MLT.name: Malta
MLT.summary:
Malta decriminalised same-sex conduct on 29 January 1973. Civil unions were introduced in 2014 and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2017; adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2014, and transgender people may serve openly in the armed forces. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender.

On 15 April 2014 the Maltese parliament approved a constitutional amendment naming gender identity as a protected ground, the first European state to do so, and introduced civil unions in the same sitting. Transgender Europe was among the first non-governmental organisations to welcome gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

Statutory discrimination protections extend to sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and hate-crime provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity offences. ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map scores Malta by category across asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime and hate speech, and the national equality body.

Legal gender recognition requires no surgery, nonbinary identity is recognised, and a December 2016 amendment allows minors aged 16 and over to change their legal gender without a court application or parental approval.

Malta was the first EU country to ban conversion therapy. The Affirmation of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression Act passed its final reading unanimously on 6 December 2016, after a bill targeting minors was first tabled by Civil Liberties Minister Helena Dalli in December 2015. The Malta Chamber of Psychologists and related professional associations backed the ban.

The 2015 Gender Identity, Gender Expression and Sex Characteristics Act introduced a ban on sterilising or invasive surgery on intersex infants, described as a worldwide first. Equaldex records a full ban on intersex infant surgery.

Bathroom access is protected under Maltese law, and Equaldex reports that 84 per cent of respondents rate Malta a good place for gay people.

Treatment of LGBTI arrivals at Malta's borders is the subject of a pending case before the European Court of Human Rights. In M.S. v. Malta, an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in April 2023 received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024. The International Commission of Jurists and partners filed observations on 30 July 2025 raising Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention, concerning non-refoulement, conditions of detention, and the absence of an individualised assessment before detention.

Reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms, and LGBTIQ+ people report a higher share of harassment and online hatred than the general population.
MLT.outOfScopeNotes:
The M.S. v. Malta case remains pending before the European Court of Human Rights; the observations filed on 30 July 2025 set out the applicant's claims, and no judgment has been issued.

The Correctional Service Agency's divergence from Malta's gender-identity legislation is documented as a continuing gap rather than a resolved matter, and the extent to which current practice has changed since the 2024 interviews is not established.

No figures for the scale of anti-LGBTQ+ violence in Malta are stated here: survey-based measures place reported SOGIE victimisation at the lower end among EU member states, a level at or below the general rate that carries no trans-specific risk signal.

sources.title: Seven transgender prison inmates awarded €5,000 each in damages for 'truly disgusting' treatment (Malta Today)
sources.summary: Malta Today (29 May 2018): the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

sources.title: The lived experiences of transgender inmates at Malta's Correctional Service Agency (Oriana Vidal, University of Malta, 2024)
sources.summary: University of Malta master's dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of Malta's Correctional Service Agency (CSA), a cohort spanning the last 25 years. It records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform CSA practice allowed TGD inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and conclude that CSA practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report (Agius, Malta Today) of seven TGD inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

ISL.name: Iceland
ISL.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Iceland rests on the 2019 self-determination law, which took effect on 1 January 2020 and was implemented in January 2021. It permits legal gender change with no restrictions, makes an X third-gender marker available, allows minors to change their legal gender with parental consent, and prohibits medical interventions on intersex children against their will except where health-related. Non-binary identity is recognised in law.

Anti-discrimination and hate-crime law covers both sexual orientation and gender identity. Amendments to the Penal Code in 1996 made it illegal to publicly attack a person or group with mockery, defamation, abuse or threats because of their sexual orientation, and a 2014 amendment added gender identity to the anti-discrimination grounds. Discrimination is illegal, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity, and bathroom access is protected. Conversion therapy is banned; the 2023 measure passed 53 to 0 with three abstentions.

Relationship and family recognition is settled. Same-sex marriage is recognised, following a unanimous 49 to 0 parliamentary vote in 2010. Stepchild adoption has been permitted since 2000, and from 27 June 2006 same-sex couples gained equal access to joint adoption and publicly funded IVF insemination. Registered partnerships, available from 1996, already carried many of the same rights and benefits as marriage, including stepchild adoption.

Reporting and redress routes exist. The national emergency service, 112, defines hate crime as offences committed from prejudice or hatred and publishes guidance for victims alongside reporting routes; it states that queer people are more likely to be victims of violence. Police-recorded potential hate crimes numbered 16 in 2023, triple the figure for the previous year, 11 in 2024, and 7 in the year to date when the report was published. The queer rights group Samtökin 78 has called for stronger hate-crime legislation. The Equality Complaints Committee is the official mechanism for discrimination complaints.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal nationwide for men and women. Outright International describes Iceland's laws as progressive while noting acknowledged gaps in protection. Equaldex ranks Iceland first of 121 jurisdictions for gay and lesbian people at 93 per cent, and records gender change with no restrictions, non-binary recognition, hate-crime protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity, a full ban on intersex infant surgery, a conversion therapy ban and protected bathroom access. That index measures conditions for gay and lesbian people rather than trans people specifically. UK travel advice states that same-sex sexual activity is legal and same-sex relationships are recognised in law, and provides dedicated LGBT+ guidance for visitors.
ISL.outOfScopeNotes:
The Equaldex ranking is an index of conditions for gay and lesbian people and does not measure trans-specific conditions. Its 93 per cent score and first-place ranking should be read on that basis.

Police-recorded hate crime figures are raw counts of potential hate crimes, are not disaggregated by the group targeted, and are small in absolute terms; they do not establish a trans-specific risk rate.

The OSCE hate crime pages on Iceland's legislation and national frameworks produced no usable findings, and the Pink Iceland page for trans and non-binary travellers likewise produced no usable finding.

Outright International refers to acknowledged gaps in protection without specifying them. The 2019 Reykjavík Grapevine piece predates the implementation of the self-determination law and does not itemise the challenges it attributes to activists.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Iceland's 1996 Penal Code amendments made it illegal to publicly attack a person or group with mockery, defamation, abuse or threats because of their sexual orientation, and a 2014 amendment added gender identity to anti-discrimination grounds. Public expression is visibly supported: Reykjavík Pride drew about 100,000 people in 2015 (roughly 30% of the population), and in 2016 President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson became the first president to attend a gay pride parade. The country has a visible gay scene of bars and cafés in Reykjavík, though elsewhere the sparse population means there is almost no gay scene (Akureyri has no gay bars). Wikipedia country coverage: Stepchild adoption (a person adopting their partner's biological child) has been permitted since 2000, and on 27 June 2006 same-sex couples gained equal access to joint adoption of children alongside public IVF insemination treatment. Registered partnerships from 1996 already granted same-sex couples many of the same rights, responsibilities and benefits as marriage, including the ability to adopt stepchildren. A 2000 Gallup poll found 53% of Icelanders supported lesbian and gay adoption rights, with 35% against. Wikipedia country coverage: Section 178 of the Penal Code criminalized same-sex relations between 1869 and 1940, and public antipathy towards LGBT people remained high until the 1980s: some of the earliest Icelanders to come out publicly, Hörður Torfason and Anna Kristjánsdottir, initially faced public discrimination and ridicule. State hostility has since reversed — the 1996 anti-discrimination amendments, the 2010 unanimous (49–0) same-sex marriage vote, and the 2023 conversion therapy ban (53–0, 3 abstentions) mark the shift. One lingering restriction was the blood donation ban on men who have sex with men, challenged by a lawsuit in 2014, relaxed to a 4-month deferral in September 2021, and lifted entirely from September 2026. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2008 it has been illegal to discriminate against people on the basis of their sexual orientation in education. Since 2016 the town of Hafnarfjörður has included information about same-sex relationships in its eighth-grade (ages 14–15) sex education lessons, and the Queer Student Association of Iceland runs social activities and field trips for University of Iceland students. On gender, the 2019 self-determination law (effective 1 January 2020, implemented January 2021) lets minors change their legal gender with parental consent, adds an 'X' third-gender option, and bans medical interventions on intersex children against their will except for health-related reasons. The age of consent was set at 14 in 1992 and raised to 15 in 2007, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

A criminal code provision criminalised same-sex relations between 1869 and 1940, and public antipathy towards LGBT people remained high until the 1980s; some of the earliest residents to come out publicly initially faced discrimination and ridicule. The 1996 anti-discrimination amendments, the 2010 marriage vote and the 2023 conversion therapy ban mark the reversal. The 2019 self-determination process replaced an earlier law that had itself been among the most progressive in the region.

A blood donation restriction on men who have sex with men was challenged by a lawsuit in 2014, relaxed to a four-month deferral in September 2021, and is lifted entirely from September 2026.

Public expression is visible. A pride event in the capital drew a crowd equivalent to roughly a third of the population in 2015, and in 2016 the head of state became the first head of state to attend a gay pride parade. Bars and cafés serving a gay clientele are concentrated in the capital; outside it the sparse population means there is almost no gay scene, and a smaller town has no gay bars.

The age of consent was set at 14 in 1992 and raised to 15 in 2007, regardless of gender or sexual orientation. A 2000 poll by a polling organisation found 53 per cent of residents supported lesbian and gay adoption rights, with 35 per cent against.

ESP.name: Spain
ESP.summary:
Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, governs legal gender recognition. Article 43 lets any person aged 16 or over apply directly to the Civil Registry to change the gender mention on their own entry, by declaration, with no diagnosis and no period of medical treatment; Human Rights Watch recorded the end of the previous dysphoria-diagnosis and two-year treatment requirements when parliament passed the law. Recognition is open from age 12 under conditions set in the statute, which also regulates consent to medical procedures for minors between 12 and 16.

Bias motive is an aggravating factor in criminal law, not a stand-alone offence. A Spanish criminal-law analysis notes that gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code: the hate-speech aggravation in Article 22.4 and the penalties in Article 510 (one to four years plus a fine of six to twelve months) come from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 reformed offences against sexual freedom in Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis. Threats or violence against a trans person are prosecuted as threats, injury or coercion, with the bias motive attached to that charge.

Courts have begun attaching the aggravator. In July 2026 a court in Vigo applied the transphobia aggravating circumstance for the first time at first-instance level, in a case of WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman; the defendant was fined EUR 300. In Valencia a group harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them; the only adult defendant was sentenced to six months' imprisonment and two minors were dealt with separately.

Facility access follows legal gender self-determination rather than a birth-sex rule, and no blanket statutory bar stops a trans person using the facilities of their gender. Coverage contrasts this with the United Kingdom, where the Equality and Human Rights Commission's statutory code moves toward stricter single-sex provision applied case by case.

Marriage and joint adoption have been open to same-sex couples since 2005, and Ley 4/2023 extends parental recognition to unmarried couples, including couples the statute classes as same-sex. Legal change of gender has not required surgery or sterilisation.

The 2023 statute also bans non-consensual normalising surgery on intersex children, adds anti-discrimination measures in healthcare, employment and housing, expands assisted reproduction and strengthens sexuality education.

Official and commercial assessments are uniformly positive. UK consular travel advice describes Spain as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers with active communities and venues; a travel operator's country guide rates it safe and welcoming, naming Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia as the strongest hubs while noting more conservative attitudes outside the large cities. The national tourism institute lists eight flagship destinations (Madrid's Chueca district, Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cadiz, the Canary Islands, Sitges and Torremolinos) and a Destinations for Diversity certification for destinations and venues meeting its open, discrimination-free standard.

Survey evidence is dated but consistent. In a 2016 survey of 23 countries Spain ranked the most trans-supportive, the only country where a majority backed unrestricted change of legal gender designation, with restroom access support above 70 percent and a quarter of respondents saying they knew a trans person. A 2013 Pew poll recorded 88 percent acceptance, the highest of the 39 countries surveyed.

Protection is not uniform across the country. In 2023 the incoming regional government of Madrid repealed the region's non-discrimination law, repealed its conversion-therapy ban as it applies to trans people, removed the penalties attached to conversion therapy and repealed several regional trans legal recognitions. The national statute remains in force there; the regional layer of protection does not.
ESP.outOfScopeNotes:
Gender expression has no free-standing hate-crime offence in the Criminal Code; protection depends on the bias aggravator being attached to an underlying offence, and the Vigo ruling is a first-instance decision rather than appellate authority.

No consolidated national dataset of prosecutions or convictions for gender-identity bias crimes was located in the sources reviewed, and the available trend figures conflict between the national security ministry and regional monitors.

The attitude data cited here dates from 2013 and 2016 and predates Ley 4/2023; no post-2023 national survey was found in the sources reviewed.

The scope of the Madrid regional repeals, in particular which regional trans legal recognitions were withdrawn, is not detailed in the sources reviewed.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Spain has a long history of state and political hostility toward LGBTQ people, alongside pockets of present-day backlash. Under Franco's dictatorship (1936-1975), thousands of gay men and women were jailed, held in camps or confined to mental institutions; some were sent to special prisons called galerías de invertidos, and vagrancy laws were applied arbitrarily to suspected dissidents on the basis of actual or perceived homosexuality. Trans people were prosecuted under public scandal offences and municipal legislation until the end of the 1980s. In 2023 a newly elected far-right government in the Madrid region repealed that region's non-discrimination law, repealed the local conversion therapy ban insofar as it applies to trans people, removed penalties for conversion therapy, and repealed several trans legal recognitions. In 2013 Interior Minister Jorge Fernández Díaz stated that same-sex marriage endangered the survival of the human species and opposed equal legal protection for such marriages. Public opinion is overwhelmingly accepting, with 88% acceptance recorded in a 2013 Pew poll, the highest of 39 countries. Violence statistics conflict: the Secretary of State for Security reported a 4% decrease in 2018, while the Observatorio Madrileño reported a 7% increase and Catalonia's Observatori contra l'Homofòbia a 30% increase in early 2019.

Trans people were prosecuted under public scandal offences and municipal ordinances until the end of the 1980s. In 2013 the interior minister said same-sex marriage endangered the survival of the human species and opposed equal legal protection for such marriages.

Reporting on anti-LGBT violence is inconsistent between monitors, which limits what any single figure shows. The Secretary of State for Security reported a 4 percent decrease in 2018, while the Observatorio Madrileño recorded a 7 percent increase and Catalonia's Observatori contra l'Homofòbia a 30 percent increase in early 2019. None of the three publishes a denominator alongside the change.

NLD.name: Netherlands
NLD.summary:
Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

What such a passport can contain is constrained. Legal gender change still requires a letter from a medical expert, and the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure that takes between three and nine months. The self-identification bill was withdrawn in July 2025. Since a law passed in December 2013 took effect in 2014, changing gender on birth certificates and other official documents has no longer required surgery or sterilisation, which had been mandatory under the 1984 and 1985 laws.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations is expressly prohibited by the Equal Treatment Act as amended by initiative Law 34.650, adopted by the Tweede Kamer on 3 July 2018 and the Eerste Kamer on 12 March 2019 (64 votes to 11), published 25 September 2019 and in force from 31 October 2019. Before that amendment the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Sexual orientation and disability were formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution in February 2023; gender identity is not among the grounds named there.

Since 1 July 2025 a private-member's bill has placed discriminatory motive into law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, alongside expanded victims' rights. Dutch legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a police Centre of Expertise Discrimination. One comparative database states that hate-crime protections in Dutch law cover sexual orientation only.

Official victimisation figures are substantial. More than 10% of LGBTIQ+ people in the Netherlands have experienced physical or sexual violence, rising to 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in verbal abuse, intimidation and violence; in 2022 one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

Police recorded about 4,800 discrimination and violence reports concerning LGBTQIA+ people last year, 7.5% more than in 2024 and 81% above the 2,654 recorded in 2022. Reports concerning transgender people rose 51% in a single year, from 264 to 399. Only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were secured in that year. These are raw counts with no per-capita denominator in the source, so the increase is a trend in reporting rather than a measured rate of risk.

Amsterdam is one data point within that national pattern. Mayor Halsema told the city council that discrimination and violent incidents would be tackled with priority during World Pride 2026, with police, enforcers and organisers agreeing to act fast; recent Prides drew between 25 and 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene. More than 70 people reported discrimination during the opening of WorldPride Amsterdam through the RITA platform, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants, and RITA warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened its 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected.

Detention carries a documented and unresolved exposure. No law, regulation or official policy governs the placement of transgender detainees; the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees. The Prison Service confirmed that placement rests on the gender designation in municipal population records together with case-by-case factors including gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background and physical or mental health, while a specialist body was drafting unpublished guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently held on an 'Extra Care Facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman held on a regular male wing on arrival before transfer to such a wing; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, where she reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; a Limburg district court sentencing ruling of 17 October 2017 concerning a trans woman facing placement in a men's prison; and an appeals court ruling of 29 June 2020 concerning a trans man in a women's prison, the courts treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights advised the Minister for Legal Protection on 21 February 2024 to create rules aligned with international detention-monitoring standards placing transgender detainees by gender identity, and recorded that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the country.
NLD.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether hate-crime aggravation under the law in force from 1 July 2025 applies to gender identity as well as sexual orientation is unresolved in the sources: the government announcement describes discriminatory motive generally as an aggravating ground, while one comparative database states that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. Dutch law also has no statutory definition of 'hate crime', so the boundary of the recorded category is not fixed by statute.

The number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands is not sourced; the Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights states that no official figures exist, and the guidelines the specialist body was drafting in February 2024 were unpublished at that date.

There is no general legislation for the 'X' gender marker, so its availability remains dependent on individual court rulings, and the sources do not state whether the withdrawal of the self-identification bill in July 2025 leaves the medical expert letter as the sole route to legal gender change or whether any replacement instrument is pending.

The incident counts for 2022, 2024 and last year are raw totals without population denominators, and the source gives no per-capita comparison; the 81% increase therefore measures reporting volume, not comparative risk against other countries or against the general population. The 17% transgender physical and sexual violence figure has no general-population benchmark in the inventory, so its position relative to background violence is not sourced.

Whether Article 1 of the Constitution will be extended to name gender identity, given that the February 2023 amendment added sexual orientation and disability only, is not addressed in the sources.

sources.title: NJCM adviseert demissionair Minister voor Rechtsbescherming over plaatsing van transgender gedetineerden (Nederlands Juristen Comité voor de Mensenrechten)
sources.summary: The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM), criminal-law working group, announced (site date 22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which NJCM calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and the relevance of CPT standards, pointing to the full letter (PDF) to Minister Weerwind (21 Feb 2024).

sources.title: Advies plaatsing transgender gedetineerden — brief aan de Minister voor Rechtsbescherming (NJCM Werkgroep Strafrecht, 21 februari 2024)
sources.summary: NJCM letter to Minister Weerwind (Leiden, 21 Feb 2024) documenting Dutch placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees — and DJI (Prison Service) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the BRP (municipal records) together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while DIZ said it was (unpublished) drafting guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling (21 Mar 2016, 15/4323/GB) on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in the men's prison; and sentencing rulings by the Limburg court (17 Oct 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624, trans woman facing placement in a men's prison) and The Hague appeals court (29 Jun 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108, trans man in a women's prison) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asks the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage of the Netherlands: gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, after the House passed the bill 127-23 in 2018 and the Senate 64-11 on 12 March 2019, following earlier cases in which the Dutch Institute for Human Rights treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender'. Since February 2023 sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution. Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Legal gender recognition has been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilization imposed by the 1984-85 laws. Care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrEP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices, projected to save €33 million in HIV treatment costs; assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple; the 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organizations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16; in July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate; conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was ultimately banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026. Youth and education: a 2018 Statistics Netherlands survey found 11.4% of LGBTQ youth faced online bullying and harassment, more than double the rate for heterosexual young people, and a 2020 Movisie estimate put homeless LGBTQ youth at 900-2,000, three times the rate for heterosexual youth, with rejection at home a stated cause. The government-financed religious-school 'single fact construction' loophole that let schools fire staff, as in a 2005 case of a teacher in a same-sex relationship, was closed by bills passed in 2014 (House 141-9) and 2015 (Senate 72-3), effective 1 July 2015, so LGBTQ students and teachers cannot be fired over sexual orientation. The age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1971, ending the 1911 Article 248bis rule that set 21 for same-sex activity. Acceptance among adolescents is falling: the Utrecht University/Trimbos HBSC study found positive attitudes toward homosexuality among secondary-school boys dropped from 40% to 22% and among girls from 78% to 51% between 2021 and 2025.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Netherlands (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Equal Treatment Act 1994 was extended in 2019 to explicitly ban discrimination based on gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, after approval by the House 127-23 on 3 July 2018 and the Senate 64-11 on 12 March 2019. The right of transgender people to change legal gender was established by parliament votes in 1984 and 1985 but required gender-affirming surgery and forced sterilization in force between 1985 and 2014, replaced by a law taking effect in 2014 allowing change of gender on birth certificates and other official documents without sterilization or surgery following overwhelming parliamentary approval in December 2013. The state issued a formal apology in December 2020 and implemented a €5,000 compensation scheme that same month for the estimated 2,000 victims sterilised under the prior law, with the cabinet apologizing in November 2020 and announcing in November 2021 that individuals subjected to surgery and sterilization under the 1985 law would be eligible for compensation after a February 2020 class-action lawsuit. Since 1993 a birth certificate may state "sex cannot be determined" when a newborn's sex is unclear, and courts have extended X markers: the District Court of Limburg granted "sex cannot be determined" on 28 May 2018, Leonne Zeegers received a Dutch passport with an "X" in October 2018 and Nanoah Struik in July 2019 with no general legislation so X designation remains court-decided, while a July 2021 district court allowed a gender X birth certificate for a self-identified non-binary individual and a December 2021 ruling dropped psychologist certification for X in passports. Transgender people are allowed to serve openly in the military, top surgery is available to patients older than 16, and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport 2016 guidelines endorsed by eight Dutch medical and patient organizations recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents of at least Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, with a July 2026 Dutch Health Board review continuing to recommend gender-affirming medical care for trans youth citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and low regret rate. A bill banning conversion therapy defined as attempting to change sexual orientation or gender identity passed the House in September 2025, the Senate on 16 June 2026 and was ratified on 8 September 2026, while offering organizations are ineligible for subsidies and such therapies have been blocked from healthcare insurance coverage since June 2012. In July 2020 it was announced that the Netherlands was considering abolishing gender markers on official identity documents from 2025, and in December 2019 the House unanimously adopted a motion calling on the government to investigate the extent of intersex medical interventions. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been legal since 1811 when the Napoleonic Code repealed sodomy laws, with no new sodomy laws after independence in 1813 except Nazi-imposed Paragraph 175 during World War II which was repealed after the war and Christian-party Article 248bis in 1911 raising the age of consent for same-sex activity to 21 versus 16 for heterosexuals. Article 248bis was repealed and the age of consent equalised at 16 regardless of gender and sexual orientation in 1971, homosexuality was declassified as a mental illness in 1973 paving the way for gay people to serve in the military, and a ban on discrimination based on sexual orientation in the military was enacted. The Equal Treatment Act 1994 bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, a "single fact" loophole allowing religious schools to dismiss teachers for same-sex conduct was removed by a bill approved 141-9 in the House on 27 May 2014 and 72-3 in the Senate on 10 March 2015 taking full effect 1 July 2015, and protections against discrimination on basis of sexual orientation were formally added to Article 1 of the Constitution in February 2023 after Senate approval 56-15 on 17 January 2023. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples began 1 January 1998, the Netherlands became the first country to legalize same-sex marriage with the law effective 1 April 2001 after House passage 109-33, marriages can be performed in European Netherlands and Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba with marriages performed elsewhere in the Kingdom required to be recognized under Article 40 of the Charter, and since 2014 all marriage officiants are prohibited from refusing services to same-sex couples. Same-sex joint and stepchild adoption was legalized alongside marriage in 2001 with overseas adoption allowed from 2009, lesbian couples have access to IVF and parentage rights with assisted insemination covered by health insurance, altruistic surrogacy is legal while commercial surrogacy is illegal, and at least two IVF clinics began offering surrogacy services to same-sex couples in 2019. Men who have sex with men were subject to a lifetime blood-donation ban until 2015, replaced by a 12-month deferral announced 28 October 2015 after a 6 March 2015 Sanquin/Maastricht University report, shortened to 4 months in February 2019, and since September 2021 gay men in monogamous relationships may donate without waiting while those in non-monogamous relationships retain a 4-month wait, with full PrEP coverage introduced 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices. The legislative history for banning conversion practices targeting sexual orientation includes May 2019 House motions to investigate extent and to legislate a ban, a May 2019 ministerial statement seeing no need to ban, and final passage of the ban bill in September 2025 in the House, 16 June 2026 in the Senate and ratification 8 September 2026. A 2016 report from the Netherlands Institute for Social Research found most Dutch people have a positive attitude towards homosexuality, with only 7% viewing homosexuality and bisexuality negatively and 10% viewing transgender people negatively. The 2023 Eurobarometer found that 91% of Dutch people agreed that "transgender people should have the same rights as anyone else". The same 2023 Eurobarometer found that 84% of people thought that "transgender persons should be able to change their civil documents to match their gender identity". The article provides no transgender-specific victimization rate, reporting violence and vulnerability figures only for gays and lesbians at 3.8% victims of violence compared to 2.4% of heterosexuals and for LGBTQ youth generally, thereby preserving the distinction from the transgender-specific tolerance figures above.

sources.title: Constitution of the Netherlands, Article 1 amendment
sources.summary: The Netherlands adopted initiative Law 34.650 on 3 July 2018 in the Tweede Kamer and 12 March 2019 in the Eerste Kamer amending the Algemene wet gelijke behandeling to explicitly prohibit unjustified distinction on grounds of sex to include sex characteristics, gender identity and gender expression, thereby providing express equal-treatment protection for transgender and intersex persons, published 25 September 2019 and entered into force 31 October 2019.

The 'X' marker has no general legislation behind it and remains court-decided. In July 2020 the government announced it was considering abolishing gender markers on official identity documents from 2025.

Transgender people may serve openly in the military, a position in place since homosexuality was declassified as a mental illness in 1973. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing the harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate.

A bill banning conversion therapy defined as attempting to change sexual orientation or gender identity passed the Tweede Kamer in September 2025, the Eerste Kamer on 16 June 2026 and was ratified on 8 September 2026; such therapies have been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and organisations offering them are ineligible for subsidies.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples began on 1 January 1998 and same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 April 2001, with same-sex joint and stepchild adoption legalised alongside it. Since 2014 all marriage officiants are prohibited from refusing services to same-sex couples. A trans person in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex therefore enters a recognised marriage or partnership, and no officiant may decline it.

Placement of transgender detainees rests on the gender designation in municipal population records plus case-by-case assessment, with no governing law or published policy, and the Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights has asked the Minister for Legal Protection to write rules placing detainees by gender identity.
NLD.blindSummary:
Visa requirements for the country depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.

What such a passport can contain is constrained. Legal gender change still requires a letter from a medical expert, and the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure that takes between three and nine months. The self-identification bill was withdrawn in July 2025. Since a law passed in December 2013 took effect in 2014, changing gender on birth certificates and other official documents has no longer required surgery or sterilisation, which had been mandatory under the 1984 and 1985 laws.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations is expressly prohibited by the national equal-treatment act as amended by an initiative law adopted by the lower house on 3 July 2018 and the upper house on 12 March 2019 (64 votes to 11), published 25 September 2019 and in force from 31 October 2019. Before that amendment the national human-rights institute had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Sexual orientation and disability were formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution in February 2023; gender identity is not among the grounds named there.

Since 1 July 2025 a private-member's bill has placed discriminatory motive into law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, alongside expanded victims' rights. National legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a police discrimination expertise centre. One comparative database states that hate-crime protections in national law cover sexual orientation only.

Official victimisation figures are substantial. More than 10% of LGBTIQ+ people in the country have experienced physical or sexual violence, rising to 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in verbal abuse, intimidation and violence; in 2022 one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.

Police recorded about 4,800 discrimination and violence reports concerning LGBTQIA+ people last year, 7.5% more than in 2024 and 81% above the 2,654 recorded in 2022. Reports concerning transgender people rose 51% in a single year, from 264 to 399. Only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were secured in that year. These are raw counts with no per-capita denominator in the source, so the increase is a trend in reporting rather than a measured rate of risk.

The country's largest city is one data point within that national pattern. Its mayor told the city council that discrimination and violent incidents would be tackled with priority during a major Pride event in 2026, with police, enforcers and organisers agreeing to act fast; recent Prides drew between 25 and 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene. More than 70 people reported discrimination during the opening of the 2026 Pride through a reporting platform, mostly festival-goers leaving a music festival and Pride Walk participants, and the platform warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. The city broadened its designated 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence to cover a church, a museum, the city archive, hotels and a central platform location, with 1.4 million visitors expected.

Detention carries a documented and unresolved exposure. No law, regulation or official policy governs the placement of transgender detainees; the national penitentiary act separates only male and female detainees. The national prison service confirmed that placement rests on the gender designation in municipal population records together with case-by-case factors including gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background and physical or mental health, while a specialist body was drafting unpublished guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently held on an 'Extra Care Facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman held on a regular male wing on arrival before transfer to such a wing; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to a women's prison, where she reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; a district court sentencing ruling of 17 October 2017 in one province concerning a trans woman facing placement in a men's prison; and an appeals court ruling of 29 June 2020 concerning a trans man in a women's prison, the courts treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. A national committee of jurists advised the justice minister on 21 February 2024 to create rules aligned with international detention-monitoring standards placing transgender detainees by gender identity, and recorded that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the country.
NLD.blindOutOfScope:
Whether hate-crime aggravation under the law in force from 1 July 2025 applies to gender identity as well as sexual orientation is unresolved in the sources: the government announcement describes discriminatory motive generally as an aggravating ground, while one comparative database states that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. National law also has no statutory definition of 'hate crime', so the boundary of the recorded category is not fixed by statute.

The number of transgender detainees in the country is not sourced; a national committee of jurists states that no official figures exist, and the guidelines the specialist body was drafting in February 2024 were unpublished at that date.

There is no general legislation for the 'X' gender marker, so its availability remains dependent on individual court rulings, and the sources do not state whether the withdrawal of the self-identification bill in July 2025 leaves the medical expert letter as the sole route to legal gender change or whether any replacement instrument is pending.

The incident counts for 2022, 2024 and last year are raw totals without population denominators, and the source gives no per-capita comparison; the 81% increase therefore measures reporting volume, not comparative risk against other jurisdictions or against the general population. The 17% transgender physical and sexual violence figure has no general-population benchmark in the inventory, so its position relative to background violence is not sourced.

Whether Article 1 of the Constitution will be extended to name gender identity, given that the February 2023 amendment added sexual orientation and disability only, is not addressed in the sources.

The country ranks #13 on a regional rights map for 2026.

A rights organisation's overview (March 2026): legal gender change still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination; the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months; the self-identification act was withdrawn in July 2025; compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules.

Official government material on combating anti-LGBTIQ+ discrimination and violence: over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence — 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people — and incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 national programme against discrimination and racism (in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation).

Official national announcements (laws in force 1 July 2025): a private member's bill puts discriminatory motive into law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data — the aggravating-factor mechanism in force since 1 July 2025.

Comparative rights data: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change legal but requires medical diagnosis, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only, discrimination illegal, employment and housing discrimination prohibited on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support (52% support LGBT openness; ranked #2 of 121 regions as a 'good place').

News reporting (Apr 2026) citing police figures: 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year — up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022 — with reports about transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399); a national LGBTQ advocacy organisation calls it 'extremely worrying', noting only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year.

News reporting (Jul 2026): more than 70 people reported discrimination during the start of Pride via a reporting platform — mostly festival-goers and Pride march participants — with the platform warning the reports are 'only a fraction of the total'.

News reporting (Jun 2026): the capital broadened safer-spaces reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during Pride — landmark buildings, museums, archives, hotels plus a central reporting location — with 1.4 million visitors expected.

News reporting (Jun 2026): the mayor told the council the capital will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during Pride (police, enforcement and organiser agreements to act fast); recent Prides drew 25-45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports (vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation, serious assault), typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

An international monitoring-frameworks page: national legislation contains no statutory definition of "hate crime", while police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a dedicated police expertise centre.

A national human-rights lawyers' committee announced (22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker minister for legal protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which the committee calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees, and the relevance of regional human-rights standards, pointing to the full letter (21 Feb 2024).

A human-rights lawyers' committee letter (21 Feb 2024) documenting placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the penitentiary principles legislation only separates male and female detainees — and the prison service confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in municipal records together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while the custodial-institutions agency said it was drafting unpublished guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'extra-care facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an extra-care facility wing; a 2016 parole-board appeals ruling on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to a women's prison, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation while there; and 2017 and 2020 sentencing rulings treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. The committee asks the minister to create rules aligned with regional human-rights standards placing transgender detainees by gender identity.

USA.name: United States
USA.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest immediate risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary determined at conception or birth, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The order also mandated that federal agencies use "sex" rather than "gender," required removal of materials that promote what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces.

The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents, while existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992; the policy remains challenged in federal courts. Trans and nonbinary travellers have reported passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs.

Entry screening carries additional exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as inadmissible for fraud. Multiple foreign governments, including at least eight European countries such as Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidance for their trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States following detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Facilities access is restricted at both federal and state level. Executive Order 14168 bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity. At state level, bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in 9 states and 1 territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules are diverging sharply. In March 2026 Kansas enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template, and further targeting bills are pending in other state legislatures. State driver's licence, birth-certificate and name-change rules for trans people vary, with some states permitting gender-marker changes and others prohibiting them.

Federal custody and enforcement present documented risks. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion-therapy-style treatment for transgender inmates, including forced hair cutting, removal of hormone medication, and substitution of psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met with beatings, solitary confinement, and reports of severe sexual abuse.

Official hostility extends to advocacy and speech. In December 2025 the attorney general instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called "radical gender ideology," describing such activists as "domestic terrorist groups." In May 2026 the White House counterterrorism strategy stated that national counterterrorism activities would "prioritize the rapid identification and neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared the administration's actions to the early stages of genocide.

Other federal orders in force or contested include Executive Order 14183 (military ban), Executive Order 14187 (describing gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," after which some hospitals paused care, and in summer 2025 the DOJ subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full patient records under 19), Executive Order 14190 (directing law enforcement to investigate schools promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers facilitating a trans minor's social transition), and Executive Order 14201 (banning trans athletes from women's sports). Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court. In October 2025 an HHS rule proposal would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18; gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states.

Censorship measures include a January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT" distributed within government health agencies, removal of words from federal agency websites including the Stonewall National Monument site, and revocation of scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialized LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; in August 2025 it threatened to pull federal funding from sex education programs mentioning transgender people, with 11 states and 2 territories complying by November 2025.

Protection machinery remains uneven. Twenty-two states plus Washington, D.C. outlaw discrimination based on gender identity or expression, and Bostock v. Clayton County (2020) holds gender identity is included under "sex" under the Civil Rights Act of 1964 for employment. Hate crimes based on gender identity are punishable federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, but only 23 states cover gender identity in state bias-motivated violence statutes. Same-sex marriage is recognized nationwide under Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015) and the Respect for Marriage Act of December 2022, though recognition still varies in American Samoa and across sovereign Native American tribal nations.

A national risk assessment published 13 July 2026 flagged Idaho as the latest state designated "Do Not Travel" for trans people, bringing the total to 4 states so flagged, with the 2026 legislative season continuing to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends. A separate travel guide notes there is no national sodomy law and that safety varies by state, advising travellers to check recent violence reports before travel.
USA.outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of Executive Order 14168's facilities clause as applied to privately operated but federally funded spaces is not resolved in the sources; the order bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, but which categories of facility qualify is not specified.

Whether the ACLU's suit against the State Department over passport marker policy will succeed is unresolved; the policy remains challenged in federal courts, and the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect while other challenges proceed.

Several federal orders are described in the sources as blocked or enjoined in court, but which specific orders remain enjoined as of the source dates is not consistently specified; the current enforceable status of each order should be verified against court records.

The claim that Idaho is the latest state flagged "Do Not Travel" for trans people, bringing the total to 4, comes from a single advocacy risk map published 13 July 2026; the criteria behind the designation and the identities of the other 3 states are not detailed in the inventory.

The report of conversion-therapy-style policies at the Federal Bureau of Prisons from 2026 and the report of forced labour in ICE custody derive from a Wikipedia survey citing imprisoned transgender individuals and advocates; primary documentation and current status of these practices are not independently confirmed in the inventory.

The characterization of the administration's actions as "the early stages of genocide" is attributed to advocates, not to any formal legal finding; no source in the inventory documents an official determination of genocide.

Whether the State Department's February 2025 visa fraud designation for applicants listing a gender other than assigned sex remains in force, and how it interacts with the passport marker policy, is not resolved in the sources.

AP (Feb 2026): 'New law puts Kansas at vanguard of denying trans identities on drivers licenses, birth certificates' — Kansas prevents transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and licenses; rights groups call it a template for other states.

MAP equality map: state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in 9 states + 1 territory; outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states (29 states + 4 territories + D.C. have no such ban); some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances.

sources.title: Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration
sources.summary: Wikipedia survey: EO 14168 (sex-as-binary, documents, facilities clause, care-funding halt), EO 14183 (military ban), EO 14187 (care for minors), EO 14190 (schools), EO 14201 (sports), January 2025 federal funding freeze; several orders blocked or enjoined in court. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates: their hair would be cut short, they would be taken off hormone medication, and instead put into psychiatric therapy and given psychiatric drugs. Imprisoned transgender individuals reported being denied access to care, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced labor programs, with guards justifying it with statements like "If you wanna be a man, I'll treat you like a man"; those who refused faced punishments including beatings and solitary confinement, and many also reported severe sexual abuse. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): In December 2025 Attorney General Pam Bondi instructed the FBI to begin offering cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called "radical gender ideology," describing such activists as "domestic terrorist groups." In May 2026 the White House's "United States Counterterrorism Strategy" stated that national counterterrorism activities would "prioritize the rapid identification and neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." The source text also reports beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse against transgender people in ICE custody, and notes that advocates have compared the administration's actions to the early stages of genocide. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): Executive Order 14168 (January 20, 2025) redefined sex for the federal government as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). On the same day Trump rescinded Executive Order 13988, which had sought to protect LGBTQ rights in federal prisons and prevent discrimination. Other measures include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers providing gender-affirming care to transgender youth; the Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): The source text states that during the second Trump presidency the US government has taken actions to persecute transgender people, accompanied by anti-transgender rhetoric and misinformation often to dehumanize and scapegoat them. Anti-transgender campaigning was a large part of the 2024 Trump campaign, with spending on anti-transgender advertising exceeding spending on housing, immigration, or the economy; Trump repeatedly made false claims that schools were performing "gender-affirming surgeries on children without their parents' consent," claims conservative groups called "valid" while acknowledging they were untrue. Censorship measures include a January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT" in health agencies, removal of words from federal websites including the Stonewall National Monument site, and revocation of scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): Executive Order 14190 (January 29, 2025), "Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling," directs law enforcement to investigate schools for promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers who facilitate a transgender minor's social transition — including using preferred names or pronouns — potentially as sexual exploitation of a minor and/or practicing medicine without a license, with federal funding revoked for violating schools. Executive Order 14187 (January 28, 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the DOJ subpoenaed "over 20" hospitals for full records of patients under 19 including names, social security numbers and doctors' notes. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialized LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; in August 2025 it threatened to pull federal funding from sex education programs mentioning transgender people (11 states and 2 territories complied by November 2025); and in October 2025 proposed HHS rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, with gender-affirming care for children already banned in 27 states. Persecution of transgender people under the second Trump administration (Wikipedia): In January 2025 a list of "forbidden terms" was distributed within government health-related agencies instructing employees to avoid words including "gender," "transgender," or "LGBT," and such words were widely removed from federal agency websites including the National Park Service Stonewall National Monument site. Executive Order 14168 mandated federal agencies use "sex" instead of "gender," remove materials that "promote gender ideology," and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in federal workplaces. Executive Order 14190 additionally directs law enforcement to criminally prosecute educators who refer to a student using preferred name and pronouns or describe a student as "non-binary," and the counterterrorism strategy frames "radically pro-transgender" ideology as a security threat.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: United States: same-sex marriage is recognized nationwide under Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015), and the Respect for Marriage Act of December 2022 repealed DOMA and required all states to recognize existing same-sex marriages; DOMA had barred federal recognition of same-sex unions until it was ruled unconstitutional in 2013. Recognition still varies: same-sex marriages are not licensed or recognized in American Samoa, status differs across sovereign Native American tribal nations, and adoption remains state-dependent, with some states allowing same-sex couple adoption and others banning all unmarried couples. Berkeley, California became the first jurisdiction to recognize same-sex unions in 1984 through domestic partnership health benefits for city employees, California passed the first state domestic partnership law in 1999, and Vermont was the first state to legalize civil unions. Expression has been both suppressed and asserted: during the reservation era, Christian missionaries and federal agencies forced Native American LGBTQ people into prescribed dress and grooming, such as making males cut their hair and females wear dresses, while both Native and non-Native LGBTQ people lived in hiding because homosexuality was a criminal offense. William Dorsey Swann, born enslaved in Maryland, organized drag balls in Washington, D.C. in the 1880s and 1890s and was arrested repeatedly, including the first documented case of arrests for female impersonation on April 12, 1888. The military's Don't Ask, Don't Tell policy (1990s-2011) explicitly barred soldiers from coming out, and gender expression-related bullying contributed to a wave of teenage and young adult suicides in 2009-2010 that prompted the It Gets Better Project. Gallup found 7.6% of U.S. adults identified as LGBTQ or another non-heterosexual orientation in 2024, rising to 22.3% among Gen Z (born 1997-2012) and 9.8% among Millennials, versus 1.1% of the Silent Generation. Visibility grew through media: Ellen was cancelled in 1998 after its star came out, while Will & Grace premiered that same year and is credited with helping increase public acceptance, and Gay Straight Alliance clubs are linked to greater safety, inclusion, wellbeing and educational attainment for LGBTQ students. The FBI reports bias against sexual orientation has consistently accounted for between one-seventh and one-fifth of single-bias reported hate incidents this century, 37 states still lacked anti-bias statutes for gender-identity crimes as of 2019, and the Transgender Day of Remembrance is held annually for transgender murder victims.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On January 20, 2025 President Donald Trump issued an executive order directing the United States government to remove all federal protections for transgender individuals and remove all recognition of transgender identity, declaring that only male and female genders are recognized and that official documents must reflect biological sex assigned at birth. Previously it was possible for US passport holders to receive either gender marker, or an "X" marker, simply by declaration during a passport application. Trump also banned trans people from military service and halted financing to gender-affirming care for individuals younger than 19, while references to transgender people were scrubbed from government websites and over 350 pages about the LGBTQ community at large were removed entirely. Twenty-two states plus Washington, D.C. outlaw discrimination based on gender identity or expression, and in June 2020 the Supreme Court in Bostock v. Clayton County held gender identity is included under "sex" as a prohibited ground of employment discrimination under the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Hate crimes based on gender identity are punishable by federal law under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, but many states lack such laws and only 23 states cover gender identity in state bias-motivated violence statutes. In 2023 more than 190 of over 470 introduced anti-LGBTQ bills were specifically anti-trans, with most passed bills focused on banning gender-affirming health care, while top contested areas are bathroom access, athletics, and transgender-related healthcare for minors. Beginning with Illinois in 1962, states began to decriminalize same-sex sexual activity, and in 2003 through Lawrence v. Texas all remaining laws against same-sex sexual activity were invalidated, though 12 states have still not formally repealed their sodomy laws. Beginning with Massachusetts in 2004, states began to offer same-sex marriage, and in 2015 through Obergefell v. Hodges all states were required to license and recognize it, with adoption of children by same-sex married couples legal nationwide since that ruling. Twenty-three states plus Washington, D.C., Guam, and Puerto Rico outlaw discrimination based on sexual orientation, while U.S. federal law does not explicitly include protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. In June 2020 the Supreme Court ruled in Bostock v. Clayton County that sexual orientation is included under "sex" as a prohibited ground of employment discrimination in the Civil Rights Act of 1964, effectively meaning no employer can fire an employee on the basis of sexual orientation. Hate crimes based on sexual orientation are punishable by federal law under the Matthew Shepard Act, and 34 states cover sexual orientation in state statutes criminalizing bias-motivated violence or intimidation. Open service by gays, lesbians and bisexuals has been permitted since September 20, 2011 after the Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act of 2010, with military sodomy provisions limited by Lawrence and Article 125 later amended to forcible sodomy in 2013 and repealed in 2017. The article states "Public opinion on transgender issues is divided." It identifies top issues regarding gender identity as bathroom access, athletics, and transgender-related healthcare for minors. A 2025 Gallup poll cited found 69% of Americans supported laws requiring transgender athletes to participate in sports aligned with their assigned sex at birth, including 90% of Republicans, 72% of independents and 41% of Democrats. The same polling found 66% of Americans supported laws requiring assigned sex at birth to be listed on government documents such as drivers licenses and passports, including 89% of Republicans, 66% of independents and 38% of Democrats. Only 40% of Americans believed that gender transition is morally acceptable, including 70% of Democrats, 45% of independents and only 9% of Republicans. The article also notes transgender people faced significant erosions in rights on the state level in Republican-run states over the course of three years before the 2025 federal actions.

sources.title: Executive Order of January 20, 2025 - Trump gender recognition order
sources.summary: On January 20, 2025 the executive order Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism And Restoring Biological Truth To The Federal Government establishes that the U.S. federal government recognizes only two immutable sexes, male and female as determined at conception/birth, and directs federal agencies to enforce sex-based distinctions on that basis, requiring federal IDs including passports and visas to reflect birth sex rather than gender identity, mandating single-sex federal facilities and housing of federal prisoners by birth sex, and prohibiting federal funding and promotion of gender-identity policies.
