USA.comparisons: Compared to the UK (0.66): the US shares bathroom-law enforcement and border hostility but adds foreign-government traveler warnings and documented foreign-visitor detention, which the UK lacks. The US scores above Peru (0.48) — Peru's higher baseline street violence is offset by the US's unique institutional hostility (traveler warnings, border detention, bathroom arrests) — and level with Mexico (0.50): Mexico's far higher lethal anti-trans violence (~50+ murders/year, police extortion) is balanced against the US's documented traveler-detention cases and state-level legal enforcement, which Mexico lacks. Different risk profiles converging at the same score.
USA.blindSummary:
Travel documents are the sharpest immediate risk for a trans visitor to the country. An executive order signed 20 January 2025 redefined sex for national purposes as a male-female binary determined at conception or birth, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the national justice department to "correct the misapplication" of a 2020 Supreme Court employment-discrimination ruling. The order also mandated that national agencies use "sex" rather than "gender," required removal of materials that promote what the order calls gender ideology, and rescinded policies requiring use of names and pronouns consistent with a person's gender identity in national workplaces.

The foreign ministry stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents, while existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a foreign-ministry policy in place since 1992; the policy remains challenged in national courts. Trans and nonbinary travellers have reported passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad, and a national civil-liberties union has sued the foreign ministry on behalf of seven plaintiffs.

Entry screening carries additional exposure. In February 2025 the foreign ministry announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as inadmissible for fraud. Multiple foreign governments, including at least eight governments in one region, adjusted travel guidance for their trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country following detentions of their citizens over visa issues.

Facilities access is restricted at both national and sub-national level. The executive order bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity. At sub-national level, bathroom bans applying to trans people in schools and some government buildings are in force in 9 state/provinces and 1 state/province, with outright bans on facility use per gender identity in additional state/provinces; some state/provinces make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a trans student was arrested in a women's restroom at a state/province capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state/province's bathroom-restriction law.

Sub-national document rules are diverging sharply. In March 2026 one state/province enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template, and further targeting bills are pending in other legislatures. Sub-national driver's licence, birth-certificate and name-change rules for trans people vary, with some state/provinces permitting gender-marker changes and others prohibiting them.

National custody and enforcement present documented risks. From 2026 the national prison service adopted policies mandating conversion-therapy-style treatment for transgender inmates, including forced hair cutting, removal of hormone medication, and substitution of psychiatric drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the prison service stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met with beatings, solitary confinement, and reports of severe sexual abuse.

Official hostility extends to advocacy and speech. In December 2025 the justice minister instructed a national law-enforcement agency to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists promoting what she called "radical gender ideology," describing such activists as "domestic terrorist groups." In May 2026 the national counterterrorism strategy stated that counterterrorism activities would "prioritize the rapid identification and neutralization of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared the government's actions to the early stages of genocide.

Other executive orders in force or contested include a military ban, an order describing gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," after which some hospitals paused care and in summer 2025 the justice department subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full patient records under 19, an order directing law enforcement to investigate schools promoting "gender ideology" and to criminally prosecute teachers facilitating a trans minor's social transition, and an order banning trans athletes from women's sports. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court. In October 2025 a health-department rule proposal would bar public insurance reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18; gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 state/provinces.

Censorship measures include a January 2025 list of "forbidden terms" including "gender," "transgender" and "LGBT" distributed within government health agencies, removal of words from national agency websites including a national monument site, and revocation of scientific grants mentioning LGBT topics. In July 2025 the government shut down specialized LGBTQ youth services on a national crisis lifeline; in August 2025 it threatened to pull funding from sex education programs mentioning transgender people, with 11 state/provinces and 2 state/provinces complying by November 2025.

Protection machinery remains uneven. Twenty-two state/provinces plus the capital region outlaw discrimination based on gender identity or expression, and a 2020 Supreme Court ruling holds gender identity is included under "sex" under the national Civil Rights Act for employment. Hate crimes based on gender identity are punishable nationally under a national hate-crimes statute, but only 23 state/provinces cover gender identity in sub-national bias-motivated violence statutes. Same-sex marriage is recognized nationwide under a 2015 Supreme Court ruling and a December 2022 statute, though recognition still varies in one state/province and across sovereign tribal nations.

A national risk assessment published 13 July 2026 flagged one state/province as the latest "Do Not Travel" designation for trans people, bringing the total to 4 state/provinces so flagged, with the 2026 legislative season continuing to degrade trans rights while national policies drove nationwide trends. A separate travel guide notes there is no national sodomy law and that safety varies by state/province, advising travellers to check recent violence reports before travel.

BRA.name: Brazil
BRA.summary:
Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the age of consent does not vary with sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework applies throughout the country. The Supreme Federal Court ruled in 2018 that legal gender recognition does not require surgery. In 2019 the same court held that constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Outright International's March 2026 country review records that LGBTIQ people nonetheless continue to face significant violence and discrimination in practice.

Passports and identity cards allow an unspecified or X gender marker under ICAO standards, and state-issued identity cards have been required to offer it since 11 January 2024. A 2025 decision of the Superior Court of Justice permitting a neutral gender entry on the civil registry binds only the plaintiff, though it is treated as a precedent.

Spousal-visa equality and the gender-marker rules apply nationwide, and a marriage recognised in Brazil is recognised for immigration purposes. Partners in registered stable unions are recognised as dependents on health plans and insurers.

The public health system provides sex reassignment surgery free of charge as a matter of constitutional right, following a 2007 ruling by the 4th Regional Federal Court; roughly 250 such operations were performed between 2000 and 2007 at three university hospitals. Access is constrained in practice: the Health Ministry left qualification decisions to local officials, and long waiting lines and poorly equipped public facilities push those who can afford it into private hospitals and clinics. In July 2026 the 3rd Panel of the Superior Court of Justice ruled that health insurance plans must cover facial feminisation surgery, and in March 2024 the Supreme Federal Court extended five-day paid paternity leave to the non-pregnant mothers of lesbian couples.

Adult access to surgery within the public system requires a patient to be at least 21, to carry no diagnosis of personality disorder, and to complete at least two years of psychological evaluation.

Gender-affirming care for minors was banned by the Federal Council of Medicine in April 2025, in the same resolution that lowered the minimum age for gender-affirming surgery from 25 to 21. Advocates filed a Direct Action of Unconstitutionality at the Supreme Federal Court. The Federal Court of Acre blocked the resolution on 25 July 2025, restoring care for minors nationwide; on 2 October 2025 Flávio Dino overturned that block and reinstated the ban. Continuity of medication for trans adolescents, and travel across state lines to obtain care, remain live issues.

Custody placement for LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned is governed nationally by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person is consulted about their preference; the judge must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or specific wings or cells. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited. The resolution entered into force after publication, 120 days later, extended to 180 days by Resolution 366/2021.

Practice diverges from the national norm. A peer-reviewed census study of travestis and transgender women in the Rio de Janeiro state prison system interviewed 138 self-declared travesti or trans-woman inmates across eleven units classified as masculine in the metropolitan region between April and June 2021, drawing on the state prison administration's own database. It documents that travestis and trans women in that system are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and characterises placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. A 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law grants them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics.

Violence and hostility directed at trans people are documented. An investigation published in May 2024 found that drink-spiking robberies known locally as 'boa noite, Cinderela' victimise LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo, as the city prepared for a Pride event drawing thousands of tourists. In October 2024 nearly 1,000 transgender candidates stood in municipal elections across every state amid threats and intimidation; the number of trans officeholders has tripled since the previous cycle.

Courts have applied the anti-discrimination framework to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing; the first-instance decision in Barra Bonita had ordered R$4,000 in compensation. Lower courts pushed the Superior Court of Justice to extend the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, which it did unanimously. The São Paulo Municipal Council's parliamentary inquiry into violence against trans and travesti persons issued a final report carrying 189 recommendations.
BRA.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 Superior Court of Justice decision allowing a neutral gender entry on the civil registry was decided for the individual plaintiff; its effect on other applicants is not established.

Litigation over the Federal Council of Medicine's April 2025 resolution is unresolved. The Direct Action of Unconstitutionality remains pending, and the lower-court block and its reversal leave the position of trans adolescents uncertain.

The prison census covering travestis and transgender women is limited to the Rio de Janeiro state system and does not establish conditions in other states.

No trans-specific entry or airport screening practice is documented in the source inventory, and no trans-disaggregated homicide data with a comparable denominator is sourced.

sources.summary:
Overview: same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013; legal gender change without surgery has been allowed since 2018 under a Supreme Federal Court ruling; the age of consent is equal regardless of orientation; and a federal anti-discrimination framework applies.

Brazil was the first country in Latin America to recognize same-sex unions for immigration benefits. On 25 November 2003 Judge Ana Carolina Morozowski of the 5th Civil Court of Curitiba granted permanent residency to the British partner of gay activist Toni Reis, and a week later the National Immigration Council issued Administrative Resolution No. 3 granting temporary or permanent visas to partners without distinction of sex. The government was slow to cable consulates, leaving binational same-sex couples confused about how to apply; Immigration Equality and the Brazilian Rainbow Group met officials at the New York consulate in February 2004 to press for clarity. A Florianópolis judge also barred immigration authorities from deporting an Italian woman partnered with a Brazilian lesbian.

Identity documents reflect gender. Passports and ID cards allow an unspecified or X marker under ICAO standards, mandatory for state-issued ID cards since 11 January 2024, and a 2025 Superior Court of Justice decision permitting a neutral gender on the civil registry affects only the plaintiff but sets a precedent.

The public health system (SUS) provides sex reassignment surgery free of charge as a basic constitutional right, per a 2007 ruling by the 4th Regional Federal Court, and roughly 250 such surgeries were performed between 2000 and 2007 at three university hospitals. Access is constrained in practice: the Health Ministry left qualification decisions to local officials, and long lines and poorly equipped public facilities push those who can afford it toward private hospitals and clinics. Partners in registered stable unions are recognized as dependents on health plans and insurers. In July 2026 the 3rd Panel of the Superior Court of Justice ruled that health insurance plans must cover facial feminization surgeries, and in March 2024 the Supreme Court extended five-day paid paternity leave to the non-pregnant mothers of lesbian couples.

Gender-affirming care for minors was banned by the Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) in April 2025, alongside a reduction of the minimum age for gender-affirming surgery from 25 to 21; LGBTQ+ advocates filed a Direct Action of Unconstitutionality at the Supreme Court. The Federal Court of Acre blocked the resolution on 25 July 2025, restoring care for minors nationwide, but on 2 October 2025 Federal Judge Flávio Dino overturned that block and reinstated the ban, leaving youth medication continuity and cross-state travel a live issue. Adult access to surgery within the public system requires patients to be at least 21, diagnosed with no personality disorder, and to undergo at least two years of psychological evaluation.

Conversion therapy has been forbidden by the Federal Psychology Council since 1999, though a Brasília federal judge approved it in September 2017 before reversing course in December 2017; the Supreme Court ultimately banned it, and in 2019 Justice Cármen Lúcia issued an injunction overturning the judge's decisions. Blood donation restrictions on gay and bisexual men, requiring 12 months without same-sex activity, were struck down as unconstitutional by the Federal Supreme Court in May 2020.

Hostility is documented both in violence and in legislative opposition. Senator Marcelo Crivella attacked the pending federal anti-discrimination bill, arguing homosexuals would receive a protection that 'should have been given to women, the elderly and children,' while conservative senators framed the law as an aggression on religious freedom. In January 2019 openly gay representative Jean Wyllys left Brazil after death threats, replaced in February by David Miranda. Grupo Gay da Bahia reported 343 LGBTQ murders in 2016, 387 in 2017 and 420 in 2018, and the figures are disputed: Veja columnist Reinaldo de Azevedo called the GGB methodology 'unscientific' because it counts all media-reported murders of LGBTQ people regardless of motive, and scholars note that international comparisons are flawed because figures reflect documentation capacity rather than crime totals. The Catholic Church and radical evangelical groups have been identified as sources of rising intolerance, and a 2007 incident saw a judge brought before São Paulo's Justice Council for calling soccer a 'virile, masculine sport and not a homosexual one.'

Education is a direct battleground. In June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that public and private schools must fight discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, sexist bullying against cisgender and transgender girls, and homotransphobic bullying. Since 2020 the Court has been overturning state and municipal laws banning gender and sexuality courses in schools, and since 2023 it has been overturning laws banning gender-neutral language in schools. Youth-specific risks include the April 2025 CFM ban on gender-affirming care for minors and labour exploitation: in the central, north and northeastern regions, transgender people from extremely poor families sometimes begin sex work as early as age 12 after expulsion from home, and travestis commonly work the streets as young as 16 or 17 in southern and southeastern regions and major capitals. On the more favorable side, the 2004 government initiative Brasil Sem Homophobia was designed to protect LGBTQ students, and a 2010 Rio de Janeiro State University and University of Campinas survey found that 95% of homosexual youth had revealed their orientation by age 18, many by 16, compared with after 21 for the 1980s generation.

Country overview (updated Mar 2026): constitutional and federal criminal provisions — after the 2019 Supreme Court ruling — prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, yet LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination in practice.
Expat legal guide (updated 5 Apr 2026): same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules apply nationwide, forming the entry and family framework for a trans visitor or partner.
Investigation (May 2024): 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies victimise LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo; the city prepares for a Pride drawing thousands of tourists.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Death threats assail Brazil's trailblazing trans candidates as they campaign' — nearly 1,000 transgender politicians run in municipal elections across every state amid threats and intimidation, as the number of trans officeholders has tripled since the last cycle.

São Paulo Court of Justice (27th Private Chamber) upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing — the Barra Bonita first instance had ordered R$4,000 compensation.

Analysis (2022): lower courts pushed the Superior Court of Justice (STJ) toward unanimously extending Maria da Penha Law and Feminicide Law remedies to trans women — inclusion of trans people in violence-prevention law.
São Paulo Municipal Council parliamentary inquiry (CPI) on Violence Against Trans and Travesti Persons: final report carrying 189 recommendations.

Canada travel advisory (updated Aug 2026) for Brazil: exercise a high degree of caution because of high crime rates and gang-related urban violence, avoid demonstrations, and avoid border drug-trafficking zones. The guidance applies to all visitors and contains no trans-specific finding.
Tour operator guide: Brazil 'progressive' on LGBTQIA+ rights and generally safe, but flags that practical safety issues can arise for LGBTQIA+ travellers.
Historical essay (Mar 2000): historian James N. Green on early-1900s Rio homosexual subculture — Glória monument site functioning as a meeting venue in the 'tropical Paris' era.

RUS.name: Russia
RUS.summary:
Russia offers no route to legal gender recognition. A law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 prohibits gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents. A trans visitor's passport, visa and identity papers therefore remain as issued, and no Russian procedure exists to align them with the holder's gender.

The Supreme Court designated the non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist in November 2023. Human Rights Watch counted 101 extremism-related convictions by June 2025 for alleged participation in the movement or display of its symbols, with charges brought under both administrative and criminal codes. Arrests have followed for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Between March and May 2026 nine organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

The propaganda statutes reach expression. The 2013 law covered material concerning minors; a December 2022 amendment extended it to all age groups, and it now prohibits material promoting "non-traditional" sexual relationships and material that gives minors a "desire to change their sex". More than 180 enforcement cases were opened in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined, with fines of about 26 million rubles. Meduza reported in June 2025 that propaganda cases had grown eighteenfold over the previous decade and that fines under the statutes brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in two years.

Enforcement has reached venues. SAU.name: Saudi Arabia
SAU.summary:
Saudi Arabia has no codified penal code. Judges apply an uncodified interpretation of sharia drawn from the Quran and the Sunnah, so penalties for same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity are unpredictable: fines, flogging, lengthy or indeterminate imprisonment, and death in the most severe cases. Same-sex relations are illegal for men and women.

Deviation from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence, not merely incidental conduct attached to another charge. No legal gender recognition is available, there is no protection from discrimination, and no relationship recognition. LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

Enforcement is documented. In October 2021 five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media. In April 2005, dozens of men caught dancing and behaving like women at a Jeddah party described as a gay wedding were sentenced to a total of 14,200 lashes and up to two years' imprisonment, after a closed trial without defence lawyers.

Enforcement reaches visitors and reaches expression. Amnesty International documents visitors imprisoned over social media posts, including a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 August 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for posts published before he had arrived in the country.

Official posture is mixed. In May 2023 the Saudi Tourism Authority's FAQ page was updated to state that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, are welcome, and VisitSaudi states that privacy will be respected; homosexuality remains illegal and enforcement is described as not universal. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office advises that same-sex relations are illegal although legal action is uncommon, and that couples should avoid public affection. Being transgender is not recognised, and trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care.

Tourist visas were introduced in 2019 alongside a Public Decency Law that fines public displays of affection and immodest clothing.

Entry and exit visa paperwork does not ask about sexual orientation, but it does ask nationality, sex, religion and marital status. Foreigners face deportation as a penalty for homosexuality. Work-visa applicants must pass an HIV test on arrival and before permit renewal, with infected foreigners deported.

In June 2022 officials in Riyadh seized rainbow-coloured products in a crackdown framed as curbing promotion of homosexuality. The seizure targeted "the young generation," confiscating children's hair accessories, backpacks, pencil cases and rainbow-striped crayon packs.

Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman, died in Saudi custody after a roundup of 34 people at Azizia prison in Riyadh. Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes, aggravating a chronic heart condition; Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack, an account her family and trans-rights activists dispute.

The government has designated several hospitals to treat people with AIDS/HIV, but other hospitals often refuse care or treat patients without compassion, and condoms were until recently rarely available outside certain hospitals or medical supply stores.
SAU.outOfScopeNotes:
No published statute sets out the penalty range for same-sex conduct or gender nonconformity, so the range cited by monitors rests on judicial application of uncodified sharia rather than a published schedule, and cannot be stated with precision.

In September 2013 Gulf states discussed a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners; officials later downplayed it as a mere proposal, and the sources do not record it being enacted.

Assessments differ on how consistently the law is enforced. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office describes legal action as uncommon, while monitors document prosecutions and a custodial death. The sources do not reconcile the two.

AFG.name: Afghanistan
AFG.summary:
Afghanistan under Taliban rule offers no legal protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the EUAA country-of-origin report of February 2026 finds this was true both before and after the 2021 takeover. Amnesty International's position, recorded in that report, is that same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Criminalisation operates in layers. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, updated 19 January 2026, states that Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on sodomy and inciting sodomy carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the Code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity.

The Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law of 31 July 2024 adds a preventive surveillance duty. Article 22 obliges the overseer to prevent listed evils including lesbianism and homosexuality 'even if with one's own spouse', codifying moral surveillance over same-sex conduct alongside adultery and gambling.

Enforcement is documented and escalating. OutRight International's February 2023 report, based on 22 interviews conducted between September and October 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country, found Taliban security officials pursuing gay men and trans women more systematically than in the movement's earlier rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed such punishments on social media. CNN reported in November 2024 that LGBTQ Afghans face beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody.

Human Rights Watch and OutRight's January 2022 report, based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans, found Taliban members and their supporters attacking, threatening and expelling LGBT people from their homes, with abuse by family, neighbours and partners surging after the takeover; many went into hiding or fled.

A DW feature of October 2021 profiled a trans man and a gay friend in their mid-20s hiding in Kabul after the takeover, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave, and documenting street attacks on men read as gay.

JURIST's November 2024 feature, drawing on the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan, reports systematic persecution after August 2021, notes that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework, and states that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks, including exploitation and violence.

The UN human-rights office reported in March 2026 that at least 1,110 people were flogged in 2025, nearly double the 2024 figure, and warned that women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for moral crimes such as adultery, illicit relationships and sodomy. Article 398 offered lesser punishment for vigilante honor killings that can target minors found engaging in homosexuality, and Article 373 imposes fines or murder-equivalent penalties for spreading a 'dangerous disease'. Persons convicted of homosexuality were generally sentenced to prison in the cities under the Islamic Republic.

No law addressed discrimination or harassment on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and political parties were prohibited from advocating anything opposing Islamic morality. The 2017 U.S. State Department report found that LGBTI community members 'did not have access to certain health services' and could be fired from jobs because of sexual orientation, and that organizations protecting LGBTI freedom 'remained underground because they could not legally register with the government', a status the 2020 report confirmed.

Before 2003 little or no HIV-AIDS education or treatment existed; the 2008 official count was 504 people living with HIV-AIDS, though the true figure was suspected to be in the thousands. Low literacy, weak infrastructure and social taboos impede comprehensive public health education.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.summary:
The Gender Recognition Act 2004, in force since 4 April 2005, allows a transgender person to apply to a Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate after two years of transition, without mandatory surgery, and to obtain a new birth certificate and full legal recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. The framework followed Goodwin v United Kingdom (2002), in which the European Court of Human Rights found the UK in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the Convention, and reversed Corbett v Corbett (1970), which had barred any change to the sex marker on a birth certificate. Medical gender reassignment is formally approved and available through the National Health Service or privately, and a December 2002 government policy document states that transsexualism is not a mental illness.

Since December 2023 the government no longer accepts gender recognition certificates issued by around 50 countries and US states, among them Sweden, New York State and Belgium, on the stated ground that those jurisdictions permit transition too easily. Holders from those places must apply for a new certificate under British law to change their gender in the UK. Women and Equalities Minister Kemi Badenoch called the change long overdue; Shadow Equalities Minister Anneliese Dodds warned of diplomatic consequences, noting the list excluded Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand.

A certificate will not be issued to a married applicant unless the spouse consents, and if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated. Same-sex marriage has been legal in England and Wales since 13 March 2014 under the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013, in Scotland since 16 December 2014, and in Northern Ireland since 13 January 2020. Civil partnerships, available since 5 December 2005, confer most but not all rights of marriage and are not recognised in every other country.

On 19 June 2026 in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Judge Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, struck down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory guidance on trans custody as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in establishments matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The case had been heard in February 2026, when the court was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible; the claimant, For Women Scotland, was challenging a policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy in April 2025 after the Supreme Court gender ruling, adopting an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth. Under the previous policy, trans women officers could conduct intimate searches of women holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Campaign group Sex Matters welcomed the change. Police Scotland published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 providing that searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex in custody and stop-and-search contexts, and that where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

New Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance on single-sex spaces came into force in August 2026, giving organisations practical examples of compliance; Sex Matters' Maya Forstater said the law is clear and the code is practical. Northern Ireland, which operates under different equality legislation, is still assessing the impact of the Supreme Court ruling.

Health Secretary Steve Barclay announced in October 2023 that trans hospital patients in England would be banned from female-only and male-only wards, alongside a commitment that a patient's request for intimate care by someone of the same biological sex would be respected, with an update to the NHS Constitution to follow consultation. The Department of Health and Social Care said it would consult on updates to ensure the privacy, dignity and safety of all patients, and Barclay ordered a reversal of NHS website changes and stopped the NHS requiring staff to declare pronouns to each new patient. The Trans Legal Clinic documents how this policy direction translated into fatal delay: Joelle, a 27-year-old trans woman with an aggressive but usually curable lymphoma, was removed from an available cancer ward bed at Wolverhampton NHS Trust once staff saw she was a trans woman, and spent 16 days in a side room without cancer pain management while emergency chemotherapy was withheld; her abdominal tumour reached 98cm and the delay was unsurvivable. Her mother Jane states the refused bed was in a multi-bed women's ward, the day after the health minister announced plans to block trans women from women's wards. The Clinic is pursuing an Article 2 inquest and a clinical negligence claim, and notes that the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling's effect on trans people's access to hospital wards has drawn far less attention than its effect on toilets.

NHS England stopped prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people in March 2024 following the Cass Review of April 2024, renewed that pause indefinitely in December 2024, and will reconsider it in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the NHS had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the Cass Review, with some families turning to black-market or overseas hormones instead. The Tavistock gender identity service for children closed in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services.

Transgender people are covered by the Equality Act 2010, but UN human rights experts warned on 18 August 2026 that proposed revisions to the Act risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people. Under ILGA-Europe's 2026 assessment the UK maintains explicit legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically difficult, and provides hate-crime and hate-speech protection on gender identity and sex characteristics only in some parts of the country.
GBR.outOfScopeNotes:
Surrey Police's searching and biological-sex policy, released under the Freedom of Information Act, could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), so its terms and whether they match the Police Scotland or British Transport Police approach remain unresolved.

The final wording of the NHS Constitution update on single-sex wards is unresolved: the sources record a 2023 announcement and a consultation commitment, but not the text as adopted. Whether the proposed revisions to the Equality Act 2010 flagged by UN experts in August 2026 have been enacted is likewise not sourced here.

Northern Ireland's assessment of the Supreme Court ruling's impact under its separate equality legislation is described as ongoing, with no outcome recorded. The Trans Legal Clinic's Article 2 inquest and clinical negligence claim over Joelle's death have no documented outcome in the sources, and the completeness of the December 2023 list of jurisdictions whose gender recognition certificates are no longer accepted is not independently verified.

Large LGBT communities exist in Brighton, Blackpool, Manchester and London, with gay villages and annual pride festivals.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in United Kingdom (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Following Corbett v Corbett (1970) transgender people could not change the sex marker on birth certificates, and in Goodwin v United Kingdom (2002) the UK was found in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights, leading to the Gender Recognition Act 2004 effective 4 April 2005. Since that date transgender people may apply to a Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate after two years transitioned, without mandatory sex reassignment surgery, to obtain a new birth certificate and full legal recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. Medical gender reassignment is formally approved and available through the National Health Service or privately, and a December 2002 Government policy document categorically states that transsexualism "is not a mental illness." European anti-gender discrimination law was held to apply to trans people in P v S and Cornwall County Council (1996). Under the Gender Recognition Act 2004 as originally enacted a married transgender applicant was required to divorce or annul the marriage before issuance of a certificate, and a married couple including a transgender partner could not directly re-register but had to dissolve, obtain recognition, then register a civil partnership with associated paperwork and costs. ILGA-Europe's executive expressed concern about a "hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups" as the UK fell from highest-ranked in 2015 to 9th in 2020 and 22nd in 2025. Male same-sex acts were decriminalised in England and Wales by the Sexual Offences Act 1967 under conditions of consent, privacy and age 21, extended to Scotland by the Criminal Justice (Scotland) Act 1980 effective 1 February 1981 and to Northern Ireland by the Homosexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 1982 effective 8 December 1982, while lesbian acts were never criminalised as civilian offences. An equal age of consent at 16 for all was achieved via the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000 effective 8 January 2001, later consolidated by the gender-neutral Sexual Offences Act 2003 effective 1 May 2004 and the Sexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 2008 lowering Northern Ireland from 17 to 16 in 2009. Discrimination protections for LGBT people existed since 1999 and were extended to all areas under the Equality Act 2010, Section 28 prohibiting "promotion of homosexuality" was repealed in 2003, and the ban on open service in the armed forces was subject to non-enforcement since 2000 and formally lifted in 2016. Civil partnerships under the Civil Partnership Act 2004 effective 5 December 2005 gave most rights of marriage, and same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales by the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 effective 13 March 2014 with first marriages 29 March 2014, in Scotland by the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014 effective 16 December 2014, and in Northern Ireland effective 13 January 2020 under the Northern Ireland (Executive Formation etc) Act 2019 with first ceremony 11 February 2020. Adoption by same-sex couples was enabled in England and Wales by the Adoption and Children Act 2002 effective 30 December 2005, in Scotland effective 28 September 2009, and in Northern Ireland in December 2013, with 12% of England adoptions in 2018 involving same-sex couples. Historic convictions were addressed by "disregards" under the Protection of Freedoms Act from 2012, the so-called Alan Turing law in the Policing and Crime Act 2017 effective 31 January 2017 for England and Wales, automatic pardons in Scotland in June 2018, and Northern Ireland law effective 28 June 2018, plus the Merchant Shipping (Homosexual Conduct) Act 2017 repealing sections 146(4) and 147(3) of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994. Female homosexuality was never a civilian offence but the government announced in June 2023 pardons for women penalised for homosexuality under the Army Act 1955, Air Force Act 1955 and Naval Discipline Act 1957. The article documents no poll measuring societal acceptance of transgender people specifically, reporting only sexuality-specific tolerance figures of 86% agreeing homosexuality should be accepted in 2019 and 77% supporting same-sex marriage in 2017. For the transgender-specific climate, it quotes ILGA-Europe's executive concern about a "hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups" by 2020. It further describes anti-trans rhetoric in UK media as "increasing and becoming more vitriolic" since 2016 and becoming "super-charged" since 2018. It links this climate to backsliding in ILGA-Europe rankings from highest in Europe in 2015 with 86% progress to 9th in 2020 with 66% and 22nd in 2025 with 45%, the third steepest drop from 2024. It notes large LGBT communities and annual pride festivals across cities including Brighton, London, Manchester and others, but does not attribute transgender-specific tolerance levels to those communities.

sources.title: ILGA-Europe Annual Review of LGBTI Rights - 2015, 2020, 2025 reports
sources.summary: As of the 2026 assessment, the United Kingdom maintains explicit bans or other legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically impossible and provides hate-crime and hate-speech protection on sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics only in some regions.

sources.title: Justice for Joelle — Trans Legal Clinic case account (Wolverhampton NHS Trust)
sources.summary: The Trans Legal Clinic documents the death of Joelle, a 27-year-old trans woman with an aggressive lymphoma that is 'almost always curable when treated as a medical emergency'. A bed was available on the cancer ward when she arrived at Wolverhampton NHS Trust; after staff saw she was a trans woman she was removed from the ward and placed in a side room on the other side of the hospital. She spent 16 days there 'deteriorating in agony, without cancer pain management', and was told emergency chemotherapy could not start until she was on the right ward, though she pleaded for a bed on either the male or the female ward. By the time treatment started it was too late; her abdominal tumour measured 98cm and the delay was unsurvivable for this lymphoma. Her mother Jane states that Joelle was refused the available bed on the cancer ward because it was in a multi-bed women's ward, and that the day before, health minister Steve Barclay had announced plans to block trans women from women's wards. The Clinic is pursuing an Article 2 inquest into systemic failures and a clinical negligence claim, and notes that the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling's effect on trans people's access to hospital beds has received far less attention than its effect on toilets: if trans people are blocked from appropriate hospital wards, Joelle's case 'could become a matter of policy across the country'. For a trans visitor this documents how a policy-level restriction translates into a life-threatening delay in emergency care.

sources.title: Trans hospital patients in England to be banned from female- and male-only wards (The Guardian, 3 Oct 2023)
sources.summary: The Guardian reported that trans hospital patients in England would be banned from female- and male-only wards under plans announced by health secretary Steve Barclay at the Conservative party conference, alongside a commitment that a patient's request for intimate care by someone of the same biological sex would be respected, and an update to the NHS constitution to give effect to the proposals after consultation. The article records the backlash: the first openly transgender MP, Jamie Wallis, called it a non-issue and cited freedom-of-information requests to hospital trusts across the UK asking whether any biologically female inpatient had complained about a trans patient's presence — none were recorded; another Conservative MP questioned what tangible change was needed 'given that the future of hospitals is in individual rooms anyway'. Barclay told delegates 'we know what a woman is'. NHS Providers' chief executive said any changes to the NHS constitution should have inclusivity at the heart and be subject to wide consultation, and Unison's head of health called the speech 'deflection politics at its worst'.

sources.title: Government commits to updating NHS constitution (GOV.UK press release, Oct 2023)
sources.summary: The Department of Health and Social Care announced it would consult on proposed updates to the NHS Constitution for England to 'ensure the privacy, dignity and safety of all patients is respected', with changes brought forward ahead of the next routine update. Speaking at the 2023 Conservative conference, Health and Social Care Secretary Steve Barclay said the changes would 'recognise the importance of different biological needs and protect the rights of women', criticised NHS diversity spending, and confirmed he had ordered a reversal of NHS website changes and stopped the NHS 'ordering staff to declare pronouns to each new patient'. The release states the government would consider Equality and Human Rights Commission advice on 'balancing the rights of different protected characteristics of patients in certain settings'.

GBR.localsOnly:
Residents seeking a Gender Recognition Certificate apply to a Gender Recognition Panel after two years of transition, with no surgery requirement, but must secure spousal consent or dissolve the marriage first. Under the Act as originally enacted a married applicant had to divorce or annul before issuance, and a couple including a transgender partner could not re-register directly but had to dissolve, obtain recognition and then register a civil partnership with associated paperwork and costs.

Transgender youth are covered by the Equality Act 2010. Bell v Tavistock (December 2020) found children under 16 could not independently consent to puberty blockers, a judgment overturned on appeal in September 2021, before the Cass Review closed the Tavistock service and halted puberty-blocker prescribing. The Girls' Day School Trust barred admissions for trans girls without a Gender Recognition Certificate in January 2022, and in July 2022 the RFU and RFL implemented a single-sex policy for under-12s excluding trans girls from girls' teams.

Hate-crime and hate-speech protection covering gender identity and sex characteristics applies only in some parts of the country under ILGA-Europe's 2026 assessment, so protection varies by where a resident lives. Residents also face the practical effect of the hospital ward policy and of the Police Scotland and British Transport Police search rules in custody, which are keyed to sex at birth.
GBR.blindSummary:
The country's Gender Recognition Act 2004, in force since 4 April 2005, allows a transgender person to apply to a recognition panel for a certificate after two years of transition, without mandatory surgery, and to obtain a new birth certificate and full legal recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. The framework followed a 2002 judgment in which an international human rights court found the country in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the Convention, and reversed a 1970 precedent that had barred any change to the sex marker on a birth certificate. Medical gender reassignment is formally approved and available through the national health service or privately, and a December 2002 government policy document states that transsexualism is not a mental illness.

Since December 2023 the government no longer accepts gender recognition certificates issued by around 50 other jurisdictions, including several foreign countries and one sub-national jurisdiction abroad, on the stated ground that those places permit transition too easily. Holders from those places must apply for a new certificate under national law to change their gender in the country. The equalities minister called the change long overdue; the shadow equalities minister warned of diplomatic consequences, noting the list excluded several other major countries.

A certificate will not be issued to a married applicant unless the spouse consents, and if the spouse does not consent the marriage must be terminated. Same-sex marriage has been legal across the country's three nations since 13 March 2014, 16 December 2014 and 13 January 2020 respectively. Civil partnerships, available since 5 December 2005, confer most but not all rights of marriage and are not recognised in every other country.

On 19 June 2026, in a challenge brought by a campaign group against the relevant ministers, a judge of the outer house of a national court struck down one devolved administration's non-statutory guidance on trans custody as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in establishments matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The case had been heard in February 2026, when the court was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible; the claimant was challenging a policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

A national transport police force amended its strip-searching policy in April 2025 after a highest-court gender ruling, adopting an interim position that trans women are strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth. Under the previous policy, trans women officers could conduct intimate searches of women holding a recognition certificate. A campaign group welcomed the change. The devolved police service published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 providing that searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex in custody and stop-and-search contexts, and that where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

New guidance from the national equality body on single-sex spaces came into force in August 2026, giving organisations practical examples of compliance; a spokesperson for the campaign group said the law is clear and the code is practical. One devolved administration, which operates under different equality legislation, is still assessing the impact of the highest court's ruling.

The health secretary announced in October 2023 that trans hospital patients would be banned from female-only and male-only wards, alongside a commitment that a patient's request for intimate care by someone of the same biological sex would be respected, with an update to the national health service constitution to follow consultation. The national health department said it would consult on updates to ensure the privacy, dignity and safety of all patients, and the secretary ordered a reversal of health-service website changes and stopped the service requiring staff to declare pronouns to each new patient. A trans legal clinic documents how this policy direction translated into fatal delay: Joelle, a 27-year-old trans woman with an aggressive but usually curable lymphoma, was removed from an available cancer ward bed at a hospital trust once staff saw she was a trans woman, and spent 16 days in a side room without cancer pain management while emergency chemotherapy was withheld; her abdominal tumour reached 98cm and the delay was unsurvivable. Her mother states the refused bed was in a multi-bed women's ward, the day after the health minister announced plans to block trans women from women's wards. The clinic is pursuing an Article 2 inquest and a clinical negligence claim, and notes that the April 2025 ruling's effect on trans people's access to hospital wards has drawn far less attention than its effect on toilets.

The national health service stopped prescribing puberty blockers to children and young people in March 2024 following an independent review published in April 2024, renewed that pause indefinitely in December 2024, and will reconsider it in 2027. In April 2025 it was reported that the health service had issued no new prescriptions of gender-affirming hormones to minors in the year since the review, with some families turning to black-market or hormones from abroad instead. The national gender identity service for children closed in March 2024, with only two of eight planned regional centres opened and many 16- and 17-year-olds transferred to adult services.

Transgender people are covered by the national equality statute, but UN human rights experts warned on 18 August 2026 that proposed revisions to that statute risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people. Under a region-wide rainbow index's 2026 assessment the country maintains explicit legal limitations making legal gender recognition practically difficult, and provides hate-crime and hate-speech protection on gender identity and sex characteristics only in some parts of the country.
GBR.blindOutOfScope:
A police force's searching and biological-sex policy, released under freedom-of-information law, could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), so its terms and whether they match the other forces' approach remain unresolved.

The final wording of the national health service constitution update on single-sex wards is unresolved: the sources record a 2023 announcement and a consultation commitment, but not the text as adopted. Whether the proposed revisions to the national equality statute flagged by UN experts in August 2026 have been enacted is likewise not sourced here.

One devolved administration's assessment of the highest court's ruling under its separate equality legislation is described as ongoing, with no outcome recorded. The trans legal clinic's Article 2 inquest and clinical negligence claim over Joelle's death have no documented outcome in the sources, and the completeness of the December 2023 list of jurisdictions whose recognition certificates are no longer accepted is not independently verified.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.summary:
Prisons in Germany house people under statutory separation into men's and women's units. The Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony reads § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement matching a prisoner's gender identity has been granted only in exceptional cases; the institute runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. A trans visitor who is arrested and remanded should not assume that a changed gender entry will determine where they are held.

The case of Marla-Svenja Liebich, a neo-Nazi convicted of incitement, shows how placement is decided. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor in Halle said she would serve her 18-month sentence at the women's prison in Chemnitz, with placement reviewed at intake. After extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison instead, although her gender entry had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act. The authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. Critics of the act described her gender change as an abuse of it.

Penelope Frank, a climate activist from the Last Generation group who is legally recorded as male, faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. Reporting on her case in 2023 found that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates and that housing runs on a binary model.

Airport screening is a documented point of friction. The trans DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, alleging that officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity and describing the episode as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment. She provided a copy of the statement she submitted to the airport.

Access to sex-segregated leisure facilities is set by operators rather than by statute. In January 2025 a guideline from the Deutscher Sauna-Bund restricted women's saunas to people whose primary sex characteristics correspond to the facility, prompting argument about whether registered trans women would be admitted. Saunas and similar venues in Berlin have been working out their practice since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025, after months of public dispute over women-only spaces. The trans woman Alessia Dorigo rejected the premise that a trans identity can be claimed on a whim.

Legal gender recognition runs through the Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024 and passed by the Bundestag in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251. Adults, including transgender, intersex and nonbinary people, change their gender entry by self-declaration on three months' notice. The previous Transsexuals Act of 1980 required genital surgery and sterilisation; the Federal Constitutional Court struck those requirements down in January 2011.

Since 1 January 2019 a 'divers' option has been available on birth certificates, passports and driver's licences under the Third Gender Act. It requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status, a condition LGBT organisations criticised, and in April 2019 the option was clarified as applying to intersex people only and not to transgender people.

The General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in health services and in education. It is the instrument under which the airport screening complaint was brought.

Registered life partnerships have existed since 2001, carrying rights in inheritance, alimony, health insurance, immigration, hospital and prison visitation, and name change. Marriage has been open to same-sex couples since 1 October 2017, after the Bundestag vote of 30 June 2017, with full marital and adoption rights. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has the same route to marriage and to the residence rights attached to it.

STOP the HATE, a prevention and empowerment campaign in northern Germany, runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
DEU.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the transfer of Marla-Svenja Liebich to a men's prison was reviewed by a court, and on what statutory basis, is not established in the sources. The number of transgender prisoners placed according to gender identity, and how many states have amended their prison statutes, is not quantified. What individual saunas and similar venues in Berlin actually do, as distinct from the association guideline and the public argument around it, is not documented. The outcome of the complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over the Frankfurt Airport screening is not reported. Whether the proposed safe-country-of-origin designations were adopted is not stated. The current status of the bill on the parentage of non-biological mothers is not established.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Paragraph 175 of the German Empire's Penal Code recriminalized same-sex sexual activity between men in 1871. Nazi Germany extended these laws during World War II, resulting in convictions multiplying to about 8,000 per year and 5,000–15,000 suspected offenders interned in concentration camps. East Germany decriminalized in 1968 and West Germany in 1969. In 2002 the government overturned Nazi-era convictions, and in 2017 the Bundestag unanimously passed a bill to pardon around 50,000 men convicted after the war, with compensation of €3,000 per conviction plus €1,500 per year of jail time; a compensation scheme was implemented in September 2021.

Transgender people have been allowed to change their legal gender since 1980 under the Transsexuals Act, which originally required genital surgery and sterilization. In January 2011 the Federal Constitutional Court ruled those requirements unconstitutional. Effective 1 November 2024, the Self-Determination Act, passed April 2024 by 374–251, allows adults to change gender by self-determination with three months' notice and applies to transgender, intersex and nonbinary adults. Since 1 January 2019 an intersex 'divers' option has been available on birth certificates, passports and driver's licenses under the Third Gender Act, though a doctor's statement confirming intersex status is required, which LGBT groups criticized; in April 2019 the option was clarified as applying to intersex people only, not transgender people.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is illegal in health services throughout Germany under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force 18 August 2006, and in education under the same act. Since May 2020 Germany has had a nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors, making it the fifth country to do so, with penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to conversion therapy. Regarding blood donation, men who have sex with men were previously banned; a one-year deferral took effect in summer 2017, was reduced to four months in September 2021, and an individual risk-based assessment replaced the deferral from 1 April 2023. The German Medical Association is against explicit legalisation of assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and directs members not to perform such procedures, though this directive is not legally binding.

Same-sex couples have been legally recognized since 2001 through registered life partnerships, providing rights in inheritance, alimony, health insurance, immigration, hospital and jail visitations, and name change. Same-sex marriage became legal on 1 October 2017 after the Bundestag passed the bill on 30 June 2017 by 393–226, granting full marital and adoption rights. Same-sex stepchild adoption became legal in 2005 and expanded to 'successive adoption' in 2013. A Federal Court of Justice ruling in October 2018 held that the non-biological mother in a married lesbian couple is not automatically recognized on a child's birth certificate and must adopt, unlike heterosexual couples where the non-biological father is automatically recognized; a bill to rectify this inequality, initiated by the Greens in June 2018, was pending in the Bundestag.

In May 2019 the Federal Minister of Family Affairs recommended that teachers use gender-neutral forms, such as 'parent 1 and parent 2' instead of 'mother and father'. The age of consent was equalized at 14 years in East Germany in 1989 and in unified Germany in 1994. According to the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2013 survey, two-thirds of 20,000 German LGBT respondents concealed their sexual orientation at school and in public life.

DEU.localsOnly:
Several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity. A new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 without any press coverage. Writing in March 2026, a commentator argued that trans prisoners need no discriminatory special law and that ordinary anti-discrimination law should govern their placement and treatment.

The Berlin prison service publishes information for trans, inter and non-binary people in custody, setting out rules and contacts across its facilities.

A nationwide ban on conversion therapy for minors has been in force since May 2020, with penalties of up to one year in prison for practitioners and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Stepchild adoption became available in 2005 and successive adoption in 2013. A Federal Court of Justice ruling in October 2018 held that the non-biological mother in a married lesbian couple is not automatically recorded on the birth certificate and must adopt, unlike a non-biological father in a heterosexual couple. A bill to correct the inequality was introduced in June 2018.

DEU.blindSummary:
Prisons in the country house people under statutory separation into men's and women's units. A regional criminological research institute reads § 170(2) of one state/province's correctional act as the operating rule and reports that placement matching a prisoner's gender identity has been granted only in exceptional cases; the institute runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. A trans visitor who is arrested and remanded should not assume that a changed gender entry will determine where they are held.

The case of a prisoner convicted of incitement shows how placement is decided. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor in one city said she would serve her 18-month sentence at a women's prison in another state/province, with placement reviewed at intake. After extradition from a neighbouring jurisdiction in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison instead, although her gender entry had been changed to female under the self-determination act. The authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility. Critics of the act described her gender change as an abuse of it.

A climate activist who is legally recorded as male faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. Reporting on the case in 2023 found that prisons in the country offer few safe spaces for trans inmates and that housing runs on a binary model.

Airport screening is a documented point of friction. A trans DJ and producer filed a complaint under the national equal treatment act over a screening at a major airport on 23 November 2024, alleging that officers deliberately disregarded her gender identity and describing the episode as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment. She provided a copy of the statement she submitted to the airport.

Access to sex-segregated leisure facilities is set by operators rather than by statute. In January 2025 a guideline from a national sauna association restricted women's saunas to people whose primary sex characteristics correspond to the facility, prompting argument about whether registered trans women would be admitted. Saunas and similar venues in the capital have been working out their practice since the self-determination act took effect on 1 January 2025, after months of public dispute over women-only spaces. A trans woman rejected the premise that a trans identity can be claimed on a whim.

Legal gender recognition runs through the self-determination act, in force since 1 November 2024 and passed by the national legislature in April 2024 by 374 votes to 251. Adults, including transgender, intersex and nonbinary people, change their gender entry by self-declaration on three months' notice. The previous gender-recognition statute of 1980 required genital surgery and sterilisation; the national constitutional court struck those requirements down in January 2011.

Since 1 January 2019 a 'divers' option has been available on birth certificates, passports and driver's licences under a third-gender statute. It requires a doctor's statement confirming intersex status, a condition LGBT organisations criticised, and in April 2019 the option was clarified as applying to intersex people only and not to transgender people.

The national equal treatment act, in force since 18 August 2006, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in health services and in education. It is the instrument under which the airport screening complaint was brought.

Registered life partnerships have existed since 2001, carrying rights in inheritance, alimony, health insurance, immigration, hospital and prison visitation, and name change. Marriage has been open to same-sex couples since 1 October 2017, after the national legislature's vote of 30 June 2017, with full marital and adoption rights. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has the same route to marriage and to the residence rights attached to it.

An anti-hate crime campaign in the north of the country runs a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including a crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.

JPN.name: Japan
JPN.summary:
Most transgender travellers to Japan encounter little direct hostility in ordinary contact, and the day-to-day risk posture is low, particularly in major tourist destinations. LGBTQ visibility is limited, social attitudes are often reserved, and legal equality lags behind comparable developed economies. The practical friction a trans visitor meets is institutional and spatial rather than violent: gendered facilities, document handling, and the absence of any anti-discrimination statute covering them.

The governing statute is the Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity, enacted by the National Diet in June 2023. Its official translation defines gender identity, obliges the government to publish annually the implementation status of policies promoting understanding of sexual orientation and gender identity diversity, and establishes a national basic plan. The text passed in weakened form after sustained political contestation over transgender issues, and it creates no individual enforcement mechanism.

Japan has no national anti-discrimination statute and no statutory guarantee of protection against violence motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation. Full marriage equality is likewise absent. Legal progress has come through litigation rather than legislation.

In July 2023 the Supreme Court upheld a finding that a national ministry, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, acted unlawfully in barring a transgender woman employee from the women's bathroom at work. She had challenged the denial in 2015; a Tokyo district court ruled in her favour in 2019, holding that living by her self-identified gender was an important legal interest, and awarded damages. The Supreme Court decision establishes that excluding a trans employee from facilities matching her gender is illegal, though it rests on public-service law rather than a general equality statute.

A Japanese court has ruled unconstitutional the requirement that a person undergo sterilising surgery before changing the gender marker on official documents, in litigation brought by Gen Suzuki. The ruling targets the surgical condition attached to legal gender recognition; the statutory scheme itself has not been replaced by self-identification.

For foreign nationals, the marker route runs through the country of nationality: a visitor or resident changes gender in their home registry and then reports the change to the Immigration Services Agency for their residence card. This conflict-of-laws arrangement can break down in practice. In 2018 the gender change of US national Elin McCready was refused recognition by Tokyo ward offices.

Same-sex marriages performed abroad are not legally recognised in Japan, and bi-national couples cannot obtain a dependent visa on the basis of the relationship. The Ministry of Justice applies a general practice of granting the discretionary designated activities visa to same-sex married spouses, which is discretionary rather than an entitlement. Since March 2009 Japanese nationals have been permitted to marry same-sex partners abroad, with the Justice Ministry instructing local authorities to issue the single-status certificates required for the foreign ceremony.

Bathhouses are gender-segregated and are the facility most consistently reported as difficult by trans and non-binary visitors. Onsen, sento and super-sento operate on binary changing and bathing areas, and trans visitors describe discretion, timing and venue choice as the main coping strategies. Private-bath bookings and co-ed pool facilities are the documented alternatives, and a number of venues are listed as LGBTQ-friendly.

Criminal law poses no risk to a trans visitor: same-sex sexual activity was criminalised only briefly, from 1872 (elsewhere dated 1873) until repeal by the Penal Code of 1880, in force from 1882. Consensual sexual activity in private is lawful regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and the age of consent has been 16 since June 2023, applied equally to same-sex and opposite-sex relations.

Institutional direction is mixed but has moved in favour of trans claimants: two Supreme Court decisions favourable to transgender rights and one favourable to gay rights sit alongside the missing marriage and violence-protection guarantees.
JPN.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the statutory surgery requirement for legal gender change has been formally amended or repealed following the ruling in Gen Suzuki's case is unresolved in the sources reviewed; the court's finding of unconstitutionality is documented, the legislative aftermath is not.

No national data on violence directed at transgender people was identified, and none is reported here. The 2009 CEDAW submission is the only broad institutional assessment in the inventory and is more than fifteen years old.

The scope of the 2023 promotion statute's practical effect on private businesses, medical providers and accommodation is not established by the sources; the text as translated sets government obligations, not duties on private parties.

sources.title: Prison warned over treatment of transgender inmate | The Asahi Shimbun
sources.summary: Asahi Shimbun (9 Sep 2023): Gifu's Kasamatsu Prison — a women's prison — holds an inmate who is listed as female on her family register but identifies as a man (diagnosed with gender identity disorder). The Gifu Prefecture Bar Association demanded the prison allow him male clothes and a male hairstyle; after years with no policy change, the bar association issued a formal 'warning' to the prison in Sep 2023. The case shows Japan places convicted trans inmates in facilities matching their registered (family-register) sex rather than their gender identity, while treatment conditions inside remain contested at the prefecture level.

sources.title: Japan Should End Abusive Detention Conditions for Transgender People | Human Rights Watch
sources.summary: HRW (11 Jun 2025): Tomoya Asanuma, a prominent transgender activist, was arrested in March 2024, held for more than 100 days in pre-trial detention and charged with assault; he was detained among men at a pre-trial detention centre, initially denied hormone treatment (until a doctor recommended it), mocked for his transgender identity in interrogations, and only allowed to shower away from other detained men after requests. HRW frames this as part of Japan's 'hostage justice' detention abuse and the legal limbo trans people face. For the prison-housing axis, it documents that a trans man's custodial placement followed his male legal sex, with accommodations (hormones, segregated showers) granted only grudgingly.
