THA.name: Thailand
THA.summary:
The Immigration Bureau runs 'Welcome Pride by Immigration', launched on 5 August 2024, which addresses the concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports do not match their current appearance or gender and eases immigration scrutiny on arrival. It is the one entry-side accommodation a trans visitor can rely on before landing.

Legal gender recognition remains absent. There is no mechanism to change the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID card or passport, and title prefixes stay locked to sex at birth; the Persons' Name Act 1962 offers only a partial workaround through name change, with approval discretionary to individual administrators. Human Rights Watch reported in December 2021 that even affirmative measures such as first-name change leave that discretion with officials, and that anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 22 January 2025, after the bill passed its final Senate reading in June 2024, making Thailand the first country in Southeast Asia to do so; the statute uses gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms. Couples who married after that date gain access to property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims from which they were previously excluded.

Thai law contains no hate-crime designation. In April 2025 a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya after she refused his request for sex; the community called the killing a hate crime, but bias-motivated violence is handled as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties and no collection of bias-motivated crime data. LGBTQ+ groups pressed for new hate-crime protections in the aftermath, and the accountability gap was still documented as of November 2025.

The Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558, passed 13 March 2015 and in force 9 September 2015, bans discrimination based on gender identity and was the first Thai law to contain language mentioning LGBTQ people. Penalties reach six months' imprisonment and a fine of up to 20,000 baht, subject to exceptions for education, religion and the public interest. A 2021 Human Rights Watch report describes implementation as spotty and inadequate, and a 2019 UNDP survey found only 44% of LGBTQ respondents knew the law existed.

Detention carries specific exposure. The Department of Corrections has separated LGBT prisoners from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; a trans woman stopped by police in 2016 expected to be held with men because her documents still carried the title 'Mr.' and was instead placed in the separated wing. Placement elsewhere turns on a prison doctor's verification of stated gender and sexual orientation, so only medically transitioned trans women are routinely placed with women, while transgender women in other facilities usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary confinement. In 2015 the trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; officials told her that under Thai law she remains a man, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections subsequently announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility, and activists welcomed it while insisting that placement should be an option rather than an obligation.

Gender-affirming surgeries have been performed in Thailand since 1975 and the country is among the most popular destinations globally for them; puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones are also available. Care settings are not uniformly respectful: a hospital refused to allow a transgender woman who had undergone sex reassignment surgery to stay in a woman's ward.
THA.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether 'Welcome Pride by Immigration' operates at every port of entry, and what written procedural basis or staffing it carries beyond the government announcement of 5 August 2024, is not sourced here.

The current status of the Min Buri LGBT prison pilot is unresolved. The reporting that documents it dates from 2016 and 2017, and no later source in this inventory confirms whether the facility, the dedicated block at Pattaya Remand Prison, or nationwide separation of LGBT prisoners continues on the same terms.

Whether the July 2019 proposal to allow surgical applicants to change legal gender on official documents, or any subsequent gender-recognition bill, has advanced into law is unresolved. Advocates were still urging the government to expedite a gender-recognition law at a Pride in Action forum in 2025, which indicates the measure remained pending at that date.

Whether the April 2025 Pattaya killing resulted in charges, a conviction, or any judicial finding about motive is not sourced. The absence of a hate-crime designation is documented as of November 2025; no later legislative change creating one appears in this inventory.

Enforcement data for the Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558 beyond the 2021 Human Rights Watch assessment and the 2019 UNDP awareness figure is not sourced, and no aggregate data on how often conscription exemptions are granted to transgender women appears here.

sources.title: Thailand Separates LGBTQ Inmates, Considers Segregated Prison (NBC News/AP)
sources.summary: NBC News/AP (29 Jan 2017): the Thai Department of Corrections says LGBT prisoners have been separated from other inmates nationwide since 1993; at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men. Trans woman Theerayut Charoenpakdee, stopped by police and expecting to be 'thrown in prison with all the men because I still have the title of Mr.,' was instead held in the separated wing. The government was also discussing what could be the world's first exclusively-LGBTQ prison facility (the Min Buri pilot), while accepting that transgender women elsewhere usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary. Of roughly 300,000 Thai prisoners, more than 6,000 were registered as sexual minorities.

sources.title: Exclusion or protection? Activists skeptical about LGBT prison (Coconuts Bangkok)
sources.summary: Coconuts Bangkok (30 Aug 2016): trans activist Nachacha Kongudom, arrested in June 2015 while protesting the junta, was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; prison officials told her that under Thai law 'she remains a man' and no Thai document can identify a trans woman as female, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The Department of Corrections then announced a pilot using Bangkok's Min Buri prison as an LGBT facility to prevent abuse of trans inmates, after Pattaya men's prison had already begun separating trans prisoners from cis men following reports of abuse. DOC figures: ~4,448 of ~300,000 prisoners identified as LGBT, 34 of them transgender. Activists welcomed the pilot but feared it 'could encourage exclusion' and insisted placement 'should be an option, not an obligation.'

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Thailand (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558 passed 13 March 2015 and in force 9 September 2015 bans discrimination based on gender identity and was the first law in Thailand to contain language mentioning LGBTQ people, punishable by up to six months in prison and a fine of up to 20,000 baht with an exception for education, religion and the public interest, with implementation described as spotty and inadequate in a 2021 Human Rights Watch report and low awareness in a 2019 UNDP report finding only 44% of LGBTQ respondents knew about the law. Gender-affirming surgeries have been performed since 1975 with Thailand among the most popular destinations globally, and puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones are available to minors, but there is no legal gender change mechanism as the Persons' Name Act debated in 2007 created an avenue to change names but not legal gender with approval discretionary to individual administrators. Post-operation male-to-female transgender government employees are not granted the right to wear female uniforms and are still expected to perform military service, and specific inequality includes a hospital refusal to allow a transgender woman who had undergone sex reassignment surgery to stay in a woman's ward, while a July 2019 proposal would allow those who underwent surgery to change legal gender on official documents plus name changes, marriage rights and conscription. All citizens age 21 and over assigned male at birth must undergo conscription via volunteering or lottery, with transgender women exempt on the basis of having gender identity disorder only if they can prove gender through medical examination described as stressful and humiliating, where those with hormone replacement therapy or breast augmentation have a high chance of exemption and those without must submit to extensive psychological evaluation. Blood donation rules allow transgender women who have not had sex with a male partner to donate while men who have sex with men remain banned, and prison policy places inmates in cells based on stated gender and sexual orientation as verified by a prison doctor meaning only medically transitioned trans women or kathoeys are placed with other women while non-transitioned kathoeys can request placement with other kathoeys. The Department of Corrections reported 4,448 LGBTQ prisoners in 2016 including 1,804 katoey and 34 male-to-female transgender people, with plans for a central prison for only LGBTQ inmates delayed over concerns about placement away from hometowns and relatives, and homosexual male prisoners like all male prisoners have heads shaved while female inmates are not allowed make-up but gay male inmates are. Transgender people face substantial employment barriers including full-time work, executive positions or promotions with daily discrimination and humiliation cutting short careers, and in education most schools require gendered uniforms according to sex assigned at birth causing discomfort, mental trauma and dropout, with a 2019 UNDP survey finding 32% of trans women faced workplace discrimination and among trans women 61% verbal abuse, 22% sexual assault, 11% physical abuse and 8% police harassment. Private, adult, consensual and non-commercial sodomy was decriminalized in 1956, the age of consent was set at fifteen regardless of gender or sexual orientation through the Penal Code Amendment Act of 1997, homosexuality was no longer regarded as a mental illness or disorder by the Ministry of Health in 2002, and in 2007 the definition of sexual assault and rape victim was expanded to include both women and men with marital rape prohibited. Same-sex marriage began performance and recognition on 23 January 2025 after the bill passed the House on 27 March 2024 and the Senate on 18 June 2024, was endorsed and published in the Royal Gazette on 24 September 2024 effective 120 days later, making Thailand the first Asian UN member state and 38th country with a comprehensive same-sex marriage law, amending the Civil and Commercial Code to replace men and women and husband and wife with individuals and spouses. Adoption by married same-sex couples became legal on 23 January 2025 under the Marriage Equality Act while single people and unmarried couples regardless of orientation or sex cannot adopt except single women for a special-needs child, and the law does not replace mother and father with gender-neutral parent raising activist concern over parental rights, with in vitro fertilisation access expected but requiring law change and surrogacy law amendment pending. Commercial surrogacy for foreigners travelling to Thailand was banned by Parliament in 2015 with only married couples as Thai residents allowed commercial surrogacy contracts, and Bangkok's Dusit district issued legally non-binding partnership certificates to same-sex couples from 14 February 2023 as the first jurisdiction. The same Gender Equality Act B.E. 2558 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation with the same penalties and exceptions, while the Thai Armed Forces lifted the ban on LGBT serving in 2005 after prior exemption as mental disorder, and the Thai Red Cross Society reaffirmed in May 2009 and October 2021 the ban on men who have sex with men donating blood citing higher HIV risk and a requirement that the rate fall below 1 in 100,000. Violence data includes the 2009 Chiang Mai pride parade violently protested leading to cancellation commemorated as Saturday the 21st with 21 February observed as the day against violence against LGBTQ, and a 2019 UNDP survey showing 53% verbal harassment, 16% sexually assaulted, 42% pretended straight, 49% contemplated suicide and 17% attempted, with corrective rape and murders categorized as crimes of passion noted due to absence of a hate crimes concept. The article states that "those whose gender expression or behavior falls out of social norms are less likely to be tolerated or accepted." The article states that "Transgender people are quite common in Thai popular entertainment, television shows and nightclub performances; however, transgender people lack various legal rights compared to the rest of the population, and may face discrimination from society." Employment exclusion is documented by the statement that "the doors of government agencies and large corporations are still closed to transgender women." Additional conditions include 2015 International Labour Organization research finding daily discrimination and humiliation cutting short transgender careers and discouraging job seeking, and a 2014 Matthayom 1 textbook describing transgender people as suffering from gender confusion khon long phet with officials reported to investigate after criticism that kham phet was more suitable. School uniform requirements according to sex assigned at birth cause discomfort, mental trauma and dropout pushing many toward sex work or high-risk behaviour, while broader surveys show 47.5% experienced family discrimination and difficulty accessing mental health and health care with discrimination.

sources.title: Marriage Equality Act - Amendment to Civil and Commercial Code
sources.summary: The 2 July-6 August 2020 draft to amend Books 1, 5 and 6 of the Civil and Commercial Code would allow same-sex as well as different-sex couples to lawfully engage at age 17 as 'engager'/'engaged person' and marry at age 18 (earlier with court permission for reasonable cause), replacing 'man/woman' with 'person' and 'husband/wife' with 'spouse' to extend identical spousal rights and duties on cohabitation, maintenance, property, debts, contracts, divorce, compensation, guardianship, adoption and spousal inheritance to same-sex spouses.

sources.title: Bangkok Post op-ed 2016 by Paisarn Likhitpreechakul, Sogi Foundation board member
sources.summary: By 8 September 2013 Thailand's Tourism Authority had launched the 'Go Thai Be Free' campaign to market Thailand as a pink/LGBT destination while same-sex marriage and civil union remained impossible, transgender men and women remained legally identified as their sex at birth with no gender-title change, and the Civil Partnership Bill after five reviews and public hearings in all four regions including a House Committee on Justice and Human Rights forum two months earlier remained off the House agenda after securing 20 MP signatures but only about 4,000 of the required 10,000 public signatures, leaving same-sex and transgender partners without spouse/partner inheritance, medical-care decision, and government spousal-benefit protections, so trans visitors receive tourist-oriented economic welcome and anonymity but not legal recognition or resident-equivalent rights.

THA.tangentialFactors:
The Thai government has pursued a strategy of positioning the country as an LGBTQ+ tourism hub, analysed by Fulcrum/ISEAS in June 2025 against the backdrop of Bangkok Pride on 4 June and marriage equality; the analysis weighs the opportunities and challenges of a state push whose motives range from genuine commitment to economic opportunism. That framing matters to how welcoming institutions are pitched to visitors, and it sits alongside a longer pattern: the Tourism Authority launched its 'Go Thai Be Free' campaign by 8 September 2013 to market Thailand as a pink/LGBT destination while same-sex marriage and civil union remained impossible and transgender people remained legally identified by their sex at birth.

Social climate runs ahead of the legal framework. Reporting from NZZ in May 2025 records that the conservative government introduced progressive trans laws including free hormone treatments with little public opposition, and that trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than is typical in the West. Recognition questions have nonetheless been live for decades: a GlobalGayz archive from 2007 to 2010 indexes campaigns around the National Human Rights Commission and constitutional charter rights, acceptance and rejection accounts from Phuket, and the 'Please call me Miss' debate over trans legal titles.

The legislative path to marriage equality ran through a public consultation held from 2 July to 6 August 2020 on draft amendments to Books 1, 5 and 6 of the Civil and Commercial Code, which would have replaced 'man' and 'woman' with 'person' and 'husband' and 'wife' with 'spouse' and extended identical spousal rights over cohabitation, maintenance, property, debts, contracts, divorce, compensation, guardianship, adoption and inheritance. The Marriage Equality Act later carried those changes into force.
THA.localsOnly:
Conscription applies to all citizens aged 21 and over who were assigned male at birth, through volunteering or the lottery. Transgender women are exempt on the basis of gender identity disorder only if they can prove gender through a medical examination described as stressful and humiliating: those on hormone replacement therapy or with breast augmentation have a high chance of exemption, while those without must submit to extensive psychological evaluation. Post-operation male-to-female transgender government employees are not granted the right to wear female uniforms and are still expected to perform military service; the armed forces lifted their ban on LGBT service in 2005.

Employment and education remain structured around sex assigned at birth. Transgender people face substantial barriers to full-time work, executive positions and promotions, with daily discrimination and humiliation cutting careers short; the doors of government agencies and large corporations are still closed to transgender women, and 2015 International Labour Organization research found the same pattern. Most schools require gendered uniforms according to sex assigned at birth, causing discomfort, mental trauma and dropout. A 2019 UNDP survey found 32% of trans women faced workplace discrimination, and among trans women 61% reported verbal abuse, 22% sexual assault, 11% physical abuse and 8% police harassment; the same survey recorded 53% verbal harassment, 16% sexual assault, 42% pretending to be straight, 49% contemplating suicide and 17% attempting it. A 2014 Matthayom 1 textbook described transgender people as suffering from gender confusion, prompting official investigation after criticism of the terminology.

Blood donation rules allow transgender women who have not had sex with a male partner to donate, while men who have sex with men remain banned; the Thai Red Cross Society reaffirmed the MSM ban in May 2009 and October 2021, citing higher HIV risk and a requirement that the rate fall below 1 in 100,000.

Adoption by married same-sex couples became legal on 23 January 2025 under the Marriage Equality Act, while single people and unmarried couples cannot adopt regardless of orientation or sex, except a single woman for a special-needs child. The law does not replace 'mother' and 'father' with gender-neutral terms, which raised activist concern over parental rights; in vitro fertilisation access is expected but requires a law change, and surrogacy law amendment remains pending. Commercial surrogacy for foreigners travelling to Thailand was banned by Parliament in 2015, with only married couples who are Thai residents permitted commercial surrogacy contracts. Bangkok's Dusit district issued legally non-binding partnership certificates to same-sex couples from 14 February 2023, the first jurisdiction to do so.

Prison population figures are reported as raw counts without per-capita context: the Department of Corrections recorded 4,448 LGBTQ prisoners in 2016, including 1,804 in a local third-gender category and 34 male-to-female transgender people, and a 2017 report put the figure at more than 6,000 registered sexual minorities out of roughly 300,000 prisoners. Plans for a central prison reserved for LGBTQ inmates were delayed over concerns about placing inmates away from hometowns and relatives.
THA.blindSummary:
The national immigration authority runs a pride-welcome programme for LGBTQ+ travellers, launched on 5 August 2024, which addresses the concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports do not match their current appearance or gender and eases immigration scrutiny on arrival. It is the one entry-side accommodation a trans visitor can rely on before landing.

Legal gender recognition remains absent. There is no mechanism to change the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID card or passport, and title prefixes stay locked to sex at birth; a 1962 name statute offers only a partial workaround through name change, with approval discretionary to individual administrators. An international human rights organisation reported in December 2021 that even affirmative measures such as first-name change leave that discretion with officials, and that anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 22 January 2025, after the bill passed its final upper-chamber reading in June 2024, making the country the first in its subregion to do so; the statute uses gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms. Couples who married after that date gain access to property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims from which they were previously excluded.

The law contains no hate-crime designation. In April 2025 a foreign tourist murdered a trans woman in a coastal city after she refused his request for sex; the community called the killing a hate crime, but bias-motivated violence is handled as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties and no collection of bias-motivated crime data. LGBTQ+ groups pressed for new hate-crime protections in the aftermath, and the accountability gap was still documented as of November 2025.

A gender equality statute, passed 13 March 2015 and in force 9 September 2015, bans discrimination based on gender identity and was the country's first law to contain language mentioning LGBTQ people. Penalties reach six months' imprisonment and a fine of up to 20,000 currency units, subject to exceptions for education, religion and the public interest. A 2021 report by an international human rights organisation describes implementation as spotty and inadequate, and a 2019 survey by a UN development programme found only 44% of LGBTQ respondents knew the law existed.

Detention carries specific exposure. The national corrections department has separated LGBT prisoners from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and at a remand prison in a coastal city transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; a trans woman stopped by police in 2016 expected to be held with men because her documents still carried a male title and was instead placed in the separated wing. Placement elsewhere turns on a prison doctor's verification of stated gender and sexual orientation, so only medically transitioned trans women are routinely placed with women, while transgender women in other facilities usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary confinement. In 2015 a trans activist arrested while protesting the military government was sent to a men's prison against her request for a women's facility; officials told her that under the country's law she remains a man, and during intake she was harassed and ordered to expose her body. The corrections department subsequently announced a pilot using a prison in the capital as an LGBT facility, and activists welcomed it while insisting that placement should be an option rather than an obligation.

Gender-affirming surgeries have been performed in the country since 1975 and it is among the most popular destinations globally for them; puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones are also available. Care settings are not uniformly respectful: a hospital refused to allow a transgender woman who had undergone sex reassignment surgery to stay in a woman's ward.

Advocates were still urging the government to expedite a gender-recognition law at a pride forum in 2025, which indicates the measure remained pending at that date.

Whether the April 2025 killing in the coastal city resulted in charges, a conviction, or any judicial finding about motive is not sourced. The absence of a hate-crime designation is documented as of November 2025; no later legislative change creating one appears in this inventory.

MEX.name: Mexico
MEX.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Mexico rests on a patchwork of state procedures rather than a single national statute. An Outright International assessment dated 12 March 2026 records that 22 of Mexico's 32 states allow people to update official documents without invasive medical or psychological evaluations. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many states operate administrative recognition procedures while implementation differs sharply between them, and called on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requesting identity documents exposes trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

The federal judiciary and the regional human-rights system have set the floor beneath that patchwork. On 17 October 2017 the Mexican Supreme Court held, in a ruling described as the first of its kind, that a transgender person may change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, whose American Convention on Human Rights Mexico has signed, ruled that recognition of gender identity on official documents is a protected human right. Article 1 of the Federal Constitution was amended on 10 June 2011 to prohibit discrimination motivated by gender, sexual preferences or any other ground attacking human dignity, with the object of nullifying or impairing rights and freedoms.

Statutory recognition arrived state by state. Mexico City allowed changes of gender and name on birth certificates from 13 March 2004, eased the procedure in September 2008, and adopted a gender identity law on 13 November 2014 that made the process much quicker and simpler. The Michoacán Congress approved comparable legislation on 13 July 2017, Nayarit on 20 July 2017, Coahuila on 13 November 2018 with easier access to birth certificates reflecting new legal gender, Hidalgo on 25 April 2019, and San Luis Potosí began authorising legal gender changes on 17 May 2019.

Where procedure is missing or slow, the cost is documented. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. That report was set against murders including a trans woman found in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Homosexual conduct is not a criminal offence in current Mexican law; the country decriminalised same-sex sexual acts in 1871, and the encyclopaedic coverage of LGBTQ life in Mexico records no present statutory criminalisation, citing only historical executions in 1658 and the 1901 Dance of the Forty-One.

A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship faces no legal penalty. Same-sex marriage had taken effect in every state by 31 December 2022, though only twenty allow adoption, and civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz. Mexico City's marriage law, which also covered adoption, loan applications, inheritance and insurance sharing, passed on 21 December 2009 and took effect on 4 March 2010, upheld 9-2 by the Supreme Court on 5 August 2010 with the adoption law upheld four days later. Coahuila approved civil unions on a 20-13 vote in January 2007, the third jurisdiction in Latin America to do so after Mexico City and Buenos Aires, with adoption and custody barred for those couples.

Targeted violence against trans people is documented and largely unpunished. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" criminalising transfemicide in July 2024, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists told reporters the law was critical to feeling safe. In early 2024 at least three transgender people were killed, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, an attack that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the preceding year. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure the source ranks second only to Brazil's 100. These are raw counts without population denominators: the ranking reflects totals rather than per-capita risk, and the sources give no general homicide rate against which to read them.

Formal rights and their enforcement diverge. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice, and she cautioned explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture.

Police conduct is a specific exposure. Coverage of LGBTQ life in Mexico records police as corrupt and prone to extortion, and transvestites as subject to police abuse.
MEX.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses trans-prisoner housing placement, that is whether placement follows birth sex or gender identity, nor special units, solitary confinement or segregation practice for trans detainees in Mexico. The prison material available covers conjugal visits only.

No sourced rule was identified on restroom or facility access by gender identity for visitors, on restrictions or prohibitions affecting gender-affirming healthcare, or on immigration screening, port-of-entry document checks or visa processes that could flag a gender marker. Whether any of these exist and how they operate remains unresolved on this evidence.

The state-by-state picture of legal gender recognition is incomplete here: the sources give the count of states with procedures, 22 of 32 as of 12 March 2026, and name six states with statutes, but do not identify the ten entities without recognition procedures or the conditions in each. The Human Rights Watch dispatch of 31 March 2025 and the Outright assessment of 12 March 2026 are date-stamped and the count may have moved since.

The transfeminicidio figures from Transgender Europe are raw counts with no population denominator and no accompanying general homicide rate, so they cannot be converted into a rate or compared with background violence on this evidence. Several factual claims here rest on encyclopaedic sourcing rather than primary documentation, including the police-abuse and Zona Rosa material, the family-rejection and UAM mental-health percentages, and the prison conjugal-visit entry.

AP (Jan 2024): 'Wave of transgender killings in Mexico spurs protests' — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca shot in Mexico City, drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

Agencia Presentes (Jun 2024): 'Violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders increased in the last year' in Mexico — data report on rising attacks against trans people and killings of defenders.

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; Mexico section)
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ people in prison' article, Mexico section, records one Mexico-specific policy: in July 2007, through the efforts of the National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the Mexico City prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate, applying to all Mexico City prisons. The article contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice for Mexico.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Mexico's Wikipedia coverage describes no current statutory criminalisation of homosexuality, citing only historical executions in 1658 and the 1901 Dance of the Forty-One; street prostitution is recorded as illegal in jurisdictions including Mexico City. Same-sex marriage took effect in Mexico City on 4 March 2010, and Coahuila approved civil unions in January 2007. Pride parades have run annually in Mexico City since 1979 (over 1,000 people in 1979, 350,000 at the XXXI edition) and in Guadalajara since 1996, alongside events in over a dozen other cities. The coverage describes a norm of "sexual silence" in which gay men and lesbians conceal their orientation and lead double lives. Police are recorded as corrupt and prone to extortion, and transvestites as subject to police abuse. Government operatives have targeted Zona Rosa nightclubs since 2007 on drug, prostitution and safety grounds, which LGBT groups denounced as homophobic, and some Zona Rosa sites of cohabitation lack safety measures such as emergency exits. Mexican youth are reported committed to psychiatric clinics after coming out to their families, with some 16% rejected by family and a greater percentage physically attacked by relatives. A UAM study found 27% of LGBTQ respondents suffering mental disorders and risk of alcoholism, some 40% with thoughts of suicide and 25% having attempted it. The National Center for the Prevention and Control of HIV/AIDS is listed as an official resource, and Pride events include consciousness-raising about AIDS and HIV, highlighting youth-specific vulnerability in accessing safe care.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mexico (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 13 March 2004 amendments to the Mexico City Civil Code allowing transgender people to change gender and name on their birth certificates took effect. In September 2008 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a law making it easier for transgender people to change their gender on birth certificates, and on 13 November 2014 it approved a gender identity law making the process much quicker and simpler. Similar gender identity laws were approved by the Michoacán Congress on 13 July 2017, in Nayarit on 20 July 2017, in Coahuila on 13 November 2018 allowing easier access to birth certificates reflecting new legal gender, in Hidalgo on 25 April 2019, while San Luis Potosí began authorizing legal gender changes on 17 May 2019. On 17 October 2017 the Supreme Court held in a ruling described as the first of its kind that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, to whose American Convention on Human Rights Mexico is a signatory, ruled that recognition of gender identity on official documents is a protected human right. In July 2003 Amaranta Gómez became the first transgender woman to run for a seat in Congress, and on 17 May 2019 the President declared 17 May the National Day of Fighting Against Homophobia, Lesbophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia with actions including labor inclusion regardless of gender identity, joint work with teachers to eradicate discrimination, and a protocol of action against hate crimes. In 1871 adoption of the Napoleonic Code following intellectual influence of the French Revolution and the 1862-67 French occupation meant sexual conduct in private between adults regardless of gender ceased to be a criminal matter, decriminalizing same-sex sexual acts. On 2 September 1999 Mexico City passed an ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, the first of its kind, followed by a federal anti-discrimination law passed 29 April 2003 creating a national council to enforce it, a 2001 amendment of Article 1 of the Federal Constitution prohibiting discrimination under the vague term preferences, and insertion of the precise term sexual orientation into Article 1 in June 2011. On 21 December 2009 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a bill legalizing same-sex marriage, adoption by same-sex couples, loan applications, inheritance and insurance sharing, signed eight days later and effective 4 March 2010, upheld 9-2 by the Supreme Court on 5 August 2010 with the adoption law upheld four days later. On 3 June 2015 the Supreme Court released a jurisprudential thesis changing the legal definition of marriage to encompass same-sex couples and deeming man-and-woman-only laws unconstitutional, requiring validation of same-sex unions through amparo injunction, with a similar nationwide jurisprudence for same-sex adoption finalized 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling though only twenty allowed adoption, while civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacán, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz. On 21 March 2014 Mexico declared 17 May the National Day Against Homophobia by presidential decree, and the rule that five amparo rulings with the same outcome override a statute has often not been followed, with almost 20 injunctions before 2015 legalization in Chihuahua and fines in Tamaulipas for failure to legalize. Acceptance of transgender identities has been documented among various indigenous peoples of Mexico, most notably the Isthmus Zapotecs and Yucatán Mayas. The Isthmus Zapotecs recognize a traditional third gender known as muxe, an intermediate between male and female, assigned male at birth but typically acting and behaving like women and doing both women's and men's work. The article documents that "Having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck and a blessing." It further documents that "Although they are perceived to be different from the general heterosexual male population, they are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities." It notes that Isthmus Zapotecs have been dominated by Roman Catholic ideology for more than four centuries despite this tolerance. It also notes that mestizos, especially mestizo police, occasionally harass and even persecute muxe boys, but Zapotec parents, especially mothers and other women, are quick to defend them and their rights to "be themselves" because "God made them that way."

sources.title: Mexico City Civil Code Amendments - Transgender birth certificate changes

MEX.tangentialFactors:
Indigenous recognition of gender diversity is documented alongside the formal legal regime. The Isthmus Zapotecs of Oaxaca recognise a traditional third gender, muxe, assigned male at birth but typically behaving and working as women do; the encyclopaedic source states that having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck and a blessing, and that although muxes are perceived as different from the general heterosexual male population they are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities. The same source notes that mestizos, especially mestizo police, occasionally harass and persecute muxe boys, while Zapotec parents defend their right to be themselves. Acceptance of transgender identities is also documented among the Yucatán Mayas, and a travel-industry guide points to Oaxaca's muxé tradition for visitors.

Public visibility is substantial in the largest cities. Pride parades have run annually in Mexico City since 1979, from just over 1,000 participants in the first year to 350,000 at the XXXI edition, and in Guadalajara since 1996, alongside events in more than a dozen other cities. Mexico City's Zona Rosa is described as a gay hub with an annual Pride and LGBT-friendly hotels, bars and tours, and Cancún as a mainstream destination for LGBTQ+ travellers; the same guide advises caution outside tourist hubs.

That visibility has drawn official pressure. Government operatives have targeted Zona Rosa nightclubs since 2007 on drug, prostitution and safety grounds, which LGBT groups denounced as homophobic, and some Zona Rosa sites of cohabitation are recorded as lacking safety measures such as emergency exits.

Comparative framing in the sources places Mexico ahead of most of its region on paper: Coahuila's 2007 civil-union vote made it the third Latin American jurisdiction to adopt such unions after Mexico City and Buenos Aires, and every state had legalised same-sex marriage by the end of 2022. The enforcement gap identified by the LSE analysis is the counterweight to that ranking.
MEX.localsOnly:
Family and institutional responses shape daily life for LGBTQ residents. Mexican youth are reported committed to psychiatric clinics after coming out to their families; roughly 16% are rejected by family and a greater percentage are physically attacked by relatives. A UAM study found 27% of LGBTQ respondents suffering mental disorders and at risk of alcoholism, some 40% with thoughts of suicide and 25% having attempted it.

A norm of "sexual silence" is described in which gay men and lesbians conceal their orientation and lead double lives. Street prostitution is recorded as illegal in jurisdictions including Mexico City.

Anti-discrimination machinery has a long domestic history: Mexico City passed an ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation on 2 September 1999, the first of its kind, followed by a federal anti-discrimination law on 29 April 2003 creating a national council to enforce it, a 2001 amendment of Article 1 of the Federal Constitution prohibiting discrimination under the term preferences, and insertion of the precise term sexual orientation into Article 1 in June 2011. The President declared 17 May the National Day of Fighting Against Homophobia, Lesbophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia on 17 May 2019, with measures including labour inclusion regardless of gender identity, joint work with teachers to eradicate discrimination, and a protocol of action against hate crimes; a similar declaration had been issued on 21 March 2014.

Political and custodial facts for residents: Amaranta Gómez became the first transgender woman to run for a seat in Congress in July 2003. In July 2007, through the efforts of the National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the Mexico City prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate, applying to all Mexico City prisons. The National Center for the Prevention and Control of HIV/AIDS is listed as an official resource, and Pride events include consciousness-raising about AIDS and HIV.

The rule that five amparo rulings with the same outcome override a statute has often not been followed: almost 20 injunctions preceded the 2015 legalization in Chihuahua, and fines were imposed in Tamaulipas for failure to legalize.
MEX.blindSummary:
Legal gender recognition in the country rests on a patchwork of state/province procedures rather than a single national statute. An LGBTI rights group's assessment dated 12 March 2026 records that 22 of the country's 32 state/provinces allow people to update official documents without invasive medical or psychological evaluations. A international human-rights organisation reported on 31 March 2025 that many state/provinces operate administrative recognition procedures while implementation differs sharply between them, and called on those without such procedures to adopt them; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requesting identity documents exposes trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

The national judiciary and the regional human-rights system have set the floor beneath that patchwork. On 17 October 2017 the national supreme court held, in a ruling described as the first of its kind, that a transgender person may change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity. On 9 January 2018 the regional human-rights court, whose regional convention the country has signed, ruled that recognition of gender identity on official documents is a protected human right. The constitution's anti-discrimination article was amended on 10 June 2011 to prohibit discrimination motivated by gender, sexual preferences or any other ground attacking human dignity, with the object of nullifying or impairing rights and freedoms.

Statutory recognition arrived state/province by state/province. The capital permitted changes of gender and name on birth certificates from 13 March 2004, eased the procedure in September 2008, and adopted a gender identity law on 13 November 2014 that made the process much quicker and simpler. One state/province legislature approved comparable legislation on 13 July 2017, another on 20 July 2017, a third on 13 November 2018 with easier access to birth certificates reflecting new legal gender, a fourth on 25 April 2019, and a fifth began authorising legal gender changes on 17 May 2019.

Where procedure is missing or slow, the cost is documented. A human-rights report of 6 March 2024 found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in one state/province leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. That report was set against murders including a trans woman found in a river in August 2023.

Homosexual conduct is not a criminal offence in current national law; the country decriminalised same-sex sexual acts in 1871, and encyclopaedic coverage of LGBTQ life records no present statutory criminalisation, citing only historical executions in 1658 and a 1901 private gathering suppressed by authorities.

A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship faces no legal penalty. Same-sex marriage had taken effect in every state/province by 31 December 2022, though only twenty allow adoption, and civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in seven state/provinces. The capital's marriage law, which also covered adoption, loan applications, inheritance and insurance sharing, passed on 21 December 2009 and took effect on 4 March 2010, upheld 9-2 by the supreme court on 5 August 2010 with the adoption law upheld four days later. One state/province approved civil unions on a 20-13 vote in January 2007, the third jurisdiction in the region to do so after the capital and a neighbouring jurisdiction's largest city, with adoption and custody barred for those couples.

Targeted violence against trans people is documented and largely unpunished. The capital's legislature approved a law criminalising transfemicide in July 2024, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists told reporters the law was critical to feeling safe. In early 2024 at least three transgender people were killed, among them an activist shot in the capital, an attack that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. A regional LGBTI+ news agency reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the preceding year. A regional human-rights commission urged national and state/provincial authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

A regional monitoring project records 593 transfeminicidios in the country from 2008 to September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure the source ranks second only to another regional jurisdiction's 100. These are raw counts without population denominators: the ranking reflects totals rather than per-capita risk, and the sources give no general homicide rate against which to read them.

Formal rights and their enforcement diverge. A university research blog analysis of 22 November 2024 found that the country's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice, and the author cautioned explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture.

Police conduct is a specific exposure. Encyclopaedic coverage of LGBTQ life records police as corrupt and prone to extortion, and transvestites as subject to police abuse.
MEX.blindOutOfScope:
No source in the inventory addresses trans-prisoner housing placement, that is whether placement follows birth sex or gender identity, nor special units, solitary confinement or segregation practice for trans detainees. The prison material available covers conjugal visits only.

No sourced rule was identified on restroom or facility access by gender identity for visitors, on restrictions or prohibitions affecting gender-affirming healthcare, or on immigration screening, port-of-entry document checks or visa processes that could flag a gender marker. Whether any of these exist and how they operate remains unresolved on this evidence.

The state/province-by-state/province picture of legal gender recognition is incomplete here: the sources give the count of state/provinces with procedures, 22 of 32 as of 12 March 2026, and name six with statutes, but do not identify the ten entities without recognition procedures or the conditions in each. The human-rights dispatch of 31 March 2025 and the rights group's assessment of 12 March 2026 are date-stamped and the count may have moved since.

The transfeminicidio figures from a regional monitoring project are raw counts with no population denominator and no accompanying general homicide rate, so they cannot be converted into a rate or compared with background violence on this evidence. Several factual claims here rest on encyclopaedic sourcing rather than primary documentation, including the police-abuse and nightclub-raids material, the family-rejection and mental-health percentages, and the prison conjugal-visit entry.

BRN.name: Brunei
BRN.summary:
Brunei's Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 criminalises a man dressing as a woman or a woman dressing as a man "without reasonable excuse" or "for immoral purposes", an offence under Section 198(1). Human Rights Watch's survey of laws criminalising same-sex relations and gender expression identifies Brunei as one of at least two countries whose national law expressly penalises "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex. The provision is enforced. On 17 October 2014 religious law enforcers detained a 38-year-old unmarried Muslim civil servant at Bangunan Bumiputera in Bandar Seri Begawan, finding women's personal items in his bag; he pleaded guilty to cross-dressing in a public place and on 11 March 2015 was fined B$1,000 with 60 days' imprisonment in default.

The United States Department of State's 2017 human rights report recorded no known convictions under the cross-dressing ban that year and stated that morality provisions covering cross-dressing, alcohol, Ramadan eating and religious propagation were enforced, while the sharia implementing regulations remained unissued.

A trans visitor cannot align travel documents with presentation. Brunei does not permit a change of name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not permitted in the country.

Penalties for sexual conduct escalate sharply. Under the Syariah Penal Code Order the de jure penalty for sex between men is death by stoning where the parties are married and the evidentiary threshold is met, either by admission or by the testimony of four adult male Muslim eyewitnesses. Where that threshold is not met the maximum is seven years' imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping, which is also the penalty applied while the death penalty moratorium continues. For unmarried men the penalty is one year in prison or 100 lashes. Sex between women carries any two of three penalties: forty lashes of caning, up to ten years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000.

The third stage of the Syariah Penal Code Order took effect on 3 April 2019, introducing stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, and forty strokes of the cane for sex between women. The code applies principally to Muslims, roughly two-thirds of the population. Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957.

In May 2019 the government extended its moratorium on the death penalty to cover the Syariah Penal Code Order, so the stoning provisions are not carried out while the moratorium holds. The moratorium was still in effect as of May 2023 and was confirmed in force at a check on 27 September 2026. It is revocable at any time by the absolute monarch with minimal process and without warning.

Secular law also criminalises "carnal intercourse against the order of nature". A July amendment to Chapter 22 of the Penal Code Order raised the minimum sentence to between 20 and 50 years' imprisonment; it is applied primarily in cases of rape or child abuse where both the attacker and the victim are male.

Reporting from April 2019 recorded no assurance that the new provisions would not be enforced against foreigners, and anonymous accounts from Brunei described a climate of fear among the people affected.
BRN.outOfScopeNotes:
The text of Brunei's Penal Code, including the Syariah Penal Code provisions, could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), and a related academic paper on the sharia penal code was likewise unavailable (HTTP 403). The statutory wording cited here rests on secondary sources.

No entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to transgender travellers were located, and no sourced account was found of how immigration or security screening treats a trans visitor's documents or presentation.

The 2017 finding of no known convictions under the cross-dressing ban is a null result and does not establish that the provision goes unenforced. The claim that a person convicted of "tarnishing the image of Islam" may be heavily punished is recorded without citation to a provision or a stated penalty.

The duration of the death penalty moratorium is unresolved beyond the last confirmed check; the sources state only that it remains revocable without notice.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Brunei (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Brunei does not allow changing one's name or gender on official documents. Sex reassignment surgery is not allowed. The Syariah Penal Code prohibits men from dressing as women or women dressing as men "without reasonable excuse" or "for immoral purposes". On 11 March 2015, a civil servant was fined B$1,000 under the Syariah Penal Code Order for cross-dressing. In 2017, there were no known convictions during that year. Members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex community reported unofficial and societal discrimination in public and private employment, housing, recreation, and in obtaining services including education from state entities, intimidation by police including threats to make public their sexuality to hamper obtaining a government job or bar graduation from government academic institutions, monitoring by the government of their activities and communications, and restrictions on assembly and expression with denial of permits for events on LGBTI topics. Same-sex sexual activity became illegal in Brunei in 1906 under Straits Settlements law applied by the 1906 Courts Enactment as updated by the Courts Enactment 1908, and remained illegal after independence in 1984. Before 2019 implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order, homosexual acts were punishable by up to 10 years imprisonment even if private and consensual. From 2014 Brunei began staged implementation of Sharia law, with Syariah Penal Code Order adultery and sodomy provisions prescribing death by stoning and corporal punishments scheduled to come into force on 3 April 2019. In May 2019 the government extended its moratorium on the death penalty to encompass the Syariah Penal Code Order, so death-by-stoning provisions are not enacted while the moratorium continues, with the moratorium still in effect as of May 2023 but revocable at any time by the absolute monarch with minimal process and without warning. Under the Syariah Penal Code Order the de jure penalty for same-sex relations between men is death by stoning if married provided they admit to the acts or four male adult Muslim eyewitnesses testify to the acts. If those evidentiary standards are not met the maximum penalty is seven years imprisonment and whipping of thirty strokes, which is also the de facto penalty while the moratorium continues, while for unmarried men the penalty is one year in prison or 100 lashes. Sexual relations between women is punishable by a combination of any two of three stipulated penalties: a caning of forty lashes, a maximum prison term of 10 years, and a fine of up to B$40,000. Secular law criminalizes "carnal intercourse against the order of nature," with a July amendment to Chapter 22 of the Penal Code Order increasing the minimum sentence to between 20 and 50 years incarceration primarily applied in cases of rape or child abuse where both attacker and victim are male, while the Syariah Penal Code bans liwat (anal intercourse) between men or between a man and a woman who is not his wife with death by stoning if implemented.

sources.title: 11 March 2015 Syariah cross-dressing enforcement case
sources.summary: On 17 October 2014 at 10.35pm religious law enforcers caught 38-year-old unmarried Muslim civil servant Roslani Hj Metasan posing as a woman at Bangunan Bumiputera in Bandar Seri Begawan with women's personal items in his bag, and he pleaded guilty to cross-dressing in a public place under Section 198(1) of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 and was sentenced to a $1,000 fine with 60 days' imprisonment in default.

BRN.tangentialFactors:
Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal in Brunei since 1906, under Straits Settlements law applied through the 1906 Courts Enactment as updated in 1908, and remained illegal after independence in 1984. Before the 2019 implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order, homosexual acts were punishable by up to ten years' imprisonment even when private and consensual.

Human Rights Watch's global survey counts at least 67 countries criminalising same-sex relations and at least nine criminalising gender expression. Brunei is one of at least two countries, alongside Oman, whose national law expressly criminalises "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex; a state-level sharia analogue exists in Malaysia.

The final stage of the code drew condemnation from the United Nations and from foreign governments, and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged Brunei to halt it. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as having the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in Southeast Asia.
BRN.blindSummary:
The country's religious penal code order criminalises a man dressing as a woman or a woman dressing as a man "without reasonable excuse" or "for immoral purposes", an offence under Section 198(1). A global survey of laws criminalising same-sex relations and gender expression by an international human rights organisation identifies the country as one of at least two whose national law expressly penalises "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex. The provision is enforced. On 17 October 2014 religious law enforcers detained a 38-year-old unmarried Muslim civil servant at a government building in the capital, finding women's personal items in his bag; he pleaded guilty to cross-dressing in a public place and on 11 March 2015 was fined 1,000 in local currency with 60 days' imprisonment in default.

A foreign government's human rights report for 2017 recorded no known convictions under the cross-dressing ban that year and stated that morality provisions covering cross-dressing, alcohol, Ramadan eating and religious propagation were enforced, while the implementing regulations for the religious code remained unissued.

A trans visitor cannot align travel documents with presentation. The country does not permit a change of name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not permitted there.

Penalties for sexual conduct escalate sharply. Under the religious penal code order the de jure penalty for sex between men is death by stoning where the parties are married and the evidentiary threshold is met, either by admission or by the testimony of four adult male Muslim eyewitnesses. Where that threshold is not met the maximum is seven years' imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping, which is also the penalty applied while the death penalty moratorium continues. For unmarried men the penalty is one year in prison or 100 lashes. Sex between women carries any two of three penalties: forty lashes of caning, up to ten years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to 40,000 in local currency.

The third stage of the religious penal code order took effect on 3 April 2019, introducing stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, and forty strokes of the cane for sex between women. The code applies principally to Muslims, roughly two-thirds of the population. The country has carried out no execution since 1957.

In May 2019 the government extended its moratorium on the death penalty to cover the religious penal code order, so the stoning provisions are not carried out while the moratorium holds. The moratorium was still in effect as of May 2023 and was confirmed in force at a check on 27 September 2026. It is revocable at any time by the absolute monarch with minimal process and without warning.

Secular law also criminalises "carnal intercourse against the order of nature". A July amendment to Chapter 22 of the penal code order raised the minimum sentence to between 20 and 50 years' imprisonment; it is applied primarily in cases of rape or child abuse where both the attacker and the victim are male.

Reporting from April 2019 recorded no assurance that the new provisions would not be enforced against foreigners, and anonymous accounts from the country described a climate of fear among the people affected.

PRT.name: Portugal
PRT.summary:
Portugal's legal position for transgender visitors is currently permissive. Homosexuality is legal, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, gender-affirming care is lawful, and legal gender and name change runs under the 2018 self-determination law, which permits self-declaration from age 16 without a medical requirement. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, conversion practices have been banned since 2024, surgery on intersex infants is prohibited, and access to facilities matching a person's gender is protected.

That framework is under active legislative attack. On 20 March 2026 the Assembly of the Republic gave preliminary approval to three bills brought by PSD, Chega and CDS-PP that would reverse the 2018 gender identity law, the first parliamentary vote to roll back self-identification. Reported tallies differ: one account records 124 votes to 79, another 151 to 79. The package was sent to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees. In first reading the bills would reintroduce a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the self-declaration regime available from age 16.

Opposition has been broad. The psychologists' order and trans organisations have described the package as a 'retrocesso' (regression); socialist deputies invoked the 2006 killing of Gisberta, a trans woman murdered by youths in Porto, during the debate, and hundreds protested outside the Assembly. A joint statement by IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warned that the bills, debated on 19 March and voted on 20 March 2026, would seriously attack trans and intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition; the organisations estimate that adoption would cost Portugal at least four places on the Rainbow Map, dropping it below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France.

The bills also threaten the existing prohibition on forced medical interventions on intersex children, alongside legal gender recognition.

Hate-crime law remains in force. The Penal Code treats sexual orientation and gender identity as explicit grounds for aggravated offences: Articles 132, 144 and 145 aggravate an offence determined by hatred on those grounds, with aggravated assault carrying up to four years, and penalties of one to eight years apply to organising discrimination on those grounds or to genocide-denial-style apology.

Institutional scrutiny of the roll-back is under way. The Ombudsman (Provedoria da Justiça) has requested a constitutional review of Article 176-C of the Penal Code, the provision criminalising acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. A member of the European Parliament has filed written question E-001183/2026 asking the Commission about the repeal process for the 2018 self-determination law and its health and safety impact on trans people.

Take-up of legal gender and name change has risen. Justice Ministry data show changes climbing back toward the high-water mark of two years earlier, with the largest share recorded in Lisbon. The figure is a raw count concentrated in the country's largest city and does not by itself indicate risk.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map 2026 places Portugal 12th at 67%, noting no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban. The score sits below Malta, Iceland and Belgium but above most of Europe.
PRT.outOfScopeNotes:
The three roll-back bills had passed only a first reading and were before the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees; whether they become law, and in what final form, is unresolved in the sources.

Reported vote tallies for the 20 March 2026 approval differ between sources (124-79 and 151-79); the discrepancy is not resolved.

The outcome of the Ombudsman's constitutional review request on Article 176-C is not sourced.

Written question E-001183/2026 is a question; no answer from the Commission is recorded.

Whether the mandatory medical opinion will in fact be reimposed, and from what date, is not established.

Three draft bills given preliminary approval on 20 March 2026 by a 151-79 vote would ban the inclusion of 'gender ideology' in school curricula, and hundreds protested outside the Assembly against them. Annual pride parades in Lisbon and Porto attract thousands of participants and spectators, and Lisbon hosts Queer Lisboa, one of Europe's largest LGBT film festivals. IRL.name: Ireland
IRL.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Ireland rests on the Gender Recognition Act 2015 (No. 25 of 2015), commenced on 4 September 2015 by S.I. 369/2015 and amended by statutory instrument through 2026. Adults change legal gender by self-declaration; the law imposes no psychological evaluation and no medical requirement. Ireland is one of only 11 European countries whose law allows gender recognition through self-determination alone. Nonbinary identities have no recognition in Irish law, so a visitor whose documents carry an X marker cannot obtain an equivalent domestic marker, and a decade of operation has produced renewed calls over remaining gaps in trans rights and healthcare rather than further statutory change.

Same-sex relations between men and between women are legal throughout the state and marriage is open to same-sex couples. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has a route to civil marriage here, and the police and courts treat that relationship as recognised.

The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 has been in force since 31 December 2024 and expressly covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; it has been described as the toughest and broadest hate-crime legislation in Europe. It was preceded by the Cabinet's October 2022 decision to add gender identity to the protected grounds of the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989, where a first offence carries a fine of up to €1,000 or six months' imprisonment, rising on indictment to €10,000 or two years.

Garda reports of hate crime rose 15 percent in 2025, with racism and xenophobia the most commonly recorded motives. These are raw counts of reported incidents rather than a per-capita rate, and while gender identity is a protected ground under the 2024 Act it is not the most frequently recorded motive. A University College Dublin study published in July 2025 found that discrimination against sexual and gender minorities in Ireland has increased despite the protective statutory framework.

Custody is the one area where recognition is under legislative pressure. A trans woman who held both a gender recognition certificate and a Department of Social Protection certificate recognising her as female was found guilty at Limerick Circuit Court in May 2022 on seven counts of threatening to kill or cause serious harm to her mother, and was acquitted in October 2024 of separate alleged threats to a fellow prisoner and a prison officer at Limerick Prison. As of late 2025 a proposed amendment to the Gender Recognition Act 2015 that would limit the effect of a certificate "for the purposes of imprisonment" had passed its first legislative stage; if enacted it would mean a recognition certificate no longer determines where a trans person is held in custody.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare is lawful for adults but tightly rationed. A November 2022 Transgender Europe study found waits of 2.5 to 10 years for a first gender-affirming appointment in Ireland, with a single public trans health provider that was severely understaffed. Patients reported being refused care for reasons including being on social welfare, holding an ADHD diagnosis, or not answering highly sexualised questions in the expected way, which pushed many into the private sector or to self-administered hormone therapy. The HSE defends its comprehensive multidisciplinary model of care. Gender-affirming care is recorded as legal but restricted for minors.

Two protection gaps sit alongside the hate-crime framework. Employment and housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only, not gender identity. No ban on conversion practices is in force and no ban on intersex infant surgery is in force. Public opinion is comparatively favourable: 61 percent support for LGBT openness, ranked fourth of 26 regions surveyed.

Open expression is visible. Dublin Pride drew an estimated 60,000 people in 2018, alongside the Dublin Gay Theatre Festival and the GAZE International LGBT Film Festival, with community infrastructure including the Outhouse LGBTQ+ Centre and established scenes in Dublin, Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford. Institutional friction is documented as well: in April 2019 Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Council cancelled Glitter Hole's Drag Storytime, first calling it not age-appropriate and then citing a high level of homophobic abuse on social media.

sources.summary:
Ireland forbids incitement to hatred based on sexual orientation under the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989, with penalties up to a €1,000 fine or 6 months' imprisonment on first offence, rising to €10,000 or 2 years on indictment; gender identity was formally added to protected grounds by the Cabinet in October 2022. The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024, described as the toughest and broadest hate crime legislation in Europe, has been in force since 31 December 2024 and explicitly covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics.

Open expression is visible: Dublin Pride drew an estimated 60,000 people in 2018, alongside the Dublin Gay Theatre Festival, the GAZE International LGBT Film Festival and gay-friendly venues nationwide. Community facilities include the Outhouse LGBTQ+ Centre, gay and gay-friendly pubs, restaurants, clubs, bars and saunas, with visible LGBT scenes in Dublin, Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford. In April 2019 Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Council cancelled Glitter Hole's Drag Storytime, first calling it "not age-appropriate" and then citing a high level of homophobic abuse on social media.

Health facilities are a serious gap: a November 2022 Transgender Europe study found wait times for a first gender-affirming healthcare appointment in Ireland of 2.5 to 10 years, with only one public trans health provider, which was severely understaffed. Patients there were reportedly denied care for reasons including being on social welfare, having an ADHD diagnosis, or not answering "highly sexualized questions" in "the right way", pushing many to the private sector or self-administered hormone therapy. A free PrEP programme through community pharmacies was established by the Department of Health in November 2019.

The Irish state itself was the historical source of hostility: male homosexual acts were criminalised under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 and Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885 until decriminalisation in 1993, and in Norris v. Attorney General (1983) the Chief Justice invoked the "Christian nature of [the Irish] State" to uphold those laws. On 19 June 2018 Taoiseach Leo Varadkar and Justice Minister Charles Flanagan issued formal public apologies to the LGBT community for state-caused suffering and criminal convictions. Residual state hostility persists in policy: Section 81E(5) of the Pensions Act 1990 bars pensioners who retired more than a year before the 2010 civil partnership law from claiming a survivor's pension for their civil partner, and Labour Minister Brendan Howlin defended refusing equal pension opt-in rights to gay men, a stance condemned by the Irish Examiner on 24 June 2015. In the courts, Judge McKechnie in Foy's case reproached the government for inaction and said Ireland was "very much isolated" among Council of Europe members on transgender recognition.

Sex education in Ireland has been described by students and teachers as "archaic", "inadequate", "biased" and "largely religious based", with reports of non-virgin students being humiliated and LGBT issues never mentioned. The Provision of Objective Sex Education Bill 2018, which would have covered consent, contraceptives, abortion, LGBT issues and sexuality, passed second reading in the Dáil in April 2018 but lapsed with the dissolution of the Oireachtas in 2020. Many LGBT youth still experience bullying, and before the 1970s LGBT individuals would mostly stay in the closet, move to England, or commit suicide. A November 2019 report by Minister Regina Doherty recommended extending self-declaration gender recognition to 16- and 17-year-olds with parental consent, and Senator Fintan Warfield's March 2018 bill to ban conversion therapy (which explicitly would not ban supportive practices for questioning LGBT youth) remained stalled in the Seanad as of April 2022 despite a coalition pledge to ban it.
