IRL.blindSummary:
Legal gender recognition in the country rests on a 2015 gender recognition statute, commenced on 4 September 2015 by a commencement instrument and amended by statutory instrument through 2026. Adults change legal gender by self-declaration; the law imposes no psychological evaluation and no medical requirement. The country is one of only 11 countries in the region whose law allows gender recognition through self-determination alone. Nonbinary identities have no recognition in national law, so a visitor whose documents carry an X marker cannot obtain an equivalent domestic marker, and a decade of operation has produced renewed calls over remaining gaps in trans rights and healthcare rather than further statutory change.

Same-sex relations between men and between women are legal throughout the country and marriage is open to same-sex couples. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has a route to civil marriage here, and the national police and courts treat that relationship as recognised.

A 2024 hate offences statute has been in force since 31 December 2024 and expressly covers sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; it has been described as the toughest and broadest hate-crime legislation in the region. It was preceded by the government's October 2022 decision to add gender identity to the protected grounds of a 1989 incitement to hatred statute, where a first offence carries a fine of up to €1,000 or six months' imprisonment, rising on indictment to €10,000 or two years.

Reports of hate crime recorded by the national police rose 15 percent in 2025, with racism and xenophobia the most commonly recorded motives. These are raw counts of reported incidents rather than a per-capita rate, and while gender identity is a protected ground under the 2024 statute it is not the most frequently recorded motive. A university study published in July 2025 found that discrimination against sexual and gender minorities in the country has increased despite the protective statutory framework.

Custody is the one area where recognition is under legislative pressure. A trans woman who held both a gender recognition certificate and a certificate from a national department recognising her as female was found guilty at a regional court in May 2022 on seven counts of threatening to kill or cause serious harm to her mother, and was acquitted in October 2024 of separate alleged threats to a fellow prisoner and a prison officer at a prison. As of late 2025 a proposed amendment to the 2015 gender recognition statute that would limit the effect of a certificate "for the purposes of imprisonment" had passed its first legislative stage; if enacted it would mean a recognition certificate no longer determines where a trans person is held in custody.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare is lawful for adults but tightly rationed. A November 2022 study by a trans advocacy organisation found waits of 2.5 to 10 years for a first gender-affirming appointment in the country, with a single public trans health provider that was severely understaffed. Patients reported being refused care for reasons including being on social welfare, holding an ADHD diagnosis, or not answering highly sexualised questions in the expected way, which pushed many into the private sector or to self-administered hormone therapy. The national health service defends its comprehensive multidisciplinary model of care. Gender-affirming care is recorded as legal but restricted for minors.

Two protection gaps sit alongside the hate-crime framework. Employment and housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only, not gender identity. No ban on conversion practices is in force and no ban on intersex infant surgery is in force. Public opinion is comparatively favourable: 61 percent support for LGBT openness, ranked fourth of 26 jurisdictions surveyed.

Open expression is visible. The capital's pride march drew an estimated 60,000 attendees in 2018, alongside gay theatre and international LGBT film festivals, with community infrastructure including an LGBTQ+ centre and established scenes in several cities. Institutional friction is documented as well: in April 2019 a local council cancelled a drag storytelling event, first calling it not age-appropriate and then citing a high level of homophobic abuse on social media.

BEL.name: Belgium
BEL.summary:
Belgian law provides for legal gender recognition by self-determination. Under the Law of 25 June 2017, in force since 1 January 2018, a trans person changes registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, with no medical conditions, surgery or sterilisation attached. The Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019; the Federal Justice Department states that applications continue to be handled under the existing procedure pending replacement provisions.

For minors the route is narrower. A person aged 12 to 16 may change a first name only. At 16 and 17, a change of sex marker requires parental consent together with a psychological opinion confirming that the decision is freely made.

The Brussels-Capital Region's own page on changing gender registration still lists a medical certificate attesting to sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision, among the documents required alongside a valid identity document, and states that the procedure is free of charge and takes three to six weeks. That requirement conflicts with the federal self-determination regime and its current status is unresolved.

Discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are prohibited. Prosecution is nonetheless hampered by the absence of a statutory definition: Belgian legislation does not define hate crimes and no code exists to record them as such, so violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions.

Equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men report rising violence and intimidation against LGBTQI people, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases Unia handled in a year, 35 per cent involved physical assault and 35 per cent serious intimidation.

A recurring pattern is the dating-app trap: perpetrators use fake profiles to arrange a meeting, then ambush the victim in an isolated place to rob, humiliate or assault them. In May 2025 the Brussels Criminal Court heard the case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims. Police have recorded a significant number of such incidents, and many go unreported because of fear or shame.

A 2019 study found that 90 per cent of LGBT people in Brussels had experienced verbal or psychological harassment.

Hate motive has been recognised in court. On 22 December 2014 a Liège jury convicted four people of the homophobic murder of Ihsane Jarfi, the first Belgian crime officially qualified as hate-motivated on grounds of sexual orientation.

Conversion practices were banned on 20 July 2023, with penalties of eight days to two years' imprisonment and fines of 208 to 2,400 euros.

A 2023 femicide law covers all gender-based homicide.

Marriage and adoption are open to same-sex couples on the same terms as opposite-sex couples, and lesbian couples have access to IVF. Since 1 January 2015 a mother's female partner is recognised as co-mother without an adoption procedure, removing an inequality that had persisted under the Civil Code.

Hostility at the level of major institutions is largely absent, but party politics has been a vector. The Flemish Block/Vlaams Belang and the National Front voted against same-sex marriage; Vlaams Belang later stated it would not campaign for repeal, and in 2019 its chairman condemned an MP who had criticised same-sex marriage and adoption. N-VA was criticised for joining a European parliamentary group containing homophobic parties.

The ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map entry gives an overall index score and per-category compliance without the underlying scores appearing in the inventory.

FRA.name: France
FRA.summary:
The documented exposure points for transgender travellers in France are detention and the border. In accommodation, services and public movement, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition, and the rights ombudsman has issued formal guidance to service providers in response.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure to strip-searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its own 2010 opinion, notwithstanding the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. In an interview, the national preventive mechanism explained that a new opinion was necessary because the 2010 opinion produced no improvement, the gender-recognition law and terminology had changed, and coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees; it identified structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable people and in suicide prevention, built on a decade of letters from detained trans people.

Placement by birth sex remained the practice in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October, according to 20 Minutes of 4 February 2025. A deputy raised her incarceration as an oral question to the Keeper of the Seals in the National Assembly, arguing that her case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; the placement question remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At the border, the documented friction is document-based and public. The trans woman Giovanna Rincon described, in a first-person account published by StreetPress on 7 March 2017, ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at an airport, questioned in front of other travellers. French law contains no visa, asylum or border-entry provision specific to LGBTQ people, so entry decisions turn on ordinary documentary checks in which a mismatch between presentation and documents can be raised openly.

Transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by imprisonment since 2017, and the law of 31 December 2004 covers injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with penalties increased where an assault or killing is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Enforcement indicators point the other way: a report released on 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults during 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against around 1,380 in 2018. Those are raw counts with no population denominator supplied, so they indicate direction of travel rather than a rate.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming from case files and association testimony that fundamental-rights violations persist, citing the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and setting out official guidance for service providers.

Partner recognition is settled at the baseline: France's marriage-equality law took effect in May 2013, and the country's first same-sex wedding was performed days later. The Court of Cassation ruled in December 2019 that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven and slow. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, and recommended an informed-consent and self-determination model. Gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979, but trans rights organisations stated that the 2010 decree removing gender identity disorder as a diagnosis changed nothing in practice. A visitor needing continuity of treatment should expect the same waiting times and geographic inequity that the report describes for residents.

No source addresses sex-segregated facilities such as hostel or hotel bathrooms, changing rooms or spas as they would apply to a trans visitor. One reported incident from a Lyon hostel in August 2024, sourced to Women's Forum Australia, concerns a dispute in which a manager invoked transphobia against a complaining guest; it does not establish how French law or establishment practice treats a trans guest's access, and remains unresolved on that point.

The 2019 figure of around 1,870 police-identified victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks is a raw count with no denominator and no breakdown separating trans victims from gay and lesbian victims, so it cannot be read as a trans-specific rate.

Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has changed facility-level practice since issuance is not documented in the inventory; the most recent placement case reported, Louna's in February 2025, postdates it.

The status of the Senate bill banning medical transition under 18 has had no update since 23 July 2024 in the sources supplied, and its final disposition is unresolved.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
French law decriminalised sodomy in the Penal Code of 1791. A 1960 ordinance (the Mirguet amendment, article 330, 2nd alinea) doubled penalties for indecent exposure when homosexual in nature and remained in force until 1980. The Vichy government's 1942 article 334 set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, equalised at 15 in 1982 under Mitterrand. In Alsace and Lorraine, LGBTQ people were persecuted and interned in concentration camps after the 1940 Nazi annexation, and were also persecuted under the Vichy regime despite no laws criminalising homosexuality. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 before 1980, still awaiting a Senate vote. Conversion therapy was banned effective 1 February 2022, punishable by two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine.

A 31 December 2004 amendment made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment. Civil liberty groups including Reporters Without Borders criticised it as a serious infringement on free speech, while the Chirac government cited rising anti-gay violence. MP Christian Vanneste of Chirac's own UMP party became the first person convicted under the law in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Homosexuality and cross-dressing were historically treated as immoral and LGBTQ people faced legal harassment under public morality and order laws. Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and LGBT people may serve openly in the French Armed Forces.

French law contains no visa, asylum or border-entry provision specific to LGBTQ people. The nearest entry-related finding concerns citizenship of children born abroad: France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens until 2015, leaving many in legal limbo, and the Court of Cassation ruled in December 2019 that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France.

A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare in France: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent and self-determination model. Transsexualism is covered under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979, but French trans rights organisations said the 2010 decree removing gender identity disorder as a diagnosis changed nothing in practice. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and a "primarily social problem" and advised extreme caution, though this did not change actual practice. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state coverage for women under 43, the MSM blood donation deferral was removed entirely on 16 March 2022, and intersex people retain significant gaps in protection from non-consensual medical interventions.

The December 2004 law amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with penalties increased when a physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. A report released on 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against around 1,380 in 2018; in October 2018 President Macron denounced the violence as "unworthy of France" and promised unspecified "concrete measures". Transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison in 2017. Overseas, Mayotte sees frequent reports of family rejection, harassment and discrimination, and a 2006 Lifou Island proposal for a "family code" envisaged eviction or lynching of LGBTQ people; it was not approved.

In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all forms of gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender-affirming care, which called such care a "health scandal" and youth transness a "social contagion"; the resulting bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, provoking large-scale protests, but is opposed by the Macron government and has had no update since 23 July 2024. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the interministerial body fighting anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory, which had called gender-affirming healthcare "mutilation"; one committee member resigned and the president stepped away. The Académie Nationale de Médecine's "epidemic-like" framing of trans people seeking care is a further state-actor hostility marker. Historically the National Assembly voted 293–222 against same-sex marriage in June 2011, and conservative outrage greeted the use of "parent 1" and "parent 2" on French school enrolment forms reported in February 2019.

In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos made fighting discrimination including homophobia one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009, and in January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign Tous égaux, tous alliés, which gives students reporting services and a helpline and requires all French schools to provide guidance about LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions must use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. Youth are the direct target of the pending under-18 medical transition ban (Senate, May 2024), while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for medical care of trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 alongside calcium and vitamin D. The Vichy-era discriminatory age of consent (21 for homosexual relations versus 15 heterosexual) was equalised at 15 in 1982, and the association Le Refuge estimated 3–4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy before the 2022 ban.

A 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 77% of the French population believed homosexuality should be accepted, one of the highest of 39 countries polled, with 81% acceptance among 18–29 year-olds; the 2019 Eurobarometer found 79% backed same-sex marriage across Europe and 85% believed LGBT people should have equal rights, and the 2023 Eurobarometer found 79% and 84% respectively. Gabriel Attal was one of the few openly gay heads of government in the world during his January–September 2024 premiership, and Paris Mayor Bertrand Delanoë came out publicly in 1998 before his 2001 election. Paris Pride drew 500,000 people in 2019, the city's third-largest event after the marathon and Techno Parade, and pride events now run in dozens of cities nationwide, with Le Marais, Quartier Pigalle and Bois de Boulogne hosting a thriving LGBTQ nightlife. Acceptance is markedly lower overseas: a 2014 study found about 20% of overseas residents saw homosexuality as a sexuality like any other against 77% in metropolitan France, with Mayotte particularly taboo and the first same-sex marriages in Saint Martin and French Polynesia triggering public demonstrations.

Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with national coverage for women under 43, the MSM blood donation deferral was removed entirely on 16 March 2022, and intersex people retain significant gaps in protection from non-consensual medical interventions.

Homosexuality and cross-dressing were historically treated as immoral, with LGBTQ people facing legal harassment under public morality and order laws; LGBT people may serve openly in the armed forces. The legislature voted 293–222 against same-sex marriage in June 2011, and conservative outrage greeted the use of "parent 1" and "parent 2" on school enrolment forms reported in February 2019. In October 2018 the head of government denounced homophobic and transphobic violence as "unworthy" of the country and promised unspecified "concrete measures".

A report released on 16 May 2020 recorded police identifying around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019 against around 1,380 in 2018; these are raw counts without a population denominator.

CHE.name: Switzerland
CHE.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland runs on self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 a person registered in a Swiss municipality can change their sex marker, their first name, or both by personal declaration before a civil registrar. The route requires no surgery, no medical diagnosis and no court proceeding. About 350 people had used it in its first months, according to SWI swissinfo reporting of 7 August 2022.

Marriage for All has been in force since 1 July 2022, opening civil marriage to same-sex couples together with adoption and access to IVF; the reform passed a referendum with 64.1% approval. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status can marry and have that marriage recognised on the same terms as any other couple.

Federal criminal law protects against discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds. Since 1 July 2020, public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on those grounds is punishable under Art. 261bis of the Criminal Code. Switzerland has no general hate-crime provision; ODIHR's 2024 country report notes that hate crimes are handled through the anti-discrimination provisions and that recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes, with police not recording bias motivation. The available sources do not record an equivalent federal criminal provision enumerating gender identity. UNHCR's country guidance records that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited.

Reported anti-LGBTIQ+ hate crime runs at roughly six cases a week. Monitoring by the LGBTIQ Helpline recorded 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020.

On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons, covering 2026 to 2030. It rests on three pillars: support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence. The Federal Office for Gender Equality coordinates implementation.

Employment protection covers name and gender presentation at work. Employers must protect employees' personal dignity under Art. 328ff of the Code of Obligations, concretised for trans people by the Equality Act. Trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any official document change.

In June 2023 the Federal Supreme Court upheld a cantonal school's dismissal of a teacher who refused to call a transgender student by his chosen male first name. The court held that the school's duty to protect the student's privacy and self-determination outweighed the teacher's religious objections.

Conversion therapy is unregulated at federal level. The National Council adopted a national ban on 12 December 2022 by 143 votes to 37 with 11 abstentions; the measure remains pending in the Council of States. Neuchâtel banned the practice in 2023, and Valais and Vaud in 2024. The Federal Council has stated that such therapies are ineffective and cause significant suffering to the young people subjected to them, and that they breach professional duties; a 2026 report confirms it condemns the practice while leaving further federal regulation open.

Detention placement for trans people has no federal provision and is handled cantonally, with no Swiss case law on the subject and no special trans units or federal solitary-confinement practice. Basel-Stadt's detention law, adopted by its Grand Council on 13 November 2019, requires the separation of female and male detainees and stipulates that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible; the prison directorate may deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority.

Support infrastructure includes a helpline launched by Swiss LGBT groups in November 2016, Dialogai (founded 1982) with helplines and advice, and Transgender Network Switzerland, which advises on legal sex and name changes, the armed forces and asylum.
CHE.outOfScopeNotes: The age at which a minor may change legal sex without guardian consent is unresolved. Minors aged 12 to 18 originally required guardian consent; the National Council suppressed that requirement while the Council of States set 16 as the age below which consent is needed. The wording finally in force is not established by the available sources.

AUT.name: Austria
AUT.summary:
The legal position a trans visitor meets in Austria is broadly permissive. Sex between men was decriminalised in 1971, marriage has been open to same-sex couples since 2017, and full adoption rights have applied since 2016. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in what Austrian law would classify as a same-sex relationship therefore stands inside the ordinary marriage and family framework rather than outside it.

The Equal Treatment Act has prohibited employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2004. Recent amendments broaden its use of "gender" to cover gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics; gender identity and intersex status have no separate listing and are handled under that term. Since January 2017 every federal state has extended anti-discrimination protection to goods and services, Lower Austria being the last to do so, which places hotels, restaurants, shops and other commercial venues inside the regime.

Hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1 January 2016, and an offence committed on that ground is treated as an aggravating factor at sentencing. The 1993 Security Police Act obliges officers to avoid actions perceived as biased on grounds of sexual orientation. No data on complaints against police or on disciplinary outcomes under that duty appears in the sources.

The serious documented risk is a coordinated ambush campaign. Police arrested 15 people, aged between 14 and 26, in March 2025. At least 17 people were lured through fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, set upon by masked groups, filmed, and falsely accused of being paedophiles; investigators said the true number of victims was probably much higher. The network behind the attacks is described as neo-Nazi, and the recordings were circulated. The lures targeted men seeking men, so a trans man who uses such applications and is read as a man falls within the group the accounts were aimed at.

Police recorded 6,751 suspected hate crimes in 2025, logged 7,327 prejudice motives, and counted 1,575 people as victims of prejudice-related violence. These are raw counts and the police data are acknowledged to under-record. Within the same reporting year, offences classed as homophobic rose while transphobic incidents declined.

Official documents can carry an "X" marker or no gender entry, following the Constitutional Court's June 2018 ruling that gender identity must be accurately reflected in official records; the first such passport and a birth certificate marked "divers" went to an intersex applicant. Intersex people may also choose "diverse", "inter", or no designation. Legal gender recognition is described as available without mandatory medical procedures, although other accounts state that a change of legal gender or name is conditional on submitting a psychiatric opinion, and that the Interior Ministry restricted the "divers" designation to holders of a medical panel certificate of intersexuality.

The national ombuds institution has issued guidance on gender-inclusive administrative forms for intersex and non-binary people.

If a trans visitor is taken into custody, the Justice Ministry's answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 of May and June 2025 sets out the official rules on housing transgender people in penal institutions. A 2025 national report by the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute, produced within a programme funded at European level, covers the legal framework governing LGBTIQ detainees, their situation and rights in detention, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection.
AUT.outOfScopeNotes:
The requirements attached to legal gender recognition are not settled in the sources. One account states that a change is possible without mandatory medical procedures; another states that a psychiatric opinion is required; a third reports that the Interior Ministry confined the "divers" designation to holders of a medical panel certificate of intersexuality. Whether the certificate requirement applies only to the third marker or also to binary changes is unresolved, and the sources do not establish whether an "X" marker is available to trans applicants who are not intersex.

The 2025 hate-crime figures are raw counts. The inventory carries no per-capita breakdown by victim group and no general homicide rate against which the trans-specific figures could be compared, so no magnitude of trans-specific risk can be calculated from them; the police data are additionally described as under-recorded.

No information on how the Security Police Act duty is enforced in practice, or on complaints and disciplinary outcomes, appears in the inventory.

The legal status of conversion therapy rests on a non-binding parliamentary resolution; no enacted prohibition is sourced, and the position after the review period is not established. On compensation for historical convictions, the only sourced statement is that no expungement or compensation scheme had been implemented as of July 2020; nothing later is available.

A report (March 2025): police arrested 15 people over a wave of hate attacks in which at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured via fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed, and falsely accused of being paedophiles. Investigators believe the real victim count is much higher.

Reporting (July 2026): the country recorded 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives in 2025, with 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence; police data broken down by who faces violent hate crime, while acknowledging under-recording.

Official hate-crime statistics for the reporting year show homophobic offences rising while transphobic incidents declined — against 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence in 2025.
Reporting (Sept 2024): the far right won the most votes in a national election for the first time since the war, raising concerns about what a far-right-led government could mean for LGBTQ+ people.

Country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity legal since 1971, marriage equality since 2017, full adoption rights since 2016. Legal gender recognition is possible without mandatory medical procedures, and individuals may obtain an 'X', indeterminate, or no gender marker; intersex people can choose 'diverse', 'inter', or no designation. An equal treatment act covers sexual orientation, with recent amendments broadening 'gender' to include gender identity, expression and sex characteristics.

AUT.blindLocalsOnly:
Conversion therapy has no enacted statutory ban. The national legislature passed a non-binding resolution in July 2019 calling for a government bill prohibiting the practice on minors, with all parties supporting it at the final vote. In 2018 an association was found running classes for minors that presented sexual orientation as changeable; a state/provincial education authority banned its workshops pending review, the association was banned in April 2019, and the parliamentary resolution followed.

Legal gender change and name change do not require prior sex-reassignment surgery, but are conditional on submitting a psychiatric opinion. Public health insurance payment for sex-change treatment is likewise bound to the submission of psychiatric opinions.

Puberty blockers for adolescents experiencing gender dysphoria are endorsed by the national societies of child and adolescent psychiatry and of gynaecology and obstetrics. Lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF. Transgender people have been permitted to serve openly in the armed forces since 2014.
AUT.blindTangential:
A far-right party took 29.2 per cent in the September 2024 national election, the first time it had won the largest share of the vote since the Second World War; parties of the right have historically opposed LGBT rights. Against that, openly LGBT politicians have held national office since 2019 and the head of state took part in a 2019 Pride parade.

A petition for dedicated queer sauna time slots in the capital was rejected, leaving no municipal provision of that kind there. The national education ministry issued new rules restricting outside providers of sex education in schools.

Advocacy organisations operate openly, the oldest founded in 1979. Community infrastructure exists in several cities, and an annual Pride parade is held in the capital.

ITA.name: Italy
ITA.summary:
Same-sex relations are legal throughout Italy for men and women, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, a parity that predates the twentieth century. Cross-dressing is legal. The penal code of the 1920s–1940s banned it and police targeted transgender people during that period; a police officer was reportedly dismissed in 2006 for cross-dressing in public while off duty.

Italy has no single comprehensive law covering sexual orientation and gender identity; protection rests on court rulings and sectoral statutes. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, which implements EU Directive 2000/78/EC; Law no. 101 of 2008 removed the exemptions that had covered police, armed forces and rescue services. No other nationwide law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and no Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, leaving transgender people exposed to discrimination in goods and services, housing, education and health care. ILGA-Europe's 2021 review recorded the absence of nationwide protection in goods and services. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that firing a transgender professor amounted to sex discrimination.

Two legislative attempts to widen protection failed or narrowed. A broader anti-discrimination and hate-crime bill passed the Chamber of Deputies 265–193 on 4 November 2020 and died in the Senate on 27 October 2021 on a 131–154 secret ballot. A separate bill banning homophobic and transphobic advertising in streets and on vehicles passed the Chamber 271–16 on 28 October 2021 and the Senate 190–34 on 4 November 2021, was signed by President Mattarella and took effect on 10 November 2021; the government forced a single up-or-down vote on the whole text, so members who opposed that provision had to vote for it.

Nine regions have adopted their own anti-discrimination statutes: Tuscany (2004), Liguria (2009), Marche (2010), Sicily (2015), Piedmont (2016), Umbria (2017), Emilia-Romagna (2019), Campania (2020) and Apulia (2024). Coverage therefore varies by region.

Legal gender change has been available since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country in the world to permit it; since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, recognised non-binary people as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 of the Constitution but declined to create a non-binary registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary; the same judgment struck down the requirement of judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. Courts in Trento (15 February 2023) permitted legal gender change for transgender minors with parental consent and psychological consultation, and in Trapani (6 July 2023) allowed a name and gender change without surgery or hormones.

On 14 April 2025 the Court of Cassation ordered Italian identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the earlier wording discriminatory.

Partner recognition is partial. Marriages between people of the same legal sex performed abroad are registered as civil unions rather than marriages (Court of Cassation, May 2018). Citing the Constitutional Court's 2010 ruling that recognised same-sex couples as a "legitimate social formation", the Court of Cassation ordered a questura to grant a residence permit to an Algerian citizen married to a same-sex Spanish spouse. Persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity is recognised as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU; Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force from 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including people persecuted on those grounds.

Health care access is comparatively broad. Since February 2019 puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones have been provided free of charge under the National Health Service, and since 2020 hormone therapy has been fully covered. In 2018 the Italian National Bioethics Committee and the Italian Medicines Agency backed puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria case by case with safeguards; access still requires medical evaluation, parental consent and the exhaustion of other interventions, a position supported by the Italian Society of Endocrinology, the Italian Academy of Pediatrics and six other paediatric and adolescent medical societies. Gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate blood since 2001.

Violence against transgender people is documented, and some cases have produced convictions. On 5 July 2024 a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton. Convictions for the assault of transgender tourists were upheld on appeal (ANSA, Campania, April 2026). ILGA-Europe's 2026 review, covering 2025, records continuing homophobic and transphobic violence, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes targeting gay men. In March the Civil Court of Asti recognised for the first time physical and psychological harm caused by homophobic mistreatment. Progetto Gionata describes transphobia as the most severe and widespread discrimination facing transgender people in Italy.

Official and political signals are mixed. ILGA-Europe's 2026 review records that the Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 states that political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people contributes to a hostile environment in Italy.
ITA.outOfScopeNotes:
No nationwide prohibition on transphobic discrimination in goods and services is sourced beyond the 2021 ILGA-Europe finding, and no later statute closing that gap is sourced.

The Constitutional Court's July 2024 judgment left the creation of a non-binary registry marker to Parliament; no legislation on that point is sourced.

Enforcement data on hate-crime prosecutions and on the regional anti-discrimination statutes is not sourced, so the practical effect of the regional patchwork is unresolved.

The 2006 dismissal of a police officer for cross-dressing rests on a single reported account.

The sentence imposed in the assault on transgender tourists is not stated in the available reporting.

sources.summary: Association for Legal Intervention news (13 Mar 2024): a regional court had placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreigners; after NGO intervention the Border Guard commander ordered her release. Her hormone therapy had been interrupted for three months because the centre refused medication supply; the case also documented her prior violence and sexual-assault history. Evidence Polish detention practice can endanger trans detainees' health until challenged.

TGEU (16 Jul 2024): on 11 July the ECtHR found Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 (and rejected Article 3) by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy; damages of EUR 8,000 ordered. Directly relevant precedent: trans prisoners in Poland can litigate medication denial and win.

Amnesty International report 'A Thousand Cuts' (2025): documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against Poland's LGBTI community on X, including LGBT-free-zone legacy (2019-23), lack of legal inclusion, and X's policy reversals (misgendering/deadnaming rule removed Apr 2023, reinstated 2024). Online abuse climate, not visitor law.

HRW World Report 2025 (Poland, events of 2024): LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government was 'slow and insufficient'; in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the Ziobro directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September the ECtHR ruled Poland's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in a 'illegal vacuum' violating their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (Jan-Dec 2024): Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; March draft Penal Code amendment raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech/violence, passed Government Legislation Centre in May but approval was postponed; a second bill followed in late October; Prosecutor General set up a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Global Affairs Canada travel advisory for Poland lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance, and notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days.

Przeglad Sejmowy 2024/5, Podgorska-Rykala & Kepa: scholarly legal analysis of Poland's administrative regime for transgender persons under the Civil Status Records Law, Population Register Act and Identity Cards Act; asks whether citizens are equally treated and whether protection is sufficient, especially on civil status. Evidence of how gender-marker documents work in practice in Poland.

HRW news release (18 Mar 2007): the then government proposed fast-track legislation 'punishing anyone who promotes homosexuality' in schools - dismissal, fines or prison for teachers/students, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education, with deputy minister Orzechowski announcing teachers who reveal homosexuality would be fired; HRW wrote to PM Kaczynski. Historical precedent for state-led school censorship.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: homosexuality was decriminalised in independent Poland in 1932 but criminalised under partition — Congress Poland 1818, Austria 1852, Prussia 1871, Russia 1845, penalised by forced resettlement to Siberia — and recriminalised from 1939 under the German occupation. Polish men in same-sex relationships were punished under Article 175, especially in annexed areas, and the General Government's criminal police could deport them or impose the death penalty; camp prisoners under Paragraph 175 were classified 'political prisoners' with red triangles. Two earlier sodomy sentences were carried out: Wojciech Skwarski of Poznań, burned at the stake in 1561 on a sentence that also counted theft and murder, and Agnieszka Kuśnierczanka in 1642, publicly beaten and exiled; the 1925 Suwałki case sentenced Stefan Góralski and Marjan Kuleszyński to three months under paragraph 516 of the 1903 Russian Penal Code. Post-war, the 1948 law set the age of consent at 15 for all sexual acts and otherwise left the liberal interwar law intact; Operation Hyacinth of 15 November 1985 registered around 11,000 suspected gay men in a national database, and 'pink files' were still held by the Institute of National Remembrance as of 2005 despite activists' requests to destroy them. A 1 January 2004 law barred workplace discrimination on sexual orientation; on 8 July 2024 the Tusk government added a registered-partnership bill (no joint adoption) to the Sejm agenda after its October 2024 presentation by Equality Minister Katarzyna Kotula. Open discussion of homosexuality stayed taboo outside literary circles: the Second Republic magazine Wiadomości Literackie and figures such as Tadeusz Boy-Żeleński and Irena Krzywicka broke taboos on contraception and homosexuality, founding the Liga Reformy Obyczajów in 1935, and 1933 produced three novels with openly lesbian themes including The Well of Loneliness with Krzywicka's preface. Communist authorities censored information about the Kinsey Report, while a 1985 Polityka article 'Jesteśmy inni' triggered a national discussion and Selerowicz's conspiratorial 1983–84 meetings produced the samizdat bulletin Etap; press came-outs followed with actor Marek Barbasiewicz in Kobieta i Życie (September 1992) and Izabela Filipiak in Viva (1998). Media has also carried hostility: the right-wing Gazeta Polska distributed 'LGBT-free zone' stickers, later reworded 'LGBT Ideology-Free Zone' after a court ordered distribution halted; President Andrzej Duda stated in the 2020 election that 'LGBT is not people, it's an ideology, which is more harmful than Communism'; Lech Kaczyński opposed official Pride in 2004–05. Cultural visibility includes the 1987 Polish premiere of Larry Kramer's The Normal Heart in Poznań with a 4 May 1989 TVP broadcast, Karolina Breguła's 2023 'Let Them See Us' billboard campaign, frequently vandalised, and Lambda's Queer Museum in Warsaw, opened 6 December 2024 as the first of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe. Café Fiolka at Puławska 257 in Warsaw, the first official gay club, opened 7 October 1990 and closed in 1992 after repeated vandalism; earlier police targeted cruising spots, with Warsaw's 6th Sanitary-Moral Brigade, joined by the female 1st Brigade in 1925, hunting cruising areas in 1927 and arresting mostly working-class men identifying as 'ciota'. Health and support infrastructure developed around the AIDS crisis: the Ministry of Health established a Plenipotentiary for AIDS and a ten-person expert team in 1985, a year before Poland's first recorded AIDS case; Lambda was registered by the Warsaw Voivodeship Court on 23 February 1990 to spread tolerance and prevent HIV; and the Kochaj, nie zabijaj campaign began in spring 1990. Organisations include Campaign Against Homophobia (2001), the Polish Feminist Lesbian Archive OLA-Archiwum (registered 1998, publishing Furia Pierwsza), the Trans-Fuzja foundation co-founded by MP Anna Grodzka, and Razem for Polish LGBT immigrants in New York (1995). Medical services are documented from the first sex reassignment surgery in 1963 at Szpital Kolejowy in Międzylesie, infrequent for some twenty years, and the first recorded transgender meeting on 10 December 1985 at Warsaw's Department of Sexology. Homophobia is described as a common public attitude driven by Catholic Church influence and widespread social conservatism, with the Church later 'a factor in making homosexuality something scandalous in many social circles' and influencing the 1988 blocking of the Warsaw Gay Movement's legal registration. After 2015, several municipalities and four voivodeships declared 'LGBT-free zones', partly in response to mayor Rafał Trzaskowski's pro-LGBT declaration; in August 2019 LGBT community members said they felt unsafe amid a rise in violence including attacks on the first Białystok Equality March and a foiled bombing attempt at a Lublin march; at a Kalisz rally on 11 November 2021 the organizer called 'LGBT, pederasts and Zionists' enemies of Poland. ILGA-Europe's 2020 report ranked Poland worst among EU countries, and on 7 August 2020 47 people were arrested in the Rainbow Night mass arrest, some peacefully protesting activist Margot's arrest, drawing criticism from the Polish Ombudsman; 50 ambassadors and representatives wrote an open letter on 27 September 2020 affirming that 'Human Rights are not an ideology'. Visibility milestones run from the first Equality Parade in Warsaw in 2001 (over 300 attendees), through banned 2004–05 Prides — the 11 June 2005 march drew about 2,500 in civil disobedience with several brief arrests and a 600–1,000-person 2004 Freedom Veche — to the 2011 election of Poland's first out LGBT MPs, Robert Biedroń and Anna Grodzka; questioned villagers in the 1925 Suwałki case reported no 'abnormality' and accepted the two men in their community.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Poland (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are allowed to change their legal gender following certain requirements which include undergoing hormone replacement therapy and receiving a medical diagnosis, with legal gender changes performed since the 1960s. Only after the legal gender has been changed does a transgender individual gain the right to undergo sex reassignment surgery because any surgery resulting in infertility is prohibited by Penal Code art. 156 §1 with few exceptions such as uterine cancer or myoma, making castration on request illegal. In July 2015 the Sejm approved a transgender recognition bill allowing change without physical interventions on statements from mental health experts of gender dysphoria by 252 to 158, approved by the Senate in August, vetoed by President Andrzej Duda in October, with Parliament failing to override the veto. Until March 2025 a transgender individual had to file a lawsuit against their parents, but on 4 March 2025 the Civil Chamber of the Supreme Court resolved the process should be a non-trial vital-records rectification on request alone with the spouse as the only possible other participant and immediate effect upon positive review. Openly transgender people are officially barred from military service on medical grounds, with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria resulting in automatic assignment as permanently and completely unfit for service in both conflict and peace. No current hate-crime protections exist, with a bill pending as of 2019 for penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by gender, gender identity, age, disability or sexual orientation, legislation agreed by Prime Minister Donald Tusk in November 2024 to add sexual orientation, gender, age and disability to hate speech laws, vetoed on 17 April 2025 by President Duda. The 2019 EU LGBTI Survey II found 1 in 5 trans and intersex people in Poland were physically or sexually attacked in the past five years. Consensual male and female same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by the 1932 Penal Code with an equal age of consent of 15, reaffirmed in 1948, while homosexual prostitution remained illegal until legalized in 1969 and homosexuality was removed from the list of diseases in 1991. Article 18 of the Constitution places marriage as a union of a man and a woman under protection, and the Supreme Court, Constitutional Tribunal and Supreme Administrative Court have ruled it limits marriage to opposite-sex couples requiring a constitutional amendment, with no legal recognition of same-sex couples except limited rights of shared tenancy, refusal to testify as the closest person under Penal Code Article 115(11), and residency under EU law. On 20 March 2026 the Supreme Administrative Court ruled registries must recognise and transcribe marriage certificates of same-sex couples married in another EU member state, first implemented in Warsaw on 14 May 2026, but on 28 July 2026 the Constitutional Tribunal ruled transcription incompatible with the Constitution, while on 29 May 2026 the Sejm passed the Act on the Status of the Closest Person granting limited notarized cohabitation rights pending Senate and presidential approval opposed by President Karol Nawrocki. Anti-discrimination provisions were added to the Labour Code in 2003 banning employment discrimination based on sexual orientation, the Constitution guarantees equality without enumerated sexual orientation after a 1995 proposal was rejected, the equal-treatment law in force from 1 January 2011 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment only, and in 2019 the Constitutional Tribunal found unconstitutional the Petty Offence Code provision punishing denial of goods and services without just cause after the Supreme Court in 2018 had found a Łódź printer acted illegally refusing banners for an LGBT group. Gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood after the 2005 Ministry of Health replaced risk groups with risk behaviours, and gays and bisexuals are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces since the 1990s with discrimination officially forbidden though an unwritten don't ask, don't tell persists. Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt and lesbian couples do not have access to IVF, with a July 2020 presidential proposal for a constitutional ban on adoption by same-sex relationships and a March 2021 government announcement to ban adoption by same-sex couples including vetting single applicants for same-sex cohabitation, although in October 2018 the Supreme Administrative Court allowed a lesbian couple to register their 4-year-old boy. In February 2019 MPs submitted a draft bill to ban using, promoting or advertising gay conversion therapy, while in August 2020 the Episcopal Conference recommended counseling centres to help regain natural sexual orientation and dismissed scientific consensus on ineffectiveness and harm as political correctness. On 20 July 2019 the first Equality March in Białystok with about 800 marchers was confronted by more than 4,000 counter-protesters throwing stones, bricks, firecrackers, flash bombs, rotten eggs and bottles filled with urine, requiring heavy riot police intervention to prevent mass casualties.

A rights organisation's 2025 report documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against the country's LGBTI community online, including the LGBT-free-zone legacy (2019-23), lack of legal inclusion, and platform policy reversals (a misgendering/deadnaming rule removed April 2023, reinstated 2024).

A world-report chapter on the country (events of 2024) says LGBT-rights reform was slow and insufficient; in June 2024 the directive blocking recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad was revoked, and in September a human-rights court ruled the lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum, calling for a recognition framework.

A national travel advisory lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status; it links generic LGBTQ2+ travel guidance and notes visa-free stays of up to 90 days for tourists. Generic advisory, limited country-specific finding.

A scholarly legal analysis of the country's administrative regime for transgender persons under the civil-status-records law, population register act and identity-cards act asks whether citizens are equally treated and whether protection is sufficient, especially on civil status — evidence of how gender-marker documents work in practice.

A 2007 news release reports a then-government proposal for fast-track legislation punishing anyone promoting homosexuality in schools — dismissal, fines or prison for teachers and students, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education; a rights organisation wrote to the prime minister. Historical precedent for national school censorship.

HUN.name: Hungary
HUN.summary:
Hungary's civil regime bars transgender people from correcting their legal gender. Administrative refusal became routine from 2018, and the barrier became explicit law in May 2020, when the government legislated by emergency decree during the COVID-19 pandemic to stop passports and identity cards from reflecting an acquired gender, including for people already legally recognised. The same law redefined nem (sex) in the civil code as immutable biological sex. Human Rights Watch records the 2020 provision as banning legal gender change for transgender and intersex people. A trans visitor should expect to enter, be screened and be documented under the marker assigned at birth, with no domestic administrative route to correcting it. Same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1961, so the exposure is documentation, recognition and official treatment of the visitor rather than criminal liability for who they are.

A supranational litigation layer runs against that domestic position. On 13 March 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in C-247/23 (Deldits), on a reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration case, that Article 16 of the GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data once it has changed and no longer complies with the accuracy principle in Article 5(1)(d); the judgment is the operative authority for updating gender markers on official records. In September 2024 a CJEU Advocate General had already called on the Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in the national registries. In April 2026 the Court of Justice found that Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ laws, including the under-18 gender-change ban argued under child-protection law, breached EU rules on several counts, and made an unprecedented finding that Hungary had breached Article 2 of the EU Treaty; the same ruling held that the 2021 child-protection law discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents. That judgment came nine days after the general election.

The political setting changed in April 2026. The 12 April election ended sixteen years of Fidesz rule and returned the Tisza party with 138 seats. Repeal of the anti-LGBTQ laws requires a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly. Budapest Pride's spokesperson, Johanna Majercsik, has named restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent issue, and Tisza's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Prime Minister Péter Magyar leaves the pace of change open; commentators describe the election result as a return to a democratic baseline rather than liberation, while rights advocates say they are hopeful that changes will be made. In June 2026 Budapest held its 31st Pride, the first since Viktor Orbán left office, with tens of thousands marching against the backdrop of the laws adopted during his rule. For a visitor, the practical position in mid-2026 is unchanged until repeal legislation actually passes.

Official hostility is documented over more than a decade. In October 2020 Prime Minister Orbán said "gays are to leave our children alone." In May 2020 the National Assembly passed a resolution rejecting the Istanbul Convention, attacking the treaty's measures as promoting "destructive gender ideologies" and "illegal migration." In 2017 Orbán welcomed the World Congress of Families, an organisation designated a hate group by the Southern Poverty Law Center, to the National Parliament. After the Labrisz Lesbian Association published a children's book in 2021, Fidesz ran a campaign conflating homosexuality with paedophilia, and the government-linked outlet Mediaworks published an article calling Labrisz paedophiles without evidence; Labrisz won at first instance, but the Curia ruled in November 2022 that the article did not violate its right to good reputation, and the case was appealed to the Constitutional Court. At Budapest Pride in 2014 the Jobbik party displayed a sign reading "The Parliament Does Not Want Any Deviants" and verbally abused attendees.

Custody and asylum procedures carry their own risks. A 2025 national report by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society, produced under an EU-funded project on the rights of LGBTIQ detainees, examines the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention. In January 2018 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that asylum seekers may not be subjected by authorities to psychological testing aimed at determining sexual orientation.
HUN.outOfScopeNotes:
The specific findings of the 2025 Hungarian Helsinki Committee and Háttér Society report on LGBTIQ detainees are not itemised in the sources reviewed. The report's existence and scope are recorded; its conclusions on the treatment of trans detainees in Hungarian custody are unresolved here.

Whether Hungarian authorities are applying the Deldits judgment to individual gender-marker requests is not established by the sources. The ruling binds the register authority in principle, and no source reviewed describes an administrative practice of compliance.

The pace and scope of repeal after April 2026 are unresolved. No repeal legislation had passed at the time of the sources, the incoming government's position on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar had not been stated, and the Constitutional Court appeal in the Labrisz defamation case had not been decided.

GRC.name: Greece
GRC.summary:
Marriage between same-sex couples became legal in Greece in February 2024 under Law 5089/2024, making it the first country with a majority Orthodox Christian population to enact marriage equality. The same law added sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics as equal-treatment grounds in goods and services, education, healthcare, housing and social protection. Civil unions have been available since 2015, adoption and foster care by same-sex couples are permitted, and the age of consent is 15 for everyone. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Greek law can have that relationship recognised in marriage.

Legal gender change has been available on a self-declaration basis since 2017. TGEU's Trans Rights Index and Map 2025 records Greece meeting 21 of its 32 indicators; the identified gaps include age restrictions on changes of forename, the absence of a national action plan on trans rights, and no legal recognition of trans or non-binary parenthood. Greece ranked seventh in Europe on the 2025 Rainbow Map.

Conversion practices are banned for minors and intersex genital mutilation was criminalised in 2022; the ban does not extend to adults. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity was prohibited in 2023. Discrimination and hate-speech protections are in force.

In March 2024 a mob of about 150 people attacked two trans people in Thessaloniki; 21 people were arrested, 11 of them minors, and a masked group then attacked counter-protesters. In July 2025 the Crete Court of Appeal convicted three French tourists for an attack carried out in 2017. The Orthodox Church officially opposed marriage equality, and transphobic comments were directed at Eurovision contestants.

In Koutra and Katzaki v. Greece (European Court of Human Rights, application 459/16, judgment 2017), the court examined the 2013 stopping and mistreatment of transgender sex workers and their lawyer in Athens, including street stops and removal from cars; the complaints against the officers were discontinued.

The EU Fundamental Rights Agency's LGBTIQ survey III, published in 2024, found that 63% of respondents in Greece avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner, against an EU-27 average of 53%; 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault, against 29% across the EU; and only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ, against 51% across the EU.

The European Court of Human Rights condemned Greece for detaining an LGBTI Iranian refugee pending deportation, finding a violation of Article 3. A criminal case was opened over an online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people.
GRC.outOfScopeNotes:
No national action plan on trans rights exists, and trans or non-binary parenthood has no legal recognition; age restrictions continue to apply to changes of forename. These are standing gaps rather than pending measures.

The conversion-practices ban covers minors only; the sources do not establish what protection, if any, applies to adults.

Whether the March 2024 Thessaloniki arrests produced convictions is not sourced, and the outcome of the criminal case over the online incitement post is likewise not sourced.

Whether Greece has complied with the European Court of Human Rights judgment on the detained LGBTI refugee is not sourced, and no disciplinary outcome is recorded for the discontinued complaints in the Koutra and Katzaki case.

CZE.name: Czechia
CZE.summary:
Czechia's Constitutional Court on 24 April 2024, in judgment PL. US 52/23, struck down the requirement that surgery including sterilisation be a condition for official legal sex change, holding that recognition conditional on disabling reproductive function is unconstitutional, and gave the government until June 2025 to change the law. Reuters reported in June 2025 that the surgery requirement had been dropped, and in July 2025 the Czech Health Ministry announced that trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment to change legal gender. Trans*Parent welcomed the change but warned that full legislative reform was still needed to prevent a new government or minister from reversing it. On 12 September 2025 the European Court of Human Rights, in T.H. v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 33037/22), found a violation of Article 8 in the surgical and sterilisation condition and the related civil-registry treatment, with Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe intervening, and framed Convention-guaranteed recognition through self-determination.

Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1962, homosexual prostitution was decriminalised in 1990, and the age of consent was equalised at 15 in 1990, having previously been 18 for homosexuals. The 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, housing and access to goods and services.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples took effect on 1 July 2006 after a presidential veto was overturned. A 2024 compromise law enshrined same-sex partnerships in the civil code, equating them to marriage in all aspects except joint adoption while permitting step-child adoption, and took effect on 1 January 2025. Individual adoption is permitted and the ban on adoption by those in a registered partnership was struck down in 2016, but joint adoption by same-sex couples remains unavailable. A marriage-equality bill introduced in 2018 by 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs and backed by the caretaker government cleared parliamentary committees in June 2023, while a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage advanced to second reading with backing from SPD, ODS, KDU-ČSL and ANO. Since 2001, persons living in a common household have held hospital and prison visitation rights similar to those of married heterosexual couples, alongside inheritance and housing succession rights.

Detention practice is inconsistent. In March 2023 the Supreme Administrative Court rebuked the Prague Municipal Court for what it described as sarcastic moral lectures toward an HIV-positive trans man in transition held in immigration detention, and ruled that authorities must first assess whether a detainee is a potentially vulnerable person before deciding placement. In November 2025 the Supreme Court demanded that the national prison concept explicitly address the needs of people in or after transition, with the human-rights commissioner pressing for a binding regulation while the Justice Ministry maintained that the existing framework suffices; that consultation remains open.

Hate-crime protection is in flux. The government approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, which remains pending in Parliament, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened the status of 'particularly vulnerable victim'. The Criminal Code amendments abandon the hostility model for a discriminatory-selection model. The OSCE/ODIHR 2024 hate crime report records 94 hate crimes reported to police in Czechia in 2024, 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, with LGBTI-motivated incidents included in the bias breakdown; these are raw counts without a population denominator. ODIHR's key observation is that recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes.

An ILGA-Europe survey of LGBTQ+ people in Czechia found that 43% had experienced discrimination or harassment in the previous five years, with the highest rates among trans and non-binary respondents, and that 51% had been targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years. Reported anti-LGBT speech by politicians rose from 43% in 2018 to 71% in 2023, and 63% of respondents attributed rising intolerance to politicians. After the Constitutional Court ruling, the Justice Minister publicly stated that his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth', and other politicians issued transphobic statements; the far-right SPD circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists'. On 27 June 2021 President Miloš Zeman said that sex-reassignment surgery means 'you are committing a crime for inflicting self-harm' and that 'these transgenders truly disgust me', and said he did not understand transgender people at all.

Public expression is legal and visible but carries social risk. The first Prague Pride parade was held in August 2011 with mayoral support and drew negative responses from religious conservative groups and the far right, and has run annually since 2012. In June 2023 a group disrupted a Brno Pride drag story-time event with homophobic slurs. In April 2023 the Ostrava Regional Court ordered that certificates and diplomas be re-issued to a trans graduate.
CZE.outOfScopeNotes:
No transgender-specific public-opinion polling is available for Czechia. The acceptance polling cited in the sources concerns homosexuality, same-sex marriage, registered partnerships and gay or lesbian neighbours or acquaintances, and the only transgender-specific attitudinal statement documented is the former president's remarks of 27 June 2021.

The July 2025 change to legal gender recognition was announced by the Health Ministry rather than enacted in statute, and Trans*Parent has warned that a new government or minister could reverse it. Whether the June 2025 deadline set by the Constitutional Court has been met by legislation is unresolved in the sources.

The Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to gender identity remains pending in Parliament, so its enactment is not sourced.

The prison regulation sought by the human-rights commissioner remains under consultation, with the Justice Ministry disputing that a new binding rule is needed.

ODIHR notes that recorded hate-crime statistics do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes, so the 2024 figures cannot be read as a complete count of bias-motivated crime.

sources.summary: Czechia: same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1962, following research by Kurt Freund concluding that homosexual orientation cannot be altered; homosexual prostitution was decriminalised in 1990, and the age of consent was equalised in 1990 at 15, having previously been 18 for homosexuals. In May 2024 the Constitutional Court ruled that forced surgery and sterilisation of transgender individuals is unconstitutional and gave the government until June 2025 to change the laws; in July 2025 the Health Ministry announced that trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment to change their legal gender. State rhetoric also framed trans bodies as criminal: on 27 June 2021 President Miloš Zeman said sex-reassignment surgery means 'you are committing a crime for inflicting self-harm' and that 'these transgenders truly disgust me.' Public expression is legal and visible but carries social risk. The first Prague Pride parade was held in August 2011 with mayoral support and drew negative responses from religious conservative groups and the far-right; it has run annually since 2012, and since 2014 organisers have barred pedophile promotional activity at Pride venues. Brno has hosted the Mezipatra gay and lesbian film festival every November since 2000, and a Prague City Council-produced gay guide and map appeared in late 2010. In the 2012 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey of 93,000 LGBTQ people, only one in five Czech respondents was open about their orientation to all colleagues or classmates, 71% were selectively open at work or school, and 52% of gay men and 30% of lesbian women avoided holding hands in public outside gay neighbourhoods for fear of assault, threat or harassment; only one in five was open to all classmates, indicating school-level concealment. Facilities are concentrated in the capital: Prague has a large, well-developed gay nightlife scene centred on the Vinohrady district with at least 20 bars and clubs and 4 saunas, while gay venues are much more sparsely spread in other Czech towns, and the city acts as a magnet for the country's gay youth. Since 2001 the Czech Republic has granted 'persons living in a common household' hospital and prison visitation rights similar to married heterosexual couples, alongside inheritance and succession rights in housing. Blood donation opened to all citizens regardless of partner gender on 1 July 2024, replacing the previous ban on people with a same-gender partner, though people reporting anal sex with a new partner in the past four months are still excluded. Anti-discrimination protection under the 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in education as well as employment, housing and access to goods and services. Acceptance is markedly higher among younger Czechs: a 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 84% of 18–29-year-olds thought homosexuality should be accepted, versus 72% of those over 50, and a January 2020 Median poll showed younger respondents overwhelmingly supporting same-sex marriage while those aged 55 and above were mostly opposed.
