LVA.blindSummary:
The country has no dedicated statute on legal gender recognition. National law does not define "sex change"; on the available account an identity-document change has been granted on presentation of a medical certificate. In 2008 the national supreme court held that authorities should have granted recognition to a transgender person refused one in 2004 after a partial sex change. A 2009 proposal in the national parliament that would have required sterilisation as a condition of changing legal gender was rejected. Nonbinary identity is not recognised. In June 2025 coalition members of the national parliament said trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet."

Same-sex conduct is not criminalised: male homosexuality was decriminalised in 1992, female homosexuality was never criminalised, and the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1999.

One trans immigrant told a national broadcaster that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status, tying document change to immigration exposure.

Registered partnerships, codified in November 2023 and in force since 1 July 2024, carry rights similar to marriage except for adoption and inheritance. A 2006 constitutional amendment defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. In April 2023 the national parliament amended the children's rights law to bar adoption of the country's children by foreign same-sex couples, a provision that reaches a trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under local law.

Enforcement of hate-motivated offences is the main documented protection gap. In a case decided by a regional human rights court, the court found unanimously on 18 July 2024 that Articles 3, 8 and 14 had been violated after a 2020 homophobic attack in the capital: no criminal charges were brought although the aggressor admitted anti-gay slurs, and the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine. The national prosecution service reopened the criminal proceedings after the ruling.

In a separate case, two people were attacked in a second city; police closed the investigation and the national prosecution service ordered it reopened. Homophobic posts by a former regional parliamentarian were investigated; he left for a neighbouring jurisdiction.

Anti-discrimination protection documented for the country covers sexual orientation in employment; no provision addressing gender identity is documented.
LVA.blindOutOfScope:
Enforcement after the reopened proceedings in the two hate-crime cases is unresolved; no outcome is recorded in the available sources.

No education-specific findings appear in the available sources.

No sourced material addresses police treatment of transgender people specifically, bathroom or facilities access rules, or border screening practices.
blindSourceSummaries: A feature reports civil unions for same-sex couples in force since 1 July 2024; transgender and non-binary residents still lack targeted legal change — a trans immigrant says legal transition would invalidate his marriage and residency status, and coalition MPs say trans rights have not emerged as a major issue; the country was the first in the region to elect an openly gay national leader (2023).

A human-rights-court press release (18 July 2024) reports the Court unanimously found violations of three articles after a homophobic attack — no criminal charges were brought despite the aggressor admitting anti-gay slurs; the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

An annual review chapter reports an administrative court overturned denial of asylum to an LGBTI seeker; the top prosecutor reopened criminal proceedings in the hate-crime case after the court ruling; two people were attacked in a regional city, with the top prosecutor ordering the investigation reopened after police closed it; a former MEP's homophobic posts were investigated.

An analysis of the ruling clarifies the positive obligations of nations in homophobic-attack cases — thorough investigation and punishment of hate crimes, sending a message of zero tolerance; it notes the troubling pattern of regional nations failing to protect LGBTI+ persons and to investigate effectively.

An organisation's country page records the human-rights-court judgment — violations of three articles after authorities declined to prosecute a homophobic assault on a gay couple as a hate-motivated offence.

A 2007 report quotes a senior cleric calling homosexuality 'total corruption in the sexual arena' and 'an unnatural form of prostitution', demanding a referendum on same-sex marriage and counter-Pride crowds of tens of thousands, calling Pride a 'foreign-inspired action'.
A 2018 report: several thousand people marched in a regional Pride in the capital — the annual event rotating among regional capitals, organised by a local association.
LVA.blindLocalsOnly:
The national ombudsman's 2018 call for a partnership law cited that about half the country's children are born outside marriage and should have legal protections.

Any person over 25 may adopt, but two people not married to each other may not adopt the same child, so in an unmarried couple only one partner can adopt.

Lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment.

A 2020 court ruling on parental leave for same-sex couples led to a national justice ministry draft civil union law in 2022.

In September 2006 the national parliament passed labour code amendments prohibiting workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation; the then president refused to sign the bill until that protection was added.
LVA.tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe ranked Latvia 24th of 27 European Union member states for LGBT rights protection in 2023.

The European Court of Human Rights judgment restates states' positive obligations to investigate and punish hate crimes thoroughly; the Strasbourg Observers analysis reads it as a clarification of those duties.

An administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker.

A small gay scene exists in Riga; outside the capital the sparse population supports none, and the bars, clubs, shops and libraries established since the restoration of independence are concentrated there.

TUR.name: Turkey
TUR.summary:
Turkey imposes no visa, entry or border condition that applies to LGBTQ travellers as such; the exposure begins after arrival. The document rule that reaches foreign visitors is general: original photo identification must be carried at transit checkpoints in holiday areas, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance. For a trans visitor the rule matters because identity checks are the mechanism through which police contact is initiated.

In August 2025 Istanbul police stopped about 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in Beyoğlu, held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released them after 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks. Lawyers quoted by bianet argue the checks breach Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the detained women said: 'They didn't fine us, but they documented us. The new law hasn't even passed yet, but they're already enforcing it on us.'

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report for 2025 records 313 violations, about two and a half times the 2024 figure, of which 299 were detention decisions (256 recorded, 43 unrecorded), alongside systematic attacks on privacy. Trans people were disproportionately represented in the documented caseload. The report characterises the shift as hostility converted into state policy.

A draft legislative package reported by Human Rights Watch in October 2025 would effectively criminalise LGBT people through vague protections of 'the family' and 'public morals'. An earlier proposal to criminalise public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years' imprisonment was not included in the 2026 judicial package. Neither text is in force; the risk to a visitor lies in the undefined boundary of such offences rather than in any enacted provision.

Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct protection on grounds of gender identity. The European Commission's 2025 annual report found legal protection insufficient and unaligned with the EU acquis, and noted that authorities were granting official permits to demonstrations promoting exclusion and discrimination. Bills introduced by the CHP in February 2015 and constitutional protection discussed in the 2013 draft process were not carried forward; a Kaos GL case alleging ineffective remedies against Pride bans has been pending since 2023.

Pride events have been restricted for a decade. The Truth Justice Memory Center's monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found violations of international human-rights law of a kind recorded since 2015, with discriminatory statements by senior officials deepening hostility. In May 2019 police broke up a student Pride march at Middle East Technical University and arrested at least 25 students.

Sex reassignment surgery is available in Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir and Antalya from age 18, and a change of the gender marker on an identity card requires the procedure to be performed at a state hospital. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the public health system, so a visitor who needs continued medication must source and pay for it privately. A September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, following a Kayseri provincial circular that added 'gender reassignment' to the official grounds for medical-board reports, requires hospitals to issue e-reports and removes the 'other' option; Kaos GL warns it creates a profiling route and narrows access to transition care.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not available, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly. The 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 removed discriminatory provisions and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, but those ceremonies confer no marital status. Marriage eligibility is determined by the gender recorded in the civil registry rather than by trans status, so a trans visitor who has legally changed their registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender, while a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under their birth-sex status cannot.

Violence against trans people is documented with impunity outcomes. In August 2024 a trans woman, Yaşam, was stabbed by a 17-year-old in Bakırköy; the assailant was released while the victim was referred for arrest, a disparity activists cite as evidence of state policy.

If a visitor is detained, custody conditions are a further risk: trans prisoners are placed by registered sex, and LGBTI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and de facto isolation, according to a Prison Insider country profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association.

State action against trans and LGBTI+ organising has intensified. A May 2025 'Decade of Family and Population' declaration, running from 2026, cast the LGBTQ movement as a threat to children; September 2026 'My Family is Safe' operations against LGBTQ+ and HIV support organisations placed 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses under investigation. In April 2026 the İzmir youth group Genç LGBTI+ was ordered to dissolve and eleven founders were put on trial.
TUR.outOfScopeNotes:
The draft package reported in October 2025 has not been enacted and the offences it would create are not defined in the sources; whether advocacy, publication or association activity by foreign nationals would fall within it is unresolved.

No published breakdown shows how many of those detained in the 2025 identity checks were foreign nationals, or whether gender-nonconforming presentation rather than documentation triggered the stops.

Whether Turkish state hospitals will continue a foreign visitor's existing hormone prescription, and whether a foreign gender-recognition certificate is accepted for the civil-registry test that governs marriage eligibility, is not sourced.

The practical effect of the September 2025 health regulation on non-citizens is not documented; the circular that preceded it applied to provincial medical-board reporting.

sources.title: Rights groups urge probe into 'suspicious' death of transgender prisoner in Turkey (Stockholm Center for Freedom)
sources.summary: SCF (18 Dec 2025): transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkish rights groups (coordinated from Human Rights Association / IHD branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakir, Mersin and Aydin) demanded an independent investigation and changes to 'detention practices affecting transgender prisoners'. sources.title: LGBTQI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches (Kaos GL), reporting the Prison Insider 'Country Profile' on Turkey (with CİSST data)
sources.summary: Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.

sources.summary:
Turkey has no visa, entry or border rules specific to LGBTQ travelers; the available material concerns people already in the country. LGBT individuals are among the most vulnerable asylum seekers and refugees in Turkey, and their access to rights and services is limited by anti-LGBTQ sentiment among state actors and the general public.

Sex reassignment surgery is available in Turkey's major cities (Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir and Antalya) and the minimum age for the procedure is 18. To change the gender marker on an identity card, the procedure must be conducted at a state hospital. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors needing continued medication must arrange and pay for it privately.

Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no direct discrimination protection regarding gender identity in Turkish law. The EU Commission's 2025 annual report wrote that legal protection of LGBTIQ persons is insufficient and not aligned with the EU acquis, and that authorities were granting official permissions for demonstrations promoting exclusion and discrimination. Bills to introduce such protections have been repeatedly proposed (CHP, February 2015) and constitutional protection agreed in 2013 draft talks, but the drafts were cancelled; KAOS GL has a case pending since 2023 alleging ineffective remedies against discrimination such as Pride bans. The government considered legislation criminalizing public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex" with one to three years' imprisonment, though it was not included in the 2026 judicial package.

Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as joint parents. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, which made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, but these carry no legal marital status. Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, so individuals who have legally changed their registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender; LGBT marriage for non-trans people remains legally impossible.

DNK.name: Denmark
DNK.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Denmark has operated by self-declaration since 1 September 2014. A person over 18 states the wish to change registered sex and completes a six-month reflection period; no medical evaluation, psychiatric diagnosis, surgery or sterilisation is required. Parliament removed the diagnosis and surgery requirements in June 2014 by 59 votes to 52. Those requirements dated to the Act on Sterilisation and Castration of June 1929, one of the first gender-change laws in the world, which had made irreversible sterilisation a condition of the process.

Danish passports are issued with male, female and X sex descriptors, so a non-binary traveller can carry a travel document that records neither male nor female.

Gender identity is not a ground for arrest or prosecution. The F&M Global Barometers country profile records that freedom from gender-identity-based arbitrary arrest was affirmed in every year from 2011 to 2024. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1930, in force from 1933, and the age of consent has been 15 regardless of sexual orientation or gender since 1977.

Denmark removed gender identity disorder from the National Board of Health's list of mental illnesses in 2016, effective 1 January 2017, the second country to do so after France in 2010. In May 2016 the government stated it would act unilaterally by October 2016 if the World Health Organization did not remove the classification; the WHO replaced the diagnosis with gender incongruence, reclassified as a sexual health condition, in June 2018.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is prohibited in Danish law, but the statutory text is uneven. The 1996 Act on Prohibition of Unequal Treatment in the Labor Market lists sexual orientation and does not explicitly name gender identity or expression. A 2015 ruling by the Aarhus court, in a case brought by a transgender woman against a staffing agency, held that her clothing and appearance were the sole reason for her dismissal and that both the Equal Treatment Act and the Anti-Discrimination Act covered it, awarding DKK 30,000 in compensation against Jysk Mandskabsservice while acquitting the client company for insufficient proof. That judgment, the first on trans discrimination in Denmark, extended protection to gender identity and gender expression despite the absence of explicit wording. Complaints are considered by the Board of Equal Treatment, established under the 2008 Act on the Board of Equal Treatment. F&M records workplace anti-discrimination law covering gender identity since 2015, and fair-housing protection on the same ground throughout the period it measures.

Hate-crime provision is narrower than the discrimination framework. Penal Code amendments adopted in 2004 add penalties for crimes committed because of a person's sexual orientation; gender identity is not named in that provision.

Access to trans health care has tightened since 2023. Guidelines issued that year recommend puberty blockers at Tanner stage two or three, described as buying time for further exploration. Children under ten showing adequate signs of gender dysphoria trigger advisory information for parents. Children over ten face at least five investigative interviews, a psychiatric evaluation, informational sessions on hormone therapy and review of school and municipal records. Hormone treatment can be consented to from age 15 without parental involvement, and no surgical options are available before 18. Assessed barriers include psychosis and autism where dysphoria is treated as an aspect of mental illness, and a history of abuse, self-harm or suicidal ideation. Adult waiting times run about 11 to 16 months for hormone therapy and four to six years for bottom surgery, and many trans adults in Denmark seek care abroad. Patients report being required to present in ways matching stereotypical gender roles in order to obtain hormone therapy.

The Supreme Court ruled on 10 September 2024 that it is not a violation of human rights for a transgender inmate to serve in a men's prison department. That judgment is the leading Danish authority on the placement of trans people in custody.

Denmark granted asylum to a transgender woman from Guatemala in 2013, the first such grant, after accepting that return would expose her to police attacks and threats over her trans activism. She was initially refused, and the case was reopened once she demonstrated that her life would be in danger on return. She was placed in a facility for men, where she was sexually assaulted several times.

A migrant transgender woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen in July 2024, as recorded in ILGA-Europe's 2025 annual review.

Partner recognition is long established. Registered partnerships were created by a law enacted on 7 June 1989 and in force from 1 October 1989, the world's first such law, with new registrations closed on 15 June 2012. Marriage between people of the same sex has been legal since 15 June 2012, following a government bill introduced on 14 March 2012 that passed by 85 votes to 24 on 7 June and received royal assent five days later; the gender-neutral law covers marriages in the Church of Denmark.

Social climate data is mixed. The Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT+ barometer records that 38% of homosexual and bisexual respondents report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance, and that hate speech targeting sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics recurs annually. Under the UN Committee Against Torture's eighth periodic review, some trans people, QTIBIPOCs and migrants reported denial of access to spaces and services and threats, and anti-trans discourse intensified while Parliament debated lowering the age limit for legal gender recognition; the committee urged access to psychosocial counselling and a remedy for intersex people. Denmark signed a United Nations resolution against intersex discrimination in March, recorded in the 2025 annual review.

sources.title: 2015 Danish court ruling on transgender employment discrimination

NOR.name: Norway
NOR.summary:
Norwegian law contains no offence targeting trans people. Hate speech under Paragraph 135a of the Penal Code has covered sexual orientation since 1981, and the Storting amended the provision in November 2020 so that it also covers bisexual and transgender people; Reuters reported the amendment as extending criminal liability to anti-trans hate speech. Discrimination on grounds of gender identity and gender expression has been prohibited since 2013 under Section 5 of the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination on the grounds of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression, which covers actual, assumed, former and future identity or expression.

The hate-crime framework recorded by OSCE/ODIHR defines hate crimes as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability, and any offence so motivated is recorded under that framework.

Reported hate crimes rose 18 per cent in 2023, with the largest increases in offences motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression and in antisemitism, according to ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025. The national broadcaster NRK reported record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023 while the clearance rate fell from 52 per cent to 45 per cent and more cases were dropped. Many victims report little trust in the police, and a dedicated hate-crime group exists to encourage reporting.

Official figures undercount the scale of offending. A University of Oslo C-REX study drawing on more than 3,000 survey responses from LGBTQI people found that only 8 per cent of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police, citing mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, while many who did report described dismissive treatment.

Documented incidents include the 2022 Oslo Pride mass shooting, for which Zaniar Matapour was sentenced to 30 years, the strictest penalty available; a knife attack on two people that police investigated as a hate crime; and a drag bingo event that drew online threats. Norway's Police Security Service reported a significant decline in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warned that hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride, and that most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than to act.

Legal gender recognition runs on self-declaration with no medical-intervention requirement. Under the Gender Recognition Act, approved on 6 June 2016 and effective from 1 July 2016, a person resident in Norway who experiences belonging to the other gender than that registered in the National Population Register may change legal gender by application to the tax office, with no surgery, hormone or diagnosis requirement. Self-application is available from age 16; ages 6 to 16 require a joint application with holders of parental responsibility; changes below age 6 are restricted to congenital uncertain somatic sex development documented by health personnel. Changed legal gender governs the application of other laws except the establishment of parenthood, and a 2017 regulation covers citizens resident abroad. The official helsenorge.no health-rights page states that legal gender is determined by the individual's own perception of gender identity.

Gender-affirming healthcare is a separate and far narrower channel. Access requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the National Treatment Centre for Gender Incongruence (NTCGI) at Oslo University Hospital, and only about a quarter of referred patients are granted access, with those disqualified having no alternative options. Non-binary patients were still without treatment as of a 2023 report, despite a 2020 guideline calling for equal access, and patients reported negative experiences including not being taken seriously and a lack of practitioner competence in gender and sexuality diversity.

The official 2020 clinical guideline from the Directorate for Health states that gender incongruence is not a mental disorder and that psychiatric or psychological assessment is not a precondition for gender-affirming care, operating on least-invasive-first, informed-consent and multidisciplinary principles. Hormone therapy is initiated mainly in specialist care after GP referral, breast surgery is performed at regional centres and genital surgery through the national treatment service for binary and non-binary patients, with speech therapy reimbursed and hair removal covered by health trusts; for under-18s, care centres on municipal supportive counselling, with puberty-delaying analogues and sex hormones provided only through the national treatment service after paediatric multidisciplinary assessment. Sources therefore conflict on whether a psychiatric diagnosis remains a formal precondition, while the practical access restriction of roughly one in four referrals is reported consistently.

Organised ideological anti-trans hostility exists but is concentrated rather than diffuse. UiO C-REX research finds transphobic hostility in Norway manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists: the Nordic Resistance Movement's 2017 march in Kristiansand advocated crushing the gay lobby, and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as degeneracy. Anti-trans groups including Kvinneaktivistene and a Norwegian branch of Women's Declaration International formed from 2021 onward, promoted in the name of radical feminism; 2,476 feminists signed an open letter in 2020 and 2,611 feminists, including the minister of equality, called in 2023 for a reckoning with transphobia. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre stated that queer people are targets of hate, threats and violence, that incitement of hate is especially virulent against trans people, and that this will not be accepted in Norway.

The general social climate is comparatively liberal. Life in Norway's resource page notes that Norwegians generally hold liberal attitudes toward LGBT people and that Norway was among the first countries with anti-discrimination laws. The Directorate for Children, Youth and Family Affairs found the proportion holding hostile attitudes steadily decreasing, while still recording that in 2017, 11 per cent expressed hostile attitudes towards transgender people against 7.8 per cent towards gay people.

Relationship recognition is in place: same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 January 2009 with the same rights as heterosexual couples including adoption and assisted pregnancies, a registered partnership law was in effect from 1993, and unregistered same-sex cohabitation has been recognised since 1991 with limited rights such as next-of-kin medical decisions. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex is therefore in a legally recognised union.
NOR.outOfScopeNotes:
Sources conflict on whether a psychiatric diagnosis is a formal precondition for gender-affirming care: the official 2020 Directorate for Health guideline states that psychiatric or psychological assessment is not a precondition, while other accounts describe diagnosis and NTCGI referral as required. This is unresolved in the inventory and current practice may differ from the published guideline.

The figure that only about a quarter of referred patients are granted access to NTCGI care is reported without a reference year in the sources available here, and no denominator for total referrals is given.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or border screening of trans visitors, gender markers on foreign passports, airport or detention screening practices, or facilities and bathroom access. Nothing should be inferred either way from their absence.

The magnitude of undercount in official hate-crime statistics cannot be determined: the 8 per cent reporting rate establishes that recorded figures are a floor, but the inventory provides no estimate of the true volume of anti-trans offending.

Reported hate-crime trends are given as percentage changes and raw counts without population context, so year-on-year rises cannot be read as a change in per-capita risk.

For this record: official statistics undercount anti-LGBTQI hate crime by a wide margin.

OSCE/ODIHR frameworks page for Norway: hate crimes are defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability; any offence so motivated is recorded under the framework. For this record: the statutory definition behind Norway's hate-crime counting.

Nordisk Post (Apr 2025): Norway's Police Security Service (PST) reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride — most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act. sources.summary: Same-sex sexual activity between men has been legal since 1972; same-sex acts between women were never penalized. In April 2022 the government formally apologized to victims of the ban on sex between men. Conversion therapy was banned effective 1 January 2024, approved by Parliament 85-15 on 12 December 2023. Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1981 under Paragraph 135a of the Penal Code; in November 2020 the Storting amended the law to also protect bisexual and transgender people. A 2019 Norwegian Institute of Social Research report found 15% of LGBT respondents reported personal threats, mostly online, against 4% of the general population. Access to gender-affirming healthcare in Norway still requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the National Treatment Centre for Gender Incongruence (NTCGI) at Oslo University Hospital; only a quarter of referred patients are allowed access, with those disqualified having no alternative options. Non-binary people were still without treatment as of a 2023 report, despite a 2020 guideline calling for equal access. Minors aged 6-16 may change legal sex with parental consent under the 2016 self-determination law, and 2020 guidelines recommend puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 following interdisciplinary assessment. In 1981 Norway became the first country to enact a law preventing discrimination against LGBT people by amending Paragraph 349a of the Penal Code, prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation in goods/services and public gatherings. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned since 1998. Since 2013 a law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity and expression (Section 5 of the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination on the grounds of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression), and Norway is one of the few countries explicitly protecting intersex people from discrimination. In 2021 anti-transgender groups such as Kvinneaktivistene and a Norwegian branch of Women's Declaration International formed. In 2023, 2611 feminists including Norway's minister of equality called for a reckoning with transphobia. Some tabloid newspapers have been criticized for publishing transphobic content, with journalism expert Jon Martin Larsen criticizing Klassekampen for contributing to 'incitement and hatred against transgender people.' Bufdir found 11% expressed hostile attitudes towards transgender people in 2017, versus 7.8% towards gay people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 January 2009, granting lesbian and gay couples the same rights as heterosexuals including religious weddings, adoption, and assisted pregnancies. A registered partnership law had been in effect since 1993, and unregistered same-sex cohabitation has been recognized since 1991 for limited rights such as next-of-kin medical decisions. In 2024 Norway was ranked the best country for same-sex couples to legally marry. Homosexual boys reported a six times higher occurrence of bullying in schools than heterosexual boys (2013 University of Bergen survey). Queer Youth (Skeiv Ungdom) is among LGBT associations offering helplines and counselling to LGBT youth.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Norway (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2013 Norway has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression, covering actual, assumed, former or future identity or expression, and in November 2020 the Storting amended hate-speech law to protect transgender and bisexual people, building on protection for gay and lesbian people since 1981. Since 1 July 2016 legal change of sex is based on self-determination without psychiatric or psychological evaluation, diagnosis or medical intervention for people aged at least 16, with parental consent required for minors aged 6-16, introduced 18 March 2016, approved 79-13 on 6 June, promulgated 17 June, with 190 applications in the first month. Transgender persons may serve openly in the Armed Forces. Access to gender-affirming healthcare still requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the National Treatment Centre for Gender Incongruence at Oslo University Hospital, with only a quarter of referred patients granted access and no alternative if disqualified, and treatment was not offered to nonbinary patients prior to 2020. In 2020 the Directorate for Health recommended puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 following interdisciplinary assessment as reversible with no reliable evidence of adverse long-term effects, while in 2023 the independent non-governmental Healthcare Investigation Board issued a non-binding finding of insufficient evidence for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormone treatments in young people recommending a cautious approach which the Directorate has not implemented. In February 2023 provider Esben Esther Pirelli Benestad was stripped of medical licence over provision diverging from NTCGI guidelines, with licence conditionally restored in part in April 2023 on appeal. A 2023 report found many patients reported negative experiences including not being taken seriously, non-binary people still without treatment despite the 2020 guideline calling for equal access, and lack of competence on gender and sexuality diversity among practitioners. Conversion therapy prohibition came into effect on 1 January 2024 after parliamentary approval by 85-15 on 12 December 2023. Same-sex sexual activity between men has been legal since 1972, same-sex acts between women were not penalized, the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and the government made formal apologies to victims of the ban in April 2022 on the 50th anniversary. In 1981 Norway amended Penal Code Paragraph 349a to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation in provision of goods or services and access to public gatherings and Paragraph 135a to prohibit hate speech on account of sexual orientation, with employment discrimination banned since 1998. The gender-neutral marriage law granting same rights including adoption and assisted pregnancies was approved 84-41 on 11 June 2008, passed 23-17 in the Lagtinget, granted royal assent and took effect 1 January 2009, replacing the registered partnership law in effect since 1993 and building on unregistered cohabitation recognized since 1991 for limited rights including medical next-of-kin status and wrongful-death compensation. Married and committed same-sex couples are permitted to adopt, with stepchild adoption allowed since 2002 and full adoption since 2009, lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, and a married or stably co-habiting female partner of a woman pregnant through insemination has all parenthood rights and duties from the moment of conception. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people can serve openly in the Armed Forces with full rights and anti-discrimination protections since 1979. The conversion therapy ban approved 85-15 on 12 December 2023 took effect 1 January 2024 after discussion since December 2019, and the Norwegian Psychiatric Association stated in 2000 that homosexuality is no disorder or illness and orientation-change treatment is ethical malpractice. The prior MSM blood-donation ban was replaced with a 12-month deferral implemented 1 June 2017 after June 2016 announcement, with a planned 2024 policy to end discrimination indefinitely postponed, while HIV-prevention drug PrEP has been offered free of charge since the October 2016 announcement. The Directorate for Children, Youth and Family Affairs found the proportion with hostile attitudes steadily decreasing, documenting that "In 2017, 7.8 percent expressed hostile attitudes towards gay people while 11 percent expressed hostile attitudes towards transgender people." A 2013 University of Bergen survey found nine of ten LGBT respondents reported no workplace discrimination or harassment, only a small minority reported physical assault, suicide had significantly decreased since the 1990s, though homosexual boys reported six times higher school bullying than heterosexual boys. The Oslo Police District recorded 238 bias-motivated crimes in Oslo in 2018 of which 20 percent related to LGBT status, and 2019 research found 15 percent of LGBT respondents had been the target of personal threats mostly online compared to four percent among the general population. Since 2021 anti-transgender groups including Kvinneaktivistene and a Norwegian branch of Women's Declaration International formed amid rising transphobia promoted in the name of radical feminism, prompting a 2020 open letter by 2476 feminists for inclusive feminism and a 2023 call by 2611 feminists including the minister of equality for a reckoning with transphobia. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre stated "we know that queer people are the targets of hate, threats and violence. The incitement of hate is especially virulent against trans people. We will not accept this in Norway." In July 2020 the government announced priority for LGBT refugees alongside vulnerable women and children for transfer for permanent resettlement.

sources.title: Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination on the grounds of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression (Lov om forbud mot diskriminering på grunn av seksuell orientering, kjønnsidentitet og kjønnsuttrykk) - 2013
sources.summary: In 2013 Norway prohibited discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression.

sources.title: Solberg Government Legal Gender Change Law - approved 6 June 2016, effective 1 July 2016
sources.summary: Approved 6 June 2016 and effective 1 July 2016, Norway's legal-gender-change law gives persons resident in Norway who experience belonging to the other gender than registered in the National Population Register the right to change legal gender by application to the tax office with no surgery, hormone or diagnosis requirement, with self-application from age 16, joint application with holders of parental responsibility for ages 6-16, restriction of under-6 changes to congenital uncertain somatic sex development documented by health personnel, and provides that changed legal gender governs application of other laws except for establishment of parenthood.

sources.title: Oslo Police District - bias-motivated crimes statistics 2018
sources.summary: In Oslo in 2018, 238 incidents were recorded as hate crime, up 20% from 2017 and up 66% from 2015, with lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans persons comprising 20% of cases as the second-most targeted group after ethnicity at 57%.

sources.title: Norwegian Institute of Social Research - 2019 report on hate speech
sources.summary: In Norway in the year to March 2019, 23% of LGBT people versus 10% of the general population experienced hateful comments, 15% versus 4% experienced threats, mostly repeated, and 16% versus 3% experienced eliminationist statements such as 'you shouldn't have been born' or 'you don't have the right to live,' with the disparity widening further when comments targeting gender identity and gender expression are included, occurring mostly online on Facebook, Instagram and comment sections and disproportionately among young, politically/online-active people and people with two or more minority characteristics, with observing such comments toward one's group alone producing feeling unsafe, while Norwegian criminal code protection against discriminatory/hateful comments in public covered ethnic origin, religion, sexual orientation and functional ability and treated online audiences of 20-30 people as public.

sources.title: Norwegian Directorate for Health - 2020 guideline for gender incongruence
sources.summary: Since 2020 in Norway gender incongruence is not a mental disorder but confers entitlement to municipal and specialist healthcare under least-invasive-first, informed-consent and multidisciplinary assessment principles without psychiatric/psychological assessment as a precondition for gender-affirming care, with adult care requiring persistent incongruence, clarified somatic-psychiatric contraindications, information on irreversible effects and side-effects, fertility preservation and individualized follow-up before hormone therapy initiated mainly in specialist care after GP referral with GP/local hospital follow-up and before breast surgery at regional centres and genital surgery at the national treatment service for binary and non-binary patients with speech therapy reimbursed via Helfo on physician prescription and hair removal covered by health trusts, and with under-18 care centred on municipal supportive counselling and family care with no drug treatment for prepubertal children while puberty-delaying GnRH analogues after puberty onset and estrogen/androgen hormones may be provided only through the national treatment service after paediatric multidisciplinary assessment of maturity, development, psychosocial situation and coexisting conditions.

NOR.localsOnly:
Residents' healthcare pathway is governed by the Directorate for Health's 2020 guideline on gender incongruence, which frames care as an entitlement to municipal and specialist services under least-invasive-first, informed-consent and multidisciplinary assessment principles. Adult care requires persistent incongruence, clarified somatic and psychiatric contraindications, information on irreversible effects and side-effects, fertility preservation and individualised follow-up before hormone therapy, with breast surgery at regional centres and genital surgery at the national treatment service. Under-18 care is centred on municipal supportive counselling and family care, with no drug treatment for prepubertal children; puberty-delaying GnRH analogues after puberty onset and estrogen or androgen hormones may be provided only through the national treatment service after paediatric multidisciplinary assessment of maturity, development, psychosocial situation and coexisting conditions. The 2020 Directorate for Health recommendation of puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 remains in force alongside the 2023 Healthcare Investigation Board's contrary non-binding finding.

Transgender people may serve openly in the Armed Forces, and lesbian, gay and bisexual people have served openly with full rights and anti-discrimination protections since 1979. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned since 1998. The conversion therapy prohibition took effect on 1 January 2024.

The exception in the Gender Recognition Act for establishment of parenthood means a changed legal gender does not govern how parenthood is established under other laws. Rules for children are fixed by the same statute: joint application with holders of parental responsibility from ages 6 to 16, and below age 6 only for congenital uncertain somatic sex development documented by health personnel. A 2017 regulation extends the change-of-gender route to citizens resident abroad.

National support infrastructure includes FRI, Skeiv Ungdom (Queer Youth), the Transgender Association and Oslo Pride, with helplines and counselling for LGBT youth available through Queer Youth. In July 2020 the government announced that LGBT refugees would be given priority alongside vulnerable women and children for transfer to permanent resettlement.
NOR.blindSummary:
The country's law contains no offence targeting trans people. Hate speech under Paragraph 135a of the Penal Code has covered sexual orientation since 1981, and the national parliament amended the provision in November 2020 so that it also covers bisexual and transgender people; a news agency reported the amendment as extending criminal liability to anti-trans hate speech. Discrimination on grounds of gender identity and gender expression has been prohibited since 2013 under Section 5 of the national anti-discrimination act, which covers actual, assumed, former and future identity or expression.

The hate-crime framework recorded by an international hate-crime monitoring body defines hate crimes as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability, and any offence so motivated is recorded under that framework.

Reported hate crimes rose 18 per cent in 2023, with the largest increases in offences motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression and in antisemitism, according to a regional LGBTI rights organisation's annual review. The national broadcaster reported record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023 while the clearance rate fell from 52 per cent to 45 per cent and more cases were dropped. Many victims report little trust in the police, and a dedicated hate-crime group exists to encourage reporting.

Official figures undercount the scale of offending. A university extremism research centre study drawing on more than 3,000 survey responses from LGBTQI people found that only 8 per cent of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police, citing mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, while many who did report described dismissive treatment.

Documented incidents include the 2022 Pride mass shooting in the capital, for which the perpetrator was sentenced to 30 years, the strictest penalty available; a knife attack on two people that police investigated as a hate crime; and a drag bingo event that drew online threats. The national security service reported a significant decline in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warned that hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride, and that most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than to act.

Legal gender recognition runs on self-declaration with no medical-intervention requirement. Under the Gender Recognition Act, approved on 6 June 2016 and effective from 1 July 2016, a person resident in the country who experiences belonging to the other gender than that registered in the National Population Register may change legal gender by application to the tax office, with no surgery, hormone or diagnosis requirement. Self-application is available from age 16; ages 6 to 16 require a joint application with holders of parental responsibility; changes below age 6 are restricted to congenital uncertain somatic sex development documented by health personnel. Changed legal gender governs the application of other laws except the establishment of parenthood, and a 2017 regulation covers citizens resident abroad. The official national health-rights page states that legal gender is determined by the individual's own perception of gender identity.

Gender-affirming healthcare is a separate and far narrower channel. Access requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the national treatment centre for gender incongruence at the national university hospital, and only about a quarter of referred patients are granted access, with those disqualified having no alternative options. Non-binary patients were still without treatment as of a 2023 report, despite a 2020 guideline calling for equal access, and patients reported negative experiences including not being taken seriously and a lack of practitioner competence in gender and sexuality diversity.

The official 2020 clinical guideline from the national health directorate states that gender incongruence is not a mental disorder and that psychiatric or psychological assessment is not a precondition for gender-affirming care, operating on least-invasive-first, informed-consent and multidisciplinary principles. Hormone therapy is initiated mainly in specialist care after GP referral, breast surgery is performed at regional centres and genital surgery through the national treatment service for binary and non-binary patients, with speech therapy reimbursed and hair removal covered by health trusts; for under-18s, care centres on municipal supportive counselling, with puberty-delaying analogues and sex hormones provided only through the national treatment service after paediatric multidisciplinary assessment. Sources therefore conflict on whether a psychiatric diagnosis remains a formal precondition, while the practical access restriction of roughly one in four referrals is reported consistently.

Organised ideological anti-trans hostility exists but is concentrated rather than diffuse. University research finds transphobic hostility in the country manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists: a far-right movement's 2017 march in a southern city advocated crushing the gay lobby, and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as degeneracy. Anti-trans groups including a domestic feminist organisation and a branch of an international anti-trans feminist network formed from 2021 onward, promoted in the name of radical feminism; 2,476 feminists signed an open letter in 2020 and 2,611 feminists, including the equality minister, called in 2023 for a reckoning with transphobia. The prime minister stated that queer people are targets of hate, threats and violence, that incitement of hate is especially virulent against trans people, and that this will not be accepted in the country.

The general social climate is comparatively liberal. A national resource page notes that citizens generally hold liberal attitudes toward LGBT people and that the country was among the first with anti-discrimination laws. The national children and family directorate found the proportion holding hostile attitudes steadily decreasing, while still recording that in 2017, 11 per cent expressed hostile attitudes towards transgender people against 7.8 per cent towards gay people.

Relationship recognition is in place: same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 January 2009 with the same rights as heterosexual couples including adoption and assisted pregnancies, a registered partnership law was in effect from 1993, and unregistered same-sex cohabitation has been recognised since 1991 with limited rights such as next-of-kin medical decisions. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex is therefore in a legally recognised union.
NOR.blindOutOfScope:
Sources conflict on whether a psychiatric diagnosis is a formal precondition for gender-affirming care: the official 2020 national health directorate guideline states that psychiatric or psychological assessment is not a precondition, while other accounts describe diagnosis and referral to the national gender treatment centre as required. This is unresolved in the inventory and current practice may differ from the published guideline.

The figure that only about a quarter of referred patients are granted access to the national gender treatment centre is reported without a reference year in the sources available here, and no denominator for total referrals is given.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or border screening of trans visitors, gender markers on foreign passports, airport or detention screening practices, or facilities and bathroom access. Nothing should be inferred either way from their absence.

The magnitude of undercount in official hate-crime statistics cannot be determined: the 8 per cent reporting rate establishes that recorded figures are a floor, but the inventory provides no estimate of the true volume of anti-trans offending.

Reported hate-crime trends are given as percentage changes and raw counts without population context, so year-on-year rises cannot be read as a change in per-capita risk.

For this record: current threat-level assessment from the security service.

NOR.tangentialFactors:
Survey data place LGBT experiences above the general population baseline. In the year to March 2019, 23 per cent of LGBT people against 10 per cent of the general population reported hateful comments, 15 per cent against 4 per cent reported threats, mostly repeated, and 16 per cent against 3 per cent reported eliminationist statements such as claims that a person should not have been born or has no right to live. The disparity widens further when comments targeting gender identity and gender expression are included, and the incidents occur mostly on Facebook, Instagram and news comment sections, concentrated among young, politically and online-active people and people carrying two or more minority characteristics. Observing such comments directed at one's group alone was associated with feeling unsafe.

City-level police counts give a further comparison point: the Oslo Police District recorded 238 bias-motivated crimes in 2018, up 20 per cent on 2017 and 66 per cent on 2015, with offences against lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans people accounting for 20 per cent of cases, the second-largest category after ethnicity at 57 per cent. These are raw counts from one city in one year and carry no per-capita denominator, so they indicate composition rather than comparative risk. Separate 2019 research found 15 per cent of LGBT respondents had been targets of personal threats, mostly online, against 4 per cent of the general population.

Tabloid and partisan newspapers have been criticised for publishing transphobic content, with journalism expert Jon Martin Larsen criticising Klassekampen for contributing to incitement and hatred against transgender people.

Protection machinery around the visitor-facing framework includes the conversion therapy prohibition approved 85 to 15 on 12 December 2023 and effective 1 January 2024, hate-speech protection on grounds of sexual orientation dating from 1981, the 1981 amendment to Paragraph 349a of the Penal Code making Norway the first country to prohibit discrimination in goods and services and public gatherings, employment discrimination prohibitions from 1998, and Norway's explicit statutory protection of intersex people from discrimination. SWE.name: Sweden
SWE.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Sweden was revised by two acts the Riksdag approved in April 2024, one on legal gender and one on medical procedures performed on genitalia, both in force from 1 July 2025. The Legal Gender Recognition Act simplifies the procedure for changing legal gender but stops short of full self-determination; medical conditions remain part of the process, so a trans visitor updating Swedish documentation may still have to satisfy them.

The April 2024 vote was 234 to 94. From 1 July 2025 the minimum age for legal gender change without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis fell from 18 to 16, on a doctor's or psychologist's statement plus approval from the National Board of Health and Welfare, with guardian consent required for 16 and 17 year olds. Genital surgery is restricted to those 18 and over, and gonad removal to those 23 and over unless an exceptional reason applies.

Changing-room access is not settled. In October 2025 the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their own changing rooms, a restriction that reaches ordinary public facilities rather than any specialised setting.

Transgender identity and expression were added to Swedish hate-crime legislation on 1 July 2018, and to the hate-speech provision with effect from 1 January 2019; sexual orientation had been covered in hate-crime law since 2010 and in hate speech since 1 January 2003. The National Council for Crime Prevention (Brå) published report 2024:13, a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences where police recorded LGBTQI hate-crime motives, which is the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

Application of the hate-speech law has been contested. Authorities declined to prosecute a Halmstad imam who described homosexuality as a virus in 2015, and the Pentecostal preacher Åke Green was convicted and then acquitted through to the Supreme Court, which held that European Convention protections for religious speech barred punishment.

Clinical access has narrowed. In March 2021 the Karolinska Institute stopped providing puberty blockers and gender-affirming hormones to under-16s, and to 16 to 18 year olds outside approved clinical trials. On 22 February 2022 the National Board of Health and Welfare issued guidance that puberty blockers should be used only in exceptional cases and rested on uncertain evidence; this is guidance rather than a statutory ban, and misinformation that Sweden had banned gender-affirming care for minors circulated abroad and was cited by US Republican politicians. Board data released in 2026 showed that prescriptions of puberty blockers to trans children had risen slightly since the 2022 guidance.

A bill before the Riksdag would extend protection to victims of conversion practices carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure.

Trans status was removed from the national illness classification by the National Board of Health and Welfare in January 2017, ending the diagnostic framing of trans identity in Swedish health records.

Until 2013 a legal gender change required sterilisation and sex reassignment surgery. The requirements were ruled unconstitutional in January 2013 and removed by the Riksdag that July; a law passed in March 2018 compensated roughly 600 to 700 people 225,000 SEK each for forced sterilisation.

On partner recognition, the Church Council of the Church of Sweden decided in November 2025, by 141 votes, that newly ordained priests must be willing to marry couples the church classes as same-sex.

Opposition to trans rights is organised. The Sweden Democrats and the Christian Democrats oppose trans legal reform while presenting it as defence of women's rights and Swedish values, and the Swedish Women's Lobby, an umbrella of 57 associations, launched the Women's Platform for Action International in 2025 to promote sex-based rights. Scholars describe the pattern as de-democratisation and record political violence and intimidation against trans advocates, feminist scholars and racialised activists, including online harassment, threats and public vilification.
SWE.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no visa or entry rules for LGBTQ travellers. The nearest material is a 1978 state inquiry into the living conditions of gays and lesbians that suggested granting refugee status to persecuted LGBTQ people, a historical recommendation rather than a statement of current asylum practice.

Country coverage dates the declassification of transgender status inconsistently, to 2017 in one place and 2009 in another; the 2017 date is the one corroborated by the reporting on the National Board of Health and Welfare decision.

No disaggregated data on hate-crime prosecutions or convictions, and no trans-specific violence rate with a usable denominator, appears in the inventory.

sources.summary: A Library of Congress entry dated April 2024 records Sweden's parliament approving new acts on legal gender and on medical procedures performed on genitalia.

TGEU report of 16 July 2025: Sweden's new Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025, simplifying the procedure but falling short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining.
SVT reported in October 2025 that the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their changing rooms, an everyday facility-access restriction affecting trans visitors.

Brå (National Council for Crime Prevention) report 2024:13: supplements Swedish hate-crime statistics with a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences where police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives - the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025): a bill would extend protection of victims of conversion practices when carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure. In November the Church of Sweden decided new priests must be willing to marry same-sex couples, passing 141 votes at the 2025 Church Council.

Open-access article in Sexuality Research and Social Policy (4 February 2016, vol 13, pp 119-129): traces LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014 - the historical record behind current service conditions.

2019 edition of the Spartacus Gay Travel Index reported by Newsweek: Canada, Portugal and Sweden tied as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations - third-party evidence on Sweden's standing as a visitor destination.

TT/The Local, 28 January 2017: Sweden's main national board decided transgender people will no longer be classified as 'mentally ill', the depathologisation step for trans residents' diagnostic status.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity was legalized in Sweden in 1944 (age of consent 18); an equal age of consent of 15 was set in 1972. Homosexuality was declassified as an illness in October 1979; the coverage dates declassification of transgender status inconsistently, to 2017 in one place and 2009 in another. A 1987 law banning sex in gay saunas and prostitution, passed to combat HIV, was repealed in 2004. Until 2013, legal gender change required sterilization and sex reassignment surgery; these requirements were ruled unconstitutional in January 2013 and removed by the Riksdag in July 2013, with roughly 600–700 people later compensated 225,000 SEK each (law passed March 2018) for forced sterilization. Sweden's hate speech law covers sexual orientation (added by Riksdag vote in 2002, effective 1 January 2003) and 'transgender identity and expression' (effective 1 January 2019); transgender identity and expression were added to hate crime legislation on 1 July 2018, with sexual orientation added in 2010. The law has been criticised as 'selectively applied': authorities refused to prosecute a Halmstad imam who called homosexuality a 'virus' in 2015, and Pentecostal preacher Åke Green was convicted then acquitted through to the Supreme Court, which held European Convention religious-speech protections barred punishment. Anti-gender actors also target expression through knowledge production, labelling gender studies and intersectional feminist scholarship 'ideological or unscientific'. The source contains no visa or entry rules for LGBTQ travellers; the nearest material is that a 1978 state inquiry into the living conditions of gays and lesbians suggested granting refugee status to persecuted LGBTQ people, and that RFSL counselling centres in Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö assist people with contact to authorities and 'legal assistance with, for example, asylum and wills'. A 2021 study found migrant LGBTQ people have worse sexual health, avoid healthcare more, are more exposed to sexual violence and are more dissatisfied with their sexual life than other groups. Sweden has seen a rise in domestic anti-gender campaigns tied to a transnational movement opposing gender equality and transgender rights, mobilising around the pejorative concept of 'gender ideology'. Actors include the far-right Sweden Democrats and Christian Democrats, who oppose trans-rights legal reforms while framing opposition as protecting women's rights and Swedish values, and 'gender-critical' radical feminist groups — notably the Swedish Women's Lobby (SWL, founded 1997, umbrella for 57 associations representing over 130,000 women and girls), which in 2025 launched the Women's Platform for Action International (WoPAI) promoting 'sex-based rights'. Scholars document 'insidious de-democratization' and report growing political violence and intimidation against trans advocates, feminist scholars and racialized activists, including online harassment, threats and public vilification. Separately, misinformation that Sweden had banned gender-affirming care for minors spread on social media and was cited by US Republican politicians to justify outright bans. In March 2021 the Karolinska Institute stopped providing puberty blockers or gender-affirming hormone therapy to children and teens under 16, and to 16–18-year-olds outside approved clinical trials; on 22 February 2022 the National Board of Health and Welfare said puberty blockers should be used only in 'exceptional cases' backed by 'uncertain science' (guidance, not a ban). In 2021 the Board cut gender-affirming clinics from seven to three (those three yet to be chosen). In April 2024 the Riksdag approved new laws (234 for, 94 against) effective 1 July 2025 lowering the minimum age for legal gender change without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis from 18 to 16, requiring a doctor/psychologist statement plus National Board approval, and guardian approval for 16–17-year-olds; genital surgery is limited to 18+ and gonad removal to 23+ absent exceptional reason. Nationwide Board data released in 2026 showed trans children prescribed puberty blockers had slightly increased since the 2022 guidance. Anti-gender efforts also target gender studies and feminist scholarship in education, and Sweden's age of consent has been equal at 15 since 1972.

The April 2024 vote was 234 to 94. From 1 July 2025 the minimum age for legal gender change without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis fell from 18 to 16, on a doctor's or psychologist's statement plus approval from the national health authority, with guardian consent required for 16 and 17 year olds. Changing-room access is not settled. In October 2025 a national swimming-pool chain stopped trans customers from choosing their own changing rooms, a restriction that reaches ordinary public facilities rather than any specialised setting.

Transgender identity and expression were added to national hate-crime legislation on 1 July 2018, and to the hate-speech provision with effect from 1 January 2019; sexual orientation had been covered in hate-crime law since 2010 and in hate speech since 1 January 2003. A bill before the national parliament would extend protection to victims of conversion practices carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure.

FIN.name: Finland
FIN.summary:
Finland does not criminalise trans people. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1971, the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1999, homosexuality was declassified as an illness in 1981 and transvestism in 2011. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation became a criminal offence in 1995 and on grounds of gender identity in 2005. Section 8(1) of the Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and other personal characteristics, whether based on fact or assumption; the Act on Equality between Women and Men covers sex and gender identity, and a 2014 amendment extended its protections to employment, goods and services, education and health services.

Legal gender recognition was reformed in 2023: the age limit is 18, down from a proposed 15 with guardian permission, with a 30-day reflection period and a limit of one change per year. Until April 2023 applicants had to be sterilised or otherwise infertile and to hold a mental disorder diagnosis; those requirements are no longer in force.

Police recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences, the highest total ever logged, with defamation and assault the most common types. The Police University College reports the sexual-orientation and gender-identity-or-expression category rising across six reported years, from 72 cases to 241. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 gives the same headline total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes, a 13% increase since 2023, and identifies sexual orientation and gender identity as recurrent motives, present in 12% of cases. The Criminal Code contains no hate-crime category, so motive is recorded only in police reports; SOGI-motivated incidents are counted as reported suspicion rather than as charges.

Finland's first conversion-practices case was prosecuted as assault, with convictions in March. Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices by 125 votes to 49 in March; a full statutory ban remained pending.

Marriage equality took effect on 1 March 2017, together with joint adoption. Registered partnerships had been available from 2002 until that date, carrying the rights of married couples except adoption and joint surname, and giving immigration rights to a foreign partner. Stepchild adoption became legal in 2009. A 2018 change to the Maternity Act recognised both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of birth, fixing second-parent registration at birth rather than through adoption. An April 2019 law, passed 122 to 42, gave lesbian couples full maternity pay and parentage rights without intra-family adoption. Surrogacy remains illegal for all couples.

Gender-affirming care for minors is delivered through the country's two centralised gender identity units. A Seta survey found over 40% of trans respondents entirely unable to access the care they needed, most reporting extended waiting times. In 2020 the Council for Choices in Health Care revised clinical recommendations for gender dysphoria under age 25, prioritising psychosocial therapy over medical transition and restricting puberty blockers and hormone treatment; the recommendations are not mandates, so puberty blockers remain available case by case and cross-sex hormones can be considered where the identity is of a permanent nature causing severe dysphoria.

Finnish police reported 73 violent attacks and assaults against LGBT people in 2018, a 27% increase on 2017 and the only hate-motive category to rise that year. In November 2019 the Institute of Health and Welfare reported that LGBT children and youth face significantly more bullying, and more physical, psychological and sexual violence, than heterosexual peers, and are more likely to suffer violence at home.
FIN.outOfScopeNotes:
The two sources reporting the 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences differ on the year: the Police University College attributes the figure to 2024, while ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 attributes it to 2025. The discrepancy is unresolved in the material reviewed.

The 1,808 figure is a raw count without a population denominator, and the Criminal Code has no hate-crime category, so the total reflects reported suspicion rather than prosecutions or convictions. The 73 attacks recorded in 2018 are likewise a raw count.

Whether the conversion-practices ban endorsed by Parliament in March has since been enacted is not established by the sources reviewed.

TWN.name: Taiwan
TWN.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Taiwan remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national ID. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining a document that matches their presentation, which turns every ID-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, into a potential site of distress and discrimination. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands.

In August 2024 a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change her ID marker without surgery or a psychological evaluation; the rights group supporting her indicated an appeal was likely. No tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction access occurred during 2025.

Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and gender characteristics in education under the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, with a NT$100,000 fine for schools that discriminate in admission, instruction or assessment; sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties were added in June 2011. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since the 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000. The Long-Term Care Services Act of January 2017 carries an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 of 24 May 2017 held that the Constitution's Article 7 discrimination grounds are illustrative rather than exhaustive, extending the right to equality to sexual orientation.

Public facilities are a documented pressure point. The Ministry of Environment is spending NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms from 623 to 1,246 by 2029, and an LGBTQ+ rights group found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage. Among trans and gender-nonconforming survey respondents who reported discrimination, 17% of the incidents occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.

For a trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship, partner recognition is partial. Same-sex couples can legally adopt: since May 2023 legislation has granted full adoption rights, replacing the stepchild-only rights in place since 2019, and a January 2022 court order had already allowed one couple to adopt before the legislature codified full rights. Single individuals, including individual LGBT people, may adopt depending on circumstances. The Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, excluding both single women and couples the law reads as same-sex.

Conversion therapy is effectively banned under a Ministry of Health and Welfare letter of 22 February 2018, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.

Political hostility to trans rights has grown. Organisations in the anti-gender movement have aligned with anti-trans policies promoted abroad, and the Taiwan Solidarity Party has called for a 'two genders' position. The seventh annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people in November 2025 despite rain, with international participants, and called for an end to discrimination against trans people.
