sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Historically, a 1740 Qing decree criminalised voluntary homosexual intercourse between adults (punishable by a month in prison and 100 heavy blows), while the Republic of China's provisional criminal code abolished explicit prohibitions on 'consenting ji jian' around 1912 and sodomy was decriminalised when the ROC took over Taiwan after World War II under the 1935 criminal code. During martial law, LGBT people were harassed and detained under general public order laws (Temporary Provisions against the Communist Rebellion), repealed in 1991. Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression is open and expanding: the first Taiwan Pride was held in Taipei on 1 November 2003 with over 1,000 attendees, growing to about 80,000 by 2015, 137,000 in 2018 and 170,000 by 2019, with pride events also held in Kaohsiung (since 2010) and Taichung (20,000 in 2016). LGBTQ representation in literature and film — from Pai Hsien-yung's novel Crystal Boys in the 1970s to Ang Lee's Brokeback Mountain (2005) and Zero Chou's Spider Lilies (2007 Berlin Teddy Award winner) — is described as instrumental in raising public awareness. In 2022 Taiwan withdrew from hosting WorldPride 2025 over the disputed name 'WorldPride Kaohsiung,' which the public and government considered offensive, and the event moved to Washington, D.C. in June 2025. Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex couples can legally adopt, and since May 2023 legislation has granted full adoption rights, replacing the partial (stepchild-only) adoption rights in place since 2019. Until 2023 they could only adopt the biological child of their partner; a January 2022 court order had already allowed a same-sex couple to adopt before the legislature codified full rights. Taiwan law also permits single individuals, including individual LGBT people, to adopt depending on circumstances, while the Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, specifically excluding same-sex female couples and single women. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004 (fine of NT$100,000 for schools discriminating in admission, instruction or assessment). Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000. The Long-Term Care Services Act (January 2017) contains an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 (24 May 2017) held that the Constitution's Article 7 grounds of discrimination are 'illustrative, rather than exhaustive,' so sexual orientation is protected by the right to equality. Wikipedia country coverage: Discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in education has been banned since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, with sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties added in June 2011. In November 2018 voters passed a referendum question to ban LGBT-inclusive sex education in schools (Question 11) and rejected the pro-inclusion Question 15; Education Minister Yeh Jiunn-rong said LGBT content would be reviewed against the result, and an earlier Ministry of Education curriculum reform (announced March 2010, effective 2011) had already been watered down to 'respecting diverse sexual orientations' after anti-LGBT opposition. Following that referendum, suicide hotlines reported a 40% surge in calls from LGBT individuals, particularly adolescents and young adults. Youth-relevant health measures include the 22 February 2018 Ministry of Health and Welfare letter effectively banning conversion therapy, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.

TWN.blindSummary:
Legal gender recognition in the country remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national identity document. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining a document that matches their presentation, which turns every document-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, into a potential site of distress and discrimination. The national health ministry has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands.

In August 2024 a court in the capital denied a transgender woman's request to change her identity-document marker without surgery or a psychological evaluation; the rights group supporting her indicated an appeal was likely. No tangible policy change on abolishing the surgery requirement or expanding assisted reproduction access occurred during 2025.

Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and gender characteristics in education under the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, with a fine of 100,000 in the national currency for schools that discriminate in admission, instruction or assessment; sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties were added in June 2011. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since the 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of 300,000 to 1,500,000 in the national currency. The Long-Term Care Services Act of January 2017 carries an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and a constitutional-court interpretation of 24 May 2017 held that the constitution's equality grounds are illustrative rather than exhaustive, extending the right to equality to sexual orientation.

Public facilities are a documented pressure point. The national environment ministry is spending 280 million in the national currency over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms from 623 to 1,246 by 2029, and an LGBTQ+ rights group found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage. Among trans and gender-nonconforming survey respondents who reported discrimination, 17% of the incidents occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms.

For a trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship, partner recognition is partial. Same-sex couples can legally adopt: since May 2023 legislation has granted full adoption rights, replacing the stepchild-only rights in place since 2019, and a January 2022 court order had already allowed one couple to adopt before the legislature codified full rights. Single individuals, including individual LGBT people, may adopt depending on circumstances. The Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, excluding both single women and couples the law reads as same-sex.

Conversion therapy is effectively banned under a national health ministry letter of 22 February 2018, with violators liable under the criminal code or the child welfare and rights legislation.

Political hostility to trans rights has grown. Organisations in the anti-gender movement have aligned with anti-trans policies promoted by a foreign government, and a political party has called for a 'two genders' position. The seventh annual transgender march in the capital drew an estimated 3,000 people in November 2025 despite rain, with international participants, and called for an end to discrimination against trans people.

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is lawful in South Korea; the criminalising statute reaches only military personnel. Military Criminal Act article 92-6 penalises consensual same-sex conduct among service members with up to two years' imprisonment, and the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Transgender people are excluded from military service. Prosecutions have followed: in 2017 the military criminally charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and one soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex.

The most fully documented case of state harm to a transgender person is that of Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as having occurred in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available but has been conditioned by judicial guidelines the courts have since narrowed. A 2011 Supreme Court ruling required applicants to be over 20, single and without children. On 24 November 2022 an en banc panel of the Supreme Court held that transgender people with minor children may have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an eleven-year-old precedent that had uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors. On 8 May 2024 the Yeongdong district court declined to require sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissal of such applications; the five plaintiffs had been assigned male at birth and had been on hormone therapy for years.

South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTI organisations can register, though registration has been contested: an NGO won before the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017, the government appealed to the Seoul High Court and the Supreme Court, and Human Rights Watch described the litigation as years of bureaucratic obstruction. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records an overall relatively positive environment with free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.

Health care is a documented gap. The National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation, and the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, stating that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult. A peer-reviewed nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, published in Epidemiology and Health on 27 June 2025, documented a pervasive discrimination burden across school, work and transition-related care.

Police conduct toward a transgender person has been found unlawful. The Seoul Central District Court held, in a decision final on 2 July 2024 with no appeal, that police advice to a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed her personal rights, and awarded 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

Public LGBT events have drawn organised, sometimes violent opposition. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protesters attacked participants; organisers filed charges against pastors and accused police of failing to act. At Busan's 2018 Pride, some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters.

Partner recognition is limited. National law recognises neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. The Constitutional Court ruled in 2024 on same-sex partners' healthcare rights, a decision travel material treats as a landmark. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship cannot rely on marriage or civil union for partner recognition.

Outing through state data practices is documented. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing exposed LGBTQ people's identities, and doxing and online harassment increased.
KOR.outOfScopeNotes:
The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor entry on a Supreme Court decision allowing a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register could not be retrieved (HTTP 403). Its detail is unverified here.

No source in the inventory describes how transgender prisoners are housed in the civilian prison system. No birth-sex versus identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary-confinement or segregation practice is documented.

The sources do not state whether the 8 May 2024 ruling against requiring surgery for legal sex change applies beyond the case before that court.

IND.name: India
IND.summary:
Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route. Legal recognition now covers historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, together with intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition pathway. The government presents the change as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Human Rights Watch and activists including Akkai Padmashali describe it as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, and the BBC reports critics saying it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. The 2011 census recorded roughly 480,000 people identifying as transgender; independent estimates put the population at about two million.

Identity documents are a live friction point. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person whom passport authorities had required to undergo a medical examination. In November 2024 airport security personnel stopped an openly transgender law student at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 even though she presented her PAN card. A trans woman in Kolkata alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at a station under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam described degrading treatment in custody. The UK government's December 2025 policy note assesses reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited, more likely in conservative rural areas, and not systemic.

The constitutional baseline offers protection. The Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that reasoning in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018. India has no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, and courts have recognised same-sex couples as family units, which leaves a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status without a route to local marital recognition. In June 2021 the Madras High Court, in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, issued guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ people from police harassment, ordered police sensitisation, banned conversion therapy, and directed the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

The replacement of the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans people from sexual violence. Trans people report fearing a rise in assaults as a result, which bears directly on how a complaint of sexual violence would be framed and received.

Transition-related healthcare sits in a mixed framework. The Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for members of the transgender community. Conversion therapy is banned under the 2021 Madras High Court ruling and a 2022 National Medical Commission measure, though clandestine networks continue to operate nationwide. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance confirmed that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.
IND.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document how the 2026 recognition categories are being applied in practice at state welfare boards, or whether documents issued to people recognised under the 2019 law remain valid after the amendment.

It is unresolved whether passport or airport identity procedures will change in response to the February 2026 Allahabad High Court case, and how frequently passport authorities demand medical examination of trans applicants.

Trans-specific violence data disaggregated from general crime statistics are not sourced, and no figure is available on prosecutions under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita where a trans complainant is involved.

sources.summary:
Constitutional protection covers expression: the Supreme Court has ruled that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls under Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by "sex," and the Allahabad High Court extended this in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. The University Grants Commission prohibits bullying and ragging aimed at students based on sexual orientation or gender identity in higher education. Conservative groups such as the Vishva Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal have labelled same-sex marriage a "Western attack on Indian culture" and have occasionally targeted Pride events.

Facilities for trans people are largely state-level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards that coordinate housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pension schemes, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Federally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors face coercive surgery: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male via non-consensual operations, prompting the Madras High Court in April 2019 to order Tamil Nadu to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants. Acceptance is notably higher among urban youth and students at top-tier universities such as the IITs, which host support groups like Indradhanu (IIT Delhi) and Saathi (IIT Bombay). Colleges such as the American College in Madurai teach specialised curricula on genderqueer and intersex human rights using works by transgender activists A. Revathi and Kalki Subramaniam. Bans on conversion therapy (Madras High Court 2021, National Medical Commission 2022) coexist with clandestine networks still operating nationwide.

Public opinion is mixed and shifting: a 2025 Pew Research Center survey found 59% of respondents still call homosexuality "morally unacceptable," a 2023 Gallup poll showed 53% support same-sex marriage, and a 2021 Ipsos survey of urban internet users found 17% identifying as non-heterosexual or non-cisgender. Demographic studies report a high prevalence of verbal abuse and physical violence against sexual minorities, and the 2011 census recorded roughly 480,000 people identifying as transgender. Organisations like GayBombay, Good as You (Bangalore) and Sappho for Equality (Kolkata) operate alongside Pride events held annually in dozens of cities since the first parade in Kolkata in 1999. Political visibility includes Shabnam Mausi (first transgender elected official, 1998), transgender mayors and judges, and Menaka Guruswamy, who in March 2026 became India's first openly LGBTQ+ member of the national Parliament.

CHN.name: China
CHN.summary:
Chinese law contains no explicit anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and hate crime provisions cover neither. LGBTI organisations cannot register, and legal gender recognition is unavailable. A trans visitor arrives in a jurisdiction where the state offers no protective machinery of any kind and where the space for gender-nonconforming expression has contracted markedly since the mid-2010s.

The most direct visitor-facing evidence concerns the border. In May 2025 the Thai trans YouTuber Nisamanee 'Nut' Lertvorapong alleged that Chinese immigration officials laughed at, mocked and questioned her during a family trip, posting video to Instagram with the statement that no one should be treated differently on the basis of gender. A visibly trans traveller should anticipate intrusive, derisive handling by immigration officers, with no recourse mechanism.

Remedy through the courts does exist, narrowly. In November 2024 the performance artist Ling'er, 28, won a record monetary payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment, the first time a trans person had successfully challenged such treatment in China; she said she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights. The New York Times investigation of December 2024 documents that such conversion practices remain in routine use across the country, and psychiatric facilities and psychiatry textbooks continue to treat homosexuality as a mental disorder and to offer conversion therapy, because the 2001 declassification by the Chinese Society of Psychiatry was never reflected in National Health and Family Planning Commission regulations.

Gender-affirming care is heavily gated. Even adults must obtain parental consent to undergo gender-affirming surgery and to change their legal gender, and must produce proof of parental death where a parent has died, so disputes are pushed inside families. The minimum age for sex reassignment surgery was lowered to 18 from 20. In December 2022 Chinese authorities banned the online sale of estradiol and androgen blockers even with valid prescriptions, forcing in-person purchase. As of 2025 seven medical centers treat transgender youth, three of which offer puberty suppression, the first such clinic opening in 2021 at the Children's Hospital of Fudan University in Shanghai; a 2022 Chinese expert consensus recommends puberty blockers for transgender youth.

Public expression is censored and venues are closing. Around Pride month in 2026 platforms scrubbed prominent LGBT social media accounts, foreign films and events with LGBT themes, which Human Rights Watch read as illustrating a deteriorating rights situation and deepening repression of expression and association. Radio Free Asia reported in January 2024 that the crackdown against 'foreign ideologies' has made LGBTQ+ activism all but extinct on the mainland, that displaying rainbow flags or accessories is no longer permitted even inside venues, and that in August 2023 officials removed an LGBTQ+ anthem titled 'Rainbow'. The broadcast regulator's 2016 guidelines banning depictions of 'abnormal sexual behaviour' remain the censorship baseline and now extend to social platforms. Cancellation of nationwide shows by the famous transgender dancer Jin Xing in early 2025 led some in China to fear a wider LGBTQ+ crackdown, and a Zurich drag artist on tour in China in August 2026 found the space for queer subcultures shrinking first-hand.

Relationship recognition is effectively absent. The Marriage Law of the PRC, adopted 10 September 1980, defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, so same-sex couples cannot marry; same-sex couples cannot adopt, and households headed by them are ineligible for the legal protections available to heterosexual couples. The one entry-related concession is that Beijing provides dependent residency status to the same-sex partners of legal residents such as expats. Since the October 2017 National People's Congress amendment allowing adults to appoint guardians by mutual agreement, some same-sex couples have used that route for limited protections, but face refusal or discriminatory conditions: one Hunan notary office held a six-hour meeting on whether approval would disrupt public order or morality, a Guangzhou office demanded a 100,000 yuan deposit not required of heterosexual applicants, and a 2021 China Notary Association report says some notary employees were disciplined for providing voluntary guardianship services to same-sex couples. On 12 April 2021 the Shenyang Intermediate People's Court ruled that a 79-year-old woman could not sue her female partner of 50 years over 294,000 yuan because their relationship is not recognised as a marriage.

Violence with an official response is documented but rare: days before the International Day Against Homophobia in 2018, two women wearing rainbow badges were attacked and beaten by security guards in Beijing, and the security company dismissed the three guards involved shortly thereafter. Chinese institutions are hostile on their own terms: a Peking University survey found trans female students face strong discrimination across sex-segregated enrolment, uniforms, bathrooms, dormitories, physical education examinations and conscription, all tied to legal gender marker.
CHN.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no visa, entry or border provision specific to LGBTQ travellers beyond the dependent residency status Beijing extends to same-sex partners of legal residents; entry requirements for trans visitors, including document-marker rules and screening practice, are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

No trans-specific killing or violence figure for China is carried in these sources, and no comparison against the country's general homicide rate is available, so no magnitude of trans-directed violence can be stated. The 2018 Beijing badge attack is documented with an outcome but is a single incident rather than a patterned rate.

Sub-national detail is thin: the Shanxi Province rule on minors applying for gender-marker change is one data point and does not indicate how other provinces handle the same procedure. Wikipedia-derived material in this inventory is country-level coverage of variable sourcing depth and has not been independently verified against primary statutes.

In May 2025 a trans content creator from another jurisdiction in the region alleged that immigration officials laughed at, mocked and questioned her during a family trip, posting video to Instagram with the statement that no one should be treated differently on the basis of gender. A visibly trans traveller should anticipate intrusive, derisive handling by immigration officers, with no recourse mechanism.

Remedy through the courts does exist, narrowly. In November 2024 a performance artist, 28, won a record monetary payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment, the first time a trans person had successfully challenged such treatment in the country; she said she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights. A national newspaper investigation of December 2024 documents that such conversion practices remain in routine use across the country, and psychiatric facilities and psychiatry textbooks continue to treat homosexuality as a mental disorder and to offer conversion therapy, because the 2001 declassification by the national psychiatric society was never reflected in national health commission regulations.

Gender-affirming care is heavily gated. Even adults must obtain parental consent to undergo gender-affirming surgery and to change their legal gender, and must produce proof of parental death where a parent has died, so disputes are pushed inside families. The minimum age for sex reassignment surgery was lowered to 18 from 20. In December 2022 the authorities banned the online sale of estradiol and androgen blockers even with valid prescriptions, forcing in-person purchase. As of 2025 seven medical centers treat transgender youth, three of which offer puberty suppression, the first such clinic opening in 2021 at a children's hospital in a major city; a 2022 national expert consensus recommends puberty blockers for transgender youth.

Public expression is censored and venues are closing. Around Pride month in 2026 platforms scrubbed prominent LGBT social media accounts, foreign films and events with LGBT themes, which an international human rights organisation read as illustrating a deteriorating rights situation and deepening repression of expression and association. A external broadcaster reported in January 2024 that the crackdown against 'foreign ideologies' has made LGBTQ+ activism all but extinct in the country, that displaying rainbow flags or accessories is no longer permitted even inside venues, and that in August 2023 officials removed an LGBTQ+ anthem titled 'Rainbow'. The broadcast regulator's 2016 guidelines banning depictions of 'abnormal sexual behaviour' remain the censorship baseline and now extend to social platforms. Cancellation of nationwide shows by the country's most famous transgender dancer in early 2025 led some to fear a wider LGBTQ+ crackdown, and a foreign drag artist on tour in August 2026 found the space for queer subcultures shrinking first-hand.

Relationship recognition is effectively absent. The national marriage statute, adopted 10 September 1980, defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, so same-sex couples cannot marry; same-sex couples cannot adopt, and households headed by them are ineligible for the legal protections available to heterosexual couples. The one entry-related concession is that the country provides dependent residency status to the same-sex partners of legal residents such as expatriates. Since the October 2017 parliamentary amendment allowing adults to appoint guardians by mutual agreement, some same-sex couples have used that route for limited protections, but face refusal or discriminatory conditions: one notary office held a six-hour meeting on whether approval would disrupt public order or morality, another demanded a 100,000 yuan deposit not required of heterosexual applicants, and a 2021 national notary association report says some notary employees were disciplined for providing voluntary guardianship services to same-sex couples. On 12 April 2021 an intermediate people's court ruled that a 79-year-old woman could not sue her female partner of 50 years over 294,000 yuan because their relationship is not recognised as a marriage.

Violence with an official response is documented but rare: days before the International Day Against Homophobia in 2018, two women wearing rainbow badges were attacked and beaten by security guards in the capital, and the security company dismissed the three guards involved shortly thereafter. Institutions are hostile on their own terms: a university survey found trans female students face strong discrimination across sex-segregated enrolment, uniforms, bathrooms, dormitories, physical education examinations and conscription, all tied to legal gender marker.

No trans-specific killing or violence figure for the country is carried in these sources, and no comparison against the general homicide rate is available, so no magnitude of trans-directed violence can be stated. The 2018 capital badge attack is documented with an outcome but is a single incident rather than a patterned rate.

Sub-national detail is thin: the one province's rule on minors applying for gender-marker change is a single data point and does not indicate how other provinces handle the same procedure. Open-encyclopedia material in this inventory is country-level coverage of variable sourcing depth and has not been independently verified against primary statutes.

CHN.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents live under a discriminatory institutional regime that a short-stay visitor will only glimpse. A university survey found trans female students face strong discrimination across sex-segregated enrolment, uniforms, bathrooms, dormitories, physical education examinations and conscription, all tied to legal gender marker. One province has allowed minors to apply for gender-marker change since 2014 with a guardian's ID, the only sub-national flexibility noted.

Outness carries measurable cost. A 2016 regional development survey found less than five percent of LGBT people are fully out at school, work or in their religious community, and about fifteen percent are out to their families. Guardianship by mutual agreement, introduced by the October 2017 parliamentary amendment, remains unevenly available to same-sex couples and is policed by notaries, with disciplinary action reported against notary staff who provided it voluntarily. CHN.tangentialFactors:

Human Rights Watch read the June 2026 censorship wave as evidence of deepening repression of expression and association for LGBT people, and the Foreign Policy account of January 2025 describes gender transition being treated as 'a family affair', with families forced to resolve disagreements internally.

Public opinion and official positions diverge. MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at both federal and state level. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, for any person regardless of gender, consent or whether the act is private; the maximum penalty is 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, and Human Rights Watch records the whipping as mandatory. The offence reaches foreign nationals and tourists, and sodomy was first criminalised in 1871. Section 377D adds "gross indecency", an undefined offence carrying up to two years that remains a discretionary prosecutorial tool.

Every state and the federal territories maintain Sharia enactments criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, including provisions against "a man posing as a woman". These offences apply only to Muslims, so a Muslim trans visitor carries exposure that a non-Muslim visitor does not; the penalties reach three years' imprisonment, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of the cane. The enactments include the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019, which covers sodomy and sexual intercourse against the order of nature. Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed such enactments; all 13 bar Muslim men from dressing as women, three also bar women posing as men, and none supplies a legal definition of transgender dress. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments.

Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but that pattern is prosecutorial discretion rather than legal protection, and it has been withdrawn under political pressure. Raids on queer venues are documented and current: on 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022, with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet releases were delayed, with over 130 men still held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Police raided a second sauna in Penang days later. Earlier actions include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar raided by police and religious enforcement in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants raided in 2022, and 11 shopping malls raided in May 2023 over pride-themed watches.

Trans people face documented state-sanctioned targeting. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists condemned and demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her over "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and obtained UNHCR protection. Violence accompanies this: a transgender woman was killed in Klang in 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months, in a record that also documents police mistreatment and impunity. Sixteen trans women were mass-arrested at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Identity documents are a live exposure point. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card with his gender identity and chosen name, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity as a male, but that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented gender-marker change is historical: in 1975 the National Registration Department recognised a trans woman as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti allowed her to marry under sharia law. A 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and remains so after sex reassignment surgery; it was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery and shapes administrative practice.

The sources contain no explicit visa or entry rule for transgender visitors. The only stated entry policy is a 2001 remark by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay and warning gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners.

Detention carries prescribed custodial and "rehabilitation" facilities. Sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months under Federal Territories s.56, Kedah s.52, Selangor s.54 and Sarawak s.53, and may order cross-dressing or other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months under Kelantan s.19-20 and Pahang s.66, extended to one year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment. Prison terms for Sharia offences run from four months to three years and are served in male wards where sexual violence is documented. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021.

Access to care is restricted. Conversion therapy is practised regularly and openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders, the 1982 fatwa bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex, transgender people face discriminatory denial of health care and employment, and the National Blood Centre of Malaysia prohibits homosexuals and bisexuals from donating blood.

There are no Malaysian laws protecting the LGBTQ community against discrimination and hate crimes, and no route to recognition for same-sex couples. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. Hate speech rules do cover orientation through the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, s.6.1(ii), enforced via s.211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act, while in 1994 the government banned anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual from state-controlled media and LGBT events and media content continue to be censored.
MYS.outOfScopeNotes:
No background or general homicide rate is sourced for Malaysia, so the 2019 killings of trans women cannot be placed against a population-level comparison; the sources document the incidents, police mistreatment and impunity without a denominator.

No explicit visa or entry rule specific to transgender visitors appears in the sources. The 2001 statement about deporting gay foreign ministers is the only entry policy recorded, and its current status is not sourced.

The status of the Home Minister's 2 December 2025 suggestion that the section 377 provisions be revisited is unresolved in the sources, as is whether the 208 charges from the Chow Kit raid proceeded after the magistrate's refusal of the remand extension.

The 1982 fatwa was never gazetted, so its formal legal weight remains unresolved even though it ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery and is applied by administrators.

The joint United Nations Development Programme and Asia Pacific Transgender Network publication on Malaysia is listed without its findings, so no claim is drawn from it.

No youth-specific health-care or medication-carrying finding appears in the sources.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile — Malaysia: federal Penal Code section 377 criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping). Sharia enactments across the states prohibit 'cross-dressing' or 'males posing as females', including the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 covering 'sodomy' and 'sexual intercourse against the order of nature'. The profile places Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise, and lists active litigation alongside cases from Mauritius and Namibia.

Human Rights Watch report (10 August 2022) 'I Don't Want to Change Myself', based on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 across seven states plus journalists and lawyers: every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia codes criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity ('a man posing as a woman'), while the federal penal code punishes oral/anal sex with up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping. Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events/media content were censored. The 2021 Nur Sajat case shows enforcement reach — 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt her over 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection.

Human Rights Watch (25 June 2019): a transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb — the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months — with the piece documenting violence against trans people alongside police mistreatment and impunity ('The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself').
Reuters (August 2023): LGBT people in Malaysia face growing fears as Islamist opposition forecloses reform.

The Diplomat (10 December 2025): on 28 November police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B — the largest such raid since 2022 — with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked, suspending 17 civil servants identified among them. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed; over 130 remained held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang. Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.
Human Rights Law Centre case summary: the Malaysian High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional.
United Nations Development Programme and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network have published a joint publication on Malaysia.

International Commission of Jurists (July 2020): Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons; the ICJ condemned the order, demanded its revocation and called for non-discrimination guarantees. Documents state-sanctioned targeting of trans people in the federal territories.

Malaysia4U legal guide (updated July 2026): sections 377A/377B criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' for any person regardless of gender or consent — maximum 20 years plus whipping — and apply to tourists; state Syariah offences (liwat, musahaqah, cross-dressing) apply only to Muslims (max 3 years, RM5,000 fine, 6 strokes). The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted. No same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; sodomy first criminalised in 1871.

Human Rights Watch (24 September 2014) 'I'm Scared to Be a Woman': since the 1980s every one of Malaysia's 13 states has passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all 13 bar Muslim men from 'dressing as women' and three also bar 'women posing as men' — enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. Documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over 20 times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the Registration Department (a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery), and prison terms of four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Follows the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that triggered the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge (Court of Appeal decision then expected 7 November 2014).

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.summary:
Sex between men is no longer a criminal offence in Singapore. Parliament repealed Section 377A on 29 November 2022, in the same sitting as a constitutional amendment reserving to Parliament, rather than the courts, the power to define marriage. Same-sex relations are lawful for men and women, and a Reuters feature in June 2023 recorded that the LGBT community felt safer after the repeal. Public-order law still reaches conduct in public places: Section 294 of the Penal Code covers obscene acts and carries up to three months' imprisonment, a fine, or both, and gay men were charged with soliciting in 11 cases between 1990 and 1994, with fines of S$200 to S$500.

Legal gender recognition depends on genital surgery, and a February 2025 stakeholder report on transgender health and well-being found the cost of the required procedures prohibitive for much of the community. A traveller whose documents, presentation or recorded sex do not align should expect the recognition framework to offer no straightforward route.

No form of same-sex relationship is recognised in Singapore: not marriage, not civil union, not domestic partnership. The Women's Charter provides that a marriage not between a woman and a man is void, and the constitutional amendment of 29 November 2022 reserves the definition of marriage to Parliament, leaving legalisation by simple majority open in future. Couples without recognition are excluded from the healthcare benefits, inheritance rights and social security benefits available to married couples. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no partner-recognition route, and a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status carries no spousal standing.

A workplace fairness law that took effect in January 2025 is Singapore's first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but it does not list gender identity or expression as protected grounds, so transgender staff have no statutory recourse against workplace discrimination.

The media regulator limits the promotion or glamorisation of the homosexual lifestyle on television and radio and imposes higher age ratings (NC16, M18, R21) on shows or films depicting same-sex sexual activity. In 2019 rapper Joshua Su (The G3sha) withdrew from a TEDx radio talk after being asked not to make sensitive comments about his sexuality.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Singapore, a structural gap that survives decriminalisation. Pride expression continues regardless: Pink Dot SG has been held annually since 2009, with record crowds of approximately 28,000 in recent years.

Gender-neutral toilets exist at Yale-NUS College and Tembusu College of the National University of Singapore. During Wikimania 2023 at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre (16 to 19 August 2023) a female toilet was temporarily converted to a gender-neutral one, drawing public backlash: the Facebook group We Are Against Pinkdot in Singapore threatened a boycott of Suntec and users sought petitions against the conversion. Pink Dot SG and the non-profit Oogachaga responded that gender-neutral toilets complement gendered toilets rather than replace them. Government representatives noted in 2014 that gay bars and clubs operate in Singapore.

On clinical care, Health Minister Gan Kim Yong wrote in May 2020 that the Ministry of Health expects doctors to practise evidence-based best practice and to respect patients' preferences and circumstances including sexual orientation, with complaints to the Singapore Medical Council as the recourse. No such complaint had been received from self-declared LGBTQ patients in the preceding three years.

No sourced account was located of how immigration officers at Singapore's checkpoints treat a traveller whose documents or presentation do not match recorded sex, or of screening practice specific to transgender arrivals. This is unresolved.

No trans-specific violence data for Singapore was located that would allow comparison against the general homicide rate. The absence of such figures is not evidence that targeting does not occur.

The January 2019 statement that adoption law would be strengthened has not been enacted; the operative position rests on the Women's Charter and on case law.

Enforcement of Section 294 is not disaggregated by gender identity in the available sources, and the soliciting prosecutions cited date from 1990 to 1994.

The refusal of registration to LGBTI organisations is documented, but the governing statutory basis and any appeal route are not sourced here.

Composite index scores for Singapore exist but aggregate de jure protection and lived-experience measures, yielding no discrete finding for a visitor.

A May 2019 National University of Singapore study estimated 210,000 men who have sex with men in Singapore, more than double the previous estimate of 90,000, who "could be at risk of a concentrated epidemic of HIV." Same-sex couples cannot access the healthcare benefits available to heterosexual couples because their relationships are unrecognised. On youth acceptance, a 2021 TODAY Youth Survey found 80% willing to work with LGBTQ people (6% disagreed), 75% willing to form close friendships (10% disagreed) and 58% willing to accept LGBTQ family members (18% disagreed).

Singapore does not recognise same-sex relationships in any form, whether marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and does not recognise adoption of children by same-sex couples generally. On 29 November 2022 Parliament passed both the repeal of Section 377A and a constitutional amendment protecting Parliament's right, rather than the judiciary's, to define marriage, leaving open a future simple-majority legalisation of same-sex marriage or civil unions. Combined with the Women's Charter precedent that a marriage not between a woman and a man is void, only heterosexual marriages are recognised. Without recognition, same-sex couples cannot access healthcare benefits, inheritance rights or social security benefits.

IRN.name: Iran
IRN.summary:
The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to the death penalty. Articles 233 to 239 define the offences in anatomical terms and set 100 lashes for the receptive partner in sodomy, 100 lashes for intercrural sex, 31 to 74 lashes for other intimate acts between men, and 100 lashes for tribadism with death on a fourth conviction; the code does not distinguish consensual from non-consensual conduct, and NGOs report that in assault cases both victim and perpetrator are held criminally liable. The UK Home Office country report (CPIN, version 5.0, December 2025) records that the code carries no discrimination protections of any kind and that convictions are frequently brought on the pretext of more severe charges. Outright International confirms that same-sex relations are illegal nationwide for both sexes.

The enforcement backdrop is documented and long-standing. Human Rights Watch recorded two men executed for homosexual conduct on 21 November 2005; an encyclopaedia compilation cites at least 107 executions on homosexuality-related charges between 1979 and 1990, a raw count with no population denominator and no per-capita basis for comparison. Raids on private gatherings recur across provinces: 87 people arrested at a birthday party in Isfahan in May 2007, 30 men arrested at a party in Isfahan in February 2008 and held without a lawyer, and an April 2017 IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province in which agents fired weapons and used electric Tasers, with detainees taken to Dastgerd Prison and told they would be executed. Security forces raid houses and monitor internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, those accused of sodomy face summary trials, and 6Rang has documented forced anal or sodomy tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct.

Recognition of trans status exists but is conditional and surgical. Legal-religious authorisation traces to a 1964 fatwa issued while Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini was in exile, an 1983 fatwa allowing operations as a cure for diagnosed transsexuals, and a 1985 reaffirmation, with practice legal since the mid-1980s under medical approval. The CPIN states that recognition follows only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; that the surgery is invasive and often carried out to sub-standard practice; and that an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution. Petitioners must invoke Article 215 of the civil code on 'rational benefit' with medical approval supporting a dissonance between assigned and experienced gender.

That tolerance is coercive. Some gay people are pressured to undergo sex reassignment surgery to avoid legal and social persecution for being gay, with medical-legal endorsement framing reassignment as a route to heteronormative conformity. Business Insider describes the state funding of gender-reassignment surgery as purchased at the price of dignity, and LGBTQ Nation reported in 2025 that trans medical tourism is booming in Iran, with foreign patients seeking subsidised surgery while Iranian trans people face pressure to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty.

Trans visibility in public space is subject to official restriction: Tehran authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid busy areas. Custodial violence against trans detainees is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted rape in an open letter from a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognised, and no legislation addresses discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The death penalty is legally available from age 18 and for murder from age 15, and documented cases involving young people include the January 2008 arrest in Sardasht of two men aged 18 and 19 on sodomy and mohārebe charges, the reported 2006 hanging of two youths in north-eastern Iran, the 2022 Maragheh case in which death sentences for 'sodomy by force' stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy were commuted to life imprisonment, and the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared allegedly by relatives after the military mailed him an exemption document because of his sexual orientation. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship enters this same statutory exposure.
IRN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents entry, visa or airport-screening treatment that is differential to trans or gender-nonconforming travellers into Iran. Whether Iranian authorities apply any document-marker check, targeted anatomy inspection or secondary screening to foreign trans visitors is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory contains no trans-specific killing or violence rate for Iran and no denominator against which one could be measured, so no comparative magnitude of trans-targeted violence can be stated. The execution and raid figures cited are raw counts covering different periods and charge types, with no population or per-capita context, and they rank nothing.

The dating of the founding religious authorisation differs across accounts: one source gives a 1964 fatwa issued in exile, an 1983 fatwa and a 1985 reaffirmation, while other accounts of the same authorisation cite 1987. This discrepancy is unresolved.

Several legal and case details here derive from encyclopaedia compilations rather than primary legal texts or court records, including the article-by-article penalty schedule, the age thresholds for the death penalty, and the individual case dates. Whether the surgical-recognition rules apply to, or are recognised for, documents issued abroad is not sourced.

Frequency of enforcement against trans people specifically, as distinct from the documented enforcement against gay men, is not established by these sources.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Under Article 20, Clause 14, a person who has had sex reassignment surgery may legally change name and gender on birth certification by court order, and corrected identity documents have reportedly been issued efficiently and transparently. Supporters of reassignment also invoke Article 215 of the civil code, covering acts serving a 'rational benefit', though approval by a doctor is required. New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders, a disclosure 6Rang warned identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognized, and no legislation addresses discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Because the government does not allow any political party or organization to endorse LGBTQ rights, that role has fallen to exiled groups such as the Green Party of Iran, the Worker Communist Party of Iran, the Worker's Way, the Glorious Frontiers Party, and the Constitutionalist Party of Iran. Mullah Taha, an Iranian Shia gay cleric, was forced to flee Iran in 2016 after conducting same-sex marriages, and gay Iranian couples report being afraid to be seen together in public while traditional families strongly influence who and when their children marry. The law sets the death penalty as legal for those above 18, and for murder, at the age of 15, and the 2017 US State Department report noted concerns about LGBTI minors. Documented cases involving young people include the January 2008 arrest of Hamzeh Chavi (18) and Loghman Hamzehpour (19) in Sardasht on sodomy and mohārebe charges, the reported 2006 hanging of two youths in north-eastern Iran for 'sex crimes', the 2022 case of two gay men in Maragheh whose death sentences for 'sodomy by force', a charge stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy, were later commuted to life in prison, and the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared allegedly by relatives. The 2017 report described an April 13, 2017 IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province in which agents reportedly fired weapons and used electric Tasers; the Canadian nonprofit Iranian Railroad for Queer Refugees reported that those arrested were taken to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan, where they were led to the prison yard and told they would be executed. In February 2008, police in Isfahan raided a party and arrested 30 men who were held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity. Since the mid-2000s the government has provided transgender persons grants of up to 45 million rials (about $1,240) and loans up to 55 million rials (about $1,500) for gender reassignment surgery, and the Ministry of Cooperatives, Labor, and Social Welfare required health insurers to cover such surgery; HIV/AIDS medication is given free of charge to all Iranian citizens and several clinics offer free testing and counselling. Many LGBTQ Iranians seek UNHCR refugee status to be resettled in Australia, Canada, or the United States, and some middle-class Iranians have received education in Western nations. Outcomes have been mixed: the UNHCR rejected a plea in 2001 from an Iranian man who had entered the country illegally and was later convicted of killing his boyfriend; Japan rejected an Iranian gay man's asylum claim in 2005, and Sweden rejected a similar appeal that same year; LGBTQ activist Zahra Seddiqi Hamedani was reported to be living in Cologne, Germany in December 2023. The Netherlands stopped deporting gay men back to Iran temporarily in 2006: in March 2006 Dutch Immigration Minister Rita Verdonk stated there was 'no question of executions or death sentences based solely on the fact that a defendant is gay,' but after internal and external pressure she reversed course in October 2006 and announced Iranian LGBTs would not be deported. The United Kingdom drew criticism for continued deportations, with news reports documenting gay Iranians who committed suicide when faced with deportation, though campaign-backed cases such as Kiana Firouz and Mehdi Kazemi ended in asylum grants. The 2017 report also noted that security forces raided houses and monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, and 6Rang documented forced 'anal' or 'sodomy' tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct. On education, the government approved a booklet explaining condoms and distributed it to high school students and ran comprehensive HIV/AIDS education by the late 1990s, but no educational campaign for LGBTQ people has been allowed to exist; Kaveh Khoshnood noted that without acknowledging homosexuality's existence, no programs for LGBTQ people can be developed. Youth-facing cultural resources include the 2015 graphic novel Yousef and Farhad, published in English and Persian by OutRight Action International, and Maryam Keshavarz's 2011 film Circumstances about changing Iranian youth mores on sex and dating.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Iran (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender identity is legally recognized only through sex reassignment surgery, with Article 20 Clause 14 allowing a person who has surgery to legally change name and gender on birth certification upon court order. Legal-religious authorization traces to a 1964 fatwa by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini approving surgery while in exile, a 1983 fatwa allowing operations as a cure for diagnosed transsexuals, and a 1985 reaffirmation, with practice legalized since the mid-1980s under medical approval and partially financially supported by the state. Petitioners invoke Article 215 of the civil code on rational benefit and require medical approval supporting dissonance between assigned gender and true gender, while a 1976 Iranian Medical Association ruling deemed such surgeries unethical except for intersex individuals. Religious authority remains split, with Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei legally recognizing reassignment while Grand Ayatollah Yousef Madani Tabrizi called it unlawful and not permissible, and several Marja stress reassignment is not permissible for cross-dressers or those engaging in same-sex behavior. Some homosexual individuals have been pressured to undergo sex reassignment surgery to avoid legal and social persecution for being gay, with medical-legal endorsement framing reassignment as a means to conform to heteronormative standards and avoid same-sex acts termed hamjinsbaz. Security forces harassed, arrested and detained individuals suspected of being gay or transgender, in some cases raiding houses and monitoring internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, with those accused of sodomy often facing summary trials. No legislation exists to address discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Since the 1979 Revolution the legal code based on Islamic law forbids any sexual activity outside heterosexual marriage, with consensual same-sex activity criminalized and carrying maximum punishment of death, alongside imprisonment, corporal punishment and fines. Article 233 defines sodomy as penetration of genital organ up to foreskin into anus of a male, Article 234 imposes death on the receptive partner and on the insertive partner if force or coercion, married status, or non-Muslim with Muslim receptive partner applies and otherwise 100 lashes, Article 235 punishes intercrural sex with 100 lashes, Article 237 punishes other physically intimate acts between men with 31 to 74 lashes, Articles 238-239 punish tribadism with 100 lashes with death on fourth conviction under Article 136, and Article 114 allows reduction to flogging, imprisonment or reprimand or pardon request if offender repents. The law does not distinguish between consensual and nonconsensual same-sex intercourse, with NGOs reporting victim and perpetrator both held criminally liable in assault cases, and does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation. Enforcement has been stricter against gay men than lesbians, with records of at least 107 executions with charges related to homosexuality between 1979 and 1990, death sentences after a video confession in Tehran in March 2005, alleged public hangings in Gorgan in November 2005, hanging of two youths in July 2006, public execution in Kermanshah in November 2006, arrest of 87 including 80 suspected gay men at an Isfahan birthday party in May 2007, raid and arrest of 30 men in Isfahan in February 2008, and arrest of 30 men in Isfahan Province in April 2017 charged with sodomy, drinking alcohol and using drugs. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognized, traditional families exercise strong influence over marriage and dating, few LGBTQ Iranians come out for fear of rejection, and gay couples report fear of being seen together and stereotyping as sex-obsessed child molesters, rapists and disease-ridden. Homosexuals, bisexuals and lesbians are banned from donating blood, and no educational campaign for LGBTQ people on HIV/AIDS has been allowed despite general HIV clinics, free testing, counseling and medication programs. Trans men and trans women are treated differently from each other in Iranian society regarding visibility and acceptance. The documented transgender-specific tolerance statement is: "Trans men are more visible socially and are able to find acceptance in society more easily than trans women, who are often misgendered and put in the same category as gay men." Hujjat al-Islam Kariminia asserts that society is largely unaware of the clear distinction between homosexuality and transsexuality, comparing the gap between the two to the Great Wall of China. For sexuality as distinct from transgender status, few LGBTQ Iranians come out to family due to fear of rejection, traditional families prohibit dating and exercise strong influence over marriage, and gay couples report fear of being seen together amid widespread stereotyping. Documented anti-LGBT violence includes the May 2021 murder of 20-year-old Ali Monfared allegedly by his half-brother and cousins days after the military mailed him an exemption document because of his sexual orientation. LGBTQ Iranians have fled Iran in recent years hoping to gain asylum in Europe, while no domestic protection machinery prohibits sexual-orientation or gender-identity discrimination.

IRN.blindSummary:
The national penal code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to the death penalty. Articles 233 to 239 define the offences in anatomical terms and set 100 lashes for the receptive partner in sodomy, 100 lashes for intercrural sex, 31 to 74 lashes for other intimate acts between men, and 100 lashes for tribadism with death on a fourth conviction; the code does not distinguish consensual from non-consensual conduct, and NGOs report that in assault cases both victim and perpetrator are held criminally liable. A foreign government's country-of-origin report (version 5.0, December 2025) records that the code carries no discrimination protections of any kind and that convictions are frequently brought on the pretext of more severe charges. An international LGBTI organisation confirms that same-sex relations are illegal nationwide for both sexes.

The enforcement backdrop is documented and long-standing. A human-rights organisation recorded two men executed for homosexual conduct on 21 November 2005; a compilation cites at least 107 executions on homosexuality-related charges between 1979 and 1990, a raw count with no population denominator and no per-capita basis for comparison. Raids on private gatherings recur across provinces: 87 people arrested at a birthday party in one province in May 2007, 30 men arrested at a party in the same province in February 2008 and held without a lawyer, and an April 2017 raid by the national guard on a private party in that province in which agents fired weapons and used electric Tasers, with detainees taken to a prison and told they would be executed. Security forces raid houses and monitor internet sites for information on LGBTI persons, those accused of sodomy face summary trials, and an exiled LGBTI group has documented forced anal or sodomy tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct.

Recognition of trans status exists but is conditional and surgical. Legal-religious authorisation traces to a 1964 ruling issued while the country's founding religious authority was in exile, an 1983 ruling allowing operations as a cure for diagnosed transsexuals, and a 1985 reaffirmation, with practice legal since the mid-1980s under medical approval. The country-of-origin report states that recognition follows only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; that the surgery is invasive and often carried out to sub-standard practice; and that an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution. Petitioners must invoke Article 215 of the civil code on 'rational benefit' with medical approval supporting a dissonance between assigned and experienced gender.

That tolerance is coercive. Some gay people are pressured to undergo sex reassignment surgery to avoid legal and social persecution for being gay, with medical-legal endorsement framing reassignment as a route to heteronormative conformity. News coverage describes the state funding of gender-reassignment surgery as purchased at the price of dignity, and a 2025 report states that trans medical tourism is booming in the country, with foreign patients seeking subsidised surgery while local trans people face pressure to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty.

Trans visibility in public space is subject to official restriction: authorities in the capital publicly warned transgender people to avoid busy areas. Custodial violence against trans detainees is documented. An imprisoned trans rights activist recounted rape in an open letter from a national intelligence ministry detention facility.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legally recognised, and no legislation addresses discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The death penalty is legally available from age 18 and for murder from age 15, and documented cases involving young people include the January 2008 arrest in a western town of two men aged 18 and 19 on sodomy and mohārebe charges, the reported 2006 hanging of two youths in the north-east, a 2022 case in which death sentences for 'sodomy by force' stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy were commuted to life imprisonment, and the May 2021 murder of a 20-year-old man allegedly by relatives after the military mailed him an exemption document because of his sexual orientation. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship enters this same statutory exposure.
IRN.blindOutOfScope:
No source in this inventory documents entry, visa or airport-screening treatment that is differential to trans or gender-nonconforming travellers into the country. Whether authorities apply any document-marker check, targeted anatomy inspection or secondary screening to foreign trans visitors is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory contains no trans-specific killing or violence rate for the country and no denominator against which one could be measured, so no comparative magnitude of trans-targeted violence can be stated. The execution and raid figures cited are raw counts covering different periods and charge types, with no population or per-capita context, and they rank nothing.

The dating of the founding religious authorisation differs across accounts: one source gives a 1964 ruling issued in exile, an 1983 ruling and a 1985 reaffirmation, while other accounts of the same authorisation cite 1987. This discrepancy is unresolved.

Several legal and case details here derive from encyclopaedia compilations rather than primary legal texts or court records, including the article-by-article penalty schedule, the age thresholds for the death penalty, and the individual case dates. Whether the surgical-recognition rules apply to, or are recognised for, documents issued abroad is not sourced.

Frequency of enforcement against trans people specifically, as distinct from the documented enforcement against gay men, is not established by these sources.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private were not enforced after a 1953 attorney-general directive and a 1963 Supreme Court ruling, and the Knesset formally removed them from the criminal code in 1988; the age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual acts. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited in employment since 1992, with exemptions for religious organisations, extended in 1997 to defamation motivated by sexual orientation under the Libel and Slander Law, and in 2000 to products, services and entry into places of entertainment and public places. Every violent crime motivated by sexual orientation is treated as a hate crime carrying double punishment.

Legal recognition of sex reassignment dates to 1986. Since 2015 the Health Ministry has allowed transgender people to change legal gender without undergoing surgery, and a 2024 Knesset law allows transgender individuals to remove a previous name from identity cards, which Israeli law had previously required to be recorded. On 27 July 2025 the High Court of Justice blocked a fast-track attempt to reverse a gender change, holding that the 2021 certificate remains valid. A June 2013 Knesset bill to eliminate gender markers on national identity cards did not pass.

Border screening is the sharpest visitor-specific exposure. A first-person account published by Haaretz on 3 May 2023 documents a transgender traveller subjected to gender-identity humiliation at an Israeli airport, with security personnel insisting "if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male". In May 2023 Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing searches of transgender people, following complaints about humiliating searches of transgender detainees and travellers.

Anti-LGBTQ violence rose during 2025, with official data cited by the Jerusalem Post showing an increase in attacks and Ynet reporting a record high in assaults, including dating-app traps and organised ambushes used to lure victims. These are raw counts without per-capita context. Earlier attacks include an armed assault on a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv on 1 August 2009 that killed two people and injured 15, and the stabbing of three marchers at the 2005 Jerusalem Pride parade by Yishai Schlissel, who after his 2015 release stabbed six more marchers and killed teenager Shira Banki.

Same-sex marriage cannot be performed in Israel because there is no civil non-religious marriage, but since 2006 the state registers civil same-sex marriages performed abroad with the same legal rights, and it was the first country in Asia to recognise unregistered cohabitation between same-sex couples. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to give same-sex couples the same citizenship rights as opposite-sex couples; previously same-sex spouses of Israeli citizens waited up to seven years and typically received only permanent residency. A December 2004 Tel Aviv District Court ruling barred the deportation of the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule to common-law and same-sex couples, and in March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted a residency permit to a gay Palestinian from Jenin to live with his partner in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life in the West Bank. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect that registration route rather than a local marriage.

Treatment for gender dysphoria can be paid for through public health insurance with approval from the Committee for Sex Reassignment at Sheba Medical Center in Tel HaShomer, composed of an endocrinologist, a urologist and a plastic surgeon and organised by the Health Ministry; all sex reassignment surgery in Israel is performed by Dr. Haim Kaplan at Sheba under the committee's approval. Many transgender Israelis have had difficulty obtaining approval because of stringent views on gender dysphoria, and many pay out of pocket for hormone replacement therapy or travel abroad for surgery.
ISR.outOfScopeNotes:
A source addressing trans rights in Israel, covering laws, protections and gaps, returned an HTTP 404 at research time and could not be verified.

Outright International, last updated 12 March 2026, states that Israel has no legal gender recognition and that LGBTI organisations cannot register. That conflicts with court and ministry records of gender recognition since 1986 and with the 2015 and 2024 document changes; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Violence figures are raw counts without per-capita denominators, and the sources do not provide a general homicide rate for comparison, so the trans-specific share of risk cannot be quantified.

The anti-discrimination and hate-crime provisions are framed by the sources around sexual orientation; whether they extend to gender identity is not stated in the available sources.
