sources.title: New Israel Fund – Victory for Transgender Rights in Israeli Prisons
sources.summary: October 2019 precedent-setting case: an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one, after ACRI petitioned. The prisoner was initially placed in a separate wing of the women’s prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition to have her housed with the general population — showing case-by-case placement review by the courts, and that trans women have at times been held in men’s prisons in Israel.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Public expression has expanded but repeatedly drawn violence: Israel's first LGBT pride march (Alizada) was held 17 September 1977, Tel Aviv's first Pride parade in 1993, and Eilat Pride began in 2001. Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned it; the 2005 march was attacked by Haredi man Yishai Schlissel (3 stabbed, 10-year sentence), and after his 2015 release he stabbed six marchers, killing teenage girl Shira Banki. The 2018 Aguda-organized LGBTQ strike drew over 100,000 to a Tel Aviv rally, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022. The 2025 Tel Aviv Pride (13 June) was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets, while in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset. Wikipedia country coverage: In December 2004 the Tel Aviv District Court ruled the government acted illegally in trying to deport the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule barring deportation of foreign nationals married to Israeli citizens to common-law and same-sex couples. In March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted a rare residency permit to a gay Palestinian from Jenin to live with his partner of 8 years in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life in the West Bank. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to give same-sex couples the same citizenship rights as opposite-sex couples; previously same-sex spouses of Israeli citizens waited up to seven years for citizenship and typically received only permanent residency. Wikipedia country coverage: In 2008 the City of Tel Aviv opened the Municipal LGBT Community Center, the first of its kind in the country. On 1 August 2009 an armed attacker killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv, condemned by PM Netanyahu and President Peres. Community infrastructure also includes the Jerusalem Open House, which staged the 21 June 2007 Jerusalem parade after police allocated thousands of personnel to secure the area, and a central Jerusalem square to be renamed "Tolerance Square" in memory of Shira Banki. In 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality hung Pride flags with the Hebrew inscription "equality in life" along the parade route. Wikipedia country coverage: On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued an executive directive banning licensed medical professionals (psychologists, social workers, Ministry of Health-licensed therapists) from conducting conversion therapy, though it does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset. Reproductive care was restricted: a July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples, but the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the ban violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022. Trans healthcare was historically denied — Attorney General Haim Cohn blocked Rina Natan's sex reassignment surgery in 1954, and legal recognition of sex reassignment only came in 1986; in July 2025 the High Court blocked a fast-track attempt to undo a gender change, holding the 2021 certificate "remains valid." Youth-specific: the governing coalition defeated a bill to ban conversion therapy on 24 February 2016, and the same day defeated a bill to train health professionals on gender and sexual orientation issues. Wikipedia country coverage: Under the British Mandate, official questionnaires documented "unnatural" sexual expression including sodomy between school boys, and Britain pushed criminalization into Palestinian schools and society, a policy carried into the Israeli state. In 1943 the Acre district court tried Mustafa Naif, aged 16, alongside Mustafa Zaharan for sodomy; Naif recanted to protect his friend, was convicted of perjury instead, and faced a sodomy charge carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment. Youth are also direct targets of violence: Shira Banki, a teenage girl, was stabbed to death at the 2015 Jerusalem Pride parade. On family formation, between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded (versus over a thousand heterosexual couples), until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure; the Knesset also voted in July 2018 to keep single men and same-sex couples out of surrogacy.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Israel (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Treatment for gender dysphoria in Israel can be paid for using public health insurance if a patient receives approval by the Committee for Sex Reassignment operating out of Sheba Medical Center in Tel HaShomer, composed of an endocrinologist, a urologist, and a plastic surgeon and organized by the Health Ministry, and all sex reassignment surgery operations in Israel are performed by Dr. Haim Kaplan at Sheba under this committee's approval. Many transgender Israelis have had trouble getting approval due to stringent opinions on gender dysphoria, and thus many pay out of pocket for hormone replacement therapy and/or go overseas for sex reassignment surgery. Since 2015 the Health Ministry has allowed transgender people to change legal gender without undergoing sex reassignment surgery or a sex change operation, while a June 2013 Knesset bill to eliminate gender markers on National Identity Cards did not pass. In 2024 the Knesset passed a law allowing transgender individuals to remove their deadname from ID cards, where Israeli law previously required individuals to record all previous names regardless of gender identity. The IDF does not consider gender dysphoria a disqualifying condition for service and considers certain transition-specific medical treatment (hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery) and counseling medically necessary for those diagnosed with transsexualism and thus pays for said treatments. The IDF determines gender-specific army regulations (length of service, which gender to be housed with, whether to wear a male or female uniform, etc.) on a case-by-case basis for transgender soldiers, but because law makes it difficult to begin transition until age 18 and does not normally allow surgery before age 21, only Shachar Erez has undergone surgery while serving as the first openly transgender officer. Many draftees diagnosed with gender dysphoria can receive exemption from military service at their own request, and officially IDF policy does not prohibit intersex persons from service. Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private were not enforced after a 1953 Attorney General directive by Haim Cohn and a 1963 Supreme Court ruling, and were formally repealed by the Knesset in 1988 by omission from the criminal code, with the age of consent at 16 years for both homosexual and heterosexual acts. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation was prohibited in employment in 1992 with some exemptions for religious organizations, broadened in 1997 to the Libel and Slander Law prohibiting defamation motivated by sexual orientation, with every violent crime motivated by sexual orientation considered a hate crime doubling punishment, and the 2000 Prohibition of Discrimination in Products, Services and Entry into Places of Entertainment and Public Places Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation by providers of products, public services or public places. In April 2020 the Beersheba Magistrate's Court ruled a local print shop must compensate an LGBTQ rights group after refusing to print posters, holding that when beliefs conflict with necessity of providing service to all in public space, the last value holds superior. Same-sex marriage cannot legally be performed in Israel due to absence of civil non-religious marriage, but since 2006 Israeli law recognizes civil same-sex marriages performed elsewhere for registration with the same legal rights, and Israel became the first country in Asia to recognize unregistered cohabitation between same-sex couples, with Tel Aviv recognizing unmarried couples including gays and lesbians as family units for municipal service discounts. Openly gay, lesbian and bisexual soldiers serve without hindrance in all branches after the IDF formally opened the draft to all regardless of sexual orientation in 1993 and ceased linking orientation to security clearances in 1998, with discrimination in recruitment, placement and promotion and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited and same-sex couples including widows and widowers recognized. In October 2014 the Ministry of Health stated conversion therapy creates false impressions of scientific recognition with no scientific evidence of success and may cause harm and created a complaints committee, while a February 2016 Knesset bill to ban conversion therapy for minors failed 37-45, the Israel Medical Association in January 2019 banned members from performing it, and in July 2020 MPs passed a bill to begin outlawing it requiring two more approvals. Since 1 June 2017 gay and bisexual men were allowed to donate blood following a one-year deferral, with a January 2018 Health Ministry pilot allowing donation regardless of last sex, and from October 2021 gay and bisexual men can donate regardless of when they last had sex.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.summary:
Argentina's Gender Identity Law 26,743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies by 167 votes to 17 with 7 abstentions and by the Senate on 9 May 2012, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis labelling abnormality, or approval by a doctor or judge. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

On 20 July 2021, Decree 476/2021 required the national civil registry, RENAPER, to offer a third gender marker X on all national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents who hold Argentine identity cards. Mendoza Province and Santa Fe Province had earlier allowed applicants to leave the sex entry blank.

The 2012 law also grants adults access to sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy through public and private health care plans, with equal health care access for non-binary, transgender or gender non-conforming people. Since 2010 no mental-health diagnosis may be made exclusively on the basis of sexual choice or identity. A 2007 Supreme Court ruling recognised a 17-year-old's right to undergo the sex-change process and change documents; Marcela Romero won legal identity change in 2009, and in October 2013 a six-year-old designated male at birth became the first transgender child to have her name officially changed without a judicial process.

In February 2025 the government issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for people under 18, alongside a second decree on the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts described the decrees as illegal and unconstitutional. In April 2025 a Federal Court ruled the care ban unconstitutional and restored access nationwide.

Penal Code Article 80(4), amended in 2012, imposes life imprisonment for a killing motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression. The aggravating circumstance for a gender-motivated killing is not currently applied: on 5 April 2025 the Supreme Court left standing the life sentence of Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravator that a cassation court had removed in 2020.

As of 2019 no national law expressly dealt with discrimination or harassment on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation; only Buenos Aires city and Rosario provided local coverage, and a 2010 amendment approved by the Chamber of Deputies was never voted by the Senate. The national anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024. Discrimination against National Public Administration employees on the basis of sexual orientation has been illegal since 2006.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record year averaging one every 38 hours. The figure is a raw count that aggregates sexual orientation and gender identity and is not disaggregated by victim group; no population denominator is provided, so it cannot be read as a per-capita magnitude or as a trans-specific rate.

Trans activists interviewed in Buenos Aires on 4 April 2025, among them figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Outright International's current country assessment records negative ratings on gender recognition, same-sex relations and organisation registration, and an overall deterioration.

Marriage for same-sex couples has been legal since 15 July 2010, the first such law in Latin America, carrying the same benefits and protections as opposite-sex couples, including adoption since July 2010. Nationwide unión convivencial took effect on 1 August 2015, after earlier civil-union schemes endorsed in Buenos Aires city and Río Negro Province in 2002-2003 and in Villa Carlos Paz in 2007 and Río Cuarto in 2009 without adoption. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has the same route to legal recognition as other couples.
ARG.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 hate-crime total aggregates sexual orientation and gender identity and is not broken down by victim group; the sources provide no general homicide rate against which any trans-specific rate could be compared, so no severity comparison can be made from this figure.

Attitudinal polling cited for Argentina concerns homosexuality rather than transgender people: about 76 per cent acceptance in a 2020 Pew poll, highest in South America; 74 per cent in a 2013 poll rising to 81 per cent among younger respondents; two-thirds favouring same-sex marriage in a 2009 survey; and 75 per cent supporting marriage in an early 2007 Buenos Aires poll. No transgender-specific public-attitude polling was identified.

The April 2025 Federal Court ruling restored gender-affirming care access nationwide, but the sources do not record subsequent government compliance with it or any appeal.

Outright International's current assessment records negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration without further detail, and the scope of those ratings is not elaborated in the source.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (Apr 10, 2025): interviews in Buenos Aires (Apr 4, 2025) with trans activists — including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán (stabbed to death 2015) and Lohana Berkins — saying President Milei's policies have made the community more vulnerable to violence; the situation described as 'chaotic, desperate'.

Agencia Presentes (Mar 19, 2026): the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — a record year, averaging one every 38 hours, marking an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

Reuters (Feb 2025): Argentina's decree bans gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors.

Outright International Argentina overview (updated Mar 12, 2026): Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality (2010) and passed one of the world's most progressive gender-identity laws in 2012 allowing legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval; anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. The overview's current assessment records negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration.
Buenos Aires safety guide (updated May 28, 2026) gives a first-person account of walking Buenos Aires at every hour, offering practical safety impressions for gay visitors to the Argentine capital.

The World Health Organization cited Argentina in 2015 as an exemplary country for providing transgender rights, and BBC Mundo assessed in 2014 that Argentina led the trans revolution in the world, tying that judgement to the law, alternative schools and the first transgender community centre rather than to tolerance polling.

Military reform passed on 27 February 2009 and took effect six months later, allowing gay, lesbian and bisexual service and banning sexual-orientation discrimination in the armed forces. The ban on gay and bisexual men donating blood was abolished in September 2015.

Reports of bullying against LGBT people, especially young people, remain common, and sex education under the 2006 law is criticised for insufficient prevention of LGBT bullying. In 2015 a judge reduced the sentence for the rape of a six-year-old boy on the basis of the child's homosexual orientation, a decision condemned as a disgrace.
ARG.localsOnly:
Formal employment exclusion persists, with most trans women limited to sex work. Reported life expectancy for trans people is 35 years, and 5 in 10 trans men report suicidal ideation with 4 in 10 reporting attempts. Family expulsion and hostile treatment are reported particularly in the more socially conservative provinces.

Conditions in custody and health settings shifted after the 2012 law: physical mistreatment of detained trans women fell from 48.3 per cent to under 10 per cent and sexual abuse from 43 per cent to under 10 per cent; avoidance of health centres for fear of discrimination fell from nearly half to 5.3 per cent, with hospital placement by affirmed gender and name. In 2005 a judge ordered Córdoba prison authorities to allow conjugal visits between gay prisoners and their partners.

Trans community infrastructure includes a publicly funded Casa Trans scheduled to open in December 2014 in Caballito, Buenos Aires, the Mocha Celis school in Chacarita serving as an educational refuge, and a proposed tax exemption for firms hiring trans workers. By May 2014 over half of the trans population had updated their DNI.

On parenting, a 2013 law approved 204 to 1 with 10 abstentions gave lesbian couples equal access to IVF, and Article 562 provides for filiation by procreative will. In 2024 the Supreme Court rejected a gay couple's surrogacy claim seeking a new birth certificate omitting the surrogate woman.
ARG.blindSummary:
The 2012 gender identity law was approved by the lower legislative chamber by 167 votes to 17 with 7 abstentions and by the upper chamber on 9 May 2012, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis labelling abnormality, or approval by a doctor or judge. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

In 2021 a decree required the national civil registry to offer a third gender marker X on all national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents who hold national identity cards. Two provinces had earlier allowed applicants to leave the sex entry blank.

The 2012 law also grants adults access to sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy through public and private health care plans, with equal health care access for non-binary, transgender or gender non-conforming people. Since 2010 no mental-health diagnosis may be made exclusively on the basis of sexual choice or identity. A 2007 supreme court ruling recognised a 17-year-old's right to undergo the sex-change process and change documents; in 2009 an activist won legal identity change, and in October 2013 a six-year-old designated male at birth became the first transgender child to have her name officially changed without a judicial process.

In February 2025 the government issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for people under 18, alongside a second decree on the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts described the decrees as illegal and unconstitutional. In April 2025 a national court ruled the care ban unconstitutional and restored access nationwide.

The penal code, amended in 2012, imposes life imprisonment for a killing motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression. The aggravating circumstance for a gender-motivated killing is not currently applied: on 5 April 2025 the highest court left standing the life sentence of the convicted man for the 2015 murder of a trans activist but rejected attempts to reinstate the gender-motivated-killing aggravator that a cassation court had removed in 2020.

As of 2019 no national law expressly dealt with discrimination or harassment on the basis of gender identity or sexual orientation; only the capital and one other city provided local coverage, and a 2010 amendment approved by the lower legislative chamber was never voted by the upper chamber. The national anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024. Discrimination against national public administration employees on the basis of sexual orientation has been illegal since 2006.

A national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record year averaging one every 38 hours. The figure is a raw count that aggregates sexual orientation and gender identity and is not disaggregated by victim group; no population denominator is provided, so it cannot be read as a per-capita magnitude or as a trans-specific rate.

Trans activists interviewed in the capital on 4 April 2025, among them figures from organisations named for two murdered activists, said the government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. An international rights organisation's current country assessment records negative ratings on gender recognition, same-sex relations and organisation registration, and an overall deterioration.

Marriage for same-sex couples has been legal since 15 July 2010, the first such law in the region, carrying the same benefits and protections as opposite-sex couples, including adoption since July 2010. Nationwide cohabitation union recognition took effect on 1 August 2015, after earlier civil-union schemes endorsed in the capital and one province in 2002-2003 and in two other cities in 2007 and 2009 without adoption. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has the same route to legal recognition as other couples.
ARG.blindOutOfScope:
The 2025 hate-crime total aggregates sexual orientation and gender identity and is not broken down by victim group; the sources provide no general homicide rate against which any trans-specific rate could be compared, so no severity comparison can be made from this figure.

Attitudinal polling cited for the country concerns homosexuality rather than transgender people: about 76 per cent acceptance in a 2020 poll, said to be the highest in the subregion; 74 per cent in a 2013 poll rising to 81 per cent among younger respondents; two-thirds favouring same-sex marriage in a 2009 survey; and 75 per cent supporting marriage in an early 2007 poll in the capital. No transgender-specific public-attitude polling was identified.

The April 2025 national court ruling restored gender-affirming care access nationwide, but the sources do not record subsequent government compliance with it or any appeal.

An international rights organisation's current assessment records negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration without further detail, and the scope of those ratings is not elaborated in the source.

ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.summary:
Entry screening at United Arab Emirates airports tests a traveller's appearance against the sex recorded in the passport. In 2025 two Israeli transgender women were held for several hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to establish whether their genital anatomy matched the female marker in their passports, mocked by staff, refused entry and had their passports confiscated.

Earlier refusals follow the same pattern. In March 2022 the Thai model Rachaya Noppakaroon, runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe contest, was stopped at Dubai immigration, questioned for nine hours and deported to Thailand ahead of an Expo 2020 appearance because her passport recorded male sex. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport and her passport confiscated after officials declined to treat her gender as valid. In May 2025 the Armenian transgender rights defender Lilit Martirosyan was detained while transiting Dubai and told she could not enter the country as a transgender person before being allowed to leave.

Federal Decree-Law No. 31 of 2021, in force since 2 January 2022, carries the offence most often used against gender expression. Article 412(2) punishes a man who disguises himself as a woman to enter a space reserved for women with up to one year in prison and a fine of up to AED 10,000. It replaced the broader Article 359 of the 1987 penal code, which prohibited clothing deemed inappropriate for one's sex in any circumstances. Legal reviews of the UAE record that the criminal law penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles and that unconventional appearance routinely produces arrest, confinement or expulsion.

The most fully documented prosecution of visitors is that of the Singaporean transgender woman Nur Qistina Fitriah Ibrahim and her companion Muhammed Fadli Abdul Rahman. They arrived in Abu Dhabi on 8 August 2017 and were arrested the next day in a mixed-gender shopping mall, wearing jeans, sneakers and long-sleeved shirts, for looking feminine. They were charged under Article 359 and under a local public morals provision carrying up to two years and AED 15,000. On 20 August 2017 they were sentenced to one year each without legal representation. They spent nearly three weeks in custody, part of it in a cell designated for effeminate detainees, where guards shaved their heads and discarded Ibrahim's hormone pills. The sentences were converted to deportation and a fine on 27 August and they were deported the following day. Other transgender women and feminine-appearing people were held in the same facility solely for looking feminine in mixed-gender public places.

Arrests for dress and appearance recur. In December 2013 two Brazilian transgender women in Dubai who called police to report prejudice they had witnessed were themselves arrested for imitating women, held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. A June 2011 Dubai police campaign targeted transsexuals and boyat, further arrests for disguising as a woman were recorded in March, July and December 2012, and foreign residents were arrested and deported in 2020 for clothing deemed inappropriate for their sex. In 2005 Abu Dhabi police raided a hotel gathering and arrested 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a gay wedding; twelve were convicted, eleven receiving five-year sentences and one a single year, with initial reports that some were offered hormone treatment in exchange for lighter sentences.

Article 409(1)(b) criminalises consensual same-sex relations with a minimum of six months' imprisonment and no prescribed maximum, and Article 409 also reaches unmarried different-sex couples. Under Article 409(5) a prosecution requires a complaint by a spouse or guardian, which may be withdrawn at any time; because civil guardianship ends at 18, the sources conclude that no eligible complainant exists for consensual conduct between adult men, while a father or male relative acting as wali, or a husband, can supply one where a woman is concerned. The 2020 amendments removed stoning and flogging, and the 2021 law does not provide the death penalty for consensual same-sex conduct; capital punishment for sexual offences is confined to non-consensual acts such as rape of a minor or rape causing death, and no death sentence for homosexual activity is documented. United States State Department reporting records no known arrests or prosecutions for consensual same-sex conduct since at least 2015, but public decency prosecutions continue: two Indian men received six months and deportation in 2012 for sex in a public bus-station toilet, a British man and another man received three years and deportation for drunken public sex the same year, a Belgian man received a year and deportation in June 2012 after admitting a relationship with a Filipino man, and police broke up a party of 30 men in Dubai on 21 March 2012.

No legal gender recognition exists. Sex reassignment surgery is confined to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances. No UAE law or policy prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. LGBTI organisations cannot register and none operates openly; Dubai has no formal LGBTQ organisations or nightclubs, and a nightclub that hosted a dedicated LGBTQ night was shut down by the government. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, so a trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship has no partner recognition, and the relationship itself falls within Article 409.

Detention carries specific risk. Transgender detainees have been held in cells designated for effeminate people. Reports describe beatings and forced anal examinations amounting to torture following suspected or established same-sex conduct. Involuntary hormonal and psychological treatment has been administered, including in connection with suspected same-sex conduct, and no law or regulation prohibits or discourages conversion practices.

A Brazilian transgender woman was held in the UAE from September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, and accused her consulate of negligence; the case is the clearest record of a trans foreign national in prolonged custody.

Official posture is openly hostile. Officials have stated publicly that there is no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE. The Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 over a same-sex relationship and Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a transgender flag reading Protect Trans Lives. The sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word gay or sex, and Amazon blocked 150 search terms including lgbtq and pride on its UAE site in June 2023 under threat of penalties.
ARE.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 account of X-ray examination at Dubai airport rests on the testimony of the two travellers; no response from UAE authorities appears in the source inventory.

No UAE statistics on arrests or prosecutions for gender expression or same-sex conduct are published. The absence of recorded prosecutions since 2015 rests on diplomatic human-rights reporting rather than court records, and the practical operation of the Article 409(5) complaint requirement in recent years is not documented.

Whether Article 412(2) is applied outside women-only spaces is unresolved in the sources; the 2017 convictions used the predecessor Article 359 together with a local public morals provision. The outcome of the Brazilian national's custody is not recorded.

The reports that men detained after the 2005 Abu Dhabi raid were offered hormone treatment in exchange for lighter sentences are initial reports, not confirmed sentencing records.

No general homicide or violence data for the UAE appears in the inventory, so no trans-specific violence rate can be stated or compared against a background rate.

sources.summary: Ynetnews (2025): two Israeli trans women describe being detained for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched their female passport records, mocked by staff, and denied entry with passports confiscated — a direct visitor-experience account of gender-document screening at UAE entry.

VICE (Mar 21, 2022): Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon (2014 Miss Tiffany Universe runner-up) was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand before her Expo 2020 appearance because her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

Metropoles (Apr 2023, Portuguese): a Brazilian trans woman detained in the UAE since September 2022 — arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test — accused the consulate of negligence; a documented case of a trans foreigner in prolonged UAE custody.

Cairo 52 legal review of the United Arab Emirates: the UAE employs various legal mechanisms that explicitly acknowledge and penalise nonconformity with traditional gender roles; transgender expression and unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion — the legal-framework basis for visitor risk.

Outright International UAE country overview (last updated Mar 12, 2026): a new federal criminal code enacted in early 2022 criminalised consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment (Article 409 also covers unmarried different-sex couples); charges require a complaint basis; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

TMZ (Aug 9, 2016): trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained at Dubai airport, headlined as 'Dubai won't let me in because I'm transgender' — an early high-profile case of a trans visitor refused UAE entry on identity grounds.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organizations operate openly anywhere in the UAE; in Dubai no formal LGBTQ organizations or nightclubs exist, and a nightclub that sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes toward homosexuality and varied gender expression, together with the likelihood of state repression, prevent the establishment of such organizations or community education. Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances, and detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people. Involuntary medical and psychological treatments, including hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatments, have occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation. No protections exist under any UAE law or policy against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), carrying a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed. Under Article 409(5), no action may be brought except upon a complaint by the spouse or guardian of the complainant, who may withdraw it at any time; because civil guardianship ends at age 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male conduct between adults, so federal prosecution is not possible, whereas for female-female relations an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative may qualify as guardian under the Islamic wali concept and a married woman's husband as spouse, so prosecution remains possible where such a complainant exists. Under Article 412(2), men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space may be imprisoned for up to one year and fined up to AED 10,000, replacing a broader previous ban on clothing 'inappropriate for one's sex'. The UAE does not recognise same-sex marriage. Censorship targets youth-facing material and LGBTQ content: the country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex'; the Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag; the Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation in 2022, with an edition withdrawn over dialogue using the Arabic word مثلي (mithli); Amazon blocked 150 search terms including 'lgbtq', 'pride' and 'closeted gay' on its UAE site in June 2023 under threat of penalties, removing listings including Roxane Gay's Bad Feminist. Officials have publicly declared there is 'no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE', and the band Steps refused a Dubai show in June 2023 over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality. Reports of mistreatment in detention, including beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture, have been consequences of suspected or established same-sex conduct. Police raids and arrests for same-sex conduct and cross-dressing include the 2005 Abu Dhabi desert resort raid on 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding', of whom 12 were found guilty, 11 receiving five-year sentences and one receiving a year, with initial reports that some were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences; a 2012 raid breaking up a gay party of 30 men in Dubai; and two Indian men arrested that year for consensual sex in a public toilet who received six months each plus deportation. In December 2013, two Brazilian transgender women who called police about prejudice they witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. Gigi Gorgeous was detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport in August 2016 because authorities did not recognise her gender as legitimate, and her passport was confiscated. In July 2007 in Dubai, a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy was kidnapped and raped, was initially treated by police as a suspect, and fear of being charged under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country, though he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation; a 17-year-old acquaintance was implicated in luring him, and the family accused UAE authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention. Youth are directly criminalised and vulnerable, and the UAE ranked 85th with a score of 37 on PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in United Arab Emirates (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited circumstances which are highly regulated by the state. In December 2013 two transgender women in a major city who called police to report prejudice they had witnessed were themselves arrested for imitating women, held until March 2014, fined 10,000 dirhams and ordered deported. A June 2011 police campaign in a major city targeted transgender and gender-variant people, further arrests for disguising as a woman were recorded in March, July and December 2012, and foreign residents were arrested and deported in 2020 for clothing deemed inappropriate for their sex. In 2005 police in the capital raided a hotel gathering and arrested 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a gay wedding; twelve were convicted, eleven receiving five-year sentences and one a single year, with initial reports that some were offered hormone treatment in exchange for lighter sentences.

Article 409(1)(b) criminalises consensual same-sex relations with a minimum of six months' imprisonment and no prescribed maximum, and Article 409 also reaches unmarried different-sex couples. Under Article 409(5) a prosecution requires a complaint by a spouse or guardian, which may be withdrawn at any time; because civil guardianship ends at 18, the sources conclude that no eligible complainant exists for consensual conduct between adult men, while a father or male relative acting as guardian, or a husband, can supply one where a woman is concerned. The 2020 amendments removed stoning and flogging, and the 2021 law does not provide the death penalty for consensual same-sex conduct; capital punishment for sexual offences is confined to non-consensual acts such as rape of a minor or rape causing death, and no death sentence for homosexual activity is documented. Annual human rights reporting by a foreign government records no known arrests or prosecutions for consensual same-sex conduct since at least 2015, but public decency prosecutions continue: two men received six months and deportation in 2012 for sex in a public bus-station toilet, two other men received three years and deportation for drunken public sex the same year, a third man received a year and deportation in June 2012 after admitting a relationship with another man, and police broke up a party of 30 men in a major city on 21 March 2012.

No legal gender recognition exists. Sex reassignment surgery is confined to limited, highly regulated circumstances at the national level. No law or policy in the country prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. LGBTI organisations cannot register and none operates openly; a major city has no formal LGBTQ organisations or nightclubs, and a nightclub that hosted a dedicated LGBTQ night was shut down by the government. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, so a transgender visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship has no partner recognition, and the relationship itself falls within Article 409.

Detention carries specific risk. Transgender detainees have been held in cells designated for effeminate people. Reports describe beatings and forced anal examinations amounting to torture following suspected or established same-sex conduct. Involuntary hormonal and psychological treatment has been administered, including in connection with suspected same-sex conduct, and no law or regulation prohibits or discourages conversion practices.

A foreign transgender woman was held in the country from September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, and accused her consulate of negligence; the case is the clearest record of a transgender foreign national in prolonged custody.

Official posture is openly hostile. Officials have stated publicly that there is no room for homosexual and queer acts in the country. The national media regulator banned an animated feature in June 2022 over a same-sex relationship and a superhero animation in June 2023 over a scene showing a transgender flag reading Protect Trans Lives. The sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word gay or sex, and a major online retailer blocked 150 search terms including lgbtq and pride on its local site in June 2023 under threat of penalties.

A visitor reporting a sexual assault cannot assume the complaint will be handled solely as a complaint.

ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.summary:
The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, prohibits unfair discrimination on grounds that include sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act of 2000 gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court, which hears complaints of unfair discrimination, hate speech and harassment on grounds including gender identity. The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act, signed into law in May 2024, places sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics inside a statutory hate-crime and hate-speech regime; its hate-speech offence requires a clear intention to be harmful, to incite harm or to promote hatred.

Nothing in South African law criminalises gender identity or consensual adult sexual conduct. The common-law offences of sodomy and unnatural sexual act were struck down by the Constitutional Court in 1998 and applied retroactively to 27 April 1994.

On 14 November 2025 the Gauteng High Court sitting as an Equality Court, in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Case 2024/070075), held that refusing a transgender inmate the gender-affirming health care prescribed for her falls below the required standard of health care, and that refusing her feminising clothing and accessories is likewise unlawful. The orders compel the Department of Correctional Services to provide prescribed hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing her gender identity, to implement the accommodations she requires and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission welcomed the ruling the same day as an affirmation of the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities.

Detention therefore carries a documented, now enforceable floor rather than an assumed one. Reporting in August 2025 recorded that the Department of Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners, while rights organisations doubted that it was being implemented in practice; the November 2025 orders direct enforcement of that procedure.

Legal gender recognition runs through the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act, in force since 2003, which allows a person to change sex status in the population registry and obtain identity documents and passports carrying their gender identity. Surgery is not required, but medical or surgical treatment such as hormone replacement therapy is, a requirement that rights organisations describe as pathologising identity and that locks people out of recognition; reform toward self-determination was still pending as of March 2026. The binary classification also excludes non-binary people entirely. The cost of affirming one's gender is described as dauntingly high, and mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 report by Gender Dynamix documents a trans woman refused help in filing a domestic-violence case after showing her identity document, amid police mockery.

In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans to introduce gender-neutral identification on South African identity cards, which would make the country the first African state to do so, with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents. The head of policy confirmed the changes would take a few years as they move through consultation to legislation.

Facility access remains contested. A 2024 academic analysis asks whether excluding transgender and non-binary people from gender-segregated bathrooms constitutes unfair discrimination under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act read with section 9 of the Constitution, and concludes that trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in access to facilities.

Violence against visible trans women is documented. Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a Tshwane tavern on 26 December 2024 that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; an arrest was reported the following month. A country overview updated in March 2026 finds that violence disproportionately affects black lesbian, transgender and gender-nonconforming people in township communities.

Gender-affirming care is available but unevenly. Hormone replacement therapy can be accessed from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. Private care is concentrated in the main urban centres while public systems face long waits, which pushes rural patients to travel to major cities. In December 2024 activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over treatment delays running to a year.

Partner recognition is established. The Civil Union Act of 2006 provides for same-sex marriage, and court decisions before and after it extended immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption to same-sex couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex falls within the class those decisions protect.

sources.summary:
South African law and public-opinion context relevant to trans and LGBT visitors.

Criminal law history: Sex between men was a common-law crime of 'sodomy' and 'unnatural sexual offence' inherited from Roman-Dutch law. Under the National Party (1948-1994) homosexuality carried up to seven years in prison, used to break up gay events and harass activists (e.g. the January 1966 Forest Town raid), and a 1969 amendment to the Immorality Act barred men from erotic conduct with more than two people present. Male same-sex conduct was legalised in 1994 (female same-sex conduct was never illegal), and in 1998 the Constitutional Court confirmed in National Coalition for Gay and Lesbian Equality v Minister of Justice that sodomy and 'unnatural sexual act' offences were unconstitutional, applying retroactively to 27 April 1994. A residual Sexual Offences provision kept the age of consent at 19 for homosexual acts versus 16 for heterosexual acts until the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act equalised it at 16 in gender-neutral terms in 2007 (the inequality was declared unconstitutional in Geldenhuys v NDPP in 2008, retroactive to 1994). As of a 2017 ILGA poll, 24% of South Africans still said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals, while 57% disagreed.

Hate-crime and equality law: The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (2000) prohibits hate speech and harassment on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds and set up Equality Courts; before this, South Africa had no statutory hate-crime penalty regime and courts treated homophobic hatred only as an aggravating sentencing factor. The Prevention and Combating of Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Bill was passed by the National Assembly in March 2023 and the National Council in November 2023 and signed into law by President Ramaphosa in May 2024, its hate-speech wording tightened after 2016 public consultation so that it requires a 'clear intention' to be harmful, incite harm or promote hatred on grounds including gender or gender identity and sexual orientation. Human Rights Watch and other legal experts warned the bill is vague, threatens freedom of expression, and has been likened to the Suppression of Communism Act, 1950. The Department of Justice's National Task Team (2011) and National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities (April 2014) addressed sex- and gender-based violence, with a rapid response team for unsolved cases.

Legal gender recognition and documents: The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act lets a person change their sex status in the population registry and obtain identity documents and passports indicating their gender identity, requiring medical or surgical treatment such as hormone replacement therapy (sex reassignment surgery is not required); hormone therapy is available from age 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. In October 2021 the Department of Home Affairs announced plans to introduce gender-neutral identification on South African ID cards — the first African country to do so — with an identity-management document estimating 530,000 non-binary residents, though the head of policy confirmed changes will take a few years as they move through consultation to legislation. Court decisions extending to same-sex couples before and after the Civil Union Act include immigration benefits, employment and pension benefits and joint adoption. South Africa ranks among the world's best in the 2025 Spartacus Gay Travel Index and Equaldex LGBT Equality Index, and the official South African Tourism site offers in-depth travel tips for gay travellers.

Screening: The source text contains no provisions on border checks, entry screening or security screening of travellers. The only screening-type policy described is blood donation: until 2014 the South African National Blood Service required men who have sex with men to abstain from sex for six months before donating, replaced by a gender-neutral rule barring any donor with a new sexual partner in the last six months or more than one partner.

Youth: Homosexual acts were gated at 19 versus 16 for heterosexual acts until the 2007 Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act set a uniform 16 in gender-neutral terms (inequality declared unconstitutional in Geldenhuys, 2008, retroactive to 1994). South Africa has no specific anti-bullying law, though the Protection from Harassment Act 17 of 2011 and Child Justice Act 75 of 2008 cover homophobic harassment and youth offenders; per the Department of Basic Education, South African pupils are the 'most bullied kids in the world' — a 2015 TIMSS survey found 44% of Grade 5 pupils (age 10-11) bullied weekly and 34% monthly, the highest of 38 countries, 48% of public-school pupils bullied weekly, and Grade 9 pupils (14-15) third-most bullied at 17% weekly and 47% monthly. A bill introduced in 2021 would ban conversion therapy on children — still not prohibited under the Children's Act 38 of 2005 — after three teens aged 15-19 died at a conversion therapy camp whose owners were convicted of murder and child abuse in February 2015. Transgender minors access hormone therapy from 16 and surgery from 18 (or younger with parental consent), with private care mostly urban and public systems facing long waits, forcing rural youth to travel to major cities; a non-binary teenager, Zade de Kock, petitioned Home Affairs over being forced to use inaccurate gender markers throughout his schooling. Active LGBT student organisations exist at Wits, UCT, Stellenbosch, UJ and UWC.

Visibility and public opinion: The first Lesbian and Gay Pride march was held in Johannesburg on 13 October 1990 (about 800 people), and Pride is now held annually in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Durban, Pretoria and Soweto, with smaller cities including Bloemfontein, Polokwane, Port Elizabeth, Mbombela, East London, Pietermaritzburg and Knysna hosting LGBT events — Knysna's Pink Loerie Mardi Gras draws visitors nationwide. Cape Town is called one of the world's friendliest LGBTQ+ cities, with the De Waterkant gay village, a permanent rainbow crosswalk and the Pink Lane. Public opinion is mixed but comparatively favourable: the 2015 Progressive Prudes study found 55% would accept a gay family member and 51% that gay people should have the same human rights; Afrobarometer (2016) put South Africa second in Africa at 67% comfortable with a same-sex couple next door versus a 21% Africa-wide average; ILGA (2017) found 67% back equal rights for gay and lesbian people and 72% for transgender people; and an Ipsos poll in May 2021 found 71% support some legal recognition for same-sex couples, 18% having attended a same-sex wedding. Violence remains a gap: lesbians have been murdered, beaten and subjected to 'corrective rape' (including among pupils), activists accuse police of negligent handling including nine allegedly related murders of gay men between 2010 and 2013, and ActionAid has condemned impunity; in 2012 Contralesa petitioned to remove LGBT rights from the Constitution, but the ANC parliamentary caucus rejected it.

Overview by an international human-rights organisation (updated Mar 2026): a marriage-equality law has been in force since 2006; since 2003 trans/intersex people can amend sex markers under the sex-description act (medical requirements pathologise identity; reform toward self-determination pending); a 2024 hate-crimes and hate-speech act explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; violence disproportionately hits lesbian/trans/gender-nonconforming people.

Opinion piece (27 Jun 2025): ordinary administrative tasks are fraught with risk for trans people — medical requirements under the sex-description act lock people out of legal gender recognition, binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; a 2024 local report documents a trans woman denied filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID (police mockery).

News report (6 Jan 2025): a trans woman survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern on 26 Dec 2024, left with severe facial injuries and physical/emotional scars — she spoke out publicly; illustrates violent hate-crime risk against visible trans women in social venues.

Rights-watch report (Dec 2024): local activists spotlighted trans healthcare access — a memorandum to a hospital over year-long treatment delays; escalating hate violence with five LGBTQIA+ murders reported; also covers the tavern attack (arrest made).

Academic article (2024): analyses whether gender-segregated bathrooms to the exclusion of transgender/non-binary persons constitute unfair discrimination under consumer-protection law read with the constitutional equality clause — argues trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access; relevant to visitor facility anxiety.

Opinion piece (19 Jan 2026): makes the legal gender recognition case — mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and even arrest threats for 'fraud'; defines legal gender recognition as changing marker/name on official documents to align with identity; argues recognition should be a right grounded in dignity.

News report: the justice minister launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence, citing the constitution's equality clause — early (2010s-era) government recognition of LGBTI violence as a policy problem; historic context for the later hate-crimes act (2024).
ZAF.blindLocalsOnly:
Conversion therapy is not prohibited under the country's children's statute of 2005. A bill introduced in 2021 would ban it on children; it followed the deaths of three teenagers aged 15 to 19 at a conversion therapy camp whose owners were convicted of murder and child abuse in February 2015.

Transgender minors can access hormone therapy from 16 and surgery from 18, or younger with parental consent. Private provision is mostly urban and public systems face long waits, so rural young people must travel to major cities for care. A non-binary teenager petitioned the national home affairs department over being compelled to use inaccurate gender markers throughout his schooling.

Residents seeking legal gender recognition must satisfy the medical requirements of the alteration-of-sex statute, and the binary registry structure offers no route for non-binary people; advocacy toward a self-determination model remained unresolved as of March 2026.

Reporting domestic violence while carrying an identity document that does not match presentation can end the encounter before it begins. A 2024 advocacy-organisation account of a trans woman turned away from filing a case, with police mockery, indicates the risk sits at the point of reporting rather than only in the underlying offence.
ZAF.blindTangential:
The 2024 hate-crime statute drew sustained criticism before and after assent. International human rights monitors and other legal experts warned that its wording is vague, threatens freedom of expression, and has been likened to a mid-century anti-subversion statute; the hate-speech provision was tightened after 2016 public consultation to require a clear intention to harm.

State machinery addressing LGBTI violence predates the statute. The national justice department established a national task team in 2011 and a national intervention strategy for LGBTI communities in April 2014, covering sex- and gender-based violence with a rapid response team for unsolved cases; earlier, the justice minister launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence citing the Constitution's equality clause.

Public opinion is comparatively favourable but not uniform. A 2017 international poll found 67% backing equal rights for gay and lesbian people and 72% for transgender people, while 24% still said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals against 57% who disagreed. A national poll in May 2021 found 71% supporting some legal recognition for same-sex couples. The country ranks among the strongest performers in two international LGBT equality indices published in 2025.

Enforcement of protection is contested. Activists have accused police of negligent handling of killings, including nine allegedly related murders of gay men between 2010 and 2013, and an international aid agency has condemned impunity; lesbians have been murdered, beaten and subjected to so-called corrective rape, including among pupils. In 2012 a traditional-authority body petitioned to remove LGBT rights from the Constitution and the governing party's parliamentary caucus rejected the request.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. In Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

Physical risk is rising. Reporting in August 2026 documents vigilante mobs attacking transgender women and ties the surge to officials' statements and to an October 2025 presidential decree of President Prabowo Subianto declaring the spread of LGBTQ culture a non-military national threat, placed alongside separatism and terrorism. An academic commentator cited by ABC News states that the regulation moves the rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy, framing LGBTQ people as risks to be monitored and controlled.

Custody risk is documented. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard graduate student and trans woman, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali. During a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release; she alleges police beat him. He died in custody, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's deputy director Wirya Adiwena called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

Expression is criminalised. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction penalises any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. The national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal in March 2016. The government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related terms, including Grindr, and closed the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni; a bill explicitly prohibiting online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised on Indonesian documents, with no third gender or X option. Transgender Indonesians have gender at birth printed on identification papers unless they have obtained court recognition; legal gender can be changed after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which marriage to someone of the opposite legal gender is possible. The sources do not describe how Indonesian border or airport authorities treat foreign identity documents carrying an X marker or a marker that differs from the holder's presentation.

No specific law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. The protection machinery that exists is narrow: a police circular issued since 2015 directs the processing of hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and Regulation of the Head of National Police Number 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.
IDN.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not describe entry, visa or airport document screening for trans visitors, including treatment of foreign passports carrying an X marker or a marker that differs from the holder's presentation. The only airport-related account in the inventory is the 2022 arrest in Bali.

Whether the 2025 bill explicitly prohibiting online content presenting LGBT behaviour has been enacted is unresolved in these sources, as is whether the extra-marital sex provision of the new penal code has been applied to foreign nationals.

Enforcement in South Sumatra is not documented beyond the province's criminalising statute; no prosecution or sentence under that statute appears in the inventory, and the same is true of the national provision outside Aceh.

No denominator-based violence data is available. The sources give no population figure or general homicide rate against which attacks on transgender people could be measured, so the magnitude of the physical risk cannot be quantified from this inventory.

Whether the October 2025 presidential decree has produced specific enforcement directives affecting foreign visitors, as distinct from domestic policy and monitoring, is not sourced.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Indonesia censors expression deemed to promote homosexuality: the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction criminalizes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations (up to 7 years prison), and in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned TV/radio programs making LGBTQ behavior appear 'normal.' The government has banned websites and apps containing 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words (including Grindr), shut down the Instagram account of the comic Alpantuni, and in 2025 a new bill was being discussed to explicitly prohibit online content presenting 'lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behavior.' In October 2025, President Prabowo Subianto declared the spread of LGBTQ culture a 'non-military national threat' in a presidential decree, placing it alongside separatism and terrorism.

Transgender Indonesians can change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. Since June 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers (Kartu Tanda Penduduk) across multiple provinces including Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung, and Papua, because many were undocumented, especially where families disapproved, leaving them without access to work or social services. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognized, with no third gender or X option, and transgender Indonesians have their gender at birth printed unless they have already obtained court recognition.

Since 2018, the Jakarta Social Agency has declared transgender women (waria) 'socially dysfunctional,' regularly conducted raids against them, and taken detained trans individuals to city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres where they are incarcerated alongside homeless people and released only after signing a promise not to repeat their 'offence'; officials stated this is meant as a deterrent against being transgender. Conversion therapy is widely practiced and openly advertised in rehabilitation centres, including corrective rape from family members against lesbian women. LGBTQ groups are working on setting up safe houses and evacuation plans, and the Yayasan Srikandi Sejati organization provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic; Yogyakarta has the only madrasa for transgender people in the world.

As of 2019, no specific law exists to protect Indonesian citizens from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Theoretically, protection against discriminatory employment practices on any ground is guaranteed in the Constitution and Human Rights Law (No. 39/1999), and the Attorney General's Office rescinded a public job offer declaring LGBTQ persons need not apply after advice from the National Commission on Human Rights. A police brigadier (TT) was fired for being gay after colleagues outed him; his lawsuit was rejected by the Semarang State Administrative Court in May 2019 on procedural grounds. The police have issued a circular since 2015 to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, and Regulation of the Head of National Police Number 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation.

The institutional posture predates the current escalation. Human Rights Watch's report of 10 August 2016, 'These Political Games Ruin Our Lives', records the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaiming same-sex orientation and transgender identities mental illnesses and recommending psychological rehabilitation, while the Jokowi government remained mostly silent. That report marks the origin point of the institutionalised anti-LGBT posture on which later legal measures build.

Human Rights Watch reported on 7 July 2026 a surge in abuse against LGBT students, following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia. The organisation has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016, and Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organisation, documented 94 cases. In early July 2026 officials called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

The extra-marital sex provision is not drafted in same-sex terms; it reaches any consensual sex outside marriage. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex therefore faces that national provision together with the province-level offences where they apply, while a heterosexual visitor outside marriage faces the national provision alone. Because prosecution is reported as selective, exposure depends on complaint and locality rather than on a uniform enforcement pattern.

PAK.name: Pakistan
PAK.summary:
Pakistan's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognises self-perceived gender identity and prohibits discrimination in education, employment, healthcare, housing and access to goods and services. Rules issued under the Act in 2020 added a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents, and a 2010 Supreme Court order had directed free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people.

Those protections face an unresolved constitutional challenge. On 19 May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court, ruling across 12 shariat petitions, held that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act, covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. The provisions remain in force pending appeal. Amnesty International, which had warned the government on 17 May 2023 against adopting amendments that breach human-rights standards, described the verdict as a blow to transgender and gender-diverse people.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Penal Code section 377, punishable by two years to life imprisonment. The provision's definition is unclear and it is framed around male-to-male sex; Human Dignity Trust's December 2024 assessment is that only men are criminalised under it. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls within the exposure the section describes.

Lethal violence against transgender women is documented and recurring. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there within a week. In September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi. A February 2026 report described a wave of violence that has left transgender Pakistanis afraid to go out, and a night-time shooting at activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana in Karachi in which three bullets were fired through a door and the two narrowly escaped. No per-capita rate for violence against transgender people in Pakistan is available in these sources, so the incidents establish a pattern of targeted attacks rather than a measurable risk level.

Protection in custody and at police stations is a documented failure. Justice Project Pakistan's policy brief finds that legal advances have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment, and identifies implementation failure rather than the absence of law as the central problem; it makes recommendations on custody and police safeguards. Transgender people report suspicion and ridicule at police stations.

Healthcare access is another failure point. In 2016 the transgender activist Alisha, aged 23, was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to place her in the men's or women's ward; men there taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was HIV-positive. Transgender women use hormones and silicone under poor medical conditions without proper equipment or supervision, and sex-change surgery is rarely available in Pakistan. Transgender people also report being turned away at hospitals.

Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity; Part II article 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family and to oppose obscenity, and Part IX article 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council. Penal Code article 496 punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. A small clerical body in Lahore, Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat, declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016.

Official hostility to transgender recognition continues. Senator Mushtaq Ahmad has proposed a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control transgender people's official gender identity.

Expression carries its own risk. Pakistani media censors LGBTQ-related news: the website Queerpk.com was blocked in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times (Express Tribune) left a blank space where a photograph accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code article 292 bans the sale, distribution, exhibition, ownership or importation of 'obscene' books, pamphlets or images; article 294 prohibits 'obscene' public acts, songs, music or poems; article 153 penalises inducing students to political activity that disturbs public order with up to two years' imprisonment; and article 141 designates an assembly of five or more people an 'unlawful assembly' if its common object is to commit any offence. A person living openly as LGBTQ is likely to face treatment from non-state actors including Islamist and terrorist groups.
PAK.outOfScopeNotes:
The appellate status of the Federal Shariat Court's 19 May 2023 verdict is unresolved in the sources: the challenged sections remain in force pending appeal, and it is not sourced whether they will be restored, amended or struck.

The status of the proposed government 'gender re-assignment board' is not sourced beyond its being proposed; no text, timetable or vote is documented.

Whether the 2020 Rules' neutral 'X' marker remains operational in practice after the 2023 verdict is not sourced.

HIV prevalence estimates for Pakistan are contested and span two orders of magnitude, from a 2004 government figure of nearly 3,000 to a UNAIDS figure of possibly up to 210,000; no single figure is reliable.

No per-capita or population-adjusted data on violence against transgender people in Pakistan is available in the sources, so the documented killings cannot be compared with the general homicide rate.
