sources.summary:
Wikipedia country coverage: Pakistani media censors LGBTQ-related news stories. The government blocked the website Queerpk.com in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times (Express Tribune) left a blank space where a photo accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code provisions reinforce this: Article 292 bans sale, distribution, exhibition, ownership or importation of 'obscene' books, pamphlets or images, Article 294 prohibits 'obscene' public acts, songs, music or poems, Article 153 penalises inducing students to political activity that disturbs public order with up to two years' imprisonment, and Article 141 designates an assembly of five or more persons an 'unlawful assembly' if its common object is to commit any offence. Open expression carries personal risk: LGBTQ Pakistanis are generally reluctant to be open about their sexuality for fear of forced marriage, honour killings, humiliation, blackmail or violence, and a person living openly as LGBTQ is likely to face treatment from non-state actors such as Islamist and terrorist groups. A 2016 article by a young Pakistani man in the UK-based Gay Star News had his surname omitted for his security.

Healthcare access is a documented failure point for trans people. In 2016, 23-year-old transgender activist Alisha was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to take her to the men's or women's ward; men there discriminated against and taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was 'HIV-positive'. Some transgender women use hormones and silicone under terrible medical conditions without proper equipment or supervision, since expensive sex change surgery is rarely available in Pakistan due to lack of education and social taboos. In 2010 the Supreme Court ordered provision of free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people, and the 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act prohibits discrimination in healthcare, education, employment, housing and access to goods and services, though the source notes locals often deny trans people basic education and healthcare. The HIV epidemic began in Pakistan in 1987; government estimates (2004) put nearly 3,000 people living with HIV while critics suggest 70,000 to 80,000 and UNAIDS reports possibly up to 210,000, and a 2009 survey found male and transgender sex workers at high risk, with prostitutes lacking access to condoms and little public health education provided.

Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity, Part II 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family and oppose obscenity, and Part IX 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council. Article 496 of the Penal Code punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. Same-sex couples can live together only in secret; the source notes the LGBTQ community can socialise, organise, date and, in rare cases, live together as couples, if done mostly in secret, and in 2005 a tribal council in the Khyber region ordered a man who married a fellow tribesman to leave the area or face death. For trans people, a small clerical body in Lahore (Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat) declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016, while in May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court struck down sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act on self-perceived gender, with provisions remaining in force pending appeals.

PAK.blindSummary:
The country's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognises self-perceived gender identity and prohibits discrimination in education, employment, healthcare, housing and access to goods and services. Rules issued under the Act in 2020 added a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents, and a 2010 Supreme Court order had directed free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people.

Those protections face an unresolved constitutional challenge. On 19 May 2023 a national religious court, ruling across 12 shariat petitions, held that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act, covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. The provisions remain in force pending appeal. An international human-rights organisation, which had warned the government on 17 May 2023 against adopting amendments that breach human-rights standards, described the verdict as a blow to transgender and gender-diverse people.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under the penal code, section 377, punishable by two years to life imprisonment. The provision's definition is unclear and it is framed around male-to-male sex; a human-rights monitoring organisation's December 2024 assessment is that only men are criminalised under it. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls within the exposure the section describes.

Lethal violence against transgender women is documented and recurring. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near a large city, the second deadly attack on the community there within a week. In September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway outside that city. A February 2026 report described a wave of violence that has left transgender people in the country afraid to go out, and a night-time shooting at two activists in which three bullets were fired through a door and the two narrowly escaped. No per-capita rate for violence against transgender people in the country is available in these sources, so the incidents establish a pattern of targeted attacks rather than a measurable risk level.

Protection in custody and at police stations is a documented failure. A national legal advocacy organisation's policy brief finds that legal advances have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment, and identifies implementation failure rather than the absence of law as the central problem; it makes recommendations on custody and police safeguards. Transgender people report suspicion and ridicule at police stations.

Healthcare access is another failure point. In 2016 a 23-year-old transgender activist was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at a public hospital while staff argued over whether to place her in the men's or women's ward; men there taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was HIV-positive. Transgender women use hormones and silicone under poor medical conditions without proper equipment or supervision, and sex-change surgery is rarely available in the country. Transgender people also report being turned away at hospitals.

Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity; Part II article 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family and to oppose obscenity, and Part IX article 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council. The penal code, article 496, punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. A small clerical body in a city declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016.

Official hostility to transgender recognition continues. A senator has proposed a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control transgender people's official gender identity.

Expression carries its own risk. The country's media censors LGBTQ-related news: an LGBTQ news website was blocked in late 2013, and an international newspaper's local edition left a blank space where a photograph accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. The penal code, article 292, bans the sale, distribution, exhibition, ownership or importation of 'obscene' books, pamphlets or images; article 294 prohibits 'obscene' public acts, songs, music or poems; article 153 penalises inducing students to political activity that disturbs public order with up to two years' imprisonment; and article 141 designates an assembly of five or more people an 'unlawful assembly' if its common object is to commit any offence. A person living openly as LGBTQ is likely to face treatment from non-state actors including Islamist and terrorist groups.

PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.summary:
The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or transgender identity, and same-sex relations have never been criminalised. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Public sexual conduct or displays of affection can be prosecuted under Article 200 of the Revised Penal Code on Grave Scandal, which carries arresto mayor and public censure for highly scandalous conduct not covered by another article.

A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band, and 81 for HIV-positive travellers.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The only affirmed exception is a marker change granted on intersex status. A bill drafted with trans Filipinos would let applicants, including consenting minors, choose markers beyond male and female, such as X or nonbinary; its drafter, Chase Go, links the absence of a recognition process to social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence. Allies planned to endorse the bill to the 20th Congress on 28 July.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination law exists. The SOGIESC Equality Bill has been before Congress for 25 years: it passed the House 198-0 on 20 September 2017, died in the Senate in June 2019, was reintroduced in July 2019, and was rejected by the government in November 2022 as unacceptable. Protection instead comes from a patchwork. Nine provinces prohibit SOGI discrimination, Aklan (2025), Albay (2022), Agusan del Norte (2014), Bataan (2021), Batangas (2015), Cavite (2014-18, with gender identity added in 2018), Dinagat Islands (2016), Ilocos Sur (2017) and Iloilo (2016), alongside ordinances in 32 cities and municipalities. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment. The Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days, and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and the 2013 Anti-Bullying Law's implementing rules list sexual orientation and gender identity as prohibited bullying grounds.

Local ordinances restrict gender expression. Marawi City's December 2004 ordinance bans men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings, and also bans skintight blue jeans and tube tops; the mayor described it as part of an Islamic 'cleaning and cleansing' drive. Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence.

Two killings in June 2025 drew national attention: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a General Santos clinic the same day. Bahaghari cited both as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIESC Equality Bill. Murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming people have been reported from at least 2012, including killings by pro-ISIS groups in Marawi, and after the five-month siege of Marawi some residents blamed the city's LGBTQ community for the militias' wrath while individuals perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps. In May 2025 a foreigner was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. On 6 April 2024 drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at Bayambang, Pangasinan's Kalutan Concert; she called the attack traumatic and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. The Commission on Human Rights has called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'. These are raw counts; no per-capita denominator is published, so they do not establish a rate.

Detention conditions place trans women in male facilities. At Manila City Jail, transgender women and gay men are held in the ordinary male dormitories, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory, and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates are widely used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. BJMP-Davao relocates LGBT detainees in batches to the Davao City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse', alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings living in the annex since its establishment.

Police have arrested Pride participants. On 26 June 2020 in Manila, police arrested at least 20 participants in an LGBT Pride protest where there were no allegations of violence and participants wore masks and followed social-distancing protocols, subsequently charging them under the 2019 Law on Reporting of Communicable Diseases and the 1985 Public Assembly Act.

Same-sex unions are not recognised as marriage or civil unions; the Family Code recognises only marriages between 'a man and a woman', while the Constitution is silent. House Bill 1015, the Civil Partnership Act, and Senate Bill 449, the Civil Unions Act, seek recognition, benefits and protection. Same-sex couples may not file for joint adoption because their unions are unrecognised, though no explicit law bars LGBTQ+ individuals from adopting and eligibility requirements do not consider sexual orientation or gender identity; adopters may still be deemed unfit for lacking 'good moral character', a term the Civil Code, Family Code and Child and Youth Welfare Code leave open to state interpretation. In June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other through a special power of attorney, rolling out first to government-owned hospitals.
PHL.outOfScopeNotes:
No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute exists, and the fate of the SOGIESC Equality Bill in the 20th Congress is unresolved.

Enforcement of the Marawi City and Kabacan ordinances is not documented in the sources beyond the text of the ordinances themselves.

The methodology and sample behind the 2026 travel-risk scores are not published.

Sources differ on the number of provinces with SOGIE ordinances: one names eight, another nine, the additional province being Aklan in 2025.

No per-capita denominator accompanies the reported killings of trans people, so no rate can be derived from them.

Whether the Davao City Jail annex practice of segregating LGBT detainees applies in other facilities is not sourced.

Provides basis-level evidence of the school-setting climate for gender-diverse youth, and includes a Tagalog summary and recommendations.

sources.title: BJMP-Davao transfers LGBT inmates to annex facility for safety (SunStar Davao, by Ian Carl Espinosa)

Shows the official Philippine response is administrative segregation of LGBT detainees into a separate annex for “safety”.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Philippines (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Under the Clerical Error Law of 2001 (RA 9048), transgender persons cannot change sex on birth certificates, as "no correction must involve the change of nationality, age, status or sex of the petitioner" without a judicial order, with the only affirmed exception being a Supreme Court decision allowing a marker change due to intersex status. No national law criminalizes cross-gender behavior, but cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequences, including documented refusals of entry and service to gender-diverse people. Marawi City in December 2004 banned men from appearing in public wearing female attire, makeup, earrings "or other ornaments to express their inclinations for femininity," and banned skintight blue jeans, tube tops and other skimpy attire, while women only must not "induce impure thoughts or lustful desires," described by the mayor as part of an Islamic "cleaning and cleansing" drive. Kabacan municipality in Cotabato in November 2019 prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims under penalty of imprisonment. Murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming persons have been reported from at least 2012, including killings by pro-ISIS groups in Marawi, and after the five-month siege of Marawi some residents blamed the city's LGBTQ community for the militias' wrath while individuals perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps. In late 2016 the Department of Social Welfare and Development with the Department of Education allowed students to use uniforms matching their gender identities, and in July 2017 the Department of Education's Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy required review of public school curriculum for all gender stereotypes including LGBTQ-based and mandated observance of June as Pride Month. Protection machinery includes nine provinces prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity — Aklan (2025), Albay (2022), Agusan del Norte (2014), Bataan (2021), Batangas (2015), Cavite (2014-18, gender identity added 2018), Dinagat Islands (2016), Ilocos Sur (2017), Iloilo (2016) — plus an anti-bullying law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, Executive Order No. 51 of 22 December 2023 establishing the Special Committee on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer, Intersex, and Asexual Affairs, and the 2016 election of Geraldine Roman as the first openly transgender woman to Congress. Non-commercial, private, consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal with no recorded evidence of enforced penalties, and the age of consent is equally 16 regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity. Public sexual conduct or affection may be punished under Article 200 of the Revised Penal Code on Grave Scandal, providing penalties of arresto mayor and public censure upon any person who shall offend against decency or good customs by highly scandalous conduct not falling within any other article. Same-sex unions are not legally recognized as marriage or civil unions, with the Family Code recognizing only marriages between "a man and a woman" while the Constitution is silent, though 19th Congress proposals House Bill 1015, the Civil Partnership Act, and Senate Bill 449, the Civil Unions Act, following 2022 refiling of two civil union bills, seek recognition, benefits and protection. Same-sex couples may not file for joint adoption because unions are unrecognized, but no explicit law bars LGBTQ+ individuals from adopting and eligibility requirements do not consider sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTQ adopters may still be deemed unfit for lacking "good moral character" because the Civil Code, Family Code, and Child and Youth Welfare Code require parents to provide moral formation, leaving the term open to state interpretation. In 2025 the Supreme Court ruled concealment of one's homosexuality from a spouse constituted fraud as a valid basis for annulment of marriage. The national SOGIE Equality Bill/Anti-Discrimination Bill seeking equal treatment regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity passed the House 198-0 on 20 September 2017 after 17-18 years but died in the Senate in June 2019 after opposition and failure to tackle, was reintroduced in July 2019, rejected by the government in November 2022 as unacceptable, while Quezon City in June 2023 launched the Right to Care Card via special power of attorney allowing LGBTQ couples to make medical decisions despite hospitals recognizing only legal spouses and next of kin.

Executive Order No. 51 of 22 December 2023 established the Special Committee on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer, Intersex and Asexual Affairs. Geraldine Roman was elected to Congress in 2016 as the first openly transgender woman to sit there.

PHL.blindSummary:
The country does not criminalise same-sex relations or transgender identity, and same-sex relations have never been criminalised. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Public sexual conduct or displays of affection can be prosecuted under a provision of the criminal code on grave scandal, which carries arresto mayor and public censure for highly scandalous conduct not covered by another article.

A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores the capital at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band, and 81 for HIV-positive travellers.

No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. A 2001 clerical error law bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and a 2008 ruling by the highest court held that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. The only affirmed exception is a marker change granted on intersex status. A bill drafted with trans residents would let applicants, including consenting minors, choose markers beyond male and female, such as X or nonbinary; its drafter links the absence of a recognition process to social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence. Allies planned to endorse the bill to the legislature on 28 July.

No national SOGI anti-discrimination law exists. An equality bill has been before the legislature for 25 years: it passed the lower chamber 198-0 on 20 September 2017, died in the upper chamber in June 2019, was reintroduced in July 2019, and was rejected by the government in November 2022 as unacceptable. Protection instead comes from a patchwork. Nine state/provinces prohibit SOGI discrimination, one in 2025, one in 2022, one in 2014, one in 2021, one in 2015, one in 2014-18 with gender identity added in 2018, one in 2016, one in 2017 and one in 2016, alongside ordinances in 32 cities and municipalities. A public social workers' statute penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment. A women's statute and a safe spaces statute punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days, and a sensitivity seminar. A statute prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and an anti-bullying statute's implementing rules list sexual orientation and gender identity as prohibited bullying grounds.

Local ordinances restrict gender expression. A city in the south's December 2004 ordinance bans men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings, and also bans skintight blue jeans and tube tops; the mayor described it as part of a religious 'cleaning and cleansing' drive. A municipality prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for members of a religious community in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence.

Two killings in June 2025 drew national attention: an 18-year-old transgender woman was found dead in a river in the north on 23 June after being reported missing, and a transgender woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in a southern city the same day. An advocacy group cited both as an urgent reason to pass the equality bill. Murders of transgender and gender-nonconforming people have been reported from at least 2012, including killings by armed groups in a southern city, and after a five-month siege of that city some residents blamed its LGBTQ community for the militias' wrath while individuals perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps. In May 2025 a foreigner was arrested for raping a transgender woman in a province. On 6 April 2024 a drag performer was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in a northern town; the performer called the attack traumatic and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. The national human rights commission has called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'. These are raw counts; no per-capita denominator is published, so they do not establish a rate.

Detention conditions place transgender women in male facilities. At a city jail, transgender women and gay men are held in the ordinary male dormitories, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory, and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates are widely used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. The national jail authority in a southern city relocates LGBT detainees in batches to a jail annex 'to prevent abuse', alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, with three LGBT groupings living in the annex since its establishment.

Police have arrested Pride participants. On 26 June 2020 in the capital, police arrested at least 20 participants in an LGBT Pride protest where there were no allegations of violence and participants wore masks and followed social-distancing protocols, subsequently charging them under a 2019 communicable diseases reporting statute and a 1985 public assembly statute.

Same-sex unions are not recognised as marriage or civil unions; the family code recognises only marriages between 'a man and a woman', while the constitution is silent. A civil partnership bill and a civil unions bill seek recognition, benefits and protection. Same-sex couples may not file for joint adoption because their unions are unrecognised, though no explicit law bars LGBTQ+ individuals from adopting and eligibility requirements do not consider sexual orientation or gender identity; adopters may still be deemed unfit for lacking 'good moral character', a term the civil code, family code and child and youth welfare code leave open to national interpretation. In June 2023 a major city launched the country's first right-to-care card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other through a special power of attorney, rolling out first to government-owned hospitals.

Enforcement of the two local ordinances is not documented in the sources beyond the text of the ordinances themselves.

The methodology and sample behind the 2026 travel-risk scores are not published.

Sources differ on the number of state/provinces with SOGIE ordinances: one names eight, another nine, the additional one dating to 2025.

No per-capita denominator accompanies the reported killings of trans people, so no rate can be derived from them.

Whether the jail annex practice of segregating LGBT detainees applies in other facilities is not sourced.

CHL.name: Chile
CHL.summary:
Chile's gender identity law, Law 21.120, has been in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry, without therapy or surgery. Applicants aged 14 to 18 must go before a family court with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and under-14s cannot use the law at all, although it recognises them as transgender.

On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional, in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl. The ruling is confined to that case and does not alter the law's age thresholds generally.

Civil unions have existed since 2015, and marriage and joint adoption have been open to same-sex couples since March 2022. A trans visitor in a relationship that is read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has recourse to marriage. Outright International records that birth certificates carry a third sex option for intersex children.

The 2012 anti-discrimination law, known as the Zamudio Law, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and was extended to gender expression in 2018; hate-crime motivation is an aggravating circumstance in criminal proceedings. A bill criminalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020.

The Migration and Immigration Law, enacted 11 April 2021, bans arbitrary discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and extends protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 allows complementary protection to be granted to asylum seekers who are not recognised, and a foreigner holding complementary protection may not be expelled or returned to a country where their life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk because of, among other grounds, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Article 373 of the Penal Code, which covers offences against morals and good customs, was historically used by police to harass gay men, including for holding hands in public. A 2015 Movilh report recorded that for the first time in seven years no police abuses against LGBT people had been reported, which it credited to the Carabineros human rights department.

Anti-trans violence is documented and has produced emblematic cases. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered and his body hidden for 24 hours; an acquaintance confessed to the killing, which national coverage treats as the emblematic anti-trans homicide case in the country. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour at a hotel in Santiago; the victim described his attacker saying he wanted to kill him.

Institutional discrimination has been litigated. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in April 2025, alleging she was relegated to administrative tasks, that her private life was exposed without her consent and that support was denied.
CHL.outOfScopeNotes:
No enactment or rejection of the incitement-to-hatred bill that passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020 is sourced.

No sentence is recorded for the killing of Ever in 2023; the sources establish only that an acquaintance confessed.

Prosecution or conviction figures under the hate-crime aggravating circumstance are not available.

The effect of the Constitutional Court's 9 April 2025 ruling beyond the individual case is unresolved; the wording was declared inapplicable to that case only.

The F&M Global Barometers composite indices, which include a Global Barometer of Transgender Rights, cover Chile, but no scores are available.

Movilh's 24th annual human rights report on sexual and gender diversity (2025) is cited without its findings.

The CEI 57 recommendations are non-binding and no legislative follow-up is sourced.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: The 2012 anti-discrimination law (Zamudio Law) protects against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. A bill criminalizing incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020. Article 373 of the Penal Code, covering offenses to morals and good customs, was historically used by police to harass homosexuals even for holding hands in public; a 2015 Movilh report noted that for the first time in seven years no police abuses against LGBT people were reported, credited to the Carabineros Human Rights Department. The Migration and Immigration Law, enacted 11 April 2021, bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that unrecognized asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk because of, among other grounds, sexual orientation or gender identity. A Ministry of Education circular of April 2017, Rights of girls, boys and trans students in the field of education, requires schools nationwide to provide bathroom and shower facilities that respect the gender identity of trans students, alongside guarantees of social name use and gender-conforming uniforms, and non-compliance is sanctionable. A 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centers in Chile to call and register transgender people by their social name. Since 2009 the National Organization of Gendarmeries has ended disciplinary sanctions against inmates that prevented them from dressing according to their gender identity. Since 2013, sex reassignment surgeries and hormone therapy have been funded by Chile's public health system (Fondo Nacional de Salud). In June 2024 the Ministry of Health's Circular 7 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court (7-3) annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law that had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) via the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run program continues providing support in medical centers. The Gender Identity Support Program Crece con Orgullo has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17. The Gender Identity Law 21.120 (effective 27 December 2019) lets those over 18 change name and sex by request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, while 14-to-18-year-olds must go before family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and under-14s cannot use the law but are recognized as transgender. In April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the over 14 years old wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, though the ruling applies only to that case. Education protections include the 2009 General Law of Education, the 2011 School Violence Law requiring Good School Coexistence Committees, the 2013 Superintendence of Education handbook ordering non-discriminatory treatment, the 2015-2018 National School Coexistence Policy incorporating the International Day Against Homosexuality and Transphobia into the 2016 School Calendar, the School Inclusion law effective March 2016, and the April 2017 ministerial circular on trans students' rights. Law 21,430 (published 15 March 2022) is the first regulation explicitly protecting LGBTIQA+ children and adolescents, including non-discrimination on sex characteristics and the right to develop gender identity, and obliges state bodies to create programs on sexual rights and diversity. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report (56-30-6), a non-binding recommendation proposing to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors, and repeal Circular 812 protecting gender identity in schools.

Movilh's annual assessment, reported in March 2025, judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTQ rights in Chile, citing stalled equality and trans-rights legislation and attributing the failure to advance to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction.

The criminal-law response to anti-LGBT violence runs through aggravating circumstances attached to ordinary offences rather than a standalone incitement or hate-crime offence. A bill criminalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression has passed only the Chamber of Deputies, on 9 January 2020.

COL.name: Colombia
COL.summary:
Colombia's formal legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal, targeted violence. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned. Her mother, Sandra Borja, said: "They killed her for being who she was." President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers, from March 2024, carrying a kill list of named individuals and stating that all will be military targets, expressly including trans people. In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; a trans salon owner, Tatiana Cespedes, was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, trans women in the department have few economic options beyond sex work, and a friend of interviewee Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. Reporting frames these repeated killings as calculated brutality persisting through the country's decades-long armed conflict.

The recorded tolls are raw counts without population denominators and cannot be read as a per-capita risk rate: more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023; the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025; 13 trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Colombian institutions have treated parts of this violence as conflict-driven persecution. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence amounted to gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. The UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence to be urgently addressed as killings rise.

Access to public and commercial facilities has been protected by court order, including judgment T-314 of 2011 on the Tequendama Hotel's refusal of access, judgment T-909 of 2011 ordering Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali to be trained so as not to repress public affection, and judgment T-301 of 2004 ordering Santa Marta police to stop harassing people at the city boardwalk. In custody, a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling protecting the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty.

In care, the 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care, and the 2016 report Cartografía de derechos trans in Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilisation as a prerequisite for other physical changes. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025.

On partner recognition, same-sex marriage has been available since 2016 and adoption since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country; couples presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as other spouses. A trans visitor whose marriage would be read as same-sex under the sex marker on their documents is therefore recognised in the same terms.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Wikipedia country coverage on Colombia states that consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized in 1981, that law reforms in the 1990s equalized the age of consent at 14 for homosexual and heterosexual sex, and that Judgment C-507 of 1999 declared unconstitutional the military prohibition on 'homosexual acts'. Congress passed a law in 2011 penalizing discrimination based on sexual orientation with one to three years' imprisonment plus fines. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed: the 'Inconvertibles' bill of Congressperson Mauricio Toro, introduced 10 May 2022, had failed by 2024, and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposed the similar bill 'Quiérele siempre' in 2025.

The coverage records the Constitutional Court's repeated protection of public expression of same-sex affection. In 1994 the Court disapproved the National Council of Television's refusal to air a commercial featuring a same-sex couple. Judgment T-268 of 2000 permitted a gay pride parade the Mayor of Neiva had blocked. Judgment T-301 of 2004 ordered Santa Marta police to stop harassing homosexuals at the city boardwalk. Judgment T-314 of 2011 held the Tequendama Hotel's refusal of access to homosexuals at two events as discriminatory. Judgment T-909 of 2011 ordered Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali to take a course so as not to repress homosexuals expressing affection in public. As of 2020 military culture still discouraged discussion of same-sex attraction under a 'se puede ser, pero no demostrar' (you can exist, but not show off) norm.

In March 2016 the first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

The coverage states that access to public and commercial facilities has been protected by court order, citing judgment T-314 of 2011 on the Tequendama Hotel, judgment T-909 of 2011 on Cosmocentro mall's guardianship officials and security firm, and judgment T-301 of 2004 on Santa Marta police at the boardwalk. The 2016 Ministry of Interior presidential decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup. A May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. Bogotá and Medellín have thriving gay neighbourhoods, bars and counselling and legal advice centres.

The Constitutional Court extended social security (health insurance) benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008, so same-sex couples now enjoy the main benefits heterosexual couples have under the same terms. In 2012 the Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation and ordered the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to rewrite donation regulations so they assess risk by sexual behaviour rather than orientation. The 2016 government decree specifically addresses LGBTI rights in health care. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilization as a prerequisite for other physical changes. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025.

Colombian society remains generally conservative despite supportive media coverage, including gay characters in programmes such as the prime-time soap opera Dr Mata and a lesbian scene in A corazón abierto. A bloc of conservative senators defeated the civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007. The country's Inspector General asked the Constitutional Court in 2015 to invalidate all same-sex marriages approved in Colombia. By 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress, and a Congress committee shelved it 20 to 12 in May 2017. An Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% against 47% opposed, and adoption at 36% in favour against 62% opposed, while 2016 polls showed 37% to 40% support for marriage and only 22% for adoption. That referendum drive targeted exactly these rights for children of same-sex couples.

The coverage states that in 1998 the Constitutional Court ruled that public school teachers cannot be fired for revealing their sexual orientation and that private religious schools cannot ban gay students from enrolling. After student Sergio Urrego committed suicide in August 2014 following discrimination by his teachers, the Constitutional Court ruled for his family and ordered the Ministry of Education to review, within a year, the manuals of coexistence of all schools nationwide so that they contain no articles discriminating against children by sexual orientation or gender identity, meaning schools across the country cannot discriminate against students on those grounds. Youth-relevant family policy has also shifted: since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers.

NGA.name: Nigeria
NGA.summary:
Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct nationally and reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch, in its October 2016 report on the act, found that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and documented police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice for Nigeria, reported in August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, restates the exposure to up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity and identifies a death-penalty risk under Sharia law in the northern states.

Reporting on the tenth year of the act (Context, August 2024) describes the law as having fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and as effectively sanctioning abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and an increase in attacks since it passed. The 2014 act is described in the same coverage and elsewhere as reinforcing criminalisation inherited from the colonial period rather than introducing it.

Enforcement is documented as violent and predatory. A 24-year-old man stopped by police in Lagos was struck in the mouth with the butt of a police gun and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, the officers' stated reason being that he 'looked gay' (TimesLIVE, March 2025). People affected by the law describe it as weaponised and as having created a climate of hostility.

Raids on private gatherings and hotels have produced mass arrests. More than 100 people attending a party at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, were arrested in June 2018; 57 young men were arrested at a hotel in Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; 67 people were arrested in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people were arrested at a party in Gombe State in October 2023. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by the end of 2011.

A documented killing of a transgender woman remains unprosecuted. The beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman known as Abuja Area Mama, who had a social-media following, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend. The police account described the victim as 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the Abuja police commissioner ordered a thorough and discreet investigation; six months later no suspect had been charged (The Dial, February 2025). The same reporting notes that Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the police response to the killing is documented as having produced no arrests.

Custody practice for transgender women is discretionary. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty on 5 April 2024 to four counts of abuse of the naira currency and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing (BBC Pidgin) asked publicly which prison 'they will keep the crossdresser in', an indication that placement is decided case by case, and the available account does not record whether she was held in a male or a female section. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that her placement in a maximum-security prison breached the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Dating applications are used as traps. 'Kito' gangs lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where they are beaten, filmed and blackmailed under threat of being outed; community members have responded with exposure forums, including one administrator's alert page with 43,000 followers, and with sting operations against the gangs (Context, April 2024). A visitor who uses dating or hook-up applications is exposed to the same luring and blackmail pattern, in which the threat of disclosure is the leverage.

Proposals to criminalise cross-dressing have been reported and were met with fear among transgender Nigerians (Reuters, September 2022). Many LGBTQ+ Nigerians also fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes to the police because of arrest and 'kito' extortion risk.
NGA.outOfScopeNotes: Whether any of the reported proposals to criminalise cross-dressing were enacted is not established by the sources surveyed. The account of the 2024 custody case does not record whether the prisoner was assigned to a male or female section, so placement can be described as discretionary while its typical result cannot. No published figures for prosecutions or convictions under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 were located, so the frequency of enforcement against any individual cannot be quantified. The August 2026 travel warning is reported through a Nigerian news outlet rather than retrieved from the issuing government's own publication. The disposition of the men arrested in Bauchi in 2007 after their case lapsed at the end of 2011 is not recorded.

sources.title: Bobrisky — Wikipedia (Nigerian transgender woman; 2024 imprisonment at Kirikiri)
sources.summary: Wikipedia biography of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman: she pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine. She served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing (BBC Pidgin) openly asked 'which prison they will keep the crossdresser in', reflecting discretionary placement; the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section. Outcome/ruling: an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by end-2011, and mass arrests occurred at hotels (Asaba, Delta State, June 2018, 100+ party-goers; Egbeda, Lagos, August 2018, 57 young men; Warri, Delta State, August 2023, the 'Warri 67'). LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure risk: the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after its members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes because of arrest and 'kito' extortion risk, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work. The 2015 survey by Bisi Alimi's organisation found only 30% of Nigerians agree LGBTQ persons should receive education, healthcare and housing, while the Constitution (Section 17(3)(d)) nominally guarantees adequate medical and health care to all citizens. NGOs Global Rights and The Independent Project provided LGBT groups with HIV/AIDS awareness training (US State Department 2011 report). The Federal Ministry of Education has a national policy on safety, security and violence-free schools in all Nigerian schools that prohibits discrimination explicitly including on 'sexual orientation', though there is no enacted legislation protecting against discrimination generally, and no political party endorses LGBTQ rights. Youth are heavily targeted by enforcement: in October 2023, 76 people were arrested at a party in Gombe state. Religious institutions play a crucial role in education, and mainstream interpretations of Islam and Christianity drive stigmatization of LGBTQ students.

NGA.blindSummary:
The 2014 same-sex marriage prohibition act criminalises same-sex conduct nationally and reaches well beyond marriage. An international human rights organisation, in an October 2016 report on the act, found that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and documented police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it.

A foreign government's country policy and information note (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve state/provinces in the north of the country criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state/province-level Zina provisions. The same government's travel advice, reported in August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, restates the exposure to up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity and identifies a death-penalty risk under Sharia law in the northern state/provinces.

Reporting on the tenth year of the act (a news organisation, August 2024) describes the law as having fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and as effectively sanctioning abuse, with LGBTQ+ people reporting lost job prospects and an increase in attacks since it passed. The act is described in the same coverage and elsewhere as reinforcing criminalisation inherited from the historic era rather than introducing it.

Enforcement is documented as violent and predatory. A 24-year-old man stopped by police in one city was struck in the mouth with the butt of a police gun and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 in local currency demanded, the officers' stated reason being that he 'looked gay' (a news outlet, March 2025). People affected by the law describe it as weaponised and as having created a climate of hostility.

Raids on private gatherings and hotels have produced mass arrests. More than 100 people attending a party at a hotel in one state/province were arrested in June 2018; 57 young men were arrested at a hotel in another state/province in August 2018; 67 people were arrested in a third state/province in August 2023; and 76 people were arrested at a party in a fourth state/province in October 2023. Men arrested in one state/province in August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by the end of 2011.

A documented killing of a transgender woman remains unprosecuted. The beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman with a social-media following was found on a highway in the capital in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend. The police account described the victim as 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the capital's police commissioner ordered an investigation described as thorough and discreet; six months later no suspect had been charged (a news outlet, February 2025). The same reporting notes that no legal protections exist for LGBTQ+ people in the country, and the police response to the killing is documented as having produced no arrests.

Custody practice for transgender women is discretionary. A prominent transgender woman pleaded guilty on 5 April 2024 to four counts of abuse of the national currency and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine; she served the term in a maximum-security prison and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing asked publicly which prison 'they will keep the crossdresser in', an indication that placement is decided case by case, and the available account does not record whether she was held in a male or a female section. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that her placement in a maximum-security prison breached the national correctional service act because she was a first-time offender.

Dating applications are used as traps. Extortion gangs lure LGBTQ+ people through dating applications to meetings where they are beaten, filmed and blackmailed under threat of being outed; community members have responded with exposure forums, including one administrator's alert page with 43,000 followers, and with sting operations against the gangs (April 2024). A visitor who uses dating or hook-up applications is exposed to the same luring and blackmail pattern, in which the threat of disclosure is the leverage.

Proposals to criminalise cross-dressing have been reported and were met with fear among transgender people in the country (September 2022). Many LGBTQ+ people also fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes to the police because of arrest and extortion risk.

The August 2026 travel warning is reported through a domestic news outlet rather than retrieved from the issuing government's own publication. The disposition of the men arrested in one state/province in 2007 after their case lapsed at the end of 2011 is not recorded.

KEN.name: Kenya
KEN.summary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in Kenya. Section 162 of the Penal Code makes carnal knowledge against the order of nature a felony punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment, rising to 21 years where the act is committed without consent or where consent is obtained by force, threats, fear of bodily harm or false representations as to the nature of the act. Section 163 punishes an attempt with 7 years, and section 165 punishes acts of gross indecency between males with 5 years. The provisions apply regardless of the nationality of those involved. In 2019 the High Court declined to declare sections 162 and 165 unconstitutional in Eric Gitari v Attorney General (Petition 150 of 2016); the Court of Appeal hearing was scheduled for May 2026 and a decision is pending.

No Kenyan statute governs gender identity, and there is no codified pathway for legal gender recognition. Intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender, according to the UK Home Office country policy and information note of February 2025.

On 20 May 2026 the Milimani High Court in Nairobi ruled that Kenyans must be allowed to change gender markers on identification documents. The decision, delivered by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, followed a suit filed in 2020 by the transgender activist Audrey Mbugua and two others seeking to amend birth certificates. Evidence before the court showed that 94 per cent of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans had been refused by civil registration offices, with some applicants spending close to four years' wages on document corrections that failed.

On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court directed the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act, finding that prisons fail to protect the dignity and privacy of transgender detainees. The petition came from a transgender Kenyan who was subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and a court-ordered gender determination during incarceration. In the same month the High Court found that violations of a specific transgender person's rights, including freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, equality and non-discrimination, dignity, freedom and security of the person, and privacy, were unconstitutional, and ordered parliament to enact the Transgender Protection Rights Act or, in the alternative, to amend the Intersex Persons Bill 2024.

Police treatment of transgender people is documented as routine rather than exceptional. Interviews with 26 trans and intersex people in Mombasa and Nairobi recorded detention on pretexts such as drunk and disorderly, on-the-spot extortion with demands such as "look for 5,000 shillings", and the use of traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through society safely. The Kenya Human Rights Commission in 2011 and the National Gay and Lesbian Human Rights Commission in 2020 and 2021 reported routine police harassment, detention in remand beyond the constitutional period without charge, presentation on trumped-up charges, extortion and blackmail for bribes, demands for bribes and sexual favours from men who have sex with men, and rape by state security officers.

On 22 March 2018 the Court of Appeal in Mombasa ruled forced anal examinations on persons accused of same-sex relations unconstitutional, reversing a 2016 High Court decision. Police in February 2015 had arrested two men in Kwale County and subjected them to forced anal examinations and HIV and hepatitis B tests at Mombasa's Madaraka Hospital; a later anal examination was halted by the Kangundo magistrate court for two men taken from Kakuyuni to Kangundo Level 4 hospital. Compensation in the forced-testing litigation was awarded in 2024.

Violence against sexual and gender minorities is documented and in at least one case prosecuted. In December 2024 a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's September 2025 report Lives on the Line is the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering October 2023 to September 2024, and it challenges the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16 of 2019 that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

Article 45(2) of the Constitution, in force since 27 August 2010, authorises marriage only between a man and a woman, and no legal recognition exists for a relationship the state classifies as same-sex, which is the classification a trans visitor's relationship would attract where the couple's recorded birth sexes match. The Children Act 2001 makes homosexuals and unmarried couples ineligible to adopt.

There are no explicit protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 27(4) and (5) non-discrimination provisions are argued to allow claims on sexual orientation grounds, and the government agreed with that interpretation in a May 2012 submission to the United Nations.

Two custody and facilities risks follow from the absence of gender recognition. Police face difficulty deciding whether to detain transgender individuals in male or female cells when arrested. Transgender people also report fearing the use of sex-designated bathrooms in entertainment areas, for fear of being accused of using bathrooms for sexual crimes.
KEN.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Protection Rights Act directed by the High Court in August 2025 has been enacted is not established by the sources reviewed; the directive and the alternative route of amending the Intersex Persons Bill 2024 remain the recorded outcome.

The Court of Appeal hearing on the constitutionality of sections 162 and 165 was scheduled for May 2026 with the decision pending, so the appellate position on the criminal provisions is unresolved.

The Family Protection Bill's current status is unresolved: it is recorded as stalled before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years, with no sourced vote or withdrawal.

Some evidence is dated. The US State Department report covers the 2010 reporting year and the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights findings date from April 2012; both describe conditions that later court rulings and the 2025 Kenya Human Rights Commission report address only in part.

Sample limitations are not resolved by the sources. The police-harassment account rests on interviews with 26 people in two cities, and the Lives on the Line report used purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, so neither is a population-level measure.

CNN 'A Equals' interactive on trans and intersex Kenyans: 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion ('look for 5,000 shillings...'), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

KHRC 'Lives on the Line' (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

KHRC press release: Eldoret High Court handed transgender Kenyans a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.
