Reuters (Dec 2024): a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

OutRight International Kenya profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The Star (23 Sep 2025) on the KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

US State Department Human Rights Report for Kenya (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya (GALCK) were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Kenya (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The article states there are no statutory provisions relating to transgender rights and no legal means to change gender in Kenya. The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights reported in April 2012 that transgender people suffer stigma and discrimination and are unable to access gender re-assignment therapy, citing a witness who had undergone all processes but was declined surgery by Kenyatta National Hospital without reasons and whose appeal to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentist's Board was unsuccessful. The same report states police face difficulties deciding whether to detain transgender individuals in male or female cells when arrested, and that transgender people fear using sex-designated bathrooms in entertainment areas for fear of being accused or mistaken as using bathrooms for sexual crimes. It further records that when opposite-sex partners demanding sexual relationships discover they are not female or male, they scream and attract members of the public to the hotel room causing public nuisance, stigma and embarrassment to the transgender person. The article states transgender people face stigma, discrimination and violence in Kenya, with discrimination in particular prevalent as is sexual violence, in areas including government recognition of a third sex, access to justice, employment and other spheres of public life. In August 2025 the High Court found violations of a specific transgender person's rights "including freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, equality and non-discrimination, dignity, freedom and security of the person, and privacy were unconstitutional" and ordered parliament to implement "the enactment of the Transgender Protection Rights Act, or, in the alternative, the amendments of the Intersex Persons Bill 2024". On 20 May 2026 the High Court ruled Kenyans must be allowed to change gender markers on identification documents in response to a lawsuit filed in 2020 by transgender activist Audrey Mbugua and two others seeking to amend birth certificates. Section 162 of the Penal Code makes carnal knowledge against the order of nature a felony liable to 14 years' imprisonment, rising to 21 years where committed without consent or where consent was obtained by force, threats or intimidation, fear of bodily harm, or false representations as to the nature of the act, while Section 163 punishes attempt with 7 years and Section 165 punishes acts of gross indecency between males with 5 years. On 24 May 2019 the High Court refused to declare Sections 162 and 165 unconstitutional in Eric Gitari v Attorney General & another Petition no. 150 of 2016, with a Court of Appeal hearing scheduled for May 2026 and decision pending. On 22 March 2018 the Court of Appeal in Mombasa ruled forced anal examinations on persons accused of same-sex relations unconstitutional, reversing a 2016 High Court decision, after police in February 2015 arrested two men in Kwale County and subjected them to forced anal exams, HIV and hepatitis B tests at Mombasa's Madaraka Hospital, with a later anal examination halted by the Kangundo magistrate court for two men taken from Kakuyuni to Kangundo Level 4 hospital. Article 45(2) of the Constitution effective 27 August 2010 authorises only opposite-sex marriage, the state recognises no same-sex relationships, and the Children Act 2001 makes homosexuals and unmarried couples ineligible to adopt. There are no explicit protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, though Article 27(4)-(5) non-discrimination provisions are argued to allow claims on sexual orientation grounds and the government in a May 2012 UN submission agreed with that interpretation. The Kenya Human Rights Commission in 2011 and the National Gay and Lesbian Human Rights Commission in 2020-2021 reported routine police harassment, detention in remand beyond the constitutional period without charges, presentation on trumped-up charges, extortion and blackmail for bribes, demands for bribes and sexual favours from MSM sex workers, and rape by state security officers. The Family Protection Bill file DLS/NA/BILLS/2/18/2023 introduced in 2023 by MP George Peter Opondo Kaluma would allow "aggravated homosexuality" to be punished with death, criminalize all promotion of LGBTQ+ activity, restrict privacy, assembly and public demonstration, prohibit pride parades, provide for monitoring of private and public spaces, remove LGBTQ+ topics from school curricula, and overturn a 2023 Supreme Court decision affirming the right to form associations, remaining stalled before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years. These provisions concern same-sex sexual activity and are listed separately from transgender-specific issues, and in 2010-2012 ICCPR and Universal Periodic Review responses the government said it would not decriminalize same-sex unions as taboo and culturally unacceptable while stating it did not support discrimination in access to services including HIV/AIDS prevention under the 2006 Act.

KEN.tangentialFactors:
The Family Protection Bill, introduced in 2023 by the MP George Peter Opondo Kaluma under file reference DLS/NA/BILLS/2/18/2023, would allow aggravated homosexuality to be punished with death, criminalise all promotion of LGBTQ+ activity, restrict privacy, assembly and public demonstration, prohibit pride parades, provide for monitoring of private and public spaces, remove LGBTQ+ topics from school curricula, and overturn the 2023 Supreme Court decision affirming the right to form associations. It has remained stalled before the Committee on Social Protection for close to two years.

In responses to the ICCPR and the Universal Periodic Review between 2010 and 2012, the government said it would not decriminalise same-sex unions, describing them as taboo and culturally unacceptable, while stating that it did not support discrimination in access to services, including HIV/AIDS prevention under the 2006 Act.

Access to HIV services has been contested locally: in February 2010 religious leaders in Mtwapa demanded the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

Court-driven change has been uneven. The 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruling against forced anal testing, the 2023 Supreme Court decision upholding freedom of association and allowing LGBTQ organisation registration, and a petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination sit alongside the 2019 High Court refusal to strike down the criminal provisions and the 2019 dismissal of violence claims in Petition 16 of 2019.
KEN.localsOnly:
Access to transition-related care is obstructed. The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights reported in April 2012 that transgender people are unable to access gender reassignment therapy; a witness who had completed all required processes was declined surgery by Kenyatta National Hospital without reasons, and an appeal to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentist's Board was unsuccessful.

Societal discrimination reaches employment and education. A US State Department human rights report for the 2010 reporting year recorded widespread discrimination based on sexual orientation causing loss of employment and education, while organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya were permitted to register and operate.

Transgender Kenyans face stigma, discrimination and violence, with discrimination and sexual violence reported in areas including government recognition of a third sex, access to justice, employment and other spheres of public life. A documented risk arises on disclosure: when partners demanding sexual relationships discover that a person is not female or male, they have screamed and drawn members of the public to the hotel room, causing public nuisance, stigma and embarrassment to the transgender person.

Community infrastructure exists but operates under pressure. The Lives on the Line report was built with more than 14 community organisations, and active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence. The Star reported that the report used purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, and that despite the dignity guarantee in Article 28 of the Constitution, the data paints a blunt picture.
KEN.blindSummary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in the country under a colonial-era statute, carrying imprisonment of up to 14 years, and the provision is applied regardless of the nationality of those involved. No statute of the country governs gender identity, and there is no codified pathway for legal gender recognition; intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender, according to a foreign office country policy note of February 2025.

Legal gender recognition is obstructed in practice. Evidence before the High Court in the largest city, in a decision delivered on 20 May 2026 by the assigned judge in a petition filed in January 2020, showed that 94 per cent of trans and gender-diverse residents had been refused by civil registration offices, with some applicants spending close to four years' wages on document corrections that failed. The country has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.

Courts have ordered state action. On 12 August 2025 a High Court sitting in a regional centre directed the national government to enact a transgender protection rights act, after finding that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections; the petition was brought by a trans resident subjected to non-consensual medical procedures and a court-ordered 'gender determination' while incarcerated.

Police harassment is routine for trans people. Twenty-six interviewees in two large cities described detention on pretexts such as being drunk and disorderly, on-the-spot extortion demands of 5,000 shillings, and the practice of using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through public life safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Violence against LGBT people is documented and sometimes lethal. In December 2024 a man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist. A national human rights commission report of September 2025, produced with more than 14 community organisations, is the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities, covering October 2023 to September 2024; it explicitly challenges a 2019 High Court ruling that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

LGBTI civil-society groups may register and operate, but only within a restrictive civic space. A Court of Appeal ruling in 2018 held forced anal testing unconstitutional, with compensation awarded in 2024, and the Supreme Court upheld freedom of association in 2023, allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; a petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination remains before the courts. Societal discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is widespread and has caused loss of employment and education.
KEN.blindOutOfScope:
Enforcement data on prosecutions under the statute's same-sex conduct provision are not sourced in this inventory; the record establishes the offence and its maximum penalty, not how often it is used against visitors or residents.

Whether the transgender protection rights act directed by the High Court on 12 August 2025 has been enacted, and in what form, is unresolved here.

The practical effect of the High Court's 20 May 2026 decision on civil registration offices, including whether refusals of document corrections have declined, is not sourced.

The scope of intersex third-gender recognition in practice, including which documents carry the marker and whether it extends to non-intersex trans people, is not established by these sources.

Only the killing of an LGBTQ activist and the resulting 50-year sentence are documented; broader patterns of anti-trans homicide with dates and outcomes are not itemised in this inventory.

International news feature on trans and intersex people: 26 interviewees describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion (demands for cash), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Report (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in the country, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges a 2019 High Court ruling that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

Press release: a High Court handed transgender people a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the government to enact a transgender protection rights act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans person subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.

Report on a High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026: follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse people were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; the country has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news report (Dec 2024) covers a man sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

News report (23 Sep 2025) on the national human rights commission's report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite the constitutional dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

Human rights report (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 local religious leaders demanded closure of an HIV research institute.
KEN.blindLocalsOnly:
A national human rights commission report of September 2025 draws on purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data collection and service provision, and was built with more than 14 community organisations; it covers the period October 2023 to September 2024.

Residents may register and run LGBTI organisations following the Supreme Court's 2023 affirmation of freedom of association, and a petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination has been filed by advocates.

The High Court judgment of 12 August 2025 obliges the state to legislate a transgender protection rights act and to remedy prison conditions that fail dignity and privacy for trans detainees.

The direction of travel is court-driven rather than statutory: constitutional litigation has produced recognition of forced anal testing as unconstitutional, freedom of association for LGBTQ organisations, and a 2025 order to legislate transgender protection, while the underlying criminal provisions remain in force.

Health and research services have been targeted on religious grounds. In February 2010 religious leaders in one town demanded the closure of a national medical research institute's HIV research facility, an episode that bears on access to care for men who have sex with men. ROU.name: Romania
ROU.summary:
Emergency Ordinance No. 89/2001, adopted 21 June 2001 and in force 26 June 2001, repealed Penal Code Article 200 and decriminalised consensual adult same-sex relations; Articles 197, 198, 201 and 202 were redefined in gender-neutral terms applying equally to sexual acts with persons of different or same sex. Pending investigations, trials and custodial sentences under former Article 200(2)–(4) were preserved only where the facts remained punishable under other provisions, with reclassification by the execution court. Same-sex relations are legal nationwide.

Government Ordinance 137/2000 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex and sexual orientation, and a 2000 law extends that prohibition across employment, goods and services, housing, education, health care, audiovisual programming, justice, public services and social security, enforced by the National Council for Combating Discrimination (CNCD). Outright International records that institutional follow-through on this protection is limited. The CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials during 2023.

The Penal Code was amended in 2006 to add incitement to discrimination, homophobic bias as an aggravating circumstance permitting higher sentences, and incitement to hatred and harassment on sexual-orientation grounds. These provisions are framed on sexual orientation and do not expressly cover gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics; ILGA-Europe's rainbow map records for 2025 that hate-crime and hate-speech protections lack express coverage of those grounds, and the application of the 2006 provisions is described as difficult to assess or not yet applied.

Legal gender recognition exists and is court-based. Since 1996 a person who has undergone sex reassignment surgery has been able to change sex in official documents, but the governing law is vague and incomplete, producing inconsistent judicial practice in which some authorities have refused recognition unless a surgical intervention had occurred. A change of civil status requires a court decision based in practice on a certificate from the Institutul Național de Medicină Legală (INML) issued through an intrusive and ad hoc procedure. The difficulty of that procedure frequently prevents documents reflecting gender identity from being obtained, which in turn creates problems in accessing health care, transport passes and banking services. ILGA-Europe's rainbow map records that during January–December 2025 Romania had no fair, transparent, self-determination-based framework free from abusive requirements, and no non-binary option.

In October 2024 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Romania had infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition in Romania of a UK gender recognition certificate, and held that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. On 31 March 2026 the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity; the ruling became definitive when the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates. ACCEPT Romania, announcing the outcome on Trans Day of Visibility, urged others who had changed their documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

Marriage is limited to a union between a man and a woman under Civil Code Article 259 and implementing legislation, and no civil-partnership regime exists. The 2018 referendum to amend the constitution to ban same-sex marriage failed on low turnout, same-sex marriage and civil-partnership bills were rejected in 2013–2015, and the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017. The European Court of Human Rights ruled on 23 May 2023 that a failure to allow marriage or partnership breaches Article 8, and the Prime Minister stated in November 2023 that Romania will not legalise either. In Coman and Others in June 2018 the Court of Justice of the European Union held that same-sex spouses married in an EU country have residence rights, and Romania's highest courts ruled the same year for equivalent residency and legal rights.

Anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign. Candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February 2025, Prime Minister Marcel Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes and in October 2025 opposed amendments to identity documents for legal gender recognition as creating confusion and eroding traditional norms, and in the same month political figures claimed children could choose their gender without parental consent. A Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements. ACCEPT Romania's chapter in the ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report states that eight of nine country submissions reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people, and cites the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.

Regulatory follow-up did occur. After B1 TV's News Pass programme on 5 June 2025 framed Pride as a provocation with derogatory portrayals of LGBTI visibility, the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to the channel in August 2025 for breach of the Audiovisual Code prohibition on generalised defamatory statements against groups defined by sexual orientation, following an ACCEPT complaint.

Pride events proceeded in 2025 amid documented hostility. The Bucharest Pride march on 7 June 2025 drew approximately 31,000 people demanding simplified legal gender recognition procedures, civil-union legislation and protection against hate speech and prejudice-based crimes; AP reported the 20th anniversary march in June 2025 as drawing tens of thousands. In July 2025 Oradea Pride went ahead despite a third-year municipal ban attempt, under heavy police supervision, with nine organisers and participants fined and a subsequent application to the European Court of Human Rights; Pride events in Cluj-Napoca, Brașov, Timișoara and Iași took place without incidents.

Attempts to legislate against gender identity and homosexuality have so far been blocked or stripped. A June 2020 parliamentary amendment imposing a blanket ban on gender identity studies without public debate was struck down by the Constitutional Court in December 2020; the anti-LGBTQ provisions of April 2022 Senate bills banning 'gay propaganda' in schools and discussion of homosexuality and gender identity in public spaces were removed from the final version; and anti-discrimination provisions in March 2024 education-law drafts drew protests from 13 religious groups and a counter-response from more than 50 organisations. LGBTI organisations can register and operate, and in October 2025 three training-of-trainers sessions were held for police officers, prosecutors and social workers to recognise, investigate and respond to hate crimes targeting LGBTI people.

Whether the hate-crime and hate-speech provisions added in 2006 have been applied in any prosecuted case is described in the source as difficult to assess or not yet applied; no case-level confirmation appears in the inventory.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Romania (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 1996 it has been possible for someone who has gone through sex reassignment surgery to legally change their sex in official documents. The governing law is vague and incomplete, resulting in inconsistency in judicial practice, with authorities in some cases denying recognition unless a sex-reassignment intervention had occurred. Changing civil status requires a court decision based in practice on a certificate issued by the Institutul Național de Medicină Legală following an intrusive and arbitrary procedure developed ad hoc to fill a legal vacuum. The difficult procedure often makes it impossible to obtain documents reflecting gender identity, leading to difficulties in health care, transportation passes and banking services. In June 2020 parliament passed an education-law amendment placing a blanket ban on gender identity studies without public debate, which Romania's Constitutional Court struck down in December 2020. In April 2022 the Senate passed bills banning "gay propaganda" in schools and banning discussion of homosexuality and gender identity in public spaces, approved by the Human Rights Commission pending Chamber of Deputies approval, but the anti-LGBTQ parts were removed in the final version. Stated anti-discrimination, hate-crime aggravation and incitement provisions are framed on the basis of sexual orientation, not expressly as transgender-specific protections. There are no laws explicitly against gay citizens aside from denial of same-sex marriage rights, with an equal age of consent since 2002 at 15 years, raised to 16 in 2020 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. Article 200 criminalizing same-sex relations was eliminated by Emergency Ordinance no. 89/2001 adopted in January 2001 and effective in January 2002 after presidential signature, with the last person imprisoned for being gay released in 1998. Marriage is limited to a union between a man and a woman under Civil Code Article 259 and implementing legislation, with same-sex marriage and civil partnership bills rejected in 2013-2015 and constitutional ban attempts withdrawn. The European Court of Justice ruled in Coman and Others in June 2018 that same-sex spouses married in an EU country have residence rights, Romania's highest courts ruled in 2018 for same residency and legal rights, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled on 23 May 2023 that failure to allow marriage or partnership breaches Article 8, while the Prime Minister said in November 2023 Romania will not legalise either. A 2000 law bans sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, goods and services, housing, education, health care, audiovisual programming, justice, public services and social security, enforced by the National Council for Combating Discrimination, including a fine against TAROM for refusing same-sex partners couples discounts in 2005. The Penal Code was amended in 2006 to add incitement to discrimination, discriminatory homophobic bias as an aggravating circumstance allowing higher sentences, and incitement to hatred and harassment on sexual-orientation grounds, though application is described as difficult to assess or not yet applied. Men who have had sex with men remain banned from blood donation under a rule found illegal sexual-orientation discrimination in September 2007, with a January 2008 Health Ministry removal law not yet implemented. In 2021 the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 8 and 11 for failure to effectively investigate the 20 February 2013 homophobic disruption of an LGBTQ film screening, finding discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds. "Attitudes in Romania are generally conservative, with regard to the rights of gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender citizens." A 2019 poll of approximately 3,200 people found 53% of LGBTI people were "(Almost) never open" about being LGBTI, with 23% rarely open, 18% fairly open and 7% very open. An ACCEPT 2010 survey reported 68.2% had suffered discrimination or exclusion because of sexual orientation or identity, with over 50% insulted, 30% threatened with physical violence, 25% deliberately excluded or avoided and 25% suffering sexual harassment, occurring most on streets at 49.5% followed by gay venues at 27.9%. A 2013 Fundamental Rights Agency survey framed in terms of homophobic behavior and sexual minorities ranked Romania third after Croatia and Bulgaria, with 21% reporting attack or threat of violence in the past five years in settings including streets and schools. Open homosexuality remains uncommon outside major urban centers with rural gay and lesbian Romanians typically remaining closeted, while visible LGBTQ communities and annual pride parades exist in Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, Iasi and Timisoara, with the 18th Bucharest Pride drawing a record 25,000 participants. Most attitude surveys cited concern gay, lesbian, homosexuality or LGBTQ rights generally, without a separate transgender-specific tolerance figure beyond the conservative-attitudes statement.

Discrimination complaints on grounds of sex or sexual orientation fall to the national anti-discrimination council, which has investigation and fining powers; it has acted against employers and service providers, including a 2005 fine against the national airline for refusing same-sex partners couples discounts, and investigated printing houses that refused LGBT and gender-equality materials in 2023. Hate-crime aggravation and incitement provisions added to the Penal Code in 2006 rest on sexual-orientation grounds rather than gender identity, and their practical application is described as difficult to assess or not yet applied.

Open homosexuality remains uncommon outside major urban centres, with rural LGBTI residents typically remaining closeted; visible communities and annual pride parades exist in the capital and three other cities. A 2019 poll found 53% of LGBTI respondents were almost never open about their identity. LGBTI organisations are able to register and operate, and the national LGBTI organisation advises residents who changed documents in another member jurisdiction to pursue transcription here following the March 2026 definitive judgment.

A regional human-rights body's thematic review published in January 2023, 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People', is a national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 covering legal and policy frameworks, applicable regional human-rights court case-law and international standards. In 2021 that court found violations of Articles 8 and 11 for the failure to investigate effectively the 20 February 2013 homophobic disruption of an LGBTQ film screening, finding discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds.

Survey evidence available here concerns sexual orientation and LGBTI identity generally and contains no separate transgender-specific tolerance or victimisation figure beyond a general statement that attitudes in the country are conservative regarding the rights of gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender citizens. A 2019 poll of about 3,200 people found 53% of LGBTI people were '(Almost) never open' about being LGBTI; a 2010 survey by the national LGBTI organisation reported 68.2% had suffered discrimination or exclusion on grounds of sexual orientation or identity, most often on streets at 49.5%; and a 2013 survey by a union-level rights agency ranked the country third of the surveyed jurisdictions after two neighbouring ones, with 21% reporting attack or threat of violence in the previous five years.

Men who have sex with men remain barred from blood donation under a rule found to be illegal sexual-orientation discrimination in September 2007; a January 2008 health-ministry removal of the ban is recorded as not yet implemented. A union-level rights agency's commissioned legal study of February 2008 maps how national law implemented the union's employment equal-treatment directive and free-movement rules for LGBT partners, including national anti-discrimination concepts, the anti-discrimination council's enforcement powers and NGO complaints, and serves as a dated baseline for the country's protection architecture. A 2023 pride survey found 51% of residents agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition.

BGD.name: Bangladesh
BGD.summary:
Bangladesh's Penal Code of 1860 criminalises "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" under Section 377, punishable by imprisonment for life or by a term of up to ten years plus a fine. The explanation attached to the section treats penetration as sufficient and extends its ambit to any sexual union involving penile insertion, including consensual acts. Parliament declined to repeal the provision in 2009 and again in 2013. Prosecutions are rare, but police use the section to arrest, harass and extort people presumed to be LGBTIQ, and it has been invoked to restrict registration of LGBTI organisations. Whether the section reaches sex between women is unresolved: a UK Home Office country policy note updated in April 2026 records the ambiguity, noting that a 2019 ILGA report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere describing the provision as relevant to all genders.

Enforcement operates through raid, extortion and public exposure rather than courtroom conviction. In a 2017 raid recorded in country human rights reporting, the paramilitary force RAB entered the Chayaneer Community Center in Keraniganj Upazila during an LGBTI dinner, separated the 120 people present into small groups, beat them and arrested 28 on suspicion of homosexual activity, allowed media to photograph some of those detained, and later stated the arrests were for narcotics possession. Four were remanded, twelve held for questioning and twelve sent directly to jail.

Visibly trans people, hijras in particular, face predatory policing. After hijras refused to pay police extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 September 2025 police in Narayanganj arrested twelve hijras for collecting money from expatriate-carrying vehicles, a traditional livelihood.

Transit points are not exempt. In April 2024 five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, according to the monitoring group JMBF.

Third-gender recognition exists on paper. On 11 November 2013 the cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina recognised hijras as a separate gender alongside male and female, and hijras hold legal third-gender status with gender-marker change permitted. Voter lists carry a third-gender option, and in April 2019 officials added "hijra" to voting forms. The recognition is narrow and unregulated: no policy sets out what a person must undergo to change gender on official documents, no criteria define who qualifies as a hijra, and no anti-discrimination protection covers hijras. Transgender communities other than hijras are neither recognised nor protected. A January 2015 Ministry of Health memorandum directed steps to identify hijras through medical check-ups requiring them to strip and have their genitals confirmed, with photographs later circulated to establish that hijras were "really men".

No form of relationship recognition exists. Bangladeshi law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships or adoption by same-sex couples, and same-sex couples have been detained and can be imprisoned or fined. A trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship has no legal standing to protect a partner, and any couple read as same-sex under birth-sex status is exposed to detention.

The August 2024 ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina changed the security environment. A Washington Blade assessment published on 5 August 2025, a year after the protests, found LGBTQ people increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats. Hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground after the 2024 change, and trans people who had previously lived visibly were reported to be living in hiding.

Lethal violence against visible trans people continues. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district, on 3 February 2025; five unidentified individuals were accused and no outcome is documented.

JMBF's annual report, published in April 2026, documents 260 human rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across Bangladesh in 2025, described as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022. The conduct includes murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. The figure is a raw count of documented cases without a population denominator, so it indicates the direction and scale of reporting rather than a per-capita risk rate.

Official statements reinforce the climate. Responding on 17 April 2022 to the U.S. Bangladesh 2021 Human Rights Report, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared that treating LGBT rights and same-sex marriage as human rights was a regrettable and uncalled-for imposition of values by a select few countries. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019, in an asylum appeal by a Bangladeshi gay man, records Home Office country material describing Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues.

Institutional exclusion extends into education. In November 2023 transgender woman Hochemin Islam was excluded from the North South University women's carnival on security grounds amid student threats of unrest and an exam boycott. In August 2025 transgender woman Sahara Chowdhury, a final-year English student at Metropolitan University in Sylhet, was expelled for life on grounds she denied. In January 2024 a BRAC University lecturer publicly tore a seventh-grade textbook story about a hijra character, prompting student protests against LGBTQ content and a five-member Education Ministry review that four months later found nineteen words "incompatible" with Bangladeshi society and recommended their omission.
BGD.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Section 377 reaches sex between women is unresolved in the sources. A 2019 ILGA report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere describing the provision as relevant to all genders, and the UK Home Office note records the ambiguity without resolving it.

No sourced criteria define who qualifies as a hijra, and no policy sets out the steps required to change gender on official documents. The recognition date appears as 2013 in cabinet records and as 2014 in some advocacy summaries.

The JMBF figure of 260 violations affecting 426 individuals for 2025 is a documented-case count without a population denominator; the sources do not establish true incidence.

The February 2025 Rangamati killing of Shila is recorded with five unidentified accused and no documented outcome.

Enforcement frequency under Section 377 is not quantified in the sources; the characterisation that prosecutions are rare rests on advocacy and government country assessments rather than case statistics.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Bangladesh (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 11 November 2013 the Bangladeshi Government in a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina recognized hijras as a separate gender alongside males and females for identification on official documents, with a Ministry of Social Welfare survey counting 10,000 registered hijras as of 2013. Voter lists offer third-gender options and hijra candidates have run for government positions, and in April 2019 officials introduced 'hijra' as a third-gender option on voting forms for the first time to allow voting under proper gender identity. Bangladesh has no policies outlining measures individuals must undergo to legally change gender on official documents, no clarity about who may qualify as a hijra, and no protections from discrimination for hijra, while other transgender communities beyond hijras remain unrecognised and unprotected from discrimination. In December 2014 the Ministry of Social Welfare invited hijras to apply for government employment, but in January 2015 the Ministry of Health issued a memorandum requesting necessary steps to identify hijras by conducting thorough medical check-ups that required hijras to strip and have genitals confirmed, with photographs later released to confirm hijras are 'really men'. In July 2015 after a hijra witnessed the murder of a secular blogger and helped arrest the perpetrators the government announced plans to recruit and enlist hijras as traffic police. A government housing scheme for homeless or landless individuals includes transgender people for the first time, with at least 140 transgender community members provided government-built houses across the country. Bangladesh opened its first religious school for transgender people in Dhaka with classes starting 7 November 2020 for more than 150 expected students in Islamic and vocational subjects for free with no age limit, while hijras continue to face severe discrimination and unequal access to housing and health care. Formal laws against homosexuality imposed by the British in 1860 through the Indian Penal Code effective in 1862 were carried into the Pakistan Penal Code after the 1947 partition and retained in Bangladesh's legal code since 1971 independence, and Parliament refused to overturn Section 377 in 2009 and 2013. Section 377 ("Unnatural offences") provides: "Whoever voluntarily has carnal intercourse against the order of nature with any man, woman or animal, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine," with explanation that penetration is sufficient and ambit extends to any sexual union involving penile insertion, including consensual heterosexual fellatio and anal penetration. The law is used to arrest, harass and extort individuals based on sexual orientation, with LGBTI groups reporting police used it as pretext to bully LGBTI individuals and those considered effeminate and to limit registration of LGBTI organizations, plus harassment under a suspicious behavior provision of the police code. In May as cited in the 2017 report, RAB forces raided the Chayaneer Community Center in Keraniganj Upazila during an LGBTI dinner, separating 120 present into small groups, beating them, and arresting 28 on suspicion of homosexual activity while allowing media to photograph some, later claiming arrest for narcotics possession (yaba and cannabis) with 4 remanded, 12 detained for questioning and 12 sent directly to jail. Bangladeshi law does not recognise same-sex relationship, civil unions, domestic partnership, or any adoption route for same-sex couples, and same-sex couples have been detained and can be imprisoned and/or fined. Labor law prohibits wage discrimination on the basis of sex or disability but does not prohibit other discrimination based on sex, disability, social status, caste, sexual orientation or similar factors, and there are no legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation. The article states: "While hijras are generally more accepted and have historically held culturally important roles, they also face severe discrimination and unequal access to various social services like housing and health care." The 2017 U.S. Department of State report as cited states: "The transgender population has long been a marginalized, but recognised part of society, but it faced continued high levels of fear, harassment, and law enforcement contact in the wake of violent extremist attacks against vulnerable communities." That report adds LGBTI members received threatening messages via telephone, text and social media with some harassed by police, and that following the raid and continued harassment many members including leadership reduced activities and sought refuge inside and outside the country, severely weakening advocacy and support networks, with organizations specifically assisting lesbians rare. It also notes social stigma against HIV and AIDS and higher-risk populations could be a barrier for accessing health services, especially for the transgender community and men who have sex with men. In November 2023 transgender woman Hochemin Islam faced exclusion from the North South University women's carnival on security grounds amid student threats of unrest and exam boycott and rally banners explicitly expressing "no transgender" sentiments. In August 2025 transgender woman Sahara Chowdhury, final-year English student at Metropolitan University in Sylhet, was expelled for life on stated grounds of online threats and carrying a weapon causing fear, which she denied as following her sharing a satirical caricature involving Asif Mahtab Utsha and Dr. Mohammad Sorowar Hossain. On 19 January 2024 part-time BRAC University lecturer Asif Mahtab Utsha publicly tore the seventh-grade History and Social Science textbook story 'Sharifar Golpo' in which Sharif born male later identifies as woman Sharifa living as Hijra claiming it promotes homosexual and transgender concepts, prompting student protests stating 'Say No To LGBTQ' and class boycott calls, his removal from lectures, and a five-member Education Ministry review that four months later found nineteen words 'incompatible' with Bangladeshi society and recommended omission.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Vietnam and has never been criminalised in Vietnamese history. The Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 without regard to gender or sexual orientation. The 1812 Gia Long Code, Article 332, prohibited prostitution and illicit sexual activity including extra-marital sex, and prosecutions of homosexual conduct could in rare cases be brought under those labels, but enforcement before the colonial period was inconsistent and little to no state action is recorded.

Official hostility has a documented history. In 2002 the Ministry of Labour, Invalids and Social Affairs declared homosexuality a "social evil" comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use, and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and to arrest same-sex couples. Fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013, effective 11 November 2013.

Legal gender recognition rests on Article 37 of the 2015 Civil Code, passed by the National Assembly on 24 November 2015 by 282 votes to 84 and effective from January 2017. It allows people who have undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex. A further implementing bill is still required, so the provision is not fully enforced. A law granting official transgender recognition that was promised for 2017 has not been implemented; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of February 2026, seven years after the National Assembly was expected to complete a draft law by 2020.

Under the Law on Citizen Identification, effective 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their ID card when undergoing gender transition but must present confirmation documents, and the change's legal effect depends on the Gender Affirmation Law being passed first.

Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, which forced transgender people to travel to Thailand for the procedure.

Conversion therapy has been prohibited since 3 August 2022 under Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC from the Ministry of Health, which states that homosexuality, bisexuality and being transgender are not illnesses and that LGBTQ+ people may not be forced into "treatment". The dispatch also required enhanced public communication across medical facilities nationwide so that staff and patients better understand LGBTQ+ individuals, and advised that psychological support be provided by people with an understanding of gender identity. A study published by Lighthouse Vietnam in October 2024 documents the forms conversion efforts take in Vietnam and the experiences of LGBTIQ people subjected to them.

Healthcare access is uneven. Transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters, including being asked "Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?", heightened scrutiny, and a risk of physical and sexual violence driven by economic pressure and stigma, with transgender women in northern provinces and from ethnic minorities particularly exposed. UGA.name: Uganda
UGA.summary:
Uganda's Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023 provides the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality", lengthy prison terms for the promotion of homosexuality, and penalties reaching 20 years for other offences under the Act. In April 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld the Act's core provisions, including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years, and dismissed challenges arguing that public participation requirements had not been met. The same court had earlier voided a comparable 2013 statute on procedural grounds, leaving the 2023 Act fully in force.

Aggravated homosexuality includes sexual intercourse with a person younger than 18 and is punishable by death. Purporting to contract a same-sex marriage, or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony, carries ten years' imprisonment. A clause in the 2023 bill that would have criminalised merely identifying as gay or non-binary with ten years in prison was proposed and excluded from the enacted text. Marriage between persons of the same sex has been constitutionally prohibited since 29 September 2005, when President Museveni signed an amendment stating that such marriages are prohibited.

Enforcement has produced arrests, raids on shelters, evictions and public outings of people perceived to be LGBT, with many living in hiding; a pressure group reported in June 2024 that rights violations against the community were escalating. In February 2026 police in Arua detained two women after neighbours reported them for allegedly kissing in public, among the first known arrests under the 2023 Act.

Violence against transgender people is documented. In January 2024 a transgender woman in Kampala was mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false allegation circulated on TikTok, and sheltered with 20 others at a safe house in the city. Attacks and harassment are frequently carried out or incited by state officials, and discrimination is actively incited by conservative political, religious and community leaders.

In June 2021 a raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala resulted in 44 arrests, with police claiming an illegal same-sex wedding was being held; several detainees alleged that police performed invasive anal examinations.

Digital exposure is a documented enforcement route. Access Now reported in May 2025 that the anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online, with digital entrapment among the main tactics authorities use through apps, and that the companies behind popular apps do too little. Amnesty International reported in October 2024 that criminalisation had shrunk online civic space, with widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence including doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation, and a climate of impunity that forces people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

Legal gender recognition is documented in a single case: in October 2021 a transgender woman, Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro, was issued identification documents identifying her as female, the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised.

Note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying news report (June 2024) covers rights violations against the country's LGBTQ community escalating, per a pressure group.

A news outlet (7 Jan 2024): fear across the main city after the anti-gay laws — a transgender woman mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false social-media allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a city safe house; notes the death penalty for aggravated same-sex conduct, international condemnation, and continued political support for the law in some other countries.
Note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying foreign-government travel advisory for the country includes LGBT-specific warnings under a 'Do Not Travel' advisory.

A digital-rights organisation (15 May 2025): the country's anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online — digital entrapment is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people via apps, while the companies behind popular apps do too little; shares 2025 case research and safety recommendations — directly relevant to visitor device and app risk under the law.

An international rights organisation (23 Oct 2024) report: the devastating impact of criminalisation on digital spaces for LGBTQ people in the country — widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxxing, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the 2023 law fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.
A news outlet (Feb 2026): police arrested two women for allegedly kissing in public — they were detained in a town after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 law.

A foreign government's 2011 human-rights report for the country: the most important problems included violence and discrimination against marginalised groups — women, children, persons with disabilities, and the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community — from the era of the anti-homosexuality bill debates.
UGA.blindTangential:
A 2011 national human rights report listed violence and discrimination against marginalized groups, including the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender community, among the three most important human rights problems in the country, during the period of the anti-homosexuality bill debates.

International condemnation of the 2023 statute has not shifted political support for comparable laws in the subregion.

Public opinion is hostile. A 2013 survey found 96 percent of people in the country believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, while a 2017 poll found 59 percent agreed that gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people.
UGA.localsOnly:
A person convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in childcare facilities in Uganda even after release. Minors convicted of homosexuality face three years' imprisonment.

In June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality. Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest.

In October 2010 the tabloid Rolling Stone published the names, addresses, photographs and hangouts of 100 allegedly gay and lesbian Ugandans with a call for their execution; activist David Kato was murdered in 2011 shortly after winning a lawsuit against the paper.

A 2018 article in African Health Sciences stated that Uganda's high HIV rate has roots in stigma against same-sex sexual behaviour and sex work. Human Rights Watch reported in 2005 that Uganda's abstinence-until-marriage programmes discriminated on the basis of sexual orientation, denying young LGBTQ people information that could save their lives and reinforcing stigma.

Human Rights Watch reported in May 2025 that a small group of Ugandan mothers were speaking publicly for their LGBT children.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.summary:
Egypt's immigration law gives the Ministry of Interior broad authority to refuse entry to, or order the removal of, anyone deemed to disturb public order or morality. The Cairo 52 study 'Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here' (27 November 2023) analyses that statute and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents from 2018 to 2022, and finds the power applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans in cases where no charge was ever upheld. Removal does not require a conviction, or any offence at all, under Egyptian law.

No penal provision names homosexual conduct. Prosecutions proceed instead through the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, whose Article 9(C) the Economic Courts have read together with Penal Code provisions; Cairo 52 reported on 24 January 2024 that this marks a shift from de facto to explicit criminalisation. Court of Cassation rulings in the 1970s had already stripped out the requirement of financial exchange, holding that habitual or multiple partners were sufficient. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, describes public-morality and debauchery provisions being used routinely for arrests that carry prison sentences.

Police entrapment through dating apps is documented. A BBC investigation found officers running fake profiles on apps used by LGBT people, with victims describing blackmail and arrest; no explicit homosexuality statute was needed because the debauchery law supplied the charge. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights documents the same method aimed particularly at transgender women, through fake accounts on dating apps and websites, and records violations continuing inside police stations.

Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing records coerced anal examinations alongside rising arrests of gay and trans people, and states that the authorities turn a blind eye. Forced anal testing was also used on those detained in the 2017 crackdown.

Sentencing exposure attached to online activity is severe. In 2004 a seventeen-year-old private university student received a seventeen-year prison sentence, including two years' hard labour, for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site.

Health care is a further barrier. TIMEP, in a 6 January 2025 submission for Egypt's fourth Universal Periodic Review cycle, reports that transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices that violate the right to health, and that barriers to equitable health services have persisted since the previous review, with pervasive discrimination on grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation in healthcare.

Personal status and family law follow the religious law of the person's recognised religion, and Egyptian law recognises marriage only between a man and a woman. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status should assume no recognition, and should assume that if the relationship becomes known to police it may be treated as evidence in an indictment under provisions against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality.

No law or policy prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression or sex characteristics, as recorded by Outright International and Bedayaa. State officials and police routinely harass, abuse and torture LGBT people, particularly trans people, producing arrests that do not hold up and abuse in custody.

Pew Research Center polling found that 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and no political party or human rights NGO expresses public support for LGBT rights.
EGY.outOfScopeNotes:
The 12 incidents from 2018 to 2022 cited by Cairo 52 are not itemised in the source, and no breakdown by nationality, point of entry or outcome is available.

No consolidated official figures exist for arrests, prosecutions or deportations under the morality and debauchery provisions. The counts that circulate come from NGO and press documentation and cover specific windows, such as the 84 arrests recorded between 25 September and the end of November 2017.

Whether the immigration powers are exercised at ports of entry, as opposed to inside the country, is not separately documented in the sources reviewed.

The Human Rights Watch material dates from 2004 and describes the Queen Boat period; it evidences a pattern rather than current practice. The 2017 media order and the 2018 social-media legislation are reported without published enforcement statistics. The 2014 bathhouse case ended in acquittals and the source does not record the legal basis for them.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Egypt's morality and public order provisions criminalize 'any behavior, or the expression of any idea' deemed immoral or offensive to religious teachings, giving police broad leeway to prosecute LGBTQ expression. In 2017 the Supreme Media Regulatory Council issued an order preventing 'the appearance of the homosexuals' or 'promoting their slogans' in media. In August 2018 the government introduced legislation placing any social network user with more than 5,000 followers under increased scrutiny and prosecution under media laws. In 2013 comedian Bassem Youssef was charged by the Morsi government with 'propagating and promoting homosexuality and obscenity.' State officials and police routinely harass, abuse and torture LGBTQ people, particularly trans people, leading to unfair arrests and abuse in custody. After the September 2017 rainbow flag incident, TV hosts Ahmed Moussa and Mohamed Al Gheity repeatedly incited violence against the community; Moussa shared personal information of flag-raisers, leading to at least 84 arrests between 25 September and the end of November 2017, many subjected to forced anal tests. In December 2014 TV presenter Mona Iraqi collaborated with police to raid a public bathhouse, arresting around 26 men, later acquitted. In January 2019 host Mohamed El Gheity was jailed for one year for hosting a gay man on his TV show. In 2009 newspaper Al Balagh Al Gadid was shut down and two reporters jailed for printing a story about actors' involvement in homosexual prostitution. Personal and family law is governed by the religious law of the person's recognized religion (Islam, Coptic Orthodox Christianity), none of which recognize homosexual relationships, so Egyptian law only recognizes marriage between a man and a woman. If a same-sex relationship becomes public, police may use it as evidence in a criminal indictment under laws against Satanism, prostitution and public immorality. In 2004 a seventeen-year-old private university student received a 17-year prison sentence, including two years' hard labor, for posting a personal profile on a gay dating site. The September 2017 crackdown caused a state of trauma and despair among young Egyptian LGBTQ individuals, with many attempted suicides. Sarah Hegazi, detained for three months after the incident, fled to Canada, was granted asylum and died by suicide in 2020. Many Egyptian LGBTQ youths and individuals left the country due to social and political threats. Pew Research Center found 95% of Egyptians believe homosexuality should not be accepted by society, and polling suggests only a minority support LGBTQ rights, so Egyptian political parties and human rights NGOs do not express public support. The term 'khawalat', historically male cross-dressing dancers, has been stigmatized and used as a derogatory term for passive and gay men. Egyptian cinema has portrayed queer characters almost exclusively in a mode of stereotyping and defamation. After the 2011 revolution LGBTQ activists became more visible and online campaigns against homophobia and transphobia went viral on Twitter and Facebook by 2013, though this did not translate into legal reform. In August 2021 the Central Bank of Egypt confirmed that rainbow holograms on new banknotes were an anti-counterfeiting feature after online critics suggested they were covert LGBTQ support.

Legal gender recognition is being closed off. A Ministry of Interior directive to civil-registry heads nationwide ends the route under the Civil Status Law 143/1994 that allowed transgender Egyptians to correct their gender markers through governorate committees, as reported by Cairo 52 on 12 December 2024.

Egyptian nationals carry the same enforcement exposure without the option of leaving. Bedayaa records rising arrests of gay and trans Egyptians, and the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights documents entrapment aimed particularly at transgender women. Detention conditions and the position of trans people inside the country are documented in Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing as a reference for work on sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics.

PER.name: Peru
PER.summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is lawful in Peru under the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to those for rape. The age of consent is 14 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation, following a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity is not itself an offence.

No legal protection against discrimination or hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is in force. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code. Congress voted 66 to 29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition for removal carrying one million signatures; the repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members, who argued the President lacked authority to issue the decree. President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms matching their gender identity. It followed the April 2025 "Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents", which requires restroom entry to be determined by "biological sex" and prohibits inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity". The measures originated in bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by congressmen Muñante and Montoya; in February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously for plenary the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, presented by Jorge Montoya and the Honor y Democracia party. Human Rights Watch reports that vague child-protection articles, article 4 on media and advertising and article 5, permit censorship of identity, artistic and educational content, and that the minimum sentence for obscenity offences rose from three to four years.

The human-rights institute at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru (IDEHPUCP) assesses the restroom provision as open discrimination against trans and non-binary people, implicitly framing them as harassment risks. It cites Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, which holds that gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons. The restroom law is a state-imposed restriction on trans people's daily movement that can intensify hostile encounters in transit spaces.

Trans Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published on 8 November, permitting a gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law, introduced on 4 November 2016, would allow legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity; it remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021. There is no self-declaration procedure.

In May 2024 the government decreed "transsexualism" a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 the Ministry of Health revised the term to "gender discordance" for health-insurance classification. Human Rights Watch reported in June 2024 that health authorities had removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance. In May 2024 the ministry reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases. Conversion therapy is banned for medical professionals.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years in prison for the torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case. Monitoring organisations report that trans women are the group most affected by hate crimes in the country.

Outright International records that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, ruling on an activist legal challenge, found an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. An April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs allows authorities to revoke registrations on "public order or security" grounds, creating a route to act against queer organising.

Organisations working on trans rights list unmet demands including equal marriage and recognition of diverse families, alongside HIV medication supply, revision of outdated medical rules, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.
PER.outOfScopeNotes:
Official hate-crime counts are described by monitoring organisations as a sub-registry, so no reliable magnitude of trans-specific violence in Peru can be stated from the available figures.

The current status of the Gender Identity Law after March 2021 is not sourced. Whether the restroom restriction is being enforced in practice, and how, is not documented in the available material.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): Congress's committee approved unanimously (for plenary) the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 (presented by Jorge Montoya and Honor y Democracia party) that threatens trans people's rights by restricting their use of public bathrooms; the article also records community demands — HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.

IDEHPUCP (PUCP human-rights institute) analysis: the bathroom-restriction article openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks — the institute cites IACtHR Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights; also quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024): report finds hate crimes rose in Peru with trans women most affected; co-author Gianna Camacho (trans human-rights defender/journalist) stresses recorded numbers are only a sub-registry; cites the 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work.

BBC News Mundo (19 Dec 2025): three police officers sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, trans woman and LGBTI activist — Peru's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per the article, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history (case reached the Court via the CIDH).

Infobae Peru (15 Dec 2025): officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León sentenced to 17 years for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas, nearly 20 years after the attack. The judgment was issued after years of litigation.

HRW (19 May 2025): the April-2025 'Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents' mandates public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people — including trans youth — from facilities matching their identity; vague child-protection articles (art.4 media/advertising ban, art.5) enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content; obscenity-minimum sentence raised 3→4 years; HRW says child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating.

sources.summary: Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Peru since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalized sodomy with penalties akin to rape. Age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation per a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, applicable to trans and cis youth. Discrimination and hate crimes on sexual orientation and gender identity were criminalized by governmental decree Nº 1323, in effect 7 January 2017, under Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code; Congress voted 66–29 in May 2017 to strip the provisions but Kuczynski's veto stood. Law 32331 (enacted 13 May 2025) prohibits trans people from using public restrooms, a state-imposed restriction on trans people's daily movements that could intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces. Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity; in 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a 21 October 2016 ruling published 8 November, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021. In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 MINSA revised the term to 'gender discordance' for health-insurance classification purposes. The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and 'not a voluntary choice'. Opinion polls show age-based variation: 18–24-year-olds (66%) were markedly more favourable toward homosexuals than the population overall (49%), and younger people showed higher approval of same-sex marriage (8.3% approval among Peruvians in 2010, higher among younger respondents). No legal protection against discrimination or hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is in force. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the criminal code. The national legislature voted 66 to 29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, after an April committee vote and a petition for removal carrying one million signatures; the repeal was carried by members of two political parties, who argued the president lacked authority to issue the decree. The president's veto stood at that point, and the protections were removed as the criminal code was reworked. The country is one of only three jurisdictions in the subregion, with two neighbouring jurisdictions, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms matching their gender identity. It followed the April 2025 "Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents", which requires restroom entry to be determined by "biological sex" and prohibits inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity". The measures originated in bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by two congressmen; in February 2025 a legislative committee approved unanimously for plenary the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, presented by a congressman and a political party. An international human rights organisation reports that vague child-protection articles, article 4 on media and advertising and article 5, permit censorship of identity, artistic and educational content, and that the minimum sentence for obscenity offences rose from three to four years.

A university human-rights institute assesses the restroom provision as open discrimination against trans and non-binary people, implicitly framing them as harassment risks. It cites a regional human rights court advisory opinion, OC-24/17, which holds that gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also quotes a congressman's dehumanising comparisons. The restroom law is a national restriction on trans people's daily movement that can intensify hostile encounters in transit spaces.

Trans people in the country may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the constitutional court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published on 8 November, permitting a gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law, introduced on 4 November 2016, would allow legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity; it remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021. There is no self-declaration procedure.

In May 2024 the government decreed "transsexualism" a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 the national health ministry revised the term to "gender discordance" for health-insurance classification. An international human rights organisation reported in June 2024 that health authorities had removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance. In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years in prison for the torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It is the country's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination, and the regional human rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case. Monitoring organisations report that trans women are the group most affected by hate crimes in the country.

An international LGBTIQ organisation records that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination. In July 2025 a constitutional court in the capital, ruling on an activist legal challenge, found an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. An April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs allows authorities to revoke registrations on "public order or security" grounds, creating a route to act against queer organising.

Organisations working on trans rights list unmet demands including equal marriage and recognition of diverse families, alongside HIV medication supply, revision of outdated medical rules, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.
