URY.name: Uruguay
URY.summary:
Uruguay's trans-protection framework is statutory and national. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law No. 19684) was promulgated by the Executive on 26 October 2018 and guarantees identity, health and anti-discrimination rights, obliges authorities to treat trans people respectfully, and bars denial of health services. It builds on Law No. 18.620 of 2009, which establishes the right to free development of personality in accordance with self-perceived gender identity, independent of biological, genetic, anatomical, morphological, hormonal or assigned sex.

Legal gender recognition is administrative and rests on self-declaration. Since October 2018 no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis is required to change legal gender on official documents. Adults have been able to change name and legal gender since October 2009; minors may do so with parental consent under the 2018 law. Under Law No. 18.620 the route runs through a voluntary Family Court process with a specialised multidisciplinary report, requiring proof of discordance with the registered name or sex and that the identity has been stable and persistent for at least two years; changes are notified to civil-identification and electoral authorities, and the person retains the same identity, passport and civic-credential number while exercising the rights attached to the new sex condition.

Official documents carry only female and male markers. Article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognises non-binary people in its definitions, but no third marker exists; a 2022 survey of non-binary people cites the absence of such a marker as deterring use of the legal change procedure.

Hate-crime and anti-discrimination machinery covers sexual orientation and sexual identity. Incitement to hatred on those grounds has been prohibited since 2003, and Penal Code article 149ter provides enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by them. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created an Honorary Commission to Combat Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and other forms of Discrimination, with a mandate covering sexual orientation and sexual identity. The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers; intersex bodily-autonomy protections remain incomplete.

Partner recognition is settled. Civil unions have been available since 1 January 2008 under a law signed on 27 December 2007, requiring at least five years of cohabitation and granting health, inheritance, parenting and pension rights. Marriage has been open to same-sex couples since August 2013, and joint adoption by same-sex couples in a civil union has been permitted since September 2009, the first such provision in Latin America. The 2013 marriage law allows lesbian couples access to in vitro fertilisation, and on 3 October 2018 a family judge ruled that barring an unmarried lesbian couple from giving twins both surnames constituted sexual orientation discrimination.

Open service in the military has been permitted since May 2009 under a Defence Minister decree ending orientation discrimination in recruitment. Since 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men donate blood under the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending the previous 12-month abstinence requirement. The age of consent has been equal at 15 regardless of orientation or gender since 1934.

Violence against trans residents is documented and, in at least one case, prosecuted. Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder. Survey data cited in country coverage records that about two-thirds of transgender Uruguayans report having been victims of physical violence, and state health service figures put transgender life expectancy at about 45 years against a national average of 77.

Enforcement against discrimination is uneven. In May 2024 a trans health-service user, Andreina Stuart, denounced mistreatment and discrimination at San Carlos hospital in Maldonado; a criminal complaint is pending and the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation once the judicial stage concludes, with local officials pressing for health-system updates. In a separate case, Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued the state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

In custody, national authorities have stated that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to decide whether to be placed in a men's or women's prison, and trans women are currently held in female prisons. A new prison planned for Montevideo is to include a specific sector for the trans population, and the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for trans inmates. The Parliamentary Commissioner for the prison system, Juan Miguel Petit, described the sector as good news for a very vulnerable population and estimated it would be ready in under two years; National Rehabilitation Institute director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that the laws are advanced but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line. Official figures record 14,965 people deprived of liberty, including 28 trans women and nine trans men.

Political opposition to the 2018 law exists but has not prevailed. A pre-referendum to repeal it went to the polls on 4 August 2019 and failed, with turnout of about 10 percent against the 25 percent of the electoral roll, roughly 650,000 voters, required to trigger a repeal consultation; the law remains in force. The Archbishop of Montevideo had called same-sex adoption a serious error, and about 69,360 signatures were gathered between November 2018 and March 2019 for the pre-referendum. Freedom House rated Uruguay Free in 2024 at 96/100, with political rights at 40/40 and civil liberties at 56/60. A 2014 poll found about 71 percent of Uruguayans supported same-sex marriage, the highest in South America, and Montevideo Pride has run annually since the 1990s, drawing an estimated 120,000 people in 2018, with Punta Pride held in Punta del Este each February.

Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, legal gender recognition is available, and LGBTI organisations can register. Equaldex records that in Montevideo, where national law applies, marriage, legal gender change, non-discrimination protections, the conversion-therapy ban and an equal age of consent are all in force, and hate-crime rules cover sexual orientation and gender identity.
URY.outOfScopeNotes: Several items remain unresolved. The criminal complaint over the alleged mistreatment of Andreina Stuart at San Carlos hospital was pending, with the hospital's administrative investigation deferred until the judicial stage concludes. The outcome of Beccah Rivas's suit against the state bank BROU is not recorded in the sources consulted. The trans sector in the planned Montevideo prison was estimated in July 2023 to be ready in under two years; no source confirms whether it has opened. Intersex bodily-autonomy protections are described as incomplete, and no third gender marker has been introduced despite article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognising non-binary people in its definitions.

Adults have been able to change name and legal gender since October 2009; minors may do so with parental consent under the 2018 law. Under Law No. 18.620 the route runs through a voluntary family court process with a specialised multidisciplinary report, requiring proof of discordance with the registered name or sex and that the identity has been stable and persistent for at least two years; changes are notified to civil-identification and electoral authorities, and the person retains the same identity, passport and civic-credential number while exercising the rights attached to the new sex condition.

Official documents carry only female and male markers. Article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognises non-binary people in its definitions, but no third marker exists; a 2022 survey of non-binary people cites the absence of such a marker as deterring use of the legal change procedure.

Hate-crime and anti-discrimination machinery covers sexual orientation and sexual identity. Incitement to hatred on those grounds has been prohibited since 2003, and the penal code provides enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by them. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created a national anti-discrimination commission with a mandate covering sexual orientation and sexual identity. The 2017 Mental Health Law (Law No. 19529) bars any mental-health diagnosis made on the exclusive basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Article 22 of Law No. 19580, in force since January 2018, prohibits unnecessary medical procedures on intersex children and teenagers; intersex bodily-autonomy protections remain incomplete.

Partner recognition is settled. Civil unions have been available since 1 January 2008 under a law signed on 27 December 2007, requiring at least five years of cohabitation and granting health, inheritance, parenting and pension rights. Marriage has been open to same-sex couples since August 2013, and joint adoption by same-sex couples in a civil union has been permitted since September 2009, the first such provision in the region. The 2013 marriage law allows lesbian couples access to in vitro fertilisation, and on 3 October 2018 a family judge ruled that barring an unmarried lesbian couple from giving twins both surnames constituted sexual orientation discrimination.

Open service in the military has been permitted since May 2009 under a defence ministry decree ending orientation discrimination in recruitment. Since 16 December 2020 gay and bisexual men donate blood under the same conditions as the rest of the population, ending the previous 12-month abstinence requirement. The age of consent has been equal at 15 regardless of orientation or gender since 1934.

Violence against trans residents is documented and, in at least one case, prosecuted. A 29-year-old trans woman was shot dead in her home in the capital on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder. Survey data cited in country coverage records that about two-thirds of transgender people in the country report having been victims of physical violence, and national health service figures put transgender life expectancy at about 45 years against a national average of 77.

Enforcement against discrimination is uneven. In May 2024 a trans health-service user denounced mistreatment and discrimination at a hospital in a coastal department; a criminal complaint is pending and the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation once the judicial stage concludes, with local officials pressing for health-system updates. In a separate case, a trans woman sued a state-owned bank over discriminatory handling by a private security contractor and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; a prosecutor compelled the bank to produce material, and the complainant says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

In custody, national authorities have stated that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to decide whether to be placed in a men's or women's prison, and trans women are currently held in female prisons. A new prison planned for the capital is to include a specific sector for the trans population, and the new women's prison at a second site would for the first time account for trans inmates. The parliamentary commissioner for the prison system described the sector as good news for a very vulnerable population and estimated it would be ready in under two years; the director of the national rehabilitation institute told a parliamentary hearing that the laws are advanced but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line. Official figures record 14,965 persons deprived of liberty, including 28 trans women and nine trans men.

Political opposition to the 2018 law exists but has not prevailed. A pre-referendum to repeal it went to the polls on 4 August 2019 and failed, with turnout of about 10 percent against the 25 percent of the electoral roll, roughly 650,000 voters, required to trigger a repeal consultation; the law remains in force. A senior religious leader in the capital had called same-sex adoption a serious error, and about 69,360 signatures were gathered between November 2018 and March 2019 for the pre-referendum. An international rights monitor rated the country Free in 2024 at 96/100, with political rights at 40/40 and civil liberties at 56/60. A 2014 poll found about 71 percent of the population supported same-sex marriage, the highest in the region, and the capital's pride march has run annually since the 1990s, drawing an estimated 120,000 individuals in 2018, with a coastal pride event held each February.

Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, legal gender recognition is available, and LGBTI organisations can register. A rights-tracking database records that in the capital, where national law applies, marriage, legal gender change, non-discrimination protections, the conversion-therapy ban and an equal age of consent are all in force, and hate-crime rules cover sexual orientation and gender identity.
URY.blindOutOfScope: Several items remain unresolved. The criminal complaint over the alleged mistreatment of a trans health-service user at a hospital in a coastal department was pending, with the hospital's administrative investigation deferred until the judicial stage concludes. The outcome of a trans woman's suit against a state-owned bank is not recorded in the sources consulted. The trans sector in the planned prison in the capital was estimated in July 2023 to be ready in under two years; no source confirms whether it has opened. Intersex bodily-autonomy protections are described as incomplete, and no third gender marker has been introduced despite article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognising non-binary people in its definitions.

URY.blindLocalsOnly:
Youth and adult outcomes for trans residents are severe. Twenty-five percent of transgender people in the country left home before the age of 18 after family rejection, 87 percent did not finish secondary school, and other studies record about 75 percent expelled from the education system. Only 23 percent hold formal employment, and 67 percent report engaging in prostitution for income. The 2018 law mandates that transgender people receive 1 percent of public and private educational scholarships, calls on government to include them in housing programmes, and provides monetary reparations to transgender people persecuted during the country's period of authoritarian rule, estimated at around 50 people. In July 2019 the national water utility began offering jobs to transgender people in compliance with the law.

Country coverage estimates the transgender population at about 1,000 people. The period of authoritarian rule involved torture, sexual violence and unjustified imprisonment of trans people.
URY.blindTangential:
Regional comparisons place the country at the top of rankings on LGBT inclusion in the region. A 2015 social-climate index ranked it fifth with a score of 73, on a par with higher-income jurisdictions elsewhere, and in 2016 a regional affairs publication named it the most LGBT-friendly country in the region, calling it a model for social inclusion. The country hosted the region's first international LGBT rights conference in July 2016, with hundreds of diplomats, politicians and activists attending.

Commercial and social infrastructure is concentrated in the capital, which has several gay bars, restaurants and pubs and is frequently described as one of the most gay-friendly cities in the region; a coastal resort city hosts a pride event each February. These indices describe general social climate rather than conditions specific to trans residents, whose documented outcomes in health, education and employment diverge sharply from the country's overall standing.

QAT.name: Qatar
QAT.summary:
Qatar criminalises consensual same-sex relations under Article 296 of the Penal Code (Law 11/2004), which carries one to three years' imprisonment. The provision applies to Muslims and non-Muslims alike and covers sexual acts between men and between women. For Muslims convicted in sharia courts a capital sentence remains a theoretical possibility; it has never been imposed. No statute repealing or legalising this exposure appears in the sources. Article 296 replaced Article 201 of the 1971 Penal Code, which had carried up to five years, and before that Article 171 of the 1956 code and the Indian Penal Code imposed through Order in Council in 1938.

Trans people face a separate detention power. They may be held for up to six months without trial or charge on suspicion of "impersonating the opposite gender" or of violating "public morality" and "community protection" provisions.

Qatar does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and cohabitation is itself illegal. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex has no route to formal recognition, and shared accommodation with a partner carries its own exposure.

Enforcement reaches visitors. Human Rights Watch documented six cases of severe repeated beatings and five cases of sexual harassment in police custody between 2019 and 2022, with arrests in public places made solely on the basis of gender expression and searches conducted unlawfully; mistreatment continued as recently as September 2022, as Qatar prepared to host the World Cup.

On 4 February 2024 a dual British-Mexican citizen was arrested after police ran a fake Grindr profile. He was held for 44 days, interrogated about other gay men, forced to sign documents in Arabic without a translator and denied a lawyer. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention raised concerns about his treatment. Detainees in that case were also denied access to antiretroviral medicines needed to live with HIV, a denial the Working Group flagged.

In May 2023 Gilbert Ignatius, a Qatar Airways employee, was detained by the Criminal Investigation Department over his appearance, with tinted moisturizer, designer clothing and a bag cited as evidence of prostitution. An officer told him "You have no rights. This is Qatar," and struck him when he asked to contact the Indonesian embassy. He was later deported, fired and banned from Qatar without official explanation. Ignatius reported that post-World Cup secret police operations especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand.

Earlier cases include the Polish Instagram figure King Luxy, held for two months in 2016 on suspicion of being homosexual, and an American visitor sentenced in 1998 to six months in prison and 90 lashes for homosexual activity. In the 1990s the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration told Philippine workers that gay workers were prohibited in Qatar, following mass arrests and deportations.

Abuse in custody has included beatings, torture and forced "conversion therapy". A May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed, the first Qatari to come out publicly as gay, described LGBTQ people being held and physically abused, then promised safety from further torture if they agreed to inform on others. Trans detainees are required to undergo forced physical detransition, including surgical removal of breast tissue, while held, and must attend conversion "therapy" on release, according to BBC-sourced information that Qatari authorities "categorically rejected".

Public expression is policed. Nasser Al Khater said in December 2021 that public display of affection "is frowned upon", and Major General al-Ansari warned that rainbow flags could be confiscated to "protect" fans. In May 2022 the Emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, said LGBTQ visitors would be welcomed to the World Cup but must respect the nation's culture; the 2013 bid chief Hassan Al-Thawadi had said all were welcome provided they refrained from public displays of affection. Some hotels on FIFA's official recommended accommodation list refused to serve same-sex couples outright in May 2022, while others accepted them only if they hid the relationship in public; FIFA said it would remind hotels of non-discrimination requirements.

Campaigning for LGBTQ rights is not permitted. In 2022 police arrested protesters who criticised Qatari law.

In 2013 Kuwait proposed banning gay foreigners from entering any Gulf Cooperation Council country. The GCC agreed to discuss the proposal and then backtracked, possibly over concerns about the effect on Qatar's 2022 World Cup hosting.
QAT.outOfScopeNotes:
The capital sentence for same-gender sex has never been imposed, and one line of argument holds that because same-gender couples cannot marry, the penalty applies only to Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions. The sources do not resolve how that reading would operate in practice.

The account of forced surgical detransition of trans detainees is attributed to BBC-sourced information; Qatari authorities "categorically rejected" it. No independent confirmation appears in the inventory.

The Government Communications Office pledged an investigation into the 2018 censorship of articles on gay and transgender rights from the Doha edition of The New York Times International Edition; the outcome is not sourced.

Whether the 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council proposal to ban gay foreigners from entry was abandoned permanently, or only shelved, is not established by the sources.

sources.summary:
Qatar's Penal Code Article 296 (Law 11/2004) punishes sodomy with one to three years' imprisonment. It replaced Article 201 of the 1971 code, which had carried up to five years, and before that Article 171 of the 1956 code and the Indian Penal Code imposed through Order in Council in 1938. Sexual acts between males and between females are illegal and punishable by up to three years in prison for Muslims and non-Muslims alike; for Muslims duly convicted in sharia courts a capital sentence remains a theoretical possibility, though never imposed. Trans people may be detained for up to six months without trial or charge on suspicion of "impersonating the opposite gender" or of violating "public morality" and "community protection" provisions. The government does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and cohabitation is itself illegal. Because same-gender couples cannot marry, the local death penalty for same-gender sex is argued to apply only to Muslims through extramarital-sex provisions.

Detentions and prosecutions have targeted visitors and residents. On 4 February 2024 a dual British-Mexican citizen was arrested after police ran a fake Grindr profile; he was held 44 days, interrogated about other gay men, forced to sign documents in Arabic without a translator and denied a lawyer. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention raised concerns about his treatment, and the detainees in that case were denied access to antiretroviral medicines needed to live with HIV, a denial the Working Group also flagged. In 2016 the Polish Instagram star King Luxy spent two months in custody on suspicion of being homosexual. In 1998 an American visitor was sentenced to six months in prison and 90 lashes for homosexual activity. In May 2023 Gilbert Ignatius, a Qatar Airways employee, was detained by Qatar's Criminal Investigation Department over his appearance, with tinted moisturizer, designer clothing and a bag cited as evidence of prostitution; an officer told him "You have no rights. This is Qatar," and struck him when he asked to contact the Indonesian embassy. He was later deported, fired and banned from Qatar without official explanation. Ignatius reported that post-World Cup secret police crackdowns especially target people who appear to be from the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand. In the 1990s the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration told Philippine workers that gay workers were prohibited in Qatar after mass arrests and deportations.

Abuse by police and other authorities against LGBTQ people has included beatings, torture and forced "conversion therapy". An October 2022 Human Rights Watch report alleged systemic police brutality based on eyewitness accounts from 2019 to 2022. A May 2022 account by Naser Mohamed, the first Qatari to publicly come out as gay, described LGBTQ people being held and physically abused, then promised safety from further torture if they agreed to become informants against others. Trans detainees are required to undergo forced physical detransition, including surgical removal of breast tissue, while held, and must attend conversion "therapy" on release, according to BBC-sourced information that Qatari authorities "categorically rejected". The government does not allow people in Qatar to campaign for LGBTQ rights, and in 2022 police arrested protesters who criticised Qatari law.

In 2013 Kuwait proposed banning gay foreigners from entering any Gulf Cooperation Council country and the GCC agreed to discuss it, then backtracked, possibly over concerns about the effect on Qatar's 2022 World Cup hosting. In May 2022 the Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said LGBTQ visitors would be welcomed to the World Cup but must respect the nation's culture, and in 2013 bid chief Hassan Al-Thawadi said all were welcome provided they refrained from public displays of affection. In May 2022 some hotels on FIFA's official recommended accommodation list refused to serve same-sex couples outright, while others accepted them only if they hid their relationship in public; FIFA said it would remind hotels of non-discrimination requirements. The Australian men's national team publicly called in October 2022 for Qatar to recognise same-sex marriage.

Qatar voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity at the Human Rights Council in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025. In 2018 nine articles on gay and transgender rights were censored from the Doha edition of The New York Times International Edition, prompting the Government Communications Office to pledge an investigation. A 2016 Doha News opinion piece by a gay Qatari man writing as "Majid Al-Qatari" drew extremely strong reactions for allowing the topic to be discussed. In June 2019 state-linked AJ+ marked LGBTQ Pride Month, prompting criticism of the paradox with domestic censorship, and in 2022 Transport for London banned Qatari advertising after Qatar moved to block rainbow armbands, with Qatar subsequently reviewing its London investments. Nasser Al Khater said in December 2021 that public display of affection "is frowned upon", and Major General al-Ansari warned that rainbow flags could be confiscated to "protect" fans.

QAT.comparisons: Unlike Kuwait (statute repealed, courts awarding compensation) or Bahrain (rare enforcement), Qatar's targeting of gender expression is systematic, current, and unreformed — placing it below both despite their shared Gulf context.

KWT.name: Kuwait
KWT.summary:
Kuwait's Penal Code Article 198 was amended in 2007 by Article 199 bis, which criminalised an indecent act in a public place or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars, about US$3,500. The amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support. Human Rights Watch found that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor obtain protection from the policing it authorised.

In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck down the provision as unconstitutional, after an individual who had been targeted by police challenged it. The ruling removed the criminal exposure the article created; it did not end the dress-code policing that preceded and outlasted it. Human Rights Watch called on parliament to repeal the law outright rather than leave the matter to the court's decision.

Enforcement of the 2007 provision was immediate. Within two weeks of it taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, in coffee shops and in taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as a punishment. Appearance-based policing continued after the article's annulment: in 2017 a social media figure was arrested in Kuwait for allegedly looking too feminine and held for two weeks before release.

Penal Code Article 193 continues to punish consensual same-sex relations between men by up to seven years in prison, and adultery by up to five. Public morality laws are strictly enforced and prosecutions of LGBTQ people are routine. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship, or whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status, falls within the reach of that provision.

A year after the Constitutional Court ruling, DAWN MENA reported that discrimination against transgender people continued in practice and that the decision had not opened a path to recognising transgender rights. The ruling is a limit on state power, not a change in the wider legal regime.

Kuwait's communications regulator, CITRA, has blocked LGBTQI+ material online, including advocacy and legal information. Censors banned the film 'The Danish Girl', and in August 2023 banned 'Barbie' on the claim that it promoted homosexuality; in July 2019 the Ministry of Commerce carried out a crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops.

On entry screening, it was announced in September 2013 that all Gulf Cooperation Council states had agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of testing to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners. Officials later insisted it was only a proposal, and concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar was cited as a reason for backtracking. No source documents the proposal being implemented.

Foreigners found to be infected with HIV/AIDS are deported, while Kuwaiti citizens who are infected are entitled to outpatient care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence has remained under 0.1 percent through the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25 to 49 making up 47 percent of those with HIV. In 1992 the National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV.
KWT.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council testing proposal was ever implemented is unresolved. Officials described it as a proposal only and cited the 2022 World Cup as a reason for backtracking; no source documents testing at Kuwaiti ports of entry.

Parliament had not repealed Article 198 as of the sources. Human Rights Watch's call for outright repeal and Cairo 52's analysis of post-abolition steps leave the legislative position unresolved.

The scale of dress-code policing after February 2022 is not quantified. DAWN MENA documents continuing discrimination but no systematic enforcement data.

Sources describe the struck provision both as Article 198 and as the 2007 amendment Article 199 bis; the two references are not reconciled in the available material.

No youth-specific or minor-specific HIV care access provisions are documented, and whether the 2019 reapplication for an LGBTQ association received a response is not sourced.

sources.summary: Brian Whitaker's overview essay (2016) on transgender issues in the Middle East: gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans people especially vulnerable; notes 'The Danish Girl' was banned by censors in Kuwait among other countries; discusses cross-dressing as a crime across the region.

HRW (17 Feb 2022): Kuwait's Constitutional Court struck down the 2007 anti-transgender provision ('imitating the opposite sex') as unconstitutional; HRW urged parliament to repeal the law outright — the ruling removed criminal exposure but not the underlying dress-code policing practice.
A Library of Congress country entry records the Kuwait Constitutional Court ruling that struck down Article 198 of the Penal Code.

US State Dept 2023 Country Report on Kuwait (via ecoi): communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information; no candidate ran for National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation — documents censorship and invisibility of LGBT political participation.

HRW World Report 2024, Kuwait (events of 2023): penal code art. 193 still punishes consensual same-sex relations between men by up to 7 years and adultery by up to 5 years; positive step noted — Feb 2022 Constitutional Court ruling unconstitutional the 2007 art. 198 'imitating' provision.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute (11 Jul 2024): the 2007 amendment criminalising 'imitating the opposite sex' was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei with overwhelming parliamentary support, and abolished by the Constitutional Court in 2022 after an individual targeted by police challenged it — analysis of the steps still needed after abolition.

DAWN MENA (13 Feb 2023, Nora Noralla): a year after the Constitutional Court overturned the anti-transgender law, transgender discrimination continues in practice — the ruling was not a first step toward recognizing transgender rights, with social and employment discrimination persisting.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' (16 Apr 2018): regional study of LGBT activism in 22 MENA jurisdictions incl. Kuwait, based on interviews with 34 activists; six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or activism.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: In September 2013 it was announced that all Gulf Cooperation Council states had agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of 'testing' to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners; officials later insisted it was only a proposal, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking. Same-sex sexual activity between men is illegal under Kuwait's penal code with penalties of up to seven years in prison, and public morality laws are strictly enforced, leading to regular prosecutions of LGBTQ people. In 2017 Instagram star King Luxy was arrested in Kuwait for allegedly looking too feminine and spent two weeks in custody before release. A 2022 Constitutional Court ruling overturned the criminalisation of 'imitation of the opposite sex', though discrimination by officials persists. Foreigners found to be infected with HIV/AIDS are deported, whereas Kuwaiti citizens who are infected are entitled to outpatient medical care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence has remained under 0.1 percent through to the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25-49 making up 47 percent of those with HIV, and in 1992 the National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV; no youth-specific or minor-specific care access provisions are documented. No known association or charity exists in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or to organise educational and social events for the LGBTQ community. In 2007 a group of Kuwaitis applied to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form such an association and never received a formal reply, and in July 2019 they announced they would reapply after a Ministry of Commerce crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops. In August 2023 Kuwait banned the film 'Barbie', claiming it promoted homosexuality; no youth- or education-specific findings about minors are documented.

KWT.tangentialFactors:
Cross-dressing is criminalised across much of the region, and gender segregation combined with enforced dress codes leaves trans people especially vulnerable; a 2016 regional survey records this pattern and notes that censors in Kuwait banned 'The Danish Girl' alongside other jurisdictions.

Human Rights Watch's 2018 study of LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa covered 22 jurisdictions and drew on interviews with 34 activists. Six interviewees, from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco, had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or their activism.

The 2022 annulment came from an individual challenge by someone the police had targeted, not from a legislative initiative. Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute's July 2024 analysis set out the steps still required after abolition, and the 2007 amendment's passage with overwhelming parliamentary support stands in contrast to the court's later decision.
KWT.blindSummary:
The country's penal code article 198 was amended in 2007 by article 199 bis, which criminalised an indecent act in a public place or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars, about US$3,500. The amendment was proposed by a member of the national assembly and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support. An international human rights organisation found that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor obtain protection from the policing it authorised.

In February 2022 the constitutional court struck down the provision as unconstitutional, after an individual who had been targeted by police challenged it. The ruling removed the criminal exposure the article created; it did not end the dress-code policing that preceded and outlasted it. The organisation called on the national assembly to repeal the law outright rather than leave the matter to the court's decision.

Enforcement of the 2007 provision was immediate. Within two weeks of it taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, in coffee shops and in taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as a punishment. Appearance-based policing continued after the article's annulment: in 2017 a social media figure was arrested in the country for allegedly looking too feminine and held for two weeks before release.

The penal code article 193 continues to punish consensual same-sex relations between men by up to seven years in prison, and adultery by up to five. Public morality laws are strictly enforced and prosecutions of LGBTQ people are routine. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship, or whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status, falls within the reach of that provision.

A year after the constitutional court ruling, a regional rights organisation reported that discrimination against transgender people continued in practice and that the decision had not opened a path to recognising transgender rights. The ruling is a limit on state power, not a change in the wider legal regime.

The national communications regulator has blocked LGBTQI+ material online, including advocacy and legal information. Censors banned a film about a transgender woman, and in August 2023 banned another film on the claim that it promoted homosexuality; in July 2019 the national commerce ministry carried out a crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbows in shops.

On entry screening, it was announced in September 2013 that a regional bloc of states had agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of testing to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners. Officials later insisted it was only a proposal, and concern over hosting a regional sporting event in a neighbouring jurisdiction was cited as a reason for backtracking. No source documents the proposal being implemented.

Foreigners found to be infected with HIV/AIDS are deported, while nationals who are infected are entitled to outpatient care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital. HIV incidence has remained under 0.1 percent through the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25 to 49 making up 47 percent of those with HIV. In 1992 the national assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV.
KWT.blindOutOfScope:
Whether the 2013 regional testing proposal was ever implemented is unresolved. Officials described it as a proposal only and cited a regional sporting event as a reason for backtracking; no source documents testing at the country's ports of entry.

The national assembly had not repealed article 198 as of the sources. The call for outright repeal and the legal research institute's analysis of post-abolition steps leave the legislative position unresolved.

The scale of dress-code policing after February 2022 is not quantified. The regional rights organisation documents continuing discrimination but no systematic enforcement data.

Sources describe the struck provision both as article 198 and as the 2007 amendment article 199 bis; the two references are not reconciled in the available material.

No youth-specific or minor-specific HIV care access provisions are documented, and whether the 2019 reapplication for an LGBTQ association received a response is not sourced.

BHR.name: Bahrain
BHR.summary:
Bahrain repealed its British colonial-era sodomy statute in 1976 and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression as such. The 1976 penal code sets the age of adulthood for consensual same-sex acts at 21.

That baseline does not translate into safety from arrest. Police apply the morality and indecency provisions of the penal code, Articles 324, 329 and 350, which carry between three months and two years' imprisonment, fines of up to 200 Bahraini dinars, and deportation for non-Bahrainis. The government has used these articles against people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of cross-dressing. In 2009 a man was sentenced to one month in jail for wearing an abaya and carrying a purse in public; in 2011 police raided a party described as a same-sex wedding. The Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation in February 2024.

Entry screening is a documented risk. The Interior Minister has stated that "suspected" effeminate homosexuals are barred from entering Bahrain and that airport checks are used to identify them. Bills before parliament have proposed expressly banning LGBTQ foreigners from entering the kingdom or holding residency permits. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council states agreed to discuss a proposal for testing to bar gay foreigners from entry; officials later retreated from it.

Legal gender recognition runs through the courts and is effectively closed. Judges require medical documentation of a "sex change operation" or of medical necessity before a marker can be changed. A 2023 ruling held that sex-reassignment procedures contravene Islamic law where the case is treated as arising solely from gender dysphoria, which confines eligibility in practice to people with intersex traits. In a May 2023 judgment a lower court refused a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and for gender-affirming care on Sharia grounds, and also refused the Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he had requested. Gender-affirming care is correspondingly restricted for anyone who needs it while in the country.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. Article 309 of the penal code protects religious groups from hate speech but extends no equivalent protection to LGBTQ people, and hostile speech against them carries no legal consequence.

Article 330 requires anyone charged with prostitution or "fujoor" to be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and allows relocation to a medical facility. For a trans person taken into custody, that provision places a compulsory medical examination inside the arrest process.

There is no LGBTQ community infrastructure to fall back on. The US Department of State records no approved LGBTQ-related organisations, and ILGA judges it improbable that any sexual- or gender-diversity group could register, since the body that approves associations may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order. No LGBTQ-specific shelters or facilities are documented.
BHR.outOfScopeNotes:
The 1976 decriminalisation date rests on ILGA-sourced and Wikipedia infobox material and on Outright International's country page; no Bahraini statute text confirming the repeal was located in this inventory. The Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board's 2016 finding that homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain is not reconciled with that reading.

The September 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council proposal to test and bar gay foreign nationals was discussed but never adopted; officials publicly retreated from it, and no implementing measure is documented.

The bills restricting entry and residency for LGBTQ foreigners, the October 2021 gatherings bill and the proposed teacher-guidance measures are recorded as proposals. Whether any has been enacted is not established by the sources here.

Violence data specific to trans people in Bahrain is not sourced in this inventory.

OMN.name: Oman
OMN.summary:
Oman criminalises same-sex conduct under the 2018 Penal Law, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment. The law applies to both men and women, and suspects may be prosecuted without a prior complaint where the act causes a public scandal. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would class as same-sex falls within the same exposure. The same statute set reaches gender expression and presentation, and the offences are enforced against foreign nationals.

Article 265 of the Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018) covers public indecency, punishable by 10 days to 3 months' imprisonment and a fine of OMR 100 to 300. Article 266 covers impersonation and entering women-only venues while disguised, carrying 1 month to 1 year; Article 266(d) is the route through which gender non-conformity is punished. Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content judged to violate public morals, offline and online, with penalties of up to 1 year and 10 days to 1 month respectively. The Cyber Crime Law 2011, Articles 17 and 31, has been used against LGBT expression, carrying 1 month to 3 years and fines of OMR 100 to 3,000. The 2018 code added the provision punishing any man who appears to dress in women's clothing.

The Public Prosecution has stated that any male who appears in female clothing or demeanour may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed for up to one year, with additional charges available for publishing such material on social media.

Enforcement is documented. In September 2018 a Salalah preliminary court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photographs of themselves in women's clothing on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video. The Royal Oman Police had arrested a group of men in January 2018 for dressing as women after social-media photographs circulated. In July 2020 Human Rights Watch wrote to the authorities about arrests and convictions under the imitating-the-opposite-sex provision, including arrests announced by the Royal Oman Police of men in women's clothing after photographs from a private party in Salalah circulated, and the case of an Asian expatriate detained in an abaya and niqab during a women-only park hour in Al Buraimi.

Border and airport screening carries a direct risk of outing and mistreatment. A genderqueer, non-binary Indian model and activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa in February 2023 said her friends cleared immigration while she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers.

Foreign nationals face an additional consequence. Article 60 requires deportation for a foreign national convicted of a felony, permanently, and permits it for a misdemeanour for 3 to 15 years.

Prosecution is often triggered by digital evidence found during unrelated investigations rather than by a family complaint; Article 49 provides a dual-criminality exception. The state internet service provider, Omantel, enables surveillance. Outing therefore carries both social and criminal risk.

Legal gender recognition is not available, and gender-affirming healthcare is explicitly banned. A joint stakeholder submission by Cairo 52 and White Tent to Oman's fourth-cycle UN Universal Periodic Review in August 2025 documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people, states that recent legislative developments have deepened the criminalisation of gender expression, and records that Oman has not acted on earlier UPR recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access. The submission recommends ending criminalisation, adopting anti-discrimination legislation and permitting legal recognition.

Assembly and advocacy are restricted through the Civil Associations Law, and advocacy for LGBT rights is treated as a criminal act.
OMN.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Oman could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403). Its documented content on the criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression could not be verified directly against the source.

Sources give inconsistent article numbering for the relevant provisions. The cross-dressing offence is cited as Article 22 in one report and as Article 266 in the statute extraction; the same-sex conduct provisions are cited as sections 33 and 223. The numbering is unresolved.

No source states where inside the prison system gender-nonconforming people convicted in Oman were housed.

No source provides a documented statement on societal tolerance of transgender people specifically in Oman; the available material addresses LGBT populations generally.

A scholarly source on religious and legal frameworks distinguishes criminalisation of homosexual acts from criminalisation of identity in some jurisdictions, but offers no Oman-specific finding and is not relied on here.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Oman (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 2018, four men who cross-dressed as women in Salalah were arrested. They were imprisoned following the arrest. They were also punished with fines at maximum amounts. The enforcement action was taken under laws against "indecent" dress and behaviour. No separate transgender-specific penal code section number is stated in the article for this enforcement. The homosexuality provisions in §§ 33 and 223 are sexuality-law facts and are not included as transgender-specific facts here. Homosexuality in the Sultanate of Oman is illegal under §§ 33 and 223 of the penal code. The punishment is a prison sentence of up to three years. The law applies to both men and women. Suspects of homosexual or lesbian intercourse shall be prosecuted without a prior complaint if the act results in a public scandal. In September 2013, all Gulf Cooperative Countries agreed to discuss a proposal to devise a test for homosexuality intended to single out gay foreigners and prevent them from entering any of the countries. The suggested reason for backtracking was concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar and fears of controversy if football fans were screened, with officials insisting it was a mere proposal. LGBTQ people in Oman face significant social and legal challenges not experienced by non-LGBTQ residents. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically, so no transgender-specific tolerance quote can be reproduced. Advocacy for LGBTQ rights in Oman is a criminal act, as in other Gulf countries. Activists use social media with an alias to protect their identities, with very rare exceptions. These advocacy-related facts are stated for LGBTQ advocacy generally and are not stated as transgender-specific.

The law applies to both men and women, and suspects may be prosecuted without a prior complaint where the act causes a public scandal. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would class as same-sex falls within the same exposure. The same statute set reaches gender expression and presentation, and the offences are enforced against foreign nationals.

Article 265 of the penal law covers public indecency, punishable by 10 days to 3 months' imprisonment and a fine of 100 to 300 in local currency. Article 266 covers impersonation and entering women-only venues while disguised, carrying 1 month to 1 year; Article 266(d) is the route through which gender non-conformity is punished. Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content judged to violate public morals, offline and online, with penalties of up to 1 year and 10 days to 1 month respectively. A 2011 cybercrime law, Articles 17 and 31, has been used against LGBT expression, carrying 1 month to 3 years and fines of 100 to 3,000 in local currency. The 2018 code added the provision punishing any man who appears to dress in women's clothing.

The national prosecution service has stated that any male who appears in female clothing or demeanour may be fined up to 3,000 in local currency and jailed for up to one year, with additional charges available for publishing such material on social media.

Enforcement is documented. In September 2018 a court in a city sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and fined them 3,000 each in local currency for cross-dressing and sharing photographs of themselves in women's clothing on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video. Border and airport screening carries a direct risk of outing and mistreatment. A genderqueer, non-binary foreign national arriving at an international airport on a 10-day tourist visa in February 2023 said their friends cleared immigration while they were held for a separate examination, made to remove their shirt and touched inappropriately by officers.

BGR.name: Bulgaria
BGR.summary:
Bulgaria criminalises neither gender identity nor gender expression, and no statute governs which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in 1968. A foreign passport is examined on ordinary terms at the border, and a recorded gender marker raises no separate question; no entry rule or screening procedure turns on a visitor's gender identity.

Legal gender recognition is closed. The Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 holds that "the only meaning of the term sex should be its biological one" and that the legal system rests on "the binary existence of humankind", which bars legal gender change. The Constitutional Court's verdict on the Istanbul Convention condemned legislation providing for legal gender recognition.

The European Court of Human Rights found in Y.T. v Bulgaria in 2020 that refusal of legal gender recognition violated Article 8, and in its December 2024 revision decision made clear that those obligations were unaffected by the 2024 registry revision, consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria. Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic.

External pressure on the ban is live but unresolved. In September 2025 an Advocate General of the Court of Justice of the European Union issued an opinion that EU law precludes national legislation such as Bulgaria's refusing a trans person identity documents matching their presented gender, and the court concurred with the Advocate General's proposed reasoning. The full judgment was pending.

Anti-discrimination protection is layered and incomplete. The Protection Against Discrimination Act took effect on 1 January 2004, covering direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and healthcare, and was expanded in 2015 to cover "sex" including "sex change". Gender identity and gender expression are not explicitly named in that revision. Health services fall under the sexual-orientation discrimination ban in force since 1 January 2004.

Hate-crime law exists; enforcement is the documented failure. Amnesty International reported in February 2015 that authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate bias crimes, that attacks spiked in 2013 according to the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee, and that the Sofia prosecution opened only some cases. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw such hate crimes was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections. Heavier penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation were adopted on 28 July 2023.

Documented violence includes the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to "cleanse" the park of gay men, and the assault in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 of children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of the Botev football club. The first Sofia Pride in 2008, with about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles, and more than 60 hooligans were arrested.

Public LGBT visibility is secured by police presence rather than settled tolerance. The 2011 Sofia Pride passed without incident under heavy police guard with only a "Family NGO" protest, after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions. Ahead of the 10 June 2017 march, Human Rights Watch urged authorities to protect participants after the National Resistance group rallied counter-demonstrators to "cleanse Sofia from garbage".

State hostility also operates through education law. On 7 August 2024 parliament amended the education law to prohibit "propaganda, promotion, or incitement... directly or indirectly" of ideas about "non-traditional sexual orientation and/or gender identity other than the biological one", defined as attraction contrary to Bulgaria's legal concept of opposite sexes. President Rumen Radev signed it and it entered into force on 16 August 2024; the amendment was introduced by the Revival party with the backing of GERB.

At municipal level, the Pazardzhik District Council voted in November 2009 to forbid the "public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation". The Administrative Court struck it down in October 2010 for procedural errors and upheld it on appeal in July 2011.

Partner recognition is contested and inconsistent. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, banning same-sex marriage; the Constitution does not prohibit civil unions, but none exist, so couples are denied inheritance, medical decision-making and joint property rights. A Sofia court granted an Australian woman and her French wife, married in France in 2016, the right to reside in Bulgaria on 29 June 2018 under the Coman ruling, after they had been refused a year earlier, and a Bulgarian court recognised a same-sex marriage performed in France in 2019. A couple married in the United Kingdom had their recognition claim rejected by the Sofia Administrative Court in January 2018, and the LGBT organisation Deystvie pursued an appeal. In September 2023 the European Court of Human Rights held that Bulgaria's refusal to recognise same-sex couples is an "infringement of human rights"; that case was subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. Same-sex couples are barred from adopting, and a 2021 Court of Justice of the European Union ruling forced Bulgaria to issue identity documents to the child of a lesbian couple after it refused a birth certificate. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Bulgarian law, recognition depends on litigation that has gone both ways.

Whether the 2015 revision of the Protection Against Discrimination Act reaches gender identity and gender expression is not resolved by the sources; the amended text names "sex" including "sex change" only.

The constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, banning same-sex marriage; the constitution does not prohibit civil unions, but none exist, so couples are denied inheritance, medical decision-making and joint property rights. A court in the capital granted a woman and her wife, married in another jurisdiction in 2016, the right to reside in the country on 29 June 2018 under a regional court ruling, after they had been refused a year earlier, and a court in the country recognised a same-sex marriage performed in another jurisdiction in 2019. A couple married in another jurisdiction had their recognition claim rejected by an administrative court in the capital in January 2018, and an LGBT organisation pursued an appeal. In September 2023 a regional human rights court held that the country's refusal to recognise same-sex couples is an "infringement of human rights"; that case was subject to appeals and awaiting a government response. Same-sex couples are barred from adopting, and a 2021 regional court ruling forced the country to issue identity documents to the child of a lesbian couple after it refused a birth certificate. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under the country's law, recognition depends on litigation that has gone both ways.
BGR.blindOutOfScope:
The September 2025 opinion of the regional court had not produced a final judgment in the sources reviewed, so its effect on the country's recognition ban is unresolved.

The September 2023 finding of the regional human rights court on non-recognition was subject to appeal, and a government response was awaited.

Whether the 2015 revision of the anti-discrimination act reaches gender identity and gender expression is not resolved by the sources; the amended text names "sex" including "sex change" only.

Current levels of hate-crime investigation and prosecution are not sourced here. The enforcement failure is documented in a 2015 report, and later reporting carries the pattern forward without updated figures.

The sources do not state whether the municipal ban remains in force after the July 2011 appeal decision.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: in August 2024 a law banning representation of LGBTI identities in schools was introduced (spearheaded by a nationalist party leader); the country continues rejecting asylum requests by LGBTI people from two other states and unlawfully detains LGBTI asylum-seekers from a conflict region in closed detention; a performer at the capital's Pride event received death threats; an LGBTI youth organisation faced institutional checks.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004, expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex change' under 'sex'. But a constitutional marriage-definition provision bans same-sex marriage, and there is no legal gender recognition. A 2023 regional human-rights court judgment (brought by two same-sex couples) found this country in violation of its obligations on non-recognition of same-sex relationships.

A regional union rights agency's LGBTIQ survey country sheet for this country (2024): 75% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (union-wide: 53%); 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (union-wide: 29%); only 27% are open about being LGBTIQ (union-wide: 51%); 28% felt discriminated against at work or looking for work. Indicates a strongly hostile day-to-day climate.

Foreign public broadcaster (Sept 2025): an advocate general of the regional union's court of justice issued a non-binding opinion that this country must not refuse a trans woman ID documents matching her presented sex ('lived gender identity') - the case concerns a trans woman on hormone therapy refused documents; such opinions are followed by the court in roughly two-thirds of cases.

Regional human-rights court analysis blog (Dec 2024) of a line of cases against this country: the original 2020 judgment found a violation of the convention's private-life article over refusal of legal gender recognition; on revision (July 2024) the application was declared inadmissible for abuse of process, but the court confirmed the country remains obliged (under a later judgment) to provide a framework for legal gender recognition - which it still lacks.

International human-rights organisation report (Feb 2015): the country's failure to adequately investigate and prosecute hate crimes fuels fear, discrimination and violence against asylum seekers, migrants, religious minorities and LGBT people; authorities consistently fail to identify bias motivation.
An international rights group (Jun 2017): urges this country's authorities to protect the capital's pride event and showcase a tolerant side of the country.

News outlet (June 2011): the 4th capital Pride march passed without incidents under heavy police guard - after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 parades; only a 'traditional family' NGO protested.
BGR.blindLocalsOnly:
Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the "easier operation", with parents "rarely informed" of later harm to the child's gender identity, and there are no laws concerning intersex people.

An LGBTI support organisation, founded in 2016, works with LGBTI youth on coming out and affirmation, and launched the country's first licensed online support chat in October 2017 for LGBTI youth, families and allies.

A 2008 survey of 15 schools in the capital and two other cities found 10.5% of students identified as bisexual and 1.8% as gay; 29% said they would refuse to sit next to a gay classmate, 5% said they would bully gay classmates and 39% said they would protect them.

Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred from donating blood. The donor form, under a health ministry ordinance of 19 July 2004, does not ask orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV or STI-risk practices.
BGR.blindTangential:
A regional advocacy ranking placed the country 37th of 49 jurisdictions in the region for LGBT rights protection in 2020.

Billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in two cities were vandalised in December 2018, and the dominant religious institution calls pride events a "sinful demonstration".

Anti-LGBT rhetoric rose in 2020 and 2021, a period in which "gender became a slur"; a far-right group advocated brooms and shovels against pride attendees, and a far-right party mounted protests.

The 1964 show trial of 26 men, including two public figures, was described by experts as "a masquerade for the public" about "decadent Western culture".

SVK.name: Slovakia
SVK.summary:
Slovakia presents no entry or documentation obstacle specific to a trans visitor. Movement into and residence in the country falls under European Union free-movement rules. Under the Court of Justice of the European Union's Coman ruling of 5 June 2018, couples resident in Slovakia who married in an EU state where one partner holds EU citizenship enjoy full residency rights, and the Interior Ministry announced immediate compliance.

Legal gender recognition exists in principle but the procedure is medicalised and restrictive. In practice surgical sterilisation has usually been required before identity documents can be amended, and registry offices are refusing to process gender-change applications pending new standards. The Ministry of Health's standards of care were revoked on 18 May 2022 under pressure from the Conference of Slovak Bishops and legislators, leaving no valid standards; by 18 November 2022 healthcare providers were refusing transgender care, forcing people to seek treatment abroad. Standards were republished on 3 March 2023, but their implementation in care access and civil registries remains to be seen. A guideline that had permitted document change without surgery was revoked on 21 November 2023 on grounds of government coalition stability.

Legislative attempts to criminalise trans lives have recurred. Bills tabled by ĽSNS on 12 February 2021 and by the Republic Movement on 23 September 2021 and again on 13 January 2023 sought to ban legal gender change and, in the 2023 version, to outlaw medical transition with a prison sentence of at least four years. All failed, mostly on abstentions. A separate bill of 24 February 2023 restricting legal gender change to people whose sex was 'wrongly assigned at birth', provable only by a karyotype test, passed first reading with 87 votes.

Hate-crime and anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation more explicitly than gender identity. A Criminal Code amendment of May 2013 added sexual orientation as a hate-crime ground carrying harsher penalties and outlawed hate speech on that basis. The Anti-Discrimination Act, adopted in 2004 to meet EU requirements and broadened in 2008, outlaws discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity across employment, education, housing, social care and the provision of goods and services, and applies to the military, where LGBT people serve openly; a 2005 Pravda report described a 'very homophobic environment' in the armed forces.

Violence against LGBT venues has been lethal. On 12 October 2022 a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger, with the Bratislava LGBT bar Tepláreň as a fallback, arrived about 18:35 and at 19:11 fired eight shots at the bar, killing two people and injuring one; the perpetrator also died. Rights groups described the attack as marking a new era for trans people in the country, and the aftermath brought greater fear about the future. In an April 2023 letter to the National Council, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović wrote that six months after the attack there was no discernible progress, that the human rights of LGBTI people appeared more, not less, at risk, and that she was concerned by regressive legislative proposals including the legal-gender-recognition ban bill.

Official hostility has come from within government. On 3 July 2024 the serving Minister of Culture, Martina Šimkovičová, made a public homophobic and racist statement claiming Europe is dying because of an excessive number of LGBT people.

Partner recognition is narrow. Slovakia recognises no civil unions or same-sex marriage; bills introduced in 1997, 2000, 2012, 2018, 2021 and 2022 were all rejected, including 94 votes against to 14 for in 2012, 31 of 150 in support in 2018, and 7 for against 67 against in 2021. A constitutional amendment of June 2014 (Article 41) defining marriage as 'a unique union between a man and a woman' passed 102 to 18, potentially rendering future recognition laws unconstitutional. Any existing marriage is invalidated on change of legal gender, and as of 2025 only married couples may adopt, barring same-sex couples, single people and unmarried partners. Since 1964 the law recognises only a 'close person', a sibling or spouse, with limited rights, mainly inheritance. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no recognition of that relationship under Slovak law.

The wider climate is hostile by EU standards. Slovakia is described as having some of the worst LGBTQ rights in the European Union and less supportive public opinion than the Czech Republic. Support is volatile: 66% acceptance in a 2007 Pew survey, 29 to 57% backing civil unions in 2019, falling to 40% after the 2022 attack; the 2015 Eurobarometer put Slovakia fourth-lowest in the EU on same-sex marriage at 24%, and PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index ranked Slovakia 47th against Czechia's 18th. The gay scene is small, consisting of a few bars and clubs in Bratislava.
SVK.outOfScopeNotes:
The fate of the 24 February 2023 bill after its first reading is not established by the sources reviewed.

Whether the standards of care republished on 3 March 2023 are being applied in registries and clinics, and whether registry offices continue to refuse gender-change applications, is unresolved.

An Amnesty International statement of May 2023 and a Pew Research Center survey on religion and minorities produced no usable finding for this record.

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.summary:
Belarusian law treats transgender visibility as criminal material. In April 2024 the definition of pornography was amended to bring depictions of same-sex relationships and of transgender people inside it, and a Ministry of Culture decree issued the same year grouped "homosexualism" with paedophilia and necrophilia under the category of "non-traditional relationships". Production and distribution carry up to four years' imprisonment, rising to thirteen years where children are involved. Prosecution proceeds under Article 343 of the Criminal Code. Human Rights Watch described the change as an explicit attack on the dignity of LGBT people. The offence attaches to depiction rather than conduct, so a trans person's own image or public presence can be treated as pornographic material.

An April 2026 law bans propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia. The inclusion of gender reassignment means that advocacy of, or representation of, transition falls within the prohibition. The Prosecutor General's Office has announced plans for a further administrative-penalty law against "LGBTI propaganda"; it had not been tabled at the time of the ILGA-Europe review for 2024.

Enforcement has been immediate. TG House Belarus reported that more than fifteen LGBTQ+ people were detained in September 2024 alone, eight of them transgender; most were charged with hooliganism and two with pornography. Those held reported physical and psychological abuse in custody, and some left the country afterwards. Activists say police beat LGBTQ+ people while arresting and charging them and that charges are coerced.

Foreign visitors are exposed through the same machinery. In 2004, when an international gay and lesbian festival was targeted, the authorities made threatening telephone calls stating that foreigners attending workshops and discussions would be immediately expelled under the article on intervention in domestic affairs. A trans visitor attending meetings or events connected to LGBT organising can expect the same treatment.

Belarus offers no protection against persecution on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Persecution on the basis of sexual orientation is not recognised in Belarusian law as a ground for refugee status, and partners are not recognised for immigration purposes, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no immigration route here. No anti-discrimination protection exists and there is no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Belarus is not a member of the Council of Europe, so there is no appeal to the European Court of Human Rights.

Official hate-crime data is not published. Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights since 2015 and has no National Point of Contact for that reporting; figures for 2024 come from civil-society organisations including Human Constanta. Police do not register brutality cases against sexual minorities or investigate homophobic motives, and officers collect personal data, passport details and photographs of gay people at known cruising areas, as reported by Vstrecha in Brest and Gomel.

Transgender people who suffer violence have little expectation of redress. In September 2008 two transgender men raped in Minsk did not report to police because they were unsure police would help. Detention carries a further risk: in prisons, homosexuality is subject to speculation, blackmail and extortion, gay and lesbian prisoners are largely unprotected, and turnkeys often encourage other prisoners to abuse them.

LGBT venues have been closed, raided or tolerated only intermittently. The gay club Oskar was closed by the authorities in February 2000 and its owner Ivan Suchinski was later killed; riot police raided a 1999 pride party; police have carried out unprovoked actions in bars frequented by homosexuals in Gomel and Minsk.

Psychological care is scarce. Qualified psychological help is generally unavailable and no trans-specific facilities are documented.

Public opinion is hostile. A Pew Research Center survey in May 2017 found that 84 per cent of Belarusians believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society and 81 per cent opposed same-sex marriage, with 16 per cent in favour. A 2002 Lambda Belarus survey found that 47 per cent thought gay people should be imprisoned, and many Belarusians treat homosexuality as a psychiatric illness. Among younger people attitudes are comparatively less hostile but still largely negative: the 2017 poll found 22 per cent of younger respondents in favour of legal gay marriage against 14 per cent of older ones, and a 2007 vote of young people in Gomel region found that 47.6 per cent held negative feelings towards sexual and gender minorities and 10 per cent wanted homosexual relations criminalised. Gay life is largely underground, most LGBT people conceal their orientation in public, and those who are open face harassment and physical violence.

State propaganda reinforces the climate. State television has equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and described them as "a weapon in the hands of the West", and TG House recorded an increase in hate speech in state propaganda. A new National Security Concept emphasises "traditional values". ILGA-Europe recorded that at least ten transgender people left Belarus in a year because of discrimination and repression.
BLR.outOfScopeNotes:
Figures on detentions and abuse in custody rest on reporting by non-governmental organisations and activists and have no official confirmation; the state publishes no hate-crime data.

Whether the April 2026 law is in force and how its provisions are applied to foreign visitors is not established in the available sources.

The sources do not describe the procedure for legal gender recognition in Belarus, or whether foreign identity documents recording a gender different from that assigned at birth are accepted at the border, in hotels or in dealings with officials.

No transgender-specific accommodation or care facilities are documented, and no findings on youth-specific access to care are recorded.
