Explicitly aimed at LGBT dignity — a persecution vector for visitors and residents alike.

JURIST (28 Sep 2024): TG House Belarus reports 15+ LGBTQ people detained in one month, incl. 8 transgender — most charged with hooliganism, two with pornography; custody abuse (physical and psychological) reported and some fled the country.

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Belarus: Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since 2015 and has no National Point of Contact; civil-society reports for 2024 came from Human Constanta and others. No official data available.
AP: 'Activists say police in Belarus beat LGBTQ+ people while arresting and charging them' — rights groups report beatings, coerced charges and expanding 'LGBT propaganda' repression.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Belarus: state TV equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and called them 'a weapon in the hands of the West'; TG House recorded increased hate speech in state propaganda; the Prosecutor General's Office plans an administrative-penalty law against 'LGBTI propaganda' (not yet tabled); at least ten trans people left Belarus in a year due to discrimination and repression; a new National Security Concept emphasises 'traditional values'.

Report 'Are all equal before the law?' (Bortnik & Sementsov, citing Amnesty International 2006-2007 context): Belarus's constitutional equality guarantee (Article 22) versus reality - clampdown on civil society, harassment of activists, arbitrary detentions, death penalty retained; the legal and political climate facing LGBT people in Belarus.

sources.summary:
Persecution on the basis of sexual orientation is not explicitly recognised in Belarusian law as a ground for refugee status, and same-sex partners are not recognised for immigration purposes. After the fall of the communist regime many Belarusians sought and received political asylum abroad, most often citing formal or informal police harassment; Amnesty International and AILGBT-Belarus documented individuals granted asylum in the Czech Republic, France, the Netherlands and Sweden. Belarus is not a member of the Council of Europe, so activists cannot appeal to the European Court of Human Rights. In 2004, when an international gay and lesbian festival was targeted, authorities made threatening phone calls stating that foreigners attending workshops and discussions would be immediately expelled from the country under the article on intervention in domestic affairs.

Qualified psychological help is generally unavailable in Belarus, and no trans-specific facilities are documented; the three Minsk universities offering full psychology courses (Belarus State University, Belarus Pedagogical University, European Humanities University) do not address the problems of sexual minorities. Suicide rates are high among gays, lesbians, bisexuals and transgender people. LGBTQ venues have been shut or raided: the gay club Oskar was closed by authorities in February 2000 and its owner Ivan Suchinski was later killed, riot police raided a 1999 pride party, and police have conducted unprovoked actions in bars frequented by homosexuals in Gomel and Minsk. In prisons, homosexuality is subject to speculation, blackmail and extortion, gays and lesbians are largely unprotected, and turnkeys often encourage prisoners to abuse homosexuals. Police do not register brutality cases against sexual minorities or investigate homophobic motives; officers instead collect personal data, passport details and mugshots of gay people at known cruising areas, as reported by Vstrecha in Brest and Gomel. In September 2008 two transgender men raped in Minsk did not report to police because they were unsure police would help. No youth-specific access-to-care findings are recorded beyond this general pattern of concealment and unavailable support. Blood donation carries no particular limitations for gay and bisexual men; all procedures and requirements are the same for all donors.

In May 2003 the administration of the European Humanities University in Minsk banned a screening of the documentary Outlawed about discrimination of gays and lesbians, with staff saying the ban came under pressure of the Russian Orthodox Church. The April 2026 law bans propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia; in July 2001 the Organising Committee of the 1st Belarusian Youth Congress voted against admitting Lambda Belarus delegates; in March 2002 the youth organization Young Front published homophobic statements, with leader Paval Sieviaryniec calling homosexuality a death-worthy sin and perversion. Opinion among the young is comparatively less hostile but still largely negative: Pew's May 2017 poll found 22% of younger Belarusians favour legal gay marriage against 14% of elders, while a 2007 vote of Gomel region youth found 47.6% had negative feelings toward sexual and gender minorities and 10% wanted to criminalize homosexual relations.

Homosexuality remains highly stigmatized. A May 2017 Pew Research Center survey found 84% of Belarusians believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society and 81% opposed same-sex marriage with only 16% in favour; a 2002 Lambda Belarus survey found 47% of Belarusians think gays should be imprisoned, and many believe homosexuality is a psychiatric illness. Gay life is largely underground, most LGBTQ people hide their orientation in public, and those who are out face harassment, violence and physical abuse. State hostility is codified: the April 2026 law prohibits propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia, compared by critics to Russia's 2013 law, and a 2024 Ministry of Culture decree categorized homosexualism alongside paedophilia and necrophilia as pornography, enabling prosecution under Article 343 of the Criminal Code with up to four years in prison. Pride events from 1999 to 2010 were repeatedly banned, raided or forcibly prevented, no official organization represents gays and lesbians in Belarus with other initiatives working outside the legal framework, and there is no anti-discrimination protection and no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

BLR.localsOnly:
Belarusian law does not recognise persecution on the basis of sexual orientation as a ground for refugee status, so LGBT residents have no domestic protection route and must seek asylum abroad. After the end of communist rule many Belarusians sought and received political asylum, most often citing formal or informal police harassment; Amnesty International and AILGBT-Belarus documented individuals granted asylum in the Czech Republic, France, the Netherlands and Sweden.

The constitutional guarantee of equality before the law, Article 22, has not protected LGBT people in practice; the wider environment includes a clampdown on civil society, harassment of activists, arbitrary detention, and retention of the death penalty. The three Minsk universities offering full psychology courses, Belarus State University, Belarus Pedagogical University and the European Humanities University, do not address the problems of sexual minorities.

No official organisation represents gay and lesbian people in Belarus, and other initiatives work outside the legal framework. Pride events between 1999 and 2010 were repeatedly banned, raided or forcibly prevented.
BLR.comparisons: Belarus scores just above Russia (0.12 — nationwide "extremist movement" designation and LGR ban) and below Uganda (0.17).
BLR.blindSummary:
National law in the country treats transgender visibility as criminal material. In April 2024 the definition of pornography was amended to bring depictions of same-sex relationships and of transgender people inside it, and a ministry decree issued the same year grouped "homosexualism" with paedophilia and necrophilia under the category of "non-traditional relationships". Production and distribution carry up to four years' imprisonment, rising to thirteen years where children are involved. Prosecution proceeds under Article 343 of the Criminal Code. A human-rights organisation described the change as an explicit attack on the dignity of LGBT people. The offence attaches to depiction rather than conduct, so a transgender person's own image or public presence can be treated as pornographic material.

An April 2026 law bans propaganda of homosexual relations, gender reassignment, childlessness and paedophilia. The inclusion of gender reassignment means that advocacy of, or representation of, transition falls within the prohibition. The national prosecution service has announced plans for a further administrative-penalty law against "LGBTI propaganda"; it had not been tabled at the time of a regional advocacy organisation's review for 2024.

Enforcement has been immediate. A local transgender rights organisation reported that more than fifteen LGBTQ+ people were detained in September 2024 alone, eight of them transgender; most were charged with hooliganism and two with pornography. Those held reported physical and psychological abuse in custody, and some left the country afterwards. Activists say police beat LGBTQ+ people while arresting and charging them and that charges are coerced.

Foreign visitors are exposed through the same machinery. In 2004, when an international gay and lesbian festival was targeted, the authorities made threatening telephone calls stating that foreigners attending workshops and discussions would be immediately expelled under the article on intervention in domestic affairs. A transgender visitor attending meetings or events connected to LGBT organising can expect the same treatment.

The country offers no protection against persecution on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Persecution on the basis of sexual orientation is not recognised in national law as a ground for refugee status, and partners are not recognised for immigration purposes, so a transgender visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no immigration route. No anti-discrimination protection exists and there is no prohibition of hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The country is not a member of a regional human-rights body, so there is no appeal to the region's human rights court.

Official hate-crime data is not published. The country has not reported hate-crime data to a regional security organisation's hate-crime monitoring mechanism since 2015 and has no national point of contact for that reporting; figures for 2024 come from civil-society organisations. Police do not register brutality cases against sexual minorities or investigate homophobic motives, and officers collect personal data, passport details and photographs of gay people at known cruising areas, as a civil-society group reported in two provincial cities.

Transgender people who suffer violence have little expectation of redress. In September 2008 two transgender men raped in the capital did not report to police because they were unsure police would help. Detention carries a further risk: in prisons, homosexuality is subject to speculation, blackmail and extortion, gay and lesbian prisoners are largely unprotected, and prison staff often encourage other prisoners to abuse them.

LGBT venues have been closed, raided or tolerated only intermittently. A gay club in the capital was closed by the authorities in February 2000 and its owner was later killed; riot police raided a 1999 pride party; police have carried out unprovoked actions in bars frequented by homosexuals in the capital and a provincial city.

Psychological care is scarce. Qualified psychological help is generally unavailable and no transgender-specific facilities are documented.

Public opinion is hostile. A 2017 polling survey found that 84 per cent of the population believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society and 81 per cent opposed same-sex marriage, with 16 per cent in favour. A 2002 survey by a local organisation found that 47 per cent thought gay people should be imprisoned, and many people treat homosexuality as a psychiatric illness. Among younger people attitudes are comparatively less hostile but still largely negative: the 2017 poll found 22 per cent of younger respondents in favour of legal gay marriage against 14 per cent of older ones, and a 2007 vote of young people in one part of the country found that 47.6 per cent held negative feelings towards sexual and gender minorities and 10 per cent wanted homosexual relations criminalised. Gay life is largely underground, most LGBT people conceal their orientation in public, and those who are open face harassment and physical violence.

State propaganda reinforces the climate. State television has equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and described them as a weapon in the hands of outside powers, and a local transgender rights organisation recorded an increase in hate speech in state propaganda. A new national security concept emphasises "traditional values". A regional advocacy organisation recorded that at least ten transgender people left the country in a year because of discrimination and repression.
BLR.blindOutOfScope:
Figures on detentions and abuse in custody rest on reporting by non-governmental organisations and activists and have no official confirmation; the state publishes no hate-crime data.

Whether the April 2026 law is in force and how its provisions are applied to foreign visitors is not established in the available sources.

The sources do not describe the procedure for legal gender recognition in the country, or whether foreign identity documents recording a gender different from that assigned at birth are accepted at the border, in hotels or in dealings with officials.

No transgender-specific accommodation or care facilities are documented, and no findings on youth-specific access to care are recorded.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.summary:
Being trans is not criminalised in Ukraine. Sexual activity between men was decriminalised in 1991, sexual activity between women was never an offence, and the age of consent is 16 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation. Legal gender recognition exists and does not require surgery: following an August 2016 court ruling, new identity documents are issued before any surgical procedure, and married applicants or those with an underage child may apply. The requirement to petition a board of mental health professionals and to spend a month in a psychiatric facility was removed effective late December 2016. Transsexuality nonetheless remains classified as a psychiatric disorder, and sex reassignment surgery is legal only for those over 25.

Obtaining the diagnosis that unlocks document amendment has become harder. ZMINA reported on 28 July 2026 that trans women face stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers when seeking a diagnosis, and that the friction is documentary as much as medical, affecting both the transition procedure and border crossing. A Ukrainian court ordered changes to passports and all other documents for two trans people without requiring sterilisation, a ruling reported in August 2016.

Border crossing carries a specific exposure. Gender Stream documents that since martial law, holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service, and the organisation assists trans people with processing and reissuing documents, including for those planning to cross legally. Cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and confirmation by the Military Medical Commission; an activist describes commission hours of 8am to 8pm and gatekeeping in which a doctor's word determines the state's classification.

An international broadcaster reported in June 2022 that Ukraine's trans community was caught in the crosshairs of the war.

Partner recognition is unresolved and contested. Article 51 of the 1996 Constitution defines marriage as a voluntary union of a man and a woman, and the Justice Ministry confirmed in June 2018 that neither same-sex marriage nor civil partnership has legal recognition. A 2015 government action plan promised a civil partnership bill by 2017; the Ministry of Justice declared in 2018 it could not proceed because of pressure from religious organisations. A civil unions bill was introduced in Parliament in March 2023, and the government's EU accession roadmap of 14 May 2025 set a Q3 2025 deadline for a registered partnerships law. President Zelenskyy said in 2022 that marriage could not be introduced during wartime because the Constitution cannot be amended under martial law, and answered "Yes!" on 16 November 2024 when asked whether he would sign registered partnerships legislation. On 10 June 2025 the Desnianskyi District Court recognised the existence of actual marital relations between two Ukrainian men, the first such ruling, and in March 2026 the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognising same-sex couples as de facto family.

The draft Civil Code submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would define family as cohabitation between a man and a woman and automatically annul a marriage if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, removing family recognition from a trans spouse at the point of transition.

Hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. The Criminal Code provides harsher penalties only for racial, national or religious intolerance; an April 2020 draft to add gender identity and sexual orientation as aggravating grounds was withdrawn in September 2020. The Cabinet's 14 May 2025 rule-of-law roadmap plans gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances, administrative liability for discrimination, criminal liability for public calls for violence, and free secondary legal aid with registration in the Unified register, all by Q2 2026. Gender identity discrimination at work was banned by a Labour Code amendment approved on 12 November 2015, and a December 2022 media bill passed unanimously bans hate speech and discrimination based on gender identity.

Enforcement of protection is weak. Amnesty International reported in May 2013 that violent attacks on a sexual-orientation or gender-identity basis were routine and frequently used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and public events, and urged Parliament to legislate against such discrimination and to vote down proposals to criminalise. In 2011 there were frequent reports of harassment and violence, with many people saying they had to conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity to avoid discrimination or violent harassment, and a perception that such violence was tolerated by the government. Ukrainian police hardly ever detained attackers. Pride events required heavy protection: 1,500 participants in Kyiv on 12 June 2016 were guarded by 5,500 police and 1,200 National Guard, and earlier events were cancelled in May 2012 and July 2014 over safety guarantees. In June 2012 the activist Taras Karasiichuk was attacked near his Kyiv apartment, sustaining a concussion and a broken jaw, the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; police did not respond immediately despite a medical referral, and Human Rights Watch called for an investigation into a homophobic motive.
UKR.outOfScopeNotes:
The draft Civil Code submitted on 22 January 2026 and the 14 May 2025 roadmap targets, including registered partnerships by Q3 2025 and gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances by Q2 2026, are proposals and deadlines. Whether they have been enacted is not established by the sources.

The April 2020 draft to add gender identity and sexual orientation as hate-crime grounds was withdrawn in September 2020, and no subsequent enactment of those grounds is recorded in the sources.

Sources conflict on the diagnosis requirement. One account lists the diagnosis of transsexuality among the requirements removed in 2016, while 2026 reporting describes the diagnosis as the operative bottleneck for document amendment. The current status of that requirement is unresolved.

No trans-specific shelter, accommodation or facility provision is described in the sources.

No per-capita data on violence against trans people in Ukraine is available in the sources. The documented incidents are individual cases and do not establish a rate.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch essay (15 May 2024) 'When Laws Fail to Protect Trans People': Ukraine-trans war-displacement case work — cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating Military Medical Commission confirmation; a Ukrainian activist notes commission hours (8am-8pm) and gatekeeping ('if a doctor says I'm a woman, the state can shrug').
France24 (June 2022) reports on Ukraine's trans community caught in the crosshairs of war.

ZMINA (28 Jul 2026): trans women in Ukraine now find it harder to obtain a diagnosis — stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers; Trans Forum 2026 (Kyiv, early June 2026) discussed the new draft Civil Code's effect on transition procedure and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation — visitor-relevant documentary friction for trans Ukrainians and those crossing borders.

Gender Stream (Ukrainian NGO): consultations and support — advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families evacuating from frontline regions to western Ukraine/EU, and helps with processing/reissuing documents for transgender people, including those planning to legally cross the border; documents that since martial law, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service.

European Parliament written question E-002018/2022 (Jun 2022): on the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion, in the context of Parliament's resolution on war's impact on women.

Amnesty International (16 May 2013) report 'Nothing to Report': Ukraine's government must legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on a sexual-orientation/gender-identity basis amid a pervasive climate of homophobia; lawmakers urged to vote down proposals to criminalise; attacks routinely used as pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and peaceful public events.

Erasing 76 Crimes (30 Aug 2016): among three-country advances, a Ukrainian court ordered changes requested by two trans people to their passports and all other documents WITHOUT requiring sterilisation — a concrete legal-gain data point for document amendment.

Human Rights Watch (26 Jun 2012): LGBT activist Taras Karasiichuk was attacked near his Kyiv apartment — the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; diagnosed concussion and broken jaw, police did not immediately respond despite medical referral; HRW urged investigation into homophobic motive.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Ukraine's first LGBTQ rights group, Our World (Nash Svit), was created in 1998 as a community centre and human rights advocacy organization. In 2008, LGBTQ organizations formed the Union of Gay Organizations of Ukraine coalition, and the Gay Alliance of Ukraine was founded in 2009. The source text does not describe trans-specific facilities or shelters. Clause 211 of the Family Code of Ukraine explicitly bans same-sex couples from adopting children, while single Ukrainian citizens of any sexual orientation are permitted to adopt. Lesbian couples have greater parenting access than gay male couples because IVF and assisted insemination treatments are legal. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would automatically annul marriages if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, directly targeting trans people's family recognition. Foreign adopters must be married in a registered different-sex marriage.

Ukraine's path to partner recognition has been long and uneven: a 2015 government action plan promised a civil partnership bill by 2017, but the Ministry of Justice declared in 2018 it could not proceed due to pressure from religious organizations. A civil unions bill was introduced in Parliament in March 2023, and on 14 May 2025 the government's EU accession roadmap (p. 3.11) set a Q3 2025 deadline for a registered partnerships law. On 10 June 2025 the Desnianskyi District Court recognized actual marital relations between two Ukrainian men, the first such ruling in Ukraine, and on 22 January 2026 the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognizing same-sex couples as de facto family. A January 2023 NDI/KIIS poll found 56% of Ukrainians supported civil partnership registration for same-sex couples. A June 2024 KIIS poll found 28.7% supported civil partnerships without adoption, 35.7% opposed and 25.6% indifferent.

A summer 2015 British Council survey found one in five Ukrainian youth would be uncomfortable having lesbian and gay people as friends. Most Ukrainians grew up with little or no comprehensive, fact-based public education about human sexuality, sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap the source says promotes viewing homosexuals as dangerous and as sources of HIV/AIDS. The Ukrainian Council of Churches opposed the Istanbul Convention partly on grounds it could "distort" younger generations' sexual identity, framing anti-LGBTQ policy as youth protection. One source anecdote describes a 19-year-old confined indoors for over a year by parents after they discovered messages to his boyfriend. At a 14 November 2024 meeting with the Ukrainian Students Association, a student representative asked President Zelenskyy whether he would sign registered partnerships legislation and he replied "Yes!"

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Ukraine (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transsexuality is classified as a psychiatric disorder in Ukraine, and sex reassignment surgery is legal only for those over age 25. In 2011 the Civil Code was amended to allow transgender people who had undergone gender-affirming surgery to change their name to reflect gender identity, with seven surgeries and five new documents reported in 2014. Since December 2016 new identity documents are issued before surgery following an August 2016 ruling ordering passport and document changes for two transgender people without surgery, and married people or those with an underage child may also apply for transition. Previously applicants required permission from a Ministry of Healthcare special commission, 30 days in a psychiatric hospital, typically in wards with patients considered "mentally ill," and a diagnosis of transsexuality, requirements now removed. On 12 November 2015 Parliament approved a Labor Code amendment banning gender identity discrimination at work as an EU visa-free requirement, and in December 2022 Parliament unanimously passed a media bill banning hate speech and discrimination based on gender identity. The Criminal Code provides harsher penalties only for racial, national or religious intolerance, not gender identity, and an April 2020 draft to add gender identity and sexual orientation as hate-crime grounds was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of those terms in legislation. On 14 May 2025 the Cabinet approved a rule-of-law roadmap planning registered-partnership status by Q3 2025 and, by Q2 2026, administrative liability for discrimination, gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances, criminal liability for public calls for violence, and free secondary legal aid with registration in the Unified register, while a 22 January 2026 draft Civil Code would define family as man-woman cohabitation and automatically annul marriage if a spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment. Male same-sex sexual activity was legalized in 1991, female same-sex activity was never a crime, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, with law as of 2018 only addressing prostitution involving minors or public conduct violating public decency. Article 51 of the 1996 Constitution defines marriage as a voluntary union between a man and a woman, with no legal recognition for same-sex marriage or civil partnerships, confirmed by the Justice Ministry in June 2018 after a 2015 action-plan promise of partnerships by 2017 was declared unimplementable in early 2018. After a July 2022 petition exceeding 28,000 signatures, President Zelenskyy asked the Prime Minister to review same-sex civil partnerships but said marriage could not be introduced during wartime because the Constitution cannot be changed under martial law, later answering "Yes!" on 16 November 2024 when asked if he would sign registered partnerships, with a 14 May 2025 EU roadmap scheduling partnership legislation for Q3 2025. On 10 June 2025 the Desnianskyi District Court recognized "existence of actual marital relations" between two men in a first for Ukraine, and in March 2026 the Supreme Court in Kyiv rejected a challenge to a lower-court ruling recognizing same-sex couples as de facto family. Single citizens may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, but same-sex couples are explicitly banned under Clause 211 of the Family Code, foreign adopters must be in registered different-sex marriage, and lesbian couples have IVF and assisted insemination access. On 12 November 2015 Parliament banned sexual orientation discrimination at work after failures on 5 and 9 November, and in December 2022 unanimously banned sexual-orientation hate speech and discrimination in mass media to align with EU Directive 2018/1808, while hate-crime aggravation still excludes sexual orientation. Homosexuality is not a legal ground for exemption from military service, and on 8 February 2022 the Health Ministry enacted 2016-proposed rules allowing gay and bisexual men to donate blood after previously listing homosexuality as "risky behaviour" barring donation. "Sexual orientations and gender identity remain taboo subjects in Ukraine." "Most Ukrainians affiliated with the Orthodox or Catholic Church tend to view homosexuality and non-traditional gender roles as signs of immorality," compounded by lack of fact-based sexuality education and Soviet-era labeling of non-heterosexual relations as abnormal. The article states the "ex-gay" movement "believes that lesbian, gay, or bisexual sexual orientations, as well as transgender identities, can be 'cured' through therapeutic or religious programs," with the largest group Love Against Homosexuality viewing LGBTQ people as "sexual perverts" needing cure. In 2011 there were frequent reports of harassment and violence against LGBTQ people, many reported needing to lie about sexual orientation or gender identity to avoid discrimination or violent harassment, with a perception that such violence is frequently tolerated by the Government. Ukrainian police "hardly ever detain attackers," creating pressure to remain in the closet especially for public figures, while pride events required heavy protection, e.g., 1,500 participants guarded by 5,500 police and 1,200 National Guard in Kyiv on 12 June 2016 and earlier cancellations in May 2012 and July 2014 over safety guarantees. General LGBTQ acceptance polling rose from 28% in a 2010 European study saying LGBT individuals should live freely however they like to 70.4% in 2024 agreeing LGBTQ people should have same rights, up from 67.3% in 2023 and 63.7% in 2022, with 28.7% approving civil partnerships without adoption, 35.7% opposed and 25.6% indifferent.

Trans Forum 2026, held in Kyiv in early June 2026, discussed whether it should be, alongside the draft Civil Code's effect on the transition procedure. Confirmation by the Military Medical Commission is part of the wartime pathway for trans women, with commission hours of 8am to 8pm and a gatekeeping structure in which a doctor's assessment determines the state's classification.

Adoption is restricted by family law. Clause 211 of the Family Code bans same-sex couples from adopting, while single Ukrainian citizens of any sexual orientation may adopt. Foreign adopters must be married in a registered different-sex marriage. The "ex-gay" movement holds that lesbian, gay or bisexual orientations and transgender identities can be "cured" through therapeutic or religious programmes, and the largest such group, Love Against Homosexuality, views LGBTQ people as "sexual perverts" needing cure.

Family pressure can amount to confinement. One documented case describes a 19-year-old confined indoors for over a year by his parents after they discovered messages to his boyfriend.
UKR.comparisons: Ukraine scores far above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) — no criminalisation, no state persecution, functioning NGOs — and below Serbia (0.64) and Moldova (0.65), reflecting wartime institutional strain and weaker legal protections rather than active hostility.

An international human rights organisation reported in May 2013 that violent attacks on a sexual-orientation or gender-identity basis were routine and frequently used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and public events, and urged the national legislature to legislate against such discrimination and to vote down proposals to criminalise. In 2011 there were frequent reports of harassment and violence, with many people saying they had to conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity to avoid discrimination or violent harassment, and a perception that such violence was tolerated by the government. National police hardly ever detained attackers. Pride events required heavy protection: 1,500 participants in the capital on 12 June 2016 were guarded by 5,500 police and 1,200 national guard personnel, and earlier events were cancelled in May 2012 and July 2014 over safety guarantees. In June 2012 an activist was attacked near his apartment in the capital, sustaining a concussion and a broken jaw, the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; police did not respond immediately despite a medical referral, and an international human rights organisation called for an investigation into a homophobic motive.
UKR.blindOutOfScope:
The draft civil code submitted on 22 January 2026 and the 14 May 2025 roadmap targets, including registered partnerships by Q3 2025 and gender identity and sexual orientation as criminal aggravating circumstances by Q2 2026, are proposals and deadlines. Whether they have been enacted is not established by the sources.

The April 2020 draft to add gender identity and sexual orientation as hate-crime grounds was withdrawn in September 2020, and no subsequent enactment of those grounds is recorded in the sources.

Sources conflict on the diagnosis requirement. One account lists the diagnosis of transsexuality among the requirements removed in 2016, while 2026 reporting describes the diagnosis as the operative bottleneck for document amendment. The current status of that requirement is unresolved.

No trans-specific shelter, accommodation or facility provision is described in the sources.

No per-capita data on violence against trans people in the country is available in the sources. The documented incidents are individual cases and do not establish a rate.
blindSourceSummaries: Human-rights organisation essay (15 May 2024): trans war-displacement case work — cross-border networks became critical support for trans women, arranging assessments and diagnoses including the often-humiliating military medical commission confirmation; an activist notes the commission's gatekeeping ('if a doctor says I'm a woman, the authorities can shrug').
Note: one cited news account (June 2022) was not retrievable at research time; it covered a trans community caught in the crosshairs of war.

Media report (28 Jul 2026): trans women find it harder to obtain a diagnosis — stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers; the June 2026 trans forum discussed a new draft civil code's effect on transition procedure and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation — documentary friction for trans people and those crossing borders.

Local support organisation: advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families evacuating from frontline regions, and helps with processing and reissuing documents for transgender people including those planning to legally cross the border; documents that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by border service officials.
Parliamentary written question (June 2022): on the situation of transgender people amid an invasion, in the context of a resolution on the war's impact on women.

Rights organisation report (16 May 2013): the government must legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on a sexual-orientation and gender-identity basis amid a pervasive climate of homophobia; lawmakers urged to reject criminalisation proposals; attacks routinely used as pretext to deny LGBTI people rights to expression and peaceful public events.
Rights blog (30 Aug 2016): a court ordered the passport and all other document changes requested by two trans people without requiring sterilisation — a concrete data point for document amendment.

Human-rights organisation (26 Jun 2012): an activist attacked near his home — the second violent attack in six weeks after threats forced cancellation of a pride parade; diagnosed concussion and broken jaw; police did not immediately respond despite a medical referral; the organisation urged an investigation into a homophobic motive.
UKR.blindLocalsOnly:
Being trans is not a legal ground for exemption from military service. A national forum held in the capital in early June 2026 discussed whether it should be, alongside the draft civil code's effect on the transition procedure. Confirmation by a military medical commission is part of the wartime pathway for trans women, with commission hours of 8am to 8pm and a gatekeeping structure in which a doctor's assessment determines the state's classification.

Adoption is restricted by family law. A clause of the family code bans same-sex couples from adopting, while single citizens of the country of any sexual orientation may adopt. Foreign adopters must be married in a registered different-sex marriage. Lesbian couples have greater parenting access than gay male couples because IVF and assisted insemination treatments are legal.

Conversion practices are promoted by organised groups. The "ex-gay" movement holds that lesbian, gay or bisexual orientations and transgender identities can be "cured" through therapeutic or religious programmes, and the largest such group views LGBTQ people as "sexual perverts" needing cure.

Family pressure can amount to confinement. One documented case describes a 19-year-old confined indoors for over a year by his parents after they discovered messages to his boyfriend.
UKR.tangentialFactors:
The European Parliament took up the situation of transgender people in Ukraine in a written question in June 2022, in the context of its resolution on the war's impact on women.

The Ukrainian Council of Churches opposed the Istanbul Convention partly on the grounds that it could "distort" younger generations' sexual identity, framing anti-LGBTQ policy as youth protection.

Public opinion has moved. A 2010 European study found 28% saying LGBT individuals should live freely as they like; by 2024, 70.4% agreed LGBTQ people should have the same rights, up from 67.3% in 2023 and 63.7% in 2022. A January 2023 NDI/KIIS poll found 56% of Ukrainians supported civil partnership registration for same-sex couples. A June 2024 KIIS poll found 28.7% supported civil partnerships without adoption, 35.7% opposed and 25.6% indifferent.

A summer 2015 British Council survey found one in five Ukrainian youth would be uncomfortable having lesbian and gay people as friends. Most Ukrainians grew up with little or no comprehensive, fact-based public education about human sexuality, sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap the source links to viewing homosexuals as dangerous and as sources of HIV/AIDS.

Sexual orientation and gender identity remain taboo subjects in Ukraine, and most Ukrainians affiliated with the Orthodox or Catholic Church tend to view homosexuality and non-traditional gender roles as signs of immorality.

MDA.name: Moldova
MDA.summary:
Moldova's anti-discrimination statute names both sexual orientation and gender identity. Law No. 2 of 2023 lists gender identity, and separately sexual orientation, among grounds protected from "any kind of discrimination"; an employment discrimination ban covering sexual orientation has been in force since 1 January 2013, and Article 11 of the audiovisual media code, effective 1 January 2019, prohibits broadcasting incitement to hatred founded on intolerance, including on grounds of sexual orientation. Hate speech and hate crimes have been criminal offences since 2022 with both grounds named, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover them. Consensual sex between men has been legal since 1995 and the age of consent was equalised in 2002. ILGA-Europe ranked Moldova last among 49 European countries for LGBT legislation in 2012 and 23rd by 2023.

Enforcement does not match the statute. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious problem with no meaningful state response, a finding the European Commission's country report echoes, and notes that political hate speech rose during the election period. Amnesty International's 2025 report describes discrimination against LGBTI people as commonplace and freedom of expression and assembly as arbitrarily restricted, with impunity for past violations. A 2024 ECOM legislative analysis, benchmarked against international standards and built on a survey of local partner organisations, identifies legal barriers for LGBT people and people living with HIV in access to justice and in the operation of hate-crime and discrimination provisions.

Changing legal name and gender marker is permitted but conditional on a psychiatric diagnosis confirming "transgenderism". The mismatch this creates in ordinary transactions is documented: a trans woman was refused bank service because her documents did not match her appearance, and the Equality Council confirmed discrimination and recommended preventive measures.

Public assembly is contested. Pride has been held since 2002 but has repeatedly been banned or cancelled. In May 2008 the mayor banned the parade the evening before, police stood by while crowds surrounded and attacked participants, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2012 that the cancellation violated the convention. The May 2017 march was cancelled by police shortly after it began when Orthodox groups attacked participants, and then-president Igor Dodon publicly endorsed the attacks. In May 2018 police used tear gas to repel counter-protesters and the march completed. Moldova Pride 2024 proceeded openly with participants of all ages.

Partner recognition is absent. The Constitution defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman, and there is no same-sex marriage or civil union, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no access to spousal recognition, residence rights or the next-of-kin protections attached to marriage.

In Russian-occupied Transnistria, legislation adopted in the reporting period prohibits the promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations", per Amnesty International's 2025 report.

Social attitudes remain hostile. The Equality Council study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022", published in January 2023, found acceptance of LGBT+ people extremely low: 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% would not accept them as work colleagues, the social-distance score stood at 5.7, and marginalisation increased during 2022. Politicians frequently make derogatory remarks about the community.

Impunity extends to attacks on advocates: in May 2019 a human rights lawyer representing GENDERDOC-M suffered an arson attack on her car in central Chisinau, and police declined to investigate on the ground that the damage was not "significant".

Official acknowledgement of the problem exists. Following reporting on a transgender detainee, the authorities stated that homophobia persists in state institutions and that they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment.
MDA.outOfScopeNotes:
No survey data specific to transgender people's social acceptance is available in the sources; the Equality Council's 2022 figures measure attitudes to LGBT+ people generally, and the material reviewed records no documented statement on societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

The Brumarețchi case is unresolved. The National Penitentiary Administration denies that his rights were violated and says the discrimination claims were unconfirmed; he has said he will bring proceedings in Moldovan courts and at the European Court of Human Rights, and no outcome is recorded.

Whether the Transnistria legislation is being enforced, and against whom, is not sourced.

The account of Moldova Pride 2024 comes from a travel publication and describes the atmosphere of the event rather than legal conditions.

Attitude (2 February 2026) revisits Moldova Pride 2024: participants of all ages and backgrounds joined the festivities, in a country described as "slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity". Public Pride proceeds openly.

sources.title: Trăind de gardă/ Deținut transgender – dublu condamnat în închisoare de către „oamenii cu epoleți”
sources.summary: Ziarul de Gardă (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man registered female at birth in 1972 whose documents were changed to male in 2007. He served his sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit ('izolator disciplinar'), supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12, the unit for detainees requiring protection, was refused. He describes forced strip body searches, 'go to the gynaecologist' calls over the intercom, staff opening his bathroom door, and being called 'Natașa' at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration (ANP) replied that he was detained alone 'at his own written request' with no rights violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR, and ZdG has notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. The case amounts to de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system, prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

sources.title: Deținuți ai prejudecăților în instituțiile de stat. Persoane LGBT+, la un pas de suicid. Povestea tragică a unui locuitor al satului Dubna
sources.summary: Observatorul de Nord (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: Igor Brumarețchi from Dubna village (Soroca district) spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the full investigation appeared on anticoruptie.md. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee in Moldovan prison No. 6 as of 2025.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Moldova (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people in Moldova are allowed to change their legal name and gender on official documents but require a psychiatric diagnosis confirming their "transgenderism" to do so. Law No. 2 (2023) includes gender identity among grounds protected from "any kind of discrimination," a transgender-specific protection distinct from the law's parallel protection for sexual orientation. Moldova's rise from last among 49 European countries in ILGA-Europe's 2012 LGBT legislation ranking to 23rd place by 2023 is attributed to continued expansion of anti-discrimination laws with regard to sexual orientation and gender identity. On 30 April 2013 the Parliament of Gagauzia approved a bill forbidding "propaganda" of homosexuality, bisexuality and transness such as same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples with no administrative sanctions or fines but with provisions banning registration of LGBT-related organizations and banning LGBT-related clubs and entertainment establishments, which were invalidated by court decision on 20 June 2013 for violating freedom of speech and human rights. In June 2011 Moldova voted against the UN Human Rights Council resolution condemning discrimination and violence against individuals based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The May 2017 march coinciding with the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia was cancelled by police shortly after it started due to safety concerns after fundamentalist Orthodox groups began attacking participants. Consenting adult same-sex sexual activity in private has been legal since 1995, with new laws in September 2002 equalising the age of consent. The Constitution explicitly defines marriage as between a man and a woman, with no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions and consequently little to no legal protection for same-sex couples. Parliament adopted a law banning discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment on 25 May 2012, signed by President Nicolae Timofti on 28 May 2012, effective 1 January 2013. The media law effective 1 January 2019 provides in Article 11 of the Codul serviciilor media audiovizuale al Republicii Moldova that audiovisual programs are prohibited from propagating incitement, promotion or justification of hatred founded on intolerance or discrimination based on sex, race, nationality, religion, disability or sexual orientation. Law No. 2 (2023) separately includes sexual orientation among grounds protected from "any kind of discrimination," distinct from gender identity. Parliament passed on 23 May 2013 a bill banning propaganda of prostitution, paedophilia and "any other relations than those related to marriage and family in accordance with the Constitution and the Family Code" with fines, signed 5 July 2013 and effective 12 July 2013, which did not explicitly prohibit "propaganda" of homosexuality but could have been interpreted as such, with the interpretable content removed by a bill passed 11 October 2013. Since 2012 several cities and districts enacted bans on "propaganda" of homosexuality with no administrative sanctions or fines, including Balti enacted 23 February 2012 and struck down 28 February 2013, Drochia enacted 27 March 2012, Cahul enacted 29 March 2012, and Ceadir-Lunga enacted 10 April 2012. The article states discrimination and violence against members of the LGBT community are commonplace, society remains very conservative, and politicians often make derogatory remarks about the LGBT community. The first pride parade was held in 2002, after which pride parades encountered stiff opposition from authorities and religious leaders and were often cancelled or banned due to safety concerns. On 11 May 2008 police and authorities stood by as crowds surrounded, intimidated and attacked Moldova Pride participants after Mayor Dorin Chirtoaca banned the parade the evening before, and in 2012 the ECHR ruled Moldovan authorities violated human rights by cancelling the 2008 event. The May 2017 march was cancelled by police shortly after it started due to safety concerns after fundamentalist Orthodox groups attacked participants, with President Igor Dodon supporting the attacks stating: "I have never promised to be the president of the gays, they should have elected their own president." The May 2018 17th Moldova Pride succeeded after police protected participants from radicals using tear gas to repel them. In May 2019 human rights lawyer Doina Ioana Straisteanu representing GENDER-DOC suffered an arson attack on her car in central Chisinau and police refused to investigate because it did not consider the damage "significant." The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically, only LGBT-general, gay and lesbian, or homosexuality-specific observations, including a Ministry of Health official letter that homosexuality is not considered a disease and medical services are accessible regardless of sexual orientation.

sources.title: United Nations Human Rights Council - June 2011 SOGI resolution vote
sources.summary: On 17 June 2011 the UN Human Rights Council adopted by 23 votes to 19 its first resolution on sexual orientation and gender identity expressing grave concern at acts of violence and discrimination committed against individuals because of sexual orientation and gender identity including transgender people and establishing a formal UN process to document abuses by commissioning a global report on discrimination including discriminatory laws and acts of violence and calling for a panel discussion on discriminatory laws, practices and acts of violence against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.

MDA.localsOnly:
The clearest documented case of institutional treatment of a trans person is custodial. He describes forced strip body searches, staff calls over the intercom telling him to "go to the gynaecologist", staff opening his bathroom door, and being called "Natașa" at roll-call. He says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration replied that he was held alone "at his own written request", that no rights were violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. LUX.name: Luxembourg
LUX.summary:
Luxembourg recognises gender identity in law through a declaration-based procedure. A person changes gender status and first name(s) in the civil register by application to the Ministry of Justice; no surgery, sterilisation, divorce or other medical treatment is required. The procedure is administered through the official government portal Guichet.lu. Recognition is binary: no nonbinary gender marker is available.

Discrimination law treats "change of sex" as a form of sex discrimination, prohibiting direct and indirect discrimination in employment, education, social security, healthcare and the provision of goods and services. Sexual orientation is separately protected under the Law of 28 November 2006 on equal treatment, covering the same fields. Gender expression and sex characteristics are not protected grounds.

Hate-crime legislation recognises "change of sex" as an aggravating factor, as it does sexual orientation.

Marriage and full adoption rights for same-sex couples took effect on 1 January 2015, after a vote of 56 to 4 in June 2014; registered partnerships carrying many of the benefits of marriage have existed since 1 November 2004. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and adopt in Luxembourg on the same terms as other couples.

The LGBT Action Plan 2018-2023 committed the government to combating violence, harassment and discrimination and to equal treatment in healthcare and employment. In July 2025 the government published a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan; organisations criticised it for omitting depathologisation and other key elements. No measures address conversion practices or intersex interventions.

An equality body, CET, handles equal-treatment complaints, and Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale provides services to the LGBTIQ+ community.
LUX.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the declaration procedure is open to non-residents, and what documentation a foreign national must produce, is not established by the sources reviewed.

Enforcement data on prosecutions or sentences involving "change of sex" as an aggravating factor is not available in the sources reviewed.

The specific commitments of the July 2025 LGBTIQ+ Action Plan and its implementation status are not detailed in the sources reviewed.

sources.title: Prisons luxembourgeoises : Les détenus gays et transgenres sont protégés
sources.summary: L'essentiel (26 August 2015), reporting Justice Minister Félix Braz's parliamentary answer to LSAP MP Cécile Hemmen, documents that Luxembourg prisons place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations handled case by case (the administration gathers all available information on the prisoner); such cases are described as 'exceptional'. Requests by LGBT detainees to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the minister warned against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen 'Monsieur'/'Madame' form of address. The Justice Ministry kept no statistics on LGBT prisoners (disclosure cannot be compelled without illegal privacy interference), and the planned Uerschterhaff prison (Sanem) was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation. Outcome: placement follows disclosed identity/need on a case-by-case basis with no codified birth-sex rule and no documented special custody unit or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners in Luxembourg.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Luxembourg (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Luxembourg law prohibits direct and indirect discrimination based on "change of sex" within the definition of sex in employment, education, social security, healthcare, and the provision of goods and services. Hate-crime legislation refers to "change of sex" and recognises it as an aggravating factor. Transgender people are allowed to change legal gender on the basis of self-determination by application to the Ministry of Justice with no surgery, sterilization, divorce or other medical treatment required. Minors even under the age of 5 may apply for a sex change with consent of legal guardians. In the past Luxembourg legally required surgery, sterilization and divorce before a change of gender on identification documents. The reform was approved by the Council of Government on 12 May 2017, submitted to Parliament on 31 May, approved 57-3 on 25 July 2018, cleared by Council of State consent to skip the second vote on 27 July 2018, promulgated by the Grand Duke on 10 August, published in the official journal on 12 September, and took effect on 16 September 2018. The LGBT Action Plan 2018-2023 pledges to combat violence, harassment and discrimination, guarantee equal treatment in healthcare and employment, and assure equality of transgender and intersex individuals. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1794 when the country was a French possession, and Article 372 of the Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. An 18-year limit imposed for same-sex sexual activity in 1971 was repealed in 1992. Partnerships granting many benefits of marriage have been recognised since 1 November 2004 under the French PACS-based partenariat/Partnerschaft model, and same-sex marriage and full adoption rights passed by 56 votes to 4 in June 2014 and took effect on 1 January 2015. Direct and indirect discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited in employment, education, social security, healthcare and provision of goods and services under the Law of 28 November 2006 on equal treatment, and sexual orientation is recognised as an aggravating factor under hate-crime legislation. Luxembourgish nationals are allowed to serve in the Armed Forces regardless of sexual orientation. Since January 2021, donors who have had sexual relations with men who have sex with men are allowed to donate plasma regardless of gender, and are allowed to donate blood after 12 months without sexual contact with MSM. The LGBT Action Plan 2018-2023 pledges inclusive educational opportunities for LGBT students, combating violence, harassment and discrimination, and equal treatment in healthcare and employment.

AND.name: Andorra
AND.summary:
Andorra's legal gender recognition framework rests on the Family Law of 21 July 2022, which allows trans people to change the name and gender recorded on legal documents through a simple administrative process that requires no medical intervention. Adoption has been open to same-sex couples since the 2014 civil union law, so a trans visitor in a relationship that Andorran law reads through birth-sex status can expect the same partnership recognition as other couples.

Law 13/2019 of 15 February 2019 prohibits discrimination on grounds including gender identity and expression in employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments, and extends that protection to education settings. Law 14/2019 of the same date on the rights of children and adolescents requires that transgender children be respected in their gender identity. Offences motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract additional penalties beyond the base offence.

Enforcement of the bias-crime framework is incomplete. Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents per month during 2025, a figure covering all bias motives rather than trans complaints alone and reported without any population denominator. DiversAnd logged incidents during the June Pride period and has called for a formal system to register and classify bias-motivated violence so that it can be prosecuted as hate crime; no such classification system was in place. The Ministry of Equality ran equality measures during the year.

The head of government, Xavier Espot Zamora, has held office since 2019 and came out as gay in September 2023; he remains the serving prime minister.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the prohibiting law was abolished in 1791, and the age of consent is 16 for both same-sex and heterosexual relationships.
AND.outOfScopeNotes:
GayLawNet's Andorra page carries a limited-information marking and cites Penal Code Article 206 for the age of consent, while other sources cite Articles 162 and 163; the article numbering is unresolved.

The bias-incident figure of two to three per month is a raw count with no population denominator and no breakdown by motive, and because no formal registration and classification system exists it is not a classified hate-crime count. Whether it understates or overstates the level of anti-trans violence cannot be determined from the available material.

The review material covers calendar years 2023 and 2025; no data for 2024 was available.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Andorra protects public LGBT expression and has a visible history: the first LGBT demonstration was held on 6 September 2002, and the first gay pride parade followed on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som. The LGBT group DiversAnd was formed in 2019, after Som Com Som ended its work in 2018, and organised a pride parade in June 2019; on 17 May 2019 the Department of Equality launched the short film "#lovingdiversity" to raise online awareness. Expression-related bias is penalised: hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation carry additional legal penalties, and Law 13/2019 of 15 February 2019 bars discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression across employment, education, health care, social services, housing and public establishments. Law 14/2019 of 15 February 2019 on the rights of children and adolescents establishes that transgender children must be respected in their gender identity, and Law 13/2019 extends non-discrimination protection, including gender identity and expression, to education settings. The age of consent is 16 for both same-sex and heterosexual relationships under Penal Code Articles 162 and 163, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the prohibiting law was abolished in 1791. Preventing and addressing bullying and discrimination in schools is a stated focus of DiversAnd. Risks to LGBT youth are documented: in 2000 a 17-year-old gay man, Nuno Ribeiro, was murdered in the country because of his sexual orientation, prompting public outcry, and cases of parents expelling their children from home over their sexual orientation are also reported. Since the 2014 civil union law, adoption has been open to same-sex couples, and the Family Law passed 21 July 2022 lets trans people update name and gender on legal documents via a simple process without medical intervention. In September 2023 Prime Minister Xavier Espot Zamora publicly came out as homosexual.

AND.tangentialFactors:
A transphobic opinion piece published in El Periòdic d'Andorra on 27 September 2023 was taken down online with a public apology after DiversAnd requested its removal; the print edition had already circulated.

Andorra has an organised LGBT presence dating to the first demonstration on 6 September 2002 and the first pride parade on 23 June 2003 at Plaça del Poble in Andorra la Vella, organised by the association Som Com Som. That association ended its work in 2018; DiversAnd formed in 2019 and held a pride parade that June. On 17 May 2019 the Department of Equality released the short film #lovingdiversity to raise awareness online.
AND.localsOnly:
Gender-affirming care for adolescents was still under negotiation in 2023: DiversAnd met the Ministry of Health in August to press for protocols covering puberty blockers and hormone therapy for 16-year-olds and, in some cases, 14-year-olds, following the 2022 regulatory changes. DiversAnd also works on bullying and discrimination in schools.

Documented risks to LGBT young people include the murder of Nuno Ribeiro, a 17-year-old gay man killed in 2000 because of his sexual orientation, which prompted public outcry, and reports of parents expelling children from the home over their sexual orientation. No general homicide or crime rate for Andorra is available, so these cannot be placed against a background rate.

MCO.name: Monaco
MCO.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has been lawful in Monaco since the 18th century, and the age of consent is 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships alike. Hate crime and hate speech on the ground of sexual orientation are criminalised. Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, and reported discrimination is described as rare; one travel guide states that such discrimination is illegal only in certain contexts, which conflicts with the country overviews reporting no general prohibition.

Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added sexual orientation to Civil Code articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (5 years).

The provisions cited in the sources name sexual orientation; none of them names gender identity. A trans visitor has no equivalent statutory protection on the face of the text.

Enforcement is documented. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for five days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man.

Legal gender recognition is not available. Transgender people cannot alter their legal gender in Monaco, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking placed Monaco 45th of 49 European countries. A trans visitor's identity documents will not correspond to any Monegasque recognition procedure, because none exists.

Partner recognition is limited. Monaco does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune, signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry; cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax rather than like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and to parents and children. Same-sex partners have no equal succession rights, survivor pensions or parental leave. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Monegasque law, none of these routes produces spousal recognition.

Anti-discrimination legislation has repeatedly failed. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme in every year of the primary and secondary cycles to sensitise pupils against racism and the other article 1 discriminations, including sexual orientation. The Council of Government did not approve the bill, and the replacement introduced on 18 December 2012 dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

Visibility is low. Roughly ten people are openly out in Monaco, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is described as limited. Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo, a Council of Europe rapporteur, described the position as the sad record of Monaco.

There is no Pride in Monaco and no official gay bars, clubs or events; visitors travel to France or Italy for Pride, and the nearest comparable scenes are in Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Some gay-friendly establishments operate with community support.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report for Monaco recorded no significant changes and no reports of torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses. The significant issues it identified were the libel and lèse-majesté laws, which it described as not enforced.
MCO.outOfScopeNotes:
Sources conflict on the scope of anti-discrimination law. The Outright International overview reports that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, while a travel guide states that such discrimination is illegal in certain contexts. The specific contexts, if any, are not identified in the inventory.

No enforcement data is available for the 2019 amendments to the Civil Code, and no trans-specific violence figures for Monaco were identified in the sources.

The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's full text and the reasons the Council of Government withheld approval are not sourced.

Whether any Monegasque provision addresses gender identity in hate-crime or hate-speech terms is not established by the sources; the cited articles name sexual orientation only.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".
