sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Hate-speech protection rests on Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression, which bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). Monaco does not recognize same-sex marriage, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking (45th of 49 European countries) notes that transgender people cannot alter their legal gender. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement (contrat de vie commune), introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and parents/children. Same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. The LGBT community supports some gay-friendly establishments inside Monaco, but there are no official gay bars, clubs or events in the country, unlike nearby French cities Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it has strong cultural and economic ties with France. Monaco has no armed forces, only a National Guard; France handles defence and allows openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve. The age of consent is 15 for both same-sex and opposite-sex relationships. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme every year of primary and secondary cycles to sensitise against racism and all article 1 discriminations (including sexual orientation), but the Council of Government did not approve the bill and its 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions. Same-sex couples' inability to adopt children directly affects family formation for youth, and most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.

MCO.localsOnly:
Residents in a same-sex relationship may sign a contrat de vie commune. The agreement was introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019, and came into force on 27 June 2020, six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco. It is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry.

The agreement does not produce spousal treatment. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and to parents and children. Same-sex partners have no equal succession rights, no survivor pensions and no parental leave, and same-sex couples have no right to adopt.

Transgender residents cannot alter their legal gender. No administrative or judicial route to legal gender recognition is described in the sources.

Community infrastructure is absent. No Pride is held in Monaco, there are no official gay bars, clubs or events, and roughly ten people are openly out. Some gay-friendly establishments operate with community support.

Anti-discrimination protection for sexual orientation and gender identity is not in force. The 2011 bill's article 44 school-sensitisation requirement was not approved by the Council of Government, and the 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.
MCO.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Slovenia (0.78), below France (0.82 — functional LGR), above Italy (0.76 — active political hostility Monaco lacks).
MCO.blindSummary:
Same-sex intimacy has been lawful in the country since the 18th century, and the age of consent is 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships alike. Hate crime and hate speech on the ground of sexual orientation are criminalised. Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, and reported discrimination is described as rare; one travel guide states that such discrimination is illegal only in certain contexts, which conflicts with the country overviews reporting no general prohibition.

A 2005 law on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. An article of the civil code, amended by a 2016 law, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. A 2019 law added sexual orientation to three civil code articles, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (5 years).

The provisions cited in the sources name sexual orientation; none of them names gender identity. A trans visitor has no equivalent statutory protection on the face of the text.

Enforcement is documented. In July 2010 a court in the country jailed a man for five days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man.

Legal gender recognition is not available. Transgender people cannot alter their legal gender in the country, and a regional rights organisation's 2019 ranking placed it 45th of 49 countries in the region. A trans visitor's identity documents will not correspond to any recognition procedure in the country, because none exists.

Partner recognition is limited. The country does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement, signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry; cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax rather than like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and to parents and children. Same-sex partners have no equal succession rights, survivor pensions or parental leave. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under the country's law, none of these routes produces spousal recognition.

Anti-discrimination legislation has repeatedly failed. A 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme in every year of the primary and secondary cycles to sensitise pupils against racism and the other article 1 discriminations, including sexual orientation. The government did not approve the bill, and the replacement introduced on 18 December 2012 dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

Visibility is low. Roughly ten people are openly out in the country, and LGBTIQ visibility is described as limited. Most residents affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. A rapporteur for a regional human rights body described the position as the country's sad record.

There is no Pride in the country and no official gay bars, clubs or events; visitors travel to a neighbouring jurisdiction for Pride, and the nearest comparable scenes are in cities in a neighbouring jurisdiction. Some gay-friendly establishments operate with community support.

A national human rights report published by a third-country government recorded no significant changes and no reports of torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses. The significant issues it identified were the libel and lèse-majesté laws, which it described as not enforced.
MCO.blindOutOfScope:
Sources conflict on the scope of anti-discrimination law. One country overview reports that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, while a travel guide states that such discrimination is illegal in certain contexts. The specific contexts, if any, are not identified in the inventory.

No enforcement data is available for the 2019 amendments to the civil code, and no trans-specific violence figures for the country were identified in the sources.

The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's full text and the reasons the government withheld approval are not sourced.

Whether any provision in the country addresses gender identity in hate-crime or hate-speech terms is not established by the sources; the cited articles name sexual orientation only.

SMR.name: San Marino
SMR.summary:
San Marino criminalises neither same-sex conduct nor gender identity. Consensual same-sex acts were decriminalised in 1864; the residual Article 274 of the Criminal Code, which punished habitual homosexual acts causing public scandal with three months to one year of imprisonment, was repealed in September 2004 and was never reported as applied. No statute regulates which bathrooms or facilities a person may use.

Entry carries no documented friction. The land border with Italy is open, and no identity screening that would out an arriving trans visitor is recorded. A visitor's foreign documents govern identity throughout the stay.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. The 2026 ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map lists San Marino among the countries with no functioning legal or administrative process for changing a gender marker. The consequence falls on residents rather than travellers, since a visitor's documentation is not reissued locally.

Protection machinery covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. A 2008 amendment to the Penal Code outlawed discrimination and hate speech based on sexual orientation, effective 3 May 2008, and provides sentence enhancements for crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Gender identity is absent from that provision. In November 2019 San Marino accepted recommendations from the UN Universal Periodic Review to outlaw discrimination based on gender identity; no implementing text is recorded.

The constitutional layer stops at sexual orientation. A referendum on 2 June 2019 added sexual orientation to Article 4 of the Declaration of Citizens' Rights with 71.46 per cent in favour, after a council vote in March 2019 fell short at 35 for, 8 against and 1 abstention against the 39 required.

Partner recognition exists but is narrower than marriage. Civil unions, in force from 5 December 2018 and fully operational from 11 February 2019, are open to same-sex and opposite-sex couples and carry rights over residency, citizenship, pensions, healthcare, succession and stepchild adoption. Same-sex couples remain barred from marrying, and households headed by same-sex couples do not receive the same legal protections as opposite-sex households. A December 2017 budget-law amendment that would allow foreign same-sex couples to marry in San Marino to encourage tourism had no implementing legislation drafted as of 2024.

Violence against LGBTQ people is reported occasionally, without published figures that would allow comparison against the general crime rate.

Official representation has shifted: Paolo Rondelli's appointment as captain regent in 2022 made San Marino the first country in modern history with an openly gay head of state, on a six-month term carrying no executive power.
SMR.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2026 ILGA Annual Review's legal gender recognition chapter does not cover San Marino; its documented cases concern Albania and Andorra.

No published statistics record the application of the 2008 hate-crime enhancements or the number of anti-LGBTQ incidents.

Article 274 was never reported as applied before its repeal.

Whether implementing legislation for the 2017 provision on foreign same-sex marriages has been drafted since 2024 is unresolved.

LIE.name: Liechtenstein
LIE.summary:
Sexual relations between people of the same sex are lawful in Liechtenstein. Anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are covered by no anti-discrimination statute in force, so a trans visitor has no protected ground to invoke in a discrimination complaint. No law in the sources reviewed prohibits intersex genital modification.

Penal protection runs along the sexual-orientation axis. Since 1 April 2016 harassment and incitement to hatred on grounds of sexual orientation have been banned. Section 283(1) of the Penal Code punishes public incitement to hatred or discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation with up to two years' imprisonment, and section 283(6) prohibits discrimination in public facilities on the same grounds. The Media Act of October 2005 declares media content illegal where it incites or supports discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. These grounds turn on sexual orientation; no equivalent provision on gender identity or gender expression is recorded.

Liechtenstein has no procedure for changing a legal gender marker in official documents, so no identity document issued there can be made to match a person's gender. A traveller arriving on documents issued elsewhere is not affected by Liechtenstein practice in respect of those documents, but anyone who depends on Liechtenstein-issued identification, or who stays in the country, cannot obtain a marker consistent with their gender.

No law in force restricts access to sex-segregated facilities on the basis of gender identity.

Marriage has been open since January 2025 to couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and joint adoption is available on the same terms. A trans visitor in a relationship that Liechtenstein would class by birth-sex status can therefore marry there, and the marriage would be recognised as such domestically.

Official posture has been less protective than the statutes. The Roman Catholic Church is the state religion, and the archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality. In a January 2016 New Year interview Prince Hans-Adam II described rainbow families as irresponsible, said children have a right to a normal family, and suggested Liechtenstein could ignore an adverse ruling from the European Court of Human Rights. The LGBT organisation Flay said the remarks left it shocked, and the Freie Liste called them contrary to the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights.
LIE.outOfScopeNotes:
A Reuters feature on small European states and LGBT equality could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so any material it contains is not reflected here.

The sources reviewed report no prosecution, complaint or enforcement data under section 283 of the Penal Code or under the Media Act. Whether the criminal provisions are applied in practice is unresolved.

The absence of a rule on sex-segregated facilities follows from the absence of any gender-identity legislation. No source reviewed states a facilities rule in positive terms.

The account of everyday social conditions dates from 2012 and has not been re-verified against later sources.

VAT.name: Vatican City
VAT.summary:
No criminal provision in Vatican City law reaches consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults in private and non-commercial. The territory's legal code derives from the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 and has carried no such offence since 1890, including through the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender.

The age of consent is 18 for all persons regardless of gender. A lower age of 14 applies to sexual relations within a marriage recognised as valid by the Catholic Church and by Vatican City law.

Vatican City has no legal mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents, and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity applies in the territory. No rule governs access to single-sex facilities for a trans visitor, and no document-amendment route exists for a resident or a visitor.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It maintains a few cells for pre-trial detention, and a person sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serves the term in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. There is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented case of a trans prisoner held under Vatican City's authority.

The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document 'Male and Female He Created Them' frames 'gender theory' as denying the difference and reciprocity of man and woman and as eliminating the anthropological basis of the family. It is an educational instruction addressed to Catholic institutions rather than a rule binding visitors, but it states the governing institution's position on gender identity.

A 2023 declaration by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith permitted spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Vatican City has consistently rejected civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and the granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples. Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church while maintaining that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God.

In 2021 Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher wrote to the Italian ambassador to the Holy See objecting to an Italian parliamentary bill meant to protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination. The objection targeted the provision prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, which the letter described as a violation of freedom of speech and of religion, and asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated.

On 13 January 1998 the activist Alfredo Ormando set himself on fire on St. Peter's Square, under Vatican jurisdiction, in protest at the Catholic religion's refusal of homosexuality. He died days later in hospital from severe burns.
VAT.outOfScopeNotes:
No United States State Department human rights report chapter for the Holy See exists for 2023 or 2024, so the assessment rests on encyclopedic and institutional sources rather than a government human rights report.

The absence of a documented trans-prisoner placement case reflects the absence of a domestic prison system and of published records, not a finding that no trans person has ever been held in pre-trial detention in Vatican City.

Whether the Vatican's stated right to dismiss officials and employees who publicly acknowledge being gay has been exercised in specific cases is not documented in the sources reviewed.

Enforcement practice at entry, at screening, or in access to facilities for a trans visitor is not documented. No source records a trans visitor being stopped, questioned or refused entry on grounds of gender identity.

CYP.name: Cyprus
CYP.summary:
Cyprus does not criminalise same-sex sexual activity. Consensual conduct was decriminalised in 1998, when the European Court of Human Rights held in Modinos v. Cyprus that Criminal Code section 171 violated the right to private life. The offence of promoting homosexuality was lifted in 2000 and unequal ages of consent were equalised in 2002; the universal age of consent is 17. The former military exclusion of homosexuals, which rested on treating homosexuality as a mental illness, has been removed. In the northern part of the island, deputies voted on 27 January 2014 to repeal the provision that punished homosexual acts with up to five years' imprisonment.

Cypriot law provides no general prohibition of discrimination based on gender identity. The 2004 Equal Treatment in Employment and Occupation Law, adopted to transpose the EU Employment Framework Directive of 2000, prohibits sexual-orientation discrimination in employment only, and gender identity is not among its enumerated grounds. Coverage of sexual orientation and gender identity is reported for 2017 in social protection, social insurance, social benefits, health care, education, participation in unions and professional organisations, and access to goods and services, but an LGBTI NGO assessed the resulting framework as fragmented and inadequate, and housing benefits were found to favour "traditional" families. The European Commission's network of legal experts has reported on the transposition of EU equality rules into Cypriot law in 2020 and again in 2024.

Article 99 of the Penal Code, headed "Incitement to violence or hatred due to sexual orientation or gender identity", punishes intentional public threatening, insulting or offensive urging or incitement, spoken or written, of violence or hatred on those grounds with imprisonment of up to three years or a fine. Parliament raised the fine from €5,000 to €10,000 in October 2024. Law 87(I)/2015 criminalises public incitement to violence or hatred on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, and Law 31(I)/2017 makes prejudice motivation an aggravating factor in sentencing. The hate-speech offence dates to a 2013 penal code amendment that carried up to three years' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine.

Conversion practices were criminalised by a House Plenum vote on 25 May 2023, under Law 39(I)/2023, which bans and criminalises the practice.

No gender-recognition law is in force. A bill drafted with the support of the President and the Justice Minister, following a November 2017 meeting between President Nicos Anastasiades and Accept-LGBT Cyprus, would allow persons over 18 to change legal gender on the basis of self-determination, without diagnosis, hormonal treatment or sex reassignment surgery. The Council of Ministers approved the bill in September 2022 and it received a first parliamentary reading in November 2022; it remained pending in 2024. In June 2019 four parents of transgender children publicly urged its speedy adoption after months of delay. At the 2019 Universal Periodic Review the national report stated that legislation for correcting registered sex, for adults and minors, was in preparation and would require only a decision of the Registrar, with no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports. Queer Cyprus's guidance describes the recognition model it advocates as self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping, and records that the northern part of the island operates its own recognition process, which explicitly includes non-binary identities.

Marriage is legally recognised only as a union between one man and one woman, and no same-sex marriage is recognised. A civil-union law passed on 26 November 2015 by 39 votes to 12 with 3 abstentions and took effect on 9 December 2015, granting several marriage rights and benefits to both same-sex and opposite-sex partners under statutory legislation termed "civil unions". It does not extend to adoption, which remains reserved to heterosexual couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status can register a civil union but cannot jointly adopt.

Enforcement of the hate-speech and hate-crime provisions is inconsistent. Incitement against LGBT people has in some cases drawn no police or legal action, most visibly when committed by clergy of the Greek Orthodox Church. In a February 2019 attack on a gay man in Nicosia police failed to establish a hate-crime motive, and a second Nicosia incident four months later drew no police action. Eleven complaints were examined in 2015 and five criminal prosecutions were pending trial.

Cyprus accepted all the SOGIESC recommendations it received at its 2019 Universal Periodic Review, which covered combating discrimination and violence, criminalising harassment, adopting an action plan against homophobia and transphobia, and adopting a gender-recognition law. No anti-homophobia action plan exists. ECRI has urged that gender identity be added as a prohibited ground of discrimination.
CYP.outOfScopeNotes:
The number of SOGIESC recommendations accepted at the 2019 Universal Periodic Review is recorded as eight by ILGA and as seven in other accounts; the discrepancy is unresolved.

The Queer Cyprus booklet describes a self-determination recognition framework without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping while no gender-recognition law is in force; whether it describes current practice in the northern part of the island, the model advocated for the Republic of Cyprus, or both, is not resolved by the sources.

The status of the gender-recognition bill after 2024 is not sourced.

A 2017 account of incitement provisions carrying up to five years' imprisonment and a €10,000 fine sits against Article 99's three-year maximum; the relationship between the two is not explained in the sources.

The 2017 claim that antidiscrimination coverage extends to gender identity across several fields is not reconciled in the sources with the equal-treatment law's grounds, which do not include gender identity.

The 2015 complaint and prosecution figures are not dated as to the reporting year.

sources.summary: UPR-info Cyprus advocacy sheet (2024): Law 87(I)/2015 criminalises public incitement to violence/hatred on SOGI grounds; Law 31(I)/2017 makes prejudice motivation an aggravating sentencing factor; Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices; the legal gender recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers Sept 2022 with first parliamentary reading Nov 2022 (still pending at 2024); gender identity remains absent from equal-treatment grounds and no anti-homophobia action plan exists; prison guards received 2-day LGBTI+ training (Apr 2023) after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints to the Ombudswoman.

The European Commission Network of Legal Experts country report on gender equality in Cyprus (2024, reporting period 2023) sets out how EU equality rules are transposed into Cypriot national law, including gender-identity-related aspects of the legal framework.

Queer Cyprus Association UPR presentation (Erman Dolmacı, 4th-cycle): confirms the same three Criminal Code amendments (87(I)/2015 incitement, 31(I)/2017 aggravating factor, 39(I)/2023 conversion-practices ban), frames 'ISSUE 1' as trans and gender-diverse rights with the Sept 2022 LGR bill as the outstanding implementation step, and lists the state response to prior UPR recommendations — i.e. hate-speech law delivered, gender-identity discrimination ground and trans legislation not yet delivered.

ILGA 32nd UPR session report (29 Jan 2019): Cyprus received 8 SOGIESC recommendations and accepted all 8; national report stated new legislation for correcting registered sex (adults and minors) was in preparation requiring only a Registrar decision, no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports; ECRI had urged gender identity as a prohibited discrimination ground; Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition as 40th member (Aug 2018). Marks the reform promise the 2022 bill was meant to fulfil.

The European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Cyprus (2020, reporting period 2019) covers transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds in Cypriot law.

PinkNews (10 Oct 2013): Cyprus amended its penal code to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity, punishable by up to 3 years' imprisonment and/or a €5,000 fine; workplace SOGI protections were added in 2004. It is the hate-speech offence the 2015 law extended.

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.summary:
Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity. No sodomy statute was inherited from the French protectorate period, which began in 1867, or enacted after independence in 1953, and the age of consent is 15 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Legislation contains no non-discrimination provisions on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans visitors have no route to legal recognition. Cambodian law does not permit changes to gender markers on official documents, and gender-affirming surgery is not legally available.

Official posture is cooperative on paper. At the 2019 Universal Periodic Review Cambodia accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage, and at the 2024 review it accepted all 12 recommendations on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, seven of them on marriage equality, alongside legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity and anti-discrimination measures. A civil-society joint submission was filed in December 2023.

That posture has not been matched by statutory protection. In 2015 a Council of Ministers spokesman claimed existing law already protected LGBT people, a claim the Cambodian Center for Human Rights disputed. The same year the Ministry of Information wrote to media outlets asking them to stop mocking the LGBT community, citing the Constitution's protection of LGBT honour and rights. In February 2011 tourism businesses launched the 'Adore Cambodia!' campaign to signal welcome to LGBT tourists, which the Ministry of Tourism endorsed, saying it had no policy to discriminate and supported them.

Enforcement and street-level violence are the principal risk. A Cambodian Centre for Human Rights study documented more than 135 cases of harassment and abuse against transgender women on city streets, and recorded a Siem Reap police practice of targeting transgender sex workers and forcing them to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water; transgender sex workers there were also made to leave the area, sometimes after being forced to bathe naked, while cisgender sex workers were not documented as receiving the same treatment. A 2016 CCHR report found about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested, with over 90% of those saying the arrest was because they were transgender. The 2017 US State Department human rights report listed violence against LGBTI persons among Cambodia's most significant human rights issues, noting frequent harassment and bullying over appearance and over work in the entertainment and commercial sex sectors, with more than 100 incidents of violence or abuse reported by a local LGBTI organisation. The same report found no official discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, citizenship, education or health care.

In custody, the Cambodian Human Rights Committee president Keo Remy said in February 2025 that transgender prisoners who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from Correctional Centre 1, the men's facility, to Correctional Centre 2, the women's facility at Prey Sar. The statement was made in praise of the centre rather than as a published regulation, and no statute or formal policy text is cited.

Phnom Penh and Siem Reap have a visible LGBT scene with bars and clubs, and Pride parades have run annually since 2003, with the first Siem Reap Pride in 2018.
KHM.outOfScopeNotes:
The February 2025 statement on transferring transgender prisoners between Correctional Centre 1 and Correctional Centre 2 is not a published regulation and no statute or formal policy text has been identified; how it is applied in practice is unresolved.

The 2015 claim by a Council of Ministers spokesman that existing law already protected LGBT people was disputed by the Cambodian Center for Human Rights, and no provision has been identified that gives it effect.

The 2024 Universal Periodic Review acceptances, including on marriage equality and legal gender recognition, have not been matched by enacted legislation in the sources reviewed.

Documented case counts, including the 135 or more cases recorded by the Cambodian Centre for Human Rights and the more than 100 incidents reported by a local LGBTI organisation in 2017, are monitoring figures rather than population rates; they record what was reported to those organisations and do not establish prevalence. The 2016 finding that about 38% of surveyed transgender women had been arrested rests on a survey sample whose sampling frame is not stated in the sources reviewed.

NPL.name: Nepal
NPL.summary:
Nepal criminalises no conduct on the basis of gender identity or gender expression. Same-sex acts have been legal since the Supreme Court's December 2007 judgment in Sunil Babu Pant v. Nepal Government, which held that homosexuality is not 'unnatural'. The Criminal Codes Act 2017, which replaced the 1963 Muluki Ain, still lists 'unnatural sex' on its face and must be read in light of that ruling; the Muluki Ain criminalised 'unnatural sexual intercourse' with up to one year's imprisonment, and LGBTQI+ Nepalis were arrested under it. The age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition rests on the 2007 Supreme Court ruling recognising the right to self-determined name and gender markers, and a third-gender category has been available on official documents by self-declaration. Government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male and female marker changes lagged, so the country's progressive reputation has outrun its policy. Changing markers to female or male has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations, including intrusive post-operative genital exams. In August 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed more than 50 lawsuits since 2021. Human Rights Watch called on the government in February 2024 to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure for transgender and third-gender people to obtain official documents, an intervention that illustrates the absence of a straightforward document-change process; a Kathmandu trans woman holds a 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender. A civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition, the Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078, was published in October 2021 by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi through the Asia Pacific Transgender Network. Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective assessed in 2020 that an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community.

Judicial recognition of foreign same-sex marriages exists: Suman Pant's Supreme Court case set a precedent for same-sex spousal visas. On 28 June 2023 Justice Til Prasad Shrestha issued an interim order directing the government to 'temporarily register' marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities, and the full bench has yet to deliver a final verdict. In April 2024 the National ID and Civil Registration Department instructed local authorities to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register. Temporary registration grants no equal rights: same-sex couples cannot inherit property, receive tax subsidies, make spousal medical decisions or adopt children, and certificates label them 'groom and bride'. The first marriage of a trans woman and a cisgender man took place in November 2023, and as of June 2025 Blue Diamond Society counted at least 17 documented queer marriages. Implementation is inconsistent: the Kathmandu District Court rejected a registration in July 2023, and compliance by local governments is unknown.

A November 2024 Kathmandu Post feature on Janakpur reported that trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. Transgender Nepalis face severe gender-based violence and interrupted education, especially in rural areas.

The first gender-affirming surgery in Nepal was performed in June 2025 at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, which has since established a Gender Affirming Clinic. Hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery remain hard to reach: a six-month hormone supply costs 4,500 rupees, providers are few, and many trans Nepalis take hormones without medical supervision because of stigma. Some travel to India and Thailand for surgery.

On 30 October 2024 the Aamul Paribartan Nagarik Party held a protest rally opposing homosexuality and LGBTQ rights, with Mitini Nepal's executive director noting that anti-LGBTQ sentiments are gaining momentum in Nepal and South Asia. In April 2026 newly elected Prime Minister Balen Shah faced LGBTQ community criticism over a YouTube rap video containing derogatory and homophobic hate speech; after demands for an apology, his supporters markedly increased derogatory comments, hate speech and death threats against the community.
NPL.outOfScopeNotes:
The Supreme Court's full bench has not delivered a final verdict on the interim order directing temporary registration of marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities; whether local governments comply with the April 2024 instruction to record such marriages in a separate register is not sourced.

Whether the August 2024 ruling requiring recognition of a trans woman as a woman on all documents without medical verification has changed practice at document-issuing offices nationally is not established by the sources.

The number of providers offering hormone therapy or gender-affirming surgery in Nepal is not quantified beyond the statement that providers are few.

For this record: the landmark ruling and the pre-ruling barrier path, dated.

During the 2011 census, some enumerators demanded that a child be stripped when parents listed them as 'third gender'.

Conversion therapy is practised, including treatment in rehabilitation centres and traditional exorcism by family members. Lesbian couples are denied IVF, and research and healthcare addressing LGBT Nepalis' needs are severely lacking.

A drop-in centre with free HIV testing operates in Kathmandu through the Blue Diamond Society, which has more than 50 branches; Mitini Nepal, Parichaya Samaj and Sahaayam Nepal also provide resources. Queer Youth Group has filed writ petitions at the Supreme Court demanding legal recognition of gender identity and has advocated for the citizenship bill.

UNDP has recommended that transgender and intersex students be given access to safe toilets and bathroom facilities.

NPL.blindSummary:
The country criminalises no conduct on the basis of gender identity or gender expression. Same-sex acts have been legal since a December 2007 Supreme Court judgment holding that homosexuality is not 'unnatural'. The 2017 criminal code, which replaced the 1963 legal code, still lists 'unnatural sex' on its face and must be read in light of that ruling; the earlier code criminalised 'unnatural sexual intercourse' with up to one year's imprisonment, and LGBTQI+ people in the country were arrested under it. The age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition rests on the 2007 Supreme Court ruling recognising the right to self-determined name and gender markers, and a third-gender category has been available on official documents by self-declaration. Government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male and female marker changes lagged, so the country's progressive reputation has outrun its policy. Changing markers to female or male has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations, including intrusive post-operative genital exams. In August 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that a transgender law student must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed more than 50 lawsuits since 2021. An international human rights organisation called on the government in February 2024 to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure for transgender and third-gender people to obtain official documents, an intervention that illustrates the absence of a straightforward document-change process; a transgender woman in the capital holds a 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender. A civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition was published in October 2021 by transgender advocates through a regional transgender network. A local advocacy group assessed in 2020 that an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law is still needed to address inequalities faced by the transgender and broader community.

Judicial recognition of foreign same-sex marriages exists: a Supreme Court case set a precedent for same-sex spousal visas. On 28 June 2023 a Supreme Court justice issued an interim order directing the government to 'temporarily register' marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities, and the full bench has yet to deliver a final verdict. In April 2024 the national civil registration department instructed local authorities to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register. Temporary registration grants no equal rights: same-sex couples cannot inherit property, receive tax subsidies, make spousal medical decisions or adopt children, and certificates label them 'groom and bride'. The first marriage of a transgender woman and a cisgender man took place in November 2023, and as of June 2025 a national transgender organisation counted at least 17 documented queer marriages. Implementation is inconsistent: a district court in the capital rejected a registration in July 2023, and compliance by local governments is unknown.

A November 2024 press feature on a provincial city reported that transgender people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. Transgender people in the country face severe gender-based violence and interrupted education, especially in rural areas.

The first gender-affirming surgery in the country was performed in June 2025 at a national teaching hospital, which has since established a gender affirming clinic. Hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery remain hard to reach: a six-month hormone supply costs 4,500 in local currency, providers are few, and many transgender people take hormones without medical supervision because of stigma. Some travel to a neighbouring jurisdiction and another country in the region for surgery.

On 30 October 2024 a political party held a protest rally opposing homosexuality and LGBTQ rights, with the executive director of a national transgender organisation noting that anti-LGBTQ sentiments are gaining momentum in the country and the region. In April 2026 the newly elected prime minister faced LGBTQ community criticism over a YouTube rap video containing derogatory and homophobic hate speech; after demands for an apology, his supporters markedly increased derogatory comments, hate speech and death threats against the community.

LKA.name: Sri Lanka
LKA.summary:
Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity. Section 365 covers "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and has been applied to men; Section 365A covers "gross indecency" and was amended in 1995 to reach women, so both provisions now apply to men and women. The maximum penalty is ten years' imprisonment. Where an offence under these sections is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16, the penalty rises to ten to twenty years' rigorous imprisonment.

Prosecutions are limited. The Canada Immigration and Refugee Board's January 2012 research found no convictions under the articles, and Outright International's March 2026 overview describes prosecutions as limited. The provisions nonetheless structure everyday policing. The US State Department's country report documents police harassment of LGBT persons, and the 2012 research found that criminalisation "paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to brand all lesbian, bisexual, transgendered persons as perverts and criminals". Outright International records frequent harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services. Advocacy groups report that police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, particularly those involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Article 365 as justification, and human rights organisations have documented police using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA individuals. Article 365 remains cited to justify police harassment and moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings.

An August 2023 opinion piece published by the International Commission of Jurists, by Mathuri Thamilmaran, states that the Sri Lanka Police are the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals, and that both the Police and the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka acknowledged this in the preceding months. The piece argues that administrative circulars cannot substitute for legal reform.

Outright International reports that authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence, a practice widely condemned as torture.

No comprehensive anti-discrimination protections exist.

Legal gender recognition is available through a certification process. In 2016 the Ministry of Health issued a circular to health services and education institutions on issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka. No surgical intervention is legally required, though the certification is bureaucratic and may be onerous to obtain.

Gender-affirming surgery is relatively inaccessible. Many hospitals lack the specialised surgical units and staff required, and a physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 report said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatment for transgender patients. Patients report ignorance, curiosity and ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, which raises their treatment costs. Obtaining hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught.

The National Blood Transfusion Service bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as "risky behaviour" alongside drug use and having multiple partners.

Family law does not recognise same-sex marriage or same-sex civil unions and gives no equal rights to same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times and is based on European law. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to marriage or civil-union recognition and no equal rights as a live-in partner.
LKA.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Sri Lanka was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403). Its documented finding that the penal code criminalises same-sex activity is consistent with the sources above but could not be verified directly.

Whether the 2016 gender recognition certification process is open to foreign nationals is not addressed in the sources reviewed, and no local gender marker document available to a visitor is identified.

No youth-specific findings on access to gender-affirming care appear in the source material.

Conviction data under Sections 365 and 365A rests on the January 2012 Immigration and Refugee Board finding of no convictions; no more recent conviction figures were located.

The status of the March 2022 conversion therapy bill after July 2024 is not sourced.

Prison placement for transgender detainees remains uncodified; no statutory rule or published policy was identified.

sources.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
sources.summary: Sri Lanka's Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing today: Media Spokesperson/Commissioner Gamini Dissanayake (Oct 2024) said current prison facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, and separate accommodation is only planned for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case-by-case: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender 'where possible', while those without it go through a doctor's assessment of whether they 'can be considered a transgender' before placement, weighing inmate preference. Officials explicitly worry about people accused of sex offences 'identifying as transgender' to enter female housing with born-male offenders, a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

sources.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation
sources.summary: The Morning (original Daily Morning reporting, 4 Oct 2024) of the same Prisons Department statement: Commissioner Dissanayake said 'we always try to accommodate transgender prisoners who have the official identity card', and absent the ID a doctor assesses whether the inmate can be considered transgender, after which 'the preference of the particular inmate' feeds the accommodation decision. The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

MNG.name: Mongolia
MNG.summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy was criminalised in Mongolia's Criminal Code of 1961 and decriminalised in 1993, when all references were removed. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is spread across several instruments rather than a single equality statute. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in force since 1 July 2017, prohibits discrimination on both grounds. Article 6 of the Labour Code, in force since 2022, prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Article 1.3.2 of the revised Criminal Law adopted on 3 December 2015 bars discrimination in criminalisation and sentencing on grounds including sexual and gender orientation. No comprehensive equality law is in place.

Hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity directly. The Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 named gender identity and sexual orientation as protected grounds for hate crimes; it was scheduled for 1 September 2016 and took effect on 1 July 2017. Section 10(1)(2)(14) of the Penal Code aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is outlawed.

Legal gender recognition exists but is conditional. A June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law allows a person to change the legal gender recorded on their birth certificate or citizen identification card following sex reassignment surgery.

Constitutional marriage is restricted to a man and a woman. Article 16(11) of the Constitution defines marriage as based on the equality and mutual consent of a man and a woman who have reached the legally determined age, with State protection for family, motherhood and child. No partnership or union recognition is available to a trans visitor's relationship or to a couple read as same-sex under birth-sex status, and such households are ineligible for the protections afforded to opposite-sex couples.

Police practice shows documented, institution-level change alongside documented non-enforcement. After an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman in 2019, the LGBT Center trained police officers, prosecutors and judges on the 2017 hate-crime provisions; reporting in October 2019 puts the number trained at more than 500, and a figure of more than 300 was recorded in August 2018. The force has issued guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of the gender marker on identity documents. Against that, local reports and activists stated in August 2018 that police continue to disregard or not take seriously complaints of hate crimes against LGBTQ people, with attacks often resulting in no punishment.

Trans-specific violence in the record is historical. In September 2009 three transgender women were kidnapped in broad daylight on a promenade in Ulaanbaatar by a hyper-nationalist group, driven to a cemetery on the city outskirts, beaten, sexually assaulted and forced to perform sexual acts on the perpetrators as a warning; the incident was not reported to police for fear of victimisation and reprisal. The dossier records no later trans-specific attack of this kind. Anti-LGBT violence more broadly is documented in 2001, when a lesbian woman was raped, abducted and stabbed by two men, and in February 2014, when a gay man was sexually assaulted by a neo-Nazi group; such violence is often not reported to police.

Since 2022, Article 6 of the Labor Code bans discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression. The new Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 included gender identity as a protected ground for hate crimes, planned to come into force on 1 September 2016 but postponed to 1 July 2017. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in effect since 2017, bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, and Section 10(1)(2)(14) aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's sexual orientation. Since 2022, Article 6 of the Labor Code bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. In 2001 a lesbian woman was raped, abducted and stabbed by two men, and in February 2014 a gay man was sexually assaulted by a neo-Nazi group, with such violence often not reported to police, while in May 2014 the Government announced it would consider anti-discrimination legislation following public outcry. MNG.blindSummary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy was criminalised in the country in 1961 and decriminalised in 1993, when all references were removed from the Criminal Code. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited across several separate instruments rather than a single equality statute. Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in effect since 1 July 2017, bans discrimination on both grounds. Article 1.3.2 of the revised Criminal Law adopted on 3 December 2015 bars discrimination in criminalisation and sentencing on grounds including sexual and gender orientation. Article 6 of the Labour Code, since 2022, bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Protections remain fragmented and no comprehensive equality law is in place.

Hate-crime and hate-speech provisions expressly cover gender identity. The Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 included gender identity as a protected ground for hate crimes; the code was scheduled to take effect on 1 September 2016 and was postponed to 1 July 2017. Section 10(1)(2)(14) of the Penal Code aggravates penalties for homicides motivated by hate towards the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is outlawed.

A June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law allows transgender people to change their legal gender on birth certificates or citizen identification cards following sex reassignment surgery.

Marriage is defined in Article 16(11) of the Constitution as based on the equality and mutual consent of a man and a woman who have reached the age determined by law, with national protection for family, motherhood and child. Same-sex relationships are not recognised and same-sex couple households are ineligible for the same protections as opposite-sex couples; no union recognition of any kind is available. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore has no legal standing for that partnership.

A residual offence addressing 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' remains on the statute book despite the absence of laws specifically criminalising homosexuality.

Enforcement of hate-crime provisions remains weak in practice. As of August 2018 the LGBT Centre was training more than 300 police officers, prosecutors and judges on hate-crime handling, and after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman in 2019 the Centre trained 500 or more police officers, prosecutors and judges on the 2017 criminal code's hate-crime provisions. The force adopted guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identity documents. Despite this training, local reports and activists say police continue to disregard or not take seriously complaints of hate crimes against LGBTQ people, and attacks often result in no punishment.

Documented violence against transgender people includes a September 2009 incident in which three transgender women were kidnapped in broad daylight at a promenade in the capital by a hyper-nationalist group, driven to a cemetery on the city outskirts, beaten, sexually assaulted and forced to perform sexual acts on the perpetrators as a warning. The attack was not reported to police for fear of victimisation and reprisal. In February 2014 a gay man was sexually assaulted by a neo-Nazi group, and in 2001 a lesbian woman was raped, abducted and stabbed by two men; such violence is often not reported to police.

Violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people are fairly common and often unreported. The culture is and has remained strongly heteronormative, and despite the 2017 protections, ostracism, harassment and violence persist both socially and systemically. A 2019 report found that 79% of LGBTQ-identified young people experienced bullying, discrimination or ostracism, with several LGBTQ students reporting discrimination and bullying at schools.

Community visibility is limited. The scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism; a 2008 account describes two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees fear being outed. LGBT groups can register as organisations. The LGBT Centre in the capital has advocated publicly and organised a Pride event in 2018, and a trans man who came out in 2004 and began transition in 2011 co-founded and advises the Centre.

MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is criminalised under section 377 of the penal code, a provision introduced in 1886. It prohibits carnal intercourse with any man, woman or animal and provides for imprisonment ranging between life and a term of not less than two years, extendable to ten years, with a fine of between 400 and 1,000 rupees. The prohibition applies regardless of consent or privacy, and it reaches heterosexual anal and oral sex as well. Enforcement has been described as inconsistent, but the provision remains in active use: in November 2018 the HIV-positive advocate Aung Myo Htut was charged under it in Yangon over an alleged offence against an employee.

Transgender people are additionally targeted under section 35(c) of the Police Act 1945, known locally as the shadow law or darkness law, which allows police to detain anyone they consider to be behaving suspiciously after sunset. A related provision on face covering carries up to three months' imprisonment and is used specifically against transgender people. Other provisions cited as available against LGBT people include sections 269 and 270 on negligently spreading a sexually transmitted disease, section 290 on public nuisance with fines up to 200 rupees, sections 292, 293 and 294 on obscene material, songs or public acts, section 372 on buying or selling a prostitute under eighteen, section 469 on a marriage ceremony absent a legal marriage, and section 5(j) of the Emergency Provisions Act on anything affecting morality negatively.

Myanmar does not recognise gender identity and does not permit transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth. No legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process is described in the sources. Transgender people are consequently subject to police harassment, sexual assault including rape, mistreatment and extortion.

Documented incidents include the 2013 arrest in Mandalay of transgender women who were forced to strip and paraded naked while being photographed, which police described as a public service, and the case of the transgender woman Nat Nat We, arrested, stripped and beaten in Yangon and held for 14 days after walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work. Police violence against transgender women is routine.

Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has worsened. Authorities have carried out attacks, arrests, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people, and torture and sexual violence in detention are documented. Militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life, and a June 2024 submission to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions identified killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas, naming intensified enforcement of section 377 as an aggravating factor.

The conscription law announced in February 2024 has driven queer people into fear and displacement. In 2025 the junta banned seven LGBTQ-themed books as obscene and announced prosecutions for their publishers. The October 2022 Organization Registration Law imposes prison terms on NGOs that fail to comply, constraining the civil-society organisations that provide community support.

Myanmar has no enforceable legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The measures that exist are symbolic or non-binding: the 2019 Child Rights Law contains a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation but applies only to children and has no enforcement mechanism; the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals without legal penalties; and the 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights lists LGBTQ people as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery but is a planning document rather than law. A survey of LGBT respondents found that 50 per cent had no confidence in the legal system and more than 68 per cent feared repercussions from abusers.

Myanmar does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions. A 2014 unofficial wedding ceremony by a couple who had been together for ten years drew widespread attention and a backlash from social conservatives who questioned why the anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced against them. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be classified as same-sex under Myanmar law, there is no route to legal recognition.
MMR.outOfScopeNotes:
No legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process for transgender people is described in the available sources. Whether any administrative practice exists outside statute is not sourced.

Enforcement of section 377 is not systematically recorded. The provision has been described as not strictly enforced while remaining in active use, and no prosecution statistics are available to indicate how often it is applied.

The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights is a planning document with no enforcement mechanism, and the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines carry no legal penalties. Neither creates a remedy for a visitor or resident who experiences discrimination.

How the 2024 conscription law's medical and documentation screening treats transgender people is not addressed in the sources.

sources.summary: Outright International overview (updated March 2026): Section 377 used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence; after the 1 Feb 2021 coup risks intensified — torture/sexual violence in detention, Oct 2022 Organization Registration Law (prison terms for NGO non-compliance), compulsory military service announced Feb 2024, seven LGBTQ-themed books banned 2025. Verdict: avoid entirely.

DVB (Jan 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; the NUG recorded 17 LGBT killed and 2 critically injured since 1 Feb 2021; 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' found 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and 68%+ fear repercussions from abusers.

Human Rights Myanmar submission (June 2024) to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions: killing of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled Myanmar - 5 to 12 individuals dead since the coup; Section 377 enforcement intensified as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

RFA (10 Jan 2025): junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; colonial-era law carries up to 10 years for gay sex; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the Feb 2021 coup.

ASEAN SOGIE Caucus (March 2025, from Queers of Burma Alternative research Jan 2025): the 2024 Conscription Law drives queer people into fear and displacement; Section 377 carries life imprisonment or up to 10 years, and 1945 Police Act s.35(c) (face covering, up to 3 months) is used specifically against transgender people.

Guardian (2 Feb 2016): Colors Rainbow's work in Yangon — trans woman Nat Nat We describes arrest, stripping, a beating and 14 days' detention for walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work; documents routine police violence against trans women.

Washington Blade (2 Nov 2018): Aung Myo Htut (aka Addy Chen), an outspoken HIV-positive LGBTI advocate and Yangon restaurant owner, was charged under Penal Code 377 over an alleged offence against an employee. Section 377 remained in active use, and the community demanded fair media coverage.

HuffPost (17 Oct 2015): colonial-era criminalisation; 2013 Mandalay arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); nat kadaws (spirit mediums) are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Myanmar (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Myanmar does not recognise gender identity and does not allow transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth. Transgender people are subject to police harassment and sexual assault, including rape, mistreatment, or extortion by police. Police often target transgender people using section 35(c) of the Police Act, described as the 'shadow law' or 'darkness law,' which allows detention of anyone considered behaving suspiciously after sunset. Transgender people may face discrimination, family rejection or violence for their identity. Trans women are frequently denied equal access to many professions, limiting opportunities and leading to overrepresentation in certain jobs including spirit mediums and sex work, with only three 'respectable' career options described as beautician, fashion designer, or nat kadaw ('spirit wife' or spirit medium). As a nat kadaw, transgender Burmese people can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied to them by Burmese society, and 'Occult' is described as a local term for the transgender community in Myanmar. Same-sex sexual activity is illegal under section 377 of Myanmar's Penal Code 1861, enacted in 1886, which subjects same-sex sexual acts regardless of whether consensual or done in private to up to 10 years in prison. Section 377 prohibits carnal intercourse with any man, woman, or animal and provides imprisonment varying between life and a term of not less than 2 years but which may extend to 10 years and a fine of not less than four hundred rupees but which may extend to one thousand rupees. Heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex are also illegal, as section 377 prohibits sodomy whether heterosexual or homosexual. The law has not been strictly enforced, but in November 2018 gay activist Aung Myo Htut, also known as 'Addy Chen,' was arrested under the sodomy law. LGBTQ people are also targeted under section 35(c) of the Police Act, which allows police to detain anyone considered behaving suspiciously after sunset, and other provisions cited as usable against LGBTQ people include sections 269 and 270 on negligently spreading a sexually transmitted disease, section 290 on 'public nuisance' with fines up to two hundred rupees, sections 292, 293, and 294 on 'obscene' material, songs or public acts, section 372 on buying or selling a prostitute under eighteen, section 469 on marriage ceremony absent legal marriage, and section 5(j) of the Emergency Provisions Act on anything affecting morality negatively. Myanmar does not recognise same-sex marriages or civil unions, and a 2014 unofficial wedding by a same-sex couple together for 10 years triggered backlash from social conservatives querying why anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced. Myanmar has no enforceable legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, with limited measures described as symbolic or non-enforceable, including the 2019 Child Rights Law non-discrimination clause applying only to children without enforcement mechanisms, the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines encouraging non-discriminatory portrayals without legal penalties, and the 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights including LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group only as a planning document. Burma's social mores about human sexuality have been described as being 'extremely conservative.' In local Buddhist tradition, those born LGBTQ are perceived as facing punishment for sins committed in a past life, and historically official homophobia, limited public awareness, and lack of community role models rendered LGBTQ people invisible in Burmese society. A 2020 poll found 74% agreed being LGBTQ should be legal (23% disagreed) and 81% agreed that 'LGBT people deserve equality and equal treatment just like anyone else in Myanmar' (12% disagreed). LGBTQ activists have noted 'a growing climate of societal acceptance and tolerance toward LGBTQ people, in line with worldwide trends.' Specifically for transgender people, 'As a nat kadaw, transgender Burmese people can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied to them by Burmese society.' Mya Thet Mu, described as a gay woman from Myanmar, is documented as stating that 'lesbians are often seen as less acceptable than gay men and transgender people.'

Activists have described a growing climate of societal acceptance and tolerance.

Social mores about sexuality have been described as extremely conservative, and in local Buddhist tradition those born LGBTQ are understood as facing punishment for sins committed in a past life. Historically, official homophobia, limited public awareness and a lack of community role models rendered LGBTQ people invisible in Burmese society.

Cultural visibility for transgender people is uneven. As nat kadaws, or spirit mediums, transgender people can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied to them, and occult is a local term for the transgender community. Documented incidents include the 2013 arrest in a major city of transgender women who were forced to strip and paraded naked while being photographed, which police described as a public service, and the case of a transgender woman arrested, stripped and beaten in the largest city and held for 14 days after walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work. Police violence against transgender women is routine.

Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has worsened. Authorities have carried out attacks, arrests, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people, and torture and sexual violence in detention are documented. Militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life, and a June 2024 submission to a United Nations special rapporteur identified killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas, naming intensified enforcement of section 377 as an aggravating factor.

The conscription law announced in February 2024 has driven queer people into fear and displacement. In 2025 the authorities banned seven LGBTQ-themed books as obscene and announced prosecutions for their publishers. The October 2022 organisation registration law imposes prison terms on non-governmental organisations that fail to comply, constraining the civil-society organisations that provide community support.

The country has no enforceable legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The measures that exist are symbolic or non-binding: the 2019 child rights law contains a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation but applies only to children and has no enforcement mechanism; the 2020 national broadcasting guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals without legal penalties; and the 2022 gender policy on sexual and reproductive health and rights lists LGBTQ people as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery but is a planning document rather than law. A survey of LGBT respondents found that 50 per cent had no confidence in the legal system and more than 68 per cent feared repercussions from abusers.

The country does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions. A 2014 unofficial wedding ceremony by a couple who had been together for ten years drew widespread attention and a backlash from social conservatives who questioned why the anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced against them. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be classified as same-sex under the country's law, there is no route to legal recognition.
MMR.blindOutOfScope:
No legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process for transgender people is described in the available sources. Whether any administrative practice exists outside statute is not sourced.

Enforcement of section 377 is not systematically recorded. The provision has been described as not strictly enforced while remaining in active use, and no prosecution statistics are available to indicate how often it is applied.

The 2022 gender policy on sexual and reproductive health and rights is a planning document with no enforcement mechanism, and the 2020 national broadcasting guidelines carry no legal penalties. Neither creates a remedy for a visitor or resident who experiences discrimination.

How the 2024 conscription law's medical and documentation screening treats transgender people is not addressed in the sources.

Civil-society research (March 2025, based on local research from January 2025): the 2024 conscription law drives queer people into fear and displacement; the penal-code provision carries life imprisonment or a long term, and a historic-era police-act clause on face covering is used specifically against transgender people.

Media report (2 November 2018): an outspoken LGBTI advocate with HIV, a restaurant owner, was charged under the penal-code provision over an alleged offence against an employee — the provision in active use, with the community demanding fair media coverage.

Public opinion data points in a different direction from the legal regime. A 2020 poll found that 74 per cent agreed being LGBTQ should be legal, against 23 per cent who disagreed, and 81 per cent agreed that LGBT people deserve equality and equal treatment, against 12 per cent who disagreed. Activists have described a growing climate of societal acceptance and tolerance.

Social mores about sexuality have been described as extremely conservative, and in the majority religious tradition those born LGBTQ are understood as facing punishment for sins committed in a past life. Historically, official homophobia, limited public awareness and a lack of community role models rendered LGBTQ people invisible in the country's society.

Cultural visibility for transgender people is uneven. As spirit mediums, transgender people can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied to them, and occult is a local term for the transgender community. A gay woman from the country is documented as saying that lesbians are often seen as less acceptable than gay men and transgender people.
MMR.localsOnly:
Trans women are frequently denied equal access to many professions, which limits opportunities and pushes them towards a narrow set of occupations. Three options are described as respectable: beautician, fashion designer, or nat kadaw. Overrepresentation in spirit medium work and in sex work follows from that exclusion.

Access to healthcare is shaped by criminalisation and stigma. Section 377 was identified in 2013 by Aung San Suu Kyi as hampering the country's efforts to combat HIV, and gay men, especially those living with HIV or AIDS, are stigmatised. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights includes LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law.

In June 2019 Kyaw Zin Win, a young gay man working as a librarian at Myanmar Imperial University in Yangon, died by suicide after continuous harassment and bullying from colleagues. More than 600 people attended his funeral and a rainbow flag was wrapped around his coffin. The university opened an investigation and suspended three staff members, and the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission launched a separate investigation and called for the enactment of anti-discrimination provisions.

Same-sex couples can cohabit freely in Yangon and Mandalay and can hold ceremonial marriages without legal persecution, but these ceremonies carry no legal standing.
