CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.summary:
Private, non-commercial sexual relations between consenting adults aged 16 and over have been lawful in Cuba since 1979, when the Social Defence Code that classified homosexual practices as a social threat was repealed. The offence of public display of homosexual condition was repealed in 1987, and the offence of bothering or soliciting with homosexual requests was narrowed in 1997 to cover sexual requests only. The Public Ostentation Law of 1938 was repealed in 1988, and police were instructed not to harass LGBT people.

Article 42 of the 2019 Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and was the first Cuban constitutional text to name both grounds expressly. The definition of marriage as between a man and a woman in Article 36 was removed in the February 2019 referendum, with marriage redefined on the basis of free will and equality of rights.

The September 2022 Family Code referendum, the fourth national vote since 1959, produced legal recognition of marriage and unions between people of the same sex, adoption by same-sex couples, non-commercial surrogacy, legal gender change without surgery, shared parental rights and codified penalties for domestic violence.

The vote passed against organised religious opposition and a campaign by government opponents who voted No in order to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a victory amid the crackdown that followed the July 2021 protests, in which more than 1,400 people were arrested, and a period of record emigration. Opponents also argued that the child-welfare provisions could be turned against dissidents. The rights the Family Code recognises are contested rather than uniformly enforced.

Police enforcement has targeted gender presentation directly. In 2001 police ran a campaign against gay and trans people, preventing them from meeting in the street, imposing fines and closing meeting places. In 2004 police ran a campaign aimed at travestis, arresting those dressed in women's clothing; the crackdown in Havana that July involved detention, municipal warnings to stop dressing as women, sanctions against three people under the dangerousness law carrying up to four years' imprisonment, the closure of private clubs hosting their shows, a ban on gay parties, and refusal of entry to regular discos. Most of those affected were forced to wear men's clothing in public, and CENESEX advised against appearing in women's clothing until the crackdown passed.

Official institutions have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s. CENESEX runs a state-backed trans-rights programme that works with the police and the supreme court and carries out sexual-diversity education. Havana holds a pride march each May to mark the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia, with attendance growing every year. Cuba voted to renew the mandate of the United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025.

State persecution of gay men dates to the UMAP forced-labour camps of 1965-68, where conscripts were sent to cut cane for around 60 hours a week in Camagüey, paid seven pesos a day, and subjected to electric-shock and injection experiments presented as cures. Official policy shifted during the mid-1970s, and in 2010 Fidel Castro publicly accepted blame for the persecution of gay Cubans in remarks carried by La Jornada.
CUB.outOfScopeNotes:
No entry, visa, immigration-screening, airport-security or custody-search rule specific to trans travellers appears in the sources reviewed.

No record of police action against gender-nonconforming people after 2004 appears in the sources reviewed, and no account of current police practice on gender presentation is available.

No figure for trans-specific violence or homicide in Cuba appears in the sources reviewed, and no rate can be stated from them.

Whether the gender-identity, disability and HIV-status protections proposed in 2013 have since been enacted into the Labor Code is not established by these sources; the enumeration gap described above stands as the last confirmed position.

The administrative requirements, waiting periods and documentary conditions attached to legal gender change are referred to only as recognition without surgery; the procedure itself is not detailed.

No information on access by gender identity to bathrooms, changing facilities or other sex-segregated public facilities appears in the sources reviewed.

sources.summary: LegalClarity overview (30 May 2026): documents Cuba's arc from the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, ~60 hrs/week cutting cane in Camagüey, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — 1979 Penal Code removal of consensual same-sex acts, Castro's public acceptance of blame (La Jornada, 2010), Resolution 126 (2008) trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 Constitution (Art 42, first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 Family Code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: Labor Code Law 116 bars SOGI discrimination but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, and the Labor Code's article 2(b) covers orientation, not identity.

Americas Quarterly (15 Sept 2022): previews Cuba's 25 Sept 2022 Family Code referendum, only the 4th national vote since 1959, which would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights. Opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (1,400+ arrestees) and record emigration. The equality settlement is contested rather than state-enforced.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (23 Dec 2011): sympathetic first-person account 'Rainbow Cuba' disputing claims of systematic state homophobia — documents the UMAP camps (conscripts paid seven pesos a day), the 1975 declaration-era turning point, and CENESEX's state-backed programme: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education. Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.

Washington Blade (21 Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; the trans-specific amendment drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, while passage of the sexual-orientation ban was the confirmed outcome. The measure predates the 2019 Constitution and the 2022 Family Code.

Washington Blade (26 May 2018): documents Cuba's use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned after filing Dutch asylum claims (Jan 2018); a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained (19 May 2018), and LGBTI activists (incl. Nelson Gandulla, Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation) remained monitored. Relevant to visitors: Cuba's hostility toward emigration/asylum, not toward gender expression as such.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Cuba (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is illegal in Cuba. Since 1993, transgender persons may serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces. In 2012, Adela Hernández became the first known transgender person to hold public office in Cuba, winning election as delegate to the City Council of Caibarien in Villa Clara province. In 2001, police carried out a campaign against gay and trans people, preventing them from meeting in the street, fining them and closing meeting places. In 2004, police carried out a campaign specifically directed at travestis (transvestites), arresting those dressed in women's clothing. Pride parades in Havana are held every May to coincide with the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia, with attendance growing every year. In 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025, Cuba voted in favor of renewing the mandate of the United Nations independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity. Private, non-commercial sexual relations between same-sex consenting adults aged 16 and over have been legal in Cuba since 1979. The Social Defence Code, which characterized homosexual practices as a social threat, was repealed in 1979, the crime of public display of homosexual condition was repealed in 1987, and the crime of bothering or soliciting with homosexual requests was amended in 1997 to refer only to sexual requests. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is illegal in Cuba. The Constitution does not ban same-sex marriage, with the man-woman definition in Article 36 repealed in the February 2019 referendum and marriage now defined as based on free will and equality of rights. Following the September 2022 Family Code referendum, there is legal recognition of same-sex marriage, unions, same-sex adoption and non-commercial surrogacy. Since 1993, lesbian, gay and bisexual persons may serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces. In 1988, the Public Ostentation Law of 1938 was repealed and police received orders not to harass LGBT people.

sources.title: BBC report (2004) and Miami Herald report (2019)
sources.summary: In July 2004 Cuban police in Havana targeted travestis wearing women's clothing for detention, issued municipal warnings to stop dressing as women, sanctioned three individuals under dangerousness law carrying up to four years imprisonment, closed private clubs hosting their shows, prohibited gay parties and denied entry to regular discos, forcing most to wear men's clothing in public and leading CENESEX to advise against appearing in women's clothing until the crackdown passed.

CUB.tangentialFactors:
The legal framework is layered rather than consolidated. The labour-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation was approved in December 2013, six years before the 2019 Constitution and nine years before the 2022 Family Code, so the three instruments sit at different stages of the same reform sequence.

Cuba has held only four national votes since 1959, the 2022 Family Code referendum among them, which places the equality settlement on a narrow base of direct popular endorsement rather than on routine legislative process.

Enforcement of the liberal framework has been episodic. The documented police campaigns against gender presentation date from 2001 and 2004; the 1988 repeal of the Public Ostentation Law and the order that police stop harassing LGBT people predate them; the Family Code followed in 2022. No source reviewed here records the current operational posture of the police toward gender-nonconforming people.
CUB.localsOnly:
Labor Code Law 116 bars discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground; its article 2(b) covers orientation and not identity. The amendment approved by lawmakers in December 2013 banned employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; the amendment that passed was the sexual-orientation ban, and the trans-specific extension was not the confirmed outcome. Claims that gender-identity discrimination is illegal in Cuba rest on Article 42 of the Constitution rather than on the Labor Code's enumerated grounds, so protection is uneven across instruments.

Transgender people have been permitted to serve openly in the Cuban Revolutionary Armed Forces since 1993, as have lesbian, gay and bisexual people. In 2012 Adela Hernández became the first known transgender person to hold public office in Cuba, elected as a delegate to the city council of Caibarien in Villa Clara province.

Trans healthcare is delivered through the public health system under Resolution 126 of 2008. CENESEX operates a state-backed programme that includes a trans-rights campaign and works with the police and the supreme court.

Citizens who leave to seek asylum abroad face prosecution on return. In January 2018 Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years in prison if they returned after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands, charged with treason against the homeland. A woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018, and LGBTI activists, including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation, remained under monitoring. Charges of this kind are brought against citizens who emigrate, not against visitors.

ECU.name: Ecuador
ECU.summary:
Article 11 of Ecuador's 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, expressly including sexual orientation and gender identity. The provision sits in a secular, multinational constitutional order and is the foundation on which LGBTI claims are litigated. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition has operated on self-determination since the 2016 Gender Identity Law, which permits a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents without surgery or medical diagnosis. The National Assembly's reforms of 12 December 2023 to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree President Daniel Noboa issued on 11 June 2024, streamlined the civil-registry procedure that carries out the change. That procedure is the operative route for a trans visitor or resident updating Ecuadorian records.

Access for adolescents is in motion. Constitutional Court rulings reported by AP in April 2026 allowed trans adolescents to change name and sex on official records, in a case described as opening a path for others seeking recognition. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, still records legal gender recognition as unavailable to under-18s. The sources do not establish how far the rulings extend beyond the case decided.

Partner recognition is split. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, but adoption is constitutionally restricted to different-sex couples under Article 68, and legislation passed on 14 August 2026 by 118 votes to 0 explicitly bars single people and same-sex couples from adopting. That statute sits against a 2018 Constitutional Court decision, taken 5-3 with one abstention, ordering the Civil Registry to register a girl as the daughter of a lesbian couple; in May 2018 the court ordered registration of Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon, the daughter of Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon, with the couple's lawyer arguing that refusal violated the child's rights. A trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship can expect the marriage to be recognised and parentage through adoption to be closed.

Conversion practices are criminalised. Article 151 of the Penal Code, in force since 2014, treats them as equivalent to torture and carries 7 to 10 years' imprisonment. Enforcement is weak: as of 2023 hundreds of clinics still promoted the practice, and clinics have confined young people against their will, including a case in which parents unsuccessfully sought their daughter's release.

Violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians was reported to be increasing in January 2024 amid the country's internal armed conflict. The US State Department's 2011 human rights report recorded discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation among Ecuador's societal problems, and LGBT groups at that time said police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals. No source in this inventory supplies a trans-specific violence count with a denominator that would allow comparison against the general homicide rate.

Detention carries specific risk. Trans women are held in an almost universally male prison system, in male spaces and pavilions, and report gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. The July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty has not produced consistent practice; the trans-rights organisation Silueta X, through its PrisioTrans programme, advocates individualised housing decisions applying Inter-American standards and weighing gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, rather than a single placement rule.
ECU.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents airport or border screening practice, document-marker flagging or body-search procedure as it affects trans travellers to Ecuador; that remains unsourced.

The scope of the 2026 Constitutional Court rulings on adolescents is unresolved: AP describes a path-opening decision while Outright's March 2026 overview continues to state that legal gender recognition is unavailable to under-18s.

Trans-specific violence data for Ecuador is not available in a form that supports comparison with the general homicide rate; the January 2024 reporting establishes a direction of travel, not a magnitude.

The 2011 State Department report is the most recent official assessment in this inventory and predates the 2016 gender identity law, the 2019 marriage ruling and the 2024 security emergency.

sources.summary: Primicias (12 Jun 2024): President Noboa issued the reglamento on 11 Jun 2024 to the National Assembly's 12 Dec 2023 reforms of the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data. Los Angeles Blade (Jan 2024) reports that violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians is increasing amid the internal armed conflict.

AP (Apr 2026) reports that Constitutional Court rulings in Ecuador let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records, in a case described as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage legalised in 2019 but same-sex couples barred from adoption by constitutional ban; legal gender recognition possible since 2016 (not available to under-18s); conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.

The US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ecuador documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems in Ecuador, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption.

The 2008 Constitution of Ecuador (Georgetown/PDBA text): Article 11 principles bind the state to respect ethnic, national, social, generational and gender differences as well as sexual orientation and identity, forming the constitutional non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI rights in a secular, multinational state.

Lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said the refusal violated the child's rights, in a precedent ordering state recognition of same-sex families.

sources.summary: Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination based on sexual orientation. The 2016 Gender Identity Law lets people change legal gender and birth name on ID cards solely by self-determination, without surgery. Conversion therapy was criminalised in 2014 under Article 151 of the Penal Code as equivalent to torture, punishable by 7-10 years' imprisonment, yet as of 2023 hundreds of clinics still promote it. The first gay pride march was held in Quito in 1998. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. Adoption is constitutionally limited to different-sex couples (Article 68), and on 14 August 2026 new adoption legislation passed 118-0 explicitly prohibiting single and same-sex couples from adopting, although the 2018 Constitutional Court had ordered the Civil Registry to register a girl as the daughter of a lesbian couple, 5-3 with one abstention. The U.S. State Department's 2011 report found LGBT community members' right to equal access to formal education frequently violated, and clinics have confined young people against their will, including the daughter of parents who unsuccessfully sought her release. Despite a conservative, macho culture in which homosexuality tends to be viewed negatively, pride marches have been authorised in all major cities with police protection and official participation. The 2011 Guayaquil march included a vice prefect, a city councillor and a National Assembly member. Attendance reached about 20,000 in Guayaquil in 2017, with the Bolívar and San Martín monument lit in rainbow colours, and over 18,000 in Quito in 2018; the Presidential House was lit in rainbow colours in June 2017. Presidential candidate Nelson Zavala was fined over $3,000 and barred from office for a year in 2013 for calling gay people 'sinners' and 'immoral'. Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017. The same 2011 report said gay, lesbian and transgender people still suffered discrimination from public and private bodies, and LGBT groups claimed police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals.

ECU.blindSummary:
Article 11 of the country's 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, expressly including sexual orientation and gender identity. The provision sits in a secular, multinational constitutional order and is the foundation on which LGBTI claims are litigated. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1997, when the constitutional tribunal struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made the country the first in the region to bar discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition has operated on self-determination since the 2016 Gender Identity Law, which permits a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents without surgery or medical diagnosis. The national legislature's reforms of 12 December 2023 to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree the president issued on 11 June 2024, streamlined the civil-registry procedure that carries out the change. That procedure is the operative route for a trans visitor or resident updating national records.

Access for adolescents is in motion. Constitutional Court rulings reported in April 2026 allowed trans adolescents to change name and sex on official records, in a case described as opening a path for others seeking recognition. A trans rights organisation's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, still records legal gender recognition as unavailable to under-18s. The sources do not establish how far the rulings extend beyond the case decided.

Partner recognition is split. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, but adoption is constitutionally restricted to different-sex couples under Article 68, and legislation passed on 14 August 2026 by 118 votes to 0 explicitly bars single people and same-sex couples from adopting. That statute sits against a 2018 Constitutional Court decision, taken 5-3 with one abstention, ordering the civil registry to register a girl as the daughter of a female couple; in May 2018 the court ordered registration of the child of that couple, with their lawyer arguing that refusal violated the child's rights. A trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship can expect the marriage to be recognised and parentage through adoption to be closed.

Conversion practices are criminalised. Article 151 of the Penal Code, in force since 2014, treats them as equivalent to torture and carries 7 to 10 years' imprisonment. Enforcement is weak: as of 2023 hundreds of clinics still promoted the practice, and clinics have confined young people against their will, including a case in which parents unsuccessfully sought their daughter's release.

Violence against LGBTQ people was reported to be increasing in January 2024 amid the country's internal armed conflict. A foreign government's 2011 human rights report recorded discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation among the country's societal problems, and LGBT groups at that time said police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals. No source in this inventory supplies a trans-specific violence count with a denominator that would allow comparison against the general homicide rate.

Detention carries specific risk. Trans women are held in an almost universally male prison system, in male spaces and pavilions, and report gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. The July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty has not produced consistent practice; a trans rights organisation, through its prison-monitoring programme, advocates individualised housing decisions applying regional human-rights standards and weighing gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, rather than a single placement rule.
ECU.blindOutOfScope:
No source in the inventory documents airport or border screening practice, document-marker flagging or body-search procedure as it affects trans travellers to the country; that remains unsourced.

The scope of the 2026 Constitutional Court rulings on adolescents is unresolved: one report describes a path-opening decision while a trans rights organisation's March 2026 overview continues to state that legal gender recognition is unavailable to under-18s.

Trans-specific violence data for the country is not available in a form that supports comparison with the general homicide rate; the January 2024 reporting establishes a direction of travel, not a magnitude.

The 2011 foreign government report is the most recent official assessment in this inventory and predates the 2016 gender identity law, the 2019 marriage ruling and the 2024 security emergency.

JAM.name: Jamaica
JAM.summary:
Jamaica's Offences Against the Person Act criminalises consensual same-sex conduct, with buggery punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour, and the US State Department's 2023 human rights report confirms the provision remains in force. No statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the same report records that individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender. A trans visitor therefore has no legal gender recognition, no discrimination protection and no carve-out from the sexual-offences regime.

Enforcement offers little recourse. A US Department of Justice immigration-review country packet records that LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights found in 2012 that gays and lesbians were subject to violent persecution and fear, and Human Rights Watch documented in 2004 police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference. An Amnesty International urgent appeal in 2006 reported vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture, with gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once their orientation was known, and lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad.

Violence against gender-nonconforming people is documented and, in the defining case, unpunished. In July 2013 a mob in St. James stabbed to death Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old, at a street party after he was identified; no arrests had been made and the case remained unsolved as of 2022. A February 2024 amicus brief to the Inter-American Commission in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica argues that continued criminalisation and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable, and documents housing insecurity and educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans.

Detention carries identity-targeted risk. The State Department report states that prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived LGBTQI identity, that Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre's maximum-security cells held three times their capacity, and that a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. A 2018 study by University of the West Indies lecturer Carla Moore, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the International Bar Association and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime, found that Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender are isolated in penal institutions, that rehabilitation opportunities for them are basically non-existent, that inmates' movement is severely curtailed and access to resources limited because other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners, and that lesbians face prevalent corrective rape; it estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street belong to sexual or gender minorities. No specialised housing policy is documented. J-FLAG reported in 2012 harassment of gay and lesbian patients by hospital and prison staff and violence against gay inmates by wardens and other inmates, with few seeking recourse through the prison system.

Partner recognition is closed. The Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act, passed in 2011, explicitly bans same-sex marriage and any other kind of union from being recognised in Jamaica. In 2019 Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Peter Phillips both announced opposition to legalising same-sex marriage, and in July 2019 Maurice Tomlinson petitioned the Inter-American Commission to rule that Section 18(2) of the Constitution contravenes the American Convention on Human Rights, seeking its repeal and recognition of his Canadian marriage; the petition also asks that Jamaica allow naturalisation of same-sex spouses of Jamaican citizens on the same terms as heterosexual spouses. Jamaica recognises no legal basis for partnerships between women.

Public assembly and official protection have been withdrawn under pressure. In September 2019 Montego Bay Mayor Omar Davis and Councilor Charles Sinclair blocked the local cultural centre's use by the local LGBT group to protect the building's 'sacredness'; other venues then cancelled reservations over fear of backlash, forcing cancellation of the October 2019 Pride events, and police said they could not provide protection to LGBT Jamaicans given the whipped-up hysteria.

Entry and official messaging cut both ways. In January 2018 Jamaica barred entry to Steven Anderson, a Holocaust-denying anti-gay pastor from Arizona, after an outcry from activists. In January 2019 the Director of Tourism, Donovan White, said gay tourists are welcome and that Jamaicans harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors.

The UNDP's March 2023 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' national survey includes dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care, documenting lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.
JAM.outOfScopeNotes:
The Court of Appeal judgment in Maurice Tomlinson's challenge to the television stations' refusal to air the advertisement was reserved as of February 2016 and no outcome is recorded in the sources. The Inter-American Commission petition in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica was filed in February 2024 and no decision is recorded. Whether Jamaica operates any specialised accommodation policy for transgender prisoners is not documented; the 2018 study records isolation and the absence of rehabilitation provision without describing a housing rule.

Violence figures drawn from J-FLAG's 2012 data are raw reported counts without a population denominator, so they do not establish a rate. The UNDP survey is cited for its coverage of violence and health-care access; the inventory does not carry its specific quantitative findings.

Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

Amnesty International urgent appeal (4 Jun 2006): reports vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people in Jamaica — gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once orientation known; lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad; concern that prominent musicians promote homophobia.

sources.title: Gays ostracised in prison – study
sources.summary: Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

sources.title: Jamaica 2023 Human Rights Report (US Department of State)
sources.summary: US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
In 2012 Maurice Tomlinson sued Jamaican TV stations TVJ, PBCJ and CVM for refusing to air a 30-second advertisement, "Love and Respect," promoting recognition of LGBT people's humanity; the Constitutional Court ruled against him in November 2013, and the Court of Appeal heard the appeal in February 2016 with judgment reserved. The UN Human Rights Committee's 2011 review regretted virulent lyrics by musicians and entertainers that incite violence against homosexuals and urged Jamaica to investigate and sanction those responsible. Dancehall artists including Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Bounty Killer, Elephant Man, Sizzla and Shabba Ranks have written or performed songs advocating attacks on gay and lesbian people, and a 2005 agreement between dancehall labels and groups such as OutRage! and the Stop Murder Music Coalition sought to end anti-gay lyrics in live performance.

In January 2018 Jamaica barred entry to Steven Anderson, a Holocaust-denying anti-gay pastor from Arizona, after an outcry from activists; he said he was told at the airport he would not be allowed into the country.

LGBT Jamaicans have fled abroad for safety. Maurice Tomlinson moved to Toronto in 2011 after death threats, Gareth Henry sought asylum in Canada in 2008, and Simone Edwards was granted asylum in the Netherlands in 2008. Tomlinson's July 2019 IACHR petition asks that Jamaica allow naturalization of same-sex spouses of Jamaican citizens on the same terms as heterosexual spouses. In January 2019 the Director of Tourism, Donovan White, said gay tourists are welcome and that Jamaicans harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors.

In September 2019 Montego Bay Mayor Omar Davis and Councilor Charles Sinclair blocked the local cultural center's use by the local LGBT group to protect the building's "sacredness," and other venues then cancelled reservations over fear of backlash, forcing cancellation of the October 2019 Pride events; police said they could not provide protection to LGBT Jamaicans given the whipped-up hysteria. J-FLAG reported in 2012 harassment of gay and lesbian patients by hospital and prison staff and numerous reports of violence against gay inmates by wardens and other inmates, with few seeking recourse through the prison system. Quality of Citizenship Jamaica, founded in 2013, worked to create safe spaces for LGBT women, youth and transgender people before ending operations in 2018.

In 2011 Parliament passed the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms (Constitutional Amendment) Act, explicitly banning same-sex marriage and any other kind of union from being recognized in Jamaica. In 2019 both Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Peter Phillips announced opposition to legalizing same-sex marriage, and in July 2019 Maurice Tomlinson petitioned the IACHR to rule that Section 18(2) of the Constitution contravenes the American Convention on Human Rights, seeking repeal and recognition of his Canadian marriage. Although lesbian civil ceremonies have taken place, including the 2012 celebration in Jamaica of Jamaican-born Nicole Y. Dennis-Benn and Emma Benn, legally married in New York, Jamaica recognizes no legal basis for partnerships between women.

J-FLAG data showed that young people aged 18 to 29 bore the brunt of violence based on sexual orientation, including 68 reports of sexually motivated harassment or abuse in 2012 with 53 assault cases and at least two killings. Dr. J. Carolyn Gomes resigned as head of Jamaicans for Justice in 2013 after nationwide pushback on sexual-education leaflets for adolescents that mentioned anal sex.

Time magazine labelled Jamaica "the most homophobic place on Earth" in 2006, and in 2013 the majority of LGBTQ people in the country said they faced homophobic violence in public. J-FLAG, founded December 1998, operates underground and anonymously as Jamaica's first LGBT human rights organization, and co-founder Brian Williamson was stabbed to death in June 2004 with a crowd outside his home celebrating and chanting slurs. In 2012 about a third of the population, over 900,000 Jamaicans, believed the government was not doing enough to protect LGBT people from violence and discrimination.

Entry and official messaging cut both ways. In January 2018 the country barred entry to an anti-gay pastor from abroad after an outcry from activists. In January 2019 the director of tourism said gay tourists are welcome and that residents harboured no open hostility toward gay visitors.

A UN development programme's March 2023 national survey includes dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care, documenting lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.
JAM.blindOutOfScope:
The Court of Appeal judgment in the activist's challenge to the television stations' refusal to air the advertisement was reserved as of February 2016 and no outcome is recorded in the sources. The regional human rights commission petition concerning the gender-nonconforming teenager was filed in February 2024 and no decision is recorded. Whether the country operates any specialised accommodation policy for transgender prisoners is not documented; the 2018 study records isolation and the absence of rehabilitation provision without describing a housing rule.

Violence figures drawn from the local organisation's 2012 data are raw reported counts without a population denominator, so they do not establish a rate. The UN development programme survey is cited for its coverage of violence and health-care access; the inventory does not carry its specific quantitative findings.
blindSourceSummaries: The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books; the defining case is a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party, whose killing police failed to investigate — now before an international human-rights commission.

A 2018 academic study of the nation's prisons (about 300 of 1,800 prisoners at a major correctional centre belonging to sexual or gender minorities) reports that prisoners perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated', that rehabilitation opportunities are 'basically non-existent', that homophobia/transphobia is entrenched (other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners), and that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'.

A major foreign government's 2023 report confirms 'prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity', in facilities so overcrowded that a maximum-security centre's cells held three times capacity; a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay; the report records that the nation barred legal gender registration.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and community members report that violence against trans people is common but rarely reported; major tourist resort areas are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare.
JAM.blindTangential:
Media and cultural pressure form part of the surrounding climate. In 2012 a local activist sued three television stations for refusing to air a 30-second advertisement promoting recognition of LGBT people's humanity; the Constitutional Court ruled against him in November 2013 and the Court of Appeal heard the appeal in February 2016 with judgment reserved. A UN human rights committee's 2011 review regretted virulent lyrics by musicians and entertainers that incite violence against homosexuals and urged the country to investigate and sanction those responsible. Several dancehall artists have written or performed songs advocating attacks on gay and lesbian people, and a 2005 agreement between dancehall labels and advocacy groups sought to end anti-gay lyrics in live performance.

Public opinion polling records sustained hostility: 96% opposed legalising homosexual relations in 2001, 70% said in 2008 that homosexuals are not entitled to the same basic rights, 85.2% opposed legalising homosexuality among consenting adults in 2010, 88% disapproved of homosexuality in a 2016 poll, and 2023 polling indicates at least 60% oppose acceptance of homosexuality. In 2013 the majority of LGBTQ people in the country said they faced homophobic violence in public, and in 2012 about a third of the population believed the government was not doing enough to protect LGBT people from violence and discrimination.

Some residents have left for safety abroad: one activist moved to another jurisdiction in 2011 after death threats, another sought asylum in a neighbouring jurisdiction in 2008, and a third was granted asylum in another jurisdiction in 2008. A local organisation founded in 2013 worked to create safe spaces for LGBT women, youth and transgender people before ending operations in 2018. The head of a local human rights organisation resigned in 2013 after nationwide pushback on sexual-education leaflets for adolescents that mentioned anal sex.
JAM.localsOnly:
J-FLAG, founded in December 1998, operates underground and anonymously as Jamaica's first LGBT human rights organisation; co-founder Brian Williamson was stabbed to death in June 2004, with a crowd outside his home celebrating and chanting slurs. J-FLAG data showed that young people aged 18 to 29 bore the brunt of violence based on sexual orientation, including 68 reports of sexually motivated harassment or abuse in 2012, 53 assault cases and at least two killings; these are raw reported counts without a population denominator.

University campuses have been sites of anti-LGBT violence. Students at the University of the West Indies' Mona campus rioted in April 2006 while police protected a man chased across campus, and in November 2012 two campus security guards beat a reportedly gay student seeking refuge from a mob, after which the University of Technology established a working group on intolerance and bullying.

TTO.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TTO.summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults was decriminalised by the High Court in Jones v Attorney General in 2018, a ruling upheld on appeal. The challenge was brought by the activist Jason Jones, who stated publicly that he faced up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner, the maximum exposure under the criminal provisions at the time. Decriminalisation removed the threat of prosecution without producing legal gender recognition. The Trinidad and Tobago Transgender Coalition's director, Rae Alibey, said in 2024 that the trans community is the most marginalised group in the country and is not recognised in law: gender identity has no separate legal standing from sexual orientation, and institutional forms carry no gender-identity markers.

Entry rules still carry the older prohibition. Section 8 of the Immigration Act bars homosexual men and women who are not citizens from entering Trinidad and Tobago, and the provision is not known to have been enforced. In 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice ruled that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize had breached the freedom of movement of the Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson, but held that neither state may exclude gay nationals of CARICOM countries, because the Treaty of Chaguaramas obligations override the entry bans in domestic law.

Violence against LGBT+ people is reported through dating applications. Police warned in November 2024 that criminals create fake profiles to lure users to meetings that end in armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault, with two incidents reported in a single week. A newspaper editorial in June 2024 counted close to half a dozen app-related attacks over the preceding months. Superintendent Claire Guy-Alleyne said the legislation contains no specific hate-crime category.

No anti-discrimination protection was added by the 2024 constitutional review. The PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected the inclusion of sexual-orientation protections in the constitution, a decision announced at a special convention.

Custody carries known risk. The Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers, launched in November 2018 by the Caribbean Court of Justice, Caribbean judicial associations, UN Women and the JURIST Project, states that there are no special facilities in the penal system to accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities safely. It directs a judicial officer sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to recommend to prison authorities that provisions be made for that inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to address intersex and transgender people by their chosen pronoun and to admit them irrespective of dress. Housing for a trans prisoner therefore rests on a sentencing recommendation, and no dedicated facility exists.
TTO.outOfScopeNotes:
Section 8 of the Immigration Act is not known to have been enforced, so how immigration officers treat a trans or visibly gender-nonconforming arrival at a port of entry is not sourced. Whether prison authorities act on the sentencing recommendations in the Gender Equality Protocol is likewise undocumented in the sources reviewed.

No national attitudinal research on gender identity has been carried out; the 2009 study covered sexual orientation. No figures were located on how many app-related attacks are reported by LGBT+ people, on prosecution or conviction practice since decriminalisation, or on the number of transgender people in the penal system. A 2012 travel and culture profile describes the criminal law as it stood before 2018 and does not reflect the current position.

sources.summary: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday (July 2024): 'Long way yet for recognition, safe spaces' - TT Transgender Coalition director Rae Alibey says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised in T&T; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Newsday (Nov 2024): police warning over cyber criminals - Grindr hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

GlobalGayz (Aug 2012) travel and culture profile states that homosexuality is illegal but that the laws are mostly ignored in practice, and describes the tourist-facing social scene and island context. The profile predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling, so its statement of the law does not reflect current law.

sources.title: Protect transgender inmates'
sources.summary: Trinidad Express (Camille Hunte, 28 Nov 2018) reports on the official 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers (launched Nov 2018 by the CCJ, CAJO, UN Women, JURIST Project, TTAWJ and the Judicial Institute of TT). The Protocol states that 'in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities'. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to make recommendations to prison authorities so that provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to refer to intersex and transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and to permit court access irrespective of dress. Housing placement for trans prisoners is therefore discretionary and unsafe, resting only on sentencing recommendations, with no facility of its own.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Under Section 8 of the Immigration Act, homosexual men and women who are not citizens are prohibited from entering Trinidad and Tobago, though this law is not known to have been enforced. In 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice ruled that neither Trinidad nor Belize violated Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson's freedom of movement, but clarified that neither state can ban homosexuals from CARICOM countries from entering due to treaty obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding their laws that ban the entry of gays. Trinidad and Tobago does not recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights and benefits as opposite-sex couples. In July 2018 Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property dispute resolution between two gay partners, noting unequal treatment under current law and warning that without agreement the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law to determine property division after dissolution of a same-sex union. Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt in Trinidad and Tobago. The Silver Lining Foundation is an LGBTQ group that seeks to end bullying against LGBTQ youth. A 2009 University of the West Indies study for the Ministry of Social Development found that four of every five Trinbagonians believed in denying someone rights or equality based on sexual orientation, prompting the founding of CAISO to encourage public discussion and legislative protections.

TTO.tangentialFactors:
Partner recognition is absent. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status has no mechanism for recognition, and the property consequences of separation are unsettled: in July 2018 Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property division between two male partners, noting their unequal treatment under current law and warning that without agreement the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law.

Official rhetoric has run ahead of the statute in only one direction. In June 2016 Prime Minister Keith Rowley told Parliament that the state must protect all citizens "regardless of whom they sleep with", while refusing to repeal the criminal laws then in force. Two years later decriminalisation came from the High Court rather than from the executive or the legislature.

After the 2024 constitutional review, CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community has been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection. GHA.name: Ghana
GHA.summary: The Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill was passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and awaits presidential assent. An earlier version passed unanimously at third reading in February 2024, sharply increasing penalties and criminalising advocacy; it lapsed unsigned when parliament dissolved before the 2024 election and was reintroduced in March 2025. Human Rights Watch had called on the president to veto the 2024 bill. President John Mahama has previously signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill, and reporting attributes the 2026 passage to pressure from religious leaders on him. The Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two challenges to the legislation, with Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson holding that until there is presidential assent there is no act, and review deferred until the president signs; the petitioners' lawyers said they would explore further options.
GHA.outOfScopeNotes:
No finding in the sources establishes Ghana's legal gender recognition procedure or document-change rules for trans people. The nearest grounded items are the 1992 constitution's definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman, with Article 39 emphasising traditional values; a 2017 ILGA poll in which 55% of Ghanaians said transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender; and the pending bill's criminalisation of crossdressing and of identifying as transgender.

No entry, visa, or immigration and airport screening rule specific to trans travellers appears in the sources reviewed, and it is unresolved whether the identification offence, the crossdressing offence or the duty to report is applied to short-term visitors as distinct from residents.

No enforcement record for the 2026 bill exists yet; the Supreme Court deferred review of the legislation until presidential assent, and the most detailed documentation of violence and police conduct available is the January 2018 Human Rights Watch report and its 2017 interviews.

BBC: Ghana's Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two challenges to the anti-LGBT bill — Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson: 'Until there's presidential assent, there is no act', review deferred until the president signs; petitioners' lawyers said they would explore options. Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

HRW report (Jan 2018) 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am': full PDF - violence and discrimination against LGBT people in Ghana; section 104(1)(b) criminalises 'unnatural carnal knowledge' but is rarely enforced; documents mob violence, police abuse, and extortion.

Human Rights Watch report of 8 January 2018, 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am: Violence and Discrimination against LGBT People in Ghana', provides the full report and annex downloads. Its endnotes document 2017 victim interviews in Kumasi and Tamale and cases of police and vigilante violence.

Bachelor thesis (Diaconia University of Applied Sciences, Helsinki, 2017) by Seree Yeboa-Mensa: survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland on LGBT rights in Ghana - most opposed decriminalisation/legalisation, citing religio-cultural reasons and effects on children; most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.

sources.title: Ghana parliament passes bill criminalising gay acts
sources.summary: BBC (30 May 2026): Ghana's parliament approved a new bill criminalising homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities. Identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer carries up to three years' imprisonment, and the bill adds a duty to report prohibited acts to police. It was passed under pressure from religious leaders on President Mahama, whose ratification is still required. The bill establishes the state pathway by which trans people in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone and contains no provision on how such prisoners would be housed.

sources.title: People 'panicking' as Ghana passes sweeping law criminalising LGBTQ+ activity
sources.summary: The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison terms of three to 10 years, with up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Community groups such as One Love Sisters Ghana report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. No publicly documented policy exists in Ghana on housing trans prisoners.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of speech, expression and assembly, but these rights are actively denied to LGBTQ people, and pro-LGBTQ activism is repeatedly thwarted by the government. In 2006 the government banned an LGBTQ rights conference at the Accra International Conference Centre, and in March 2020 President Akufo-Addo banned the Pan Africa ILGA conference planned for Accra as illegal. The Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by Parliament in February 2024 (reintroduced in March 2025 and passed again in May 2026) criminalises identifying as LGBTQ (up to three years), funding or forming an LGBTQ-related group (up to five years), advocacy or intentional support of LGBTQ activities (three to five years, with some proposals at 5–10 years), public displays of same-sex affection, crossdressing, and disseminating information perceived as supporting LGBTQ people. Those identifying as an 'ally' of LGBTQ people may also face prison.

No finding exists on legal gender recognition procedures or document-change rules for transgender Ghanaians. The closest grounded items are that the 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman (Article 39 emphasises traditional values), that a 2017 ILGA poll found 55% of Ghanaians believe transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender, and that the pending anti-LGBTQ bill would criminalise crossdressing and identifying as transgender.

Facilities for LGBTQ people in Ghana have been shut down rather than provided: in February 2021 religious and political leaders forced an LGBTQ Centre in Accra to close, and LGBT+ Rights Ghana's Accra office, opened in January 2021, was raided and closed by National Security in late February 2021 after opposition from locals, religious institutions and politicians. Most LGBTQ groups operate secretly or online, with FOTHA-Ghana members using the dark web for safety. No supported housing or shelter provision exists; instead young LGBTQ people are disowned and evicted from family homes, and the Solomon-supported Solace Initiative provides human-rights-trained paralegals to defend LGBTQ people in court.

Mental health and healthcare access are severely constrained: mental health professionals in Ghana are often not trained to work with LGBTQ populations and may hold prejudiced views, and the Ghana Mental Health Authority has not fully implemented inclusive policies under its 2012 Mental Health Act. Due to fear of persecution many LGBTQ people avoid seeking healthcare altogether, creating barriers to mental and sexual health support, and rates of anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and some deaths by suicide are linked to forced evictions, blackmail and violence. Conversion therapy, which families often seek from religious groups when a young person discloses same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity, is commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings; an August 2018 report documented conversion therapy programmes run by religious leaders, and a 2018 conference claimed about 400 people had registered for such programmes. A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana are at significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than their heterosexual peers, and government HIV/AIDS campaigns present the disease as an issue for straight people, leaving gay men unaware that HIV can be transmitted through anal sex even though the country receives HIV funding.

No broad legal protections exist for LGBT people against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Enforcement of the 'unnatural carnal knowledge' law (Section 104, Criminal Code 1960, a misdemeanour carrying up to three years under Article 296(4)) overwhelmingly targets LGBTQ people while heterosexual couples doing the same acts are rarely or never prosecuted, a disparity CDD-Ghana describes as moral policing rather than criminal justice. In a 2017 ILGA poll 59% of Ghanaians agreed LGBTQ people should be protected from workplace discrimination (62% for transgender people), while 89% reported disliking LGBTQ individuals and nearly 90% said they would report a relative or co-worker to police. The UN Human Rights Committee's October 2012 recommendation to eliminate 'unnatural sexual relations' and eradicate discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity was rejected by Ghana along with all other recommendations.

Ghana does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions: the 1992 Constitution defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and no provision of Ghanaian law allows legal recognition of same-sex relationships, leaving LGBTQ people in vulnerable legal positions around long-term relationships and shared property. Same-sex couples are explicitly excluded from the adoption process, since the system does not support joint applications from non-heterosexual partnerships. The pending Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill would additionally ban same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples outright.

Young LGBTQ Ghanaians are disowned by families and communities and evicted from their homes, and families often seek conversion therapy from religious groups when a same-sex orientation or non-conforming gender identity is disclosed, reported to be commonly administered in abusive and inhumane settings, with medical bodies warning conversion therapy is ineffective and potentially harmful. A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana face significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than heterosexual peers. In January 2025 President John Mahama said he prefers teaching traditional family values through Ghana's school curriculum rather than passing anti-LGBTQ laws, and the National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education. The pending bill targets youth directly by criminalising identification as LGBTQ (three years), with Pan Africa ILGA's banned March 2020 Accra conference intended partly to protect queer youth in Africa.

GHA.tangentialFactors:
A 2017 bachelor's thesis at Diaconia University of Applied Sciences in Helsinki surveyed 113 Ghanaians living in Finland on LGBT rights in Ghana: most opposed decriminalisation or legalisation, citing religious and cultural reasons and effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.

The National Coalition for Proper Human Sexual Rights and Family Values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education, an education-policy position adjacent to the criminal-law provisions above.
GHA.comparisons: Pairwise: above Nigeria (0.19 — SSMPA in force with mob lynching culture) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts). Ghana's near-passage of an identity-criminalising bill is what separates it from Elevated band: the legal floor is currently the old 3-year statute, but the demonstrated legislative intent is far harsher.

A 2017 bachelor's thesis surveyed 113 nationals living abroad on LGBT rights in the country: most opposed decriminalisation or legalisation, citing religious and cultural reasons and effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.

A national coalition campaigning on sexual rights and family values has actively opposed comprehensive sex education, an education-policy position adjacent to the criminal-law provisions above.
GHA.localsOnly:
Young LGBTQ Ghanaians are disowned by their families and communities and evicted from their homes. When a young person discloses a same-sex orientation or a non-conforming gender identity, families commonly seek conversion therapy from religious groups; it is reported to be administered in abusive and inhumane settings, and medical bodies warn that it is ineffective and potentially harmful. An August 2018 report documented programmes run by religious leaders, and a 2018 conference claimed that about 400 people had registered for them.

A study found LGBTQ+ adolescents in Ghana at significantly higher risk of suicidal ideation and self-harm than their heterosexual peers. Anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and some deaths by suicide among LGBTQ people are linked to forced evictions, blackmail and violence.

Community infrastructure has been closed rather than provided. Religious and political leaders forced the LGBTQ Centre in Accra to close in February 2021, and the Accra office of LGBT+ Rights Ghana, opened in January 2021, was raided and closed by National Security in late February 2021 after opposition from local residents, religious institutions and politicians. Most LGBTQ groups operate secretly or online, and FOTHA-Ghana members use the dark web for safety. No supported housing or shelter provision exists.

The Solace Initiative provides human-rights-trained paralegals to defend LGBTQ people in court.

MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.summary:
Article 489 of Morocco's penal code criminalises "indecent acts" between persons of the same sex, with penalties of six months to three years' imprisonment. Outright International reports that the provision is enforced with wide police discretion and that arrests are arbitrary; 170 people were charged with same-sex relations in 2018. ILGA's State-Sponsored Homophobia survey lists Morocco among the countries whose law prohibits same-sex activity between consenting adults, and Human Rights Watch's April 2018 report "Audacity in Adversity" places Article 489 in an annex of statutes used across the Middle East and North Africa to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression.

The statute does not name transgender people, but it is applied to them. A January 2026 report by Cairo 52, "A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco", draws on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans, describes an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility, and records Article 489 being used to arrest trans people on the basis of their gender expression. The same organisation's country review finds no legal gender recognition pathway and no specific statutory provisions governing transition, with de facto criminalisation instead running through Article 498 moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies and involuntary outing.

Police conduct documented in press reporting includes an allegation by an Instagram model in November 2024 that Moroccan police forced her to display her genitals after suspecting her of being trans. In January 2019 El Pais reported that police in Marrakesh handcuffed a cross-dressing man, Chafiq, after a minor traffic accident, that bystanders and officers filmed him, and that his identity documents were photographed and posted online; he later sought asylum in Europe. Wikipedia's account of LGBTQ rights in Morocco states that police disproportionately target people perceived to be LGBTQ and that the names of arrested individuals are publicised before trial.

Morocco has no law prohibiting discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no political party has enacted LGBTQ rights legislation. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples. Official hostility is on the record: in 2017 the then Minister of Justice and Liberties, Mustafa Ramid, described homosexuals as "trash" in an interview, prompting local human rights associations to petition Prime Minister Othmani to investigate what they called his discriminatory and unconstitutional statements. Cairo 52 reports that the Grand Mufti opposes transition, and Outright International reports that the authorities block LGBTIQ organisations.

Healthcare access for trans people is not established in law or provision. Cairo 52 finds no gender-affirming healthcare framework, with some trans Moroccans self-medicating as a result, and records a 2021 recognition process that covers intersex people only. The same report describes a de facto prohibition on gender-affirming surgery for Moroccans while noting that the country once drew foreign patients for such operations: 1950s publicity around the French entertainer Coccinelle helped establish Casablanca as a place where certain doctors would perform sex change operations "albeit in clandestine circumstances", indicating unregulated care rather than a documented public facility. No current trans-specific healthcare access, identity-document procedure or shelter provision for trans visitors is recorded in the sources.

In April 2020 an online campaign targeted presumed gay and bisexual men, documented by Human Rights Watch. During that campaign some landlords ejected tenants who had been targeted, and sociologist Khalid Mouna noted that transgender influencer Sofia Talouni sought to "isolate young Moroccan homosexuals by breaking up their family unit"; journalist Hicham Tahir reported receiving "a hundred testimonies" from victims or witnesses, and one person allegedly committed suicide. In November 2022 a trans woman was violently beaten in Tangier; three minors and an adult were arrested over the assault. Outright International states that public identification as LGBTIQ in Morocco carries significant risk of violence and harassment.

Prosecutions have proceeded on thin evidence. In December 2007 a court in Ksar el-Kebir convicted six men under Article 489 after an online video of a private party, reported in the press as a "gay marriage", circulated; their lawyers said no evidence of prohibited conduct was presented, and the men received varying sentences on 17 December 2007. Dozens of people then marched through the streets of Ksar el-Kebir calling for their punishment. In 2016 two girls in Marrakesh were arrested after a cousin photographed them kissing and their mother complained to police; the case was postponed to December 2016, when both were acquitted, provoking the #freethegirls outcry.

In the 2018-19 Arab Barometer survey, 21% of Moroccan respondents said homosexuality is acceptable.
MAR.outOfScopeNotes:
The January 2026 Cairo 52 report rests on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans; its findings describe patterns reported by that group rather than a statistically representative sample.

No current official figures on prosecutions under Article 489 are published; the 170 charges cited by Outright International date from 2018. The application of Article 498 to trans people is documented by Cairo 52 without published case counts.

The November 2024 allegation that police forced a woman to display her genitals is a first-person account reported in the press and has not been independently confirmed. The reported suicide during the April 2020 outing campaign is described as alleged.

No current trans-specific healthcare access, identity-document procedure or shelter provision for trans visitors is recorded in the sources reviewed; the 1950s Casablanca reference concerns unregulated private practice, not a public facility. Details of the 2021 intersex recognition process are not set out in the sources.

MAR.localsOnly:

DZA.name: Algeria
DZA.summary:
Algeria's Penal Code, Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966, criminalises same-sex sexual activity. Article 338 punishes a homosexual act with 2 months to 2 years imprisonment and a fine of 500 to 2,000 Algerian dinars, and applies to conduct between men and between women. Where one participant is under 18, the older participant faces up to 3 years and a 10,000 dinar fine. Article 333 separately punishes outrage to public decency consisting of an act against nature with a person of the same sex, with 6 months to 3 years imprisonment and a fine of 1,000 to 10,000 dinars. The United Kingdom Home Office country policy note of 26 July 2026 confirms the 1966 Code remains the operative framework, citing a Human Dignity Trust legal summary updated in June 2026.

No transgender-specific offence, penalty, document rule, screening procedure, facility rule, custody rule, care rule or protection mechanism is documented in Algerian law. Trans people appear in the legal literature only inside the broader LGBTQ grouping. There is no legal gender-recognition route, so a change to a civil-status gender marker is blocked in practice. No legal framework exists for gender-affirming healthcare, and Articles 274 and 264 could be turned against providers, which amounts to de facto criminalisation of care. A Snopes fact-check of 5 August 2024 rated as true the claim that Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and prohibits being transgender.

Enforcement is documented. Human Rights Watch reported that after a 24 July 2020 raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, police arrested 44 people, 9 women and 35 men, most of them university students, over an alleged gay wedding. On 3 September 2020 a court sentenced two of them to prison and 42 to suspended terms, treating decorations and gay appearance as evidence. NGOs record arrests within the LGBT+ community but publish little on the trans identity of those detained, so the share of trans people among those arrested is not established.

The United States Department of State 2023 human rights report describes the offence as undefined homosexual acts carrying 2 months to 2 years imprisonment plus fines. Prison authorities separated vulnerable detainees from the general population, but LGBTQI+ prisoners had no specific legal protections, and civil society reported compounded discrimination against them. No political organisation is permitted to campaign for LGBTQ rights, and there are officially no gay-friendly establishments.

Violence against people read as gender-nonconforming is documented and frequently state-tolerated. Vigilante executions, beatings and torture have occurred, with police joining attacks, acting in complicity or turning a blind eye. Two men were stoned in the street in 2001, and two men were killed in 1994 and 1996 in what were described as hate crimes against homosexuals. In 2019 Assil Belatla, a student suspected of being gay, was murdered in his university-district dormitory, with the words he is gay painted on the wall in his blood; the killer believed he would avoid prosecution.

The law does not recognise or respect the civil rights of LGBTQ persons. Attempts at unofficial same-sex marriage are blocked by police, including one in 2005. An Arab Barometer survey for BBC News Arabic in 2018-19 found that about 26% of Algerians thought homosexuality should be accepted; that figure concerns homosexuality, and no equivalent measure for transgender people is published. Homophobic attitudes are normalised and the prevailing social attitude is openly negative.
DZA.outOfScopeNotes: No source in the inventory documents a transgender-specific offence, penalty, document rule, screening procedure, facility rule, custody rule, care rule or protection mechanism in Algeria. Whether cross-dressing is separately punishable is unresolved: the criminal provisions are described as originating in mores that treat homosexuality and cross-dressing as contrary to the Islamic faith, but no imprisonment term, fine, age threshold, arrest or case outcome is stated for cross-dressing or transgender identity itself. The number of trans people among those arrested in LGBT+ enforcement operations is not sourced. No per-capita or survey measure of attitudes toward transgender people specifically is available; the 26% acceptance figure concerns homosexuality. The 2008 ILGA entry predates the 2026 Home Office confirmation that the same 1966 Code remains in force.
