UK Home Office CPIN 'Algeria: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression' (26 Jul 2026, covering since May 2025): same-sex activity prohibited under Penal Code 1966 ('acts of homosexuality', Human Dignity Trust updated June 2026); internal relocation viable for gay males but lesbians and trans females face societal difficulties; refusals rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded — the current asylum-authority baseline.

An international human rights organisation reported that after a 24 July 2020 raid on a private home in a locality in one province, police arrested 44 people, 9 women and 35 men, most of them university students, over an alleged gay wedding. On 3 September 2020 a court sentenced two of them to prison and 42 to suspended terms, treating decorations and gay appearance as evidence. NGOs record arrests within the LGBT+ community but publish little on the trans identity of those detained, so the share of trans people among those arrested is not established.

A foreign government's annual human rights report for 2023 describes the offence as undefined homosexual acts carrying 2 months to 2 years imprisonment plus fines. Prison authorities separated vulnerable detainees from the general population, but LGBTQI+ prisoners had no specific legal protections, and civil society reported compounded discrimination against them. No political organisation is permitted to campaign for LGBTQ rights, and there are officially no gay-friendly establishments.

Violence against people read as gender-nonconforming is documented and frequently tolerated by the authorities. Vigilante executions, beatings and torture have occurred, with police joining attacks, acting in complicity or turning a blind eye. Two men were stoned in the street in 2001, and two men were killed in 1994 and 1996 in what were described as hate crimes against homosexuals. In 2019 a student suspected of being gay was murdered in his university-district dormitory, with the words he is gay painted on the wall in his blood; the killer believed he would avoid prosecution.

The law does not recognise or respect the civil rights of LGBTQ persons. Attempts at unofficial same-sex marriage are blocked by police, including one in 2005. A regional survey conducted for a regional broadcaster in 2018-19 found that about 26% of respondents thought homosexuality should be accepted; that figure concerns homosexuality, and no equivalent measure for transgender people is published. Homophobic attitudes are normalised and the prevailing social attitude is openly negative.

TUN.name: Tunisia
TUN.summary:
Tunisia criminalises same-sex conduct under Penal Code Article 230, which carries up to three years' imprisonment. The provision dates from the 1913 Penal Code, was largely modified in 1964, and covers both male and female same-sex activity, rendered in Arabic as "Liwat" and "El Mousahaka". Enforcement is active rather than dormant, and authorities use the anti-sodomy law to detain and question people about their sexual activities and orientation. Article 226, which outlaws "outrages against public decency", is applied to gender expression; cross-dressing is not expressly illegal, but transgender people are frequently accused under this article.

Amnesty International documented at least 84 people, mainly gay men and transgender women, arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. The arrests were recorded in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, indicating a national sweep rather than a single-city operation. A mass conviction on 31 October 2024 imposed prison terms of up to four and a half years; the sentences were upheld on appeal on 5 February 2025, with four people released after sentence reduction.

Detention carries specific risks for transgender people. Transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings, a systemic refusal of identity that begins at arrest and continues through the prison system. Police abuse in enforcement of Article 230 is documented: detainees interviewed by Human Rights Watch in 2016 reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment. Anal examinations have been used as evidence, with refusal treated as evidence of guilt; in June 2017 a 16-year-old was sentenced to four months' imprisonment for homosexuality after refusing examination.

Legal gender recognition is inconsistent and frequently denied. In April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man, weighing contradictory lower-court judgements, including case No. 12304/2018, and finding no consistent precedent; the question remains unsettled below the Court of Cassation. In 1993 the Court of Appeals in Tunis rejected a transgender woman's request to change her civil status from male to female, describing the change as a "voluntary and artificial operation". A transgender man did obtain a change of legal status in 2018. A separate ruling of the Court of First Instance held that gender identity disorder is a psychological condition permitting legal change of sex.
TUN.outOfScopeNotes:
Two rulings of the Court of First Instance in Tunis conflict on legal gender recognition: one refused recognition to a transgender man in April 2023 on the ground that gender identity disorder is not a valid reason, while another held that gender identity disorder is a psychological condition permitting legal change of sex. The sources do not establish which position currently governs, and the question is unresolved below the Court of Cassation.

No transgender-specific provisions on detention procedures, identity documents beyond civil-status change, screening, facilities, custody, care or protection machinery are documented. Documented tolerance figures and official statements address homosexuality or sexual orientation generally rather than transgender people specifically.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Tunisia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Legal recognition for transgender or gender non-conforming people in Tunisia is described as inconsistent. Cross-dressing is not expressly illegal, although transgender people, along with gay people, are often accused of violating Article 226 of the Penal Code which outlaws "outrages against public decency". On 22 December 1993, the Court of Appeals in Tunis rejected a trans woman's request to change her legal gender (statut civil) from male to female, declaring her gender change a "voluntary and artificial operation" that does not justify a change in legal status. In 2018, a trans man succeeded in changing his legal status in what is described as a revolutionary judgement. No transgender-specific provisions on detention procedures, identity documents beyond civil status change, screening, facilities, custody, care, or protection machinery are stated. Article 230 of the Penal Code of 1913 (largely modified in 1964) punishes private consensual sodomy between adults with imprisonment of up to three years, covering both male and female same-sex sexual activity, rendered in Arabic as "Liwat" (male homosexuality) and "El Mousahaka" (female homosexuality). Authorities occasionally use the anti-sodomy law to detain and question persons about their sexual activities and orientation. Enforcement involves anal examinations as evidence, with refusal treated as evidence of guilt, including a June 2017 case where a 16-year-old was sentenced to four months in jail for homosexuality after refusing examination. On 7 December 2016 two men were arrested in Sousse on suspicion of homosexual activity, subjected to anal probing and forced to sign confessions of sodomy, and on 11 March 2017 while on bail were given eight-month prison sentences. On 3 June two men were arrested on suspicion of same-sex conduct and subjected to attempted anal examination, followed by sentencing for homosexuality reported on 6 July 2020. Recorded enforcement totals were 56 jailed in 2016, 79 in 2017, and 127 in 2018, with at least 22 arrests by April 2019. In September 2017 Minister Mehdi Ben Gharbia agreed to stop forced anal tests, stating exams could no longer be imposed by force, physical or moral, or without consent, yet courts continued ordering anal tests throughout 2018 and 2019. LGBTQ Tunisians face both legal and social discrimination. Reports of family rejection, violence in public spaces, violence within families and suicides are quite common. No shelter, victim-protection, medical care, custody, facility-access, or other protection machinery specific to transgender visitors is described. Documented tolerance figures and official statements in the article address homosexuality or sexual orientation generally, not transgender people specifically, including opposition to same-sex marriage and support for punishing homosexuals and official descriptions of homosexuality as perversion or illness requiring treatment. The article contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically to quote.

Official statements address homosexuality rather than transgender status directly. CMR.name: Cameroon
CMR.summary:
Article 347-1 of Cameroon's penal code criminalises same-sex sexual activity between both men and women and carries a maximum sentence of five years' imprisonment. The penal code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex acts; an ordinance issued in September 1972 by President Ahmadou Ahidjo introduced Article 347bis, now numbered 347-1, and the 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations. Sentences under the earlier provision ran from six months to five years.

Enforcement reaches appearance and gender presentation, not only alleged acts. On 8 February 2021 in Douala, two transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing. Shakiro, born 29 July 1997 in Douala, had built a following on Facebook and YouTube discussing trans life. Both were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification, and each received five years' imprisonment plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs (about $370), the maximum statutory term. They had been held since February 2021 and spent five months in prison before a judge released them pending appeal. Their lawyers, Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu, described the convictions as a political decision reached without proof of any acts. Shakiro later left Cameroon and claimed asylum abroad.

A 2013 appeal shows the same pattern. Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, jailed for five years in November 2011, were acquitted on appeal; the original judge had cited their dress, their speech and their order of Baileys as proof they were gay. Alice Nkom said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcomed the acquittal. Arrests on grounds of effeminacy or appearance under the colonial-era sodomy law carry sentences of six months to five years.

Human Rights Watch reported on 11 May 2022 that violence against LGBTI people had risen that year: since 9 March, security forces had arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity. Gendarmes beat two of them in detention. HRW's senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi said the criminalisation law allows both civilians and security forces to abuse LGBTI people without consequence.

Online conduct is separately criminalised. Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime provides under Article 83(1) for one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, or one of those penalties, for same-sex sexual propositions made through electronic communications; Article 83(2) doubles the penalty where intercourse followed.

Earlier prosecutions rest on circumstantial evidence. In May 2005, eleven men were arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy; the government threatened medical examinations to prove their homosexual activity, they were detained into February 2006, trials were scheduled for March 2006 and they were released in April 2006. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347, among them Jean-Claude Roger Mbede, sentenced to three years at Kondengui Central Prison for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. On 24 November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years for oral sex in a parked car, and in the same month two young men arrested outside a nightclub were convicted on appearance and behaviour alone, the judge holding that speech manner, wearing women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor were sufficient evidence of homosexuality; that verdict was overturned on appeal.

Detention conditions are severe for people accused under these provisions. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as hell. The LGBTQ organisation Alternatives-Cameroon shut down after a police raid, removing a service base, and few lawyers are willing to defend the accused.

Official and media hostility compounds the legal exposure. In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, boosting circulation; the state communication council criticised the privacy invasion, while President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy and prosecutions of people accused of homosexual activity continued. The US State Department's 2010 human rights report recorded harassment and extortion of gays and lesbians by law enforcement and the use of false allegations to harass or extort, alongside discrimination among societal abuses. A 2020 assessment described Cameroon as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. On 30 June 2024 President Biya's daughter Brenda Biya came out as a lesbian on Instagram, prompting national backlash and, among LGBTQ Cameroonians, hope.
CMR.outOfScopeNotes:
No information on legal gender recognition, name change, or identity-document and marker procedures in Cameroon appears in the sources reviewed. No healthcare, HIV or medication access information specific to transgender visitors is documented; the only health-service finding is the 2005 threat of medical examinations to prove homosexual activity among detained men, which is coercive contact with health services rather than care.

No contemporary youth, school or minor-specific legal policy is covered. Historical ethnographic material on same-sex customs among the Bafia people in 1921 has no bearing on the current legal regime and is not treated as visitor-relevant.

No Cameroonian border screening procedure, entry-refusal practice or visa rule for LGBTQ travellers is set out in the sources; the asylum and deportation material concerns outbound cases in the United Kingdom.

Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime criminalises online same-sex sexual propositions, with Article 83(1) punishing sexual propositions to a person of the same sex through electronic communications with one to two years imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs or only one of these penalties, doubled under Article 83(2) when followed by sexual intercourse. As of 2020, Cameroon prosecutes consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. In May 2005, 11 men were arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy with threatened medical examinations to prove activity, detained into February 2006 with trials scheduled March 2006 and released in April 2006. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347, including Jean-Claude Roger Mbede sentenced to three years imprisonment at Kondengui Central Prison for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance, and on 24 November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years imprisonment for oral sex in a parked car. In November 2011 two young men arrested outside a nightclub were convicted to five years imprisonment based solely on appearance and behavior, with the judge holding speech manner, wearing women's clothing and ordering cream-based liquor sufficient evidence for homosexuality, a verdict later overturned on appeal.

CMR.tangentialFactors:
No visa policy, entry-refusal rule or border-admission procedure specific to LGBTQ travellers is documented for Cameroon. The material closest to border practice concerns Cameroonians seeking protection abroad rather than visitors arriving. In July 2010 the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities and that he is not the only gay person in Cameroon. In August 2011 a gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the UK Border Agency after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé. In May 2012 the UK Border Agency sought to return asylum-seeker Ediage Valerie Ekwedde, finding no credible evidence that he was gay, and held him in custody after he threatened to make a fuss on the return flight.

The state's public position that private same-sex conduct is not prosecuted sits against convictions resting on conduct inferred from appearance, dress and messages, and against the 2020 assessment that Cameroon prosecutes consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any other country.

CMR.blindSummary:
Article 347-1 of the country's penal code criminalises same-sex sexual activity between both men and women and carries a maximum sentence of five years' imprisonment. The penal code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex acts; an ordinance issued in September 1972 by the then head of state introduced Article 347bis, now numbered 347-1, and the 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations. Sentences under the earlier provision ran from six months to five years.

Enforcement reaches appearance and gender presentation, not only alleged acts. On 8 February 2021 in a city, two transgender women were arrested in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing. One of them, born 29 July 1997, had built a following on social media platforms discussing trans life. Both were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification, and each received five years' imprisonment plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs (about $370), the maximum statutory term. They had been held since February 2021 and spent five months in prison before a judge released them pending appeal. Their defence lawyers described the convictions as a political decision reached without proof of any acts. One of the women later left the country and claimed asylum abroad.

A 2013 appeal shows the same pattern. Two men, jailed for five years in November 2011, were acquitted on appeal; the original judge had cited their dress, their speech and their order of a cream-based liqueur as proof they were gay. A defence lawyer said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and a human-rights organisation welcomed the acquittal. Arrests on grounds of effeminacy or appearance under the colonial-era sodomy law carry sentences of six months to five years.

An international human-rights organisation reported on 11 May 2022 that violence against LGBTI people had risen that year: since 9 March, security forces had arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity. Gendarmes beat two of them in detention. A senior researcher at the organisation said the criminalisation law allows both civilians and security forces to abuse LGBTI people without consequence.

Online conduct is separately criminalised. A 2010 law on cybersecurity and cybercrime provides under Article 83(1) for one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, or one of those penalties, for same-sex sexual propositions made through electronic communications; Article 83(2) doubles the penalty where intercourse followed.

Earlier prosecutions rest on circumstantial evidence. In May 2005, eleven men were arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy; the government threatened medical examinations to prove their homosexual activity, they were detained into February 2006, trials were scheduled for March 2006 and they were released in April 2006. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347, among them a man sentenced to three years at a central prison for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. On 24 November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years for oral sex in a parked car, and in the same month two young men arrested outside a nightclub were convicted on appearance and behaviour alone, the judge holding that speech manner, wearing women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor were sufficient evidence of homosexuality; that verdict was overturned on appeal.

Detention conditions are severe for people accused under these provisions. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe a main city prison as hell. An LGBTQ organisation shut down after a police raid, removing a service base, and few lawyers are willing to defend the accused.

Official and media hostility compounds the legal exposure. In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, boosting circulation; the state communication council criticised the privacy invasion, while the head of state publicly urged respect for privacy and prosecutions of people accused of homosexual activity continued. A foreign government's 2010 human rights report recorded harassment and extortion of gays and lesbians by law enforcement and the use of false allegations to harass or extort, alongside discrimination among societal abuses. A 2020 assessment described the country as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. On 30 June 2024 the head of state's daughter came out as a lesbian on a social media platform, prompting national backlash and, among LGBTQ people in the country, hope.
CMR.blindOutOfScope:
No information on legal gender recognition, name change, or identity-document and marker procedures in the country appears in the sources reviewed. No healthcare, HIV or medication access information specific to transgender visitors is documented; the only health-service finding is the 2005 threat of medical examinations to prove homosexual activity among detained men, which is coercive contact with health services rather than care.

No contemporary youth, school or minor-specific legal policy is covered. Historical ethnographic material on same-sex customs among an ethnic group in 1921 has no bearing on the current legal regime and is not treated as visitor-relevant.

No border screening procedure, entry-refusal practice or visa rule for LGBTQ travellers is set out in the sources; the asylum and deportation material concerns outbound cases in another jurisdiction.

TZA.name: Tanzania
TZA.summary:
Tanzania criminalises same-sex sexual conduct. The Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998 provides a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for same-sex acts between men; section 138A treats 'gross indecency' as an offence carrying one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of TSh 100,000 to 300,000. Heterosexual oral and anal sex are also offences under the same framework.

Zanzibar, the semi-autonomous island jurisdiction, runs a separate criminal statute. The Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004, enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives, defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute below 12, with under-18 and marriage distinctions) and provides penalties including three years' imprisonment. Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934, as amended in 2004, outlaws sex between women with up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine. A visitor may therefore fall under two overlapping criminal regimes depending on location.

Enforcement has been documented rather than theoretical. In 2018 the Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner, Paul Makonda, announced a 17-member committee of police, lawyers and doctors to identify and punish homosexuals, scouring the internet for videos of people presented as LGBTQ; men detained in the resulting sweep were forced to undergo anal examinations and torture. A 2013 report by Human Rights Watch and the Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS organisations on the basis of 'promoting homosexuality', disrupting services.

Violence against trans people is documented. In June 2024 the UN Human Rights Office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on Tanzanian transgender activist Mauzinde of Rahaleo, who was abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut. The office called for action against discrimination and flagged possible violations of Article 20 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and Article 13 equality guarantees in Tanzania's Constitution.

Official hostility is not confined to enforcement operations. Officials including the former president John Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla have pushed persecution of LGBT people, while activists Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule have publicly backed LGBT rights. Respect for freedom of speech and assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. Amnesty International's January 2024 report documents escalating anti-LGBT sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBT people; legislation on same-sex relations was deferred after protests. The US State Department's 2013 human rights report records discrimination based on sexual orientation and describes Tanzania's human rights record as poor, with police custody abuse detailed.

State-directed online filtering constrains access to information. The Open Observatory of Network Interference documented the blocking of LGBTIQ websites, including social networks and rights sites, in Tanzania in 2024.
TZA.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Tanzania was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); its documented finding that life imprisonment is available for same-sex activity is corroborated by other sources in this inventory.

The most recent US State Department human rights report cited here dates from 2013 and may not reflect current conditions.

Whether the 2018 Dar es Salaam crackdown carried central government backing is unresolved: the Foreign Ministry stated it did not, while the operation was announced by the regional commissioner.

Amnesty International report (Jan 2024, AFR 01/75/33/2024, 'We Are Facing Extinction'): documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people in Tanzania, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment — national-level findings.

Interview (Rainer Ebert, 4 Sep 2020) with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists: documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people in Tanzania and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy; includes definitions of sexual orientation, gender identity and trans woman terms.

sources.summary: Government respect for freedom of speech and freedom of assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. The 2018 broadcast content regulations bar inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference; the online content regulations issued the same year banned such hate speech but were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation. Activists Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule have openly backed LGBTQ rights against officials such as Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla, who pushed persecution. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the basis of 'promoting homosexuality', directly disrupting services. In 2018 a 'witch hunt' against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam, where gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and torture. Also in 2018 Paul Makonda, the Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner, announced a 17-strong committee of police, lawyers and doctors to identify and punish homosexuals, scouring the internet for videos of supposedly LGBTQ people; the Foreign Ministry said the crackdown lacked government support and Denmark withheld 65 million kr (about US$9.8 million) in aid. A 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. The US State Department's 2013 report likewise details police custody abuse and describes Tanzania's human rights record as poor. There are no gay bars in Tanzania, although some places exist where gay men meet, and lesbians are less visible than gay men. Tanzania has a high HIV/AIDS rate with reportedly one million people infected. On the policy side, the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services 'regardless of age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference', counselling 'any woman, man, couple, or young person regardless of age'; the Nursing and Midwifery (practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation; and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family planning counselling language is stated. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania, so no partner can be sponsored, inherited from, or recognized as next of kin through relationship status. Adoption requires a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly. Same-sex sexual acts between men carry a maximum penalty of life imprisonment under the Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences Special Provisions Act 1998 (section 138A 'gross indecency', 1–5 years or fines of TSh 100,000–300,000 for the general offence), and Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934 (as amended 2004) outlaws sex between women with up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine. Heterosexual oral and anal sex is also illegal.

ETH.name: Ethiopia
ETH.summary:
Article 629 of Ethiopia's 2004 Criminal Code makes same-sex conduct between men and between women a criminal offence. Prosecutions are uncommon, but the provision sustains stigma, harassment and violence against LGBTIQ+ people and produces near-total concealment of identity. Stakeholder submissions to the country's Universal Periodic Review put the maximum penalty at one year, with harsher terms available under aggravating provisions; a 2009 study of the same code reports up to three years for male homosexuality. The two accounts of the ceiling have not been reconciled.

No legal gender recognition mechanism exists. Neither a surgical nor a psychiatric pathway to changing legal sex is available, so trans men remain legally women and trans women legally men. A relationship that the law reads through birth-registered sex can therefore fall inside the prohibition on same-sex conduct, and a trans visitor travelling with a partner whose registered sex matches their own is exposed to the criminal law and not only to social disapproval.

Enforcement runs through public order and morality policing rather than through the courts. On 10 August 2023 security forces raided hospitality venues in Addis Ababa, shutting guest houses and arresting managers, after the city's Peace and Security Administration Bureau announced measures against hotels, restaurants, guest houses and other entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts and called on the public to report such cases. The same month produced an online incitement campaign that ended in physical attacks.

Police conduct documented by ILGA World includes residential searches without warrants following complaints from neighbours and physical abuse during detention. In a 2014 case a detained man was refused legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, and no trial record was found. In January 2021 police disclosed the sexual orientation of two people released from detention to their families, and one of them subsequently died by suicide. Activists report surveillance and entrapment, and the US State Department recorded harassment and violence rising toward the end of 2023.

The Charities and Societies Proclamation, Article 69, bars registration of LGBTI organisations as contrary to public morality, and groups operate without legal status. Pride events are not permitted and participants are not protected. A 2008 petition for equal rights signed by hundreds of gay people was blocked before reaching the prime minister's office, and a conference scheduled for Addis Ababa in 2012 was cancelled after religious groups denounced the organisers.

No hate-crime or hate-speech legislation covers gender identity, and there is no protection against arbitrary arrest on grounds of gender identity or expression. Workplace and housing discrimination protections do not extend to gender identity. The F&M Global Barometers series scores the country 'no' on every protection axis for each year from 2011 to 2024.

Discrimination is reported across education, employment and healthcare, and being identified as LGBTIQ+ carries a risk of physical violence and ostracism. Christian and Muslim bodies campaign for heavier penalties, and the Orthodox Church set out its position in June 2024. In March 2014 the Council of Ministers endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a non-pardonable offence, then cancelled both the bill and a planned anti-gay rally, with a government spokesman saying the existing jail term was sufficient.

Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition, and no mechanism recognises a trans person's partnership according to the partner's gender rather than registered sex. An unofficial ceremony held at a hotel in Addis Ababa in 2008 had no legal effect.

Stigma attached to HIV affects access to education, employment and community life. sources.summary: Ethiopia: same-sex conduct is criminalised, and concealment of identity is the norm. In the early 2010s some Ethiopian media outlets, cooperating with the government, restricted discussion of "LGBTQ ideology" without enacting the policy into law. Internet censorship has limited LGBTQ organising; in 2008 a petition for equal rights signed by hundreds of gay people was blocked en route to Prime Minister Meles Zenawi's office, and a pro-gay conference scheduled for Addis Ababa in 2012 was cancelled after fundamentalist Christian and religious groups called organizers "missionaries of evil." In 2023 the House of Guramayle reported online harassment of self-identified gay, lesbian and transgender people on platforms including TikTok, citing an August 2 video calling for gay men to be stabbed and a threat reading "We should find them and kill them." In July 2021 German authorities ordered the deportation of a trans woman of Qatari origin holding Ethiopian citizenship. She testified that after someone discovered she was registered as male in her passport and attempted extortion, she was reported to Ethiopian authorities, held about a year in an Ethiopian men's prison and subjected to physical and sexual abuse by staff and inmates. German officials argued she would be safe because she could "pass" as cisgender, citing the absence of explicit laws regarding gender identity. On 10 August 2023 the government raided hospitality venues in Addis Ababa to crack down on alleged homosexual activity, shutting down guest houses and arresting managers, while the Addis Ababa Peace and Security Administration Bureau announced measures "against hotels, restaurants, guest houses, and other entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts" and called on the public to report such incidents. ILGA World recorded police residential searches without warrants following neighbour complaints, physical abuse during detention, and a 2014 case in which a gay man was denied legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, with no trial records found. In January 2021 police disclosed the sexual orientation of two people released from detention to their families, and one subsequently died by suicide. The AIDS Resource Center in Addis Ababa reported that the majority of self-identified gay and lesbian callers, mostly male, requested help changing their behavior to avoid discrimination, with many gay men reporting anxiety, confusion, identity crises, depression, self-ostracism, religious conflict and suicide attempts. Stigma and discrimination toward people living with HIV/AIDS affected residents' ability to receive an education, find employment and integrate into the community. In early December 2011 Christian and Muslim religious leaders tried to derail a sexual health seminar targeted at men who have sex with men; the government intervened and the seminar went ahead at a different location. Organizers of the 2014 anti-gay rally and religious figures publicly blamed gay people for the rape of children and young men, and an anonymous LGBTQ activist told the AP in 2019 of wide misconceptions that gay people may be culpable for rising rape incidence, a climate that deters young people from seeking services. The DANA Social Club, founded 2013 by Beki Abiy, campaigns for transgender people's rights to sex reassignment surgery. Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition. In 2008 an unofficial gay marriage took place at the Sheraton Addis in Addis Ababa, and in Nuer society researcher Brian MacDermot encountered a transgender woman, formerly a man who dressed as a woman, who received spiritual approval to change status and marry a husband, suggesting precolonial acceptance of gender fluidity. In December 2008 nearly a dozen Ethiopian religious figures, including the leader of Ethiopian Muslims and heads of the Orthodox, Protestant and Catholic churches, adopted a resolution urging lawmakers to ban homosexual activity in the constitution, and religious figures that month held homosexuality responsible for a rise in sexual attacks on children and young men. In March 2014 the Council of Ministers endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a "non-pardonable" offence, but the government later cancelled both that bill and a planned April 2014 anti-gay rally, with spokesman Redwan Hussien saying the current jail term was deemed sufficient. The Addis Ababa Youth Forum, together with a church group linked to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, had planned the rally for 26 April 2014 alongside debate on the proposed bill; group chairman Dereje Negash claimed "Children are being raped by gay people in this country." The US Department of State's 2011 Human Rights Report found that stigma and discrimination toward people living with HIV/AIDS impacted residents' ability to receive an education. Historically, David F. Greenberg reported that shepherd boys of the Amhara and Qemant developed homosexual relationships with one another until marriage.

US State Department reporting on Ethiopia documents torture and harsh prison conditions alongside anti-terrorism prosecutions and restrictions on civil society under the charities and societies law, an environment in which a person held on a morality charge has little external scrutiny.

Historical and ethnographic material records a transgender woman in Nuer society, encountered by researcher Brian MacDermot, who received spiritual approval to change status and marry a husband, and homosexual relationships among shepherd boys of the Amhara and Qemant communities reported by David F. Greenberg. Neither has any bearing on the current statute.

ETH.blindSummary:
Article 629 of the country's 2004 Criminal Code makes same-sex conduct between men and between women a criminal offence. Prosecutions are uncommon, but the provision sustains stigma, harassment and violence against LGBTIQ+ people and produces near-total concealment of identity. Stakeholder submissions to a UN human rights review put the maximum penalty at one year, with harsher terms available under aggravating provisions; a 2009 university study of the same code reports up to three years for male homosexuality. The two accounts of the ceiling have not been reconciled.

No legal gender recognition mechanism exists. Neither a surgical nor a psychiatric pathway to changing legal sex is available, so trans men remain legally women and trans women legally men. A relationship that the law reads through birth-registered sex can therefore fall inside the prohibition on same-sex conduct, and a trans visitor travelling with a partner whose registered sex matches their own is exposed to the criminal law and not only to social disapproval.

Enforcement runs through public order and morality policing rather than through the courts. On 10 August 2023 security forces raided hospitality venues in the capital, shutting guest houses and arresting managers, after a municipal security authority announced measures against hotels, restaurants, guest houses and other entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts and called on the public to report such cases. The same month produced an online incitement campaign that ended in physical attacks.

Police conduct documented by an international monitoring group includes residential searches without warrants following complaints from neighbours and physical abuse during detention. In a 2014 case a detained man was refused legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, and no trial record was found. In January 2021 police disclosed the sexual orientation of two people released from detention to their families, and one of them subsequently died by suicide. Activists report surveillance and entrapment, and a foreign government's human rights report recorded harassment and violence rising toward the end of 2023.

A civil-society law, Article 69, bars registration of LGBTI organisations as contrary to public morality, and groups operate without legal status. Pride events are not permitted and participants are not protected. A 2008 petition for equal rights signed by hundreds of gay people was blocked before reaching the head of government's office, and a conference scheduled for the capital in 2012 was cancelled after religious groups denounced the organisers.

No hate-crime or hate-speech legislation covers gender identity, and there is no protection against arbitrary arrest on grounds of gender identity or expression. Workplace and housing discrimination protections do not extend to gender identity. An international index scores the country 'no' on every protection axis for each year from 2011 to 2024.

Discrimination is reported across education, employment and healthcare, and being identified as LGBTIQ+ carries a risk of physical violence and ostracism. Christian and Muslim bodies campaign for heavier penalties, and the dominant religious institution set out its position in June 2024. In March 2014 the cabinet endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a non-pardonable offence, then cancelled both the bill and a planned anti-gay rally, with a government spokesman saying the existing jail term was sufficient.

Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition, and no mechanism recognises a trans person's partnership according to the partner's gender rather than registered sex. An unofficial ceremony held at a hotel in the capital in 2008 had no legal effect.

Stigma attached to HIV affects access to education, employment and community life. A health organisation in the capital reported that most self-identified gay and lesbian callers, predominantly men, asked for help changing their behaviour to avoid discrimination, and many described anxiety, depression, identity crises and suicide attempts. Public claims blaming gay people for sexual violence against children and young men deter young people from seeking services. In December 2011 religious leaders tried to stop a sexual health seminar for men who have sex with men; the government intervened and the seminar went ahead at another location.

Document markers carry direct custodial risk. In July 2021 authorities in another jurisdiction ordered the deportation of a trans woman of foreign origin who held citizenship of the country. After someone discovered that her passport recorded her as male and attempted to extort her, she was reported to the authorities, held for about a year in a men's prison and subjected to physical and sexual abuse by staff and inmates. Officials there argued that she would be safe because she could pass as cisgender, citing the absence of explicit law on gender identity.

In the early 2010s some media outlets, cooperating with the government, restricted discussion of what they termed LGBTQ ideology without any formal policy being enacted. Internet censorship has limited organising.

LBN.name: Lebanon
LBN.summary:
Lebanon's Penal Code criminalises transgender expression both directly and through general morality provisions. Article 521 prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for "men disguising themselves as women", a provision that reaches trans feminine presentation. Article 534 punishes "intercourse contrary to the order of nature" with up to one year's imprisonment and remains on the statute book. A regional country review concludes that the state applies both de facto and explicit criminalisation, with transgender women carrying the greatest exposure.

Court practice has moved against Article 534 without removing it. Multiple courts between 2007 and 2023 declined to apply the article to consensual sexual conduct, including a 2009 precedent holding that consensual sexual relations are not a criminal offence and a February 2017 ruling that questioned the legal basis for prosecution. In August 2023 a district court of appeal held that consensual sexual relations are not unlawful. The article nonetheless remains in force, and arrests and prosecutions have been brought under it.

Enforcement has included police arrests of LGBT people and intrusive anal examinations ordered by prosecutors; 36 people were arrested in a 2012 cinema raid. Human Rights Watch reported in April 2022 that trans people in Lebanon face policing and documentation barriers, and called on the state to guarantee access to legal gender recognition.

Legal gender recognition is not available. Outright International records that sexual relations between men and between women are not lawful anywhere in the country and that legal gender recognition is not possible. The judiciary has a long history of reviewing trans plaintiffs' requests to change names and gender markers, governed by the civil registry code of 1951, with an 1887-era precedent recorded as Lebanese Civil Decision 1987; medical and religious authorities hold heavy roles in those proceedings. In 2015 a judge approved a plaintiff's change of gender marker on identity documents, the start of gradual progress in that area.

Public assembly has been restricted by executive action. In June 2022 the caretaker interior minister, Bassam Mawlawi, ordered security forces to prevent LGBT gatherings; the Shura Council froze the order in November 2022 after Legal Agenda and Helem argued that it incited violence and violated constitutional rights to equality, expression and assembly. In May 2018 security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel Beirut Pride, nine days of LGBT-identity activities, in a crackdown Human Rights Watch described as a violation of freedom of assembly.

A rise in prejudice and violence against trans and queer people is documented in Beirut, including incidents responding to a decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament.

The scope of the June 2022 interior ministry order after the Shura Council freeze is not sourced, including whether any part of it remains in effect.

Whether the 2015 approval of a gender-marker change reflects settled administrative practice or an isolated ruling is not established by the sources.

JOR.name: Jordan
JOR.summary:
Jordan does not criminalise same-sex relations. The 1951 Penal Code abolished the colonial-era ban, legalising private, adult, non-commercial, consensual same-sex acts with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or orientation. That revision left no anti-discrimination protection in its place. No statute criminalises gender expression as such, though Human Rights Watch's April 2018 annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the region includes Jordan.

Formal decriminalisation does not describe enforcement. Human Rights Watch reported on 6 June 2024 that authorities in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait use public-morality and debauchery provisions in place of explicit criminalisation to harass LGBT people. IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.summary:
Iraq's legal position for a trans visitor is set by the amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution passed by the Council of Representatives on 27 April 2024, signed by the President on 29 June 2024 and in force since 1 July 2024. The amendment criminalises consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression. Human Rights Watch, the Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor and ILGA Asia all record it as the operative legal baseline, and Human Rights Watch has called for its repeal.

Penalties are custodial and severe. Consensual same-sex relations carry 10 to 15 years' imprisonment. Undergoing or performing a gender-affirming procedure carries 1 to 3 years, applied to the trans person and to the doctor, which places transition itself outside the law. The legislation also penalises "promoting homosexuality". Penalties include fines and deportation, so removal from the country is a stated consequence of a criminalised status rather than a discretionary immigration outcome.

Iraq has no legal gender recognition framework. The 2024 provisions target "biological sex changes based on personal desires and inclination" with up to three years' imprisonment for the person and the practitioner, excluding court-ordered procedures on intersex people. No route to corrected identity documents exists, and a visitor cannot rely on Iraqi documents matching their presentation.

Partner recognition is closed. The Personal Status Law 1959 Article 3 and the Iraqi Kurdistan Personal Status Law 1992 Article 1 define marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and same-sex marriage and civil unions are illegal. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no recognised status, and the relationship itself falls within the 2024 criminalisation.

Violence against LGBT Iraqis is documented over more than a decade with no effective state response. A BBC investigation found that killings of gay people had continued over successive years while the authorities turned a blind eye, and reported the UN's assessment that state neglect makes the state itself a perpetrator. In October 2023 a prominent Iraqi social media figure was fatally shot in Baghdad during a crackdown on the LGBT community. In early 2012 Shi'a militia death squads carried out the "Emo Killings", targeting teenagers accused of homosexuality on the basis of their clothing; flyers appeared in Baghdad naming individuals and threatening them unless they cut their hair and abandoned nonconformist dress. The pattern is one of impunity for anti-LGBT violence rather than prosecution of it.

Official assessments acknowledge the danger. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report for Iraq recorded societal discrimination and violence against individuals based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity, alongside sectarian violence, torture and impunity. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 3.0, July 2025) assesses risk from state, hybrid and non-state actors, the availability of protection, the feasibility of internal relocation, and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims.
IRQ.outOfScopeNotes:
The number of prosecutions brought under the 2024 amendment is not sourced; the statute's text and its entry into force are documented, but enforcement data are not available in the material reviewed.

Historical material on the 1986 order relocating Iraqis with AIDS to a prison facility is not trans-specific and is not treated as evidence of the current legal regime.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note is an asylum-decision instrument rather than a travel advisory; its risk assessment is used here for its country information on state, hybrid and non-state actors and internal relocation.

The US State Department report dates from 2012 and predates the 2024 statute; it documents the pre-statutory climate and official acknowledgment of discrimination and violence.

Saddam Hussein ordered all Iraqis with AIDS relocated to a special prison facility after the disease reached Iraq in 1986. Iraqueer (formed March 2015) runs education work including published guides on security and health safety, YouTube videos and workshops on gender and sexuality, advocacy and safety in crisis.

VEN.name: Venezuela
VEN.summary:
Venezuela does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The age of consent is 16 and applies identically to same-sex relations. The country has no hate-crime statute and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, so violence or discrimination directed at a trans person carries no dedicated penalty or aggravating circumstance.

Legality has not prevented police action. In May 2026 the Observatorio Venezolano de Violencias LGBTIQ+, Caleidoscopio Humano and Movimiento SOMOS denounced the detention of around 30 people in a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto, Lara state. Officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, extorted detainees and accused them of 'committing the crime of homosexuality', a charge with no basis in Venezuelan law.

There is no working legal gender recognition route. A 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal requires each case to be assessed individually, with certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist demonstrating the veracity of the intended sexual identity, and the Tribunal has not granted the requested name and gender changes. SAIME announced in September 2016 that transgender people could request an identity card matching their gender identity, but no administrative procedure or mechanism exists to enact the relevant article. A trans visitor cannot expect to obtain Venezuelan documents that match their gender.

Partner recognition is partial. Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children, and the law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions. Lesbian couples are permitted to access IVF. A December 2016 ruling of the Supreme Tribunal of Justice allowed a baby to be registered in the Civil Registry with both mothers' surnames and held that the state must protect all families without distinction.

Institutional protection is limited. The National Assembly unanimously passed a resolution in May 2016 establishing 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia; the Supreme Court suspended that resolution in August 2016. Venezuela has marked the International Day Against Homophobia since 2000, and the government has begun participating in Pride events.

Tamara Adrián and Rosmit Mantilla were elected Alternate Deputies in the 2015 parliamentary election, the first LGBT members of Venezuela's legislature; Adrián had run as the country's first transgender candidate for the National Assembly. In December 2015 Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla, a Voluntad Popular deputy and the country's first openly gay parliamentarian, a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody.
VEN.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal remains unresolved: no ruling granting the requested name and gender changes is recorded.

Whether an administrative procedure has since been created to implement SAIME's September 2016 identity-card announcement is not sourced.

The fate of the equal-marriage bill reported in January 2014 after its presentation to the National Assembly is not recorded, and whether the August 2016 suspension of the 17 May resolution remains in force is not sourced.

Two reference compilations are catalogued as sources: the EUAA country focus on Venezuela, covering the period through 2025, and the October 2024 LGBTQ guide published by AFS and the Vance Center. Their individual findings are not itemised separately here.

An LGBTQ guide covering Venezuela was published by AFS and the Vance Center in Oct 2024.

Sydney Morning Herald (8 Aug 2015): Tamara Adrian, Venezuela's first transgender candidate, ran for the National Assembly -- landmark trans political candidacy under Venezuela's gender-recognition law context.

Cronica Uno poll (2-3 Mar 2023): a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens; 82% know the LGBTIQ+ term (13% do not); 36% think gay/lesbian/bisexuality is innate -- dated public-opinion data.
Aporrea reported on 31 Jan 2014 that an equal-marriage bill was to be presented to Venezuela's National Assembly that week, a legislative push for same-sex marriage; no later enactment is recorded.

El Mundo (13 Dec 2015): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla -- Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian -- a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody; he turned 33 in his cell -- state persecution of an openly gay politician.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Venezuela has marked the International Day Against Homophobia since 2000, and the government has recently begun participating in Pride events. In May 2016 the National Assembly unanimously passed a resolution establishing 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia, and the Supreme Court suspended that resolution in August 2016. Tamara Adrián and Rosmit Mantilla were elected Alternate Deputies in the 2015 parliamentary election, the first LGBT members of Venezuela's legislature. Police harassment remains a serious problem: in May 2026 NGOs including the Observatorio Venezolano de Violencias LGBTIQ+, Caleidoscopio Humano and Movimiento SOMOS denounced the detention of around 30 people in a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in Barquisimeto, Lara state, where officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, extorted detainees and accused them of 'committing the crime of homosexuality', despite homosexuality being legal. The law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions, lesbian couples are allowed to access IVF, and same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children. For legal gender recognition, a 2017 constitutional action before the Supreme Justice Tribunal requires each case to be individually assessed with certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist demonstrating the veracity of the intended sexual identity, and the Tribunal still has not granted the requested name and gender changes. Trans people also remain unable to change identity-card information: although SAIME announced in September 2016 that transgender people may request a new identity card matching their gender identity, there is currently no administrative procedure or mechanism to enact the relevant article. The universal age of consent is 16, with no differential age for same-sex conduct. On 15 December 2016 the Supreme Tribunal of Justice ruled that a baby may be registered in the Civil Registry with both mothers' surnames, basing the decision on Article 75 of the Constitution, and declared that the state must protect all families without distinction, so that children and teenagers born into same-sex families enjoy all the rights and guarantees of children born into opposite-sex families. Same-sex couples are still unable to legally adopt, though a 2023 Equilibrium CenDE poll found 48% of Venezuelans supported adoption by same-sex couples (34% totally, 14% somewhat) versus 39% opposed. A 2013 Pew survey found 57% of 18–29-year-olds believed homosexuality should be accepted by society, compared with 51% of 30–49-year-olds and 45% of those over 50.

VEN.comparisons: Pairwise: above Trinidad & Tobago (0.42 — court-decriminalised with dating-app ambush pattern) and below Peru (0.48 — LGR exists). Venezuela's distinguishing factor is the absence of any legal floor whatsoever plus active regime persecution.
VEN.blindSummary:
The country does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The age of consent is 16 and applies identically to same-sex relations. The country has no hate-crime statute and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, so violence or discrimination directed at a trans person carries no dedicated penalty or aggravating circumstance.

Legality has not prevented police action. In May 2026 local NGOs denounced the detention of around 30 people in a police raid on an LGBTQ+ venue in a city in one state/province. Officers allegedly entered without proper warrants, extorted detainees and accused them of 'committing the crime of homosexuality', a charge with no basis in national law.

There is no working legal gender recognition route. A 2017 constitutional action before the national supreme court requires each case to be assessed individually, with certified birth certificates and a psychiatric and psychological report from a specialist demonstrating the veracity of the intended sexual identity, and the court has not granted the requested name and gender changes. The national identity registry announced in September 2016 that transgender people could request an identity card matching their gender identity, but no administrative procedure or mechanism exists to enact the relevant article. A trans visitor cannot expect to obtain documents of the country that match their gender.

Partner recognition is partial. Same-sex couples cannot legally adopt children, and the law sets no general healthcare or transition-care provisions. Lesbian couples are permitted to access IVF. In December 2016 the national supreme court allowed a baby to be registered in the civil registry with both mothers' surnames and held that the state must protect all families without distinction.

Institutional protection is limited. The national legislature unanimously passed a resolution in May 2016 establishing 17 May as the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia; the national supreme court suspended that resolution in August 2016. The country has marked the International Day Against Homophobia since 2000, and the government has begun participating in Pride events.

Two candidates were elected Alternate Deputies in the 2015 parliamentary election, the first LGBT members of the national legislature; one had run as the country's first transgender candidate for that legislature. In December 2015 an international human rights organisation declared an openly gay parliamentarian of a political party a prisoner of conscience held in national security custody.

BOL.name: Bolivia
BOL.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised and has been lawful since 1832. The age of consent is 14 under Criminal Code article 308bis, with a three-year close-in-age exemption.

Article 14(II) of the 2009 Constitution, in force since February 2009, prohibits and punishes discrimination on grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation, and guarantees equal recognition and exercise of rights.

The Law Against Racism and All Forms of Discrimination (Law 045), enacted on 8 October 2010, defines discrimination to include distinctions based on sex, sexual orientation and gender identity, and bars it in employment, services, education, health and other public and private spheres. It supplies definitions of transphobia, amends Penal Code article 281 to criminalise gender-identity-based discrimination, and makes dissemination and incitement punishable by one to five years' imprisonment. Since 2010, Penal Code article 40bis treats gender-identity motivation as an aggravating circumstance at sentencing.

The Gender Identity Law, passed by the Chamber of Deputies on 19 May 2016 and by the Chamber of Senators on 20 May 2016, signed on 21 May and in force from 1 August 2016, permits people over 18 to change name, sex and photograph on legal documents before the Civil Registry Service. The procedure is confidential, must be completed within 15 days, rests on a psychological test of voluntary assumption rather than surgery, and is reversible once. The first legal gender change under the law was recorded on 1 August 2016.

The changed sex marker is not recognised for marriage. In November 2017 the Supreme Court invalidated as unconstitutional a June 2017 Supreme Electoral Tribunal instruction to recognise it, and an appeal was lodged with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in May 2018.

Article 63 of the Constitution reserves marriage to heterosexual couples. Free unions between same-sex partners have been registered since 20 March 2023, when a Plurinational Constitutional Court ruling of 22 June 2022 obliging the Civil Registry Service to register them took effect; regulations were modified on 21 July 2023 to impose the same requirements and timelines as for heterosexual couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex has no access to marriage and depends on the free-union route for any recognition.

Single people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, and same-sex couples in a free union may adopt under article 84 of the Child and Adolescent Code.

Enforcement of the protection framework is weak. The Ombudsman reported in 2017 that only a minority of the murders of LGBT people recorded that year were investigated and that none produced a sentence. Reports of societal discrimination are common, and a 2024 national virtual survey, the first of its kind, documented widespread exclusion of LGBTI people.

A 2017 ILGA poll found 64% agreeing that transgender people should have the same rights, 63% that they should be protected from employment discrimination, and 53% that they should be able to change their legal gender.
BOL.outOfScopeNotes:
Sources give conflicting dates for civil-union registration: one records civil-registry recognition in December 2020, while the court ruling that obliged registration is dated 22 June 2022 and took effect on 20 March 2023.

The outcome of the May 2018 appeal to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights on marriage recognition of a changed sex marker is not recorded in the sources.

The November 2015 government bill that became the Gender Identity Law was presented with an explicit exclusion of same-sex marriage; the sources do not describe any legislative change on that point beyond the 2017 Supreme Court ruling.

Official enforcement figures are limited to 2017 Ombudsman reporting; no more recent data on investigations or sentences appears in the sources.

sources.summary: Comparative Politics article (April 2024) 'Activists, Parties, and the Expansion of Trans Rights in Bolivia': Bolivia prohibits gender-identity discrimination and passed a ground-breaking gender identity law (2016, allowing name/marker change) despite low voter support; trans activists leveraged access to ruling-party legislators; contradictory heteronormative laws passed alongside because both organised religion and LGBT activists were party constituents.
Agencia Presentes article (Dec 2024): Bolivia's first virtual survey finds the great exclusion of LGBTI people in the country.

The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia documents the constitutional guarantee against discrimination and societal discrimination against LGBT people. Its general assessment addresses arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions, and corruption.
Newsweek (Jul 2017) counted 18 countries believed to fully legalise LGBT military service following the US trans military ban, and did not single out Bolivia.

Bolivia's Constitution prohibits discrimination and protects bodily integrity, citing Art 15(II) on violence and Art 45(V) on maternity, while Penal Code Title VIII governs abortion. The 2016 gender-identity law provides self-identification, followed in Jan 2018 by an Inter-American Court opinion and in Dec 2020 by civil-registry recognition of free union for same-sex couples.

eju.tv/La Razón (25 Aug 2014, Spanish): homosexuality is taboo in Bolivia's armed forces — gay soldiers report discrimination and sanctions, testimony given anonymously; the TLGB collective and human-rights activists demand openness.

Since 2010, Penal Code article 40bis aggravates penalties for crimes motivated by grounds including gender identity. The Gender Identity Law was passed by the Chamber of Deputies on 19 May 2016, by the Chamber of Senators on 20 May 2016, signed on 21 May 2016, and took effect on 1 August 2016. It allows individuals over 18 to legally change name, sex and photograph on legal documents before the Civil Registry Service confidentially within 15 days based on a psychological test of voluntary assumption without requiring sex reassignment surgery, reversible once only. The first legal gender change under the law occurred on 1 August 2016 by activist Pamela Valenzuela. The newly assigned sex is not recognized for marriage after the Supreme Court in November 2017 invalidated a June 2017 Supreme Electoral Tribunal instruction to recognize it as unconstitutional, with an appeal filed to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights in May 2018. Bolivia allows transgender people to serve openly in the military under a 2013 Armed Forces announcement effective in 2015. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1832, with the age of consent set at 14 under Criminal Code article 308bis and a three-year close-in-age exemption. Discrimination based on sexual orientation is constitutionally prohibited and criminalized under Penal Code article 281 as amended, with one to five years imprisonment for dissemination and incitement, and article 40bis since 2010 aggravates penalties for orientation-motivated crimes. Men who have sex with men have been permitted to donate blood since 10 July 2019 under amended Supreme Decree 24547, after a prior ban labelling homosexual and bisexual men as a high-risk group. The Armed Forces announced in 2013 that LGBT citizens could serve from 2015, though homosexuality in the military remains viewed as taboo with discretion advised. Enforcement remains weak, with the Ombudsman reporting 64 LGBT people murdered in 2017 with only 14 cases investigated and none resulting in a sentence. Reports of societal discrimination against LGBT people are not uncommon. In 2017 the Ombudsman reported that 64 LGBT people had been murdered that year, with only 14 cases investigated and none resulting in a sentence. PRY.name: Paraguay
PRY.summary:
Paraguay has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. A 1993 civil court case seeking to register Ramón Fidel, who had undergone gender reassignment surgery, as a woman ended without a decision because Fidel died in a traffic accident before judgment. Trans people are not permitted to change their name or gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

Amnesty International's 2025-26 reporting records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents, evidence that the documentary gap reaches administrative encounters rather than staying theoretical.

Health settings are the one area where a chosen name is formally recognised. Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare Resolution 695, approved in October 2016, provides that trans people may use their social name on medical records, medical histories and forms, and requires officials in the Integrated Networks of Health Services to assist and treat trans patients using the name with which they identify. Law 7018 on Mental Health, enacted 15 November 2022, provides in Article 3 that mental-health care is governed by non-discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and that a diagnosis may in no case be made solely on the basis of sexual choice, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Official hostility toward trans people is documented at the national and municipal levels. In October 2017 the government imposed a ban on discussion of LGBT issues in public schools, and the Minister of Education said the ministry might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March. Horacio Cartes, a leading figure of the ruling party, said he would shoot himself in the testicles if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended.

Discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into internal and cross-border migration and into sex work, according to reporting from September 2025. Violence and discrimination against LGBT people are frequent and often ignored by police. Amnesty International counted 37 registered feminicides in 2025, a figure not disaggregated for trans victims, and in April a bill was introduced to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family.

No broad anti-discrimination law covers Paraguay. A bill introduced in November 2015 to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction, and violence and discrimination against LGBT people are frequently left unaddressed by police, leaving a visitor who is targeted with no general statutory remedy.

Partner recognition is closed at the constitutional level. Articles 49, 50, 51 and 52 of the 1992 Constitution limit marriage, de facto unions and the family to one man and one woman, and Article 140 of the Civil Code expressly prohibits marriage between persons of the same sex. An 8 January 2018 advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights held that states party to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family registration systems, including marriage; Paraguay is a party to the Convention, but its law has not been adapted and a lawsuit relying on the opinion to recognise same-sex marriage remains pending. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no route to marriage or union recognition, and the same gap applies to trans residents.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1990. The age of consent is 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct, a distinction that can bear on a younger trans visitor in a relationship local law reads as same-sex.
PRY.outOfScopeNotes:
The ten recognition lawsuits have no final rulings, and the UN Human Rights Committee communications filed by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights are still awaiting a decision. The outcome and any compliance by Paraguay are unresolved.

The lawsuit seeking recognition of a same-sex marriage on the basis of the 8 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion remains pending. Whether the domestic-law gap identified after the opinion will be closed is not sourced.

The November 2015 anti-discrimination bill has not advanced since introduction; no parliamentary schedule or vote is recorded.

Violence data is incomplete for this assessment. The 37 feminicides registered in 2025 are not disaggregated for trans victims, and no trans-specific homicide or violence count with a denominator was located in the source inventory, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made. The two identity-document refusals recorded by Amnesty International are individual cases rather than a count.

The Asunción city council's ban on the event honouring the trans human-rights defender is recorded without the resolution text, the stated grounds or any legal challenge, so whether it rests on a general municipal events rule or on the subject matter of the event is not sourced.

Elite-level anti-LGBT rhetoric.
