Paraguay is an OAS party and therefore bound by the ruling, while Bolivian, Paraguayan and Peruvian law recognise neither same-sex marriage nor unions, leaving local law lagging behind the opinion. About 300 Costa Ricans celebrated the opinion at the court.

ABC Color (30 May 2017): adoption analysis - Law 1136/97 does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or singles from adopting (prohibitions cover only infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records), a legal gap allowing same-sex adoption as couples or as single men/women, amid a society that still closes doors. Adoption-law reality check.

Ultima Hora: post-IACtHR ruling analysis says people in Paraguay must overcome difficulties adapting the country's laws to extend the right to marriage to everyone - the domestic-law gap the inter-American opinion leaves for Paraguay to close.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: During the Stroessner dictatorship (1954-1989) LGBT people faced heavy persecution. In the 1959 Caso 108, police arrested and tortured 108 gay men in Asunción and made their names public, and the government publicly encouraged hatred and violence against LGBT people. Violence and discrimination against LGBT community members remain frequent in Paraguay today and are often ignored by the police. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Paraguay since 1990, though the age of consent is 16 for homosexuals and 14 for heterosexuals. There is no broad anti-discrimination law, and a November 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction. Limited protections exist in specific contexts: Law 5162/2014 requires that collective dormitory placement for adolescents take into account age, sexual orientation and degree of psychic development; Decree 6973 under Law 577/2016 protects women from violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation; Law 6149/2018 bars discrimination against stateless persons based on sexual orientation and gender identity; Law 6534/2020 treats sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data; Article 28 of the Ministry of Public Defense internal rules prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation against employees. In October 2017 the Government of Paraguay implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues within public schools, and the Minister of Education said it might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Transgender people are not allowed to legally change their name and gender on official documents, though in December 2016 two transgender women filed a lawsuit to change their names citing constitutional free expression and identity provisions. In October 2016 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved Resolution 695 requiring that all transgender people may use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms, and that health service officials must treat transgender patients using their identified social name. Law 7018 on Mental Health (enacted 15 November 2022) states that a mental health diagnosis cannot be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Paraguay (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to legally change their name and gender on official documents. A 1993 Civil Court case seeking registration of Ramon Fidel, who had undergone gender reassignment surgery, as a woman did not result in a decision because Fidel died in a traffic accident before it was decided. In December 2016 two transgender women, Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepulveda, filed a lawsuit to change their names invoking Article 25 of the Constitution on free expression and free construction of identity and Article 42 of the Civil Code allowing change of first name. In October 2016 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare approved Resolution 695 providing that all transgender people may use their social name on medical records, medical history and forms and requiring officials in Integrated Networks of Health Services (RIISS) to assist and treat transgender patients using the social name with which they identify. Specific non-discrimination provisions expressly covering gender identity include Article 9 of Law 6149/2018 on Protection and Facilities for Naturalization of Stateless Persons, while a November 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced. Law 7018 on Mental Health enacted November 15, 2022 provides in Article 3 that in no case can a diagnosis be made in mental health on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity. In October 2017 the Government implemented a ban on discussion of LGBT issues within public schools, with the Minister of Education stating consideration of burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1990, with age of consent set at 16 for homosexuals and 14 for heterosexuals. Since 1992 the Constitution limits marriage, de facto unions and the family to one man and one woman under Articles 49, 50, 51 and 52, and Article 140 of the Civil Code expressly prohibits marriage between persons of the same sex. An 8 January 2018 advisory opinion of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights stated that states party to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family registration systems including marriage, and a lawsuit relying on that opinion to recognize same-sex marriage remains pending. Under the Adoption Law Ley 1136 de 1997 in force since 1997, single persons of any sex may adopt regardless of marital status, with equal preference given to opposite-sex marriages and de facto unions and single women. There is no broad anti-discrimination law, but limited protections based on sexual orientation exist including Article 274 of Law 5162/2014 Criminal Enforcement Code requiring consideration of sexual orientation with age and psychic development when housing adolescents in collective dormitories, Decree 6973 regulating Law 577/2016 protecting women in situations of violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation, and Article 28 of the Internal Rules of the Ministry of Public Defense prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination against employees. There is no official prohibition preventing entry of gays, lesbians and bisexuals into the Armed Forces and National Police, after the Chamber of Deputies in June 2010 rejected by 42 votes against and 4 in favor a bill that would have prohibited entry of homosexuals into the Public Force. During the dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner from 1954 to 1989 LGBT people faced heavy persecution including the 1 September 1959 Case 108 in which 108 gay men blamed for a fire in Asuncion were arrested, tortured and publicly named. The article describes Paraguay as one of South America's most conservative countries where reports of violence and discrimination against members of the LGBT community generally are frequent and often ignored by police. It attributes influence to the Catholic Church, which retains strong influence and presence and has strongly opposed measures to improve LGBT lives, alongside a recent rise in religious fundamentalism causing concern among LGBT advocacy groups. It states general population attitudes toward same-sex marriage and LGBT rights remain low compared to other South American countries, especially Argentina and Brazil, citing 15% support for same-sex marriage with 81% opposed in a Pew survey conducted 26 November 2013 to 8 January 2014 and 26% support in the 2017 AmericasBarometer. It notes LGBT groups have organised pride parades in Asuncion since 2004. These violence, church-influence, attitude and polling statements refer to LGBT people or same-sex marriage generally and are not stated as transgender-specific findings. The only transgender-specific tolerance statement documented is the Minister of Education's statement in connection with the October 2017 ban on discussion of LGBT issues in public schools that "it might even consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people."

PRY.blindSummary:
The country has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by two plaintiffs that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to a United Nations human rights treaty body under an optional protocol to an international covenant on civil and political rights and are awaiting a decision. A 1993 civil court case seeking to register a person who had undergone gender reassignment surgery as a woman ended without a decision because that person died in a traffic accident before judgment. Trans people are not permitted to change their name or gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

Human rights reporting for 2025-26 records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents, evidence that the documentary gap reaches administrative encounters rather than staying theoretical.

Health settings are the one area where a chosen name is formally recognised. A resolution of the national public health ministry, approved in October 2016, provides that trans people may use their social name on medical records, medical histories and forms, and requires officials in integrated health service networks to assist and treat trans patients using the name with which they identify. A mental health law enacted 15 November 2022 provides that mental-health care is governed by non-discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, and that a diagnosis may in no case be made solely on the basis of sexual choice, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Official hostility toward trans people is documented at the national and municipal levels. In October 2017 the government imposed a ban on discussion of LGBT issues in public schools, and the national education minister said the ministry might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. The capital city's council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March. A leading figure of the ruling party said he would shoot himself in the testicles if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended.

Discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into internal and cross-border migration and into sex work, according to reporting from September 2025. Violence and discrimination against LGBT people are frequent and often ignored by police. A human rights organisation counted 37 registered feminicides in 2025, a figure not disaggregated for trans victims, and in April a bill was introduced to merge the national women's ministry into a family ministry.

No broad anti-discrimination law covers the country. A bill introduced in November 2015 to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced since introduction, and violence and discrimination against LGBT people are frequently left unaddressed by police, leaving a visitor who is targeted with no general statutory remedy.

Partner recognition is closed at the constitutional level. Provisions of the 1992 Constitution limit marriage, de facto unions and the family to one man and one woman, and the civil code expressly prohibits marriage between persons of the same sex. An 8 January 2018 advisory opinion of a regional human rights court held that states party to a regional human rights convention should grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family registration systems, including marriage; the country is a party to the convention, but its law has not been adapted and a lawsuit relying on the opinion to recognise same-sex marriage remains pending. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no route to marriage or union recognition, and the same gap applies to trans residents.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1990. The age of consent is 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct, a distinction that can bear on a younger trans visitor in a relationship local law reads as same-sex.

GTM.name: Guatemala
GTM.summary:
Consensual, private, non-commercial same-sex sexual activity between adults has been lawful in Guatemala since 1871.

Guatemala provides no legal gender recognition. Since 2016 a person may change a legal name to match gender identity only with judicial permission; legal gender cannot be changed, and a person cannot self-report gender for official documents, which must show the sex and name assigned at birth. The resulting mismatch between presentation and identity documents exposes a trans visitor to scrutiny during identity checks.

Guatemala is bound by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion OC-24/17 of 9 January 2018, which holds recognition of gender identity on official documents to be a human right under the American Convention on Human Rights and requires states parties to grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage with all rights deriving from marriage.

Legislative movement on recognition has gone in the opposite direction. A December 2017 bill to recognise the right to gender identity and allow transgender people to change name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by both the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission, and later proposals for a gender identity law permitting change of official documents have been advocated without enactment.

Initiative No. 5940, received by the Legislative Directorate on 12 July 2021 and presented to the plenary of the Congress of Guatemala on 13 September 2021, proposes a law to guarantee the integral protection of children and adolescents against gender identity disorders and was assigned to the Human Rights, Education, Science and Technology, and Governance commissions. Bill 5490, advanced in December 2021, would remove education regarding transgender individuals in schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents from "gender identity disorders" and require censorship of media featuring transgender individuals; it was unanimously approved by the Congress's Education, Science and Technology committee and moved for full congress review.

Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations such as cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas. A May 2017 bill to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category remains unadopted, and the penal code's prohibition of discrimination on grounds including gender does not explicitly cover gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. No convictions for discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds were recorded through 2021.

Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of gender identity are reportedly tolerated by the Guatemalan government, particularly where harassment or violence is directed at transgender people, and the absence of hate-crime protection is attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles.

Trans women are held in men's prisons on birth-sex placement. A 2020 Human Rights Watch report documents that practice and the resulting sexual assault, recording no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice and no court ruling on trans custody. Bárbara Herrarte of Redmmutrans described her time in a men's prison: "Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him." The same reporting flags forced internal displacement of LGBT people from violence.

Conversion practices operate openly, mainly through Evangelical-funded centres in rural areas, and include electroshock therapy, forced marriage and coerced sex; "corrective" rape is prosecuted only as rape and not as a hate crime. Such practices remain normalised, including among mental health professionals.

Documented violence is longstanding. United Nations and NGO reports from the late 1990s recorded systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a social cleansing campaign, including the 1997 gunning down in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia. Central American governments have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, and Guatemalan officials have justified that exclusion by stating that transgender women are not "biological women".

There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples as marriage, civil union or domestic partnership. A civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Morán has not been debated since. The Protection of Life and Family initiative (5272), which would increase penalties for abortion, explicitly ban same-sex marriage, define family as "being a father, a mother and children" and describe homosexuality as "being contrary to biology and genetics", passed first and second readings in 2018 with its third reading blocked that September. Congress approved the law again on 8 March 2022; after President Alejandro Giammattei announced a veto on grounds it violated the Constitution and international agreements, Congress archived and discarded it on 15 March 2022 by 119 votes, leaving its prohibitions without effect.

An opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash against gender recognition in Guatemala and neighbouring jurisdictions. In August 2025 the Guatemalan Congress hosted the Meeting for Religious Freedom, Life and Family to advance an anti-LGBTIQ agenda, and despite the election of a more progressive government in 2024 the legislature remained predominantly conservative with no significant pro-LGBTIQ initiatives.
GTM.outOfScopeNotes:
Guatemala's compliance with the Inter-American Court's advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 is not recorded in the available sources, so the gap between the opinion's requirements and practice on document recognition and couple recognition remains unresolved.

The sources carry no trans-specific killing rate for Guatemala and no denominator against which such a figure could be read, so no comparative magnitude of trans homicide risk can be stated. Reported incidents are described qualitatively rather than as rates.

The status of Bill 5490 and Initiative No. 5940 beyond their 2021 committee and plenary stages is not sourced, and whether either was enacted, archived or withdrawn is unresolved.

No sourced material addresses airport or border screening of gender presentation, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or facilities and restroom rules for visitors; these are not covered rather than absent.

Whether the government elected in 2024 altered any policy on gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection is not documented in the inventory.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Guatemala (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2016 transgender people in Guatemala can change their legal name to match gender identity following judicial permission, but they cannot change their legal gender, and individuals cannot self-report gender for official government documents, which must show gender and name assigned at birth, causing problems accessing government services such as education and basic resources that require official ID. Guatemala is legally bound to the 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holding that recognition of one's gender identity on official documents is a human right protected by the American Convention on Human Rights. A December 2017 bill to recognize the right to gender identity and allow transgender people to change name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by both the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission, while a later legislative proposal for a gender identity law to allow change of official documents to reflect gender status has been advocated without enactment. Bill 5490 advanced in December 2021 to remove education regarding transgender individuals in schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents from “gender identity disorders” and to require censorship of media with transgender individuals, unanimously approved by the Congress’ Education, Science, and Technology committee and moved for full congress review. Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or other public accommodations such as cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas, with a May 2017 bill proposing to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category remaining unadopted. Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of gender identity are reportedly tolerated by the Government, especially when harassment or violence is directed at transgender people, with lack of hate-crime protection attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles. United Nations and NGO reports from the late 1990s documented systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a social cleansing campaign, including the 1997 gunning down in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia, and active Evangelical-funded conversion therapy centers mainly in rural areas subject persons to electroshock therapy, “corrective” rape prosecuted only as rape not hate crime, forced marriage and coerced sex. Both male and female consensual, non-commercial, private same-sex sexual activity have been legal in Guatemala since 1871, following earlier Spanish colonial punishment of sodomy with burning at the stake. There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples as marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, and a civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Morán has not been debated since. The 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage with all rights deriving from marriage, to which Guatemala is bound. In response lawmakers introduced the life and protection bill / Initiative 5272 Protection of Life and Family Act to increase penalties for abortion, explicitly ban same-sex marriage, define family as “being a father, a mother and children,” provide that “freedom of conscience and expression” protects people from being “obliged to accept non-heterosexual conduct or practices as normal,” and describe homosexuality as “being contrary to biology and genetics.” That initiative passed first and second readings but its third reading was blocked in September 2018 with no debate since, and a renewed 9 March 2022 congressional approval of Law 5272 to ban same-sex marriage and penalize abortion with 5 years in prison was archived and discarded on 15 March after President Alejandro Giammattei announced a veto as violating the Constitution and international agreements. Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations, except for the 1997 Code on Childhood and Youth safeguarding children and youth from discrimination based on sexual orientation and that of parents, repealed in 2003, with a May 2017 bill to add sexual orientation to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 unadopted. Former President Álvaro Colom supported civil unions, President Jimmy Morales supported the ban proposal stating Guatemala believes in family based in marriage of man and woman, and openly LGBT political representation began with lesbian Deputy Sandra Morán elected January 2016 and gay Deputy Aldo Dávila elected June 2019 on a platform to criminalize hate crimes and hate speech against the LGBT community. A majority of Guatemalans affiliate with the Catholic Church or Pentecostal churches, with most residents members of Catholic, Fundamentalist Pentecostal, or Eastern Orthodox faiths, and attitudes towards LGBT people tend to reflect prevailing religious mores. Those faiths have traditionally upheld socially conservative attitudes and in particular “tend to believe that homosexuality and cross-dressing are signs of immorality,” attitudes also reflected in the dominant political parties while most other parties generally ignore LGBT rights. Despite legality since 1871, negative social attitudes have prevailed with known harassment and even targeted killings of LGBT people, with only one gay bar allowed from 1976 until the late 1990s amid a strong and growing contrast from the rise of the fundamentalist Pentecostal population. Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity are reportedly tolerated by the Government, especially when directed at transgender people, attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles. Late-1990s United Nations and NGO reports documented systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a “social cleansing campaign,” including the 1997 killing of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia in Guatemala City. Since the 1990s the LGBT community has become more visible following refocus on democratization, peace and human rights, with OASIS allowed in 1993 to provide HIV/AIDS education, expanded to LGBT rights after the 1996 end of civil war, and the first gay pride parade held in Guatemala City in 2000. The article documents pre-Spanish Mayan tolerance only for homosexuality involving ritual homosexual acts by shamans and priests, not for transgender people specifically.

GTM.blindSummary:
Consensual, private, non-commercial same-sex sexual activity between adults has been lawful in the country since 1871.

The country provides no legal gender recognition. Since 2016 a person may change a legal name to match gender identity only with judicial permission; legal gender cannot be changed, and a person cannot self-report gender for official documents, which must show the sex and name assigned at birth. The resulting mismatch between presentation and identity documents exposes a trans visitor to scrutiny during identity checks.

The country is bound by the regional human rights court's advisory opinion of 9 January 2018, which holds recognition of gender identity on official documents to be a human right under the regional human rights convention and requires states parties to grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage with all rights deriving from marriage.

Legislative movement on recognition has gone in the opposite direction. A December 2017 bill to recognise the right to gender identity and allow transgender people to change name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by both the legislative points commission and the women's commission, and later proposals for a gender identity law permitting change of official documents have been advocated without enactment.

Initiative No. 5940, received by the legislative directorate on 12 July 2021 and presented to the plenary of the national legislature on 13 September 2021, proposes a law to guarantee the integral protection of children and adolescents against gender identity disorders and was assigned to the human rights, education, science and technology, and governance commissions. Bill 5490, advanced in December 2021, would remove education regarding transgender individuals in schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents from "gender identity disorders" and require censorship of media featuring transgender individuals; it was unanimously approved by the legislature's education, science and technology committee and moved for full legislature review.

National law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations such as cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas. A May 2017 bill to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category remains unadopted, and the penal code's prohibition of discrimination on grounds including gender does not explicitly cover gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. No convictions for discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds were recorded through 2021.

Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of gender identity are reportedly tolerated by the government, particularly where harassment or violence is directed at transgender people, and the absence of hate-crime protection is attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles.

Trans women are held in men's prisons on birth-sex placement. A 2020 report by an international human rights organisation documents that practice and the resulting sexual assault, recording no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice and no court ruling on trans custody. A trans activist with a national trans women's organisation described her time in a men's prison: "Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him." The same reporting flags forced internal displacement of LGBT people from violence.

Conversion practices operate openly, mainly through religiously funded centres in rural areas, and include electroshock therapy, forced marriage and coerced sex; "corrective" rape is prosecuted only as rape and not as a hate crime. Such practices remain normalised, including among mental health professionals.

Documented violence is longstanding. United Nations and NGO reports from the late 1990s recorded systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a social cleansing campaign, including the 1997 gunning down in the largest city of a transgender AIDS activist. Governments in the region have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, and national officials have justified that exclusion by stating that transgender women are not "biological women".

There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples as marriage, civil union or domestic partnership. A civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by a deputy has not been debated since. The Protection of Life and Family initiative (5272), which would increase penalties for abortion, explicitly ban same-sex marriage, define family as "being a father, a mother and children" and describe homosexuality as "being contrary to biology and genetics", passed first and second readings in 2018 with its third reading blocked that September. The legislature approved the law again on 8 March 2022; after the president announced a veto on grounds it violated the constitution and international agreements, the legislature archived and discarded it on 15 March 2022 by 119 votes, leaving its prohibitions without effect.

An opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash against gender recognition in the country and in several neighbouring jurisdictions. In August 2025 the national legislature hosted a meeting on religious freedom, life and family to advance an anti-LGBTIQ agenda, and despite the election of a more progressive government in 2024 the legislature remained predominantly conservative with no significant pro-LGBTIQ initiatives.
GTM.blindOutOfScope:
The country's compliance with the regional human rights court's advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 is not recorded in the available sources, so the gap between the opinion's requirements and practice on document recognition and couple recognition remains unresolved.

The sources carry no trans-specific killing rate for the country and no denominator against which such a figure could be read, so no comparative magnitude of trans homicide risk can be stated. Reported incidents are described qualitatively rather than as rates.

The status of Bill 5490 and Initiative No. 5940 beyond their 2021 committee and plenary stages is not sourced, and whether either was enacted, archived or withdrawn is unresolved.

No sourced material addresses airport or border screening of gender presentation, access to gender-affirming healthcare, or facilities and restroom rules for visitors; these are not covered rather than absent.

Whether the government elected in 2024 altered any policy on gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection is not documented in the inventory.

GTM.tangentialFactors:
Guatemala's social climate reflects its religious composition: a majority of Guatemalans affiliate with the Catholic Church or Pentecostal churches, and these traditions have upheld socially conservative positions, tending to treat homosexuality and cross-dressing as signs of immorality. The same attitudes are reflected in the dominant political parties, while most smaller parties generally ignore LGBT rights.

Openly LGBT political representation began with lesbian Deputy Sandra Morán elected in January 2016 and gay Deputy Aldo Dávila elected in June 2019, both on platforms to criminalise hate crimes and hate speech against the LGBT community. Former President Álvaro Colom supported civil unions, while President Jimmy Morales supported the marriage ban proposal, stating that Guatemala believes in a family based on the marriage of a man and a woman.

The Arcus Foundation reported in May 2024 that the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, with binary-framed opposition generating backlash in all four countries.

Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations, apart from a 1997 Code on Childhood and Youth safeguard that was repealed in 2003; a May 2017 bill to add sexual orientation to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 remains unadopted.

Visibility has grown since the 1990s: OASIS was permitted in 1993 to provide HIV/AIDS education and expanded to LGBT rights after the 1996 end of the civil war, and the first gay pride parade was held in Guatemala City in 2000. Only one gay bar was allowed from 1976 until the late 1990s, against a rising fundamentalist Pentecostal population.

HND.name: Honduras
HND.summary:
Honduran law does not criminalise gender identity, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1899 with the age of consent set at 15 years for both same-sex and heterosexual conduct.

The Penal Code, amended by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility under Article 27. Article 321 punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights, or refuses a professional service, on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of L.50,000 to L.300,000. LGBTQ rights groups met with Congress before the new code took effect to ensure these provisions survived; they did.

The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits police to arrest anyone who 'goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals'. LGBTQ rights organisations have documented numerous instances of police using this provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.

Violence against transgender people is documented and impunity is systemic. Human Rights Watch's May 2009 report 'Not Worth a Penny' documented police rape, assault and extortion of transgender people in Honduras. The LAWG Education Fund report 'Left in the Dark' finds that Honduras has among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, that transgender women especially face major obstacles to justice, and that impunity is driven by under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional case mishandling. The US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among significant human-rights issues. Documented killings include transgender activist Cynthia Nicole shot dead on 2 January 2022 and trans activist Thalia Rodriguez murdered on 10 January 2022 in Tegucigalpa; sixty-nine transgender people were among 174 violent LGBTQ deaths recorded from 2009 to 2014, and 264 LGBTQ people were murdered between 2009 and 2017, with those totals reported as raw counts by year range rather than per-capita rates. In June 2013 a trans woman was granted asylum in Spain after a police officer attempted to assassinate her.

Vicky Hernandez v Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case; Human Rights Watch finds that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks, with Guatemalan officials describing them as 'not biological women'.

Transgender women are held in the men's prison system. Corresponsales Clave, drawing on the torture-prevention centre CPTRT, reports that at Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module beside the mentally-ill unit, that trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women, and that conjugal visits are denied. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair; only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from the men and her belongings returned. Placement operates by birth sex with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy exists. Human Rights Watch (7 October 2020) independently confirms that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, where physical and sexual abuse can follow: a Honduran judge told HRW of a trans woman raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, and said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate. The judge's assessment was that there is no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.

Same-sex unions are not legally recognised. Decree 36 of 4 May 2005 amended Constitution Articles 112 and 116 to provide that only a man and a woman who have that status naturally may contract marriage, to prohibit marriage and de facto union between persons of the same sex, to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages or unions performed legally in other countries, and to bar same-sex couples from adopting. Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A name change for LGBTI persons is approved, though the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association described it as an 'aberration in God's eyes'; no procedure details are given.

The Government offers medical care to all citizens and has worked increasingly with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, but the socially conservative influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestants has made comprehensive public programmes difficult to implement. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups. No youth-specific care or medication provisions appear.

Political hostility is visible. The two major parties have mostly ignored LGBTQ rights; only a handful of dissident members of the Democratic Unification Party expressed interest in working with the LGBT community; and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats. President Juan Orlando Hernández said on 12 October 2018 that personally as a Christian he is against same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association urged President Xiomara Castro to stop 'immoral laws'. At the same time, trans visibility has grown: a trans activist and Asociacion Cozumel Trans co-founder ran for Congress in Francisco Morazan for the PINU party at the 26 November 2017 election, potentially the first openly trans officeholder, receiving 11,112 votes and placing 136th for a 128-seat National Congress; Kendra Stefani Jordany won a 2017 primary, Claudia Spellman ran for LIBRE in 2012, and Victoria Gomez sought asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in San Pedro Sula.

Protection machinery has a contested history. Initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays; the first organisations arose often in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing, and were essentially ignored by the Government apart from police harassment. In 2004 the Government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups despite organised protests from the Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators. International human rights organisations state that the military Government targeted LGBTQ people for harassment, abuse and murder.

Following the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 on access to marriage, Honduran activists filed suit with the Supreme Court in May 2018 to legalise same-sex marriage, while a second case was dismissed in November 2018 for technical errors. A bill for same-sex marriage was presented to the National Congress in May 2022 by Libertad y Refundacion deputy Manuel Rodriguez and remained under discussion as of 24 May 2022.

The only general social-conditions statement available is that there is a social environment of historical discrimination against LGBTQ persons motivated by prejudice and machismo; the sources document no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

HND.blindSummary:
The country's law does not criminalise gender identity, and same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1899 with the age of consent set at 15 years for both same-sex and heterosexual conduct.

The Penal Code, amended by decree in 2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility under Article 27. Article 321 punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights, or refuses a professional service, on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. Article 321-A punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred, contempt, persecution, violence or attacks on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of fifty thousand to three hundred thousand units of national currency. LGBTQ rights groups met with the national legislature before the new code took effect to ensure these provisions survived; they did.

The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits police to arrest anyone who 'goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals'. LGBTQ rights organisations have documented numerous instances of police using this provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.

Violence against transgender people is documented and impunity is systemic. A human rights organisation's May 2009 report documented police rape, assault and extortion of transgender people in the country. An education fund report finds that the country has among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, that transgender women especially face major obstacles to justice, and that impunity is driven by under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional case mishandling. A national human rights report lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among significant human-rights issues. Documented killings include a transgender activist shot dead on 2 January 2022 and a trans activist murdered on 10 January 2022 in the capital; sixty-nine transgender people were among 174 violent LGBTQ deaths recorded from 2009 to 2014, and 264 LGBTQ people were murdered between 2009 and 2017, with those totals reported as raw counts by year range rather than per-capita rates. In June 2013 a trans woman was granted asylum in a neighbouring jurisdiction after a police officer attempted to assassinate her.

A case against the country, heard at the regional human rights court, is the leading transfemicide case; a human rights organisation finds that several states in the region exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks, with officials in a neighbouring jurisdiction describing them as 'not biological women'.

Transgender women are held in the men's prison system. A trans activist's report, drawing on the national torture-prevention centre, reports that at the national penitentiary LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in a single module beside the mentally-ill unit, that trans women are forced to cut their hair and barred from presenting as women, and that conjugal visits are denied. At a second penitentiary authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair; only after torture-prevention centre intervention was she isolated from the men and her belongings returned. Placement operates by birth sex with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy exists. A human rights organisation (7 October 2020) independently confirms that the country places transgender women in men's prisons, where physical and sexual abuse can follow: a judge told the organisation of a trans woman raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, and said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate. The judge's assessment was that there is no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.

Same-sex unions are not legally recognised. A 2005 constitutional decree amended Articles 112 and 116 to provide that only a man and a woman who have that status naturally may contract marriage, to prohibit marriage and de facto union between persons of the same sex, to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages or unions performed legally in other jurisdictions, and to bar same-sex couples from adopting. Same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A name change for LGBTI persons is approved, though the president of a pastors' association in the capital described it as an 'aberration in God's eyes'; no procedure details are given.

The Government offers medical care to all citizens and has worked increasingly with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, but the socially conservative influence of religious institutions has made comprehensive public programmes difficult to implement. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups. No youth-specific care or medication provisions appear.

Political hostility is visible. The two major parties have mostly ignored LGBTQ rights; only a handful of dissident members of one smaller party expressed interest in working with the LGBT community; and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win national legislature seats. The head of state said on 12 October 2018 that personally as a Christian he is against same-sex marriage, and the president of a pastors' association urged the incoming head of state to stop 'immoral laws'. At the same time, trans visibility has grown: a trans activist and co-founder of a trans rights organisation ran for the national legislature in 2017 for a minor party, receiving 11,112 votes and placing 136th for a 128-seat legislature, potentially the first openly trans officeholder; another trans activist won a 2017 primary; a third ran for a different party in 2012; and a fourth sought asylum abroad after threats and attacks in the capital. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in July 2017 in the country's second city.

Protection machinery has a contested history. Initial efforts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays; the first organisations arose often in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing, and were essentially ignored by the Government apart from police harassment. In 2004 the Government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups despite organised protests from religious institutions and conservative legislators. International human rights organisations state that a prior military government targeted LGBTQ people for harassment, abuse and murder.

Following an advisory opinion of the regional human rights court of 9 January 2018 on access to marriage, activists filed suit with the Supreme Court in May 2018 to legalise same-sex marriage, while a second case was dismissed in November 2018 for technical errors. A bill for same-sex marriage was presented to the national legislature in May 2022 by a deputy of a left party and remained under discussion as of 24 May 2022.

The only general social-conditions statement available is that there is a social environment of historical discrimination against LGBTQ persons motivated by prejudice and machismo; the sources document no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

SLV.name: El Salvador
SLV.summary:
El Salvador has no Gender Identity Law and no legal recognition of gender identity. A trans visitor carrying documents issued in another country has no domestic mechanism through which those documents could be aligned or challenged. In 2022 the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court ordered the Name Law reformed so that individuals could change their names to match their gender identity, holding the existing regime unconstitutional because it discriminated on the basis of gender, after a case brought by a transgender activist in 2016. As of 2023 the Legislative Assembly had enacted nothing, so transgender Salvadorans still cannot update official papers.

The penal code carries an enhanced penalty for bias-motivated killing. In September 2015 the National Assembly approved reforms under which homicides motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender draw 30 to 60 years under Article 129. A 2015 hate crime law added sexual orientation and gender identity provisions to the Criminal Code, carrying three to six years' imprisonment. A 2018 Institutional Policy for the Care of the LGBT Population allows LGBT people to file legal complaints against discrimination.

Human Rights Watch reported in 2020 and 2021 that El Salvador, with Guatemala and Honduras, fails to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, driving asylum claims to the United States; the reports document obstacles to obtaining protection. Police have shown blatant refusal to cooperate in LGBT death investigations. About 500 hate crimes against LGBT people were reported between 1998 and 2015, with many unreported. Gang violence includes targeting of LGBT people through physical and sexual assault, forced recruitment, and extortion for safety.

The death of Camila Díaz Córdova, a transgender Salvadoran woman, was prosecuted as a hate crime; activists called it an advance toward El Salvador's first hate-crime homicide conviction. On 28 July 2020 a San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of the January 2019 killing and sentenced each to 20 years, the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for killing a transgender person.

Since the state of exception began in March 2022, trans women arbitrarily captured in mass raids have been held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. Jennifer, arrested on 14 April 2022 in San Salvador, was held first at the El Penalito police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman, Rosa, for outdoor punishment drills while handcuffed and forced to squat in the sun, and denied her access to an HIV clinic; a judge freed her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported, while Rosa remains imprisoned. Socorro Jurídico Humanista and Cristosal link the abuse to the absence of a Gender Identity Law.

Prison conditions are explicitly hostile: homosexual inmates are strictly forbidden from dressing or behaving in an effeminate manner, and men are targeted by police officers, soldiers and prison guards for effeminate behaviour or dress through unwarranted searches, theft of property, sexual assault and other physical violence. In the 1999 investigation of Doris and Maricela, the two transvestites were forced to wear men's clothing for their hearing.

Hospital specialists frequently dismiss trans patients' problems as a side effect of being transgender, and patients are sometimes made to wait longer or denied care. Transgender health care access is severely restricted: there is a lack of protocols and programmes for hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery, and one study found that many trans women did not seek medical help after suffering side effects from surgeries, having learned not to trust the system. In April 2009 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance published guidelines banning discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services, and a 2009 national HIV/AIDS health plan included a prohibition on sexual orientation-based discrimination in health care.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised: the Family Code's Article 11 defines marriage as a heterosexual union, individuals may adopt but same-sex couples cannot adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence does not apply to same-sex couples. Since 2006 there have been proposals to amend the Constitution to restrict recognition even of same-sex couples married legally abroad. Two legal challenges to the ban were dismissed on technical and procedural grounds on 20 December 2016 and 17 January 2019, although the Constitutional Court declared a proposed marriage ban unlawful in January 2018 and admitted a lawsuit for recognition of same-sex marriage for a hearing in August 2019, following a January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holding same-sex marriage to be a human right.

A 2013 study showed that 62 per cent of Salvadorans do not accept homosexuality and 85 per cent believe it acceptable to attack a transgender individual on the basis of their identity. A 2010 poll showed 10 per cent support for legalising same-sex marriage, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 19 per cent support.
SLV.outOfScopeNotes: The 2022 Supreme Court order on the Name Law is unresolved: the Legislative Assembly had taken no action as of 2023, and no later enactment is sourced here. The lawsuit for recognition of same-sex marriage admitted for a hearing in August 2019 has no sourced outcome. The proposals since 2006 to amend the Constitution to restrict recognition of same-sex couples married abroad are not sourced as enacted. The 'Denied deaths' dataset's homicide figures for 2000-2020 are not itemised in this record. Whether the 2015 hate-crime penalty framework has produced convictions beyond the Camila Díaz Córdova case is not sourced.

sources.summary: El Salvador's Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court ordered in 2022 that the Name Law be reformed to allow individuals to change their names to match their gender identity, holding the existing laws unconstitutional because they discriminated on the basis of gender; the case originated in a 2016 lawsuit by a transgender activist. As of 2023 the Legislative Assembly had taken no action to guarantee changes of name and gender in legal documents, so transgender Salvadorans still cannot update official papers. Same-sex marriage is not recognized: the Family Code's Article 11 defines marriage as a heterosexual union, individuals may adopt but same-sex couples cannot adopt as a couple, and the Law on Family Violence does not apply to same-sex couples. Prison conditions are explicitly hostile: homosexual inmates are strictly forbidden from dressing or behaving in an effeminate manner, and men are targeted by police officers, soldiers, and prison guards for effeminate behavior or dress through unwarranted searches, theft of property, sexual assault, and other physical violence. In the 1999 investigation of Doris and Maricela, the two transvestites were forced to wear men's clothing for their hearing. Hospital specialists frequently dismiss trans patients' problems as a side effect of being transgender, and patients are sometimes made to wait longer or denied care, though this can be done discreetly. Transgender health care access is severely restricted: there is a lack of protocols and programs for hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery, and one study found that many trans women did not seek medical help after suffering side effects from surgeries, having learned not to trust the system. For LGBT people in general, even when individuals reach out for psychological care they feel insecure and report prejudice, and such care often arrives in the form of conversion therapies, frequently deployed by parents attempting to change a child's sexual orientation; LGBT community members experience suicide ideation and attempts at higher rates than the general population. In April 2009 the Ministry of Public Health and Social Assistance published guidelines banning discrimination against LGBT and HIV-positive people in health services, a 2009 national HIV/AIDS health plan included a prohibition on sexual orientation-based discrimination in health care, and since 2005 a national HIV/AIDS policy has developed with the first National HIV testing day established in 2007. Gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood, though policy prohibits those who 'engage in risky behaviours' from donating. Same-sex marriage is not legal, and since 2006 there have been proposals to amend the Constitution to restrict recognition even of same-sex couples married legally abroad. Two legal challenges to the ban were dismissed by the courts on technical and procedural grounds (20 December 2016 and 17 January 2019), although the Constitutional Court declared a proposed marriage ban unlawful in January 2018 and admitted a lawsuit for recognition of same-sex marriage for a hearing in August 2019, following a January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion holding same-sex marriage to be a human right. A 2010 poll showed only 10% support for legalizing same-sex marriage, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 19% support. Sexuality is absent from school curriculum, in line with societal expectations, which leads many LGBT students to remain invisible in school to avoid discrimination; LGBT students, particularly those whose gender expression does not match that assigned at birth, drop out of school at high rates, and some LGBT students have been expelled outright for their sexuality and identity. No known universities or graduate programs offer Sexuality Studies programs; academic publications exist, most from the University of El Salvador, often from psychological or legal science perspectives, but with varying levels of support within them. Where LGBT children do come out, families may subject them to conversion therapy or family prayers to convert them to heterosexuality, and when these methods fail, families sometimes expel the child from the home and sever all connections. Young Salvadoran homosexuals now encourage older homosexuals to come out, and globalization is slowly changing the young LGBT community, though it still faces heavy unacceptance. A 2013 study showed that 62% of Salvadorans do not accept homosexuality and 85% believe it acceptable to attack a transgender individual on the basis of their identity, and El Salvador is described as one of the most socially-homophobic countries in Latin America. Over 50% identify as actively practicing Catholics, many of the rest attend evangelical churches, and church leaders have organized opposition to LGBT rights legislation; an embedded machismo culture holds that being Salvadoran means being virile, heterosexuals are described as afraid of defending or befriending gay people for fear of stigma and of being accused of being gay themselves, and being 'gay friendly' is seen as against nature, anti-religious, and anti-masculine. About 500 hate crimes against LGBTQ people were reported between 1998 and 2015 (with many unreported), police have shown blatant refusal to cooperate in LGBT death investigations, and gang violence includes targeting of LGBT people through physical and sexual assault, forced recruitment, and 'taxing' for safety; on 28 July 2020 a San Salvador judge convicted three police officers of killing transgender woman Camila Díaz Córdova, sentencing them to 20 years each. Entre Amigos organized El Salvador's first Gay Pride Parade in June 1997 to commemorate the massacre of trans women in the 1980s and it continues today, San Salvador authorized permanent rainbow paintings at several crossroads in July 2017, a 2015 hate crime law added sexual orientation and gender identity provisions to the Criminal Code (three to six years imprisonment), and a 2018 Institutional Policy for the Care of the LGBT Population allows LGBT people to file legal complaints against discrimination.

An international human-rights organisation's report (7 Oct 2020): this nation (with two neighbouring nations) fails to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, driving asylum claims abroad; documents obstacles to obtaining protection.

An international human-rights organisation's report (Jan 2021): violence and discrimination against LGBT people in this country — full report with recommendations to the president, the top government lawyer, the elected legislature and ministries.

An international human-rights organisation (31 Jul 2020): a judge in the capital found three police officers guilty of the January 2019 killing of a transgender woman and sentenced each to 20 years; the 28 July 2020 judgment is the first homicide conviction in this country for killing a transgender person, hailed as pivotal for transgender residents' rights.

A news report (9 Sep 2015): the elected legislature approved legal-code reforms so killings motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender draw 30-60 years — the enhanced hate-crime penalty framework on the books since.

An investigative report (26 Feb 2024): since the exceptional security regime began (Mar 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. Sexuality is absent from the school curriculum, LGBT students drop out at high rates, and some have been expelled for their sexuality and identity; no known universities or graduate programmes offer sexuality studies. Where LGBT children come out, families may subject them to conversion therapy or family prayers, and when these fail families sometimes expel the child and sever all connections. LGBT community members report suicide ideation and attempts at higher rates than the general population, and psychological care is often experienced as insecure and prejudiced, frequently arriving as conversion therapy.

A national HIV/AIDS policy has developed since 2005, with the first national HIV testing day established in 2007; gay and bisexual men are allowed to donate blood, though policy prohibits those who engage in risky behaviours from donating. A local organisation organised the country's first gay pride parade in June 1997 to commemorate the massacre of trans women in the 1980s, and the capital authorised permanent rainbow paintings at several crossroads in July 2017.

CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal in Costa Rica since 1971. The country adopted marriage equality in 2020, the first state in Central America to do so. Outright International and the ILGA World Database record the resulting legal framework covering conduct, gender recognition and legal protections.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than judicial. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, allows a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. Since May 2018, name changes on official identification are available through a simple, free procedure at the Tribunal Supremo de Elecciones. From 2013 until then, transgender people could change their legal name only by judicial order. A 2016 bill that would have allowed change of both name and gender without surgery or judicial permission was not adopted.

The state health system funds gender-affirming care. The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation, while raising concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people. She recommended intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

No explicit visa or entry policy targeting LGBTQ travellers appears in current law. In December 2018, President Carlos Alvarado Quesada signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples.

In 2020 the Legislative Assembly strengthened hate-crime penalties. Penal Code article 112 provides up to 20 to 35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation; article 380 provides 1 to 3 years for exclusion or segregation on that basis; article 386bis provides 3 to 10 years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion or blackmail on that basis.

Official posture has been supportive. The government recognised the International Day Against Homophobia on 17 May from 2008, when President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to support activities aimed at eradicating homophobia. President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial in May 2014. In 2018 President Alvarado issued a public apology for past state persecution, citing persecutions, raids, arbitrary arrests and beatings. In June 2019 he became the first Costa Rican president to march in the San José pride parade, which drew about 100,000 participants.

There is countervailing pressure. A conversion-therapy bill has been stalled since its 2019 committee report. In 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education programme and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.

Police harassment and raids of LGBTQ people and private establishments were formerly commonplace while same-sex conduct was technically legal. In 2000 the Supreme Court ruled that a gay sauna must remain open, holding that subjective criteria of morality and proper behaviour have no legal basis and violate constitutional rights.
CRI.outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the 2016 gender-recognition bill beyond its failure to be adopted is not sourced.

Enforcement of the 2020 hate-crime provisions is not documented in the available sources.

No source in the inventory documents border or airport screening practices specific to trans travellers.

The 1990 consular visa instruction is historical; no source indicates whether any comparable practice exists now.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Costa Rica has demonstrated supportive expression rights for LGBTQ people. President Luis Guillermo Solis placed a rainbow flag in the Presidential House on 15 May 2014, and President Carlos Alvarado Quesada became the first Costa Rican President to march at the annual gay pride parade in San José in June 2019, an event that drew about 100,000 participants. In 2018, President Alvarado issued a public apology to the LGBT community for past state persecution, citing state "promoted and executed persecutions, raids, arbitrary arrests and beatings." The President designated 17 May as the National Day Against Homophobia by executive order in 2008. No explicit visa or entry policy targeting LGBTQ travelers appears in current law; in December 2018, President Alvarado signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples. The historical finding is the 1990 incident when the Minister of the Interior instructed Costa Rican consulates not to grant visas to women travelling unaccompanied by men, warning all such women would be stopped at the airport, in an attempt to block foreign lesbians from attending an international meeting; this policy is decades old and not described as current. The Supreme Court ruled in 2000 that a gay sauna must remain open, holding that "subjective criteria of morality and proper behaviour have no legal basis" and violate constitutional rights. In 2011, the Supreme Court reversed its 2008 ruling and now allows same-sex couples equal access to conjugal visits in prison. Police harassment and raids of LGBTQ people and private establishments were "formerly commonplace" while homosexuality was technically legal. In 2020, the Legislative Assembly strengthened hate crime penalties: up to 20–35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation (amending article 112 of the Penal Code), 1–3 years for exclusion or segregation based on sexual orientation (article 380), and 3–10 years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion, or blackmail based on sexual orientation (article 386bis). In 1993, Universidad Internacional de las Américas was found to have a policy of expelling LGBTQ students and firing LGBTQ faculty and staff; when the Ministry of Education was informed, it said the policy would likely violate constitutional articles 20, 33, and 70 if enforced. Comprehensive sex education campaigns are described as "almost nonexistent" in Costa Rican public high schools due to opposition from the Catholic Church and other religious groups. LGBTQ rights remain a major political flashpoint affecting young people: the 2018 general election was sharply divisive over same-sex marriage, and a 2012 poll found 60% of 18–34-year-olds supported equal rights for same-sex couples. A 2016 bill to allow transgender people to change name and gender without surgery or judicial permission was unsuccessful; since 2013 transgender people can change legal name with a judicial order, and since May 2018 name changes on official IDs are permitted through a simple, free procedure by the TSE.

PAN.name: Panama
PAN.summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Panama, and the sources reviewed record no criminal provision directed at transgender people.

Legal gender recognition is available but requires surgery, and no nonbinary recognition exists.

No Panamanian statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The National Assembly blocked an amendment to the general anti-discrimination law in 2024, with the block defended on the argument that the existing text already covers the ground implicitly. A 2015 bill to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity has not advanced. No act is recognised as a hate crime, so violence motivated by a victim's gender identity or orientation is not charged or recorded as such.

At the 2025 Universal Periodic Review, multiple states urged Panama to adopt explicit anti-discrimination protections, reform gender recognition, and strengthen safeguards against violence. The reforms remain stalled, and Panama's legal position lags much of Latin America.

Partner recognition is closed. Article 40 of the Code of Private International Law, approved on 8 May 2014, states that same-sex marriages are strictly prohibited and that foreign same-sex marriages will not be recognised. The Supreme Court ruled on 27 March 2023, after a seven-year delay, that the constitution confers no positive right to same-sex marriage. A constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman was approved by the National Assembly on 29 October 2019 and withdrawn before the referendum following public protests. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Panamanian law has no route to recognition, and no civil-union alternative is in force.

Public opinion data: a 2017 survey found 78% of Panamanians opposed to same-sex marriage; AmericasBarometer in 2023 recorded 12% approval, ranking Panama 18th of 22 countries surveyed in the Americas.

In the indigenous territory of Guna Yala, an Omeggid third-gender community is described as accepted as completely normal, with matriarchal figures holding elevated status. That is one local data point on how gender diversity is received; it does not describe the country as a whole.
PAN.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document how Panamanian border or immigration officers handle a passport whose gender marker differs from the holder's presentation, and no record of screening, secondary inspection or detention on that basis was located, nor any documented pattern of police targeting transgender people. The absence of a documented practice is not evidence that none occurs.

No Panamanian statute governing bathroom, changing-room or other single-sex facility access by gender identity was located in the sources reviewed.

The practical effect of the surgery requirement on a resident's ability to obtain a corrected identity document, and the processing time involved, are not sourced.

Whether the 2024 blocked anti-discrimination amendment will be reintroduced, and whether the 2023 Supreme Court ruling leaves any pending marriage case alive, are unresolved.

DOM.name: Dominican Republic
DOM.summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the last surviving sodomy provisions is concluded, and the criminal code as it now stands contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct. Those provisions reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no corresponding offence for heterosexual acts. Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy guarantees.

Policing of same-sex affection has run through public-order law rather than a sodomy statute. A former provision criminalising acts that violated "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for displays of affection; it was repealed by a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code. In 2006 several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo were shut down as part of a police harassment programme. In 2012 police broke up the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride parade and arrested marchers on the ground that they were improperly using the national flag. Visible, politically active LGBTQ signage is frequently a target of government crackdowns, at times with the support of religious leaders.

Transgender people cannot change their legal gender or name on identity documents. In June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree allowing 35 transgender Dominicans to change their legal name to match their gender identity; television journalist Mía Cepeda was among the 35 and subsequently changed her name. No standing procedure for legal gender recognition exists. A 2017 ILGA poll found 5% of Dominicans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

Family law recognises no legal status between persons of the same sex, neither marriage nor a civil or domestic partnership. Article 55, added by the 2010 constitutional amendment, provides that the State promotes and protects family organisation based on marriage between a man and a woman, constitutionally barring same-sex marriage; households headed by such couples are excluded from the rights granted to married opposite-sex couples. Article 41 of Law 544-14 on private international law could justify recognition, since a marriage is valid if the law of the place of celebration, or the national law or domicile of at least one spouse, treats it as such. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples accession to all existing domestic family registration systems, including marriage, and several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it. A trans visitor in a relationship that Dominican law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls outside this framework, whatever the couple's own documents record.

Access to health care is a constitutional right, but health programmes for the LGBTQ community have generally concentrated on HIV/AIDS education and are largely run by non-governmental organisations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos. Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services or public accommodations. The one sector-specific provision is Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS, in force since 2011, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.

The socially conservative mores of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations carry significant weight in public policy and in prevailing attitudes. The major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. A 2017 ILGA poll found 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals.
DOM.outOfScopeNotes:
The Universal Periodic Review record shows the Dominican Republic accepted recommendations on the rights of intersex persons and on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. No domestic implementing measure for those commitments appears in the sources reviewed.

Whether Article 41 of Law 544-14 is applied by Dominican registries or courts to recognise a marriage validly celebrated abroad is not established in the sources, and it stands against the constitutional bar in Article 55.

Implementation of the January 2018 Inter-American Court advisory opinion remains unresolved: legal experts say the country must apply it, but no legislation or judgment giving effect to it is sourced.

The inventory contains no hate-crime provision, no sentencing enhancement, and no documented enforcement data for offences against transgender people; whether such protections exist is not established by the sources reviewed.
