CAN.name: Canada
CAN.summary:
Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act, and both are listed among the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code. Bill C-16 added them; the Senate passed the bill 67-11 in June 2017.

Discrimination complaints in areas of provincial responsibility run through provincial human rights codes. Ontario's code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission publishes a policy setting out the legislation and case law governing complaints under it, so a visitor or resident in Ontario has a documented route to recourse.

Changing the gender marker on official documents is a provincial function. Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the previous surgery requirement and substituted a declaration of the person's identified gender supported by a doctor's letter.
CAN.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventoried sources do not set out the federal procedure for changing a gender marker on national identity documents, nor entry, visa or border-screening rules bearing on trans travellers. No trans-specific border or screening practice is documented here.

Two publications are recorded without their findings: Egale Canada's analysis of 2024 police-reported hate-crime data affecting 2SLGBTQI people, and the survey findings of the federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan, released as quick statistics.

The national hate-crime series is not disaggregated by gender identity in the material available, so the level of anti-trans hate crime in Canada is unresolved. Prince Edward Island is the only province whose document-change procedure appears in these sources; other provinces' requirements are not sourced.

sources.summary: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026): police-reported hate crime totalled 4,882 incidents in 2024 (+1% after a 34% jump in 2022-23); incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, down from a 2023 peak of 889 — three consecutive years of increases ended.

The federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings were presented as quick stats.

Egale Canada UPR submission (2012): overview of LGBT human rights in Canada - sexual orientation in the Charter since 1995, marriage equality 2005; but trans protections limited and varying by jurisdiction, with no federal gender-identity discrimination law at the time; identifies gaps against the Yogyakarta Principles.

CBC News (Apr 2016): Prince Edward Island amended its Vital Statistics Act so a trans person changes the gender on official documents by declaring their identified gender plus a doctor's letter — the prior surgery requirement removed. A practical document-update pathway in one province.

The Globe and Mail (Jun 2017): the Senate passed Bill C-16 by 67-11, prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression and adding gender identity/expression to the Criminal Code hate-motivation provisions — framed as Canadian leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash.

Ontario Human Rights Commission policy (Part I): lays out the legal context, case law and legislation for sexual-orientation discrimination complaints under the Ontario Human Rights Code, which expressly covers gender identity and gender expression — official Ontario guidance a visitor/resident can invoke for discrimination recourse.

A 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners; a 2022 CTV report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault. AUS.name: Australia
AUS.summary:
Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that the protection extends to trans women as women and awarded damages against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member; Reuters reported the ruling as a landmark for gender-identity discrimination. A person excluded from a service on the basis of gender identity has a federal remedy, and damages have been awarded in practice.

Federal hate-crime legislation passed in February 2025 (Act 1 of 2025, effective immediately) covers sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status, with penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment. Victoria's Anti-vilification Act 2025 carries the same grounds and takes effect on 30 June 2026. Coverage outside that federal layer is uneven: New South Wales, the ACT and Victoria reach sexual orientation only, South Australia, Tasmania and Queensland include gender identity, and the Northern Territory and Western Australia cover neither. No charging or prosecution data for any of these provisions appears in the sources reviewed.

An ANROWS research briefing on threats to trans and gender-diverse rights in Australia records organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over facilities and over access to official records, and rights-rollback pressure. Facilities and records access are the documented points of friction.

Health care: Medicare covers many major sex reassignment surgeries, but the gap between the benefit and the surgeon's fee can run to thousands of dollars, and private hospital policies or insurers typically impose a waiting period of about 12 months before claims for surgery. Since November 2017 a trans child can obtain puberty blockers and hormone treatment without court approval where the child, parents and doctors agree; blockers are treated as a first, reversible stage from around age 10 and hormone therapy as a second, irreversible stage usually from 16, with surgery generally unavailable before 18.

NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.summary:
New Zealand's legal framework for trans people rests on statutory self-declaration. The Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 2021 eased correction of sex markers on identity documents, and the Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022 makes conversion practices unlawful. Marriage equality has been in place since 2013, so a trans visitor's marriage or partnership is recognised on the same terms as any other. Whether the Human Rights Act 1993 protects transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics is not settled: the New Zealand Law Commission's Issues Paper 53, 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024), is a consultation reviewing the Act's coverage of those groups.

Police-recorded hostility has risen. Data released under the Official Information Act and reported by RNZ on 17 April 2024 records 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023, against 161 in 2022, a rise of 42%. Police say the figure likely understates the true level of anti-trans hate. The same dataset shows a spike in March 2023, the month anti-trans activist Posie Parker visited New Zealand.

Survey evidence provides the first population-level picture of violence. The Counting Ourselves survey, reported by RNZ on 27 February 2025, found that almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders had been threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the previous four years, and that 8% had experienced deliberate physical violence.

A mid-2024 community-safety assessment, published as opinion in The Spinoff on 2 July 2024, describes a worsening street climate: a spate of rainbow event cancellations and a 2023 protest around Posie Parker's visit prompted calls for more security for rainbow communities. The same piece names the 2021 registration act and the 2022 conversion practices ban as statutory gains.
NZL.outOfScopeNotes:
No placement rule for incarcerated trans people is described in the sources consulted: whether housing follows birth-sex status or gender identity, and whether a special unit or segregation practice exists, are not addressed.

The scope of Human Rights Act 1993 protection for transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics remains unresolved pending the Law Commission's review.

The hate-incident count is a police-reported figure that police themselves describe as an undercount, so the true number is not established. The Counting Ourselves figures are self-reported and cover a four-year recall period.

No source in the inventory addresses border screening, document-marker flagging at entry, or airport screening practice for trans travellers arriving in New Zealand.

ALB.name: Albania
ALB.summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. The criminal code carried a ten-year prison sentence for homosexual conduct until 1995, and no equivalent provision has been reinstated.

The operative instrument is the comprehensive anti-discrimination law in force from 4 February 2010, which covers sexual orientation in employment, goods and services, education, housing and health care. In October 2020 it was expanded to prohibit discrimination on the grounds of sex characteristics and HIV status.

On 4 May 2013 the Albanian Parliament amended the criminal code to place hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity on the same footing as offences motivated by race, ethnicity, religion and disability. In the same session it passed a law punishing dissemination of homophobic information through any means, including the internet, by a fine and up to two years' imprisonment.

Enforcement of the protection machinery has been uneven. In December 2010 the Deputy Commissioner for Labour, Social Affairs and Health, Tritan Shehu, said publicly that medical staff should treat homosexuality as a hormonal and psychological disorder. The Commissioner for Protection from Discrimination reprimanded him on 30 September 2011, after a lengthy delay and after LGBT groups had already lost trust in the body over slow, bureaucratically impeded investigations.

In 2016 members of parliament removed sexual orientation and gender identity from Article 18 of the Constitution at the last moment, under pressure from faith-based leaders and contrary to earlier promises. PINK Embassy condemned the removal on 20 July 2016.

Albania recognises neither marriage nor civil unions for same-sex couples in any form, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to different-sex households. MKD.name: North Macedonia
MKD.summary:
North Macedonia imposes no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct or for being transgender. Sex between people of the same sex was criminalised until 1996, when decriminalisation was adopted as a condition of Council of Europe membership.

The Law on Prevention of and Protection against Discrimination, adopted in March 2019 with 52 votes in favour and three abstentions, took effect on 22 May 2019 and covered gender identity. The Constitutional Court struck it down on 14 May 2020 on procedural grounds, and Parliament passed a replacement bill on 27 October 2020. The 2019 amendments to the Criminal Code explicitly list sexual orientation and gender identity in the section regulating hate speech, and the constitution and law prohibit discrimination on those grounds in access to government services including health care. The 2019 US State Department human rights report found the government enforced those provisions.

Legal gender recognition is the central unresolved gap for a trans visitor carrying identity documents. In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights held that requiring sex reassignment surgery before a gender marker on identification documents could be changed violated the applicant's private life, found a violation of the right of appeal, and awarded 9,000 euros in damages. Non-governmental organisations report that the government still fails to recognise gender identity changes in identification documents. In 2023 the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry, which contained the legal gender recognition chapter, one day before Parliamentary Committee review.

Marriage and partner recognition are closed. Family law defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman, and same-sex couples and households headed by them have no access to the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. In 2014 the government submitted a constitutional motion to define marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman, ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption. In January 2015 Parliament approved a constitutional amendment to that effect, together with a requirement that marriage, family and civil unions be regulated only by a two-thirds majority, by 72 votes to 4; the final session did not conclude and the amendment failed. An earlier attempt in September 2013 also failed to reach the required two-thirds majority.

Hate speech remained serious in 2023, with numerous reports and no meaningful state response; the European Commission's country report concurs. In September the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years' imprisonment for assaulting an LGBTI activist, applying the Criminal Code's sexual orientation and gender identity aggravating grounds. The 2019 US State Department report deemed the Skopje public prosecutor ineffective in processing hate speech cases.

On 29 June 2019, during the first Skopje Pride, about 20 people chased seven activists down the street, pulled them from a taxi and beat activist Bekim Asani, threatening to kill him and the others; police arrested the assailants and opened a criminal investigation. The same 2019 report documents fellow students verbally and physically attacking a gay high school student and breaking his nose, which he reported to the principal but not to police. Civil-society monitoring in 2019 recorded violence against LGBTI people, including a verbal assault by a police officer, and noted that most such violence is never reported to police or other institutions, so no reliable rate of violence can be established.

Societal hostility is long-standing and, where measured, severe. A 2002 survey by the Center for Civil and Human Rights found more than 80 percent of respondents viewed homosexuality as a psychiatric disorder that endangered families and about 65 percent considered it a crime warranting a jail term; the same survey found women and rural inhabitants somewhat more liberal. The 2019 US State Department report states that the LGBTQ community is still prejudiced and harassed by society, the media and the authorities, and that the first Pride Parade in June 2019 triggered hate speech on social media. The report also records many reports of public humiliations, worker firings and homosexual teenagers being cast onto the streets after their sexual orientation was revealed.

Official hostility extends to municipal level. In June 2023 the mayor of Strumica, Kostadin Kostadinov, nullified all memoranda with LGBTQ organisations and vowed to veto future ones.

Comparative rankings place the country among the weaker performers in Europe. In 2019 it was ranked the tenth worst European country for LGBTQ tourists. In 2024 ILGA-Europe ranked North Macedonia 31st out of 48 European countries for LGBTI rights legislation.

Trans-specific civil society exists and is visible. TransFormA held a March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje to mark the Transgender Day of Visibility under the slogan "we march bravely", and reported a trend of religious institutions being mobilised to scapegoat the country's small trans population. EGAL works on gay and lesbian health issues, and the LGBTI Support Center in Skopje, a subsidiary of the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, offers free legal aid.
MKD.outOfScopeNotes:
No current, trans-specific measurement of societal tolerance was identified. The only attitudinal survey in the inventory dates from 2002, and the available tolerance findings address homosexuality or LGBTI people generally rather than transgender people specifically.

Implementation of the January 2019 European Court of Human Rights judgment is disputed. The Court found a violation and ordered damages, while non-governmental organisations report that gender identity changes are still not recognised in identification documents; no administrative procedure giving effect to the judgment is documented in the inventory.

Enforcement findings rest largely on the 2019 US State Department report, including its assessment that the Skopje public prosecutor was ineffective on hate speech cases; more recent systematic enforcement data are not in the inventory.

No reliable rate of violence against trans or LGBTI people is available. Civil-society monitoring for 2019 records documented incidents and states that most violence goes unreported, so the true incidence is unresolved.

A 2002 survey by a civil and human rights centre found more than 80 percent of respondents viewed homosexuality as a psychiatric disorder that endangered families and about 65 percent considered it a crime warranting a jail term; the same survey found women and rural inhabitants somewhat more liberal. A national government's 2019 human rights report states that the LGBTQ community is still prejudiced and harassed by society, the media and the authorities, and that the first Pride Parade in June 2019 triggered hate speech on social media. The report also records many reports of public humiliations, worker firings and homosexual teenagers being cast onto the streets after their sexual orientation was revealed.

Official hostility extends to municipal level. In June 2023 a municipal mayor nullified all memoranda with LGBTQ organisations and vowed to veto future ones.

Comparative rankings place the country among the weaker performers in the region. In 2019 it was ranked the tenth worst country in the region for LGBTQ tourists. In 2024 a regional rights organisation ranked the country 31st out of 48 countries in the region for LGBTI rights legislation.

Trans-specific civil society exists and is visible. A trans rights organisation held a March for Visibility of Trans People in the capital to mark the Transgender Day of Visibility under the slogan "we march bravely", and reported a trend of religious institutions being mobilised to scapegoat the country's small trans population. A health organisation works on gay and lesbian health issues, and a legal-aid centre in the capital, a subsidiary of a human rights committee, offers free legal aid.

No current, trans-specific measurement of societal tolerance was identified. The only attitudinal survey in the inventory dates from 2002, and the available tolerance findings address homosexuality or LGBTI people generally rather than transgender people specifically.

Implementation of the January 2019 regional human rights court judgment is disputed. The court found a violation and ordered damages, while non-governmental organisations report that gender identity changes are still not recognised in identification documents; no administrative procedure giving effect to the judgment is documented in the inventory.

Enforcement findings rest largely on a 2019 national government human rights report, including its assessment that the capital's public prosecutor was ineffective on hate speech cases; more recent systematic enforcement data are not in the inventory.

No reliable rate of violence against trans or LGBTI people is available. Civil-society monitoring for 2019 records documented incidents and states that most violence goes unreported, so the true incidence is unresolved.

MNE.name: Montenegro
MNE.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1977, with an equal age of consent of 14, and the prohibition has not been restored. A trans visitor faces no legal exposure for being trans or for presenting gender non-conformingly in public.

The Law on Prohibition of Discrimination, passed on 27 July 2010, lists gender identity as a prohibited ground and reaches employment, the provision of goods and services, education and health services. Criminal Code amendments adopted in 2013 and in force from 3 June 2014 prohibit hate speech based on gender identity and provide penalty enhancements where an offence is committed because of the victim's LGBT status, gender identity included.

Those enhancements are applied unevenly. The European Commission has found that prosecutors bring misdemeanour charges where hate-crime proceedings are warranted, which limits the sentencing uplift the Criminal Code provides.

No legal gender recognition statute based on self-determination exists. Change of legal gender requires a medical diagnosis, sex reassignment surgery and sterilisation, and divorce where the applicant is married. A draft Law on Legal Recognition of Gender Identity based on self-determination completed its legislative steps and consultations but was not adopted; the 2024 deadline set under the EU accession programme passed, and the law remained unadopted as of November 2025. The practical effect for a visitor is documentary: there is no administrative procedure in the country that will issue a record in an acquired gender.

The Constitution bars same-sex marriage, and households headed by same-sex couples do not receive the protections attached to opposite-sex marriage. Since 15 July 2021 same-sex couples may register a Life Partnership, approved by parliament on 1 July 2020 by 42 votes to 5, signed on 3 July 2020 and published on 7 July 2020, which carries almost all the rights of marriage except adoption, foster care and parenting. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under the country's birth-sex-based rules can have that relationship recognised only through a registration made before a registrar in the country.

Public visibility has drawn organised hostility alongside state protection. The first Pride march in Podgorica in 2013 put roughly 150 marchers on the street under a guard of some 2,000 police; opponents threw rocks and were dispersed with tear gas. The 2011 Pride had been cancelled after two attacks on gay people in the capital.

Official hostility has not disappeared. Anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric continued through 2023. In the same period a psychologist who appeared on television in gender-non-conforming clothes was subjected to hate comments, threats and several physical attacks, and the police response was monitored by the organisation recording the case. Over 222 online hate-speech incidents were reported.

A 2018 study by the ERA Western Balkans office found that 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted, a measure of how much hostility is absorbed privately rather than reported.
MNE.outOfScopeNotes:
No source records how border officers or police handle a trans traveller's documents, and no screening or marker-flagging practice at Montenegrin border points is documented.

Whether a foreign gender recognition certificate is accepted for any administrative purpose in Montenegro is not addressed in the sources.

The figure of over 222 online hate-speech incidents is a count of reports, not a rate; no denominator is published.

The outcome of police monitoring of the attacks on the television psychologist is not recorded.

Whether Life Partnership registration is open to non-residents is not stated in the sources.

Incident reporting is not disaggregated for trans people, so no trans-specific violence rate with a comparable denominator is available.

BIH.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
BIH.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina removed it from its criminal code in 1996 and Republika Srpska followed in 1998, each through its own entity-level code, so a trans visitor carries no legal exposure on that basis. The age of consent is 14 years, applied equally regardless of gender or sexual orientation, with sex below that age treated as statutory rape.

State-level anti-discrimination protection is explicit. The Anti-Discrimination Law adopted in 2016 bans discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; the 2009 Law Against Discrimination had covered sexual orientation and gender expression but omitted gender identity as originally intended. The Sarajevo Open Centre presented the 2016 amendments together with the Agency for Gender Equality after public consultations in late 2015.

Bias-motivated offences carry sentencing enhancement at entity level. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina amended its Criminal Code in April 2016 to name sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances, published on 15 June 2016; Republika Srpska and Brčko District already had comparable provisions.

Public assembly has drawn organised violence. The Queer Sarajevo Festival in 2008 was stormed by football fans and religious extremists shouting death threats; eight people, including a police officer, were injured, and in 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled that the authorities had failed to protect participants' freedom of assembly. In February 2014 Sarajevo Pride organisers were violently attacked even though they had arranged security with police about three weeks earlier, and Human Rights Watch called for prosecution of the attackers. The first BiH Pride March was held in Sarajevo on 9 September 2019 with an estimated 2,000 marchers. In March 2023 police in Banja Luka cancelled LGBTQ film screenings citing security concerns, and activists were chased and attacked afterwards.

Social attitudes recorded in surveys are hostile. A 2015 survey found 48% of respondents would try to "cure" a child who came out as gay and 16% would stop communicating with that child; 19% supported granting same-sex couples some marriage-associated rights. A 2017 Pew poll found 13% support for same-sex marriage and 84% opposed.

No legal recognition of same-sex couples exists at national or entity level. The Constitution is silent on gender eligibility for marriage, both entities' family codes limit marriage to opposite-sex couples, and households of same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections as opposite-sex households. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has no route to partner recognition. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted a request to legalise civil unions on 19 October 2018 and established a working group in January 2020, whose start was postponed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024, the annual assessment by the leading local monitor, recorded a series of negative events with significant impact over the preceding year and described a long-visible worsening trend as increasingly evident.
BIH.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not document prosecutions or convictions under the entity-level hate-crime provisions, so the practical weight of those sentencing enhancements is unresolved.

The status of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina civil-union working group after its January 2020 postponement is not sourced.

The most recent public-attitude figures in the inventory are the 2015 survey and the 2017 Pew poll; no later national polling is recorded.

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.summary:
Georgia's Parliament passed the package "On Family Values and Protection of Minors" on 17 September 2024 by 84 votes to 0, and it was signed into law on 3 October 2024. It prohibits all surgical operations and medical interventions for gender reassignment for people of all ages, and prohibits entering any gender "different from his own" on state or identity documents. The same package bars adoption of a minor by people who do not identify "as their gender", voids public or private labour obligations "aimed at neglecting biological sex", bans radio and television broadcasting, advertising and public gatherings that promote belonging to a gender different from one's own, and bans pride events and public displays of the rainbow flag. It also outlaws "alternative marriage unions" and designates 17 May as a holiday for the sanctity of the family.

A 2024 bill was described as seeking to make being transgender illegal and to remove all transgender recognition on identity documents. Those transgender-specific provisions were separate from the package's provisions on alternative marriage unions, general LGBT protections and LGBT public displays, which were framed as applying to LGBT people generally.

Legal gender recognition had been available since 2008, when transgender people could change documents and personal names after sex reassignment surgery. On 31 March 2021 the Tbilisi Civil Registry Service registered a transgender woman as female, the first such precedent. From 2024 no recognition procedure is available, so a trans visitor's passport or ID will carry whatever marker the issuing authority assigned. Legal activists had pressed for reform for more than a decade on the ground that paperwork failing to match a person's identity made job applications difficult and exposed the person to disclosure.

Transition-related care is now prohibited outright for people of all ages. The foreign agents law further endangers LGBTI service provision: organisations that refuse to register as "foreign agents" face fines and bankruptcy. ILGA-Europe reports that the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust and reduced applications for services, that large numbers of LGBTI people are leaving the country and seeking asylum documentation, and that misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

On the day after the package's final passage, transgender model and actress Kesaria Abramidze was stabbed to death; the interior ministry called it a premeditated murder. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path, and reporting after the killing described fears of hate crimes under Russia-style "gay propaganda" provisions.

Hate-crime protection exists on paper but is not enforced. Since 2012 crimes committed on the basis of gender identity are an aggravating factor under Criminal Code article 53, and Article 1 of the Law on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination, effective 7 May 2014, expressly covers gender identity and expression. There are nonetheless no official statistics on crimes on gender-identity grounds, and registered cases and studies indicate the hate-crime law is not efficient. Georgia's Public Defender reported in 2017 that prosecutors examined 86 alleged hate crimes that year, 37 of them based on gender identity; that law enforcement had no efficient strategy against hate-motivated violence and reacted only to individual cases; that numerous complaints concerned homophobic attitudes by law enforcement; and that complainants withdrew for lack of belief in a timely investigation.

Public assembly by LGBTI people has been repeatedly and violently prevented. The 17 May 2012 Identoba march was assaulted by religious counter-demonstrators, with police intervening only after fighting began and arresting victims; a 2013 rally was stormed by thousands led by priests, injuring at least 28 and trapping participants in buses and shops; the 5 July 2021 Tbilisi Pride was disrupted, leaving 53 media workers injured and NGO offices raided; and a 2021 Pride march was called off after anti-LGBT protesters stormed the Tbilisi Pride headquarters and attacked about 50 journalists. In June 2019 the Interior Ministry declared Tbilisi Pride "impossible" in its planned city-centre locations, citing safety risks, while organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel and far-right groups vowed to thwart the march. After the 2021 riots the authorities arrested 102 people, 68 of whom were released on bail and the rest held pending trial; on 9 July 2021 Tbilisi City Court denied bail and ordered pre-trial detention of four more, the judge stating the actions "in addition to being criminal, undermine the stability of the state".

A 2012 study found that 32 per cent of LGBTI respondents had experienced physical violence and 89.93 per cent psychological violence; 73 per cent of physical-violence victims never reported to police, citing ineffectiveness, fear of homophobic treatment and failure to be taken seriously, and 46.15 per cent of those who did report were dissatisfied because of homophobic police reaction.

Georgia's Constitution, adopted 13 October 2017 and in effect from 2018, provides that all persons are equal before the law and prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex or any other grounds, guarantees inviolability of human dignity with a prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, and guarantees free development of personality together with protection of life, physical integrity and liberty; universally recognised human rights apply directly and international treaties prevail over domestic acts unless they conflict with the Constitution.

Georgia does not recognise same-sex unions. The Civil Code has defined marriage as a heterosexual union since 1997, and the Constitution as passed on 26 September 2017 defines marriage solely as "a union between a woman and a man for the purpose of creating a family". A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition, and the 2024 package outlaws "alternative marriage unions" outright. Same-sex sexual activity was not formally legalised until 2000, when an amended criminal code was adopted to meet Council of Europe standards; the age of consent is equal at 16 under Penal Code articles 140 and 141.
GEO.outOfScopeNotes:
The two source accounts give different passage dates for the 2024 package: one records passage on 4 September, another records passage by 84-0 on 17 September. The signing date of 3 October is consistent across sources. The discrepancy is unresolved.

No official statistics on crimes on gender-identity grounds exist, so the enforcement gap cannot be quantified from official data.

The most recent violence-prevalence figure in the source inventory is the 2012 survey, which predates the 2024 law and the 2021 and 2023 assembly disruptions.

Whether the 2024 package's document provisions are being applied to markers already issued is not sourced.

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in Armenia in 2003, and no provision of Armenian law criminalises transgender identity or expression as such. The restrictive legislative route has been attempted: in 2013 the police proposed a bill criminalising "non-traditional sexual relationships" and LGBT "propaganda" directed at young people, modelled on Russian legislation; it failed to pass after Pink Armenia argued it functioned as a distraction tactic. A 2009 ILGA-Europe and COC fact-finding mission, Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia, documented societal and institutional homophobia, harassment and violence, and the legislation then affecting LGBT people; the pattern it described is visible in later reporting.

Legal gender recognition has operated as an administrative practice since 2006 and requires surgery. There is no recognition of non-binary identities, and gender-affirming care is restricted. A trans visitor should expect that a change of legal marker is not available on self-declaration and that access to hormone or surgical care in Armenia is limited.

Marriage is not open to a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex, or read as same-sex under birth-sex status; Armenian law bars marriage between persons of the same sex and provides no equivalent recognition. No discrimination protection exists on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and an anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence has been characterised as ambiguous since 2022.

Pink Human Rights Defender NGO's 2024 annual report documents discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, directed at LGBT people in Armenia, along with violations of private and family life, of education and work rights, and hate speech. Public acceptance is low: Equaldex records a public-opinion acceptance score of 5 out of 100.

Violence against LGBT people has drawn a slow or absent state response. In May 2012 a neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan involved a Molotov cocktail and a fire; police took 12 hours to respond, and two suspects were later detained on the basis of CCTV footage. In April 2019 Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered transgender woman, became the first transgender person to address the National Assembly; she received death threats, including from members of parliament who called for her to be burned alive. In February 2020 a nationalist party member burned incense over the same lectern, denouncing her speech as a desecration.
ARM.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no general homicide rate or per-capita baseline for Armenia, so the trans-specific violence documented by Pink Armenia and the 2012 arson attack cannot be compared against a background rate. The counts are raw, and the sources describe underreporting; no magnitude should be read from them.

Whether the surgical requirement for legal gender recognition is applied to foreign nationals, and what documentation a trans visitor would need to change or match a marker, is not sourced. Whether Armenia's hate-crime provisions have produced any prosecution is unresolved in the inventory. The 2009 ILGA-Europe and COC report is dated, and the inventory does not establish which of its findings on institutional homophobia persist beyond what the 2024 Pink Armenia report documents.

ILGA-Europe/COC fact-finding report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, HIV/AIDS, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in Armenia.

Consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised in the country in 2003, and no provision of national law criminalises transgender identity or expression as such. The restrictive legislative route has been attempted: in 2013 the police proposed a bill criminalising "non-traditional sexual relationships" and LGBT "propaganda" directed at young people, modelled on the legislation of a neighbouring jurisdiction; it failed to pass after a local LGBT rights organisation argued it functioned as a distraction tactic. A 2009 fact-finding mission by a regional LGBT rights federation and a partner organisation documented societal and institutional homophobia, harassment and violence, and the legislation then affecting LGBT people; the pattern it described is visible in later reporting.

Legal gender recognition has operated as an administrative practice since 2006 and requires surgery. There is no recognition of non-binary identities, and gender-affirming care is restricted. A trans visitor should expect that a change of legal marker is not available on self-declaration and that access to hormone or surgical care in the country is limited.

Marriage is not open to a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex, or read as same-sex under birth-sex status; national law bars marriage between persons of the same sex and provides no equivalent recognition. No discrimination protection exists on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and an anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence has been characterised as ambiguous since 2022.

A local LGBT rights organisation's 2024 annual report documents discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, directed at LGBT people in the country, along with violations of private and family life, of education and work rights, and hate speech. Public acceptance is low: a rights-comparison database records a public-opinion acceptance score of 5 out of 100.

Violence against LGBT people has drawn a slow or absent national response. In May 2012 a neo-Nazi arson attack on a gay-friendly bar in the capital involved a Molotov cocktail and a fire; police took 12 hours to respond, and two suspects were later detained on the basis of CCTV footage. In April 2019 a transgender activist, the country's first registered transgender woman, became the first transgender person to address the national legislature; she received death threats, including from members of the legislature who called for her to be burned alive. In February 2020 a nationalist party member burned incense over the same lectern, denouncing her speech as a desecration.
ARM.blindOutOfScope:
The inventory contains no general homicide rate or per-capita baseline for the country, so the trans-specific violence documented by a local LGBT rights organisation and the 2012 arson attack cannot be compared against a background rate. The counts are raw, and the sources describe underreporting; no magnitude should be read from them.

Whether the surgical requirement for legal gender recognition is applied to foreign nationals, and what documentation a trans visitor would need to change or match a marker, is not sourced. Whether the country's hate-crime provisions have produced any prosecution is unresolved in the inventory. The 2009 report by a regional LGBT rights federation and a partner organisation is dated, and the inventory does not establish which of its findings on institutional homophobia persist beyond what the 2024 report documents.

Comparison service covering this nation and two neighbours: this nation decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections ‘ambiguous’ since 2022; no protection statute; same-sex marriage banned. Public-opinion acceptance scores are very low.

Regional monitors’ fact-finding mission report (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional hostility, media coverage, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in this nation.

ARM.blindLocalsOnly:
Attitudes among the resident population are hostile. A 2012 study found that 55% of residents would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out, and 70% find LGBT people "strange".

In 2014 a newspaper published a list of dozens of LGBT social media accounts in the country, describing them as "zombies". An appellate court ruled that the newspaper had not offended anyone and ordered the plaintiffs to pay 50,000 in local currency, about US$120, to the newspaper.

A local LGBT rights organisation's 2024 report includes a chapter on pressure brought against a transgender individual in the country over participation in a beauty pageant.
ARM.tangentialFactors:

The 2013 bill was drafted on the model of Russian legislation, an import of a restrictive framework from a neighbouring jurisdiction.

Restrictions on LGBT public expression and assembly have been documented. In 2017 the organisers of the Yerevan International Film Festival cancelled the screening of two LGBT-themed films after negative public reaction. AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.summary:
The national police are the documented source of the most serious risk. In September 2017 officers in Baku detained at least 100 people in raids presented as action against prostitution; detainees were beaten, interrogated, subjected to forced medical examinations and blackmailed. A United States State Department report on the period recorded threats of rape and the use of electric shocks. At least 60 of those held were imprisoned or fined. The arrests formed part of a wave of detentions ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games, and Human Rights Watch called for an investigation and for releases. Azerbaijan acknowledged the cases in 2019, and in April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the arrests and the mistreatment.

Enforcement of this kind did not end with those arrests. In July 2023 officers raided a private birthday party in Baku; queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats that their sexual orientation or gender identity would be disclosed.

Killings of trans people are documented and the response to them is inadequate. A trans woman was murdered in Baku in March 2024, and the police investigation that followed is described by monitoring organisations as inadequate. The sources available do not give Azerbaijan's general homicide rate, so this killing cannot be measured against the background rate of violence in the country; a single documented case, not a rate, is what the sources support.

Hostility in state-aligned media is routine. After a Women's Day march in 2024 whose demands included access to trans healthcare, the state-affiliated broadcaster Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people. Monitoring by QueeRadar found that 77 per cent of 428 media items analysed were hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people. In a separate incident an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe. The 2017 United States State Department report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and the blocking of websites.

Legal recognition is absent for trans people and for couples read as same-sex. Transgender people cannot change their gender entry on official documents, although they may change their name to accord with their gender identity. Marriage and civil unions between partners of the same sex are neither recognised nor performed, and same-sex couples may not adopt children, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be classified locally as a same-sex relationship has no route to recognition of that relationship. Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not prohibited by law. The age of consent is 16 for heterosexual and homosexual sex alike.

Coercion within families is a documented pattern. A shadow report to the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, submitted by the Gender and Development Social Union, records forced marriages of lesbian, bisexual and transgender women. In a separate case a family forcibly transported an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out.
AZE.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources in this inventory carry no detail on entry rules, visa processing or airport and border screening for trans travellers arriving in Azerbaijan, and nothing on how travel documents or prosthetics would be handled at a port of entry.

The April 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling on the 2017 arrests is recorded as issued; the sources available do not set out its terms or what compliance has followed.

Whether the press council established in 2003 has assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics is not known.

A Women's Day march in 2024 demanded access to trans healthcare, which indicates that such access is contested, but the inventory contains no detail on whether gender-affirming care is legally available in Azerbaijan or how a visitor would obtain it.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Azerbaijan's constitution guarantees freedom of expression, and the Azerbaijan Press Council, founded in 2003, handles complaints under a Press Code of Conduct; it is not known whether it has assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics. Media have been criticised for spreading fear and hate toward queer people through discriminatory language, with politicians and officials using it to shape public perception; Vahid Aliyev of the Minority Azerbaijan webpage criticised this unprofessionalism. The 2017 US State Department report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and blocking of websites. LGBTQIA+ media nonetheless exists: gay.az, the first news website for LGBTQIA+ people, launched 25 May 2011 by Ruslan Balukhin, and Minority Magazine, the first LGBTQIA+ online magazine, founded by Samad Ismayilov in December 2015 and an NGO from August 2017; Ismayilov's documentary about a trans man premiered in Baku on 25 November 2017 with Dutch embassy support, drawing about 80 people. Same-sex couples are not legally recognised: marriage and civil unions are neither recognised nor performed, and same-sex couples may not adopt children. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned. ILGA-Europe has ranked Azerbaijan last, 49 of 49, in Europe every year since 2015, citing a near total absence of legal protection. The age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. Transgender people cannot change their gender on official documents, though they may change their name to match their gender identity. Azerbaijan mandates conscription for able-bodied men aged 18 to 35, under which LGBTQIA+ enlistees can be declared unfit for service under Articles 18/b (personality disorders) and 17/b (reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders) of the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations, and queer conscripts often conceal their orientation to avoid dedovshchina hazing. In September 2017 at least 100 members of Baku's LGBTQIA+ community were arrested in a crackdown ostensibly on prostitution; detainees were subjected to beatings, interrogation, forced medical examinations and blackmail, and the 2017 US State Department report added that police threatened rape and used electric shocks. By law no groups are excluded from blood donation apart from people infected with HIV/AIDS, though it is unknown whether men who have sex with men are de facto permitted to donate. The Gender Resource Center (Gender Resurs Mərkəzi), established in 2020, is a queer-feminist platform created in response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations. Gender and Development, created in 2007, runs local projects in collaboration with the Ministry of Health. AZAD LGBT ran in-person programming in Baku, including LGBTQ movie nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-film Q&As, and launched a website in 2015 providing free online LGBTQ education tools; Minority Magazine covers education topics. Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance regularly holds talks with the EU Delegation to Azerbaijan and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face. Critics have argued Azerbaijan should not be allowed to host international events because of its discrimination against LGBTQIA+ people, a controversy that flared around Eurovision 2012. In April 2019 14-year-old Elina Hajiyeva of Baku attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at her school; the principal took no action, tried to attribute the attempt to family difficulties and did not call an ambulance, and she died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus 18,500 AZN ($10,882) compensation. The case sparked a nationwide social media campaign, a video by 2011 Eurovision winner Nigar Jamal to President Ilham Aliyev, and a Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan launched 13 May 2019 with a new hotline to ensure a healthy environment in general education institutions, improve school-family relations and protect students from abuse.

KAZ.name: Kazakhstan
KAZ.summary:
Kazakhstan decriminalised consensual sex between men in late 1997, when Article 104 of the Penal Code, which criminalised "buggery", was repealed; the repeal took effect in 1998 and introduced a common age of consent of 16. Sex between women was never a criminal offence. The sources record no statute regulating clothing by gender presentation and no law restricting which toilet or facility a trans visitor may use.

A statutory ban on "propaganda of non-traditional sexual orientation" is the operative legal threat. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the law on 30 December 2025, prohibiting "information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation" in public spaces and in the media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine. The Mäjilis had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025. Kazakhstan now stands with Russia, Hungary and Georgia among jurisdictions that ban "LGBTQ propaganda" by statute. The measure grew out of a petition, "We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!", filed by the Union of Parents; in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information said it was reviewing the petition after it met the threshold for government consideration, and Human Rights Watch warned that the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide.

No law protects LGBT people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit, so a trans visitor refused service or dismissed from a placement has no statutory remedy. Public opinion is heavily adverse: 89 per cent of respondents opposed same-sex marriage in a 2015-16 Pew survey.

Bias-motivated violence goes largely unrecorded by the state. Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights since the 2018 reporting cycle and has no nominated national point of contact for hate crimes; the OSCE assessment notes the country would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures.

Documented incidents set the pattern. During 2023 an LGBTQI activist was almost run over by a car in an apparent deliberate attack that produced no investigation, and an LGBTQI+ education organisation was refused registration as an employment site after disclosing its focus, according to ILGA-Europe's review of access to services. In 2019 the Supreme Court upheld a privacy claim against a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, ordering compensation over a "moral foundations" defence; the two women left Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for their safety.

Barriers to health care for LGBT people are documented by the Eurasian Coalition on Male Health, which has recorded rights violations in the country since 2017 and reports that informal behavioural practices shaping access are missed by formal policy analysis.

Partner recognition is absent. Kazakhstan does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and households headed by same-sex couples receive none of the legal protections available to married opposite-sex couples. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status should expect no spousal recognition, no next-of-kin standing and no protection tied to the relationship.
KAZ.outOfScopeNotes:
The propaganda law's penalties are stated in statute as a 10-day administrative arrest and a fine. Whether the measure has been applied to individuals, and to whom, is not established by the sources, and no case counts or enforcement records are available.

The country's last hate-crime submission to the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights covers the 2018 reporting cycle, and no national point of contact for hate crimes is nominated. The scale of anti-trans violence is therefore unquantified; no official or independent figure is sourced.

The 2023 refusal to register an LGBTQI+ education organisation as an employment site is recorded without a resolution or appeal outcome. In the 2019 case, the Supreme Court ordered compensation, but the amount awarded and whether the video was taken down are not sourced.

How the medical-commission requirements for legal gender recognition apply to foreign nationals or visitors is unresolved; the sources describe the process only for residents. The Pew finding on opposition to same-sex marriage dates from 2015-16, and no more recent national polling is sourced.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering Jan–Dec 2023 (Kazakhstan): documents access-to-services bias (an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022.

OSCE/ODIHR Hate Crime Reporting 2024 summary for Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since the 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

HRW (10 Jul 2024): in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information said it was reviewing a 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!' petition (Union of Parents) that met the threshold for government consideration; HRW warns the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide — a live, dated legislative threat.

ECOM (2024): ECOM has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017. Its analysis identifies health-right barriers in Kazakhstan alongside informal behavioural practices that policy analysis misses.

HRW (24 Sep 2019): Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments — privacy rights upheld over a 'moral foundations' defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal since late 1997 (de jure 1998), when Article 104 of the Penal Code criminalising 'buggery' was repealed and a common age of consent of 16 was introduced; lesbianism was never a criminal offence. Wikipedia country coverage: Since 2003 transgender people in Kazakhstan may change legal gender on identity documents, but only after a diagnosis of 'gender identity disorder' involving medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission. Applicants must pay around ₸100,000 tenge, and although since 2023 commissions can in principle be assembled in every region, in practice the only functioning one is in Almaty because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months to start medical transition, and since 2011 document changes require gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation; people under 21 cannot change gender on documents at all. Deputy Minister of Education Natalya Jumadildaeva stated that a parent's sexual orientation would play a 'key role' in approval, assessed through a 'special psychological test'. Critics, including independent media, noted the law was modelled on Russian legislation. Wikipedia country coverage: Kazakhstan does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. KAZ.localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available on identity documents since 2003, but only through a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder". Applicants undergo medical tests and a 30-day psychiatric evaluation by a medical commission, and pay a fee of around 100,000 tenge.

Since 2011 changes to documents have required gender-affirming surgery, hormone therapy and sterilisation, and no one under 21 may change gender on documents at all. Although commissions may in principle be assembled in every region since 2023, the only functioning one in practice is in Almaty, because of requirements for separate specialist rooms. A positive decision yields a certificate valid for six months in which to begin medical transition.

Same-sex couples have been unable to adopt children legally since at least 2020, and in February 2024 President Tokayev signed a law prohibiting adoption of orphans by same-sex couples. Deputy Minister of Education Natalya Jumadildaeva stated that a prospective parent's sexual orientation would play a "key role" in approval, assessed through a "special psychological test".
KAZ.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Peru (0.48) and just below the USA/Mexico (0.50) — Kazakhstan has no institutional hostility machinery but a far weaker protection floor — and above Armenia (0.46) and Turkey (0.47).
KAZ.blindSummary:
The country decriminalised consensual sex between men in late 1997, when the criminal-code article prohibiting "buggery" was repealed; the repeal took effect in 1998 and set a common age of consent at 16. Sex between women was never a criminal offence. The sources record no statute regulating clothing by gender presentation and no law restricting which toilet or facility a trans visitor may use.

A statutory ban on "propaganda of non-traditional sexual orientation" is the operative legal threat. The president signed the law on 30 December 2025, prohibiting "information containing propaganda of pedophilia and/or non-traditional sexual orientation" in public spaces and in the media, with violations punishable by a 10-day arrest and a fine. The lower house of the national legislature had approved a harsher version on 12 November 2025. The country now stands with three other jurisdictions in the region that ban "LGBTQ propaganda" by statute. The measure grew out of a petition against open and hidden propaganda, filed by a parents' association; in June 2024 the national culture ministry said it was reviewing the petition after it met the threshold for government consideration, and an international human-rights organisation warned that the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide.

No law protects LGBT people from discrimination in employment, education, housing, health care, public accommodations or credit, so a trans visitor refused service or dismissed from a placement has no statutory remedy. Public opinion is heavily adverse: 89 per cent of respondents opposed same-sex marriage in a public-opinion survey conducted in 2015-16.

Bias-motivated violence goes largely unrecorded by the state. The country has not reported hate-crime data to a regional security organisation's hate-crime reporting mechanism since the 2018 reporting cycle and has no nominated national point of contact for hate crimes; that body's assessment notes the country would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures.

Documented incidents set the pattern. During 2023 an activist was almost run over by a car in an apparent deliberate attack that produced no investigation, and an education organisation was refused registration as an employment site after disclosing its focus, according to a regional advocacy organisation's review of access to services. In 2019 the highest court upheld a privacy claim against a social media user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, ordering compensation over a "moral foundations" defence; the two women left the country for eight months fearing for their safety.

Barriers to health care for LGBT people are documented by a regional health coalition, which has recorded rights violations in the country since 2017 and reports that informal behavioural practices shaping access are missed by formal policy analysis.

Partner recognition is absent. The country does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and households headed by same-sex couples receive none of the legal protections available to married opposite-sex couples. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status should expect no spousal recognition, no next-of-kin standing and no protection tied to the relationship.

UZB.name: Uzbekistan
UZB.summary:
Article 120 of Uzbekistan's 1994 Criminal Code criminalises consensual sexual conduct between men and carries a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment. Human Dignity Trust, Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 and the UK Home Office's country-policy note of July 2024 all record the offence as in force. The Home Office documents prosecutions under Article 120 between 2009 and 2023, so the provision is applied rather than dormant.

Uzbekistan has no legal gender recognition. A trans visitor remains, in law, the sex assigned at birth, and Human Dignity Trust notes that transgender people may be prosecuted under Article 120 on that basis. Human Rights Watch reports that police target gay and bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment.

Forced examinations of detainees amount to torture, according to the World Health Organization's assessment cited by Human Rights Watch, and impunity for police ill-treatment persists. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records torture, ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in custody alongside social stigma and violence against LGBT people.

The State Department's 2023 report records LGBTQI+ people arrested and then released, or threatened with arrest, unless they paid bribes, and police coercing LGBTQI+ people to inform on others under threat of prison. Human Rights Watch's March 2021 reporting describes gay and bisexual men facing discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from both state and non-state actors with almost no protection available.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Uzbekistan and operate unofficially, so formally recognised advocacy, legal aid and support structures do not exist. The Home Office note records that rural social taboo drives discrimination, and the State Department's 2023 report records continued societal harassment alongside self-censorship by websites and bloggers covering LGBTQI+ issues.

In November 2024 Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish party, announced he was drafting a law to ban discussion of LGBTQ people. In April 2023 the Constitution was amended leaving "sexual orientation" out of its enumerated protected categories while listing gender, race, religion and nationality.

ECOM's 2024 national report on violations of LGBT people's rights in Uzbekistan addresses the legislative framework, anti-discrimination provisions, the criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, and the rights to health and to work.
UZB.outOfScopeNotes:
Article 120's text addresses conduct between men. How it is applied to a trans woman, a trans man, or a foreign national is not documented in the sources reviewed, and no case involving a visitor appears among them.

No sourced information was identified on entry and visa rules, document-marker or passport-gender policy for trans travellers, border screening practice, or bathroom and facilities law in Uzbekistan.

The status of the draft law announced in November 2024 is unresolved: the sources record the announcement, not enactment or parliamentary progress.

Enforcement data is unevenly dated. The Home Office case record runs to 2023, Human Rights Watch's World Report covers 2023, the State Department material covers 2021 and 2023, and ECOM's report covers 2024. No per-capita or case-count data on Article 120 prosecutions is provided.

Wikipedia is the only source among those reviewed for the November 2024 draft law and the April 2023 constitutional enumeration; both rest on a single source and were not corroborated by the other material.

NIC.name: Nicaragua
NIC.summary:
Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or transgender identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, added by socially conservative legislators to a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner". President Violeta Chamorro signed it in July 1992 and the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality challenge in March 1994. The provision's vagueness also made it usable against LGBT-rights organising and sexual-health work. The language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender, and sexual offences under Criminal Code articles 168, 170, 172 and 175 are gender-neutral.

Formal legality does not produce protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices records a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against people perceived as opponents of the government, which authorities neither investigated nor prosecuted, and lists violence and threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex people among the country's significant human rights violations. The report's assessment is that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of state impunity.

Violence against LGBT people is widely tolerated socially and not enforced legally. Attacks are largely unreported because victims fear retaliation and expect poor legal outcomes. Trans women are the group most frequently targeted. Police are documented among the aggressors, tied with family members in the 2022 count, and assaults occur mainly in the street and in private homes.

The crackdown on protests that began in April 2018 left at least 325 people dead and more than 2,000 injured according to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. Amnesty International reported in May 2019 that journalist Miguel Mora was beaten by a pro-government mob and was targeted partly because he is gay, an instance of homophobia operating inside the political repression.

Marriage, partnership and adoption are restricted to heterosexual couples under the revised Family Code approved by Congress in June 2014 and in force from 8 April 2015; Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on the voluntary agreement of a man and a woman. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in a relationship read as same-sex under local law has no access to the legal benefits and protections available to married opposite-sex couples. Unconstitutionality actions were filed against the Family Code. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that states party to the American Convention on Human Rights must give same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration institutions, including marriage; no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.

Ministerial Resolution 671-2014, adopted by the Ministry of Health and replacing Resolution 249-2009, requires non-discrimination in public and private health units on grounds of gender identity and gender expression, alongside sexual orientation. Article 3(l) of Law No. 820 prohibits discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds in the HIV and AIDS context.

Much of Nicaragua's media has been restricted since the 2018 protests and reporting is largely suppressed, which limits independent coverage of LGBT issues and makes the record of violence and enforcement harder to verify.
NIC.outOfScopeNotes:
F&M Global Barometers records no documented finding for Nicaragua.

No youth-specific findings on access to care are recorded.

No Nicaraguan implementation of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 is recorded.

The incidence of anti-LGBT violence is unresolved. Attacks are widely underreported out of fear of retaliation and because legal outcomes are poor, and no complete count is available.

sources.summary:
A 1992 law, Article 204 of the Criminal Code, was added by social Christians to a bill originally meant to protect women from rape and made it an offence punishable by up to three years' prison to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner". President Violeta Chamorro signed it in July 1992 and the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality appeal in March 1994; the language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, so same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since. Media reporting is largely suppressed, much of the media having been restricted since the 2018 protests, which limits coverage of LGBT issues.

In June 2014 the Nicaraguan Congress approved a revised Family Code limiting marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples; it took effect on 8 April 2015, and several organizations filed an action of unconstitutionality against it. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples, and Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration figures including marriage; no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.

Sexual-orientation discrimination is barred in several settings. Article 315 of the Penal Code, covering offences against labour rights, punishes discrimination based on "sexual option" by up to one year in prison in employment. Article 3(l) of Law N° 820 prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation grounds in the HIV and AIDS context, Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 bars it in access to health services on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, and Article 36(5) of the Penal Code makes sexual-orientation discrimination an aggravating circumstance when committing any criminal offence. No youth-specific care-access findings are recorded.

Violence against the LGBTQ community is generally culturally accepted and legally unenforced, and attacks go largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes. A 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, among them 15 murders of 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with the true figure expected to be higher. NGO Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime or murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person in the first two quarters of 2024. Trans women are the most targeted group, and state police are among the aggressors, tied with family members in 2022.

Public opinion is largely opposed. A Pew survey of 9 November to 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed to same-sex marriage, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support. Visibility is uneven: gay men are generally more visible in public than lesbians, who often socialise privately, and an annual Gay Pride celebration has been held in Managua around 28 June since the country's first public pride festival in 1991.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nicaragua (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Article 1 of Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression, alongside sexual orientation, in access to health services. No transgender-specific hate-crime aggravator is stated; the Penal Code Article 36(5) aggravating circumstance described is framed as motivation by discrimination based on sexual orientation. A 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey documented 53 aggressions against LGBT people between 1999 and 2011, including 15 murders comprising 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with actual homicides and attacks expected to be higher as many victims choose not to denounce attacks to police. Programa Feminista La Corriente reported for 2021 67 assaults, 1 hate crime/murder, and 2 suicides with the majority of aggressions happening to trans women, occurring mainly in the street or in houses by family members or strangers, with acquaintances and state police each committing 10 documented aggressions. For 2022 it reported 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes, and 1 suicide with trans women continuing as the most targeted group followed by gay men, with street and home as most common places and state police tying family members in number of assaults. For 2023 it reported 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults, and 1 extortion with demographic statistics described as consistent with previous years, while partial 2024 data for two quarters as of April 2025 showed 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes, and 1 person missing. The article states violence against the LGBTQ community is generally culturally accepted and legally unenforced, with instances largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and dismal legal results and media reporting largely suppressed since the 2018 protests. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity have been legal since March 2008 under a new Penal Code effective 1 March 2008 that omitted repealed Article 204; the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender and all sexual offenses are gender-neutral under Criminal Code articles 168, 170, 172 and 175. Former Article 204, signed into law in July 1992, imposed up to three years in prison for anyone who induces, promotes, propagandizes, or practices sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner and also covered unmarried sex acts; a November 1992 constitutional challenge by the Campaign for Sexuality without Prejudices was rejected by the Supreme Court in March 1994. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same legal benefits and protections as opposite-sex married couples; in June 2014 Congress approved a revised family code limiting marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples effective 8 April 2015 with unconstitutionality actions filed, and Constitution Article 72 states marriage and stable unions rest on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. Article 315 of the Penal Code on offenses against labor rights punishes discrimination based on sexual option with up to one year in prison, and Article 3(l) of Law No. 820 on promotion, protection and defense of human rights regarding HIV and AIDS prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation. Article 36(5) of the Penal Code establishes an aggravating circumstance when a criminal offense is motivated by discrimination based on sexual orientation. On enforcement, the 2012 survey counted 10 gay men and 1 lesbian among 15 murders, La Corriente identified gay men as the second most targeted group in 2022, and the article states anti-LGBTQ violence is generally culturally accepted, legally unenforced, and largely unreported for fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes.
