The country does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or transgender identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, added by socially conservative legislators to a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner". The president at the time signed it in July 1992 and the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality challenge in March 1994. The provision's vagueness also made it usable against LGBT-rights organising and sexual-health work. The language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender, and sexual offences under Criminal Code articles 168, 170, 172 and 175 are gender-neutral.

Formal legality does not produce protection. A 2023 country human-rights report published by a foreign government records a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against people perceived as opponents of the government, which authorities neither investigated nor prosecuted, and lists violence and threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex people among the country's significant human rights violations. The report's assessment is that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of official impunity.

Violence against LGBT people is widely tolerated socially and not enforced legally. Attacks are largely unreported because victims fear retaliation and expect poor legal outcomes. Trans women are the group most frequently targeted. Police are documented among the aggressors, tied with family members in the 2022 count, and assaults occur mainly in the street and in private homes.

The crackdown on protests that began in April 2018 left at least 325 people dead and more than 2,000 injured according to a regional human-rights commission. An international human-rights organisation reported in May 2019 that a journalist was beaten by a pro-government mob and was targeted partly because he is gay, an instance of homophobia operating inside the political repression.

Marriage, partnership and adoption are restricted to heterosexual couples under the revised Family Code approved by the national legislature in June 2014 and in force from 8 April 2015; Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on the voluntary agreement of a man and a woman. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in a relationship read as same-sex under local law has no access to the legal benefits and protections available to married opposite-sex couples. Unconstitutionality actions were filed against the Family Code. A regional human-rights court's advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that states party to a regional human-rights convention must give same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration institutions, including marriage; no implementation is recorded in the country.

A 2014 ministerial resolution adopted by the national health ministry and replacing an earlier resolution requires non-discrimination in public and private health units on grounds of gender identity and gender expression, alongside sexual orientation. Article 3(l) of a national law on HIV and AIDS prohibits discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds in that context.

Much of the country's media has been restricted since the 2018 protests and reporting is largely suppressed, which limits independent coverage of LGBT issues and makes the record of violence and enforcement harder to verify.

A global barometer programme records no documented finding for the country.

No youth-specific findings on access to care are recorded.

No implementation of the regional human-rights court's advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 is recorded in the country.

The incidence of anti-LGBT violence is unresolved. Attacks are widely underreported out of fear of retaliation and because legal outcomes are poor, and no complete count is available.

NIC.blindLocalsOnly:
Article 315 of the Penal Code, which covers offences against labour rights, punishes discrimination based on "sexual option" with up to one year's imprisonment in employment.

Article 36(5) of the Penal Code makes discrimination based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance when any criminal offence is committed. The aggravator as described is framed on sexual orientation; no transgender-specific hate-crime aggravator is stated.

Couples whose relationship local law reads as same-sex, and households headed by such couples, are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. The national legislature approved the revised Family Code in June 2014 and it took effect on 8 April 2015, limiting marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples; several organisations filed an action of unconstitutionality against it.
NIC.tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is largely opposed to same-sex marriage. A Pew survey conducted between 9 November and 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 24.5% support.

Visibility is uneven. Gay men are generally more visible in public than lesbians, who often socialise privately, and an annual Gay Pride celebration has been held in Managua around 28 June since the country's first public pride festival in 1991.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 sets a regional standard on family registration that Nicaraguan law does not meet, and no domestic implementing measure has followed.

GUY.name: Guyana
GUY.summary:
Guyana criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, retained in force after independence. Section 351 punishes an act of gross indecency between men, in public or private, as a misdemeanour carrying up to two years' imprisonment. Section 353 punishes buggery as a felony carrying life imprisonment, with related provisions covering attempted buggery. Some compilations cite the same offences as sections 352 to 354. Prosecutions are rare, but the provisions structure police encounters with lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people and sustain public stigma.

A constitutional savings clause bars judicial review of laws inherited at independence. The clause prevents courts from invalidating the inherited sexual offences even where they conflict with human rights guarantees, so repeal depends on Parliament rather than litigation.

The cross-dressing offence in section 153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act was struck down by the Caribbean Court of Justice on 13 November 2018 in McEwan, Clarke, Fraser, Persaud and SASOD v Attorney General, as unconstitutionally vague and contrary to freedom of expression. The challenge followed the 2009 arrests of transgender women under the 1893 provision and three nights' detention, a 2010 Supreme Court filing with SASOD, a 2013 Chief Justice ruling permitting cross-dressing unless for an "improper purpose", and affirmance by the Court of Appeal.

Guyana provides no procedure for legal gender recognition. No sourced provision addresses transgender-specific identity documents, airport screening, facilities, custody or gender-affirming care.

Police use residual Summary Jurisdiction clauses against LGBT people. SASOD's Joel Simpson documented men in "compromising positions" threatened with arrest to extract bribes, same-sex couples harassed at seawalls and parks, and complainants who face secondary discrimination at stations and give "watered down" accounts. Loitering and vagancy clauses remain usable after the 2018 ruling, chiefly against sex workers.

Street violence and justice-system failure are documented together. Petronella Trotman, a trans woman, was stabbed in Georgetown in January 2017; on 2 March 2017 magistrate Dylon Bess refused her entry to the Georgetown Magistrates Court because she was not "dressed like a man" and her case against her attacker was dismissed. At the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights' 191st session in November 2024, a hearing requested by the Guyana Equality Forum heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition on violence against migrant women, sex workers and transgender women; Commission chair Roberta Clarke called on Guyana to take urgent action, with 69 documented cases of violence against trans women recorded for 2018 to 2022, a raw count the source gives without a population denominator.

No hate-crime legislation covering gender identity or sexual orientation exists. Simpson was beaten by six men in Georgetown on 16 June 2019 after harassment at a nightclub, filed a police complaint and called for such legislation; the Ministry of Social Protection condemned the attack while affirming acceptance.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist in Guyana. Adoption, foster care and guardianship are not barred: the U.S. Department of State reports that LGBTQ people are not disqualified, and in December 2015 the Director of Guyana's Childcare and Protection Agency stated the agency does not discriminate and encouraged LGBTQ people to become adoptive parents.

Decriminalisation carries political backing. Five of six parties in the 2025 election, including the ruling party, supported it, and President Irfaan Ali promised in September 2025 to decriminalise with SASOD. An October 2022 poll of 1,070 respondents found 72.4% accepting or tolerating LGBTQ people, up from 34.5% in 2013, with reported hatred down to 12% from 25%.
GUY.outOfScopeNotes:
Section numbering for the sexual-offence provisions is unresolved across sources: Wikipedia cites sections 351 and 353 of the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, while Outright's overview cites sections 352 to 354 for the same offences. Both describe the same conduct and penalties.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules, identity-document markers, airport or border screening, bathroom or facility access, detention or custody placement, or access to gender-affirming care for visitors. The absence of such provisions is stated where the sources speak to it; beyond that, these areas are not sourced here.

The figure of 69 documented cases of violence against trans women for 2018 to 2022 is a raw count with no population denominator and no comparison to Guyana's general violence rate, so it indicates documented pattern and official concern rather than a measurable rate of risk.

The frequency of prosecutions under sections 351 and 353 is described as rare by two sources but no case counts are given. Whether the constitutional savings clause would bar a challenge to a future repealing statute is not addressed in the inventory.

SASOD managing director Joel Simpson stated in May 2019 that discriminatory laws have enabled law enforcement to extort LGBTQ people, with recorded cases of victims blackmailed by police who threatened arrest under the sodomy laws; hate crimes often go unreported. SASOD works with health professionals on their knowledge of LGBTQ people, and with the University of Guyana and nursing schools across the country. Discrimination and violence at the hands of law enforcement, religious leaders and others are widespread, leading most LGBTQ people to hide their orientation. No youth-specific or minor-specific care findings are recorded. Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist in Guyana. sources.summary: Under Section 153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act, cross-dressing was criminalized until 13 November 2018, when the Caribbean Court of Justice in Quincy McEwan, Seon Clarke, Joseph Fraser, Seyon Persaud and SASOD v The Attorney General of Guyana ruled the provision unconstitutional and ordered it struck from the code as archaic, vague, violative of protection of the law and contrary to the rule of law. Enforcement included 2009 arrests of several transgender activists for wearing clothes of the opposite sex, followed by a 2010 Supreme Court challenge by Guyana Trans United, a 2013 Chief Justice ruling permitting cross-dressing unless for an "improper purpose," affirmance by the Court of Appeal, and CCJ oral arguments beginning 28 June 2018 addressing vagueness and the constitutional savings clause barring challenge to colonial-era laws. The article states: "Guyanese society tends to view homosexuality and transgender people negatively, though attitudes are slowly changing and becoming more accepting." In 2017 a trans woman assaulted in Georgetown reported to police and filed in Georgetown Magistrates Court but on verdict day 2 March 2017 was denied courtroom entry because she was not "dressed like a man," after which the court dismissed her case. In July 2019 Minister of Social Protection Amna Ally stated the government was working to remove legal gaps to prevent discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, stating "The government believes that every individual regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity has an inherent human right to live their life free from violence, abuse and discrimination." No article-stated provisions address transgender-specific documents, screening, facilities, custody, or gender-affirming care. Guyana is the only country in South America and the only mainland country in the Americas where homosexual acts remain illegal under the inherited Criminal Law (Offences) Act (1893). Section 351 punishes any male act of gross indecency with another male in public or private as a misdemeanour liable to two years' imprisonment, and Section 353 punishes buggery as a felony liable to life imprisonment. The Constitution's savings clause bars judicial review of British colonial-era laws even if they undermine human rights, blocking court-led repeal despite 2016 Belize and 2018 Trinidad and Tobago rulings striking down analogous bans. Legislative reform remains pending after a 2012 government national-debate announcement, a 2013 parliamentary commission receiving 2014 submissions, a 2017 referendum proposal later described as a misunderstanding and opposed by SASOD, a May 2019 SASOD call for the Law Reform Commission to remove archaic clauses, July 2025 support for decriminalization by 5 of 6 main parties, and a September 2025 presidential promise by Irfaan Ali to decriminalize with SASOD. Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist, while adoption, foster care and guardianship remain legally available as the Childcare and Protection Agency stated in December 2015 it does not discriminate and no law bars LGBTQ individuals or same-sex couples. Constitutional protection based on sexual orientation was unanimously approved in December 2000 but denied presidential assent before the March 2001 elections after religious opposition and a 2003 reintroduction was withdrawn without progress. Enforcement risk includes SASOD-documented extortion and blackmail by police threatening arrest under the buggery law with hate crimes often unreported, and a July 2019 reduction by the Court of Appeal of Clive Knights' 2015 57-year murder sentence for the 2012 killing of Bert Whyte to 30 years for manslaughter after a claim of "unwanted homosexual advances." The article states: "Guyanese society tends to view homosexuality and transgender people negatively, though attitudes are slowly changing and becoming more accepting." Pride mobilization proceeded with state tolerance: the first parade on 2 June 2018 in Georgetown by hundreds demanding decriminalization occurred without violent incident despite a Georgetown Ministers' Fellowship demand for a ban as immoral, with support from political and religious leaders including the Anglican Bishop affirming marching rights with police permission, followed by a second festival 28 May to 3 June 2019 with a 1 June parade of 200 under police protection though participants faced shouted insults, postponements in 2020-2021 for COVID-19, and the largest Georgetown event in June 2022. Widespread discrimination and violence persist with LGBTQ persons facing violence and verbal harassment from law enforcement, religious leaders and others, causing most to conceal orientation, and gay men commonly labeled "anti-men." Managing Director of SASOD Joel Simpson stated discriminatory laws contributed to extortion by authorities, and on 16 June 2019 Simpson himself was beaten by six men after harassment at Palm Court nightclub while waiting at Bourda Market, filing a police complaint and calling for hate-crime legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity, which the Ministry of Social Protection condemned while affirming acceptance. Polling shows shifting norms: the 2013 CADRES survey found 24% "hate" homosexuals, 38% "tolerant" and 25% "accepting" with 53% supporting criminalization, while the October 2022 SASOD-commissioned poll of 1,070 respondents found hatred down to 12% from 25% in 2013 and 72.4% accepting and tolerating LGBTQ persons up from 34.5%, concluding "LGBT acceptance was increasing in Guyana." No article-stated transgender-specific facilities, screening, custody or care protections are described beyond general violence and assembly facts.

sources.summary: Article 149 of Guyana's revised Constitution guarantees equality and non-discrimination, and in July 2019 the Government recognized responsibility to remove legal gaps to prevent discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity with active stakeholder dialogue toward filling them, affirmed every individual regardless of sexual orientation/gender identity has the right to live free from violence, abuse and discrimination while condemning a recent attack on a leading LGBTQ activist, and reported Society Against Sexual Orientation Discrimination cooperation with the Guyana Police Force hierarchy to retrain/train officers to respond professionally to LGBTQ complaints and service access alongside cabinet approval of a sexual and reproductive health policy inclusive of sexual orientation.

GUY.tangentialFactors:
Guyana is the only country in South America and the only mainland country in the Americas where homosexual acts remain illegal, and one of five Western-Hemisphere countries still criminalising consensual same-sex conduct. The regional comparison runs the other way on court-led reform: Belize in 2016 and Trinidad and Tobago in 2018 struck down analogous bans, routes unavailable in Guyana because of the savings clause.

Constitutional protection on sexual orientation was unanimously approved in December 2000 but denied presidential assent before the March 2001 elections after religious opposition; a 2003 reintroduction was withdrawn without progress. Legislative reform has been announced and stalled repeatedly since, including a 2012 national-debate announcement, a 2013 parliamentary commission that received submissions in 2014, a 2017 referendum proposal later described as a misunderstanding and opposed by SASOD, and a May 2019 SASOD call for the Law Reform Commission to remove archaic clauses.

Public attitudes are recorded as shifting. The 2013 CADRES survey found 24% "hate" homosexuals, 38% tolerant and 25% accepting, with 53% supporting criminalisation; LAPOP's AmericasBarometer score rose from 7.2 in 2010 to 20.6 in 2017 on a 0-100 scale against an Americas average of 26.8; a 2022 poll recorded 72% acceptance and 13 percentage points less hostility than in 2013.

Pride mobilisation has proceeded with state tolerance. The first parade took place on 2 June 2018 in Georgetown without violent incident despite a demand from a ministers' fellowship for a ban, followed by a 2019 festival with a 1 June parade of 200 under police protection during which participants faced shouted insults, postponements in 2020 and 2021 for COVID-19, and the largest Georgetown event in June 2022.

A July 2019 Court of Appeal reduction of Clive Knights' 57-year murder sentence for the 2012 killing of Bert Whyte to 30 years for manslaughter after a claim of "unwanted homosexual advances" illustrates how sexual-orientation framing enters sentencing.

SUR.name: Suriname
SUR.summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful in Suriname since 1869, for men and women, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation. Article 302 of the 1910 Penal Code, which had set 18 for same-sex acts, was amended in 2015 to remove the difference.

Suriname has no statutory procedure for changing a gender marker, and trans people have obtained recognition only through litigation. On 11 January 2017 the Kantongerecht in the Eerste Kanton ordered the civil registrar to record a post-operative trans woman as female by marginal note, holding that the conflict between her socio-psychological gender role and her birth registration breached the right to respect for private life under Article 17 of the Constitution, Article 17 of the ICCPR and Article 11 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The court found that Suriname law provided no statutory procedure for a transsexual gender-marker change and interpreted Articles 17 and 64-67a of the Civil Code under Articles 106 and 137 of the Constitution to reach that result. The applicant had undergone male-to-female surgery on 22 April 2009 and obtained a forename change on 12 January 2011. The Central Bureau of Civil Affairs appealed in February 2017. On 21 January 2022 the Hof van Justitie ruled in her favour and ordered the change recorded on her birth certificate, establishing a precedent for amending sex and name in official registers. Execution of that judgment through the Ministry of Interior Affairs was still being sought, and legislation permitting change without prolonged litigation was still absent.

On 31 January 2023 the Constitutional Court described the Civil Code as very outdated, out of step with contemporary developments and urgently requiring amendment, in a case referencing the same transgender applicant.

Anti-discrimination law names sexual orientation expressly in several instruments. In March 2015 Articles 175, 175a and 176 of the Penal Code were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the ground of sexual orientation, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine. Articles 176c and 500a forbid discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation in employment and in the provision of goods and services. The Employment Equal Treatment Act 2022 extended workplace protection to gender identity for the first time. Whether Articles 175, 175a and 176 reach gender identity is not stated in the sources available here.

Constitutional protection is implicit rather than enumerated. Article 8.2 lists 'any other status' among prohibited grounds, and the government reads that clause as covering sexual orientation and gender identity, but no statute lists either as a protected ground. A July 2024 civil-society report from Projekta Foundation with VIDS and the LGBT Platform recommended a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

Partner recognition is unresolved. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised in law. On 13 February 2025 Judge Shanti Bikhari ruled that the provisions used to refuse same-sex marriage conflict with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the American Convention on Human Rights, ordered the state to amend the relevant laws and required the Bureau of Civil Affairs to register the marriages; the ruling may still be overturned. In February 2023 the Constitutional Court had held that the ban did not violate the constitution or Suriname's obligations under the American Convention, while finding the Civil Code outdated and in need of modernisation. Suriname is bound by the January 2018 judgment of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights holding that same-sex marriage is a right protected by the American Convention.

Enforcement and social conditions lag the legal position. A submission to the UN Human Rights Committee from the LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata records that LGBTI people still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation despite constitutional protection. The US State Department's 2015 human rights report for Suriname likewise records discrimination against LGBTI persons. At the Human Rights Committee's July 2024 review of Suriname, the state said its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation and pointed to monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while committee experts pressed on implementation of the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity.

KGZ.name: Kyrgyzstan
KGZ.summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Kyrgyzstan since 1998, with the age of consent set at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The constitution has explicitly banned same-sex marriage since a 2016 amendment, and no same-sex union of any kind is recognised. No non-discrimination statute protecting LGBTQ people is described in the available sources.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. A 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status removed the provision that allowed trans people to change their legal gender markers, and amendments to the Law on Civil Acts have left trans people unable to obtain legal recognition at all since 2021. A draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 and passed at first reading on 4 June 2026 would prohibit transgender individuals from changing gender markers and from accessing gender-affirming care and surgeries, and would affect minors as well.

Transition-related care is restricted by age. Clause 47 of the Law on the Protection of the Health of Citizens was amended from 2024 to bar trans people from accessing transition-related care before age 25, where the process could previously begin at 18. This directly affects trans youth and young adults.

Expression touching on same-sex relations is regulated through child-protection law. On 14 August 2023 the president signed amendments to the child protection law (Article 2-1) expanding information deemed harmful to children to include content that promotes non-traditional sexual relations; the law does not define its key terms and does not mention sexual orientation explicitly. An earlier bill criminalising expression that creates a positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations through media or networks passed its first reading 79 to 7 in October 2014 but expired without a final vote.

Enforcement targeting is documented. Police officials were reported in 2018 to be blackmailing LGBTQ people on social media and dating sites, demanding between 5,000 and 30,000 soms, roughly 70 to 500 US dollars. ECOM data records high stigma and discrimination, particularly from law enforcement. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records anti-LGBT legislative pushes accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from members of parliament.

Reports of discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people are frequent, and after the government launched legal reforms including an anti-gay propaganda law in 2014 there was a near 300 percent increase in attacks against LGBTQ people. In March 2019, after a march of about 400 people in Bishkek described as Kyrgyzstan's first gay pride march, MP Jyldyz Musabekova publicly called for participants to be beaten, though other deputies condemned her remarks.

Public LGBTQ life in the capital has contracted. Bishkek's only gay club closed in 2017, with patrons entering furtively through a derelict yard as the atmosphere worsened, and no other gay venue remained. LGBTQ people fear social ostracism from friends and family, especially in rural areas.

On care access, an ECOM study published in 2024 examines trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and hormone replacement therapy across the region, covering Kyrgyzstan, and includes information for trans migrants.
KGZ.outOfScopeNotes:
Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 Kyrgyzstan chapter contains no content on transgender prisoners or prison housing; its only prison references concern journalists and opposition activists sentenced to prison terms, covering media repression and freedom of expression rather than the placement or conditions of trans detainees. The placement and treatment of trans detainees in Kyrgyz custody is not sourced.

The 2014 bill criminalising expression creating a positive attitude toward non-traditional sexual relations expired without a final vote, so its status is unresolved rather than enacted. The draft law proposed on 30 January 2026 has passed only a first reading and is not in force. The 2023 child protection amendments do not define their key terms and do not mention sexual orientation explicitly, leaving the scope of the restriction unresolved on the face of the text.

TGEU Trans Rights Index Map 2024: Kyrgyzstan (2021) joined Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia in removing the right to legal gender recognition; for Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan the 'bare minimum' of not banning recognition is all they score — the regional floor on trans legal status.

The same index scores the country together with neighbouring jurisdictions at only the bare minimum of not banning recognition, which the index treats as the regional floor on trans legal status.

TJK.name: Tajikistan
TJK.summary:
Consensual same-sex relations have been legal in Tajikistan since May 1998 and sex between women was never criminalised; the age of consent is 16 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation. That legality is not backed by protection. No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the country's first anti-discrimination statute, adopted in July 2022, dropped both grounds and retains only "sex". A monitoring review covering 2024 finds the law only partially aligned with international standards, and a legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners records barriers and gaps for gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, including situations where the written law protects but practice does not.

Police keep a register of LGBTIQ people, introduced in 2016; a separate account dates a government registry of "proven" LGBT persons to 2017. A regional review covering 2024 describes officers luring LGBT people into staged meetings in order to enter them in the database, harvesting contact lists from their social media and extracting money, with more than ten such cases recorded in the Sughd region.

Raids carried out in 2022 and 2023 produced forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges. Documented police conduct includes ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion. In 2024 a regional monitoring organisation recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people, among them arbitrary arrest, blackmail and extortion. That is a count of cases an organisation was able to record, not a rate, and no denominator accompanies it.

Gender-affirming medical services are not available inside Tajikistan, and a trans visitor cannot obtain hormone therapy or surgical care locally. Trans people who can travel go abroad to transition. Most doctors in the country have no expertise in the treatments involved. A 2024 regional study of trans people's access to medical services, covering HIV prevention and treatment and hormone therapy, includes a Tajikistan country coordinator and carries guidance for trans migrants. Patients report disrespectful treatment from medical staff.

Legal gender change is blocked in practice. Tajik law permits reassignment on some documents, but medical institutions issue no official papers for that purpose, so a trans visitor has no route to correcting a local record.

No relationship-recognition framework exists. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status cannot have it recognised, and same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections that attach to marriage.

Public expression of support for LGBT people is effectively suppressed, and public attitudes have been described as entirely negative. Homophobic and transphobic statements by politicians form part of ordinary political life, and the country's senior religious authority, the Supreme Mufti Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has called same-sex relations a disaster, condemned states that legalise same-sex marriage and spoken against rights activists and anti-discrimination legislation.

Where a person is known or suspected of being LGBT, disclosure brings physical and psychological abuse, including from police. Reporting from 2013, fifteen years after decriminalisation, found very little tolerance and described the community as one of the most closed in society.
TJK.outOfScopeNotes:
Prison conditions and placement of trans detainees are unresolved. A human-rights review published in 2025 records detention material concerning opposition figures and deportees only; no conditions or placement of trans detainees are documented.

Accounts differ on when police began registering LGBT people: one dates the register to 2016, another to a government registry of "proven" LGBT persons in 2017. Neither describes how the register is maintained or who may be entered in it.

Recorded violation counts depend on what a monitoring organisation can document from a community that reports anonymously. The 27 cases recorded for 2024 are not a prevalence measure, and no denominator is available.

No findings are available on LGBT minors, education-sector policies or school environments. Visa, entry and border-screening rules bearing on trans travellers to Tajikistan are not documented in the sources available.

TKM.name: Turkmenistan
TKM.summary:
Consensual sex between adult men is a criminal offence under Article 135 of the Criminal Code. The maximum sentence is two years' imprisonment, with a further two to five years in a labour camp possible under some readings of the provision. Article 19 permits increased penalties for repeat convictions. A 2019 amendment raised the maximum above the two-year ceiling set in 1997, and ILGA-Europe's 2025 annual review records that the Criminal Code adopted in April 2022 retained the sodomy provisions while increasing both the severity and the scope of the punishments attached to them.

Trans people are an unacknowledged category in Turkmen law. No provision addresses gender recognition and no legal mechanism exists to change identity documents. The same silence covers women who have relationships with women, for whom no penal provision exists. The practical exposure for a trans visitor turns on how the authorities read their birth-sex status: a trans woman whose identity documents record a male sex, or a trans man in a relationship the authorities would read as between two men, falls within the scope of Article 135.

There is no anti-discrimination legislation. The government has rejected requests to adopt one made through three Universal Periodic Reviews, and in February 2021 told the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights that it intended to 'study the option of introducing anti-discrimination legislation'. In UN human rights dialogue it has justified its framework by arguing that any deviation poses a potential threat to the fabric of Turkmen traditions and society.

Enforcement of Article 135 was rare before Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow became president in 2006. Reported consequences since then include state-sponsored violence and torture during criminal investigation, interrogation that witnesses describe as grossly humiliating, and vigilante attacks that are especially common in prison. ILGA-Europe reports that torture and inhuman treatment remain present throughout the country, with relatives reporting LGBTI people among those subjected to them. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report on Turkmenistan lists laws criminalising consensual same-sex conduct between adults among the country's significant human rights issues, alongside officials in the security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity.

Suspects in Article 135 cases face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals. In October 2019 a gay doctor was tortured by the state apparatus over a prolonged period before temporarily disappearing. In May 2020 several well-known figures from the modelling industry were arrested on charges of homosexuality.

The persecution documented in asylum proceedings is a measure of what people flee. In 2007 a US law clinic secured asylum for a Turkmen woman persecuted for being a lesbian and for her political opinions, believed to be the first such grant for a lesbian from Turkmenistan. In 2019 attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared imprisonment and torture.

A 2020 civil-society submission to the UN human rights review process concluded that LGBT people in Turkmenistan have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights, and identified Article 135 as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination.
TKM.outOfScopeNotes:
The precise penalty structure of the April 2022 Criminal Code is not set out in the available sources; the increase in severity and scope is reported without the amended text.

Whether the February 2021 stated intention to study anti-discrimination legislation produced a draft or any legislative step is not sourced.

Data on these issues is scarce: the media is entirely state-owned and no civil society organisations operate in the country, so incident counts and enforcement frequency are not independently verifiable.

No trans-specific healthcare access findings, and no youth- or minor-specific care access findings, appear in the sources reviewed.

No gender-recognition procedure is documented in the sources. The absence of a legal category for trans people is reported, but administrative practice at entry, in screening or in detention is not documented.

SYR.name: Syria
SYR.summary:
Syria's Penal Code criminalises the conduct a trans visitor may be read as engaging in. Article 520 of the 1949 code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" and carries up to three years' imprisonment; Article 517 covers public indecency. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that both provisions are applied to women as well as men, so a trans visitor is reachable under the same articles irrespective of legal sex marker or presentation.

Legal gender recognition is not available in Syria, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. No anti-discrimination protection exists in any field. The state's response to same-sex conduct is criminalisation, which removes the complaint route a visitor would otherwise have after an assault, a refusal of service or a document dispute.

Enforcement has fallen on gatherings. In the weeks before 23 June 2010, Syrian authorities raided several private parties and arrested more than 25 men; most were charged with homosexual acts, others with drug offences, and charges also included encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Reporting from Damascus in October 2020 records that homosexuality and public decency offences are illegal there and quotes a 36-year-old describing meetings with friends in gay-friendly cafes as happening "only in whispers".

Violence against LGBTQ people, including beatings and torture, occurs frequently, and non-state armed actors are among the perpetrators. Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State have both attacked LGBTQ people, and the Islamic State executed people in areas under its control on accusations of sodomy.

Armed and political figures have endorsed harsher treatment rather than restraint. A Free Syrian Army member, Nasradeen Ahme, said he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while the secular figure Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would answer "no way" to gays claiming rights.

Official stigma reaches health care. In 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly described HIV/AIDS as divine punishment for fornication and homosexuality.

Organised social space for LGBTQ people has been eliminated. The region's only gay tour, running between Damascus and Aleppo, stopped operating, and the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus were eradicated. The Aleppo and Damascus hammams that hosted the pre-2011 tour, described by its organiser as a place where "we never had any problems", ended that activity with the civil war.

sources.summary:
Expression is criminalised and chilled: Article 520 of the 1949 penal code prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" with up to three years' imprisonment, and a 2010 police crackdown arrested over 25 men on charges including homosexual acts, encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Public cultural expression has been squeezed since the civil war: the region's only gay tour (Damascus and Aleppo, run by Bertho) stopped operating, and the underground LGBTQ hubs of Damascus have been eradicated. Hammams in Aleppo and Damascus were the main venues of the pre-2011 tour, described by its organiser as "a paradise for gay people" where "we never had any problems," but the civil war ended that activity. Digital expression persists anonymously: the "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020, later moving to Twitter, with university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographing themselves by a faculty building under #oneofyou, most using fake accounts for fear of being identified; reactions ranged from defence to threats of blood before it faded amid COVID-19. Earlier literary expression includes Nizar Qabbani's 1971 poem "The Evil Poem," describing a relationship between two women.

Health care access is shaped by official stigma and under-provision: in 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected and offered free medicines, a figure NGOs estimated at least five times too low, and the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs, and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational program for youth in secondary schooling; comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist. Prevalence is low, under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 reported cases through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987. Physical safety is also a care barrier: beatings and torture of LGBTQ people occur frequently, including attacks by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State, which reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in its areas, an issue reported to the UN Security Council in August 2015 in the Council's first-ever discussion of LGBTQ concerns.

There is no anti-discrimination protection; the state criminalises same-sex conduct instead. Violence comes from non-state armed actors as well, and political actors endorse harsher treatment: Free Syrian Army member Nasradeen Ahme said he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, while secular leader Miral Bioredda said Syrian society would say "no way" to gays claiming rights. In the diaspora, Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees face discrimination and exclusion in host countries based on race, language, skin colour and religious background.

Youth are both a target and an organising force. Abdulrahman Akkad, a Syrian young man in Germany, came out publicly on Facebook in July 2017 while under family pressure to marry against his will, and his case was raised in the German Parliament's 2020 human rights session. The 2017 film Mr. Gay Syria follows two gay Syrian refugees rebuilding their lives.

LBY.name: Libya
LBY.summary:
Libya's Penal Code penalises "illicit sexual intercourse" and "indecent acts", and the indecent-acts provisions carry up to five years' imprisonment. Same-sex relations are not legal for men or women. The sources identify no provision that criminalises homosexuality by that name; enforcement instead runs through the general morality offences. A regional guide published by The Guardian on 21 June 2016 lists Libya among the states where imprisonment is the penalty and notes that where no specific law exists, other laws are used.

Cairo 52's country review records de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process itself, whether social, medical or surgical, enforced through the same indecent-acts and illicit-intercourse provisions. Religious rulings issued in recent years have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible, which narrows the ground on which a trans person can seek or be seen to have undergone care.

Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that same-sex relations are not legal for men or women, that the indecent-acts provisions carry up to five years' imprisonment, and that no legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exist. Same-sex relationships are not legally recognised, and legal gender recognition is unavailable: official identity documents cannot be changed. A visitor whose documents and presentation differ has no domestic procedure to fall back on.

Violence against people perceived as gender-nonconforming has been documented in territory held by armed groups. Human Rights Watch reported on 8 June 2015 that Islamic State killed men accused of homosexuality in areas it controlled, including Derna, where a young man was targeted by local Islamists for effeminate dress and "contemporary" clothes; the case dates from November 2014. D+C reported in June 2015 that Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in Derna in April 2015, and concluded that conditions for homosexuals in Libya were worsening as militias controlled territory.

Earlier vigilante violence is also recorded. On 26 November 2012, HuffPost reported that twelve men accused of being gay faced torture and threats of death at the hands of a Libyan militia, in the early post-revolutionary period.

A 2010 case heard in France concerned a Libyan girl who was jailed, raped and returned to her family for a forced marriage after she stated online that she was gay.
LBY.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2010 asylum account gives no age, schooling or student status for the person concerned, and the sources do not establish whether the case produced a change in Libyan practice.

The sources give a maximum of five years for indecent acts but no maximum term for illicit sexual intercourse, and no Libyan statute criminalising homosexuality by name is identified.

Reporting from Derna in 2015 moved only through the mosque, so the number of killings and assaults recorded for that period is likely incomplete and no reliable count is available.

YEM.name: Yemen
YEM.summary:
Yemen's Penal Code 1994 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Article 264 defines homosexuality between men as anal penetration and prescribes 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment for participants who are not married; the article prescribes a different penalty where the participants are married. Article 268 criminalises premeditated lesbianism and carries up to three years' imprisonment. A visitor should treat any same-sex conduct, not only conduct between men, as criminal.

The Constitution of the Republic of Yemen, as amended in 2001, does not address LGBTQ rights, and the state provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The Constitution guarantees human rights to all citizens only on condition that legislation be compatible with Islamic Shariah law, which leaves no recognised legal basis for a discrimination claim or for official protection.

Which authority enforces the law depends on where the visitor is. The penal provisions are applied in areas under the internationally recognised government's control; other parts of the country sit under different factions in the ongoing conflict, so both the applicable law and the enforcing authority vary by territory.

The documented prosecutions of 2024 came from courts run by the Houthi authorities. On 23 January 2024 the criminal court in Dhamar sentenced nine people to death, seven by stoning and two by crucifixion, and gave 23 others terms of between six months and ten years for 'homosexuality' and 'spreading immorality'. On 1 February 2024 a court in Ibb handed down further death sentences. Between them the two courts sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or imprisonment over same-sex conduct, and Amnesty International called for an immediate halt to the executions and the release of those charged. A provincial court is separately recorded as having sentenced several people to death for homosexual acts during the same year.

Routine enforcement is uneven. Erosion of the rule of law, a humanitarian crisis in which 19.5 million people need assistance, and growing militia influence mean the penal provisions are rarely applied in ordinary cases, but the same provisions are invoked to justify civilians taking action themselves. A visitor therefore faces not only the possibility of prosecution but the possibility of violence by private individuals who treat the law as licence.

Social enforcement operates alongside the statute. In the capital, a gay man described concealing his appearance, including covering long hair, and still finding his position precarious; the account describes a conservative society with no place for people known to be gay while the law treats homosexuality as punishable by death. Enforcement of this kind does not depend on a charge being brought.

Yemen is one of 14 countries covered by Human Rights Watch's 2018 study of LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited. The same study records 'breach of modesty' laws used against expression, which reaches public presentation as well as sexual conduct.
YEM.outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty Article 264 prescribes for married participants is not settled across the sources. Wikipedia states that married men face death under the article; Human Rights Watch and GayLawNet describe the article as prescribing a different penalty for married participants without specifying what it is. The capital exposure of a married participant is therefore unresolved on this inventory.

Whether the death sentences handed down in 2024 were carried out is not recorded in any source here, and no figure for the number of people currently held on same-sex conduct charges is available.

No source in this inventory documents a rule on gender markers on Yemeni identity documents, a restriction on transition-related medical care, or a provision governing access to single-sex facilities. The absence of such material is a gap in the sources, not evidence that no rule exists.

Territorial control is contested and shifts with the conflict. The sources establish that the penal provisions are applied in government-controlled areas and that other areas sit under different factions, but they do not map which governorates fall under which authority at any given date.

The account of social conditions in the capital dates from 2013. No later source in this inventory updates it, and the 2018 finding that no activists could be identified is likewise several years old.

HRW World Report 2026, Yemen chapter (events of 2025): its Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section states Yemen's penal code prohibits same-sex relations — Article 264 punishes anal sex with 100 lashes and one year in prison if participants are not married, with the article prescribing differently if married — alongside world's-worst humanitarian crisis (19.5M needing aid) and Houthi/government factional control affecting where law applies.

Amnesty International (Feb 2024): two Huthi-run courts in Yemen sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct — the Dhamar criminal court (23 Jan) sentenced nine to death (seven by stoning, two by crucifixion) with 23 more given 6 months-10 years for 'homosexuality'/'spreading immorality', and an Ibb court (1 Feb) handed further death sentences; Amnesty demanded an immediate halt.

GayLawNet Yemen laws page: consensual same-sex sex is unlawful under Penal Code 1994 Article 264 — homosexuality between men defined as anal penetration; unmarried men punishable with 100 lashes (and up to one year's imprisonment per the statute); the canonical statute citation for Yemen's criminalisation.

BTN.name: Bhutan
BTN.summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, removing Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions that carried one month to one year of imprisonment and had gone unenforced for at least 15 years. The lower house voted 43-1 for repeal in June 2019; the upper house reinserted the ban; a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. No reversal has followed.

The repeal created no protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics. LGBTIQ organisations may register, though activists describe the process as lengthy and burdensome.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. Administrative changes to a gender marker are suspended for lack of standardised guidelines; the pathway documented in official material requires a transgender applicant to submit a medical note together with a supporting letter from a civil society organisation.

Enforcement does not match the formal legal position. Bhutan Broadcasting Service reported in November 2024 that trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault as the general population. A 49-year-old trans woman described having nowhere to report violence: police dismissed her complaints on the ground that her identity card records a male marker, treating the matter as violence between two men. Families press victims to accept the outcome as fate, and referrals routed through the LGBTQIA+ committee move slowly. The practical result is impunity for anti-trans violence.

Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a setting where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served. Official guidance cuts the other way: the Bhutan Medical and Health Council's Code of Professional Fidelity, issued in 2021, protects sexual orientation, and the 2020 Standard Operating Procedure for Gender Based Violence Prevention and Response requires providers to deliver age-appropriate, culturally sensitive and sexual-orientation- and gender-identity-sensitive care, with case managers giving tailored support to people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities.

No form of legal recognition exists for same-sex relationships. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Bhutanese law cannot have a partner recognised in any legal proceeding. A marriage bill drafted with gender-neutral pronouns was discussed in the 2018 summer parliamentary session but deferred because of that year's election; the community expected the conversation to resume under the incoming government, and no sourced outcome has followed.
BTN.outOfScopeNotes:
Official material describes a gender-marker change pathway requiring a medical note and a civil society supporting letter, while other reporting states that administrative marker changes are suspended for want of standardised guidelines. Which procedure is currently operative is unresolved.

The November 2024 figure that trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault is reported without the underlying survey basis or comparison data, so the precision of the multiplier cannot be verified.

Whether the 2018 gender-neutral marriage bill will be revived has no sourced outcome.

LAO.name: Laos
LAO.summary:
Laos has never formally criminalised consensual same-sex conduct. The penal code was modelled on the French system at independence in the 1950s and contains no sodomy offence, unlike neighbouring jurisdictions that retained colonial-era prohibitions.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution does not expressly address either. At the 35th session of the Universal Periodic Review on 21 January 2020, Malta's ambassador recommended that Laos improve LGBTI rights and involve LGBTI representatives in decision-making, and Iceland's ambassador recommended comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and gender identity. In March 2025, National Assembly member Maifong Maixai proposed amending Article 36 of the 2025 revised Constitution to widen the room for non-discrimination protections for gender-diverse people.

The age of consent is 15 and does not vary by sexual orientation or gender identity.

State practice is to tolerate or ignore LGBTI people unless they campaign for LGBTI rights or are judged too publicly immodest or indecent. A 2014 decree prohibited criticism of government policies, and the government has blocked access to LGBTI-themed webpages. An October 2018 Al Jazeera investigation described a crackdown on social media in which influential Facebook users faced retribution for their posts, and reported that 'Proud to be us Laos' is the country's only LGBTI advocacy group.

Discussion of LGBTI issues in the media is rare, with trans people visible mainly as entertainment.

In 2013 the United States Department of State reported that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation, and against people living with HIV/AIDS, was prevalent.

The European Union marked the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia in Vientiane, giving LGBTI rights visible diplomatic backing in the country.
LAO.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources give no detail on school policy, bullying, or education-specific protections for LGBTI youth.

Healthcare access for trans people and trans youth is not described in the sources.

The Law on Electronic Data Protection (No. 25/NA, 12 May 2017) lists sexual behaviour among prohibited categories of data; whether the law covers gender identity is not stated.

The outcome of the March 2025 proposal to amend Article 36, and any follow-up to the 2020 Universal Periodic Review recommendations, is not established in the sources.

TLS.name: Timor-Leste
TLS.summary:
Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex sexual conduct. Both male and female same-sex activity has been lawful since 1975, and the age of consent is 14 irrespective of sexual orientation or gender. The sources record no anti-trans statute, no arrest pattern and no police targeting of transgender people, and no law barring trans people from public facilities, health care or employment.

No legal gender recognition procedure is documented in the sources reviewed. The operative document for a trans visitor is the passport or identity card issued at home, including any marker changed there; there is no domestic route to alter or regularise a marker while in the country.

Health policy is required to be non-discriminatory on gender identity grounds. Law No. 13/2022, the second amendment to the Health System Law, provides at Article 3-2(o) that health policy must ensure access to family planning, reproductive, school, visual, oral and mental health care and early diagnosis without discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. Reported practice diverges: LGBTI people are described as often verbally abused and discriminated against in some public services, medical centres among them.

Protection instruments issued in 2024 name transgender people explicitly. Ministerial Decree No. 11/MSSI/V/2024 requires children and young people, regardless of gender, nationality, sexual orientation, religion or disability, to have adequate access to protection services and protection from sexual and gender-based violence, abuse and exploitation; its standard operating procedure defines non-binary gender identity, includes transgender children within its definition of LGBTI children, states that transgender children may be at greater risk of prejudice, stigma, violence or difficulty accessing humanitarian services, and requires case managers to respond to needs on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation. Ministerial Decree No. 10/MSSI/V/2024 on gender-based violence extends protection expressly to lesbian, bisexual, transgender and intersex people, bars social workers from discriminating on grounds of gender or sexual orientation, and prohibits revealing a person's gender identity or sexual orientation without authorisation. Law No. 6/2023, Article 6(n), gives children and young people equal rights and prohibits discrimination based on sex, gender and sexual orientation.

Hate-crime and non-discrimination law covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. Bias based on sexual orientation has been an aggravating circumstance for crimes since 2009. There is no general anti-discrimination law on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; a clause barring discrimination on sexual orientation was removed from the draft Constitution by 52 votes of 88 before the Constitution took effect in 2002. Sectoral provisions reach sexual orientation only: Article 3(3) of the Penal Execution Regime Decree-Law No. 14/2014 requires imprisonment to be executed impartially without discrimination based on sexual orientation, Article 2(i) of the Land Law No. 13/2017 lists sexual orientation among vulnerable groups, and Article 3 of the trafficking law No. 3/2017 requires victim protection without discrimination on that ground.

Police conduct rules follow the same pattern. Decree-Law No. 44/2020, Article 13(1), requires respectful treatment without discrimination based on sexual orientation; Decree-Law No. 69/2022, Articles 15(6)(f) and 18(b), bans such discrimination; and Decree-Law No. 35/2024, Articles 16(f) and 17(b), requires missions and action without hindrance or discrimination by reason of sexual orientation. Physical abuse in public or by public authorities is described as uncommon, but no source documents enforcement of these provisions in a case involving a transgender person.

Partnership recognition is closed. Article 1467 of the Civil Code, Law No. 10/2011, defines marriage as a contract between two people of different sex, and Article 1517 declares a marriage contracted by two people of the same sex legally non-existent. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no spousal recognition, and no source indicates that such a partner can obtain residence, next-of-kin standing or medical decision-making authority on that basis. Protection may still be available: the Domestic Violence Law No. 07/2010 treats people who live or have lived in conditions analogous to spouses as family, without requiring cohabitation, and covers intimate relationships regardless of gender.

Violence against transgender people is documented as family and community-based rather than state-directed. CODIVA records that transgender members of the community are particularly vulnerable to harassment and discrimination, and that transgender students are more likely to be bullied and to drop out at secondary level. A November study for Rede Feto with lesbian and bisexual women and transgender men in Dili and Bobonaro documented corrective rape, physical and psychological abuse, ostracism, discrimination and marginalisation by family members. A 2017 survey of 57 young lesbian and bisexual women and transgender men found that 86 per cent had experienced physical and psychological violence, including domestic violence, forced marriages and attempts by family members to change their sexual orientation or gender identity; the sample is small and self-selected, so the figure describes that group rather than a population rate.

Senior officials have publicly endorsed the annual Pride march. The first parade, in 2017, drew a televised endorsement from the Prime Minister. A second parade was held in Dili on 20 July 2018, and the third, on 12 July 2019, drew an estimated 3,000 participants, six times the 2017 turnout, with President Francisco Guterres stating "I am a President for all people". Reporting on the same period records day-to-day rejection, including hostile messages sent to the family of the 2017 organiser.

A 2017 report by the US State Department recorded that same-sex conduct was not criminalised but that the law provided no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, that transgender people remained particularly vulnerable to societal discrimination, stigma and violence limiting access to employment, education and health care, and that no government action had been taken to prevent discrimination or violence.

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.summary:
Section 210 of the Penal Code prohibits male same-sex sexual activity. Anal or oral sex, whether heterosexual or homosexual, is punishable as sodomy with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and other same-sex sexual acts carry up to three years. Sex between women is not restricted by law. As of 2024 there is no legal recognition of transgender or gender-diverse identities, and the criminal penalties attach to sexual acts rather than to transgender identity as such.

Enforcement is sporadic. No prosecutions directed at LGBTQ people were recorded in 2012, but arrests occurred in 2015 and 2022. In the 2015 case a man charged with indecent acts between males pleaded guilty and received a suspended sentence with community service and mandatory counselling; in 2022 two men were arrested after having sex. Decriminalisation was described as not a priority in 2011, and in 2023 the government confirmed it had no intention of repealing the laws criminalising male homosexuality, stating that existing protections against violence and abuse were sufficient.

The Asian Development Bank's 2024 assessment of the legal status of sexual and gender minorities in 17 countries in Asia and the Pacific includes Papua New Guinea, with decriminalisation among the topics examined. The criminal-law position is therefore a live question in regional legal review rather than a settled matter.

Violence against trans and gender-diverse people in Port Moresby is documented. Gay and transgender people in the capital are commonly raped or beaten, in some cases by police officers, according to reporting by the documentary maker Vlad Sokhin broadcast by ABC News in October 2014. A 2011 study found police were one of the main sources of violence against men who have sex with men and trans people. Abuse commonly continues even when reported, because of the imbalance of power between victims and police, and victims are often framed as perpetrators. A 24-year-old gay man described being pelted with stones and bottles.

Hanuabada, a village built over the sea on the outskirts of Port Moresby, functions as a sanctuary. Residents live openly there, and transgender people wear women's clothes in the street without retaliation. LGBTQ people subjected to violence elsewhere in the country, including in the capital, frequently move to the village.

Transgender Papua New Guineans use the Tok Pisin word palopa, reportedly derived from the name of the American singer Jennifer Lopez, for a cultural and traditional third gender, and the Sambia recognise a traditional third gender, kwolu-aatmwol, literally a male thing transforming into a female thing. The words lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender carry heavy stigma. LGBTQ people report discrimination in daily life and difficulty finding work. Homophobia is widespread, and homosexuality is more accepted in coastal areas than in the Highlands, although no source documents societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.
PNG.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources state no transgender-specific rule on identity documents or markers, airport or police screening, detention and custody, facilities, or access to transition-related care. How the criminal provisions would be applied to a trans visitor, as distinct from the general prohibition on male same-sex acts, is not documented.

Prosecution data are limited to individual cases in 2012, 2015 and 2022; no systematic enforcement statistics were identified. The observation that homosexuality is more accepted in coastal areas than in the Highlands concerns LGBTQ people generally and is not documented as trans-specific.

The Guardian (13 Jan 2017) on HRW's annual world-report assessment of PNG: the government of Peter O'Neill has failed to protect women and children and to respond to corruption and police violence — 'police abuse, including of children, continues to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse'.

Sorcery accusations, often linked to HIV deaths, were used to conceal murders and to mitigate sentences, and police routinely took no action.

A newspaper reported in January 2017 on the same organisation's annual assessment that police abuse in the country, including of children, continued to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse. These findings concern the general enforcement climate rather than transgender-specific targeting, but they indicate the low likelihood of a complaint being pursued.

LGBTQ people report discrimination in daily life and difficulty finding work, and the vocabulary for sexual and gender minorities carries heavy stigma.

Violence drives internal movement. BWA.name: Botswana
BWA.summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Botswana. On 11 June 2019 the High Court unanimously declared Section 164 of the Penal Code unconstitutional in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General. The Government appealed in July 2019; the Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the appeal on 29 November 2021, writing that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." On 26 March 2026 paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164 were formally deleted from the statute book by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026, made under the Revision of the Laws Act. Only carnal knowledge of an animal remains an unnatural offence under that section.

Before June 2019 the exposure rested on Section 164(a) and (c), which criminalised sodomy whether heterosexual or homosexual, applied to both men and women, and carried a maximum of seven years' imprisonment. Prosecutions were rare. The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report found that police "did not target same-sex activity," and former President Festus Mogae said he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his ten years in office, while declining to change a law he said would cost him an election.

Legal gender recognition rests on two 2017 High Court rulings. In September 2017 the court held that the Registrar of National Registration's refusal to change a transgender man's gender marker was unreasonable and violated his constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection of the law, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment. The Government announced it would appeal, then decided against it in December and issued him an identity document reflecting his gender identity. In a parallel case heard in December 2017, transgender woman and activist Tshepo Ricki Kgositau, who had undergone gender confirmation surgery in December 2016, won a ruling that the Government must recognise her gender identity; she received a female identity card after a four-year legal battle and dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana."

The administrative route remains unsettled. In its 43rd-session Universal Periodic Review outcome in May 2023, Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendation to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition, and the review recorded that "a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced" (para 570). Botswana also declined the recommendation to repeal Penal Code Section 167, which covers same-sex conduct between women.

In June 2019 the High Court held that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation; legal commentator Carmel Rickard read this as giving LGBTQ Batswana a stronger constitutionally based argument against discrimination. The Employment Act 1982 has prohibited employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2010.

Botswana recognises no same-sex marriage or civil union. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classified as same-sex under local law has no route to partnership recognition, and no spousal immigration or next-of-kin status follows from it.

Documented violence against trans people is absent from the record rather than shown to be high. The U.S. State Department's 2011 report found no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity that year, and recorded societal discrimination against LGBT people. Afrobarometer's measure of tolerance rose from 43 per cent in 2016 to 50 per cent in 2021 of respondents who would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour. Official signals are mixed: in February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power; President Ian Khama deported American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson in September 2016, saying "we don't want hate speech in this country"; and in November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and deserved protection. LEGABIBO and activists described the Government's 2019 appeal as "an affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia."

Community infrastructure is legally established. The 2016 Court of Appeal ordered the registration of LEGABIBO, Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation, on freedom of association, expression and assembly grounds; it runs advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health and HIV work, and maintains Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre assessed in May 2024 that implementation of these precedents across Botswana and Namibia "has not been satisfactory so far."

A draft constitutional amendment would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities. During June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct. Civic groups criticise the wider review process; the intersex provision nonetheless signals movement toward broader protection.
BWA.outOfScopeNotes:

Whether an administrative gender-recognition procedure now exists is not sourced beyond the 2023 review's finding that none had been introduced.

No post-2011 data on violence against trans people in Botswana appears in the inventory; the 2011 U.S. State Department finding of no reported violence is the most recent figure available here, and no trans-specific homicide or assault rate with a denominator is recorded.

The sources do not record whether the Employment Act's sexual-orientation provision has been interpreted to cover gender identity, nor whether it has been enforced in any trans-specific complaint.

The 2011 U.S. State Department report's other findings (violence against women, prison conditions, discrimination against San people) are not trans-specific and are not carried here.
