NAM.name: Namibia
NAM.summary:
The criminal-law layer is unsettled. Sodomy and "unnatural sexual offences" appeared as grounds in the Immigration Act until the High Court of Windhoek declared those references unconstitutional and invalid on 21 June 2024; the government appealed in July 2024. The colonial-era sodomy offence itself remained on the statute book and was not believed to have been used since independence in 1990, and the government told the UN Human Rights Committee it had no intention of repealing it. A December 2024 UNDP review records that Namibia's courts decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2024 and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, while noting that implementation remains contested.

Public displays of affection between two men can still be treated as "immoral" behaviour punishable under the Combating of Immoral Practices Act of 1980.

Partner recognition is the sharpest exposure. On 16 May 2023 the Supreme Court ruled that same-sex marriages performed abroad must be recognised under the Immigration Act, giving non-Namibian spouses the same residence rights as opposite-sex spouses. Compliance has not followed: immigration officials told litigant Daniel Digashu that the ruling covers only the couples who brought the case, and he is issued a visitor's visa on every exit from the country. Gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than to "all persons". In December 2024 parliament passed an act explicitly forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad, overriding the 2023 judgment. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law cannot rely on the 2023 ruling to secure a spouse's residence rights.

Earlier residence litigation produced the same individualised outcomes. In 2001 a Namibian woman's German wife, Elisabeth Frank, won a Supreme Court permanent residence permit without the court endorsing same-sex relationships, and in January 2018 Daniel Digashu won a court petition to enter Namibia while his case was reviewed.

Article 10 of the constitution does not list gender identity or sexual orientation. A 2017 analysis by the Southern Africa Litigation Centre argues that "other status" should be read to include them, following the UN Human Rights Committee's position.

Health care is governed by professional rules that bar discrimination. Health professionals are bound by the Ethical Guidelines for Health Professionals (2010, Health Professions Councils of Namibia), whose Sections 2.1.5, 2.6 and 3.2.2 require that personal beliefs not prejudice patient care and prohibit discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, and the Ministry of Health and Social Services' Patient Charter makes "Impartiality" a core value requiring equal treatment irrespective of sex, gender and sexuality. Against that, the 2009 ministry regulations on scope of practice for clinical and educational psychologists still treat "sexual and gender identity" as disorders.

Media regulation offers a limited protection. The Broadcasting Code for Broadcasting Licensees 2018 (General Notice No. 602) bars licensees from broadcasting material that advocates hatred based on gender or sexual orientation, sanctions violence or unlawful conduct on those grounds, and prohibits material likely to incite hatred or severe ridicule against persons because of sexual orientation where that constitutes incitement to harm (Sections 5, 7(2), 7(3)). The UN Human Rights Committee recommended in 2016 that Namibia legislate against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Public assembly by LGBT people has proceeded without government impediment. OutRight Namibia organised the country's first pride parades: the Windhoek march of December 2013 drew about 100 people, around 200 marched in June 2017, and hundreds marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund in December 2018. The first Namibian Lesbian Festival was held in Windhoek in November 2017, bringing more than sixty young lesbians from eight regions together for a week of public poetry, story, music, drama and dance, and was repeated in November 2018.
NAM.outOfScopeNotes:
The government's July 2024 appeal against the High Court of Windhoek's 21 June 2024 ruling on the Immigration Act references has no recorded outcome in the sources reviewed; whether those references are currently enforceable is unresolved.

How the December 2024 act forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad operates against the 16 May 2023 Supreme Court judgment in practice is not sourced beyond the fact of its passage.

The 2017 Southern Africa Litigation Centre analysis of Article 10 and section 7B predates the 2023 marriage-recognition judgment and the 2024 decriminalisation ruling and has not been updated in the material reviewed.

The 2018 account of the sodomy offence being unused since independence is dated and rests on the absence of known prosecutions rather than a formal assurance.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Namibia' (2017): constitutional analysis - Article 10 omits gender identity/sexual orientation but 'other status' should include them per the UN Human Rights Committee; section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 allows gender-marker changes on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and 'not problematic' per the Legal Assistance Centre (2015).

Mambaonline (28 May 2018): Out-Right Namibia opened Namibia's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May (IDAHOT) at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. Health professionals are bound by the Ethical Guidelines for Health Professionals (2010, Health Professions Councils of Namibia), whose Sections 2.1.5, 2.6 and 3.2.2 require that personal beliefs not prejudice patient care and bar discrimination including on sexual orientation, while the Ministry of Health and Social Services' Patient Charter makes "Impartiality" a core value requiring equal treatment irrespective of sex, gender and sexuality. The 2009 Ministry regulations on scope of practice for clinical and educational psychologists still treat "sexual and gender identity" as disorders. The Namibian Gays and Lesbian Movement organises educational programs to raise awareness among LGBTQ Namibians, and MPower Community Trust provides sexual health awareness for gay and bisexual men. The SWAPO Party Youth League is listed among parties opposing LGBTQ rights; the government told the UN it had no intention of repealing the sodomy law, and in late 2024 parliament passed a law forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad.

NAM.tangentialFactors:
Political hostility to LGBT rights is organised rather than incidental. In June 2014 a Namibian party modelled on South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original. The SWAPO Party Youth League is listed among parties opposing LGBTQ rights.

The op-ed by Daniel Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre attributes part of the compliance failure to reporting that amplified the non-implementation, alongside a hostile parliamentary response of marriage bills.

Namibia sits inside the African Commission's Resolution 275 framework on LGBT rights, which the December 2024 UNDP review treats as the regional reference point for the country's decriminalisation and residency-recognition developments.
NAM.localsOnly:
Gender-marker changes are available under section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 on medical evidence, handled case by case; the Legal Assistance Centre described the process in 2015 as not problematic.

Resident health and support infrastructure is thin but present. OutRight Namibia opened the country's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May 2018 at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West, offering HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, and mental and sexual and reproductive health services, with plans to add legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. The Namibian Gays and Lesbian Movement runs educational programmes to raise awareness among LGBTQ Namibians, and MPower Community Trust provides sexual health awareness for gay and bisexual men.

NAM.blindSummary:
The criminal-law layer is unsettled. Sodomy and "unnatural sexual offences" appeared as grounds in the immigration act until a high court declared those references unconstitutional and invalid on 21 June 2024; the government appealed in July 2024. The historic-era sodomy offence itself remained on the statute book and was not believed to have been used since independence in 1990, and the government told a UN human rights body it had no intention of repealing it. A December 2024 UN development agency review records that the country's courts decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2024 and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, while noting that implementation remains contested.

Public displays of affection between two men can still be treated as "immoral" behaviour punishable under an immoral practices act of 1980.

Partner recognition is the sharpest exposure. On 16 May 2023 the highest court ruled that same-sex marriages performed abroad must be recognised under the immigration act, giving non-national spouses the same residence rights as opposite-sex spouses. Compliance has not followed: immigration officials told a litigant that the ruling covers only the couples who brought the case, and he is issued a visitor's visa on every exit from the country. Gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than to "all persons". In December 2024 the legislature passed an act explicitly forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad, overriding the 2023 judgment. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law cannot rely on the 2023 ruling to secure a spouse's residence rights.

Earlier residence litigation produced the same individualised outcomes. In 2001 a resident's foreign spouse won a permanent residence permit from the highest court without the court endorsing same-sex relationships, and in January 2018 a litigant won a court petition to enter the country while his case was reviewed.

The constitution's equality provision does not list gender identity or sexual orientation. A 2017 analysis by a regional litigation organisation argues that "other status" should be read to include them, following a UN human rights body's position.

Health care is governed by professional rules that bar discrimination. Health professionals are bound by national ethical guidelines for health professionals (2010, the national health professions council), whose sections require that personal beliefs not prejudice patient care and prohibit discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, and the national health ministry's patient charter makes "Impartiality" a core value requiring equal treatment irrespective of sex, gender and sexuality. Against that, the 2009 ministry regulations on scope of practice for clinical and educational psychologists still treat "sexual and gender identity" as disorders.

Media regulation offers a limited protection. A broadcasting code for licensees (2018) bars licensees from broadcasting material that advocates hatred based on gender or sexual orientation, sanctions violence or unlawful conduct on those grounds, and prohibits material likely to incite hatred or severe ridicule against persons because of sexual orientation where that constitutes incitement to harm. A UN human rights body recommended in 2016 that the country legislate against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.

Public assembly by LGBT people has proceeded without government impediment. A national advocacy organisation organised the country's first pride parades: the capital's march of December 2013 drew about 100 people, around 200 marched in June 2017, and hundreds marched in the capital and a second city in December 2018. The first national lesbian festival was held in the capital in November 2017, bringing more than sixty young lesbians from eight areas of the country together for a week of public poetry, story, music, drama and dance, and was repeated in November 2018.
NAM.blindOutOfScope:
The government's July 2024 appeal against the high court's 21 June 2024 ruling on the immigration act references has no recorded outcome in the sources reviewed; whether those references are currently enforceable is unresolved.

How the December 2024 act forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad operates against the 16 May 2023 judgment of the highest court in practice is not sourced beyond the fact of its passage.

The 2017 analysis by a regional litigation organisation of the equality provision and the gender-marker section predates the 2023 marriage-recognition judgment and the 2024 decriminalisation ruling and has not been updated in the material reviewed.

The 2018 account of the sodomy offence being unused since independence is dated and rests on the absence of known prosecutions rather than a formal assurance.

MUS.name: Mauritius
MUS.summary:
Mauritius decriminalised same-sex conduct on 4 October 2023, when the Supreme Court struck down Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838 as unconstitutional and ruled that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. The provision had carried penal servitude of up to five years. Prosecutions were rare: the US State Department's 2016 country report found that sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce proceedings as an aggravating factor, although a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy. The government said in 2017 that it would not repeal the section, and a decriminalisation bill brought by former Attorney General Rama Valayden failed to pass. In October 2019 a group of young people filed a constitutional challenge supported by the Young Queer Alliance and the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, alongside activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek, backed by Collectif Arc-en-Ciel.

No criminal provision in the sources targets gender expression. The State Department's 2016 report records harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing; no prosecution or detention of a visitor for gender-nonconforming presentation appears in the inventory.

Legal gender recognition is not available. The Civil Status Act of 1981 and the Central Population Database form the framework that denies it, and a July 2021 policy brief by the Young Queer Alliance argues for recognition. The sources record no administrative route by which a trans visitor or resident can change a gender marker.

Mauritius recognises neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law cannot marry or register a partnership here. In practice, resorts are described as welcoming and non-discriminatory, and no problems have been recorded with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms.

The Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The sources do not state that gender identity falls within their scope. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Government statements say hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form. LGBTQ people may face discrimination in public hospitals in particular.

Pride has been held since 2005, organised by Collectif Arc-en-Ciel, founded the same year; the 2016 march drew more than 1,200 participants when it moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis. In 2018 the march was annulled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, and a counter-protest was organised by Javed Meetoo, described as an Islamic extremist under state surveillance. Police had been deployed earlier in 2018 to protect marchers, an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support, and Cardinal Maurice Piat and other religious leaders condemned the anti-LGBTQ protest. The Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights.

During the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and other candidates used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech. Outright International, in an overview last updated 12 March 2026, records advances for lesbian, gay and bisexual people with progress for trans and intersex people 'less evident'. Conservative attitudes remain commonplace.

In 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan became the first transgender woman to compete in Miss Universe Mauritius. Analysis of her participation against the country's legal obstacles, published by AfricLaw in August 2024, concludes that legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate, and notes activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G.
MUS.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains nothing on border or immigration practice: no sourced account of airport screening, pat-downs, secondary inspection or document-marker flagging affecting trans travellers entering Mauritius.

Whether the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and the Workers' Rights Act 2019 cover gender identity, and how they are enforced in practice, is not established by the sources.

No trans-specific violence data with a denominator appears in the inventory; the sources record no homicide or assault figures for trans people in Mauritius.

The sources do not state whether the 2021 Civil Status Act's 'undetermined' registration option is available to trans adults or only to intersex newborns.

It is not sourced whether the Supreme Court's 2023 ruling has been followed by an amendment to the Criminal Code or operates only as a reading-down of Section 250.

The anti-LGBTIQ statements made during the 2024 elections are not linked in the sources to any specific policy or enforcement outcome.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's Mauritius coverage reports that Collectif Arc-En-Ciel, founded in 2005, organised the country's first Pride and has done so for fifteen years, drawing more than 1,200 participants in 2016, when the march moved from Rose-Hill to Port Louis. In 2018 the Pride march was annulled after hundreds of death threats believed to come from religious extremists, and a counter-protest was organised by Javed Meetoo, an Islamic extremist under state surveillance; a strong police force had been deployed earlier in 2018 to protect marchers, and an LGBTQ sit-in at the Caudan Waterfront followed with the Prime Minister's support. AfriGay reports that gay life is fairly quiet, existing mainly online, in private and at occasional parties, though resorts are welcoming and non-discriminatory and no problems with LGBTQ couples sharing hotel rooms have been recorded. LGBTQ people may face discrimination notably in public hospitals; according to the government, hormone therapy for transgender people is provided in public hospitals, but gender-affirming care is available only in limited form. In 2014 the Ministry of Health amended blood donation policy to allow men who have sex with men to donate, although anecdotally LGBTQI persons have still been prevented from donating on occasion. Section 250 of the Criminal Code of 1838 provided for penal servitude of up to 5 years for sodomy, the law under which a same-sex couple was arrested in 2015 on suspicion of practising sodomy; prosecutions under the law were rare, and on 4 October 2023 the Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional, ruling that it must be read to exclude consensual acts. In 2017 the government said it would not repeal Section 250, saying it would address the issue after further consideration, and former Attorney General Rama Valayden's decriminalisation bill failed to pass. Conservative attitudes remain commonplace and LGBTQ people still face discrimination; in 2018 religious extremists issued hundreds of death threats that cancelled Pride and organised a counter-protest, with Cardinal Maurice Piat and other religious leaders condemning the anti-LGBTQ protest and calling for tolerance. State actors have also shown support: police protected Pride marchers, Prime Minister Pravind Jugnauth backed an LGBTQ sit-in, and the Opposition stated that sexual orientation should not be an obstacle to equal rights. LGBTQ people may face bullying in schools, while acceptance is growing particularly among the younger generation, with polls indicating Mauritius is one of Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries. In October 2019 a group of young people filed a constitutional challenge to Section 250, supported by the Young Queer Alliance and the Love Honor Cherish Foundation, alongside activist Abdool Ridwan Firaas Ah Seek, 29, backed by Collectif Arc-En-Ciel. The Young Queer Alliance was founded on 1 September 2014 for young LGBTQ Mauritians, engaging in support, advocacy and anti-discrimination campaigns; a 2016 poll found 49% of Mauritians would like or not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour.

Polls place Mauritius among Africa's most LGBTQ-friendly countries, and a 2016 poll found that 49 per cent of Mauritians would like or would not mind having an LGBTQ neighbour. Acceptance is described as growing particularly among the younger generation.

SYC.name: Seychelles
SYC.summary:
Seychelles repealed Penal Code Section 151 in 2016, ending a colonial-era offence that had carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex intimacy. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised under the current Penal Code.

The Constitution guarantees freedom from torture under Article 16 and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex under Article 27. The constitutional list does not name gender identity expressly.

Section 5 of the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) adds sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status to protected characteristics, creating an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences.

The revised law increases prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward a victim's sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability. The Human Dignity Trust describes Seychelles as the second African country, after South Africa, to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation.

Seychelles does not recognise same-sex marriage or same-sex civil unions. In June 2015 two men, one a British national and one a Seychellois national, were married at the British High Commission in Seychelles by the British High Commissioner; the ceremony took place through a foreign mission and did not create a marriage under Seychellois law.

For a trans visitor, the statutory position is one of decriminalisation and enhanced hate-crime protection on gender-identity grounds, with no local recognition of a relationship that would be read as same-sex under Seychellois law.
SYC.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document police enforcement practice, entry or visa screening, document-marker rules, bathroom or facilities access, or access to gender-affirming care for trans travellers. One source states that legal and social conditions for visitors can vary from the statutory position but provides no specific incidents, enforcement data or locations.

No trans-specific violence data or hate-crime enforcement statistics are included in the inventory.

Travel guide: notes the 2016 decriminalisation of same-sex acts as a significant victory for the country, while advising both local residents and tourists to stay vigilant and informed about the current legal and social landscape — practical visitor guidance for the destination.

Rights-media outlet, 27 September 2024: a newly revised law calls for increased prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward victims' sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability — per a human-rights legal organisation, this country is one of only two countries to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation; before 2016 the penal code punished male same-sex intimacy with up to 14 years.
SYC.blindLocalsOnly:
Nationals and residents of the country have no access to same-sex marriage or civil unions under domestic law. The 2015 marriage at a foreign diplomatic mission was solemnised through that mission and did not establish a marriage recognised under the country's law.

The 2024 hate-crime amendments apply to residents as victims of violent offences motivated by hostility toward protected characteristics including gender identity and sexual orientation.
SYC.blindTangential: A human-rights organisation's comparison places the country after a neighbouring jurisdiction as the second jurisdiction in the region to enact statutory protection against all forms of hate-based victimisation. That comparison concerns the scope of hate-crime law, not the recognition of relationships or gender identity in civil status.

SEN.name: Senegal
SEN.summary:
Article 319 of Senegal's 1965 Penal Code criminalises an "improper or unnatural act" with a person of the same sex. The penalty is one to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 1,500,000 CFA francs, and the maximum is applied whenever the act is committed with a person under 21. The provision is drafted around the sex of the participants; it makes no reference to transgender status, gender identity or gender expression.

An amendment adopted in 2026 raises that penalty to five to ten years and fines of 100,000 to 10,000,000 CFA francs. The bill was presented on 25 February 2026, adopted on 12 March, signed on 30 March and published on 31 March. It adds an explicit ban on the promotion, financing and support of homosexuality, bisexuality and transsexuality, together with a penalty for abusive relationships conducted in bad faith. The government's draft, adopted in February 2026, raised the maximum fine from 1.5 million to 10 million CFA francs and targeted organisations promoting what it called LGBT philosophy through film, television or writing.

The promotion and support ban is the provision that reaches trans expression directly. It criminalises advocacy and funding for transsexuality rather than sexual conduct alone, so a visitor who speaks publicly, organises, or gives money to trans-related activity is exposed under the same article as the conduct offence.

Enforcement is documented. In September 2018 four LGBT people, two women and two men, were detained in Dakar on charges of "acts against the order of nature" after videos of them circulated; the detentions formed part of a wave of politically motivated arrests ahead of the 2019 elections. In February 2026, 22 gay men were arrested within two weeks, among them a man detained on 20 February at the Senegal-Gambian border while attempting to leave the country. A separate report counted 17 arrests for "acts against nature" in early February 2026. In August, 99 men were arrested; 28 were released and 71 faced up to 20 years after the maximum was doubled.

Police practice compounds the statutory risk. Arrests have been made on second-hand reports alone, and detainees have been badly treated in custody because of their sexual orientation. Two women detained in January after a kissing video circulated were released on bail without formal charge. In October, a Dakar court sentenced one man to four years and a 200,000 CFA franc fine for acts against nature plus arms and battery, and a second man to three years.

An earlier prosecution shows how far the process can run before it collapses. Nine men were arrested on 19 December 2008 in a Dakar flat and convicted on 6 January 2009 to five years for indecent conduct and unnatural acts, plus three years for membership of a criminal group. They were tortured repeatedly in police custody and held segregated because other inmates threatened them. The convictions were overturned in April 2009 and all nine were released immediately.

Senegal has no legal gender recognition procedure. No law broadly protects LGBTQ people from discrimination; the only related provisions are limited restrictions on revealing or stigmatising depiction of sexual orientation.

Violence against people read as gender-nonconforming or gay is documented. On 28 October 2023 the body of Cheikh Fall, a 31-year-old man buried in Léona Niassene cemetery, was dug up and burned in the street in Kaolack after it was revealed he was gay; four men were arrested on 30 October, while images from the scene showed a crowd of hundreds around the fire. In December 2012 a gay male couple near Dakar were beaten by a parent after being caught having sex. In May 2009 the corpse of a person locally described as goor-gigen, man-woman, was disinterred twice in Thies, left beside the grave and then dumped outside the family home after reburial.

Transgender people, counted within the LGBT population, face criminal prosecution, arrest, widespread discrimination, social intolerance and violence. Local organisations keep an exceedingly low profile because of the criminal provisions and the stigma, and the media rarely report hatred or violence directed at them.

Hostility extends to speech about the subject. A political activist and a preacher were jailed and fined 100,000 CFA francs each after posting a video attacking opposition leader Ousmane Sonko for giving a visiting French politician a platform to express support for same-sex marriage.

The US State Department's 2012 human rights report for Senegal listed pre-electoral violence, torture, and violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the country's major human rights problems.

A campaign to raise the maximum penalty to 15 years has run since 2020, with anti-LGBT forces pressing for the increase as of July 2024. The 15-year figure was not enacted; the 2026 amendment sets the range at five to ten years.
SEN.outOfScopeNotes:
The February 2026 arrest figures are not reconciled: one source reports 22 men arrested within two weeks, another reports 17 arrests for "acts against nature" in early February. Whether these describe the same operation is unresolved.

The report that 71 of the 99 men arrested in August face up to 20 years is not reconciled with the five-to-ten-year range set by the 2026 amendment. The source does not explain the doubling, and the year of that round-up is not stated.

The scope of the penalty for abusive relationships conducted in bad faith is not defined in the available sources, and it is not sourced whether it has been applied.

Whether the 2026 amendment is in force and how it is being applied to foreign visitors is not sourced. The status of the 15-year proposal after July 2024 is likewise not sourced beyond the enactment of the five-to-ten-year range.

No information was located on how the promotion and support ban is applied to non-citizens, on entry screening practice at ports of entry, or on how border officers handle travellers whose document markers differ from their presentation. The only border incident in the inventory is the 20 February 2026 detention of a man attempting to leave the country.

SEN.tangentialFactors:
Senegal refused recommendations made at the Universal Periodic Review in October 2009 and again in October 2013 to amend or repeal legislation punishing conduct on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, to establish a moratorium on Article 319, to ensure non-discrimination, protection and integration, and to criminalise orientation-based violence. The refusal was reasoned on the basis that being homosexual is not a crime although same-sex acts are.

On 6 February 2009 the president authorised a man to change his name to a woman's name in order to emphasise his feminine side, an act reported at the time as causing no controversy. It is a single documented administrative instance of a name change reflecting feminine presentation and does not amount to a legal gender recognition procedure.

The 2008 Dakar prosecution ended in acquittal on appeal in April 2009, so convictions under Article 319 are not final at first instance. The men had by then spent months in custody and been tortured, and the reversal did not alter the statute.

The demand for a 15-year maximum, pressed since 2020, was overtaken by the 2026 amendment, which sets five to ten years rather than the 15 years the campaign sought.

CIV.name: Côte d'Ivoire
CIV.summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal in Côte d'Ivoire and have never been criminalised. The country's historic-era legal inheritance did not include sodomy offences, and no statute criminalising private same-sex conduct has been enacted since.

Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes a public breach of decency with three months to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 francs. Where the breach consists of an indecent or act contrary to nature with an individual of the same sex, the penalty rises to six months to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 francs, doubled where the act is committed against a minor or in the presence of a minor under eighteen. Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for same-sex couples and 15 for different-sex couples, so conduct involving a same-sex partner aged between 15 and 17 is an offence regardless of consent.

Côte d'Ivoire provides no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and none on the basis of sexual orientation. The government does not recognise same-sex couples, and gay and lesbian individuals and couples are not legally recognised as eligible to adopt.

Official posture is mixed. In March 2010 the Ivorian representative stated that the country would begin taking measures to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, while ruling out awareness-raising programmes as not a current priority. In September 2024 the National Human Rights Council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubi (gay men and trans women) and lelé (lesbians and trans men), stating that despite their sexual orientation the members of that community remain human beings entitled to the rights enshrined in the Constitution and in international human rights treaties. Against this, in 2024 President Alassane Ouattara promised to introduce a bill to Parliament to counter the expansion of homosexuality.

Violence concentrates on gender expression rather than on sexual orientation alone. Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth face especially hostile attention because their presentation breaches social norms, and travestis have been documented as facing harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender conformity keeps them unremarked. During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis the Force Républicaines de Côte d'Ivoire beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers; complaints were not filed for fear of reprisals, and fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis. In 2012 FRCI members repeatedly raided Le Club, a bar frequented by gender and sexual minorities and mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes compelling them to remove clothing and demanding a substantial fine under threat of being taken to base.

A documented surge of violence occurred in Abidjan between early September and late October 2024, when 45 assault incidents were recorded in the city. Social media influencers called for violence, a hoax circulated that the French President had asked the Ivorian President to legalise same-sex marriage, and a homophobia-motivated attack struck a market employing gay hair stylists. Afterward people avoided going out during the day and meeting in public and remained hypervigilant. The figure of 45 incidents is a raw count for one city over roughly seven weeks; the sources give no population denominator and no comparison with the general assault or homicide rate, so it indicates a documented cluster rather than a measurable per-capita risk.

Police and state responses are a recurring barrier. The US State Department's 2023 report found that same-sex conduct is not criminalised but that LGBTQI+ persons faced violence, including three deaths reported within the community during the year; police responses to non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, Abidjan, while walking with another man. Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years, but as of 2023 many people still did not report to police, believing they would not be taken seriously.

Reported conversion therapy in 2023 included a transgender man attempting suicide after being forced to attend a prayer camp. Many transgender people lack secure housing.

Discrimination continues in healthcare, housing and employment. Documented consequences include evictions and family expulsions causing school dropout, refusal to hire or promote, and dismissal if a person is discovered; a doctor refused service on grounds of sexual orientation until protest led to care being provided. A vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preach against the community.
CIV.outOfScopeNotes:
Placement of transgender detainees is unresolved. Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners in Côte d'Ivoire; where trans detainees are placed, whether by birth sex or identity, whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any available publication. On the Human Rights Watch country page for Côte d'Ivoire, LGBT Rights appears only as a topic-facet link.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, amendment of gender markers on national identity documents or passports, or entry, visa and border-screening treatment of transgender travellers. Any assessment of those questions would be unsourced.

The violence counts available are raw counts without denominators. The 45 assault incidents recorded in Abidjan between early September and late October 2024 and the three deaths reported within the LGBTQI+ community in 2023 are not accompanied by population figures, general homicide or assault rates, or undercount estimates, so neither can be converted into a comparative risk magnitude.

No source documents societal tolerance toward transgender people specifically. The only tolerance assessment quoted concerns gay people, and the inventory contains no equivalent statement, survey or finding for trans residents or visitors.

The 2024 promise of a bill to counter the expansion of homosexuality is recorded without a bill text, parliamentary status, or date, so its content and current standing remain unresolved.

In September 2024 the National Human Rights Council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubis (gay men and trans women) and lelés (lesbians and trans men), stating "despite their different sexual orientation and contrary to our customs and traditions, the members of this ‘woubi’ community remain above all human beings and benefit from the human rights enshrined in the Ivorian Constitution and international human rights treaties." Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth are at especially high risk of violence because their gender expression breaks social norms and draws more hostile attention. Many transgender people lack secure housing, and reported conversion therapy in 2023 included a transgender man attempting suicide after being forced to attend prayer camp. During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis, the Force Républicaines de Côte d’Ivoire beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers, with complaints not filed for fear of reprisals, and fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis, defined as transgender and otherwise gender non-conforming people assigned male at birth. In 2012 FRCI members repeatedly raided Le Club, a bar frequented by gender and sexual minorities, mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes forcing them to remove clothes, and demanding a significant fine under threat of being taken to bases. Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal and have never been criminalized, due in part to Ivory Coast being a former French colony not inheriting sodomy laws. Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes public breach of decency with three months to two years imprisonment and a 50,000 to 500,000 francs fine, and where the breach consists of an indecent or contrary-to-nature act with an individual of the same sex, six months to two years imprisonment and a 50,000 to 300,000 francs fine, doubled if committed against a minor or in presence of a minor of eighteen years. Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for homosexual couples and 15 for heterosexual ones. The government does not recognize same-sex couples. Gay and lesbian individuals and couples are not legally recognized as eligible to adopt. There is no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation. In 2024 President Ouattara promised to introduce a bill to Parliament to "counter the expansion" of homosexuality. Sexual minorities, transgender and gender non-conforming people are seen as abnormal and their identities are perceived as stemming from the Global North. LGBTQ people are subject to violence, with 45 assault incidents recorded in Abidjan between early September and late October 2024, social media influencers calling for violence, misinformation including a hoax that the French President asked the Ivorian President to legalize same-sex marriage, and a homophobia-motivated attack at a market employing gay hair stylists, after which people avoided going out during the day and meeting publicly and remained hypervigilant, while wealthier people are treated with less hostility. As of 2023 state authorities are slow and sometimes ineffective at managing civilian violence but may be improving in understanding and handling complaints, yet many do not report to police believing they will not be taken seriously, with reports of police not taking violence seriously and often blaming victims. Discrimination continues in healthcare, housing and employment, with evictions and family expulsions causing school dropout, refusal to hire or promote or firing if discovered, a doctor refusing service a few years before September 2011 because of sexual orientation until protest led to care being provided, and a vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preaching against the community. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance toward transgender people specifically; the only tolerance assessment quoted concerns gay people: "There is still discrimination against gay people, but generally we are moving toward relative tolerance."

CIV.blindSummary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal in the country and have never been criminalised. The country's historic-era legal inheritance did not include sodomy offences, and no statute criminalising private same-sex conduct has been enacted since.

Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes a public breach of decency with three months to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 francs. Where the breach consists of an indecent or act contrary to nature with an individual of the same sex, the penalty rises to six months to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 francs, doubled where the act is committed against a minor or in the presence of a minor under eighteen. Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for same-sex couples and 15 for different-sex couples, so conduct involving a same-sex partner aged between 15 and 17 is an offence regardless of consent.

The country provides no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and none on the basis of sexual orientation. The government does not recognise same-sex couples, and gay and lesbian individuals and couples are not legally recognised as eligible to adopt.

Official posture is mixed. In March 2010 the country's representative stated that the state would begin taking measures to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, while ruling out awareness-raising programmes as not a current priority. In September 2024 the national human rights council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubi (gay men and trans women) and lelé (lesbians and trans men), stating that despite their sexual orientation the members of that community remain human beings entitled to the rights enshrined in the constitution and in international human rights treaties. Against this, in 2024 the head of state promised to introduce a bill to the legislature to counter the expansion of homosexuality.

Violence concentrates on gender expression rather than on sexual orientation alone. Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth face especially hostile attention because their presentation breaches social norms, and travestis have been documented as facing harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender conformity keeps them unremarked. During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis, post-crisis security forces beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers; complaints were not filed for fear of reprisals, and fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis. In 2012 members of those forces repeatedly raided a bar frequented by gender and sexual minorities and mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes compelling them to remove clothing and demanding a substantial fine under threat of being taken to base.

A documented surge of violence occurred in the largest city between early September and late October 2024, when 45 assault incidents were recorded there. Social media influencers called for violence, a hoax circulated that a foreign head of state had asked the country's head of state to legalise same-sex marriage, and a homophobia-motivated attack struck a market employing gay hair stylists. Afterward people avoided going out during the day and meeting in public and remained hypervigilant. The figure of 45 incidents is a raw count for one city over roughly seven weeks; the sources give no population denominator and no comparison with the general assault or homicide rate, so it indicates a documented cluster rather than a measurable per-capita risk.

Police and national responses are a recurring barrier. A foreign government's 2023 human rights report found that same-sex conduct is not criminalised but that LGBTQI+ persons faced violence, including three deaths reported within the community during the year; police responses to non-governmental violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim. A transgender man was beaten in a district of the largest city while walking with another man. Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years, but as of 2023 many people still did not report to police, believing they would not be taken seriously.

Reported conversion therapy in 2023 included a transgender man attempting suicide after being forced to attend a prayer camp. Many transgender people lack secure housing.

Discrimination continues in healthcare, housing and employment. Documented consequences include evictions and family expulsions causing school dropout, refusal to hire or promote, and dismissal if a person is discovered; a doctor refused service on grounds of sexual orientation until protest led to care being provided. A vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preach against the community.
CIV.blindOutOfScope:
Placement of transgender detainees is unresolved. The principal international human rights publisher covering the country publishes no document, case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners there; where trans detainees are placed, whether by birth sex or identity, whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any available publication. On that publisher's country page, LGBT Rights appears only as a topic-facet link.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, amendment of gender markers on national identity documents or passports, or entry, visa and border-screening treatment of transgender travellers. Any assessment of those questions would be unsourced.

The violence counts available are raw counts without denominators. The 45 assault incidents recorded in the largest city between early September and late October 2024 and the three deaths reported within the LGBTQI+ community in 2023 are not accompanied by population figures, general homicide or assault rates, or undercount estimates, so neither can be converted into a comparative risk magnitude.

No source documents societal tolerance toward transgender people specifically. The only tolerance assessment quoted concerns gay people, and the inventory contains no equivalent statement, survey or finding for trans residents or visitors.

The 2024 promise of a bill to counter the expansion of homosexuality is recorded without a bill text, legislative status, or date, so its content and current standing remain unresolved.

CIV.tangentialFactors:
The social climate is described as hostile to sexual and gender minorities on the grounds that their identities are seen as abnormal and as originating in the Global North. Wealthier people are treated with less hostility than poorer ones, which shapes how exposure to risk is distributed. A vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preaches against the community.

Reporting on the country has intensified alongside the documented 2024 violence: a New York Times article of October 2024 addressed the situation of LGBTQ people in Côte d'Ivoire, and a UNDP report of December 2024, African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa, includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space and inclusion.

The US State Department's 2011 human rights report for Côte d'Ivoire contains limited LGBT-specific content and instead covers the post-electoral crisis context, including some 3,000 deaths, sexual violence and displacement. That crisis is the backdrop against which the documented abuse of gay and transgender people by the Force Républicaines de Côte d'Ivoire occurred.

The only quoted assessment of societal tolerance concerns gay people rather than transgender people: one source records that there is still discrimination against gay people but that the country is generally moving toward relative tolerance. No equivalent assessment for transgender people appears in the inventory.

MLI.name: Mali
MLI.summary:
Mali's Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code on 31 October 2024. It was promulgated in December 2024 and took effect on 13 December 2024, published in Official Journal Special No. 21 of 2024. The code defines homosexuality as sexual relations between persons of the same sex and punishes it with two to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 200,000 to 500,000 CFA francs. Human Rights Watch, reporting on 6 November 2024, describes the penalties as harsh.

The code recognises no affirmed gender. The offence is fixed by sex assigned at birth, so a trans visitor in a relationship that local authorities would class as same-sex under birth-registered status falls inside its terms, and a traveller whose presentation is read as gender-nonconforming can be arrested on perceived same-sex conduct.

The statute also bans the undefined "promotion" of homosexuality and reaches any citizen seen to encourage it. Because the term is left undefined, the provision covers people well beyond those accused of conduct itself, and Human Rights Watch states the drafting is broad enough for expansive application.

Before the code took effect, same-sex conduct was not explicitly criminalised in Mali, but the vague public indecency provisions of Article 225 were already used against LGBT people and against gender-nonconforming expression, and laws against attacks on morality were actively enforced against the same groups. That enforcement record predates the criminalisation now in force and indicates how the new provisions are likely to be applied.

Since the code came into effect, reporting records a significant increase in arbitrary arrests and detentions, and in physical abuse directed at individuals on the basis of appearance or gender expression alone.

No anti-discrimination law protects against harassment or abuse on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so neither a visitor nor a resident has a domestic complaint mechanism or protection body to invoke.

The constitution adopted by referendum in June 2023 limits marriage to a union of one man and one woman, which closes partner recognition in Mali for a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law.
MLI.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Mali could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403). That organisation's profile documents the new criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

The Human Rights Watch World Report 2025 chapter on Mali, covering events of 2024, contains no transgender-specific content and no information on prison placement, special units, or solitary confinement and segregation practice for transgender prisoners. Its coverage of the junta's rule, counterterrorism sweeps and an international arrest warrant carries no transgender dimension.

No source in hand states a documented position on societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the attitude data available addresses homosexuality and men who have sex with men.

The reported increase in arbitrary arrests and physical abuse since December 2024 is described qualitatively. No count, rate or comparison with general detention figures is provided, so its scale is unresolved.

No entry rule, visa provision, screening practice or identity-document requirement specific to transgender travellers is documented in the sources consulted.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mali (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The only protection-related fact stated is LGBTQ-general: there are no anti-discrimination laws protecting the LGBTQ community from harassment and abuse on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Before December 2024, Article 225 penalizing “public indecency” was frequently used to target LGBTQ individuals and those with nonconforming gender expressions. Laws prohibiting “attacks on morality” are described as used to target LGBTQ persons and as actively enforced. The immediate result of the December 2024 penal code is described as a significant increase in arbitrary arrests and detentions as well as physical abuse directed at individuals based solely on appearance or gender expression. The 2011 human rights findings recorded no publicly visible lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender organizations in the country, with free association impeded by a law prohibiting association “for an immoral purpose.” Homosexuality has been illegal in Mali since December 2024. The Transitional National Council passed a new penal code criminalizing homosexuality on 31 October 2024, and the code went into effect on 13 December 2024. The new code also prohibits “promotion” of homosexuality, a term left undefined, thereby broadening the scope of prosecution. Before this law, same-sex sexual conduct was not explicitly illegal, but Article 225 penalizing “public indecency” was frequently used to target LGBTQ individuals. Mali’s new constitution adopted by referendum in June 2023 limits marriage to a union of one man and one woman, outlawing same-sex marriage since 2023. Article 522 of the Code des Personnes et de la Famille, passed by the National Assembly on 2 December 2011 and signed by the president, forbids same-sex couples from adopting children. The military junta ruling since 2021 justified the criminalization as defending “traditional and moral values,” and Justice Minister Mamadou Kassogue had previously described homosexuality as “unnatural” and pledged to criminalize it. The article contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. As LGBTQ-general background, societal discrimination against the LGBTQ community is described as widespread. No publicly visible lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender organizations were recorded in the 2011 findings, and a law prohibiting association “for an immoral purpose” was cited in 2005 to refuse recognition to a gay rights association in Bamako. The sexuality-specific attitude survey cited found 98 percent of Malian adults in 2007 believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, presented as a view on homosexuality, not on transgender people. The tolerance statement from health provider director Dr. Dembelé Bintou Keita that Malian society is not tolerant to MSM and that “All cultural beliefs towards MSM are negative” is presented as MSM-specific, not as a finding about transgender people.

BFA.name: Burkina Faso
BFA.summary:
Consensual same-sex relations became a criminal offence in Burkina Faso on 1 September 2025, when the Transitional Legislative Assembly passed the measure unanimously and it took effect on passage. The penalty is two to five years' imprisonment plus a fine. The criminal code in force from that date also prohibits the promotion of homosexuality or similar behaviour. Same-sex conduct had been lawful before, with an equal age of consent in place since 1996; the 2025 code ended that position.

The prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code that the junta's council of ministers approved by decree in July 2024, part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law, and which entered into force on 1 September 2025 as criminal-code law. The vote was taken in an unelected 71-member transitional parliament. Military rule dates from September 2022.

Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala has said the two-to-five-year terms and fines apply to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices", and that foreign nationals who violate the law will be deported. The offence is framed around acts rather than status, but a trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status falls within its terms, and removal from the country is the stated consequence for foreign nationals.

No arrests under the law had been reported as of 28 September 2025. Reporting by France 24 and AFP on 22 September 2025 described fear of a witch hunt and increased self-censorship within the LGBTQ community. The exposure a visitor faces is therefore statutory and discretionary rather than demonstrated through a record of prosecutions.

Article 23 of the Constitution defines marriage as the free consent of a man and a woman and describes the family as the basic unit of society owed state protection; it does not authorise same-sex marriage. Its anti-discrimination clause covers race, colour, religion, ethnicity, caste, social origin and wealth, and omits sexual orientation and gender identity. Pre-existing prohibitions on same-sex marriage and on adoption by same-sex couples remain in force. Under the adoption rules reported by the U.S. Department of State, only married, cohabiting heterosexual couples married at least five years may adopt, and single applicants are almost never permitted to adopt.

No mechanism for responding to anti-LGBT violence is documented. A 2011 human rights report found no legal discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, housing, statelessness, education or health care, while societal discrimination on those grounds persisted. LGBT people were reported as occasional victims of verbal and physical abuse; religious and traditional opinion did not accept homosexuality; and there were no reports that the government responded to societal violence or discrimination against them. LGBTQ organisations had no legal presence in the country, though they existed unofficially, with no reported violence against them. That assessment dates from 2011, before the criminalisation took effect.
BFA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a prosecution, conviction or deportation under the September 2025 law after 28 September 2025; the enforcement record beyond that date is unresolved.

The inventory contains no information on legal gender recognition. No procedure, court order or administrative rule for changing name or gender markers on Burkinabé identity documents is described, and no rule on how a trans traveller's documents would be read at entry is available.

No trans-specific violence data and no general homicide rate for Burkina Faso appear in the inventory, so no comparison of trans-targeted violence against the background rate can be made.

The sources describe a July 2024 decree approving the Personal and Family Code and a 1 September 2025 vote in the transitional assembly without fully reconciling the sequence; the code's entry into force and the assembly vote are both dated 1 September 2025.

MOZ.name: Mozambique
MOZ.summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Mozambique. The colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision was erased in the 2015 revision of the penal code, and the code now in force, Law 24/2019 (effective 2020), carries no prohibition on consensual conduct. A trans visitor faces no criminal exposure on the basis of gender identity or consensual sexual conduct.

The penal code provides hate-crime and hate-speech protections that name gender identity. Article 191 prohibits incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on the basis of gender identity, and reaches defamation, insults and threats directed at transgender people. Article 160 makes a victim's sexual orientation or gender identity an aggravating factor in homicide. The Advertising Code (2016) bars advertisements containing discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. These are the statutory protections a trans visitor could invoke.

No legal gender recognition procedure exists. There is no route under Mozambican law for a trans person to change the gender marker on identity documents. A visitor whose passport or other documents carry markers inconsistent with their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at checkpoints and in any interaction requiring identification. The sources describe no formal screening process for trans travellers and offer no assurance that none occurs.

Anti-discrimination law does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity in education, health, housing or employment. Employment protections that had been in place since 2007 were repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024. Discrimination on those grounds in education, health, housing or employment is not prohibited by law.

Violence against LGBTQ people is documented as rare, with discrimination the more common experience. Lambda Mozambique's Carina Capitine said the community is not targeted by violence as in some other African countries but does face discrimination.

Mozambique does not recognise same-sex relationships. Same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to legal recognition, and no spousal rights or protections follow from the relationship.
MOZ.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Rights Watch World Report 2024 chapter on Mozambique, published 11 January 2024, records general police detentions and election-related arrests. It carries no transgender-specific content and no information on where transgender prisoners are housed.

Enforcement of Article 191 and Article 160 is not documented in the sources. Whether prosecutions or civil claims under either provision have occurred is unresolved.

No formal screening process for trans travellers at Mozambican entry points or checkpoints is documented. The absence of a documented process is not evidence that none occurs, and no source addresses how officials handle document-marker mismatches in practice.

sources.summary: Outright International (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct legal since the 2015 penal code; no legal gender recognition procedure exists; societal attitudes broadly neutral but LGBTIQ people face family ostracisation and employment/education barriers; the 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations then disappointed. GlobalGayz archive (2006-2011): dated milestones — first newspaper article arguing gay rights (Agencia de Informacao, 7 July 2006), Maputo men petitioning parliament, the LGBT group still unregistered as of March 2011, refugee deaths en route to South Africa; documents early organising under the colonial-era law.

RWA.name: Rwanda
RWA.summary:
Rwanda does not criminalise same-sex intimacy, and the age of consent is 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. No statute targets transgender identity or consensual relationships as such.

Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no legal gender recognition path exists. A trans visitor's identity documents cannot be aligned with their lived gender under local law, and identity checks are the point at which that absence becomes an enforcement encounter.

The Human Rights First Rwanda Association's 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents law-enforcement abuse directed at transgender people: harassment during identity checks and arbitrary arrests on vagrancy and public-order grounds. Vice reported in November 2020 on violent detentions of transgender people; on Christmas Day 2018 a singer booked to perform at a hotel in Kigali was stopped by police officers on the street after her show, and her name was changed in the reporting because of concerns for her safety. A U.S. State Department report from 2016 recorded LGBTQ Rwandans being harassed, blackmailed and arrested by police under public-order and morality laws, with occasional harassment by neighbours as well as by police.

The Constitution adopted in May 2003 recognises in Article 26 only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman. Same-sex marriages, civil unions and comparable unions are not recognised. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition.

No anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's non-discrimination provisions, Articles 15 and 16, do not list those grounds; Article 16 names ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability and other grounds, but not sexual orientation or gender identity.

The Ministry of Health's Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy (2018) states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief or disability, are equally entitled to receive health services, and applies across public, private and NGO sectors.

Immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people were issued in 2024, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. The Asylum and humanitarian protection decision making Standard Operating Procedures (2024) require interviews to be conducted so that the applicant can present the grounds of their application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and of any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The Manual on Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures (2014) imposes the same requirement on hearings. Standard Operating Procedures on identifying and safeguarding vulnerable persons under the Migration and Economic Development Partnership (2024) define Vulnerable Persons to include individuals whose gender identity or sexual orientation places them at higher risk, expressly naming lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons.

Homosexuality is a taboo subject in Rwanda with no significant public discussion, and LGBTQ people face stigmatisation among the broader population. Asked about LGBT life in Rwanda at Rwanda Cultural Day in San Francisco in September 2016, President Paul Kagame said "it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem."
RWA.outOfScopeNotes:
No youth-, minor- or education-specific findings appear in the sources: school policy, bullying and the carriage of medication by minors are not documented here.

The asylum and immigration protections are documented as written procedures. Beyond the April 2022 grant of refugee status to a transgender claimant, the sources do not record how those procedures operate in practice.

The most detailed accounts of enforcement against transgender people date from 2016 and 2020; the 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee is the most recent documentation in the inventory. No later presidential statement on the subject appears in the sources, and no reform of the prohibition on changing legal gender is recorded.

In September 2019 gospel singer Albert Nabonibo came out as gay on a Christian YouTube channel, causing shock in a country where such a public assertion is described as unheard of, with horrible reactions from family and friends, though the Minister of State for East African Community Affairs, Olivier Nduhungirehe, publicly backed him. The Horizons Community Association of Rwanda has conducted public advocacy for LGBTQ rights since 2005, but its members have often been harassed by the government. The Anglican Church of Rwanda condemned non-biblical behaviors of Western churches in 2007 and refused to support ordination of LGBTQ clergy. In September 2016 President Paul Kagame said homosexuality hasn't been our problem and we don't intend to make it our problem. Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so no legal gender recognition path exists for transgender people. The Constitution (adopted May 2003), Article 26, states only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman is recognized, so same-sex marriages, civil unions and similar unions are not recognized. Same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an age of consent of 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. In 2024 the Government issued immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. The Asylum and humanitarian protection decision making Standard Operating Procedures (2024) require that interviews be conducted so the individual can present the grounds of their application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The Manual on Refugee Appeal Tribunal Standard Operating Procedures (2014) similarly requires hearings to take account of the appellant's sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. Standard Operating Procedures on identifying and safeguarding vulnerable persons under the Migration and Economic Development Partnership (2024) define Vulnerable Persons to include individuals whose gender identity and/or sexual orientation place them at higher risk, expressly naming lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons. LGBTQ Rwandans have reported being harassed, blackmailed, and even arrested by police under various laws dealing with public order and morality, and LGBTI rights groups reported occasional harassment by neighbors and police (U.S. State Department 2016 report). The Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy (2018) issued by the Ministry of Health states that all Rwandans, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief, or disability are equally entitled to receive health services to promote and maintain good health, applying across public, private and NGO sectors. No youth-specific or minor-specific care access findings appear in the source text. There are no anti-discrimination laws afforded to LGBTQ citizens, and the Constitution's non-discrimination provisions (Articles 15 and 16) do not ban discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity; Article 16 lists ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability and other grounds but not SOGI. Limited protections exist: the Human Resource Management Policy (2015) of the Office of the Auditor General of State Finances lists sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for harassment; the Code of Conduct of the Public Private Partnership Guidelines (2018) bans discrimination against bidders on grounds of sexual orientation; and Law 058/2021 on Protection of Personal Data and Privacy protects a person's sexual life as sensitive personal data. The age of consent in Rwanda is 18, regardless of sexual orientation or gender. Historically, in the old Kingdom of Rwanda male homosexual relations were common among young Hutus and Tutsis: boys training as warriors and Tutsi boys training at court formed emotional and often sexual relationships, sometimes lasting into adulthood, and were sometimes made sexually available to guests; societal acceptance disappeared after the arrival of European colonialists and Christianity. No contemporary youth-, minor- or education-specific findings (school policy, bullying, medication carriage by minors) appear in the source text.

RWA.localsOnly:
No legal gender recognition procedure exists: Rwandan law forbids changing legal gender, so transgender residents hold documents recording the sex assigned at birth.

LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, and NGO Law No. 058/2024, adopted in June 2024, raises freedom-of-association concerns. A public Pride event was held in 2021. The Horizons Community Association of Rwanda has conducted public advocacy for LGBTQ rights since 2005, and its members have often been harassed by the government.

Protections that do exist are narrow and sectoral. The Human Resource Management Policy (2015) of the Office of the Auditor General of State Finances lists sexual orientation as a prohibited ground for harassment. The Code of Conduct of the Public Private Partnership Guidelines (2018) bans discrimination against bidders on grounds of sexual orientation. Law 058/2021 on Protection of Personal Data and Privacy protects a person's sexual life as sensitive personal data.
RWA.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Venezuela (0.44 — different profiles: RWA has lower violence, more arbitrary state power) and above Trinidad & Tobago (0.42).
RWA.blindSummary:
The country does not criminalise same-sex intimacy, and the age of consent is 18 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. No statute targets transgender identity or consensual relationships as such.

The country's law forbids changing legal gender, so no legal gender recognition path exists. A trans visitor's identity documents cannot be aligned with their lived gender under local law, and identity checks are the point at which that absence becomes an enforcement encounter.

A national human rights organisation's 2025 submission to a United Nations human rights committee documents law-enforcement abuse directed at transgender people: harassment during identity checks and arbitrary arrests on vagrancy and public-order grounds. A news outlet reported in November 2020 on violent detentions of transgender people; on Christmas Day 2018 a singer booked to perform at a hotel in the capital was stopped by police officers on the street after her show, and her name was changed in the reporting because of concerns for her safety. A foreign government report from 2016 recorded LGBTQ residents being harassed, blackmailed and arrested by police under public-order and morality laws, with occasional harassment by neighbours as well as by police.

The Constitution adopted in May 2003 recognises in Article 26 only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman. Same-sex marriages, civil unions and comparable unions are not recognised. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition.

No anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's non-discrimination provisions, Articles 15 and 16, do not list those grounds; Article 16 names ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability and other grounds, but not sexual orientation or gender identity.

The national health ministry's Patients Rights and Responsibilities Policy (2018) states that all residents, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, age, religion, cultural belief or disability, are equally entitled to receive health services, and applies across public, private and NGO sectors.

Immigration and asylum protections covering LGBTQ people were issued in 2024, and in April 2022 a transgender claimant was granted refugee status. National asylum standard operating procedures (2024) require interviews to be conducted so that the applicant can present the grounds of their application comprehensively, with trained interviewers taking account of gender and of any circumstance including sexual orientation, gender identity or vulnerability. The manual on refugee appeal tribunal standard operating procedures (2014) imposes the same requirement on hearings. Standard operating procedures on identifying and safeguarding vulnerable persons under a migration partnership programme (2024) define Vulnerable Persons to include individuals whose gender identity or sexual orientation places them at higher risk, expressly naming lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons.

Homosexuality is a taboo subject in the country with no significant public discussion, and LGBTQ people face stigmatisation among the broader population. Asked about LGBT life in the country at a national cultural event in a city abroad in September 2016, the president said "it hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem."

No youth-, minor- or education-specific findings appear in the sources: school policy, bullying and the carriage of medication by minors are not documented here.

The most detailed accounts of enforcement against transgender people date from 2016 and 2020; the 2025 submission to a United Nations human rights committee is the most recent documentation in the inventory. No later presidential statement on the subject appears in the sources, and no reform of the prohibition on changing legal gender is recorded.
