AGO.name: Angola
AGO.summary:
Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in Angola with effect from 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 removed the colonial-era provision that described same-sex relationships as a "vice against nature" and, in the same instrument, attached imprisonment to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. A trans visitor therefore faces no criminal exposure under the sexual-offence provisions, and discrimination against them in employment and services on grounds of orientation is itself punishable.

The constitutional layer is narrower than the statutory one. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and expression sit across Title II articles. Protection for a trans visitor rests on those general provisions rather than on an enumerated ground.

Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations, among them Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA and Diversidade Masculina, submitted a shadow report on the country's compliance with the African Charter to the African Commission's 81st session in Banjul in October and November 2024, with support from ILGA and Synergia, documenting human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. A separate submission by Angolan organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, ahead of the state's review at the committee's 74th pre-session, raised discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people. Both filings indicate that formal legal protection is not matched by practice.

No law allows transgender people in Angola to change their gender marker on official documents or passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 provides that, in general, details entered into registration records should not be altered; section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status. That section is the only identified route to a legal gender change and its application to transgender applicants is not established. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

No entry or visa provisions specific to trans travellers are recorded for Angola. The only entry-adjacent material in the sources is external reference links to asylum information packets and to UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office travel advice on local laws and customs.

Official posture has been uneven. In 2010 the Angolan government refused to receive Isi Yanouka, an openly gay Israeli ambassador, reportedly because of his sexual orientation; the decision concerned diplomatic reception and was not a visa rule.

People living with HIV/AIDS in Angola are legally entitled to health care services and to protection from employment discrimination. No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition, and an unofficial commitment ceremony reported in 2005 was described in national news magazines as "shameless" and "abominable".
AGO.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Angolan border or immigration practice treats trans travellers differently is not sourced. No entry or visa provisions specific to trans travellers appear in the inventory, which holds only external reference links to asylum information packets and to UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office travel advice.

The gender-marker position is unresolved. No statute provides for a change of legal gender, and whether the Civil Registrar applies section 87 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 to such a change is not documented.

No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated LGBTQ facilities are recorded; the absence of a record is not evidence that none exist.

The 2024 shadow report documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people, but the inventory does not itemise individual incidents, dates or penalties. No trans-specific violence counts and no general homicide rate appear in the inventory, so no comparison of violence levels can be made. No youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education are recorded.

sources.summary:
Two LGBT groups operate in Angola, and only one, Iris Angola Association, has received official and legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018. At that time it had about 200 members, based in Luanda with offices in Benguela and Lubango. The three major political parties have not formally addressed LGBT issues in their platforms. The government does allow non-governmental organisations to exist, and some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education. In 2010 the Angolan Government refused to receive openly gay Isi Yanouka as the new Israeli ambassador, allegedly due to his sexual orientation, a diplomatic reception decision rather than a visa rule.

No specific law allows transgender people in Angola to change their gender marker on official documents and passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states that, in general, there should be no alteration of details entered into registration records, but section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status, meaning transgender people could possibly use this section to change their legal gender. A 2017 ILGA poll found 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

No entry or visa provisions are recorded for Angola; the only entry-adjacent items are external reference links to 'Asylumlaw.org: Sexual Minorities & HIV Status (Angola)' with information packets used for asylum purposes and to Angola travel advice on local laws and customs from the UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office.

Legally, people living with HIV/AIDS in Angola are entitled to health care services and protection from employment discrimination. No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded. On relationship recognition, there is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant; in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as 'shameless' and 'abominable' in national news magazines.

Education-focused work for LGBTQ Angolans is nascent and underfunded: the first association, Acção Humana (Human Action), launched in 2006 but has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programs specifically for LGBT people have struggled to get NGO funding. An HIV/AIDS educational program for LGBT people is only just beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International, and a 2007 study estimated roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men. No youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education are recorded.

COD.name: DR Congo
COD.summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo does not criminalise same-sex conduct. Same-sex activity has never been outlawed, including during Belgian colonial rule, and the age of consent is equal for partners of any sex. The absence of a ban is not matched by any protection: a March 2024 stakeholder submission by Savie asbl and co-signatories to the country's fifth-cycle Universal Periodic Review records that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights.

Public same-sex affection remains exposed to prosecution. Article 176 of the Penal Code punishes anyone who publicly outrages morals by their actions, and local ordinances are applied against LGBTQ people. GayOut's country guide notes there is no explicit national criminalisation while identifying Article 176 and those ordinances as the instruments used against LGBTQ people.

No legal gender recognition exists. Trans people have no route to change their identity documents, and the sources record no gender-identity recognition of any kind.

Relationship recognition is closed. The constitution has banned marriage between partners of the same sex since 2006, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex has no recognition route, and no other partnership status is available.

Violence against LGBTQ people is reported to involve the state's own forces. Queer In The World records violence, harassment and torture involving police, security forces and the army. GayOut reports that armed militia groups in eastern DRC have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity, and that the collapse of state authority in parts of the country leaves legal protections theoretical.

Expression is censored and can carry imprisonment. GayOut rates the country High Risk for LGBTQ+ travellers. Queer In The World advises visitors to keep a low profile and exercise discretion.

Church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral.
COD.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source prosecution counts or case outcomes under Article 176, so the frequency of enforcement against individuals cannot be stated. No sourced information is available on conditions of detention for LGBTQ detainees, on access to HIV or transition-related healthcare, or on asylum and refoulement practice.

Queer In The World's guidance covers both the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Republic of the Congo; only its DRC-specific statements are carried here, and its country-level risk rating is not broken down by region. GayOut's assessment of militia violence in eastern DRC is not accompanied by incident counts or dates.

Whether a third gender marker or any administrative gender-change procedure exists is unresolved in the inventory; the sources state only that no legal gender change is available.

sources.summary: Stakeholder submission to the DRC's 5th-cycle UPR (March 2024) by Savie asbl NGO and others: the DRC does not criminalise same-sex relations but neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights; public displays of same-sex affection can be prosecuted under indecent-exposure provisions (Article 176 of the Penal Code: 'anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions...').

Human Rights Watch, 4 Dec 2017: 120+ interviews, including nine Congolese security-force officers, UN officials and 21 M23 fighters, documented security forces recruiting ex-M23 fighters from Uganda and Rwanda in Oct–Dec 2016 and deploying them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi. State violence and impunity bear on visitor safety.

GayOut travel guide for DR Congo: rates the country 'High Risk for LGBTQ+' - no explicit national criminalisation but Article 176 ('indecent acts') and local ordinances applied to LGBTQ people; armed militia groups in eastern DRC have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity; state authority collapse means legal protections are theoretical.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror) on LGBTQ rights in the DRC: same-sex activity legal for both sexes (never outlawed, even under Belgian rule), equal age of consent; but no gender-identity recognition, no relationship recognition (same-sex marriage banned constitutionally since 2006), limited protections; church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral; public same-sex affection can trigger prosecution under indecency provisions.

ZMB.name: Zambia
ZMB.summary:
Zambian law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct and the prohibition is enforced. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law falls within the conduct the law reaches. Amnesty International's campaign account of 26 November 2024, 'Madalitso's story', describes a 36-year-old medical professional who by November 2024 had served three years of a sentence imposed for consensual same-sex acts; his imprisonment removed a trained clinician from a health system already short of staff.

Police are a documented source of risk rather than protection. The US State Department's 2021 country report records police perpetrating violence and verbal and physical harassment on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation, and prolonged detentions of LGBTQI+ people. Advocacy groups reported that police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTI individuals, with fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha, roughly $30 to $900. The 2022 report adds that when police detain LGBTQI+ people they often threaten charges under other laws to extort payment for release, and it found no credible reports that government agents condoned violence.

Prosecutions for same-sex conduct have relied on forced anal examinations. Human Rights Watch's July 2016 report 'Dignity Debased' documents the practice in Zambia, where prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal examinations as court evidence in sodomy cases, including a mass trial of about twenty men. Victims describe the examinations as painful, degrading sexual violence; Amnesty International in 2014 called them tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid, and the World Health Organization and medical authorities have condemned them.

The government rejects recognition and protection of LGBTQI+ rights. The 2021 State Department report found the government continued to reject such recognition and protection, and the 2022 report found no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ people. President Hakainde Hichilema's statement of 30 May, recorded in the 2022 report, opposed basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage and was followed by a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults.

Freedom of expression and assembly on LGBTQI+ matters is effectively barred. The government does not permit advocacy of LGBTQ rights, and the 2021 State Department report concluded that freedom of expression or peaceful assembly on LGBTQI+ matters remained nonexistent. In 1998 Vice President Christon Tembo called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona (2013), an activist arrested after calling for decriminalisation on a television talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court held he was reasonably exercising his right to freedom of expression, and the High Court rejected the soliciting, public place and immoral purposes charges. The government contested that decision.

Societal violence against LGBTQI+ people is frequent and often communal, with little recourse from police: threats, stalking, vandalism and hate crimes including murders are documented. The 2021 report found LGBTQI+ people at risk of societal violence arising from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of the law. In May 2014 residents of Marapodi in Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest, and in January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Most LGBTQI+ people in Zambia are closeted because of the risk of targeting, and lesbians are especially vulnerable within the country's patriarchal structure.

Discrimination in employment, housing, education and health continued through both reporting years. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care, but limited standards exist: the Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management on the basis of sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour. The 2021 State Department report records LGBTQI+ people facing an inability to access healthcare services.

Social attitudes are mostly negative, shaped by evangelical religious influence and colonial-era attitudes and by perceptions that homosexuality is immoral or a form of insanity. A 2010 survey found 2 percent of Zambians considered homosexuality morally acceptable. Anti-LGBTQI+ mobilisation is organised: the NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts (ZAPASA) was formed in 1999 to combat homosexuality.
ZMB.outOfScopeNotes:
No information in the source inventory addresses trans-specific healthcare or medication in Zambia.

Gender-marker and identity-document rules for trans travellers, and any entry or visa screening that could expose a traveller's status, are not sourced.

Access to sex-segregated facilities such as toilets and changing rooms is not addressed by any source.

The outcome of the government's challenge to the 2013 Kasonkomona acquittal is not recorded.

HIV service data date from July 2007 and the attitude survey from 2010; no more recent figures are available here.

ZWE.name: Zimbabwe
ZWE.summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that the offence covers sodomy and acts involving contact between males that a reasonable person would regard as indecent. Sodomy is classified in the Criminal Code as unlawful sexual conduct, defined as anal sexual intercourse or any indecent act between consenting adults, with common-law formulations reaching "unlawful and intentional sexual relations per anum between two human males" and "unnatural offences".

A 2006 revision of the Criminal Code expanded sodomy beyond sexual activity to any act involving contact between two males that a reasonable person would regard as an indecent act, and added a sexual deviancy offence criminalising holding hands, hugging or kissing between two people of the same sex. That amendment was one of fifteen additions made to the code that year. Conduct well short of intercourse therefore falls inside the criminal law, and visible affection between two people read as of the same sex is exposed to it.

Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024) examines escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people across the countries it covers, Zimbabwe among them. The deployment of law as an instrument of hostility is the risk context a visitor faces, alongside the statutory exposure itself.

Zimbabwean law provides no general protection from discrimination, violence or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The only explicit protections tied to sexual orientation concern personal information, under the Freedom of Information Act (2020) and the Cyber and Data Protection Act (2022).

The Constitution was amended in 2013 to define marriage as between a man and a woman, and in May 2019 Cabinet approved amendments to the marriage law to align the ban. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition of that partnership and no protection attaching to it.

Gender marker change is not permitted. Section 18(2) of the Births and Deaths Registration Act allows a first-name change only by application to the Registrar General with evidence justifying the need, and the Registrar General's discretion can defeat a change sought on grounds of gender identity.

Enforcement has a documented record. In 2014 the activist Rikki Nathanson was arrested for using a women's bathroom under a criminal nuisance charge; the charge was dismissed and she sued for damages and won. In 1998 former President Canaan Banana was convicted on eleven charges of sodomy, attempted sodomy and indecent assault following his 1996 arrest, sentenced to ten years' imprisonment, and released after serving six months in an open prison.

Government campaigns against homosexual men and women have run since 1995. Documented enforcement includes infiltration of GALZ, bribery, detention, beating, killing and rape by authorities, and the reported use of the Central Intelligence Organisation to beat and arrest homosexuals.

Healthcare is the clearest area of formal protection. In July 2018 the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender or non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that providing care to these groups is lawful and every provider's duty, recording that "nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups", and it was issued because patients had been avoiding clinics out of fear of mistreatment or of staff tipping off the police. Health ministry training manuals further require professionals to support the specific healthcare needs of transgender and non-gender-conforming people, alongside sex workers, men who have sex with men, and people who inject drugs.

Reachable support infrastructure is thin but present. GALZ, established in 1990, reports more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, and offers legal support covering arrests for sodomy, counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes.
ZWE.outOfScopeNotes:
How often the sodomy and sexual deviancy provisions have been charged in recent years is not established in the available sources. No charge-level figures were located, so the distance between the statute as written and its day-to-day application remains unresolved.

The text of the 2006 amendment was not obtained directly. The scope of the sexual deviancy offence and the examples attached to it rest on reference material and contemporaneous reporting.

Whether health providers in public institutions follow the 2018 handbook in practice, and whether the police tip-offs the handbook was designed to prevent continue, is not documented. Day-to-day treatment of trans patients therefore depends on staff trained under that handbook.

The May 2019 Cabinet approval of marriage-law amendments is recorded as an approval; whether those amendments were enacted, and in what final form, is not sourced.

In 1998 a former head of state was convicted on eleven charges of sodomy, attempted sodomy and indecent assault following his 1996 arrest, sentenced to ten years' imprisonment, and released after serving six months in an open prison.

Government campaigns against homosexual men and women have run since 1995. Documented enforcement includes infiltration of a national LGBTI membership organisation, bribery, detention, beating, killing and rape by authorities, and the reported use of a national intelligence agency to beat and arrest homosexuals.

Healthcare is the clearest area of formal protection. In July 2018 the national health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender or non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that providing care to these groups is lawful and every provider's duty, recording that "nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups", and it was issued because patients had been avoiding clinics out of fear of mistreatment or of staff tipping off the police. Health ministry training manuals further require professionals to support the specific healthcare needs of transgender and non-gender-conforming people, alongside sex workers, men who have sex with men, and people who inject drugs.

Reachable support infrastructure is thin but present. A national LGBTI membership organisation established in 1990 reports more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, and offers legal support covering arrests for sodomy, counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes.

How often the sodomy and sexual deviancy provisions have been charged in recent years is not established in the available sources. No charge-level figures were located, so the distance between the statute as written and its day-to-day application remains unresolved.

The text of the 2006 amendment was not obtained directly. The scope of the sexual deviancy offence and the examples attached to it rest on reference material and contemporaneous reporting.

Whether health providers in public institutions follow the 2018 handbook in practice, and whether the police tip-offs the handbook was designed to prevent continue, is not documented. Day-to-day treatment of trans patients therefore depends on staff trained under that handbook.

The May 2019 national cabinet approval of marriage-law amendments is recorded as an approval; whether those amendments were enacted, and in what final form, is not sourced.

News outlet report, 9 July 2018: the health ministry released a training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender/non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions; the manual states care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, and was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff; for a trans visitor: formal policy guarantees health-service access including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Academic article, 'The politics of sexual identities in this country: A social work perspective?' (International Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012): homosexuals live secluded lives due to prejudice; the article traces same-sex relations in this country before and after historic administration; social workers should promote social justice for the gay community.

ZWE.blindTangential:
A censorship and entertainments control statute prohibits undesirable publications, defined as indecent or obscene or offensive or harmful to public morals or likely to be contrary to public health. Section 11 of that statute has been used to harass LGBTI people and activists, an expression and materials exposure that sits alongside the person-level criminal law.

A human rights report published on 9 January 2024 places the country within a set of countries in one region where law is being turned against LGBTI populations, so travel within the region does not by itself lower the exposure described here.
ZWE.localsOnly:
Transgender Zimbabweans face difficulty accessing legal work because official documents do not reflect their gender, as documented in comments attributed to the activist Jordan Chanetsa, who also cites the documents problem as a barrier beyond employment.

Rikki Nathanson established Trans Research, Education, Advocacy & Training (TREAT) in 2015, the year after her arrest and the civil claim that followed it.

The 2018 health ministry handbook records the domestic public-health position: criminalisation of sex work, drug use and some sexual acts creates disproportionate harms, undermines HIV prevention for the whole nation, and impairs access to healthcare.

MWI.name: Malawi
MWI.summary:
Malawi's Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Section 153 covers carnal knowledge against the order of nature and permits up to fourteen years' imprisonment with or without corporal punishment, and section 154 punishes attempts with up to seven years on the same terms. Gross indecency between men, in public or private, is a felony carrying up to five years. Human Rights Watch reports the sections as exposing men to up to fourteen years and women to five.

On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court dismissed the challenge to sections 153, 154 and 156, an application brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani. The court held that the sections criminalise consensual same-sex conduct among other acts but do not discriminate against homosexual persons because they prohibit all people from certain conduct, and it rejected claims of discriminatory application, leaving any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the ruling a dark day and warned of heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence.

Jana Gonani, a trans woman, was convicted under section 153(c) by a Magistrate's Court in Mangochi on 23 December 2021 and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment, served in a men's prison. Human Rights Watch reports that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are the most likely to be targeted under these provisions, so the sections reach gender identity directly in practice.

Enforcement is documented as arbitrary and violent. Human Rights Watch's 61-page report Let Posterity Judge, released on 26 October 2018 from interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, found that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and sometimes assaulted them. Medical staff denied services on gender-expression grounds: a trans man was beaten and then refused treatment, and nurses mocked people presenting for HIV tests.

A moratorium suspending arrests and prosecutions under sections 153 to 156 was announced by the attorney general on 5 November 2012 and reaffirmed in July 2014 and on 18 December 2015 by the justice minister. The High Court in Mzuzu granted an injunction on 9 February 2016 ordering police to resume arrests and annulled the moratorium on 19 February 2016 on the ground that the executive lacked constitutional authority to suspend parliamentary laws, leaving its legality contested. Police worked around it while it stood: in April 2018 officers in Mzuzu arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, apparently to circumvent the moratorium while both laws faced constitutional challenge.

Arrest itself carries a documented secondary risk. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 on homosexuality charges, Cuthbert Kulemela and Kelvin Gonani, had their house ransacked and were assaulted by neighbours, threatened with being burned alive, subjected to attempted extortion and humiliated by community police through forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photographs distributed on social media.

A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read locally as same-sex has no recognition to rely on. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions, provides that gender is assigned at birth, and does not permit a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender.
MWI.outOfScopeNotes:
No entry, visa or passport-marker rules for Malawi are sourced in this inventory, and no airport or border screening practice specific to trans or gender-nonconforming travellers is documented. Whether a trans visitor faces document inspection, secondary screening or outing at the border remains unresolved on the available material.

The inventory provides no violence figures for trans people in Malawi against which a general homicide rate could be set, so no comparative magnitude of trans-specific violence can be stated. The 2011 protest death toll of 20 is reported by a foreign government's human rights report without a stated relation to LGBT targeting, and that relation is unresolved here.

Whether parliament has taken up the reform the Constitutional Court left to it after 28 June 2024 is not sourced. Enforcement of the 2019 broadcasting hate-speech provisions, and whether any complaint under them has been pursued, is likewise not documented. The application of section 154 to gender-identity-related conduct is not evidenced in the inventory.

SDN.name: Sudan
SDN.summary:
Gender nonconformity is itself criminalised in Sudan. Article 152 of the Penal Code prohibits wearing clothing of the opposite sex, and the provision addresses gender presentation rather than sexual conduct. A trans visitor whose appearance is read as incongruent with the sex recorded on their documents falls within its scope regardless of any other behaviour.

Sodomy is criminalised under Article 148 of the Criminal Act of 1991, as amended in 2009. The offence is defined as anal sex, whether between people of the same sex or of different sexes, and applies to men and women alike. Penalties set by the amendment adopted by the Transitional Sovereignty Council on 9 July 2020 are up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence, up to seven years for a second, and life imprisonment for a third. The same amendment abolished the death penalty for anal sex and the 100 lashes previously imposed for same-sex intimacy; before that repeal, capital punishment was available for a third offence. No executions for sodomy were documented before the repeal, and in 2011 there were no reports of the antisodomy provision being applied.

SSD.name: South Sudan
SSD.summary:
South Sudan's Penal Code criminalises gender presentation on its face. Section 379 reaches "any male person who dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman", with a penalty of up to three months' imprisonment. The provision requires no sexual conduct and no disclosure of identity, so a trans visitor presenting female is exposed on appearance alone.

The same code treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as an "unnatural offense", defined as carnal intercourse against the order of nature, punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual, the maximum rises to 14 years.

United States State Department human rights reports for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that no authorities were reported to have enforced the same-sex conduct provision. The reports describe no repeal, no moratorium and no prosecutorial policy limiting its use, so non-enforcement is reported practice rather than a legal safeguard.

The same reporting series documents security forces routinely harassing LGBTQI+ people and sometimes arresting, detaining, torturing and beating them between 2018 and 2022. Enforcement pressure falls on people who are visible or suspected rather than on the conduct provision itself.

No hate crime legislation and no anti-discrimination law protect against harassment or abuse on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. A visitor who is targeted has no statutory bias-crime route and no discrimination remedy.

South Sudan recognises no legal status for same-sex couples, and the 2011 Constitution bans same-sex marriage. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex holds no recognition and no spousal immigration or next-of-kin standing derived from it.

Stigmatisation of LGBTQ people is widespread in the wider population. The 2011 State Department report described discrimination against gay men and lesbians as "widespread", and the 2022 report found that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled the country because of "actively hostile government rhetoric and action".

No LGBTQ support organisation is known to operate in the country, leaving a visitor who runs into trouble without local advocacy or referral infrastructure.
SSD.outOfScopeNotes:
No entry, visa or passport gender-marker rules specific to trans travellers appear in the source inventory. Airport screening practice and document-marker policy for South Sudan are not sourced here.

Access to gender-affirming care, and the law or practice governing bathrooms and other sex-segregated facilities, is not covered by the inventory.

The enforcement picture rests on State Department reporting that records the absence of reported prosecutions. Absence of reports is not evidence that the conduct provision has never been used, and no sentencing data for either provision is available.

Whether Section 379 has been applied to trans women in practice, and how often, is not documented in the sources reviewed.

SOM.name: Somalia
SOM.summary:
Somalia criminalises same-sex sexual activity, and the sources give irreconcilable penalties. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of life imprisonment under a penal code it dates to 1964, together with the death penalty under sharia in some regions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report gives up to three years, and its 2022 report gives three months to three years for 'carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex'. Article 409 of the penal code, dated by Wikipedia to 1973, carries three months to three years for intercourse and two months to two years for an 'act of lust' other than intercourse; Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, intended to prevent re-offending.

Under local interpretations of sharia, same-sex conduct is punishable by death. In areas controlled by al-Shabaab and in Jubaland, capital punishment is imposed for consensual same-sex sexual activity at a judge's discretion. The 2022 State Department report records no known state-conducted executions of that kind, and the archived 2010 report noted the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control.

Enforcement by the federal authorities is undocumented. The 2022 State Department report states that no official reports of enforcement were available and that impunity generally remained the norm. Wikipedia records that in government-controlled areas civil law provides for up to three years and that LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted. The two accounts cannot be reconciled from the sources.

ILGA reported killings of people accused of homosexual activity by al-Shabaab or other non-state armed groups: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed by al-Shabaab in 2024. The inventory supplies no denominator or background homicide rate, so these counts cannot be compared with the general level of lethal violence in the country.

The law does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, as reported by the US Department of State in 2022.

The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family, which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law has no route to recognition.

Pervasive social stigma attaches to same-sex relationships, and sexual orientation is a taboo subject with no public discussion in any region of the country, per US State Department reports from 2010 and 2022. Severe societal stigma prevents LGBTQI+ individuals from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly as of 2022. For a visitor, visible gender nonconformity or a disclosed identity carries outing risk.

The 2016 report by Benjamin Christman, reported by Erasing 76 Crimes, found evidence that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia because of persecution risk, supporting refugee-status claims and forming a non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers.
SOM.outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty figures cannot be reconciled. The Human Dignity Trust records a maximum of life imprisonment under a penal code it dates to 1964; the 2021 State Department report gives up to three years; the 2022 report gives three months to three years; and Article 409 of the penal code, dated by Wikipedia to 1973, gives three months to three years for intercourse and two months to two years for an act of lust. The dating of the penal code is unresolved between the sources.

No official enforcement data is available from the federal authorities. Whether the death penalty has been carried out by state authorities for same-sex conduct is not sourced; the 2022 report records no known state-conducted executions of that kind.

The sources provide no denominator or background homicide rate for the reported killings, so no magnitude can be attached to those counts.

Since 1999, much AIDS/HIV education and care has come from international organizations such as the United Nations. Somalia has one of the lowest HIV infection rates on the continent, with adult prevalence estimated at 0.5% in 2007. ERI.name: Eritrea
ERI.summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's penal code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries a maximum sentence of seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained at independence and carried into its first post-independence penal code, adopted in 2015, with an enhanced sentence.

The law is enforced against foreign nationals as well as residents. In 2013 Paolo Mannina, an Italian citizen teaching literature at a technical school in Asmara, was dismissed and deported; the government described him as a "dangerous individual who is potentially destabilizing to the moral order and public of the country" and justified the expulsion under Article 7 of the Agreement on Italian Technical Schools, which requires compliance with local law including the penal code's prohibition. In 2004 three hotel workers from Western countries were expelled for homosexual activity, at least one of them openly homosexual. Eritrea's ambassador to Italy stated that any foreigner must respect local customs and the law prohibiting homosexual relations; Italian diplomats condemned the expulsions.

Detention facilities are used against people suspected of same-sex conduct. In 2003 six gay men arrested in a public bathroom in Asmara were transferred to the Adi Abeyto prison facility, which is known for holding political prisoners and journalists.

Openly LGBTQI+ people risk imprisonment and for that reason did not take part in the political process, according to the US State Department's 2023 human rights report, which also records continuing societal discrimination. The same reporting found no public LGBTQ organisations and tight restrictions on expression of sexual orientation and gender identity; LGBTQI+ people cannot freely assemble, associate or express themselves publicly for fear of identification, arrest, discrimination or violence. State censorship of LGBTQ issues is compounded by heavy social stigma, and in the early 2000s state-run radio and television broadcast programmes on the alleged dangers of homosexuality.

Official rhetoric is hostile. The government has labelled disloyal individuals "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles". It rejected a UN Human Rights Council Universal Periodic Review recommendation to decriminalise same-sex sexual activity as "in direct contradiction with the values and traditions of the Eritrean people", and has made no major effort to change or rescind the law.

No anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people, as the UK Foreign Office records; the UK raised the issue bilaterally and through the EU. The penal code makes no gender distinction for assault.

Criminalisation obstructs health and care access. ILGA and HIV/AIDS prevention groups have condemned the law on the ground that it makes prevention programmes directed at men who have sex with men extremely difficult, and the US State Department lists societal discrimination against people with HIV/AIDS as an area of concern. No law bans conversion therapy; OutRight Action International found conversion therapy and attempts to forcibly change sexual orientation or gender identity widespread under social stigma, and LGBTQ people have reportedly been offered conversion therapy in lieu of jail time.

Same-sex relationships have no legal recognition in Eritrea and same-sex couples cannot adopt. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law has no recognition route.
ERI.outOfScopeNotes:
Sources cite the offence both as Article 310(1) of the 2015 penal code and as Article 600 of the penal code; the relationship between the two numbering systems is not resolved here.

The 2002 account of abuse of gay and lesbian soldiers is unconfirmed.

No youth-specific care findings are recorded, and no data was identified on trans-specific violence, hate-crime enforcement, or screening and document-marker rules affecting trans travellers at Eritrean entry points.

ATG.name: Antigua and Barbuda
ATG.summary:
Consensual sexual intimacy between adults is not a criminal offence in Antigua and Barbuda. On 5 July 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Orden David et al v The Attorney General of Antigua and Barbuda, declared Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995 unconstitutional and void. The ruling struck down the country's buggery and gross indecency provisions, which Human Rights Watch described as the sodomy and gross indecency offences. The penalties those sections carried before the judgment were up to fifteen years' imprisonment for adult-on-adult buggery, five years where a minor committed the act, and life imprisonment where an adult committed it on a minor; serious indecency carried up to ten years where the target was a child under sixteen; and a person convicted of buggery as a repeat offender was placed on the Sex Offenders Register for the remainder of their life.

The same judgment read the constitutional prohibition on sex discrimination as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity. That is an interpretive holding by the court and has not been translated into a statutory protection regime. Antiguan law contains no explicit prohibition of discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Outright International records that transgender people are particularly vulnerable in Antigua and Barbuda because there is no mechanism to change legal gender markers, and only name changes are available. For a trans visitor this is the operative constraint: a change of the sex recorded on identity documents is not possible in the country, by administrative or judicial route, so travel documents and any local identity check will continue to show the sex assigned at birth.

No form of same-sex union is recognised in Antigua and Barbuda, and households headed by such couples are not eligible for the rights granted to married opposite-sex couples. A trans visitor travelling with a partner whose relationship would be classified as same-sex under local birth-sex status has no route to have that relationship recognised during the stay.

Decriminalisation followed years of official resistance. At the May 2016 Universal Periodic Review of the UN Human Rights Council, Argentina, Australia, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Nicaragua urged the government to repeal its sodomy ban and guarantee full human rights to LGBTQ people. Minister of Social Transformation Samantha Marshall described the ban as antiquated and said it should be repealed, while Parliamentary Secretary Maureen Payne-Hyman told the Council that LGBTQ people are not persecuted in the country. On 24 August 2016 the government announced it had no intention of repealing the ban, while acknowledging that a lawsuit would almost certainly strike it down given the identical jurisprudence already established in Belize.

On 1 November 2019 the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality announced it would file a legal challenge, which culminated in the 5 July 2022 ruling. The group's stated argument was that buggery and indecency laws stigmatise LGBT people and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence. The litigant, Orden David, had been bullied and physically attacked before bringing the case, including being struck in the head and knocked unconscious in daylight.

The Advocates for Human Rights filed a submission with the UN Human Rights Committee in January 2025, ahead of that body's review of Antigua and Barbuda, listing LGBTQ+ rights issues that remain open following decriminalisation.
ATG.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports trans-specific violence figures for Antigua and Barbuda, and none gives the country's general homicide rate, so no comparison between the two can be made. The inventory records one assault on a named activist before the 2022 litigation; it is a single incident and cannot be read as a rate.

Police and immigration practice toward trans visitors, including document screening and any differential treatment in custody or at ports of entry, is not addressed in the inventory.

It is unresolved whether convictions entered under Sections 12 and 15 before the 2022 judgment have been expunged, and what has become of the lifetime Sex Offenders Register entries imposed on repeat offenders. No source addresses this.

Whether the court's reading of sex discrimination to include sexual orientation and gender identity has been applied in any later case, tribunal or administrative decision is not sourced.

The January 2025 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee is described only at the level of its subject matter; the specific issues it raises are not itemised in the inventory.

BRB.name: Barbados
BRB.summary:
Same-sex conduct between men was decriminalised in Barbados in December 2022, following a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with the trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights programme. A High Court ruling on sodomy published in May 2023 found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional.

Enforcement against violence has produced a documented impunity outcome. In February 2018 Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward and suffered serious injuries, including to her throat. Coward was convicted in April 2019 and ordered to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or serve three months in prison; no jail time was imposed.

Employment protection does not reach gender identity or gender expression. Trans Barbadians are frequently fired or denied jobs for dressing wrong, and the Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status but is read by Hoffmann as excluding trans workers because neither gender identity nor gender expression is listed.

Barbados law recognises no union between two people of the same sex. In June 2016 the government ruled out changing the law to allow same-sex marriage, and in September 2020 it announced only a plan to recognise some form of civil union followed by a referendum on gay marriage. Critics called the civil union proposal unnecessarily vague and expected the referendum to fail; as of the source's account neither had been enacted.

Entry and migration policy treats LGBT people as a contested category rather than a protected one. Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct group, and the government has questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration: in 2011 it said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada, and in 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean described such applications as an attempt to abuse the Canadian refugee system, noting that two of nine Canadian applications had been denied.

The Welcome Stamp remote-work visa, introduced in July 2020, initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse; it was changed to permit same-sex spouses.

Family recognition is closed to same-sex couples. They cannot legally adopt, surrogacy is illegal although not explicitly prohibited or regulated by law, and same-sex couples are not recognised as families. The Barbados Fertility Centre offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.

Official and religious hostility is on the record. In 2016 Attorney General Adriel Brathwaite said Barbados would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage, and after David Cameron's 2011 CHOGM aid warning over sodomy laws he said Barbados would not be dictated to by the United Kingdom. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting Human Rights Watch to call the response a cheap political trick, since its report did not mention same-sex marriage. Fundamentalist groups including the New Testament Church have claimed sexual orientation is chosen and argued that discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, and human rights activists say the arrival of more American evangelical ministers has spread homophobic rhetoric more widely. The Barbados Nation's informal comment line drew opposition to a proposed gay tourism package. The Anglican Bishop of Barbados and the Catholic Church oppose the buggery law while stating respect for LGBT rights, and Prime Minister Mia Mottley, elected in May 2018, is reportedly pro-LGBT.

A regional human-rights route remains open. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154, ss.9 and 12); the Commission gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019, and failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision.

No findings were identified on the treatment of LGBT minors, the detention of unaccompanied youth, or school-based anti-bullying and gender-affirming education.

KNA.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
KNA.summary:
Consensual sexual conduct between adults is lawful in Saint Kitts and Nevis. On 29 August 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General, struck sections 56 (buggery) and 57 (indecent assault against men) of the Offences Against the Person Act as contrary to constitutional guarantees of the right to privacy and freedom of expression. The decision took immediate effect and decriminalised consensual sexual intercourse between adult men in private, and the conduct has been legal throughout the country, on both Saint Kitts and Nevis, since that judgment. The offences struck were defined in relation to men, and the change came from a civil-society constitutional challenge rather than from legislation.

The penal code contains no protection against discrimination or harassment on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no post-repeal discrimination statute has been enacted. Discrimination in employment, education and accommodation, and hate speech, remain lawful. A visitor subjected to any of these has no local statutory remedy.

No form of same-sex union is recognised, whether marriage or partnership, and households headed by same-sex couples receive none of the rights attaching to opposite-sex married couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classified locally as same-sex can expect no spousal recognition, no next-of-kin standing and no partner benefits under local law.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: there is no procedure for changing gender markers, and identity documents cannot be updated to reflect a trans person's gender. A trans visitor travels on the documents issued by their home jurisdiction and cannot have them altered locally.

Protection machinery is thin. The National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 names LGBTQ+ citizens among the groups it covers, but the Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance and ECADE told the Universal Periodic Review process in 2025 that the state has taken no tangible steps under it, and that LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement. That avoidance is a direct signal about reporting: police are not a reliable route to protection for anti-trans harassment or assault. LGBTI organisations are permitted to register.

State posture toward LGBTQ people has been documented at the point of entry. On 23 March 2005 Nevis barred a cruise ship carrying 110 passengers, most of them LGBTQ, from docking; a police boat halted the Source Events/Windjammer Barefoot Cruises vessel and the ship was ordered to sail on. Port officials announced the exclusion publicly as a cultural decision, and the port authority's acting general manager, Oral Brandy, told reporters that Nevis did not want homosexuality "to be a part of our culture."

In 2011 the Government of Saint Kitts and Nevis stated that it had "no mandate from the people" to abolish the criminalisation of homosexuality among consenting adults, a position taken while the struck offences were still in force.
KNA.outOfScopeNotes:
Prosecution, police and court practice toward trans or gender-nonconforming people after the 2022 judgment is not documented in the sources, and the frequency with which the struck provisions were applied before it is not sourced.

No trans-specific violence or hate-crime data for Saint Kitts and Nevis appears in the sources, and no comparison with the jurisdiction's general homicide rate is available.

Immigration and visa screening rules that would single out trans travellers are not sourced. The one documented exclusion at a port, the 2005 refusal of a chartered cruise ship, was an ad hoc decision by port authorities rather than a published entry rule.

Implementation of the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 rests on civil-society reporting to the Universal Periodic Review; no government implementation report was located. Country coverage in several sources comes from regional campaign and tag archives rather than country-specific enforcement reporting, so enforcement detail is unresolved.

Discrimination protections are absent in employment, education and accommodation, and hate speech is not unlawful. The criminal code does not address discrimination or harassment on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

LGBTQ+ organisations may register and operate. Civil-society organisations report that LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement, and that LGBTQ+ citizens are named in a national gender equality policy for 2022 to 2027 but that the state has taken no tangible steps under it.

DMA.name: Dominica
DMA.summary:
On 22 April 2024 the High Court of Justice in Roseau held that sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act were unconstitutional insofar as they criminalised consensual same-sex activity between adults. The case was brought by a gay man living in Dominica. The court did not strike the sections down; it ordered them read down, so that section 14(2) exempts private consensual acts between adult persons who consent, and section 16(1)(b) exempts private consensual adult acts from the ten-year penalty for buggery. Both provisions remain on the statute book in that construed form.

The provisions the court construed were broad. The Sexual Offences Act 1998, as amended in 2016, criminalised male same-sex sexual activity and female same-sex sexual activity, and also anal intercourse between persons of the opposite sex. Section 14 punished gross indecency with 12 years' imprisonment where the complainant was 16 or older, and 14 years for a first offence or 20 years for a subsequent offence where the complainant was under 16, exempting only private consensual adult male-female acts. Section 16 punished buggery with 25 years where an adult committed it on a minor, 10 years where an adult committed it on another adult, 5 years where committed by a minor, and 4 years for attempt or assault with intent, and allowed the court to order admission to a psychiatric hospital for treatment.

The ruling addresses sexual conduct only. It creates no protection on grounds of gender identity or gender expression, and no Dominican law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Dominica gives no recognition to same-sex unions, whether as marriage or as civil unions, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no route to partner recognition, spousal immigration status or next-of-kin standing through a registered union.

Policing of anti-LGBT violence has been documented as dismissive. The man who filed the July 2019 constitutional challenge to the 10-year and 12-year provisions reported that police refused to investigate a violent attack on his home because, under Dominican law, gay people were considered criminals. A 2011 academic submission to the United Nations recorded that reports by victims to police were not taken seriously and that victims were sometimes ridiculed.

Violence against people perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming is documented, including a killing. In 2010 Clement James of Portsmouth was stabbed to death after being accused of "watching" his male assailant in a public place; the accused, Davis St Jean, was reported to preach in the street about killing gay people and to have said "all battie boi must dead" before the stabbing. Reporting on LGBTQ rights in Dominica also records suspected hate crimes against individuals believed to be homosexual, and the use of slurs such as "buggerman" and "battyman" for men read as effeminate.

Hostility has been directed at visitors specifically. In 2009 the president of the Evangelical Association, Bill Daniel, said "We want the government to ensure that gay tourists do not come to the island and conduct themselves in any immoral way"; the association protested gay cruises visiting the island and the promotion of Dominica as a gay tourist destination.

No available source documents the position of transgender people in Dominica specifically. There is no cited record of a trans-specific prosecution, a trans-specific violent incident, gender-marker or documentation rules, facility-access rules, or trans healthcare access. The 2024 judgment concerns consensual sexual conduct between adults and leaves gender identity, gender expression and gender-marker policy unaddressed by any cited instrument.

LCA.name: Saint Lucia
LCA.summary:
Saint Lucia's High Court decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 29 July 2025, striking down the colonial-era buggery and gross indecency offences as unconstitutional in Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia. Human Rights Watch reported the judgment on 31 July 2025, and the Associated Press covered it as part of a wave of strategic constitutional litigation across the Eastern Caribbean. For a visitor, criminal exposure for private consensual adult same-sex conduct ended with that declaration.

The Criminal Code No. 9 of 2004, in force since 1 January 2005, remains on the books as amended by the ruling. Section 132 defines gross indecency as genital acts other than intercourse for sexual arousal or gratification and carries ten years on indictment or five years on summary conviction, but exempts private consensual acts between adults. Section 133 defines buggery as anal intercourse and carries life imprisonment where committed by force and without consent, ten years otherwise, and five years for an attempt or assault with intent, exempting private consensual acts where both parties are 16 or older.

The Domestic Violence Act, passed on 8 March 2022, is the clearest protection available to a trans visitor or resident who is a victim of violence. It uses gender-neutral definitions of spouse, cohabitant, visiting relationship, domestic relationship, applicant and respondent, and its definition of domestic violence covers economic and sexual abuse, harassment, cyber-stalking, coercion, threats and intimidation. Clause 5 requires public officers and service providers not to discriminate on grounds that include sex, gender, sexual orientation and gender identity, and transgender victims and survivors have equal access to remedies, including court protection orders.

Enforcement and protection machinery has been the subject of targeted training. A human rights sensitisation session in 2014 instructed the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force on general and LGBT-specific content, and a further session in Castries on 19 May 2015 brought together officers from the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and the Bordelais Correctional Facility with regional and international civil-society organisations. The 2015 programme built on the 2014 work.

Documented violence against sexual-orientation minorities includes the 2011 attack and robbery of three American gay men in a vacation villa, in which the assailants used anti-gay slurs, and the February 2019 stabbing murder of Michael Pooran, a 27-year-old Guyanese man, alleged to have been motivated by his perceived sexual orientation and followed by calls to denounce violence and revisit the buggery laws. In March 2019 the United Kingdom Upper Tribunal held that gay men are at risk of persecution in Saint Lucia and may claim asylum. No trans-specific violence data was identified.

Saint Lucia was the only UN member state in the Americas to formally oppose the UN declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity.
LCA.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust case digest for Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403), so the judgment's full reasoning is not sourced here.

No trans-specific violence data, no data on bathroom or facilities access rules, no data on gender-marker or document-change procedures, and no data on entry or visa screening specific to trans travellers were identified.

The 2011 and 2019 incidents are individual documented cases; no denominator or rate is available, so they cannot be used to rank Saint Lucia's risk level against other jurisdictions.

VCT.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
VCT.summary:
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines criminalises consensual sex between men. Section 146 of the criminal code, the inherited buggery offence, carries up to 10 years' imprisonment; section 148, gross indecency, carries up to 5 years. Both provisions remain in force.

On 16 February 2024 the High Court dismissed a constitutional challenge and upheld the ban, holding that outlawing homosexual activity is lawful. The Eastern Caribbean rights alliance ECADE condemned the ruling on 19 February 2024, stating that LGBTQ+ Vincentians face greater vulnerability as a result. The Prime Minister has said any change would be an OECS-wide decision, because constitutional and legislative provisions are similar across member states.

Human Rights Watch's July 2023 report, a 58-page study titled 'They Can Harass Us Because of the Laws', documents bias-motivated violence and discrimination against LGBT people in daily life and calls for decriminalisation and for sexual-orientation and gender-identity non-discrimination legislation. No law addresses discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so LGBT people have no legal protection when they speak out.

In September 2018 three cross-dressing young men were physically attacked; Prime Minister Ralph Gonsalves condemned the attacks, called the homophobia unacceptable and called for an open conversation on homosexuality. In April 2019 a cross-dressing teenager, Leswan Stewart, was the victim of a transphobic assault and was then charged with fraud for allegedly pretending to be a woman; the prosecutor withdrew the charge in May 2019 without giving a reason.

GRD.name: Grenada
GRD.summary:
Sections 430 and 431 of the Criminal Code criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Section 431, covering "unnatural crime," carries a maximum penalty of ten years' imprisonment for male same-sex acts. Section 430 addresses "grossly indecent acts" between men. A gender-neutral grossly indecent act provision reaches same-sex conduct committed willfully in public. These provisions remain in force.

United States Department of State reporting for 2023 records that the criminalising provisions are not enforced in practice, and reports no arbitrary killings, torture or enforced disappearances in Grenada that year. The absence of enforcement does not remove the exposure: the statutes remain in force with custodial penalties attached.

No legal gender recognition is available. A trans visitor's passport or other identity documents will carry the sex marker assigned at birth or issued by another jurisdiction, and there is no domestic procedure to amend it.

National law provides no protection against discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The 1973 Constitution contains no equality clause and no protection of privacy.

LGBTIQ people face discrimination in housing, education, employment and public services, and fear of prosecution inhibits reporting to police, which affects residents and visitors alike.

Grenada does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnership. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex classification has no route to spousal recognition, and no spousal protections follow from it.
GRD.outOfScopeNotes:
The gender-neutral grossly indecent act provision is cited as Section 430 in some sources and as Section 7 in others; the numbering is unresolved here.

No prosecution, conviction or sentencing data for Sections 430 and 431 appears in the sources. The finding that the provisions are not enforced rests on a single government human-rights report covering 2023.

No information is available on how police, immigration or border officers treat trans travellers, and no account of document or screening practice at ports of entry is present in the sources.

No trans-specific violence data for Grenada appears in the sources; the 2023 report records no arbitrary killings, torture or enforced disappearances.

No information is available on access to hormone therapy, surgery or other trans-specific healthcare.

BHS.name: Bahamas
BHS.summary:
Consensual sexual conduct between adults was decriminalised on 16 May 1991 under the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act, and no source records a prosecution risk for a visitor on that basis. The criminal law retains an unequal age of consent: 16 years for opposite-sex acts and 18 years for same-sex acts, so a trans visitor in a relationship that local law reads as same-sex falls under the higher threshold.

Gender identity appears in no anti-discrimination or anti-harassment statute in the Bahamas. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal, and the same gap applies to sexual orientation. The Constitution's prohibition on discrimination covers neither characteristic. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed Constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition.

No national hate-crime law exists to prevent or punish violence directed at LGBT people, and discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal.

Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign in April 2016, stating that no laws protect transgender and intersex Bahamians and advocating, through member Torri Culmer, against job termination for trans and intersex workers.

Trans people have been named as targets by a serving official. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas," urged financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island so that "they stay out of the way," and pledged $1,000 toward it. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 that he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 that a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people.

Marriage and civil unions are not available to same-sex couples. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, and maritime marriage law provides that a marriage is void if contracted between two men or two women. In 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated that such a marriage is void, calling this a community standard. Same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples.

Violence against gay and gender-nonconforming people has met with judicial tolerance. A defendant was acquitted in 2009 of murdering a gay HIV-positive man after invoking a "gay panic" defence; on 10 June 2010 the Court of Appeal president stated that "One is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent one's self-being the victim of a homosexual act"; and an accused in the 2007 Harl Taylor slaying was found not guilty. Nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved. That figure is a raw count over fourteen years with no population denominator supplied by the sources, so it supports no per-capita comparison.

A gay visitor was physically attacked during a tourist event. On 8 May 2017 The Tribune reported that Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at the Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival early that Saturday, and that he wants charges laid.

Police have moved against LGBT social space. On 6 October 2007 officers raided a gay party in downtown Nassau; no arrests were possible because no crime had been committed, guests demanded an apology, and the Ministry of Tourism issued one to the cruise company. LGBT tourist groups have also been protested: church group opposition to Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise, a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise, and in September 2007 the formation of an anti-gay committee by the Bahamas Christian Council over a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo.

No exclusively gay bars or clubs exist; the Nassau scene is underground, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations treating homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. Due to lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequalities and homophobia, many LGBT people keep sexual orientation or gender identity private.

There is no prohibition on LGBT citizens serving in the police, military or prison service, and in May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson declared that those forces do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation.

No HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded in the sources.
BHS.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source addresses entry, visa or passport gender-marker rules for the Bahamas, or how immigration and customs screening treats a traveller whose documents do not match their presentation. Nothing in the inventory speaks to this layer.

Not sourced: no material on facilities such as restrooms, changing areas or accommodation, and no record of any law or policy governing them.

Not sourced: whether gender-affirming care is available locally, whether prescriptions can be continued or obtained, or what clinical capacity exists. The inventory records only the absence of HIV-specific and trans-specific care provisions.

Unresolved: whether charges were laid following the 8 May 2017 carnival assault on Adrian Brown, and how the case was disposed of.

Unresolved: the nine unsolved murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 are given as a raw count with no denominator and no per-capita comparison, so the figure cannot be read as a rate or ranked against other jurisdictions.

Not sourced: no trans-specific violence statistic covering a stated population and period exists in the inventory; the sources document individual incidents rather than prevalence.

Unresolved: whether the May 1998 ministerial non-discrimination declaration extends beyond sexual orientation to gender identity, and whether it binds the military, prison service and police in current practice.

Not sourced: enforcement practice behind the 16/18 age-of-consent split, and the methodology or sample of the 2013 and 2015 opinion surveys.
