sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Bahamas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Gender identity is not included in any broad anti-discrimination or anti-harassment law. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal. The Constitution's prohibition on discrimination does not include gender identity. There are no national hate-crime laws to prevent or punish violence directed toward people in the LGBT community. The 2016 equality referendum bills were not inclusive to the transgender or intersex community, while marriage eligibility was framed as between a man and a woman with male and female determined at birth. A government member, Leslie Miller, publicly called for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas," urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to their own private island to ensure "they stay out of the way" and pledging $1,000 toward relocation. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults has been legal since 1991. The age of consent is 16 for opposite-sex couples and 18 for same-sex couples. Same-sex marriages and civil unions are not legal, and the Marriage Act defines Bahamian marriage as composed of a man and a woman, with maritime marriage law stating a marriage is void if between male-male or female-female. Sexual orientation is not included in broad anti-discrimination or anti-harassment law, and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal. The Constitution's non-discrimination provision does not include sexual orientation, and a 2006 reform proposal to treat citizens equally regardless of religion, political affiliation, race, sex and gender did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection. A 2001 Employment Bill clause banning workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation was removed after passage. There are no prohibitions on LGB citizens serving in police or military forces, with a 1998 ministerial declaration that the military, prison service and police did not discriminate based on sexual orientation. Socially conservative Christian denominations generally promote the belief that homosexuality and cross dressing are signs of decadence and immorality. Due to lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequalities and homophobia, many LGBT people keep sexual orientation or gender identity private, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Documented transgender-specific intolerance includes government member Leslie Miller forcefully denouncing "the growing transgender community" and calling for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas" to ensure "they stay out of the way." Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 but could not arrest anyone as no crime was committed, with guests demanding an apology and the Ministry of Tourism issuing an apology to the cruise company. Juries have acquitted or leniently sentenced killers invoking gay-panic defences, including a 2009 acquittal for murder of a homosexual HIV-positive man and a 10 June 2010 case where the Court of Appeal president stated "One is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent one's self-being the victim of a homosexual act." Numerous murders of homosexual men from 2001 to 2015 are listed as unsolved, including an accused in the 2007 Harl Taylor slaying found not guilty.

BHS.tangentialFactors:
National public-opinion surveys record strong opposition to LGBT visibility, though they measure attitudes rather than incidents and surveyed the general population, not trans respondents: 85.5% strongly disapproved of same-sex marriage in 2015 against 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproved of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive. Both figures are now a decade or more old.

Statutory protection that does exist is narrow. The criminal law retains an unequal age of consent: 16 years for opposite-sex acts and 18 years for same-sex acts, so a trans visitor in a relationship that local law reads as same-sex falls under the higher threshold.

Gender identity appears in no anti-discrimination or anti-harassment statute in the country. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal, and the same gap applies to sexual orientation. The Constitution's prohibition on discrimination covers neither characteristic. The 2006 constitutional reform commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed Constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition.

No national hate-crime law exists to prevent or punish violence directed at LGBT people, and discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal.

A national transgender and intersex organisation launched a 'trans lives matter' campaign in April 2016, stating that no laws protect transgender and intersex residents and advocating against job termination for trans and intersex workers.

Trans people have been named as targets by a serving official. A government member publicly called for the "Exile of Transgender out of the country," urged financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private state/province so that "they stay out of the way," and pledged $1,000 toward it. A former prime minister stated in 2013 that he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 that a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth. BLZ.name: Belize
BLZ.summary:
Same-sex conduct is decriminalised in Belize. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, presided over by Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, declared Section 53 of the Criminal Code unconstitutional. The challenge was filed in 2010 by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco and heard in Belize City in May 2013. The Human Dignity Trust documents the case among constitutional challenges to criminalisation statutes in the Eastern Caribbean, and Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to strike down such a law.

On 30 December 2019 the Court of Appeal upheld the ruling and confirmed that the Constitution's protections against discrimination extend to sexual orientation and that freedom of expression encompasses sexual expression. A visitor faces no criminal exposure for consensual same-sex conduct.

The government did not rest on the ruling. It announced on 17 August 2016 that it would not appeal, then reversed that position after meeting religious leaders on 9 September and filed a partial appeal against the declaration that the Constitution bars discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Catholic Church withdrew from the appeal in March 2018, leaving the government as sole appellant. Solicitor General Nigel Hawke argued that the ruling was judicial overreach in re-defining "sex" to include sexual orientation.

Immigration law is where exposure remains. Section 5(1)(e) of the Immigration Act lists "any prostitute or homosexual" among prohibited immigrants. Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson filed a challenge in 2013; the Caribbean Court of Justice granted leave in May 2014, and CARICOM joined as an interested party in October 2014. On 10 June 2016 the CCJ dismissed his case, finding no violation of his freedom of movement. In the litigation Belize contended that Section 5(1) of the Immigration Act applies only to those offering sexual services for financial gain, and that it does not interpret or enforce the act as a blanket prohibition against homosexual immigrants. The CCJ's judgment clarified that neither Belize nor Trinidad and Tobago can ban homosexuals from CARICOM countries from entering, by reason of their obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas, notwithstanding the entry bans in their own laws.

Two 2024 statutes name protected grounds. The Anti-Sexual Harassment Act 2024 expressly provides prevention and protection from sexual harassment regardless of sexual preference and gender identity. Section 8(1)(c)(i) of the Alternative Sentencing Act 2024, effective 27 April 2024, makes evidence that an offence was motivated by bias, prejudice or hate based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance. The sentencing provision names sexual orientation but not gender identity, while the harassment act names both.

In its 2018 Universal Periodic Review Belize accepted 15 of 17 recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity, the most accepted by any CARICOM country at that review, pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection; two recommendations concerning rights equality were noted rather than accepted. Accepted recommendations included concrete steps to ensure universal access to HIV treatment for LGBT people, and training for police officials to respond properly to discrimination, violence and hate crimes against LGBT people.

Belize held its first Pride Week in August 2017, with awareness and acceptance activities hosted around the country, and LGBT organisations have become more visible and active since the 2016 ruling. A 2013 UNAIDS survey of 773 Belizeans aged 18 to 64 found 34 per cent accepting and 34 per cent tolerant of homosexuals, among the highest acceptance rates recorded in the Caribbean in that polling.

The 2013 Supreme Court hearing took place amid violence and death threats received by LGBT activists. Religious bodies were openly hostile: the Council of Churches held a "Take a Stand" rally on 3 December 2011 and a "Belize Action/Family Forum" rally on 23 November 2011 that described decriminalisation as "an orchestrated plan of demonic darkness". In December 2011 Prime Minister Dean Barrow publicly rejected pressure from President Obama, saying Belize would not change its laws. A 1998 protest against a gay cruise ship docking shows that organised hostility to visible LGBT presence predates the litigation.

HTI.name: Haiti
HTI.summary:
Haiti has not criminalised same-sex conduct since 1791, but the legal framework provides no recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime enhancement. The judiciary does not function as a protection avenue in practice, so a trans visitor has no statutory remedy to invoke and no aggravated-penalty framework behind any complaint.

Two Senate measures would tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. As of November 2017 both awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies.

Visibility carries risk. The US State Department's 2018 report found that attitudes in Haiti remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince. In November 2019 Charlot Jeudy, president of the national advocacy organisation Kouraj, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince; reports of poisoning were unconfirmed. The regional network ILGALAC issued a mourning statement.

Transgender people have faced documented harassment in the post-earthquake camps. No prison-placement practice is documented for trans detainees: no rule assigns housing by birth sex or by identity, no separate units are recorded for them, and no solitary or segregation practice is recorded.
HTI.outOfScopeNotes:
Reports that Charlot Jeudy was poisoned were unconfirmed.

The status of the two 2017 Senate bills after November 2017 is not sourced. Whether they passed the Chamber of Deputies, lapsed or remain pending is unresolved.

No prison-placement rule for trans detainees is documented either way; the absence of a documented practice is not evidence that no practice exists.

The HIV prevalence figures date to 2008 and no current data is in the inventory.

Two upper-chamber measures would tighten the regime. In August 2017 the upper legislative chamber passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 bill would allow denial of a good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. As of November 2017 both awaited a vote in the lower legislative chamber.

Visibility carries risk. A foreign government's human-rights report for 2018 found that attitudes in the country remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in the capital. In November 2019 the president of a national advocacy organisation was found dead at his home in the capital; reports of poisoning were unconfirmed. A regional advocacy network issued a mourning statement.

Transgender people have faced documented harassment in the post-earthquake camps. No prison-placement practice is documented for trans detainees: no rule assigns housing by birth sex or by identity, no separate units are recorded for them, and no solitary or segregation practice is recorded.

FJI.name: Fiji
FJI.summary:
Private, adult, consensual conduct between men and between women has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the colonial Penal Code offence at Article 175, which had carried a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment. Enforcement had already stopped: in July 2006 Fiji's High Commissioner in New Zealand confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested. The enforcement era produced prosecutions — in 2005 an Australian tourist, Thomas McCosker, and a Fijian man, Dhirendra Nadan, received two-year sentences under Article 175, and the trial judge described the acts as 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Those convictions were overturned in August 2005 by Fiji's highest court as violations of the constitution then in force.

The Constitution promulgated in September 2013, Article 26(3)(a), prohibits unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, sexual orientation, and gender identity and expression. The 1997 Constitution had already barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, which made Fiji one of the first two countries in the world to do so, alongside South Africa. The Asia Pacific Alliance's 2023 case study describes the 2013 protection on gender identity and expression as unique worldwide.

Statutory layers sit beneath that guarantee. The Employment Relations Promulgation 2007 has prohibited discrimination in employment on grounds of sexual orientation since 2007, and in 2013 the government included sexual orientation and gender identity within anti-hate speech law and within law governing discrimination in certain businesses.

The Mental Health Decree 2010 provides that a person is not mentally ill for refusing or failing to express a particular sexual orientation, and it bars registered mental health professionals from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation. Outright International's overview records the same prohibition on health professionals attempting to change sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker, and they do not recognise traditional third-gender identities. The traditional third-gender population known as vaka sa lewa lewa — people assigned male at birth who dress, act and behave as female — has been accepted by Fijian society, but that cultural standing carries no legal route to recognition of gender. The Asia Pacific Alliance records the result as a headline constitutional protection with no implementation for trans people, producing documented marginalisation and discrimination. Intersex bodily autonomy is likewise unprotected.

Fiji provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions. The Marriage Act 2002 limits marriage to one man and one woman, and no statutory union other than marriage is available to a couple read as same-sex under birth-sex status. Prime ministerial opposition to any change was restated on 26 March 2013, in January 2016, and in 2019.

Documented violence includes the brutal murder of a young transgender woman in Suva in May 2018, in a setting where mistrust of police, rooted in the risk of harassment, is reported to discourage LGBTQ people and couples from reporting anti-gay violence or hateful discrimination. The dossier's other recorded incidents are older and are historical: the murder of Red Cross leader John Maurice Scott and his partner Gregory Scrivener in Suva on 1 July 2001 in an apparent homophobic attack with possible political motive, and a gay student found dead in Nasinu in September 2017. Activists additionally describe physical violence and domestic abuse operating as a form of familial conversion therapy for LGBTQ people. The sources characterise hate-crime reports as rare while listing these cases; no dataset of police-reported incidents is available.

Social climate is shaped by majority Methodist and Catholic denominations, which traditionally view transgender identities negatively, and by a Muslim minority of about 6% that tends to regard cross-dressing as sinful behaviour to be corrected. Social mores on sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative, with little public support for LGBTQ rights, and reports of societal discrimination and bullying are recorded without a figure or period. Public displays of affection are not illegal but are generally considered offensive.

In April 2017 the Ministry of Health confirmed that gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood, following the refusal of a gay man on grounds of his sexual orientation.

Political participation has advanced at one point. In 2022 the National Federation Party endorsed Divina Loloma, a transgender woman, as the first openly LGBTQ candidate ever endorsed by a political party; the leader of the All People's Party, Tuiloma Tawaivuna, denounced the nomination, calling transgender people an 'abomination' and 'Biblically wrong'.

Organising has been permitted as well as obstructed. The government has in the past cancelled gay pride marches, but activists held activities on 17 May 2013 for the international day against homophobia, biphobia and transphobia, an event in Suva in 2017 attended by activists and religious figures, and Fiji's first pride parade on 17 May 2018 in Lautoka, held with a local police escort and addressed by former President Epeli Nailatikau.
FJI.outOfScopeNotes:
Outright International's overview page (updated 12 March 2026) carries an 'at a glance' block stating that same-sex relations are illegal, listing legal gender recognition as 'No', and stating that organisations cannot register. The illegality flag contradicts the decriminalisation the same page records for 2010 and is treated here as an unresolved source inconsistency rather than as a current rule. The organisation-registration claim appears in that one source only and is not corroborated or explained elsewhere in the inventory; its meaning (which organisations, under which statute) remains not sourced.

No figures are available for police-reported incidents of anti-LGBTQ violence, for court convictions after 2010, or for the use of the constitutional discrimination guarantee. The characterisation of hate crimes as 'rare' is the source's own wording and carries no count or period, so the true frequency is unresolved.

The inventory contains no information on entry or visa screening, on airport document checks or gender-marker flagging, on detention or immigration handling of trans travellers, or on availability of gender-affirming care, hormone supply, or trans-specific healthcare for visitors. Absence of those items in the sources is not evidence that no issue exists.

Outright's 2026 overview states that health professionals are barred from trying to change sexual orientation, and the Mental Health Decree 2010 wording bars registered mental health professionals; whether unregistered practitioners fall outside the prohibition is not sourced. The scope of the 2013 anti-hate speech provision, including penalties and any prosecution to date, is likewise not stated in the inventory.

WSM.name: Samoa
WSM.summary:
Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 (Tulafono o Solitulafono 2013), in force 1 May 2013, criminalises same-sex sexual conduct through sections 67, 68 and 71. Section 67 makes the offence complete on penetration with no defence of consent, section 68 makes attempts liable to imprisonment for up to five years, and section 71 makes keeping a place of resort for homosexual acts liable to up to seven years. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records the headline penalty as five years. The same sections also prohibit heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex.

The 2007 decision Police v Poi defined the act as penetration of the anus by the offender's penis, whether of a male or female victim. Because the offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, it reaches a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship, and on that definition it also reaches anal intercourse with a female partner. Samoa should be treated as a jurisdiction where same-sex conduct remains on the statute book.

The overview source states that the law is not enforced, and the inventory records no prosecution under sections 67, 68 or 71. In June 2010 the Samoa Law Reform Commission recommended repealing all criminal penalties for sodomy and related acts in private between consenting adult males, reporting majority public support; the Government rejected that recommendation and a reported 2011 decriminalisation proposal. The provisions remain in force.

The Crimes Act 2013 also removed the former Crimes Ordinance 1961 provisions that criminalised males "impersonating" females in a public place, which had been used to target transgender women and gender-diverse people. RNZ Pacific reported on 3 May 2013 that Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief at the removal, and that the community was not then agitating to repeal the sodomy provisions. Gender presentation as such is no longer an offence.

Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 (Tulafono o Faasalaga 2016) provides for crimes motivated by gender identity, and for crimes motivated by sexual orientation, at sentencing. As a provision of a sentencing statute it operates at the sentencing stage of a separately charged offence rather than as a standalone charge.

The Mental Health Act 2007, published 2 February 2007, states that people are not to be considered mentally ill if they refuse or fail to express a particular sexual orientation, and prohibits conversion therapy by mental health professionals.

Samoa does not recognise same-sex relationships. Prime-ministerial statements in 2012, 2013 and 2017 rejected same-sex marriage on Christian and traditional grounds.

Fa'afafine, meaning people assigned male at birth who embody both gender traits, and fa'afatama, people assigned female at birth who embody both gender traits, have been recognised as gender identities or gender roles in Samoa since at least the early 20th century. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Samoa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Samoa has a large transgender or "third gender" community called fa'afafine, with fa'afatama described as people assigned female at birth who embody both gender traits. Fa'afafine are assigned male at birth and explicitly embody both gender traits ranging from extravagantly feminine to conventionally masculine, recognised as a gender identity/gender role since at least the early 20th century. On 1 May 2013, the Crimes Act 2013 (Tulafono o Solitulafono 2013) removed provisions from the now-repealed Crimes Ordinance 1961 which criminalised males "impersonating" females in a public place, which had been used to target transgender women and gender-diverse people. The Ombudsman's first National State of Human Rights Report released in August 2015 referred to fa'afafine as "the third gender that has always existed in Samoa" and noted their hard work in carrying out both men's and women's family roles and responsibilities. Crimes motivated by gender identity are criminalised under Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 (Tulafono o Faasalaga 2016). The Samoa Fa'afafine Association (S.F.A.) is described as fostering collaboration between the fa'afafine and LGBTQ communities and aiming to promote a positive attitude toward the Samoan fa'afafine community while balancing Samoan values with Western influences. Sections 67, 68 and 71 of the Crimes Act 2013 (Tulafono o Solitulafono 2013), which took effect on 1 May 2013, criminalize same-sex sexual acts and also prohibit heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex. Section 67 makes sodomy complete upon penetration with no defence of consent, Section 68 makes attempts to commit sodomy liable to imprisonment up to five (5) years, and Section 71 makes keeping a place of resort for homosexual acts liable to imprisonment up to seven (7) years. "Sodomy" was defined in the 2007 case of Police v Poi as penetration of the male or female victim's anus by the offender's penis, replacing Sections 58D, 58E, 58G and 58J of the repealed Crimes Ordinance 1961 which had criminalised same-sex acts. The article states the law is not enforced, and notes that in June 2010 the Samoa Law Reform Commission recommended repealing all criminal penalties for sodomy and related acts in private between consenting adult males with majority public support, but the Government rejected the recommendation and a reported 2011 decriminalisation proposal. Section 20(2) of the Labour and Employment Relations Act 2013 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment policies, procedures or practices, and Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 criminalises crimes motivated by sexual orientation. There is no recognition of same-sex relationships, with prime-ministerial statements in 2012, 2013 and 2017 rejecting same-sex marriage on Christian and traditional grounds, and Samoa rejecting first-cycle UPR recommendations by Canada, France and Norway to repeal criminalisation and second-cycle recommendations except Slovenia's on reducing violence, stating decriminalisation was not possible because of cultural sensitivities and Christian beliefs. In 2011 Samoa signed the UN "joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity," and the Mental Health Act 2007 published 2 February 2007 states people are not to be considered mentally ill if they refuse or fail to express a particular sexual orientation and prohibits conversion therapy by mental health professionals. The article states: "Samoan society tends to be very tolerant of being transgender, but not of homosexuality." It states Samoa is fairly progressive in terms of gender identity and expression because of its large fa'afafine community, with fa'afafine described as a recognised part of traditional Samoan customs allowing transgender people in particular trans women to be accepted as they have always been part of Samoan culture. In the UPR process Samoa stated Fa'afafine, gays and lesbians were integral members of society and heirs to family chiefly titles and lands through extended family consensus, but that sexual orientation was a sensitive issue given religious and cultural beliefs of mainstream society requiring education and sensitisation for acceptance. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association sees anti-gay laws as hindering full incorporation of both fa'afafine and gay and lesbian Samoans, stating in 2017 its priority is "the promotion of human rights and the reduction of discrimination and violence based on gender identity" and in 2018 that "marriage is the least of our worries when you don't have a job, it's not a priority." In 2009 the Censorship Board banned screening of Milk about gay activist Harvey Milk while allowing Lesbian Vampire Killers, and in 2019 banned Rocketman about Elton John, actions criticised as "hypocritical," "ignorant" and "selective morality" and protested by the Samoa Fa'afafine Association. In 2026 Samoa held its first LGBTQ Pride Week with LGBTQ residents and allies gathering to celebrate the community.

WSM.tangentialFactors:
APTN reported on 9 May 2024 that a convening in Nadi, Fiji gathered gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua and Papua New Guinea, documenting the regional MVPFAFF+ spectrum of identities that Samoa's fa'afafine community belongs to alongside fakaleiti in Tonga and fakafifine in Niue. The convening shows an organised regional network, but it is a meeting record rather than evidence about conditions inside Samoa.

Schmidt's 2001 academic article in Intersections, "Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa", analyses fa'afafine as "in the manner of a woman" and argues that the identity is both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality and transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora as a contact zone. This bears on how the term is likely to be encountered and translated by a visitor, not on legal exposure.

The UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet of August 2015 lists the fa'afafine of Samoa, American Samoa and Tokelau among diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities described as important parts of the cultural treasure of the region. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association's stakeholder report for Samoa's third-cycle UPR in 2021 describes the culturally unique third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences, aiming to establish grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation.

Censorship decisions show official selectivity toward gender and sexuality content rather than a rule bearing on visitors: in 2009 the Censorship Board banned screening of the film Milk about gay activist Harvey Milk while allowing Lesbian Vampire Killers, and in 2019 banned Rocketman about Elton John. The decisions were criticised as hypocritical, ignorant and an exercise in selective morality and were protested by the Samoa Fa'afafine Association.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence figure for Samoa, no count of incidents and no denominator, so no comparison with the general homicide rate can be drawn and none should be inferred from the absence of figures.
WSM.localsOnly:
Section 20(2) of the Labour and Employment Relations Act 2013 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment policies, procedures or practices. Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 likewise covers crimes motivated by sexual orientation. Neither provision is stated in the inventory to cover gender identity in employment.

The Samoa Fa'afafine Association is described as fostering collaboration between the fa'afafine and LGBTQ communities and promoting a positive attitude toward the Samoan fa'afafine community while balancing Samoan values with Western influences. It regards anti-gay laws as hindering the full incorporation of both fa'afafine and gay and lesbian Samoans, stated in 2017 that its priority was the promotion of human rights and the reduction of discrimination and violence based on gender identity, and stated in 2018 that marriage was the least of its worries when people do not have a job.

Fa'afafine and fa'afatama hold family chiefly titles and lands through extended family consensus, according to the government's own UPR statements, which places third-gender people inside the matai system in a way that is not mirrored in the statute book.

The conversion therapy prohibition in the Mental Health Act 2007 binds mental health professionals, and the act's provision on sexual orientation addresses diagnosis rather than gender identity; the inventory does not source a gender-identity equivalent in that statute.
WSM.comparisons: Calibration (Aug 2026, two rounds of pairwise challenge): on traveler-facing axes Samoa beats Slovakia (0.69) on public presence, outing violence, and state climate; beats Greece (0.75) on public presence, police predation, and documented violence; and beats Romania (0.67) on every axis. It sits level with Greece — its lack of EU-style institutional recourse (a resident-weighted factor) is the only axis where European comparators hold an edge, and Estonia (0.77) keeps a 0.02 edge on that basis alone.
WSM.blindSummary:
The country's Crimes Act 2013, in force 1 May 2013, criminalises same-sex sexual conduct through sections 67, 68 and 71. Section 67 makes the offence complete on penetration with no defence of consent, section 68 makes attempts liable to imprisonment for up to five years, and section 71 makes keeping a place of resort for homosexual acts liable to up to seven years. An international anti-criminalisation NGO's country profile records the headline penalty as five years. The same sections also prohibit heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex.

A 2007 court decision defined the act as penetration of the anus by the offender's penis, whether of a male or female victim. Because the offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, it reaches a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship, and on that definition it also reaches anal intercourse with a female partner. The country should be treated as a jurisdiction where same-sex conduct remains on the statute book.

The overview source states that the law is not enforced, and the inventory records no prosecution under sections 67, 68 or 71. In June 2010 the national law reform commission recommended repealing all criminal penalties for sodomy and related acts in private between consenting adult males, reporting majority public support; the government rejected that recommendation and a reported 2011 decriminalisation proposal. The provisions remain in force.

The Crimes Act 2013 also removed the former 1961 ordinance provisions that criminalised males "impersonating" females in a public place, which had been used to target transgender women and gender-diverse people. The national broadcaster reported on 3 May 2013 that the president of the national third-gender advocacy organisation expressed relief at the removal, and that the community was not then agitating to repeal the sodomy provisions. Gender presentation as such is no longer an offence.

Section 7(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act 2016 provides for crimes motivated by gender identity, and for crimes motivated by sexual orientation, at sentencing. As a provision of a sentencing statute it operates at the sentencing stage of a separately charged offence rather than as a standalone charge.

The Mental Health Act 2007, published 2 February 2007, states that people are not to be considered mentally ill if they refuse or fail to express a particular sexual orientation, and prohibits conversion therapy by mental health professionals.

The country does not recognise same-sex relationships. Statements by the head of government in 2012, 2013 and 2017 rejected same-sex marriage on religious and traditional grounds.

In the UN Universal Periodic Review the country rejected first-cycle recommendations from several foreign governments to repeal criminalisation, and rejected all second-cycle recommendations except one other government's on reducing violence, stating that decriminalisation was not possible because of cultural sensitivities and religious beliefs. In the UPR process the government stated that third-gender people, gays and lesbians were integral members of society and heirs to family chiefly titles and lands through extended family consensus, while describing sexual orientation as a sensitive issue requiring education and sensitisation for acceptance.

The locally recognised third-gender roles for people assigned male at birth and for people assigned female at birth, who embody both gender traits, have been recognised as gender identities or gender roles since at least the early 20th century. The overview source characterises society as very tolerant of being transgender but not of homosexuality, and describes the country as fairly progressive on gender identity and expression because of the size of its third-gender community. The country held its first LGBTQ Pride Week in 2026, with LGBTQ residents and allies gathering to celebrate the community.

TON.name: Tonga
TON.summary:
The Criminal Offences Act criminalises same-sex activity between men and women, with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment. Outright International's overview, updated in March 2026, records no evidence of enforcement in recent years, and the US State Department's 2010 human rights report described enforcement of the sodomy provision as rare. The provision remains in force; the absence of recent prosecutions is not a repeal.

The same Act contains an offence aimed at gender expression rather than private conduct: a male who solicits in public "for an immoral purpose" with intent to deceive as to his true sex commits an offence. Because it turns on how a person appears and speaks in public, it bears on a trans visitor's visible presentation in streets, venues and other public space in a way the sodomy provision does not.

Tonga provides no legal gender recognition. A visitor's passport and other documents will carry the sex marker assigned at birth, and no administrative or judicial procedure exists to change it. There is no route to a Tongan identity document matching a visitor's gender.

No Tongan law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment or in the provision of goods and services. The Judicial Code of Conduct 2010 requires judges to be aware of diversity including sexual orientation and bars bias on irrelevant grounds, but it binds judges alone, not employers, landlords or service providers.

Tongan law does not recognise same-sex relationships or unions in any form. No partnership, marriage or next-of-kin rights appear in the source material. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status holds no recognition or spousal standing here.

An LGBTQ activist, Polikalepo Kefu, was murdered near his home at Muʻa in 2021. LGBTQ people in Tonga face a climate of fear, discrimination and homophobia attributed to conservative values, colonial-era laws, and rising fundamentalism and religious fanaticism that has increased hostility toward LGBTQ people and fakaleitis.
TON.outOfScopeNotes:
No available source records enforcement of the public-solicitation provision, or any prosecution of a trans or gender-nonconforming person under it. Whether police apply it is unresolved.

No sourced information was identified on Tongan border, immigration or airport screening practice as it affects trans travellers, including whether document markers prompt secondary inspection.

No sourced information was identified on hate-crime or sentencing provisions covering anti-LGBTQ violence, or on police response to such violence.

The most detailed enforcement assessment available is the US State Department's 2010 report; its age limits what it establishes about current policing.

Available sources record no partnership, marriage or next-of-kin rights for same-sex couples, but do not document how Tongan authorities would classify a relationship involving a trans person whose documents carry a different sex marker.

KIR.name: Kiribati
KIR.summary:
Sections 153 to 155 of Kiribati's Penal Code criminalise sex between men. Anal intercourse carries up to fourteen years' imprisonment, attempts and assault with intent to commit it up to seven years, and acts of gross indecency between males up to five years. Sex between women is not an offence.

The provisions are not enforced. A 2015 US State Department human rights report recorded no prosecutions under them, and no prosecution of an LGBTQ person under these sections has been reported.

The same 2015 report recorded no societal discrimination or violence based on sexual orientation. That observation is a decade old and the inventory holds no later survey of the social climate.

No constitutional or statutory non-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity generally. Article 15(3) of the Constitution bars discrimination by reference to race, place of origin, political opinions, colour and creed. Gender discrimination is prohibited only in employment, a limit the 2015 State Department report described as poorly enforced.

TUV.name: Tuvalu
TUV.summary:
Sections 153, 154 and 155 of the Penal Code criminalise male homosexual intercourse, attempts to commit it, and gross indecency between males. All three are felonies, carrying maximum sentences of 14, 7 and 5 years' imprisonment respectively. The provisions date to the colonial period, and ILGA World's jurisdiction database records them as still in force.

The exposure is defined by sex. Because the offences apply to male persons, a transgender woman whom police read as male falls within their scope; what matters at charge or in custody is the classification officers apply, not how she identifies. For a trans visitor who has sex with a man in Tuvalu, the statute creates a felony exposure in principle regardless of how rarely it is used.

The male homosexual provisions also carry heavier penalties than other sexual conduct. The age of consent is 15 for heterosexual vaginal sex and for sex between women, while conduct between men is dealt with under the felony provisions above. A young trans visitor read as male is exposed to those maximums rather than to the age-of-consent regime.

Enforcement evidence is thin and dated. The US State Department's 2013 human rights report for Tuvalu records no prosecutions of consenting adults under these provisions and reports no government abuses of LGBT people that year, attributing discrimination to traditional customs that perpetuate religious and social prejudice rather than to state action. No later enforcement record was identified for this assessment.

No hate-crime legislation is documented for Tuvalu, and no hate-crime incidents or statistics are recorded. Violence or harassment directed at someone because of gender identity or sexual orientation would not meet a specific aggravated offence on the material reviewed.

In 2011 Tuvalu signed the United Nations joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. That signature records a diplomatic position and does not amend the Penal Code. No domestic measure implementing it is documented.

Tuvalu recognises neither marriage nor civil union between two people of the same sex. The 2023 constitutional amendments bar recognition of same-sex marriage, and section 43(2)(b) of the Charter of Duties and Responsibilities defines a family unit as a marriage between a man and a woman to the exclusion of all others. The Marriage Act (Cap 29) lists no such restriction among its restrictions on marriage and does not expressly prohibit recognition of foreign same-sex unions, but its provisions assume the parties are male and female. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no recognition route, and the Act contains no provision for recognising a union entered elsewhere.
TUV.outOfScopeNotes:
No finding on detention conditions, strip searches or the custody treatment of transgender detainees was identified. The custody exposure rests on the statutory maximum alone; no documented case of a transgender person held under these provisions was found.

No partner-visa, next-of-kin or foreign-union recognition provision is addressed anywhere in the sources reviewed.

No education-policy, school-bullying or youth-service findings are available, and no hate-crime incident statistics or enforcement data later than 2013 were identified.

SLB.name: Solomon Islands
SLB.summary:
The Penal Code criminalises consensual sexual activity between men and between women. The provisions are inherited from the colonial period and carry a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. ILGA World Database, the Human Dignity Trust country profile and general reference coverage record the same offence and the same statutory maximum.

No arrests or prosecutions appear in the record. United States State Department human-rights reports for 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 record no arrests or prosecutions directed at LGBT people; the 2011 report records no LGBT-specific abuses; the 2013 report records no abuses by security forces and no prosecutions under the penal-code provisions. The Human Dignity Trust documents no recorded prosecutions in recent years. Reference coverage states the law is not enforced.

Official opposition to any legal change is on the record. Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare publicly opposed same-sex marriage in a 2017 address to a church group. In June 2018 Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used a Queen's Birthday address to warn that same-sex marriage "cannot populate the world", and in the same period acknowledged that being gay or lesbian "is said to be biological and is beyond individual control" while condemning any legal change and citing both the criminal code and the Bible.

No same-sex marriage law exists and Parliament has not legislated one. No form of relationship recognition is available. No non-discrimination protection covers sexual orientation or gender identity. Reference coverage notes that LGBT people face legal challenges not experienced by other residents.
SLB.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific data is sourced. The material covers sexual orientation and same-sex conduct; nothing in the inventory records the treatment of trans people by police, courts, employers or service providers, and no trans-specific violence or discrimination figures are available.

The enforcement record rests on United States State Department reporting for 2010 to 2013 and on the Human Dignity Trust's assessment of recent years. No more recent prosecution data is sourced, and no domestic figures are available.

No information is sourced on identity-document or gender-marker rules, on entry and visa practice, or on access to facilities and healthcare.

The status of constitutional reform is sourced only to 2019.

VUT.name: Vanuatu
VUT.summary:
Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Vanuatu, and the sources record no documented pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors. The operative risk for a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming traveller comes from official posture rather than from statute.

In November 2024 the Ministry of Justice and Community Services was directed to appoint a committee to draft a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion. National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 had targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, framing V-Pride as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values. The framing attaches suspicion to advocacy and public promotion rather than to private conduct, and a foreign visitor has no standing as a resident to argue the distinction.

Parliament amended the Marriage Act in November 2024 to define marriage as the union of a male and a female. Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed that same-sex marriages cannot be registered and that pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under local law cannot marry or have a marriage registered in Vanuatu.

There is no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no general prohibition of employment discrimination on that basis. Narrow exceptions exist in the Teaching Service Act 2013, which covers teaching-service staff, and in section 2(2)(j) of the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024, which bars digital communications that denigrate a person by reason of sexual orientation.

Prosecutorial guidance offers the clearest protection a trans visitor can point to if they are a victim of crime. The Office of the Public Prosecutor's Prosecution Policy 2003, the Prosecutors Code (Gazette no. 13 of 2017) and its General Principles on vulnerable witnesses in sexual and gender-based violence cases require prosecutors to disregard sexual preference and to treat discrimination or hostility based on sexual orientation or gender identity as factors weighing toward prosecution. Vanuatu signed the UN joint statement on ending violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011.

Partner protection is thinner than the criminal law. A 2016 workshop convened by the VPride Foundation and the Vanuatu Women's Centre established that same-sex partners receive no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes instead.

The social climate is conservative. Gay and lesbian travellers and citizens are advised to avoid public displays of affection, and there is no active gay scene.
VUT.outOfScopeNotes:
The VPride Foundation's founding year is given as 2009 in one source and 2014 in another; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether the drafting committee has produced a policy, what legal form it takes, and how it would be enforced are not sourced.

Whether the Marriage Act amendment affects recognition of an existing marriage or the gender marker on identity documents is not sourced.

No data is available on how often the prosecutorial guidance on sexual-orientation and gender-identity hostility is applied in practice.

NRU.name: Nauru
NRU.summary:
Nauru repealed the criminal-code provisions that prohibited consensual same-sex conduct in 2016, a change reported on 29 May 2016. The sections struck out belonged to a criminal code inherited from Queensland in 1899, and the same repeal covered the attempted-suicide offences that sat alongside them. Consensual same-sex intimacy between adults is not a prosecutable offence under Nauruan law, and a visitor should not expect prosecution on that basis.

Marriage and union recognition is a separate matter. Same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal in Nauru, and there is no recognition route for a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex.

Kaleidoscope Trust's country assessment records that intersex and transgender people in Nauru have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and that lesbian, bisexual, trans and intersex people have no employment-discrimination protection. Nauru's most recent CEDAW state report, submitted in 2016, contained no LBTI-specific information, so the official reporting machinery carries no account of trans people's situation in the country.

One detention-specific protection is documented. The Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, prohibit discrimination against any person on the basis of sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity inside the regional processing centre. This instrument governs immigration detention rather than Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and it addresses non-discrimination rather than placement by birth sex versus identity, special units or solitary-confinement practice. No documented data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed in Nauru's corrections system, and no trans-prisoner case or ruling is recorded.
NRU.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no information on whether Nauru provides any legal gender-recognition procedure for changing sex markers on identity documents or passports; the assessment that transgender people have no explicit legal recognition is an absence-of-protection finding, not a sourced statement about a specific recognition statute or its refusal.

No data was found on housing placement for transgender prisoners in Nauru's corrections system, and no trans-prisoner case or ruling is documented. Whether the Regional Processing Centre non-discrimination rules are enforced in practice, and how complaints under them are handled, is not sourced.

The inventory records no incidents of violence against trans people in Nauru with dates or outcomes, and no trans-specific violence rate, so no assessment of relative risk can be made from these sources.

The Vexen index placement is a single publication's composite ranking; its methodology and weighting are not sourced here, and it should not be read as a measure of trans-specific exposure.

PLW.name: Palau
PLW.summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal in Palau. The Penal Code signed by President Tommy Remengesau Jr. in April 2014 took effect on 23 July 2014 and contains no offence outlawing consensual sex between people of the same sex. It repealed the sodomy offence formerly at section 2803 of Chapter 28, "Sex Crimes", Title 17, which carried up to ten years' imprisonment. Before that repeal, male same-sex sexual activity was an offence while female same-sex activity was not. Palau's Attorney General confirmed the change to the Human Dignity Trust.

Palau has no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ residents do not hold the same legal protections as non-LGBTQ residents. No protective provision specific to gender identity appears in the available material.

The Constitution defines marriage as between a man and a woman. The same-sex marriage ban was one of 22 amendments approved in the referendum of 4 November 2008, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read under Palauan law as same-sex therefore has no route to marriage or to those protections. In July 2019 President Remengesau Jr. said he supported striking down the constitutional ban as discriminatory and believed in full equality; no repeal outcome is recorded.

Palau provides no legal gender recognition. No provision for updating identity documents, no screening or facility rules, no custody rule and no gender-affirming care provision specific to transgender people is recorded in the available material, and no transgender-specific penalty or enforcement measure exists.

At its 2011 Universal Periodic Review Palau accepted recommendations to decriminalise homosexual acts and to combat discrimination, and in October 2011 the government promised to fully decriminalise homosexuality. On 22 March 2011 Palau was among the 84 countries on whose behalf Colombia delivered a joint Human Rights Council statement calling for an end to violence, criminal sanctions and related human-rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
PLW.outOfScopeNotes:
The available material contains no information on violence against transgender people in Palau, no incident records, no killing figures and no general homicide rate against which any such figure could be compared. Nothing in the inventory documents patterned or state-tolerated targeting.

Entry and visa rules, border or airport screening practice, document-marker rules, facility access, custody outcomes and access to gender-affirming care are not sourced for Palau, and no claim about them can be made from this inventory.

Whether the July 2019 presidential statement in favour of striking down the constitutional ban produced a subsequent amendment, bill or court ruling is unresolved in the available material.

Whether any administrative route to legal gender recognition exists outside the cited sources, for example under the 2014 Penal Code or subordinate regulation, is not sourced.

FSM.name: Micronesia (FSM)
FSM.summary:

MHL.name: Marshall Islands
MHL.summary:
The Republic of the Marshall Islands has no criminalisation regime covering consensual same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust dates decriminalisation to 2005, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sex or sexual orientation, so a visitor faces no statutory offence for consensual sex and no differential age threshold.

The Gender Equality Act 2019 prohibits direct and indirect discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation across all areas, naming the political, legal, economic, employment, social and domestic spheres. It obliges the government to adopt measures eliminating stereotypes, prejudice and harmful practices on those grounds, and establishes a programme to sensitise judicial and law enforcement officers and other public officials. Before 2019 no legal protection against discrimination on gender identity or sexual orientation existed in employment or in the provision of goods and services.

The Code of Judicial Conduct 2008 provides that a judge shall not manifest bias, prejudice or harassment based on sexual orientation, and shall require lawyers to refrain from such bias, prejudice or harassment.

Same-sex marriages and civil unions are not recognised, and households headed by same-sex couples are ineligible for the protections available to opposite-sex married couples. The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1988 does not expressly prohibit same-sex marriage, but section 428(1) assumes opposite-sex parties, setting minimum ages of 18 for the male and 16 for the female. Whether constitutional or statutory non-discrimination guarantees on sexual orientation, marital status and family status confer a right to marry remains unresolved, as the Supreme Court has yet to rule.

On 22 March 2011 the Marshall Islands joined the Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, which expressed concern at killings, rape, torture and criminal sanctions on those grounds. In 2016 the country received recommendations from Germany and Israel to prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation.

The 2015 US State Department Human Rights Report on the Marshall Islands listed prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence as significant problems, and recorded no reports of torture, arbitrary killings, disappearances or LGBT-specific abuses.
MHL.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether constitutional or statutory non-discrimination guarantees on sexual orientation, marital status and family status confer a right to marry in the Marshall Islands is unresolved; the Supreme Court has yet to rule.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence statistics, no entry or visa document-marker rules, no airport screening evidence of differential treatment of trans travellers, and no data on access to gender-affirming care.

BEN.name: Benin
BEN.summary:
Consensual sexual acts between adults are legal in Benin. Article 545 of the Penal Code, in force since 2018, sets an equal age of consent regardless of sex, while keeping heavier penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex. Legality is not the same as protection: the general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct, and no criminal ruling on the same-sex provisions had ever been rendered as of Benin's statement to the 2008 review, on the government's account because families would not allow children to be brought to court.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, and there is no protection on grounds of gender identity at all. Legal gender recognition is impossible. A trans visitor has no recognition pathway to rely on and no statutory protection to invoke.

The protections that do exist are narrow and mostly concern data and speech. Article 394 of Law No. 2017-20 on the Digital Code prohibits processing personal data that reveals sex life or sexual orientation; Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law bars collection or processing without express consent; Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 requires business leaders to prevent, end and punish sexual or sexist acts based on sex or real or perceived sexuality. Article 552 of the same 2017 Digital Code punishes provoking discrimination, hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation through an electronic communications network or computer system with one year's imprisonment and a five million franc fine, or one penalty only, in force since 2018.

Benin does not recognise LGBTQI+ couples or families. The one sourced exception is the grant of diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats. Article 104(d) of the Children's Code, Law 2015-08, bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption.

Healthcare access is the sharpest practical exposure. Providers regularly refuse treatment related to LGBTQ status, including gender-affirming hormone therapy, and also refuse general care such as malaria treatment. Employers often will not hire people known to be LGBTQ, with transgender and intersex people singled out.

Violence against LGBTQI+ people is documented as common, particularly outside major urban areas, and includes arbitrary detention, physical and sexual violence and degrading treatment. Anti-gay lynchings are described as commonplace and are mostly committed by civilians rather than state authorities; police rarely pursue perpetrators. The sources give no count of killings and no general homicide rate for Benin, so no comparison between trans-specific and background violence can be made here.

Reporting is suppressed. People who report violence or discrimination to police conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity for fear of mistreatment, and lesbian, bisexual and queer women rarely report at all.

Religious institutions are a significant source of hostility. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries and priests are documented calling transgender people demons. Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques take part in homophobic preaching, and imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion therapy, often coerced by families.

State responses have been limited. Benin rejected recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons at the 2012 review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting that "certain things would be rectified". At the 2023 Universal Periodic Review the government accepted two of fifteen recommendations, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against HIV.

Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restrictions on LGBT people.

No source in the inventory records tolerance toward transgender people distinct from general LGBTQ stigmatisation; the transgender-specific material is limited to the "demons" preaching and to hiring discrimination that names transgender and intersex people.
BEN.outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace is not accompanied in the inventory by a count of killings, a date range or a general homicide rate for Benin, so its magnitude cannot be assessed and no trans-specific rate can be stated.

The 2015 Washington Blade account is a decade old and is treated as context, not as evidence of the current situation.

The shelter figures appear in two forms in the sources: a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people have passed since about 2020, and 20 shelters housing 380 LGBTQ people between 2020 and 2024. Which figure is accurate is unresolved.

Whether the general indecency provision is currently used to prosecute same-sex conduct is not dated in the sources. The statement that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered on the same-sex provisions dates from Benin's submission to the 2008 review.

The 2013 note that "certain things would be rectified" is not tied to any enacted measure. Implementation of the two recommendations accepted at the 2023 Universal Periodic Review is not sourced.

Several findings, among them conversion therapy by imams, priests and traditional healers, separate Catholic cemeteries, and the refusal of gender-affirming hormone therapy, rest on a single encyclopaedic source in the inventory and are not corroborated by the other sources listed.

sources.summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (9 Apr 2024): the Hirondelles Club at Rehoboth Friendship Centre has housed LGBT+ youth in Benin since about 2020 — a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed; the report's framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. For this record: current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

Outright International country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are not criminalised anywhere in Benin, but SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. For this record: the current statutory baseline, legal but entirely unshielded, with no recognition pathway.

US State Department 2023 Country Report (Benin): the law does not explicitly prohibit SOGIESC discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. For this record: official US assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

Washington Blade (31 Aug 2015), commissioned by the European Forum of LGBT Christian Groups: LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. For this record: regional religious-institution hostility including Benin — dated 2015, treat as context not current-state evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (8 May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo (political sociology/medical anthropology, EHESS Paris) citing evidence of same-sex relationships in Benin alongside Cameroon, Zimbabwe and Burkina Faso, and Melville Herskovits' record of women-women marriages in the ancient Dahomey kingdom (modern Benin); frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a colonial import. For this record: historical baseline supporting the localsOnly framing that today's statutory legality sits on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Benin (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: There is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. Healthcare providers regularly refuse to give treatments related to LGBTQ status such as gender-affirming hormone therapy and also regularly deny general healthcare like malaria treatment to LGBTQ people. Employers often will not hire people known to be LGBTQ, especially transgender and intersex people. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries and priests are documented as "calling transgender people demons". Those reporting violence or discrimination to police conceal sexual orientation or gender identity out of fear of mistreatment, with lesbian, bisexual and queer women rarely reporting to police. Same-sex sexual acts between consenting adults are legal, with equal age of consent regardless of sex under Article 545 of the new Penal Code in force since 2018, which establishes greater penalties for an indecent or unnatural act with a minor of the same sex. Previously, Article 331 of the old Penal Code and a 1947 amendment punished an indecent act or act against nature with a minor of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years imprisonment and a fine of 200 to 50,000 francs. Article 88 of the 1996 draft Penal Code would have punished an indecent act or act against nature with an individual of the same sex with one to three years imprisonment and a 100,000 to 500,000 francs fine but was never voted into law, while the October 2008 draft includes no punishment for same-sex relations between consenting adults in private and has not been voted on, though the general indecency provision has been used to prosecute same-sex conduct. There is no recognition of legal rights for same-sex couples, except the government grants diplomatic visas and immunity to same-sex partners of foreign diplomats, and Article 104(d) of the Children's Code Law 2015-08 bars foreign homosexual couples from international adoption. Limited protections based on sexual orientation and sexual life exist: Article 394 of Law No. 2017-20 on the Digital Code (2017) prohibits processing personal data revealing sex life or sexual orientation, Article 6 of the 2009 Personal Data Protection Law similarly prohibits collection or processing without express consent, and Article 23 of Law No. 2011-26 (2012) requires business leaders to prevent, end and punish sexual or sexist acts or behavior based on sex or real or perceived sexuality infringing rights and dignity of women or girls. Article 552 on incitement to hatred and violence of Law No. 2017-20 (2017) punishes provoking discrimination, hatred or violence based on sexual orientation by electronic communications network or computer system with one year imprisonment and a five million CFA francs fine or one penalty only, in place since 2018. Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restrictions for LGBT people. For enforcement, Benin's representative stated for the 2008 review that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered although provided for by law because families would never allow children to be taken to court, and Benin rejected states' recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons in the 2012 review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting "certain things would be rectified." The LGBTQI+ community, especially outside major urban areas, faced hostility with discrimination common, alongside arbitrary detention, physical and sexual violence and degrading treatment, with violence and anti-gay lynchings common and mostly committed by civilians rather than state authorities while police rarely pursue perpetrators. Between 2020 and 2024 Hirondelles Club ran 20 shelters housing 380 LGBTQ people, and the government accepted two of fifteen 2023 Universal Periodic Review recommendations, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against HIV. LGBTQ people are frequently rejected by families and have difficulty getting jobs, and while the government provides sexual and reproductive healthcare for people who experienced sexual violence, LGBTQ people are typically denied medical care and social services. Religion is a significant source of homophobia, with Catholic churches burying LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries, Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques participating in homophobic preaching, and imams, priests and traditional healers performing conversion therapy often coerced by families. Homosexuality is perceived as unnatural and stemming from Western culture, with homosexuals considered deviants and homosexuality often called a disease brought by white people, and on 17 May 2013 LGBTQ associations in Cotonou organized a public International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event at the Institut Francais drawing 200 people while organizations can hold public events. For transgender-specific societal tolerance, the article provides only that priests are documented as "calling transgender people demons" and that hiring discrimination singles out "especially transgender and intersex people," with no separate finding of tolerance toward transgender people distinct from general LGBTQ stigmatization.
