The sources give no count of killings and no general homicide rate for the country, so no comparison between trans-specific and background violence can be made here.

Reporting is suppressed. People who report violence or discrimination to police conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity for fear of mistreatment, and lesbian, bisexual and queer women rarely report at all.

Religious institutions are a significant source of hostility. Catholic churches bury LGBTQ people in separate cemeteries and priests are documented calling transgender people demons. Evangelical temples and Muslim mosques take part in homophobic preaching, and imams, priests and traditional healers perform conversion therapy, often coerced by families.

National responses have been limited. The country rejected recommendations to improve the situation for LGBTQ persons at the 2012 review, with a 4 March 2013 meeting noting that "certain things would be rectified". At the 2023 Universal Periodic Review the government accepted two of fifteen recommendations, one to investigate and prosecute violence against LGBTQ people and one to combat stigma against HIV.

Decree No. 1999-639 imposes no specific blood-donation restrictions on LGBT people.

No source in the inventory records tolerance toward transgender people distinct from general LGBTQ stigmatisation; the transgender-specific material is limited to the "demons" preaching and to hiring discrimination that names transgender and intersex people.
BEN.blindOutOfScope:
The claim that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace is not accompanied in the inventory by a count of killings, a date range or a general homicide rate for the country, so its magnitude cannot be assessed and no trans-specific rate can be stated.

The 2015 account is a decade old and is treated as context, not as evidence of the current situation.

The shelter figures appear in two forms in the sources: a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people have passed since about 2020, and 20 shelters housing 380 LGBTQ people between 2020 and 2024. Which figure is accurate is unresolved.

Whether the general indecency provision is currently used to prosecute same-sex conduct is not dated in the sources. The statement that no criminal ruling had ever been rendered on the same-sex provisions dates from the country's submission to the 2008 review.

The 2013 note that "certain things would be rectified" is not tied to any enacted measure. Implementation of the two recommendations accepted at the 2023 Universal Periodic Review is not sourced.

Several findings, among them conversion therapy by imams, priests and traditional healers, separate Catholic cemeteries, and the refusal of gender-affirming hormone therapy, rest on a single encyclopaedic source in the inventory and are not corroborated by the other sources listed.
blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring organisation (9 Apr 2024): a local safe-housing club has housed LGBT+ youth since about 2020 — a temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from the country and the sub-region have passed; the framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace. Current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

An organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in the country, but sexual-orientation-and-gender discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

A government annual human-rights report: the law does not explicitly prohibit sexual-orientation-and-gender discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. Official assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

A news outlet (31 Aug 2015): LGBT people in several countries of the region describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. Regional religious-institution hostility relevant to this country — dated 2015, treat as context not current-evidence.

A monitoring organisation (8 May 2012): an interview with a researcher citing evidence of same-sex relationships in this country alongside several regional countries, and an anthropologist's record of women-women marriages in ancient times in the same country; frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a historic-era import. Historical baseline supporting the framing that today's statutory legality sits on long-standing practice, not recent liberalisation.
BEN.blindLocalsOnly:
LGBTI organisations cannot register in the country. Against that, a community organisation has run a 20-place temporary accommodation centre for LGBT+ youth since about 2020, through which almost 380 young people from the country and the subregion have passed.

Family rejection is common and drives the shelter need. LGBTQ people are frequently rejected by their families and have difficulty getting jobs. The government provides sexual and reproductive healthcare for people who have experienced sexual violence, but LGBTQ people are typically denied medical care and social services.

Public events are possible. On 17 May 2013 LGBTQ associations in a major city organised an International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia event at a cultural centre that drew 200 people, and organisations are able to hold public events.

The statutory legality rests on older practice rather than recent liberalisation. An anthropologist's interview cites evidence of same-sex relationships in the country alongside several other jurisdictions in the region, and an earlier ethnographic record of women-women marriages in a pre-colonial polity in the region, in what is now the modern country.
BEN.blindTangential:
The country's current statute sits against a longer legislative record. Article 331 of the old Penal Code, as amended in 1947, punished an indecent act or act against nature with a minor of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 200 to 50,000 francs. Article 88 of the 1996 draft Penal Code would have punished an indecent act or act against nature with an individual of the same sex with one to three years' imprisonment and a 100,000 to 500,000 franc fine, but was never voted into law. The October 2008 draft contains no punishment for same-sex relations between consenting adults in private and has not been voted on.

Regional religious hostility is documented across the country's neighbourhood. A 2015 account commissioned by a regional religious body records LGBT Catholics in several jurisdictions in the region describing discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. The piece is dated 2015 and is context rather than current-state evidence.

Public attitudes frame homosexuality as unnatural and as an import from outside the region, with homosexuals treated as deviants and homosexuality often described as a disease brought by outsiders.

TGO.name: Togo
TGO.summary:
Togo criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Human Dignity Trust's country profile records a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment plus a fine. The offence is defined in the 2015 Penal Code as an indecent or unnatural act committed with a person of the same sex (Article 393), carrying one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of one to three million CFA francs. The 1980 Penal Code had criminalised the same conduct at the same custodial range with a lower fine of 100,000 to 500,000 CFA francs, and the prohibition dates to 1884, when it was introduced under the German Togoland protectorate.

The law also prohibits "promotion of same-sex conduct", a clause the United States Department of State's 2023 human rights report understands to reach advocacy and gender identity expression. LGBTQ advocacy is separately criminalised under Article 392 for spoken words, writing or images perceived as violating public decency. The State Department recorded that the provision was enforced during the reporting period. Because the offence is drafted in terms of acts rather than identity, a trans visitor's exposure is not self-evident from the code; the practical risk attaches to visibility, conduct and advocacy, and the sources do not delimit where the promotion clause ends.

There is no legal route to change gender on government documents in Togo. No law protects against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

No statute explicitly bans cross-dressing, yet arrests follow the presentation. A transgender person was arrested in March 2018 for supposed cross-dressing. In 2023 the social-media personality Bobo Períta, known for cross-dressing, was arrested for violating public decency, convicted on 1 June 2023 and sentenced to a civil prison in Lomé.

A 2015 press account from Lomé reported that the capital's police are "particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists". Enforcement documented in the same period includes arbitrary arrests and disproportionate use of neutral loitering and immorality laws against LGBTQ people. In January 2021 a gay man and his partner were arrested and imprisoned until Afrique Arc-En-Ciel paid for their release.

Violence or threats of violence targeting LGBTTQI people were listed among Togo's significant human rights issues in the State Department's 2022 and 2023 reports. Intimidation, death threats and physical assault are reported, and mistreatment by civilians or state authorities tends to go unpunished; victims are deterred from reporting by stigma and by the possibility of legal consequences under the criminalisation of homosexuality and of LGBTQ advocacy. The 2011 State Department report documented security-force torture, impunity, and official as well as societal discrimination against LGBT people.

The documented transgender-specific violence is a November 2019 incident in which police followed a transgender woman home and refused to let her go until she had sex with them; the assault was prevented only by the presence of her mother.

Conditions in custody are harsh. The State Department cites cruel treatment, harsh prison conditions, arbitrary detention and criminal libel enforcement. LGBTQ prisoners are denied HIV/AIDS treatment and condoms, and prison chaplains have refused communion to LGBTQ prisoners who have not repented for homosexuality.

Providers at HIV and sexually transmitted disease treatment centres often discriminate against LGBTQ patients, which the source links to avoidance of care.

A 2023 decree (Articles 17, 27 and 39) requires passenger screening by the Passenger Information Unit to be non-discriminatory and not based on sexual life or sexual orientation, and protects sexual orientation in data processing. Article 5 of the Press and Communications Code (Law 2020-001) prohibits dissemination of defamatory comments, including homophobic defamation.

A domestic association documents LGBT rights violations and provides legal and judicial support to victims, giving visitors a documented assistance channel.
TGO.outOfScopeNotes:
No documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically was identified in the sources reviewed.

The scope of the "promotion of same-sex conduct" clause is unresolved: the sources do not delimit what conduct or expression it reaches, nor how it is applied to gender identity expression in practice.

Enforcement data are incomplete and are not accompanied by a denominator against which reported cases could be measured, so the volume of documented violations cannot be compared with other jurisdictions.

The most detailed on-the-ground account of police treatment of tourists in Lomé dates from 2015; no comparable recent account was identified.

Whether the 2023 decree's non-discrimination requirement for passenger screening is observed in practice is not sourced.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Togo (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: There is no legal way to change one's gender on government documents in Togo. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity and no law protects persons from discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. There is no law explicitly against cross-dressing, yet a transgender person was arrested in March 2018 for supposed cross-dressing. In 2023 TikTok influencer Bobo Períta, known for cross-dressing, was arrested for violating public decency, convicted on 1 June that year and sentenced to a civil prison in Lomé. In November 2019 police followed a transgender person home and refused to let her go until she had sex with them, with sexual assault prevented only by the presence of the victim's mother. These transgender-specific facts are distinct from sexuality-law provisions criminalizing same-sex intimacy, which do not on their face criminalize transgender status. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is illegal in Togo, first made illegal in 1884 under the German Togoland protectorate and continued under the Penal Code of 13 August 1980. The 1980 Code imposed one to three years imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 CFA francs. The 2015 Penal Code retained one to three years imprisonment but under Article 393 defined the offense as an indecent or unnatural act committed with a person of the same sex and increased the fine to one to three million CFA francs. LGBTQ advocacy is criminalized under Article 392 for spoken words, writing or images perceived as violating public decency, and LGBTQ organizations may register as health organizations but not as LGBTQ advocacy organizations. Enforcement includes arbitrary arrests and disproportionate use of neutral loitering and immorality laws against LGBTQ people, including the January 2021 arrest and imprisonment of a gay man and his partner until Afrique Arc-En-Ciel paid for their release. In custody and care, prison chaplains have refused communion to LGBTQ prisoners who have not repented for homosexuality, LGBTQ prisoners are denied HIV/AIDS treatment and condoms, and providers at HIV and STD treatment centers often discriminate against LGBTQ patients causing avoidance of care. Limited protection machinery includes Article 5 of the Press and Communications Code Law 2020-001 prohibiting dissemination of defamatory comments including homophobic defamation, and Decree No. 2023-116/PR Articles 17, 27 and 39 requiring passenger screening by the Passenger Information Unit to be non-discriminatory and not based on sexual life or sexual orientation and protecting sexual orientation in data processing. No documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically is provided. For LGBTQ people generally, intimidation, death threats and physical assault are reported, with mistreatment by civilians or state authorities tending to go unpunished and victims deterred from reporting by stigma and possible legal consequences from criminalization of homosexuality and LGBTQ advocacy. In 2020 there were 33 reported instances of human rights violations towards LGBTQ people, described as most likely a small fraction of overall cases. Religion plays a significant role in stigmatization of LGBTQ people generally, with Catholic bishops blaming misfortunes and disasters on homosexuality and religious programs used to perform conversion therapy. LGBTQ people generally experience discrimination in employment, housing, education and healthcare, including refusal of housing, family rejection, denial of healthcare, and additional discrimination against people with HIV such as expulsion by family or viewing illness as moral punishment. Transgender-specific violence documented consists of the November 2019 police attempt to coerce sex from a transgender person at home and the pattern of arrest for cross-dressing presentation despite no explicit ban.

The sexuality provisions and transgender status are distinct in law. The same-sex intimacy offence does not on its face criminalise transgender status, so trans-specific exposure in Togo runs through public decency, loitering and immorality enforcement rather than through the sexual-offence provision itself.

NER.name: Niger
NER.summary:
Niger criminalises same-sex conduct and transition itself. Article 25 of the Charter of Refoundation, adopted by the military junta in March 2025, bans “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the five-year transition that followed the July 2023 coup. It was the first explicit prohibition of its kind at statutory level in the country, and it sets no penalty of its own.

The February 2026 revision of the penal code supplies the penalties. Article 390 punishes “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” with five to ten years' imprisonment and fines of up to 100 million CFA francs. The same article reaches public announcement of a same-sex relationship and anyone who changes or attempts to change their birth sex, which places transition-related medical and legal steps inside the criminal provision. Article 391 punishes same-sex marriage with ten to twenty years. Article 392 covers LGBTQIA+ associations. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences are excluded.

Article 392, as reported, punishes creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, with ten to twenty years in prison and fines of up to 500 million CFA francs, roughly €762,000 or US$883,000.

The drafting is broad enough that El Espectador reports asexuality as falling within the sanctionable conduct.

Enforcement has followed. By 1 July 2026 The Guardian reported at least 40 people arrested for homosexuality and 16 men imprisoned, among them high-ranking military officials; campaigners described a witch-hunt in a toxic climate. Local media reported dozens arrested across the country after the code took effect, some of them imprisoned.

State media confirmed the criminalisation: Agence Nigérienne de Presse reported on 1 June 2026 that Niger criminalises LGBTQIA+ practice under the 2026 revision.

Justice Minister Alio Daouda said “all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be” are “not in line with our social and cultural values”.

No broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exists. The only provision that had touched the area, Article 4 of Law 2015-36 on Illicit Trafficking of Migrants, was repealed in 2023 by decree of President Abdourahamane Tiani, with prior convictions and their effects expunged.

Prosecutions predate the new code. In 2022 two young women in Maradi were prosecuted over lesbianism and acquitted because no legislation then criminalised it, but were imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos on social media that allegedly portrayed a lesbian act. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276, which carries up to three years; the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them. In Niamey in 2025 two young women reported by a third person were prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, and the judge was reportedly sanctioned for leniency.

In December 2022 lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges for want of legislation.

After the 2026 law LGBTQ people went into hiding. Historically many led socially acceptable public lives while keeping their relationships private.
NER.outOfScopeNotes:
The most recent official assessment in the source inventory is the U.S. State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report, which found no reports of violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity and no documented cases of discrimination, including in education, while noting that stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported; it recorded two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined. No comparable official accounting for the period since 2025 is available in the inventory.

The charter's Article 25 sets no penalty of its own, and the sources do not state how it operates alongside the penal code articles.

Whether the provision on changing or attempting to change one's birth sex reaches a visitor whose documents were amended outside the country is not addressed by the sources.

The arrest figures come from campaigners and local media rather than an official count.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: in March 2025 Niger explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — Article 25 of the junta's Charter of Refoundation bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the July 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276 (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

BBC News (December 2022): Niger's lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships.

The Guardian (1 July 2026): at least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, imprisoned across Niger following the introduction of a new penal code earlier in 2026. Campaigners describe a 'witch-hunt' in a 'toxic' climate, and sources fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to PrEP drugs collapses.
Agence Nigérienne de Presse (1 Jun 2026) reports that Niger criminalises LGBTQIA+ practice in the country under the criminalisation provisions adopted in the 2026 penal code revision.

Justice Minister Alio Daouda said 'all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be' are 'not in line with our social and cultural values', and President Mohamed Bazoum's 2023 proposals focused public discourse on 'social contagion'. After the 2026 law, LGBTQ people went into hiding; historically many led socially acceptable public lives while keeping relationships private, and Niger's authorities refused to recognise the 2022 protesters' refugee status.

NER.blindSummary:
The country criminalises same-sex conduct and transition itself. Article 25 of the charter adopted by the military government in March 2025 bans “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the five-year transition that followed the July 2023 coup. It was the first explicit prohibition of its kind at statutory level in the country, and it sets no penalty of its own.

The February 2026 revision of the penal code supplies the penalties. Article 390 punishes “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” with five to ten years' imprisonment and fines of up to 100 million in the local currency. The same article reaches public announcement of a same-sex relationship and anyone who changes or attempts to change their birth sex, which places transition-related medical and legal steps inside the criminal provision. Article 391 punishes same-sex marriage with ten to twenty years. Article 392 covers LGBTQIA+ associations. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences are excluded.

Article 392, as reported, punishes creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, with ten to twenty years in prison and fines of up to 500 million in the local currency, roughly €762,000 or US$883,000.

The drafting is broad enough that a news outlet reports asexuality as falling within the sanctionable conduct.

Enforcement has followed. By 1 July 2026 an international newspaper reported at least 40 people arrested for homosexuality and 16 men imprisoned, among them high-ranking military officials; campaigners described a witch-hunt in a toxic climate. Local media reported dozens arrested across the country after the code took effect, some of them imprisoned.

A national news agency confirmed the criminalisation on 1 June 2026.

The justice minister said “all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be” are “not in line with our social and cultural values”.

No broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exists. The only provision that had touched the area, Article 4 of a law on migrant trafficking, was repealed in 2023 by decree of the head of state, with prior convictions and their effects expunged.

Prosecutions predate the new code. In 2022 two young women in a southern region were prosecuted over lesbianism and acquitted because no legislation then criminalised it, but were imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos on social media that allegedly portrayed a lesbian act. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276, which carries up to three years; the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them. In the capital in 2025 two young women reported by a third person were prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, and the judge was reportedly sanctioned for leniency.

In December 2022 legislators backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by a legislator from a southern region, weeks after a court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges for want of legislation.

After the 2026 law LGBTQ people went into hiding. Historically many led socially acceptable public lives while keeping their relationships private.

TCD.name: Chad
TCD.summary:
Chad's penal code, in force since 1 August 2017, criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults under Article 354, carrying three months to two years' imprisonment and fines of 50,000 to 500,000 CFA francs (roughly 89 to 885 US dollars). A trans visitor whose conduct or relationship is read as same-sex under the provision falls within its reach. The National Assembly adopted the code on 12 December 2016 by 111 votes to one, with four abstentions.

Article 360, in Chapter III on sexual offences against minors, punishes a person who without violence maintains a sexual relationship or practices sexual touching with a person of the same sex under eighteen years of age with one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 500,000 francs (about 177 to 885 US dollars).

Chad has no legal gender recognition. There is no pathway for a trans person to amend sex markers on official documents, so a visitor's travel documents cannot be brought into line with their lived gender under Chadian law.

Because same-sex conduct is criminalised, police and prosecutors refuse to investigate or prosecute crimes committed against LGBTQ+ people, and local civil society members say dozens of LGBTQ+ people are held in prison under the pretext of other charges. The only provision in Chadian law that addresses violence targeting someone for their sexual orientation is Article 350(i), which imposes ten to twenty years' imprisonment when rape is committed because of the victim's sexual orientation. There is no general legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Enforcement predates the 2017 code. In 2013 two men were arrested in Abéché for celebrating their wedding, before the penal code formally outlawed homosexuality; the bar was ordered closed for two years, both men were fined and initially given two-year prison sentences, and those sentences were suspended on appeal after community outcry. Religious groups, women's groups and youth associations petitioned the government to punish the men.

Official hostility to the law's targets is on the record. Former Prime Minister Delwa Kassiré Coumakoye defended the 2017 criminalisation on religious grounds, saying homosexuality is condemned by all religions.

Social attitudes are hostile. LGBTQ+ people are viewed as threats to family, procreation and marriage, and homosexuality is perceived as a Western invention. In a 2024 survey, 15 percent of Chadians felt their local area would be a good place for gay and lesbian people to live. LGBTQ+ people in Chad continue to hide their identity to protect their safety.

Healthcare access is affected. Men who have sex with men are unlikely to be able to donate blood, not because of a formal ban but because of discrimination and hostility encountered when accessing healthcare.

No law formally restricts LGBTQ+ people's freedom of expression, association or peaceful assembly, but discrimination and marginalisation limit these rights in practice.
TCD.outOfScopeNotes:
The figure of dozens of LGBTQ+ people imprisoned under other charges comes from local civil society members and is not independently corroborated in the source inventory.

The 2024 attitudinal survey is reported as a single measure; the source does not describe its sample, method or margin of error.

Whether Article 350(i) has ever been applied in a prosecution is not stated in the sources.

The source inventory contains no trans-specific violence statistics for Chad, so no comparison against the country's general homicide rate can be made.

sources.summary: US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Chad: criminalisation section states the law criminalised consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults with punishments ranging from three months to two years' imprisonment — official current-law baseline for visitor exposure; report also covers societal abuses.

US State Dept 2010 Human Rights Report, Chad (pre-criminalisation baseline): law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts' with no evidence it was used against LGBT persons that year; no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, most persons discreet due to social strictures — documents the pre-2017 legal climate.

US State Department 2006 Human Rights Report for Chad documents Deby regime abuses including extrajudicial killings, torture and the MINURCAT withdrawal. The report contains no trans-specific or sexual-orientation-specific finding.

HuffPost/GroundTruth Project analysis: while further criminalisation attempts failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda, they succeeded in Chad and Nigeria — situates Chad's criminalisation drive within the broader wave of conservative anti-LGBT advocacy, relevant context for how the law's trajectory developed.

GAB.name: Gabon
GAB.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful in Gabon. The criminal provision introduced in 2019 was repealed in 2020, and no offence covering same-sex conduct is in force.

Gabon became independent in 1960 without inheriting a sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was lawful before July 2019. Law No. 042/2018, the penal code that entered into force on 5 July 2019, created the offence. Article 402 placed 'les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe' under 'atteintes aux mœurs' without using the term homosexuality. Conviction carried up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of up to five million CFA francs, reported at about US$8,500 to US$8,561.

The provision was applied. Two men were arrested under it within months of its entry into force and were released only after paying bribes to police. Police had also arrested two men accused of conducting a same-sex wedding in December 2013 and released them, four years before any statute addressed same-sex conduct.

Repeal began on 23 June 2020, when the National Assembly voted 48 in favour, 24 against with 25 abstentions, and continued with Senate approval on 29 June and presidential signature on 7 July 2020. The reversal divided public opinion.

The age of sexual majority is 15 for girls and 18 for boys, regardless of the sex of the partner. Before 2020 the thresholds were unequal, at 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts, so both the historic and current thresholds are keyed to sex rather than to the sex of the partner.

The constitution ratified by referendum on 16 November 2024, with more than 90 per cent approval on turnout of about 55 per cent, codifies privacy in Article 18 and rejected civil-society demands to restore the criminal offence. Article 16 defines marriage as a union between two people of opposite sex, effective 12 April 2025, and is entrenched as unamendable. The text was adopted under the military government that took power in August 2023, ending 56 years of rule by the Bongo family.

A trans visitor should expect no legal gender recognition in Gabon. There is no procedure for changing gender markers on identity documents, and the law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity.

Enforcement directed at gender presentation runs through general public order provisions. Police are reported to occasionally bring breaches of modesty charges against people with non-gender-conforming presentation and against same-sex couples, and this misuse of neutral laws is described as not widespread. State-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is described as not present, while harassment by private individuals is described as common. Societal stigmatisation of LGBTQ+ people is documented.

LGBTI organisations cannot register as associations in Gabon, which removes the formal civil-society bodies that would otherwise document abuses and provide support to visitors.

Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023, amending Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011, treats sexual orientation and sexual life as sensitive personal data. Gender identity is not covered by that protection.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Gabon. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship cannot marry or have the partnership recognised, and the constitutional marriage definition forecloses recognition by ordinary legislation.
GAB.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any administrative practice exists for changing gender markers on Gabonese identity documents is unresolved in the sources; they record only that no legal gender recognition is available.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence data for Gabon, and no comparison with the general violent-crime rate. The level of risk of violence faced by trans visitors relative to other visitors is not sourced.

How the sex-keyed age of sexual majority thresholds are applied to a person whose legal record and appearance differ is not addressed by any source in the inventory.

The description of breaches of modesty charges as occasional and not widespread carries no date in the inventory, so current enforcement frequency is not established.

The 2019 US State Department human rights report for Gabon is inventoried as documenting the criminalisation year and societal discrimination; its specific findings are not reproduced in the inventory and are not restated here.

Entry rules, visa practice and screening at Gabonese ports of entry are not covered by any source in the inventory.

Article 18 of the 2024 constitution has no reported application, and its practical effect on police conduct, custody or documentation procedures is unresolved.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Gabon (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Gabonese law provides no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. The criminal provisions described concern same-sex sexual activity, not gender identity. Police are reported to occasionally use 'breaches of modesty' charges to target people with non-gender-conforming presentations. Such discriminatory misuse of neutral laws is described as not widespread. State-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is described as not present, while harassment by individuals is described as common. Involuntary conversion therapies, both religious and ritualistic, are described as widespread. Same-sex sexual activity has generally been legal in Gabon except for the period between July 2019 and June 2020. Historically the age of consent was unequal, requiring 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts. On 5 July 2019 revisions to the Penal Code criminalised homosexual relations between consenting adults with a penalty of up to 6 months imprisonment and/or a fine of up to 5 million CFA francs. Two men were reported to have been arrested under that law and to have paid bribes to police to be released. On 23 June 2020 the National Assembly approved decriminalisation, followed by Senate approval on 29 June and presidential signature on 7 July 2020, setting the age of sexual majority at 15 for girls and 18 for boys regardless of partner. Police are reported to occasionally use 'breaches of modesty' charges to target same-sex couples, though such misuse is described as not widespread and state-sponsored harassment is described as not present. Limited protections based on sexual orientation and sexual life exist, including Law No. 025/2023 of 09/07/2023 amending Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011 to treat sexual orientation and sexual life as sensitive personal data, while same-sex couples have no legal recognition under a November 2024 constitutional marriage definition effective 12 April 2025 as a union between two people of opposite sex entrenched as unamendable.

sources.title: Gabon government bill to decriminalise same-sex sexual activity (2020)
sources.summary: On 23 June 2020 Gabon's lower house voted 48 in favour, 24 against with 25 abstentions to revise the 2019 law to decriminalise sexual relations between people of the same sex, removing punishment of up to six months imprisonment and a 5 million FCFA fine, while same-sex marriage remained not allowed.

sources.title: Constitution of Gabon adopted by national referendum November 2024
sources.summary: In Gabon same-sex relations were decriminalised in 2020, same-sex marriage remains prohibited, and LGBTQIA+ people face societal stigmatization.

GAB.tangentialFactors:
The 2024 constitution was drafted and ratified under the military government that took power in August 2023, which ended 56 years of rule by the Bongo family. Its privacy guarantee and its marriage definition were settled by the same process: campaigners who sought the restoration of criminalisation were refused, and the exclusion of same-sex couples from marriage was written in as unamendable.

Because the marriage definition cannot be amended, partner recognition for same-sex couples is not reachable through ordinary legislation in Gabon. Any change would require the replacement of the constitutional text.

Gabon's 2019 offence did not derive from a colonial penal code that the country carried over at independence in 1960. The lawfulness that preceded 2019 and that has applied since 2020 is the longer-standing position of Gabonese law, and the criminalisation episode ran for about twelve months.

Article 18 of the 2024 constitution has no reported enforcement record. Whether the privacy guarantee changes police conduct toward LGBTQ+ people is not evidenced by any case in the source inventory.

GAB.blindSummary:
Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults is lawful in the country. The criminal provision introduced in 2019 was repealed in 2020, and no offence covering same-sex conduct is in force.

The country became independent in 1960 without inheriting a sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was lawful before July 2019. Law No. 042/2018, the penal code that entered into force on 5 July 2019, created the offence. Article 402 placed 'les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe' under 'atteintes aux mœurs' without using the term homosexuality. Conviction carried up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of up to five million CFA francs, reported at about US$8,500 to US$8,561.

The provision was applied. Two men were arrested under it within months of its entry into force and were released only after paying bribes to police. Police had also arrested two men accused of conducting a same-sex wedding in December 2013 and released them, four years before any statute addressed same-sex conduct.

Repeal began on 23 June 2020, when the national assembly voted 48 in favour, 24 against with 25 abstentions, and continued with senate approval on 29 June and presidential signature on 7 July 2020. The reversal divided public opinion.

The age of sexual majority is 15 for girls and 18 for boys, regardless of the sex of the partner. Before 2020 the thresholds were unequal, at 15 for opposite-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts, so both the historic and current thresholds are keyed to sex rather than to the sex of the partner.

The constitution ratified by referendum on 16 November 2024, with more than 90 per cent approval on turnout of about 55 per cent, codifies privacy in Article 18 and rejected civil-society demands to restore the criminal offence. Article 16 defines marriage as a union between two people of opposite sex, effective 12 April 2025, and is entrenched as unamendable. The text was adopted under the military government that took power in August 2023, ending 56 years of rule by a single family.

A trans visitor should expect no legal gender recognition in the country. There is no procedure for changing gender markers on identity documents, and the law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity.

Enforcement directed at gender presentation runs through general public order provisions. Police are reported to occasionally bring breaches of modesty charges against people with non-gender-conforming presentation and against same-sex couples, and this misuse of neutral laws is described as not widespread. State-sponsored harassment of LGBTQ+ people as a group is described as not present, while harassment by private individuals is described as common. Societal stigmatisation of LGBTQ+ people is documented.

LGBTI organisations cannot register as associations in the country, which removes the formal civil-society bodies that would otherwise document abuses and provide support to visitors.

Law No. 025/2023 of 9 July 2023, amending Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011, treats sexual orientation and sexual life as sensitive personal data. Gender identity is not covered by that protection.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in the country. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship cannot marry or have the partnership recognised, and the constitutional marriage definition forecloses recognition by ordinary legislation.

COG.name: Republic of the Congo
COG.summary:
The Republic of the Congo does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct between adults. A systematic legislative review published by the European Union Agency for Asylum in May 2024 reached that finding, and the United States Department of State human rights reports for 2022 and 2023 record the same position. Same-sex relationships have been legal since 1940.

Penal Code Article 331, as amended in 2006, sets an unequal age of consent: 21 years for same-sex acts against 18 years for different-sex acts. It punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years imprisonment and a fine. The EUAA review, drawing on ILGA data, and the State Department reports describe the scope of that provision as applied to same-sex conduct as ambiguous, and sources treat it as a basis for justifying discrimination.

Prosecutions under Article 331 are not documented. The State Department recorded no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the provision during 2023. Police nonetheless invoke it as a pretext to solicit bribes from men perceived as gay, and officers have falsely claimed that same-sex activity is generally illegal in order to extract money. Such abuses are rarely reported because of fear of police interaction, and are investigated when they are reported.

There is no legally recognised procedure for changing gender identity in the Republic of the Congo. A trans visitor whose passport, visa or other identity documents carry a gender marker that does not match their presentation has no local route to obtain congruent documentation, and no legal protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity.

Marriage is defined in Section 2, Article 127 of the Family Code as a public act establishing a lasting union between a man and a woman, which explicitly bars recognition of same-sex marriage. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under birth-sex status has no prospect of local recognition.

No broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation exists, and there are no hate crime laws, so a visitor has no statutory discrimination or bias-crime route to pursue.

Violence and harassment against LGBTQI+ people are documented. Non-governmental organisations reported psychological and physical harassment and financial extortion by both government actors and nonstate actors. Violence rose in 2022, a trend attributed to forced confinement during the COVID-19 pandemic and to worsening economic hardship, and most of it was committed by family members. State authorities and private citizens committed violence in 2022 and 2023. Where violence is reported, law enforcement punishes it.

Social attitudes are hostile. In a survey conducted between 2021 and 2023, 73 percent of residents of Brazzaville said they would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour.

Legal protections for sensitive personal data cover sexual orientation and sexual life but not gender identity. Article 19 of Law No. 27-2020 on the fight against cybercrime prohibits placing or storing personal data revealing sexual orientation without a legal exception or express consent, punishable by one to five years in prison, a fine of one million to ten million CFA francs, or both. Articles 8, 10 and 15 of Decree No. 2025-66 on the personal data of air passengers protect sexual orientation, and Articles 4, 14 and 40 of Law No. 29-2019 on the protection of personal data protect sexual life as sensitive personal data.
COG.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. Tolerance and violence findings are framed around LGBTQ people generally or around homosexual neighbours, so the trans-specific risk picture is inferred from the wider legal and social regime rather than measured directly.

Article 331's scope as applied to same-sex conduct remains ambiguous. No court ruling, prosecution record or interpretive guidance resolving it was identified.

Violence findings in the sources are qualitative. No incident counts, rates or population denominators are given, so no comparison with the country's general violence level can be made.

sources.summary: EUAA COI Query Response Q29 (May 2024) on the Republic of the Congo: systematic review of legislation, implementation, treatment by state and society, and availability of state protection for LGBTQI+ people. Key findings: no law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults; Penal Code Article 331 (per ILGA) sets age of consent at 21 for same-sex vs 18 for different-sex acts; the under-21 'shameless act / against nature' provision's scope as applied to same-sex conduct is 'ambiguous', and sources say it is used to justify discrimination.

US State Department 2022 human rights report (Republic of the Congo), SOGI section: no law specifically prohibits consensual same-sex conduct between adults; a provision punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under age 21 (6 months–3 years plus fine), scope ambiguous and not invoked for prosecutions. Police at times cite the provision to extract bribes from gay men; local NGOs reported violence, psychological/physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by government and nonstate actors.

US State Department 2023 human rights report (Republic of the Congo): no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the ambiguous under-21 provision during 2023; police continued using the 'act against nature' law as a pretext to solicit bribes from men; NGOs reported continuing psychological/physical harassment and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by both government actors and nonstate actors, with no anti-discrimination protections in law.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Republic of the Congo (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: There is no legally recognized way to change one's gender identity. There is no broad legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. There are no laws addressing hate crimes. There are no laws addressing discrimination in education, healthcare, housing, or employment. There are no laws addressing conversion therapy or surgeries on intersex children intended to make their bodies fit expected norms. The personal-data protections cited in the article cover sexual orientation and sexual life, not gender identity. Same-sex relationships have been legal since 1940. The 1940 Penal Code as amended in 2006 only prohibits same-sex sexual behaviour with a person younger than 21 years, compared to 18 years for opposite-sex sexual activity. Same-sex marriage is explicitly banned under Section 2, Article 127 of the Family Code, which defines marriage as a public act establishing a lasting union between a man and a woman. The unequal age of consent is not used for arrests, but police have used the Penal Code to solicit bribes from young men perceived as gay and have falsely claimed same-sex activity is generally illegal to solicit bribes; such abuses are rarely reported due to fear of police interaction but are investigated when reported. There is no broad legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and no laws on hate crimes or on discrimination in education, healthcare, housing, or employment. Article 19 of Law No. 27-2020 on the Fight against Cybercrime prohibits placing or storing personal data revealing sexual orientation without a legal exception or expressed consent. Violation is punishable by one to five years in prison, a fine of one million to ten million CFA francs, or both. Articles 8, 10 and 15 of Decree No. 2025-66 relating to the Personal data of Air Passengers protect sexual orientation, and Articles 4, 14 and 40 of Law No. 29-2019 on the Protection of Personal Data protect sexual life as sensitive and personal data. The article contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; all tolerance and violence findings are framed around LGBTQ people generally or homosexual neighbors. Social stigma was linked to no significant gay or lesbian community presence in 2010, with no cases of violence or discrimination reported to non-governmental organizations or news media at that time, though instances may have been unreported. Violence toward LGBTQ+ people rose in 2022 due to forced confinement during the COVID-19 pandemic, with increasing economic hardship further contributing, and most violence was committed by family members. State authorities and regular citizens committed violence against LGBTQ+ people in 2022 and 2023, while reported violence against LGBTQ people is punished by law enforcement. In a survey conducted from 2021 to 2023, 73 percent of Congolese people in Brazzaville said they would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbor. LGBTQ civil societies were present in 2023 but had been unable to gain legal recognition. In 2020 a non-governmental organization was denied legal registration until references to the organization's focus on the LGBTQ+ community were removed.

BDI.name: Burundi
BDI.summary:
Article 567 of the Penal Code criminalises sexual relations with a person of the same sex and applies to conduct by both men and women. It was passed on 22 November 2008 and took effect on 22 April 2009; such conduct was not criminalised before that date. The penalty is three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 Burundian francs. Reporting by OutRight International as of March 2026 cites Article 250 of the Penal Code for the same offence, with up to two years in prison and a fine; the article number differs from the 2008 provision and the sources do not reconcile the two.

Burundi provides no legal gender recognition as of March 2026, so a visitor cannot obtain local documents or markers matching their gender, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register as associations.

Article 29 of the Constitution bans same-sex marriage, and Burundi recognises neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition for a spouse or partner.

In December 2023 President Évariste Ndayishimiye said homosexuals found in Burundi should be taken to stadiums and stoned, and rejected development aid conditioned on respect for LGBT rights. Human Rights Watch called on the ruling party to renounce persecution. The Iteka League, a Burundian human rights organisation working in exile, described the remarks as a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people, and members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described them as a real license to kill.

Arrests are documented while prosecutions of consensual adult conduct rarely reach conviction. On 1 July 2009 a man in Bujumbura was arrested for being gay and police sought money in exchange for his release before advocacy secured it. In 2012 two lesbians were briefly arrested and released. In September 2014 a case in Karuzi Province involving a Viettel employee and a Burundian man was dropped after three days for lack of evidence. Reporting for 2016 recorded no prosecutions during that year.

The one recorded conviction attached to a same-sex charge, on 2 November 2016 at the High Court of Cibitoke Province, sentenced a 15-year-old boy to one year in prison on charges of rape of a minor and homosexuality, following his admission of raping a seven-year-old boy.

In March 2023 twenty-four people were arrested on same-sex conduct charges; one of the accused died in detention; the group was acquitted on the conduct charge and seven were convicted of inciting debauchery. In August 2023 seven people were sentenced to one to two years in prison for homosexual acts.

United States State Department human rights reports from 2009 through 2016 list discrimination against gay and lesbian people among the country's common abuses, alongside torture, extrajudicial executions, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns, and record societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity without government protection. OutRight International describes extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, torture and sexual and gender-based violence with no meaningful legal reform. These conditions determine what protection, medical care and custody conditions a detained visitor can expect; the inventory contains no general homicide rate for Burundi, so no comparison between general and trans-specific violence levels can be made.
BDI.outOfScopeNotes:
The penal code article number is not settled in the sources: the 2008 provision is cited as Article 567, while OutRight International's March 2026 country page cites Article 250 with the same penalty range. No source explains the discrepancy or whether the code was renumbered.

Human rights reporting in the inventory records extrajudicial killings and one death in detention in the March 2023 case, but gives no general homicide rate for Burundi, so no baseline comparison is possible, and no count of violence against trans people specifically is available.

Nothing in the inventory describes border, visa or airport screening practice: whether document markers or presentation are flagged on entry, whether secondary screening occurs, or whether trans travellers face questioning is not sourced.

No information covers bathroom or single-sex facility rules. Beyond the absence of legal gender recognition, no data addresses medical or care access specific to trans people.

Enforcement data is sparse: the documented cases span 2009 to 2023, no prosecution figures for recent years are given, and nothing distinguishes enforcement against trans people from enforcement against same-sex conduct generally.

BDI.tangentialFactors:
International pressure has limited purchase. Enforcement patterns shifted in 2023. Through 2016 the documented record was of arrests and short detentions that ended without prosecution of consensual adult conduct; in March 2023 a mass arrest of twenty-four people ended in acquittal on the conduct charge but seven convictions for inciting debauchery following a death in detention, and in August 2023 seven people received prison terms of one to two years for homosexual acts.

BDI.blindSummary:
Article 567 of the penal code criminalises sexual relations with a person of the same sex and applies to conduct by both men and women. It was passed on 22 November 2008 and took effect on 22 April 2009; such conduct was not criminalised before that date. The penalty is three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 in the local currency. Reporting by an international advocacy organisation as of March 2026 cites Article 250 of the penal code for the same offence, with up to two years in prison and a fine; the article number differs from the 2008 provision and the sources do not reconcile the two.

The country provides no legal gender recognition as of March 2026, so a visitor cannot obtain local documents or markers matching their gender, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register as associations.

Article 29 of the constitution bans same-sex marriage, and the country recognises neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition for a spouse or partner.

In December 2023 the president said homosexuals found in the country should be taken to stadiums and stoned, and rejected development aid conditioned on respect for LGBT rights. An international human rights organisation called on the ruling party to renounce persecution. A local human rights organisation working in exile described the remarks as a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people, and members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described them as a real license to kill.

Arrests are documented while prosecutions of consensual adult conduct rarely reach conviction. On 1 July 2009 a man in the capital was arrested for being gay and police sought money in exchange for his release before advocacy secured it. In 2012 two lesbians were briefly arrested and released. In September 2014 a case in one province involving a telecommunications company employee and a local man was dropped after three days for lack of evidence. Reporting for 2016 recorded no prosecutions during that year.

The one recorded conviction attached to a same-sex charge, on 2 November 2016 at a provincial high court, sentenced a 15-year-old boy to one year in prison on charges of rape of a minor and homosexuality, following his admission of raping a seven-year-old boy.

In March 2023 twenty-four people were arrested on same-sex conduct charges; one of the accused died in detention; the group was acquitted on the conduct charge and seven were convicted of inciting debauchery. In August 2023 seven people were sentenced to one to two years in prison for homosexual acts.

Human rights reports by a foreign government from 2009 through 2016 list discrimination against gay and lesbian people among the country's common abuses, alongside torture, extrajudicial executions, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns, and record societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity without government protection. An international advocacy organisation describes extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, torture and sexual and gender-based violence with no meaningful legal reform. These conditions determine what protection, medical care and custody conditions a detained visitor can expect; the sources contain no general homicide rate for the country, so no comparison between general and trans-specific violence levels can be made.

CAF.name: Central African Republic
CAF.summary:
Private sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex is legal in the Central African Republic for both men and women. Criminal liability attaches only to conduct in public.

Article 85 of the criminal code punishes public expression of love between persons of the same sex as an attack on public morals. The penalty is six months to two years' imprisonment or a fine of 150,000 to 600,000 CFA francs ($300 to $1,200), a heavier sanction than the code applies to other public-morals offences. Where one participant is a child, the adult faces two to five years' imprisonment or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs ($200 to $1,600).

The US State Department's 2012 human rights report recorded no arrests or detentions by police under these provisions. Alternatives Centrafrique, a domestic organisation, has since documented arrests prompted by false accusations of same-sex intercourse, as well as mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ people by law enforcement. The 2023 State Department report recorded no reports of violence against LGBTQ people, which leaves open whether incidents were absent or went unreported.

Criminalisation of public same-sex affection, together with cultural stigma, keeps the LGBTQ community concealed. The 2023 State Department report found no known organisations promoting LGBTQ human rights. Issues of sexual orientation and gender identity are treated as taboo and described publicly as imported from Europe and contrary to African values.

Legal gender recognition does not exist in the Central African Republic. A trans visitor cannot obtain a changed gender marker and will be assessed by officials against documents as issued. Sources provide no transgender-specific criminal, documentary, screening, facilities, custody or care rule beyond that absence; the remaining rules are stated only on an LGBTQ-collective or homosexuality-specific basis, and no transgender-specific statement on societal tolerance is documented.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in health, employment, education, or access to goods and services. Marriage is defined in Article 7 of the constitution as the union between one man and one woman, and no same-sex couple can be legally recognised. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition, and family and marriage are placed under the protection of the state.

No law bars psychological or medical practices used as conversion therapy on LGBTQ people. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data treats sexual orientation as sensitive data, and Article 17 prohibits any processing of sensitive data on the ground that it risks discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms. The provision names sexual orientation; gender identity is not addressed.

The Central African Republic signed the United Nations joint statement condemning violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. It has received two Universal Periodic Review recommendations, on non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and on improving the situation of sexual minorities. The OHCHR summary of stakeholder submissions for the country's fourth-cycle review, examined at the 45th session in January 2024, includes related stakeholder recommendations.

Societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people is entrenched, and many citizens attribute homosexuality to undue Western influence. Discrimination in education, healthcare and employment is documented, and LGBTQ people conceal their identities to avoid it. Maintaining a relationship is described as dangerous.
CAF.outOfScopeNotes:
The only enforcement figure for Article 85 in this inventory dates from 2012, when no arrests or detentions were recorded; no current arrest data is sourced.

The 2023 State Department report recorded no reports of violence against LGBTQ people and could not establish whether that reflected an absence of incidents or victims not reporting. No violence data specific to transgender people in the Central African Republic is available in these sources.

No source treats gender identity separately from sexual orientation except to record the absence of a gender-recognition procedure; whether Article 17 of Law 24-001 extends to gender identity is unresolved.

No custody, screening or facilities data specific to trans travellers is sourced, and whether the absence of transgender-specific tolerance reporting reflects absent hostility or absent reporting is unresolved.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Central African Republic (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: No legal gender recognition exists. No transgender-specific criminal, documentary, screening, facilities, custody or care rule is provided beyond that absence; all other rules affecting transgender visitors are stated only on an LGBTQ-collective basis. There are no laws protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in health, employment, education, and access to goods and services. Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military. There are no laws against psychology or medical practices being used as conversion therapy on LGBTQ people. There is no ban on surgeries intended to normalize the bodies of intersex infants, with no reports of them occurring in 2023. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data protects sexual orientation as sensitive data and Article 17 provides "Any processing of sensitive data is prohibited due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms." Central African Republic signed the United Nations joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity condemning violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people, while Alternatives Centrafrique founded in 2009 and registered in 2020 documented mistreatment and torture of LGBTQ people by law enforcement. Both male and female types of same-sex sexual activity are legal. The penal code criminalizes "public expression of love" between persons of the same sex with imprisonment for six months to two years or a fine of between 150,000 and 600,000 CFA francs ($300 and $1,200). When one of the participants is a child, the adult may be sentenced to two to five years' imprisonment or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs ($200 and $1,600). In 2012 there were no reports that police arrested or detained persons under these provisions. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned under Article 7 defining marriage as "the union between one man and one woman ... Family and marriage are under the protection of the State." Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data protects sexual orientation as sensitive data with Article 17 prohibiting any processing of sensitive data due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms. Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military and Alternatives Centrafrique documented cases of arrests due to false accusations of same-sex intercourse plus mistreatment and torture by law enforcement. No transgender-specific societal-tolerance statement is documented; all tolerance and stigma statements are framed on an LGBTQ-collective or homosexuality-specific basis. The collective statement including transgender persons is: "societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons was entrenched, and many citizens attributed the existence of homosexuality to undue Western influence." Cultural stigma continues to persist and religious preaching of conversion is rarely enacted since people keep their LGBTQ identities hidden. LGBTQ people face discrimination in education, healthcare, and employment and due to criminalization of public same-sex affection plus cultural stigma the LGBTQ community has to conceal itself, with maintaining queer relationships described as dangerous. While there were no reports of violence against LGBTQ people, it is unclear if this is due to a lack of incidents or victims not reporting it. Alternatives Centrafrique, founded in 2009 and registered in 2020, submitted reports for the Universal Periodic Review third and fourth cycles, while being diagnosed with HIV is used as a source of workplace stigmatization leading to harassment, blackmail, and firings.

GIN.name: Guinea
GIN.summary:
Guinea's 2016 Penal Code, Article 274, punishes consensual same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both. The provision replaced Article 325 of the 1998 Penal Code, which criminalised the same conduct through indecency provisions and set a lower minimum fine. Where the conduct involves violence or attempted violence, the sentence rises to five to ten years, and acts with a person under 21 carry the maximum penalty.

Enforcement reaches people who are not charged with conduct. Police arrest on the basis of clothing and appearance, and Article 274 functions as a standing basis for extortion, with release commonly secured by payment to officers. A 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission reports LGBTQ people held for up to five days despite the 48-hour legal limit, most released only after paying bribes or fines. In 2023 the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals added a unit to investigate same-sex conduct. Security forces have arrested, harassed and used violence against LGBTQ people accused of disrupting social order. In 2016 and 2017 the organisation Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reported gay men jailed and fined for release.

Custody carries specific risk. LGBTQ people in detention are frequently abused, and transgender women are arrested and imprisoned on the stated pretext of protecting them from community violence, then held in male prisons where they often experience sexual violence.

Guinea has no legal gender recognition, so a trans visitor cannot obtain identity documents matching their gender, and no recognition of same-sex unions. A trans visitor in a relationship the law would read as same-sex has no route to partnership recognition.

The UPR submission describes a hostile, sometimes lethal environment with threats of physical violence and discrimination on grounds of orientation, gender identity and expression, and notes that widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence. A survey covering 2021 to 2023 found 87 percent of Guineans would dislike or strongly dislike having a gay neighbour. The State Department's 2011 report described homosexuality as socially, religiously and culturally taboo with no LGBTQ organisations in the country; its 2023 report found that LGBTQ people are cast as part of a Western imperialist agenda attributed to the United States and France.
GIN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how Article 274 is applied to foreign visitors specifically, or whether police stop, search or charge travellers on the basis of appearance at ports of entry.

The Guinea Aeronautical Regulations address PNR data handling only; the inventory contains no account of trans-specific screening, pat-down or secondary inspection practice at Conakry's airport or land borders.

The inventory contains no per-capita or comparative data on violence against transgender people in Guinea.

Whether the 2023 unit added to investigate same-sex conduct has produced prosecutions is not stated in the sources.

LBR.name: Liberia
LBR.summary:
Liberia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The sodomy offence carries up to one year of imprisonment, applies to women as well as men, and is a domestic-origin provision rather than a colonial import, so no external legal framework presses toward repeal.

Enforcement of the sodomy law is uncommon, but its existence deters victims of crime from reporting to police, and some people have been arrested on the basis of their sexuality or gender identity after attackers used their LGBTQ status as an excuse.

Legislative pressure on the statute is active rather than residual. Rep. Johnson N. Williams has been seeking lawmakers' support for an anti-homosexuality bill filed in the summer of 2024, and related proposals would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex. Earlier rounds followed the same pattern: in 2012 new legislation proposed longer jail terms for homosexuality, and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

Official hostility has been expressed at the top of the executive. In a joint interview in March 2012, then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended the laws criminalising homosexuality, remarks that drew international comment on Liberia's stance.

There is no legal gender recognition. No administrative route exists for a trans person to amend the name or gender marker on a Liberian identity document, so a visitor whose papers do not match their presentation cannot bring them into consistency before travel or during the stay.

Transition-related medical care is not available domestically. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery are not offered in Liberia, so a visitor who depends on a regular hormone supply or on post-operative follow-up has no in-country clinical fallback and must arrive with what they need.

Marriage between two people of the same sex is not recognised. In 2012 then-Senator Jewel Howard Taylor introduced a bill that would have made such a marriage a first-degree felony carrying up to ten years; it passed the Senate but not the House and never became law, and President Sirleaf had threatened to veto either of the 2012 anti-LGBTQ bills. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no recognition route.

One statutory protection sits alongside the criminal provision: Section 2.4(b)(iii) of the Decent Work Act (2015) entitles all who seek to work in Liberia to do so regardless of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation.

Community infrastructure exists but is largely private and organisational; LGBTQ Liberians often have to hide their identities in public.
LBR.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 2024 anti-homosexuality bill is unresolved in the available material: whether it has advanced, stalled or been withdrawn is not established, and no text, sponsor list or committee stage is sourced.

The scope of the proposals to imprison children as young as 10 is not detailed in the available material; the age threshold is reported but the offences and penalties attached to it are not.

A UNDP and OHCHR country report on sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia (April 2020) is a participatory review of the legal, social and human-rights environment, but no specific finding from it is carried in the available material.

No information was identified on border or airport screening practices that would risk outing a trans traveller, nor on how Liberian identity documents record gender for the purposes of entry.

The HIV prevalence figure dates from 2013 and no more recent measurement is available in the material reviewed.
