MDG.name: Madagascar
MDG.summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is lawful in Madagascar only from age 21. Article 331 of the Penal Code treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, with a reported penalty band of five to ten years' imprisonment. The age of consent is unequal, so a trans visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 carries a criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not. In a 2020 case a 33-year-old woman was arrested for statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint; the mother was allegedly acting to cover an incest and rape accusation against the father. Religious leaders offered the younger woman conversion therapy during the proceedings.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex, whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names gender identity as a cause of absolute nullity of marriage, which is a direct legal exposure for a trans person whose marriage is examined under that provision. No civil union or other form of partner recognition exists.

Adoption is restricted. Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that full adoption is only permitted to heterosexual spouses, so a trans visitor resident in the country with a partner has no route to joint adoption.

Data protection law treats sexual life and orientation as sensitive. Article 18 of Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Article 2 of Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus protects sexual orientation as sensitive data. The provisions matter where a visitor's medical or financial records would otherwise record a partner or a transition history.

Health policy addresses trans and same-sex health needs mainly through HIV programming. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programmes adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions protecting vulnerable groups, expressly including young people, sex workers, men who have sex with men and mobile populations, against HIV transmission.

The government rejected trans and LGBT protections at its fourth Universal Periodic Review in January 2025, which carried 235 recommendations. It declined recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations, Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+, responded that refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence.

Public expression is constrained by administrative action. In early July 2021 the government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of incitement to debauchery.

Same-sex conduct is not criminalised as such, but it is widely considered socially unacceptable and many people conceal it to keep their jobs and live in peace, relying on private networks and coded language. The US State Department's 2011 human rights report recorded societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community, with public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, particularly of transgender sex workers, who were frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and murder. Supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused the couple of promising homosexuality.
MDG.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records the number of prosecutions brought under Article 331, so the frequency of enforcement against the under-21 offence is unresolved. Whether the data protection provisions in Law No. 2014-038 and Law No. 2017-045 are enforced in practice, and whether they cover records held by private clinics or employers, is not sourced.

No source addresses police or border-screening practice towards trans travellers, document and marker rules at ports of entry, or access to bathrooms and single-sex facilities. No trans-specific hate-crime or anti-discrimination statute was located in the inventory, and the position on legal gender recognition is not documented here. The most detailed account of violence against transgender sex workers dates from the 2011 State Department report and no figure with a denominator accompanies it.

COM.name: Comoros
COM.summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is criminal in Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code covers any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural, and the sources disagree on the penalty it carries. Outright International records six months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs, about US$240 to US$720. The archived text of the 2020 code specifies two to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs. Human Dignity Trust gives a maximum of three years. A December 2024 press report cites Article 318 as carrying up to five years. The 1982 Penal Code that preceded the current one provided up to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs.

Enforcement is documented. In 2022 a man was prosecuted after a sexual video of him with another man was leaked online, described as the first prosecution of consensual adult same-sex activity under the 2020 code. In June 2024 two women were detained after asking an imam to marry them; the marriage allegation was not proven in court, but the women said they had previously had sexual relations together. On 12 December 2024 a court convicted them of homosexuality and sentenced them to five and six months respectively. Because the sentences were shorter than the detention already served, they were released. Human Dignity Trust described the conviction as a human rights violation, and it was the first conviction of its kind in the country.

The enforcement picture is not uniform. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report records no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct during that year and states that authorities did not actively enforce the law. Police were reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ people, and no such violence was reported in 2023. The same report lists widespread impunity among the country's major human rights problems.

No legal gender-marker change is available to transgender people, and no law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The 2012 Labor Code contains no protections for LGBTQ people.

There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples, so a trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under local law has no partner recognition or spousal protections.

Social exposure carries risk. LGBTQ people face stigmatisation among the wider population. Discrimination extends to education and employment, and some are ostracised from their homes, neighbourhoods and villages.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Comoros (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their gender markers. There is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. The Labor Code (2012) does not provide protections for LGBTQ people. There are no LGBTQ+ organizations in the country. Such organizations could potentially be prosecuted under Article 5 of Law No. 86-006/AF (1986) which prohibits organizations founded on an "unlawful cause or for an unlawful purpose, contrary to the law or public morals." Both male and female same-sex sexual acts are illegal in the Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code provides that "Any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural shall be punished with a sentence of six months to two years and a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs." Previously, the 1982 Penal Code punished such acts with up to five years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs. The government has repeatedly refused to decriminalize homosexuality when advised to by bodies of the United Nations. The first prosecution of consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults under the 2020 Penal Code was in 2022, involving a man prosecuted after a sexual video of him with another man was leaked online. In 2024, two women were detained from June until December after allegedly asking an imam to marry them, which was not proven in court, but the women said they had previously engaged in sexual activity together. They were convicted for homosexuality and sentenced to five and six months in prison respectively, and were released after the December ruling because the sentence was shorter than the detention period. There is no recognition of legal rights for same-sex couples, and the Family Code establishes marriage as the union of a man and a woman. LGBTQ persons face stigmatization among the broader population. Most LGBTQ+ people do not disclose their sexual orientation or gender identity as of 2023. LGBTQ+ people face cultural discrimination as well as discrimination while seeking education and employment opportunities. Some LGBTQ+ people are ostracized from their homes, neighborhoods, and villages. According to Gallup, 26 percent responded in 2023 that the area they lived would be a good place for LGBTQ+ people, a 10 percent increase from the previous year. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

DJI.name: Djibouti
DJI.summary:
Djibouti's penal code contains no express offence criminalising consensual same-sex conduct. Sections 353 and 354 refer vaguely to "good morals" and public morality without naming same-sex relations, and no provision states the position either way. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, nevertheless marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country in its at-a-glance assessment, and authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these articles. The practical position is that such conduct is treated as de facto illegal despite the absence of an express offence.

Public-morality and "obscene acts" provisions are used against people. No reported case law defines the outer limits of Sections 353 and 354, so the exposure of a trans visitor who is visible, or who engages in any conduct in a public setting that would be read as sexual or obscene, is undefined by statute and depends on how authorities apply the provisions.

Djibouti provides no legal gender recognition, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Wikipedia's overview records that discrimination protection exists in employment only, while the US State Department's 2023 human rights report states there is no legal prohibition of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The two sources differ on the scope of any employment protection.

Social and religious intolerance is pervasive. The 2023 State Department report describes status and conduct as taboo, with a societal pattern of discrimination and no official violence cases that can be cited. People fear family and community shunning on disclosure. Wikipedia records that no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

Complaints about discrimination can be filed with the police or with the national human-rights commission (CNDH). The 2023 State Department report cites no official violence cases, so the practical reach of that route is not documented.
DJI.outOfScopeNotes:
No reported case law defines the outer limits of Sections 353 and 354, and the 2023 State Department report cites no official violence cases, so the enforcement record is not documented.

The US State Department's 2015 human rights report for Djibouti carried limited LGBT-specific content; the remainder addressed general conditions including suppression of the opposition, prison conditions, female genital mutilation and trafficking.

A Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board response to information request covering research from 2009 to March 2012 found documentation on the treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti scarce across all consulted sources, relying on the US 2010 country report. It is a dated baseline for the legal and protection framework and support services of that period, not a current assessment.

MRT.name: Mauritania
MRT.summary:
Transgender people in Mauritania are effectively criminalised through the Penal Code's debauchery provisions. Article 264, framed around public indecency and debauchery, is applied to gender nonconformity and carries between one month and two years' imprisonment together with fines of 5,000 to 150,000 ouguiya. Gender expression alone can bring a person within reach of the criminal law. Official data on the transgender population is gravely lacking.

The sexual-conduct regime carries a heavier ceiling. Mauritania criminalises same-sex sexual activity with a possible death penalty under Sharia law, and the Penal Code retains a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men. The government confirmed a de facto moratorium on the death penalty in 2021, but arrests and detentions under these provisions have continued in recent years.

Enforcement is uneven rather than absent. Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised but the penalties are not enforced, according to the 2023 US State Department human rights report, which also records reports of violence and threats against LGBT people. Civil society has objected to the scant number of indictments, and officials have at times acted with impunity.
MRT.outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the finding that Mauritania criminalises same-sex sexual activity with a possible death penalty under Sharia law rests on the profile's documented content rather than a live retrieval.

No official data on the size or circumstances of the transgender population is available, and whether the 2021 death-penalty moratorium holds in practice is not established by the sources.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mauritania (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: There is no legal recognition of transgender people in Mauritania. There are no legal protections against discrimination or hate crimes for LGBTQ+ people, and the law criminalizes raping women but not corrective rape against LGBTQ+ people. There is no law against conversion therapy with no reports of it occurring, and intersex medical interventions on children are not banned with no reported cases in 2023. In January 2020, ten men were arrested and detained after a video allegedly showing a gay wedding was posted to social media and later revealed to be a birthday party, with the local police commissioner stating the basis was imitating women. According to the police report in that incident, eight of the men confessed to being homosexual and were subsequently persecuted, while one woman present received a one-year suspended sentence for inciting debauchery. Most LGBTQ+ people find it safer to conceal sexual orientation or gender identity or intersex variation amid reported harassment and arbitrary arrest and detention by police, road safety authorities, community members, and family. Both male and female same-sex sexual activity are illegal in Mauritania under law based on Sharia. Article 308 of the 1983 Criminal Code provides that any adult Muslim man who commits an impudent or unnatural act with an individual of his sex will face death by public stoning (Rajm), with unclear application to non-Muslim men. Women who have sex with women face three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 5,000 to 60,000 Mauritanian Ouguiya. There have been no known cases of executions caused by homosexuality charges, with no death penalty imposed since 1986 and a government-confirmed unofficial moratorium on the death penalty for sexual activity between men in 2021. In January 2020, ten men were arrested and detained after a video allegedly showing a gay wedding was posted to social media and later revealed to be a birthday party. In 2025, two men were arrested after a video of them kissing was widely shared on Facebook. Mauritanian society is largely conservative, with a widely held belief that HIV and homosexuality are brought into the country by Senegalese and Gambian refugees. A survey conducted from 2021 to 2023 found that 77 percent of respondents would either dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbor. LGBTQ+ people often experience discrimination when seeking housing, employment, education, and healthcare, and most find it safer to conceal sexual orientation or gender identity or intersex variation. LGBTQI+ persons were sometimes harassed and arbitrarily arrested and detained by the National Police, the General Group for Road Safety, community members, and family, although local non-governmental organizations report a decrease in harassment from public authorities. Groups for LGBTQ+ rights are not officially allowed and often meet discreetly, with NouakchottSolidarity founded in 2015 as the first association to promote LGBTQ+ rights. No transgender-specific societal tolerance statement is documented; the only tolerance statement is general: "There is little social tolerance for LGBTQ+ people."

MRT.tangentialFactors:
Since 2008 Mauritania has served as a refuge for Senegalese LGBTIQ people, a migration pattern that places foreign trans and LGBTIQ visitors within the same legal regime as residents.

A minimal but real public advocacy space exists. Liberals Mauritania campaigns openly from inside the country on freethinker and LGBT-adjacent causes, and its published titles include 'When the Law Deprives Rights and Freedoms' and 'The First Trans Woman to Speak Out in Mauritania's Media'.

GNB.name: Guinea-Bissau
GNB.summary:
Same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence in Guinea-Bissau. The penal code introduced by Decree 4/93 in 1993 omits same-sex offences, and the U.S. Department of State's 2011 and 2012 human rights reports both record that consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised.

There is no transgender legal framework of any kind. No legal gender recognition procedure exists, so a visitor's identity documents carry the sex marker assigned at birth, with no domestic route to alter it before or during travel, and no statute addresses gender marker change at all.

The state recognises no partnership or marriage for couples read as same-sex under local law. No statute provides for such recognition, and official practice on family-size government housing treats those couples as single-person households rather than as couples.

No anti-discrimination statute covers sexual orientation or gender identity. The U.S. Department of State's 2012 report states plainly that the country's anti-discrimination laws do not apply to LGBT individuals, while recording no official discrimination against them in access to health care, employment or education, and no reported violent incidents or human-rights abuses targeting people on that basis in the reporting period covered by that report.

Sexual orientation and gender identity do appear in one piece of protective legislation. Article 5 of the Law against Domestic Violence (Law No. 6/2014) provides that all victims, regardless of sexual orientation, enjoy the fundamental rights inherent to human dignity and are guaranteed equal opportunities to a life free from violence as well as physical and mental health.

The reported picture of societal treatment is contested and dated. The U.S. Department of State's 2011 report documents societal stigma against LGBT people, and its 2012 report notes that social taboos against homosexuality sometimes restrict freedom to express sexual orientation while finding society relatively tolerant of consensual same-sex conduct. In 2018 a local NGO director stated that there had been some cases of violence targeting people based on sexual orientation or gender identity and that legal protections for LGBTI people are absent.
GNB.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether LGBT people face greater violence than the general population is unresolved. The sources offer only two dated and conflicting observations: a 2012 government report finding no reported violent incidents on that basis, and a 2018 statement from a local NGO director reporting some such cases. No figures, rates or denominators accompany either, and no trans-specific violence data of any kind appears in the inventory.

Whether LGBTQ applicants are barred from adoption is not sourced; the available guidance is silent rather than permissive or prohibitive.

The most recent human-rights reporting in the inventory is from 2012, with the NGO statement from 2018. Current enforcement practice, any legislative drafting after those dates, and present-day police treatment of gender-nonconforming visitors are not sourced here.

No entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to trans travellers, and no documented instances of document-marker flagging or secondary screening on the basis of gender presentation, appear in the sources.

GNQ.name: Equatorial Guinea
GNQ.summary:
The penal code in force since 15 November 2022 does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity. Same-sex sexual activity is lawful and the age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. The code is a revision of a historic-era Spanish criminal code dating to the Francoist period. Article 364(2) bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the first provision explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people, and Law 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data (Articles 10 and 41) protects personal data on 'sexual life' where it entails discrimination.

Enforcement does not follow the statute. Authorities continue to apply the obsolete 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which classifies homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices. A 2020 draft law, 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals', would move the conduct squarely into the criminal code if enacted; its status is unresolved. Three further instruments institutionalise discrimination against LGBT people: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order on 'immoral' activities, and a provincial regulation. ILGA reports that state intimidation of sexually diverse individuals persists: no law explicitly criminalises homosexuality, yet LGBTQ+ people are detained and punished through public shaming.

Police and military intervene in the spaces of assembly, expression and residence of lesbian women. In Bata, police detain known lesbians collectively, on the premise that 'lesbians are members of a sect', and apply collective punishment when one lesbian is sought. Transgender women have reported harassment and sexual violence while in police custody, and security forces have subjected LGBTQ+ people to sexual violence and discrimination in the military, in jails and in prison.

Documented incidents give the pattern its shape. In 2014 four men were detained over a video found on a phone and made to explain their actions on national television. A lesbian couple in Añisok were tied up at the police station, paraded through town with banners calling them witchcraft-practicing lesbians, photographed and shamed. In August 2023 police illegally detained Trifonia Melibea Obono, founder of Somos Parte del Mundo, after her group submitted a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people to the EU headquarters in Madrid; arrests and restrictions rose significantly afterward.

Rape is sometimes used as a form of conversion therapy, and queer women are forcibly impregnated in an attempt to make them heterosexual. LGBTQ+ women and transgender men are described as vulnerable to sexual violence in the military and from family. Laws against rape are not effectively enforced: the crime is rarely reported, and police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or is in the police or military.

The 2021 US State Department report, which predates the current penal code, recorded that same-sex conduct was not specifically criminalised but that LGBT persons faced societal stigma, with no anti-discrimination protections, within a general context of repression. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition and are not eligible for the same legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status has no access to partnership recognition or the protections attached to it.
GNQ.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 2020 draft law 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' is unresolved in the sources; whether it has been enacted, withdrawn or left dormant is not established.

No sourced information was identified on legal gender recognition, document or marker change, hormone access, medication or trans-specific health services.

No sourced data was identified on trans-specific violence with a denominator that would allow comparison against the general homicide rate.

SWZ.name: Eswatini
SWZ.summary:
Same-sex relations are illegal for men and women throughout Eswatini as of 12 March 2026. No legal gender recognition exists, so a trans visitor's passport and other documents are read exactly as issued, with no administrative route to align them with lived gender. A trans visitor travelling in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship falls under the criminal law, and there is no registered advocacy body in the country to turn to for help.

LGBTI organisations cannot obtain registration. The registrar of companies refused to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities in June 2019 on grounds of morality. In April 2022 the High Court upheld that refusal while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. The gap between the constitutional finding and the registration outcome leaves no licensed national organisation able to represent or assist a visitor.

Hostility from public figures is on the record. In 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said people of the same sex cannot even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider the question; in 2014 Press Secretary Percy Simelane said the government was monitoring the situation with a view to taking a legal position. Former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law in 2012 on the grounds that so few gay people lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort. A 2021 United States State Department report recorded traditional, religious and government officials describing same-sex conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The wider political setting is an absolute monarchy rated Not Free by Freedom House in its 2024 report, with an overall score of 17 out of 100 (1 out of 40 for political rights, 16 out of 60 for civil liberties) and severely restricted civic space. The BTI 2024 country report places the refusal to register LGBTQ+ groups inside a broader pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment.

No same-sex relationship is legally recognised, and no broad legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity apply in education, health, housing or employment.

Health settings are a documented point of exposure. A 2019 survey found that 59 per cent of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities and 30 per cent had been denied healthcare services. Policy points the other way in places: section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion, and the 2021 National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence and define gender-based violence to include violence based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity.

Violence against people perceived as gender or sexual minorities is documented. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. Rock of Hope reports that, with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and that most choose to remain closeted or move to South Africa.
SWZ.outOfScopeNotes:
The statutory provision that criminalises same-sex conduct in Eswatini, the penalty it carries, and any recorded prosecution or conviction are not sourced. Enforcement practice against visitors is therefore unresolved.

Police or immigration treatment of trans travellers specifically is not documented, and no trans-specific violent incident with a recorded outcome is available. Whether the April 2022 High Court ruling was appealed, and whether the registration refusal has been revisited since, is not established.

Violence figures available are individual incidents and survey responses rather than a measured rate, and no comparison with the general homicide rate is available.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Rock of Hope states that with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa. In April 2022 the High Court, while upholding refusal to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities, accepted that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. Officials refused to register ESGM in June 2019 on the grounds of morality. Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced. There is no legal recognition of same-sex relationships. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said people of the same sex cannot even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not even ready to consider it; in 2014 Press Secretary Percy Simelane said the government was closely monitoring the situation with a view to take a legal position. A 2019 survey found 59% of LGBTQ Swazis had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities, with 30% denied healthcare services. In February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a move LGBTQ groups welcomed. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion. The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of one's sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles. The 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation. A 2013 survey found 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Limited protections exist in policy: the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law, saying so few gays lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort; in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

SWZ.tangentialFactors:
Public visibility has occurred without recorded incident. The first eSwatini Pride, held in July 2018, was declared a success, and a virtual Pride celebration in June 2021 passed without incident according to the 2021 State Department report. A church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in December 2018, documented alongside continuing discrimination in the kingdom.

Several policy instruments reference sexual orientation without creating enforceable rights. The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles, the 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as freedom from discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, and the 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and the 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation. In February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a move LGBTQ groups welcomed.
SWZ.blindSummary:
Same-sex relations are illegal for men and women throughout the country as of 12 March 2026. No legal gender recognition exists, so a trans visitor's passport and other documents are read exactly as issued, with no administrative route to align them with lived gender. A trans visitor travelling in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship falls under the criminal law, and there is no registered advocacy body in the country to turn to for help.

LGBTI organisations cannot obtain registration. The registrar of companies refused to register a sexual and gender minorities group in June 2019 on grounds of morality. In April 2022 the High Court upheld that refusal while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. The gap between the constitutional finding and the registration outcome leaves no licensed national organisation able to represent or assist a visitor.

Hostility from public figures is on the record. In 2012 the prime minister said people of the same sex cannot even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider the question; in 2014 a government press secretary said the government was monitoring the situation with a view to taking a legal position. The foreign affairs minister rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law in 2012 on the grounds that so few gay people lived in the country that drafting one was not worth the effort. A 2021 human-rights report by a foreign government recorded traditional, religious and government officials describing same-sex conduct as neither morally authentic to the country nor Christian. In May 2017 a UN human rights body pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The wider political setting is an absolute monarchy rated Not Free in a 2024 civil-liberties assessment, with an overall score of 17 out of 100 (1 out of 40 for political rights, 16 out of 60 for civil liberties) and severely restricted civic space. A 2024 governance report places the refusal to register LGBTQ+ groups inside a broader pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment.

No same-sex relationship is legally recognised, and no broad legal protections against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity apply in education, health, housing or employment.

Health settings are a documented point of exposure. A 2019 survey found that 59 per cent of LGBTQ respondents had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities and 30 per cent had been denied healthcare services. Policy points the other way in places: section 4.3 of the 2013 national sexual and reproductive health policy requires the ministry of health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion, and 2021 national guidelines on adolescent sexual and reproductive health name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence and define gender-based violence to include violence based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity.

Violence against people perceived as gender or sexual minorities is documented. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from a town in the country was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. A local advocacy group reports that, with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and that most choose to remain closeted or move to a neighbouring jurisdiction.
SWZ.blindOutOfScope:
The statutory provision that criminalises same-sex conduct in the country, the penalty it carries, and any recorded prosecution or conviction are not sourced. Enforcement practice against visitors is therefore unresolved.

Police or immigration treatment of trans travellers specifically is not documented, and no trans-specific violent incident with a recorded outcome is available. Whether the April 2022 High Court ruling was appealed, and whether the registration refusal has been revisited since, is not established.

Violence figures available are individual incidents and survey responses rather than a measured rate, and no comparison with the general homicide rate is available.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): common law criminalises consensual same-sex intimacy; no legal gender recognition and limited gender-affirming healthcare; intersex people lack safeguards; in April 2022 the high court rejected an LGBT organisation's bid for registration, but in June 2023 the supreme court declared the registrar's decision void; the commerce ministry still refuses registration, claiming the organisation's name and objectives 'seek to offend against customary principles'.

Freedom-watchdog annual assessment (2024): this country is rated 'not free' (17/100) - an absolute monarchy; political dissent harshly punished; discrimination against women and LGBT+ people among the human-rights problems.

Governance-index country report (2024) by a political foundation: the last absolute monarchy in its world region - the king and queen mother hold veto powers over all branches of government; governance and human-rights context.
A foreign government's 2021 human-rights report on this country: official assessment - sodomy laws (common law) remain; significant societal stigma; no legal protections for LGBT persons.

Media commentary site (Dec 2018): a church welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in a residential area outside the capital; an activist at an LGBT advocacy organisation welcomed it while noting religious hate speech; a regional gender-rights report described a meeting where 20+ pastors called LGBTI behaviour 'demonic' and refused to let gay people 'flaunt' themselves.

Independent news site (July 2018): history made as the country's first Pride was declared a 'perfect' success - more than 2,000 people attended in the capital, with a police-escorted march around the main stadium; the organiser, an LGBT activist, was 'beyond thrilled'.

The same independent news site (July 2019): the country's registrar of companies refused to register the leading sexual- and gender-minorities organisation, calling its objectives a 'negative mindset' - other groups had to include 'acceptable' health/HIV aims to register; that organisation's first objective is to advance LGBT rights.

LSO.name: Lesotho
LSO.summary:
Lesotho does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The common-law offence of sodomy was struck down in 2012, and male same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since; sexual activity between women was never criminalised. No general anti-discrimination protections exist for LGBTIQ+ people. A joint stakeholder submission to the Universal Periodic Review filed in October 2024 by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho confirms that same-sex conduct is lawful while recording the absence of protections. The International Commission of Jurists, in a November 2024 UPR submission, listed LGBTIQ+ rights to equality and non-discrimination among its three principal concerns for the country.

There is no legal gender recognition. No statute provides a route to change the gender marker on official documents. A 2017 constitutional analysis by the Southern African Litigation Centre argues that section 4(1) of the constitution, which refers to 'sex' and 'other status', should be read to include gender identity, consistent with the position of the UN Human Rights Committee, but no law gives effect to that reading. A briefing published in October 2020 by the Southern African Litigation Centre, the People's Matrix Association and the Women and Law in Southern Africa Research and Education Project, researched by Prof Alex Müller with community consultations, sets out the absence of any statutory route against international best practice.

The 2017 analysis warns that a transgender person travelling on a passport whose gender marker does not match their presentation could be charged with an offence. The National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011, section 8(1), requires the Director to take reasonably practicable steps to keep personal information in the Register complete, accurate and updated; this has been read as possibly permitting a change of legal gender on identity documents, but no procedure, eligibility criteria, penalties or records of granted changes are documented.

Marriage is restricted to opposite-sex couples under the Marriage Act No. 10 of 1974 and customary law. Same-sex marriages and civil unions are not recognised. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to have that relationship recognised.

The October 2024 UPR submission documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and expression. Reports describe discrimination in employment, health care, housing and education, with many LGBTI Basotho living secret lives and concealing their sexual orientation. Family rejection, violence and harassment are described as not uncommon.

The Matrix Support Group, established in 2009 and registered in 2010, is the only known LGBTI organisation in the country. It has operated freely across all ten districts and maintains a working relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service. In December 2015 police intervened to enable a lesbian who had been forced from her home by her brothers to return, and police provided an escort for a march of approximately 200 people from Lakeside to Central Park in Maseru on 21 May. The first pride march was held on 18 May 2013 in central Maseru with a supportive police escort, and marches have been held annually since, attracting a few hundred people.

No transgender-specific provisions govern screening, sex-segregated facilities, custody, detention or gender-affirming care. The 2016 United States Department of State human rights report recorded societal discrimination and official insensitivity toward LGBTI persons, described same-sex relationships as taboo and not openly discussed, and noted that no assaults were reported while incidents often went unreported for fear of stigma. No source documents societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the only tolerance assessment available is general to the LGBTIQ+ community, describing attitudes as slowly becoming more tolerant.
LSO.outOfScopeNotes:
The National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011 provision on updating the Register has not been tested in any sourced procedure; eligibility criteria, penalties and any granted changes are not documented.

No source documents societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

The 2016 State Department statement that consensual relations between men were prohibited but unenforced conflicts with the 2012 legalisation date; the discrepancy is unresolved in the sources.

No transgender-specific provisions on screening, sex-segregated facilities, custody, detention or gender-affirming care are sourced; the absence of material is not evidence either way.

sources.summary: Joint stakeholder UPR report (Oct 2024) by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho on LGBTQ+ rights in Lesotho: documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination; same-sex conduct is not criminalised but no protections exist.

ICJ UPR submission (Nov 2024) on Lesotho: highlights LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns (alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and revocation of NGO lawyers' practising certificates).

SALC + People's Matrix Association + WLSA briefing (Oct 2020): 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho' - analysis of law and policy against international best practice; Matrix is the only known LGBTI organisation in Lesotho; researched by Prof Alex Müller with community consultations.

US State Department 2016 Human Rights Report for Lesotho: documents the LDF mutiny arrests, torture of detainees, the killing of Lt-Gen Mahao, and the LGBT section noting no criminalisation but societal stigma.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Lesotho' (2017): constitutional analysis - section 4(1) 'sex' and 'other status' should include gender identity per the UN Human Rights Committee; no law allows gender-marker changes; a trans person using a non-matching passport could be charged; the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation.

Lesotho Labour Act 2024 (full text, ILO NATLEX): the new labour law - unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, forced and child labour prohibitions - the current statutory framework for workplace rights.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Lesotho (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Labour Act 2024 bans employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and defines workplace gender-based violence and harassment as violence and harassment including sexual harassment directed at workers, trainees, probationers, applicants, managers, supervisors, customers, clients, suppliers or contractors because of sex, gender or gender identity or affecting persons of a particular sex, gender or gender identity disproportionately. The National Identity Cards Act 9 of 2011 governs national identity cards and Section 8(1) provides that the Director shall take reasonable practicable steps to ensure personal information entered into the Register is complete, accurate and updated where necessary. The article states this provision could be interpreted as allowing transgender people to change their legal gender on identity documents and provides no further procedure, eligibility criteria, penalties, or granted-change outcomes. The article states no transgender-specific provisions on screening, sex-segregated facilities, custody, detention, or gender-affirming care. Historically the article documents boukonchana or inkotshane boy-wives who typically dressed as women and notes that by 1941 public cross-dressing was commonplace, while the 1914 colonial attempt to stop such practices failed and recent discussion has faced suppression and widespread denial. In 2012 male same-sex sexual activity was legalized in Lesotho after previously being illegal as an unenforced common law offence, while female same-sex sexual activity has never been outlawed. Under the Marriage Act No. 10 of 1974 and customary law marriage is permitted only for opposite-sex couples and same-sex marriages or civil unions are not recognised. The Labour Act 2024 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and Section 127(4) of the Children’s Protection and Welfare Act 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination based on sexual orientation in selection of a diversion programme, process or option with equal access for all children. Since 2013 the Credit Reporting Regulations provide that credit information relating to sexual orientation may not be contained in credit bureau records except to the extent self-evident from marital status and family member list. Under the Child Welfare and Protection Act of 2011 only married opposite-sex couples may adopt jointly and single men and same-sex couples are not permitted to adopt. The 2016 United States Department of State report section included in the article stated that the law at that time prohibited consensual sexual relations between men but authorities did not enforce it and was silent on consensual sex between women, and noted Deputy Prime Minister Mothetjoa Metsing’s June statement after the UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on HIV/AIDS that the government would look into decriminalizing same-sex relationships to stop HIV spread. Reports of discrimination, family rejection, violence and harassment against LGBTQ people are described as not uncommon, with LGBTQ Basotho facing discrimination in employment, health care, housing, education and other areas and many living secret lives and hiding sexual orientation. Lesotho is described as having the second highest HIV prevalence in the world with reportedly 25 percent of Basotho infected, with LGBTQ activists reaching out to HIV-positive people and offering prevention strategies. The Matrix Support Group, an LGBTQ NGO established in 2009 and fully registered in 2010 to build an environment where LGBTQ people can freely express human rights and contribute to development, organized the first gay pride march on 18 May 2013 in central Maseru with supportive authorities providing an escort, and pride marches have been held annually since attracting a few hundred people. The included 2016 United States Department of State report stated LGBTI persons faced societal discrimination and official insensitivity, same-sex relationships were taboo and not openly discussed, no assaults were reported but incidents often went unreported for fear of stigma, and Matrix operated freely in all 10 districts with a good working relationship with the Lesotho Mounted Police Service including police intervention in December 2015 to enable a lesbian forced from home by brothers to return and supportive police escort for the 21 May march of approximately 200 people from Lakeside to Central Park in Maseru. The same report noted Matrix public outreach through film screenings, radio programs, public gatherings, social media and an electronic billboard in central Maseru supporting LGBTI rights. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. The only tolerance statement given is LGBTQ-general, namely that attitudes towards members of the LGBTQ community are slowly evolving and becoming more tolerant and accepting, in line with worldwide trends.

sources.title: Matrix Support Group
sources.summary: Established in 2009, Lesotho's Matrix Support Group is an LGBTI organisation including transgender and intersex people that works for an environment where LGBTI individuals can freely express their human rights and contribute socially, politically and economically regardless of gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation and sex, principally through engagement with partner organisations on gender-based violence.

CPV.name: Cabo Verde
CPV.summary:
Cabo Verde does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 71 of the 1886 Penal Code had prohibited unnatural acts; a 2004 amendment removed all provisions on consensual homosexual sex, making Cabo Verde the second African country to decriminalise after South Africa. The age of consent stood at 16 at decriminalisation, the same as for heterosexual acts, and was 14 as of 2015.

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. Civil law blocked the change to a female legal name sought by Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed transgender woman in Cabo Verde, who came out in 1997 at age 19 and in a local newspaper in 1998. The sources contain no later statute or administrative procedure permitting a legal gender change. A visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation should expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility. Transgender people in the country are often referred to locally as tchindas.

Articles 45(2) and 406(3) of the Labour Code have banned workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation since 2008, with a fine set case by case. Article 406(3) extends the same penalty to unlawful dismissal on grounds of race, ethnic group, religion, sexual orientation or any other discriminatory reason. Gender identity is not covered by the protection as the sources describe it.

Cabo Verde does not recognise same-sex unions, and a trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under local law has no recognition route. On 11 July 2017 Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva said legalisation of same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from the opposition of MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro. During 2018 Pride Week in Praia, NGOs petitioned the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law.

Andrade describes Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reports verbal violence and two physical attacks. No trans-specific violence statistics are on record.

A 2020 Afrobarometer poll found 80% of Cape Verdeans would welcome or would not be bothered by having a homosexual neighbour, one of only four African countries polled with a majority in favour; 2019 to 2021 polling put acceptance of a homosexual neighbour at 82%. Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 of May 2020 names Cabo Verde among particularly tolerant countries while noting that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains weak even among younger respondents. Every tolerance finding in the sources is framed around gays, lesbians, homosexual neighbours or LGBT people generally; no equivalent data on attitudes toward transgender people is on record.

The 2010 U.S. Department of State human rights report cited in the sources found that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity continued to be a problem, and that no LGBT organisations were active in the country at that time.

STP.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
STP.summary:
Sexual conduct between people of the same sex has been legal since the Penal Code took effect in November 2012, and the provision covers both male and female activity. The age of consent applies equally regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity, but the sources disagree on the figure: two record it as 16, while others report that Law 15/2021, the First Amendment to the Penal Code, raised it to 18 in 2021. A visitor should assume 18 until the discrepancy is resolved, because if the higher figure is correct it applies to visitors as well as residents.

São Tomé and Príncipe has no legal gender-identity recognition. No procedure exists for changing the sex or gender marker on an identity document, so a traveller whose passport, visa or other papers do not match their presentation carries that mismatch into every inspection with no domestic remedy behind it. Border, immigration and hotel staff see the discrepancy wherever documents are checked, and national law and policy say nothing about how such a case should be handled.

No form of relationship recognition exists. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised and adoption by such couples is not available. A trans visitor whose relationship is locally classed as same-sex, or read as same-sex from recorded birth sex, has no route to have a partner recognised for next-of-kin, medical decision-making, immigration or inheritance purposes.

Article 16.2 of the 2019 Labour Code prohibits workplace discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. There is no general anti-discrimination protection beyond employment, so the ban does not reach housing, healthcare, goods and services, or public accommodation. Neither the Labour Code nor any other cited provision names gender identity, which means the employment protection does not on its face cover a trans employee dismissed or harassed for being trans.

Article 130(2)(d) of the Penal Code makes crimes motivated by hatred of the victim's sexual orientation eligible for enhanced sentencing. As with the employment provision, the listed ground is sexual orientation and gender identity is not included. No hate-crime provision naming gender identity and no trans-specific protection machinery are documented.

The available sources record no trans-specific violence, enforcement action or protection outcome, and none of them makes a separate finding on societal tolerance of trans people as distinct from LGBTQ people generally. LGBTQ people are described as facing stigmatisation among the wider population. Taken together, the law here does not criminalise a trans visitor, but it offers no recognition, no document remedy and no protection ground that names them.
STP.outOfScopeNotes:
The age of consent is unresolved. Two sources state 16, equal for everyone. Two others state that Law 15/2021 raised it to 18 in 2021. No primary text of the amendment appears in the inventory.

No source records an enforcement action, court ruling, police practice or government statement bearing on trans travellers in São Tomé and Príncipe. The absence of documented trans-specific incidents is an absence of monitoring and reporting, not evidence that none occur.

All four cited sources are encyclopaedic and restate the same small set of provisions, so the account of the law is consistent but thinly sourced. Nothing in the inventory reports how the Labour Code ban or the Penal Code sentencing provision has been applied in practice.

Whether the omission of gender identity from those two provisions has ever been litigated or administratively interpreted is not sourced.

MDV.name: Maldives
MDV.summary:
The Maldives criminalises same-sex conduct and same-sex marriage under its Penal Code, whose amended provisions took effect in 2015. Section 131 defines criminal sexual contact as sexual contact without a reason permitted under Islamic law, and section 411(2) names same-sex intercourse as an offence under section 411(f). Section 410(a)(8), in force since 16 July 2015, criminalises marriage between two persons of the same sex. Penalties run to one year for unlawful marriage under section 410(a)(8), up to eight years for the conduct covered by sections 411(a)(2) and 411(d), with a supplementary 100 lashes available under Sharia, and up to four years for unlawful sexual conduct under section 412. The 2014 code extended the offence beyond Muslims to all persons.

Reporting in 2015 described death-penalty provisions as theoretically in reach for the offence. The statute's own terms are narrower: sections 92(k) and 1205 make death available only for egregious purposeful killing, capital punishment has been suspended since 1953, and plans to resume executions were later abandoned.

No transgender-specific criminal provision, document rule, screening procedure, facility rule, custody rule or care rule has been identified. Codified offences and penalties concern same-sex sexual activity and same-sex marriage. There is no legal protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity, and none on grounds of sexual orientation.

Enforcement is documented. Police on Dhaandhoo arrested two men, aged 56 and 27, on 29 August 2015 after a public complaint about homosexual activity in their private home. The prosecution reached into a residence on a local island, so exposure is not confined to public space or to Maldivian nationals. Rainbow Warriors warned after the arrests that tourists could face similar threats. Prosecutions are rare, but homosexuality remains a social taboo.

Tourist infrastructure operates at a distance from the criminal regime. Private tourist islands, resorts and hotels are usually isolated from civilian population centres and are not subject to Islamic law, as the sale of alcohol there indicates. LGBTQ tourists are generally considered welcome at these properties, and LGBTQ couples visiting resorts rarely encounter the Islamic-based law that applies elsewhere. Guides advise caution over public displays of affection outside tourist areas. Anti-LGBTQ discrimination is pervasive in the country as a whole.

The Maldives holds reservations to the ICCPR, CEDAW and the CRC. In review by the UN Human Rights Committee, the government was recommended to adopt anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and to act against the stigmatisation of homosexuals. The United Nations Population Fund reported that people perceived as homosexual or transgender were the target of hate crimes and other human rights violations and recommended law reform to protect them; the Maldives noted those recommendations without accepting them. The government rejected 60 Universal Periodic Review recommendations, including matters said to contradict the Islamic faith and the Constitution, among them recommendations on lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and non-traditional forms of the family. The Maldives signed the 2008 statement opposing decriminalisation and rejected UN resolutions on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011 and September 2014.

A 2024 expert survey by the Human Rights Measurement Initiative found LGBTQIA+ people among the groups most commonly identified by human-rights experts as at risk of empowerment-rights violations, alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers. Political participation scored relatively better at 6.4 out of 10, while other civil and political rights scored considerably lower.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Maldives (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The article states there is no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity. It states the Maldives rejected 60 Universal Periodic Review recommendations that included matters said to contradict the Islamic faith and the Constitution, such as those relating to lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and non-traditional forms of the family. It states the United Nations Population Fund reported that those perceived as homosexual or transgender in the Maldives were the target of hate crimes and other human rights violations and recommended law reform to ensure protection of LGBTQ individuals. It states these recommendations were noted by the Maldives but not accepted. The article states no transgender-specific criminal provision, document, screening, facility, custody, or care rule, with all codified offenses and penalties described concerning same-sex sexual activity and same-sex marriage. The article states section 131 of the Penal Code defines criminal sexual contact as sexual contact without reason permitted under Islamic law, with section 411(2) explicitly naming same-sex intercourse as an offense defined under section 411(f). It states section 410(a)(8), in force since 16 July 2015, criminalizes same-sex marriage where two persons of the same sex enter into marriage. It states that since the amended Penal Code came into effect in 2015 laws tightened, with maximum penalties of up to one year for unlawful marriage under s410(a)(8), up to eight years for criminal conduct under s411(a)(2) and 411(d) with allowance for supplementary 100 lashes under Sharia, and up to four years for unlawful sexual conduct under s412. It states homosexual acts cannot be punished with death under Maldivian law, noting capital punishment suspended since 1953 and that under sections 92(k) and 1205 death is only available for egregious purposeful killing while the Quran specifies no punishment for homosexuality, with plans to restart executions later abandoned. It states homosexuality is rarely prosecuted and notes 2015 arrest of two local men in their private home on an island on homosexuality charges following a public complaint. It states LGBTQ tourists are generally considered welcome at most private tourist islands, resorts and hotels, which are usually isolated from civilian population centers and therefore not subject to Islamic law as evidenced by alcohol sale, while guides advise caution on public displays of affection outside tourist areas. It states there is no legal protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and that the Maldives signed the 2008 opposing document to decriminalization, rejected 2011 and September 2014 United Nations resolutions on sexual orientation and gender identity, and noted but did not accept 2015 recommendations to decriminalize consenting adult same-sex relations. The article states homosexuality is rarely prosecuted but remains a social taboo. It states those in the LGBTQ community are subject to discrimination, hate crimes and other human rights violations and that anti-LGBTQ discrimination is pervasive though LGBTQ couples visiting resorts rarely experience the reality of Islamic-based law. It cites Rainbow Warriors stating the local Maldives LGBTQ movement is mostly limited to the virtual world operating on the internet due to the intensity of homophobia in the country. It cites the 2020 United States Country Reports finding there were no reports of officials complicit in abuses against LGBTI persons although societal stigma likely discouraged reporting, and that local citizens expressing support for LGBTI rights on social media were targeted for online harassment as apostates or irreligious. It documents the 2013 neck stabbing of gay blogger Hilath Rasheed in Male and the 2014 grant of asylum in New Zealand to gay Maldivian Abraham Naim as at risk of serious harm from state agents, with a Presidents Office spokesman commenting those seeking asylum for sexual orientation discrimination would face prosecution upon return. PRK.name: North Korea
PRK.summary:
North Korea's Criminal Code of 1950, revised in 2009, appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts. Two provisions nonetheless leave enforcement to official discretion. Article 193 bans the import, keeping and distribution of "decadent culture", including sexual recordings, and Article 262 bans collective "obscene activities". Neither is defined in terms that constrain how it is applied. The US State Department's 2022 human rights report reaches the same conclusion, that no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct, and adds that the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life.

Official hostility runs alongside official denial. In April 2014 the state news agency KCNA rejected the UN Commission of Inquiry's report on the country as a political fabrication and attacked commissioner Michael Kirby as "a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality". The regime denies that homosexuality exists in the country while punishing it.

A 2023 South Korean Ministry of Unification report, the 584-page North Korean Human Rights Report, cites defector testimony that at least one male detainee in a detention camp was secretly executed for homosexuality in 2014. A 2011 Korea Times report attributed to Free North Korea Radio claimed the state executed a lesbian couple, a North Korean woman and a Japanese woman, for being influenced by capitalism and "bringing corruption of public morals". Both accounts rest on defector or exile testimony and have not been independently confirmed.

No North Korean law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the State Department states that the concepts do not appear in the legal system. The Constitution, last revised in 2024, does not address such discrimination. There is no registration route for LGBTI organisations. Outright International records no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people, a finding that sits alongside the executions reported above and reflects the near-total absence of information rather than a protective environment.

As of 2026 no North Korean law recognises same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Article 8 of the Family Law provides that "Marriage may be done only between one man and one woman". A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition, and the State Department's 2020 report records that same-sex couples could not legally adopt children.

Changing a sex marker on a birth certificate or citizen card is technically possible under "unavoidable circumstances", by application to the People's Security Agency with a state forensic medical evaluation; in practice the procedure requires surgical intervention. No law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible.

Newer statutes, among them the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act, have tightened control in the decade since the UN Commission of Inquiry reported. A novelist who left the country in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed became the first publicly known gay defector, and an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017. CNN recorded in April 2017 a defector's account of homosexuality's place in North Korean society and of the punishment it carries.
PRK.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2011 claim that a lesbian couple was executed rests on a single report in a South Korean newspaper attributed to Free North Korea Radio, an exile broadcaster, and has not been corroborated.

The 2014 detention-camp execution rests on defector testimony cited in a South Korean government report. No independent confirmation exists.

The State Department's 2020 report states that no reliable information on LGBT persons in North Korea is available. The country permits no independent human rights monitoring, so the scope and consistency of enforcement against trans and LGB people cannot be verified from outside.

Because Articles 193 and 262 are undefined, how they are applied in practice, and whether they are applied to trans visitors at all, is not documented.

PSE.name: Palestinian Territories
PSE.summary:
Two separate criminal-law regimes apply across the Palestinian Territories, and the difference between them determines what a trans visitor faces. In the West Bank, criminal law derives from the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision of its own code dropped offences covering consensual private sexual conduct, and the 1960 code carried that position forward, so no provision there criminalises consensual same-sex acts. In Gaza, Criminal Code Ordinance No. 74 of 1936 remains the governing text. Section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex "carnal knowledge" by up to ten years' imprisonment, and section 152(1)(c) sets up to fourteen years for sodomy with a child under sixteen. Neither code names trans identity. Gaza's public-morality provisions are the route by which trans people are brought within the criminal law, and the source material describes the resulting position as de facto oppression rather than formal prohibition.

The applicability of the 1936 ordinance is contested. Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force in Gaza; Amnesty International does not report same-sex acts as illegal there; the editor-in-chief Anis F. Kassim has argued the text could be read as permitting homosexuality. Palestinian law overall is a patchwork of Ottoman, British, Jordanian, Egyptian and Israeli legacies, and the Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality. Israel stopped applying the Mandate criminal code in 1977.

Enforcement against LGBT Palestinians is documented. Gay Palestinians are often arrested and tortured, and the Palestinian Authority's usual stated justification for persecution is to label the person a collaborator. Shaul Ganon of the Israeli rights group Aguda reported knowledge of two cases within a three-year window in which people were tried explicitly for being homosexual, and said that since the intifada, as police increasingly enforced Islamic law, being openly gay under the Palestinian Authority was not possible. Palestinian police banned LGBTQ activity, and after action against the organisation al-Qaws the group received a wave of hate messages that activists described as a serious threat.

No legal gender recognition provisions are set out for the Palestinian Territories, and no broad legal protections from discrimination exist for LGBTIQ+ people. The Palestinian Authority is not a signatory to key human rights treaties.

Social conditions are hostile. Palestine ranks 130 on the Global Acceptance Index with very little movement between 2010 and 2020. Interviews by Human Rights Watch and the Women's Centre for Legal Aid with twelve Palestinian women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer recorded widespread discrimination and abuse in public and in family settings. Social and family persecution makes the practical position harsher than the formal law in the West Bank.

Health care for trans and queer people is inadequate. HIV-positive people often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and stigma is high, and comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking. Ninety-eight HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered in Palestine between 1988 and 2017, seventy-nine of them AIDS and nineteen HIV-positive, with the true figure likely far higher because taboos obstruct data collection. In Gaza, the collapse of the health system and blockades since October 2023 have made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult.

Civil society groups that protect women and children in Gaza are described as vulnerable to attack.

sources.summary:
Palestinian law is a patchwork of Ottoman, British, Jordanian, Egyptian and Israeli legacies, and the Palestinian Authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality. Applicability of the British Mandate Criminal Code (1936), which criminalised sodomy with up to 14 years' imprisonment and 'act against the law of nature' with up to 10 years, is disputed: the Human Dignity Trust and Human Rights Watch hold it in force in Gaza, Amnesty does not report same-sex acts as illegal, and editor-in-chief Anis F. Kassim argues it could be read as permitting homosexuality. The 2003 draft Palestinian penal code criminalised adult consensual same-sex conduct, carrying up to five years for male-male sodomy, and it is unknown whether it was implemented. Equaldex reports no broad legal protections from discrimination for LGBTIQ+ people in Palestine, no legal gender recognition provisions are set out, Palestinian queer organisations operate from within Israel, and statelessness is cited as a structural condition of LGBTQ Palestinians.

HIV prevention and care are described as inadequate: HIV-positive queer individuals often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and social stigma is high, and comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking. Only 98 HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered in Palestine between 1988 and 2017 (79 AIDS, 19 HIV-positive), with the true number likely far higher because taboos hinder data collection. In Gaza since October 2023, collapse of the healthcare system plus Israeli blockades has made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult. In Israel, LGBTQ Palestinian asylum seekers are routinely excluded from basic healthcare programs and shelter access available to other asylum seekers, and some have faced house arrest or deportation; only in June 2022 did Israel begin issuing work permits to gay Palestinian refugees granted asylum and those fleeing domestic violence.

Section 152(1)(c) of the British Mandate Criminal Code is the only youth-linked legal provision cited, under which sodomy with a child under sixteen carries up to 14 years' imprisonment, alongside Section 152(2)(b) criminalizing 'carnal knowledge' against the law of nature with up to 10 years. Islamist actors contest LGBTQ content in education and youth spaces: the Palestinian Mujahideen Movement and the Rightly-Guided Caliphs Assembly criticized UNRWA for promoting what they see as un-Islamic values including LGBTQ issues, and the Islamic Movement in Israel opposed Israel's conversion therapy ban, with activist Maisan Hamdan noting that the movement's sole stated aim is Palestine's liberation without LGBTQ inclusion. Public acceptance is ranked Palestine 130 on the Global Acceptance Index with very little change 2010–2020, and civil society groups protecting women and children are 'vulnerable to attack' in Gaza.
