PSE.blindSummary:
Two separate criminal-law regimes apply across the state/province, and the difference between them determines what a trans visitor faces. In one state/province, criminal law derives from the penal code of a neighbouring jurisdiction, No. 16 of 1960. That neighbouring jurisdiction's 1951 revision of its own code dropped offences covering consensual private sexual conduct, and the 1960 code carried that position forward, so no provision there criminalises consensual same-sex acts. In the other state/province, a 1936 criminal code ordinance remains the governing text. Section 152(2) punishes consensual same-sex "carnal knowledge" by up to ten years' imprisonment, and section 152(1)(c) sets up to fourteen years for sodomy with a child under sixteen. Neither code names trans identity. Public-morality provisions in that state/province are the route by which trans people are brought within the criminal law, and the source material describes the resulting position as de facto oppression rather than formal prohibition.

The applicability of the 1936 ordinance is contested. A legal advocacy organisation and an international human rights organisation hold it in force in that state/province; another human rights organisation does not report same-sex acts as illegal there; a legal scholar has argued the text could be read as permitting homosexuality. The law overall is a patchwork of historic-era and neighbouring legal legacies, and the governing authority has legislated neither for nor against homosexuality. A neighbouring jurisdiction stopped applying the historic-era mandate criminal code in 1977.

Enforcement against LGBT people is documented. They are often arrested and tortured, and the governing authority's usual stated justification for persecution is to label the person a collaborator. A representative of a rights group based in a neighbouring jurisdiction reported knowledge of two cases within a three-year window in which people were tried explicitly for being homosexual, and said that since a period of uprising, as police increasingly enforced religious law, being openly gay under the governing authority was not possible. Police banned LGBTQ activity, and after action against a local LGBTQ organisation the group received a wave of hate messages that activists described as a serious threat.

No legal gender recognition provisions are set out, and no broad legal protections from discrimination exist for LGBTIQ+ people. The governing authority is not a signatory to key human rights treaties.

Social conditions are hostile. The state/province ranks 130 on an international acceptance index with very little movement between 2010 and 2020. Interviews by an international human rights organisation and a women's legal aid organisation with twelve women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer recorded widespread discrimination and abuse in public and in family settings. Social and family persecution makes the practical position harsher than the formal law in one state/province.

Health care for trans and queer people is inadequate. HIV-positive people often do not receive continuous antiretroviral therapy because medication is limited and stigma is high, and comprehensive epidemiological surveillance is lacking. Ninety-eight HIV/AIDS cases were officially registered between 1988 and 2017, seventy-nine of them AIDS and nineteen HIV-positive, with the true figure likely far higher because taboos obstruct data collection. In one state/province, the collapse of the health system and blockades since October 2023 have made access to life-saving HIV medication especially difficult.

Civil society groups that protect women and children in one state/province are described as vulnerable to attack.

SLE.name: Sierra Leone
SLE.summary:
Sexual activity between men is a criminal offence in Sierra Leone under the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act, which carries a penalty of up to life imprisonment; the Human Dignity Trust country profile records the statute as the basis of the criminalisation regime. Consensual sexual relations between women are not explicitly outlawed, according to Amnesty International's 2025 country report, though the absence of an explicit prohibition does not remove risk for a trans visitor.

Enforcement does not run through prosecution. The US Department of State's 2012 Human Rights Report records that the 1861 law was not enforced, while police continued to harass, detain, beat and denounce people perceived to be members of the LGBT community. Men dressed as women were singled out for detention, harassment and public humiliation and were not formally charged with any crime or misdemeanour. Presentation, rather than conduct, is what draws police attention.

The GlobalGayz news archive records the November 2004 rape and murder of lesbian activist FannyAnn Eddy, the arrest of her killer in January 2005, police refusal to classify the killing as a hate crime, and the alleged murderer's reported escape from custody in July 2005. The case documents both lethal violence against LGBT people and the absence of a hate-crime response.

No non-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is documented in the sources reviewed, and the State Department's 2012 report records official and societal discrimination against LGBT individuals. A visitor has no statutory route of recourse against discriminatory treatment.
SLE.outOfScopeNotes:
No prosecution under the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act is documented in the sources reviewed, and the 2025 Amnesty International report does not record any. Whether the statute has been amended or replaced since the 2012 State Department report is not established by the material available.

The reported escape of FannyAnn Eddy's alleged killer from custody in July 2005 is described in the archive as alleged, and the subsequent outcome of the case is not sourced.

XKX.name: Kosovo
XKX.summary:
The Republic of Kosovo's constitution was adopted on 9 April 2008 and entered into force on 15 June 2008. It guarantees equality before the law, treats human dignity as inviolable, and prohibits discrimination on grounds including gender and sexual orientation. The Anti-Discrimination Law was amended on 26 May 2015 and took effect in July 2015, adding gender identity to the protected grounds. It covers employment, membership of organisations, education, provision of goods and services, social security, and access to housing, and defines discrimination to include direct and indirect discrimination, harassment, victimisation and segregation. Outright International's March 2026 overview records that implementation of both the constitutional prohibition and the 2015 statute remains inconsistent in practice, so the protections a visitor can cite are broader than what is reliably delivered.

The Criminal Code in force from April 2019 provides additional penalties for hate crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity, alongside the equivalent provision covering sexual orientation.

Sexual conduct between people of the same sex has been lawful in Kosovo since independence in 2008. The 2004 UNMIK regulation set the age of consent at 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation and made all sexual offences gender-neutral.

Legal gender recognition has no administrative procedure in Kosovo and runs through the courts. Kosovo's Civil Registration Agency rejected Blert Morina's application for a name and gender-marker change on his identity documents, and constitutional review of the matter was requested in July 2018. In December 2019 the Basic Court of Pristina ruled in his favour, holding that his name and sex marker could be changed without evidence of surgical intervention or any other medical change. The Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency have stated that the judgment will not be treated as precedent and that other transgender people will have to go through a similar court procedure. No source in the inventory identifies a standing administrative route available to applicants generally, and the only documented successful route is individual litigation.

Partnership recognition has not been extended. Article 14 of the Law on Family defines marriage as a legally registered community of two persons of different sexes. The Assembly rejected a civil-partnership provision in the new Civil Code on 16 March 2022, with only 28 of 120 MPs voting in favour. Reuters reported in May 2024 that the debate over same-sex unions was proceeding amid fierce opposition in the Muslim-majority country. Prime Minister Albin Kurti announced an intent to legalise same-sex unions on 25 April 2024. As of February 2026 Parliament had still failed to adopt the new Civil Code amid opposition that included the ruling party. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no legal recognition of that partnership, in the form of either marriage or civil union.

Enforcement and reporting of anti-LGBTQ violence are weak. LGBTQ people in Kosovo tend to avoid reporting discrimination or abuse to the police. Ten bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people were reported to the authorities in 2019, with a further 13 reported only to LGBTQ organisations. In February 2019 the authorities initiated a case against a Ministry of Justice official who had called for LGBTQ people to be beheaded, and police took him into custody.

Public organising in the capital is established and visible. The first pride parade in Pristina was held in May 2016, and Pride Week has been held annually since 2017; the third annual parade was accompanied by a week of exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions organised by the Center for Equality and Liberty, under a slogan framed as both an appeal for tolerance and an invitation to join the parade. The October 2019 march from Skanderbeg Square down Mother Teresa Boulevard to Zahir Pajaziti Square was held without incident but under multiple threats; anonymous threats warning people not to attend were especially pronounced in 2017. Government engagement has included a late-2013 parliamentary bill creating a coordinating group for the LGBTQ community and a 17 May 2014 march against homophobia by politicians and diplomats, welcomed by the European Union office and the government, with a large LGBTQ flag covering the front of the government building that night.

Survey evidence documents widespread societal hostility, but not in terms specific to transgender people. A 2015 National Democratic Institute survey found that 81 per cent of LGBTQ Kosovars said they had been subjected to psychological abuse and that 29 per cent reported being victims of physical violence; the same body found that over 97 per cent of respondents would not accept a child who came out as lesbian or gay. These figures cover LGBTQ respondents generally, are not disaggregated for transgender people, date from 2015, and are given without a general-population comparison.
XKX.outOfScopeNotes:
The availability of legal gender recognition as a general rule is unresolved across the sources. One overview states that transgender people in Kosovo are not allowed to legally change their gender even if they have undergone sex reassignment surgery. That sits against the December 2019 Basic Court of Pristina judgment, which recognised a change of name and sex marker without surgical or medical evidence for the individual applicant, and against the model of case-by-case litigation described by the Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency. No source in this inventory records a later case testing whether the courts will follow the 2019 judgment, and none identifies an administrative procedure.

Data on violence and abuse are not disaggregated for transgender people. The 2015 National Democratic Institute figures cover LGBTQ respondents as a whole and are a decade old; the source provides no general-population rate against which to read them.

The hate-crime figures for 2019 are raw counts of reports, not incidence: 10 reports to authorities and 13 to LGBTQ organisations. Advocacy sources describe reluctance among LGBTQ people to report to police, so the recorded numbers understate what occurs and cannot be used to compare Kosovo's risk level with any other jurisdiction.

Whether the Civil Code will be adopted, and whether it will retain gender-neutral marriage language or a civil-union provision, was unresolved as of February 2026.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Kosovo (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to legally change their gender in Kosovo even if they have undergone sex reassignment surgery. Kosovo's Anti-Discrimination Law was amended on 26 May 2015 to add gender identity and took effect in July 2015, banning discrimination including in employment, membership of organizations, education, provision of goods and services, social security and access to housing and defining discrimination to include direct and indirect discrimination as well as harassment, victimization and segregation. The new Criminal Code that went into force in April 2019 provides additional penalties for commission of a hate crime motivated by the victim's gender identity. In 2017 Kosovar citizen Blert Morina submitted a court case seeking to change his name and gender on official identification documents after rejection by Kosovo's Civil Registration Agency, with constitutional review requested in July 2018. In December 2019 the Basic Court of Pristina ruled in Morina's favour affirming his right to change both name and sex marker on identification documents, with his lawyer stating that "for the first time the court has decided to recognize the right to gender identity without offering evidence for surgical intervention or any medical change". The Ministry of Justice and the Civil Registration Agency have stated that the judgment will not be considered precedent and other transgender people will have to go through a similar court procedure. Same-sex sexual intercourse has remained legal in independent Kosovo since 2008, following legalization under Ottoman rule in 1858, legalization of male same-sex intercourse in 1994 in the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija when part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the 2004 UNMIK setting of the age of consent at 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation with all sexual offenses made gender-neutral. Article 24 of the 2008 Constitution bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. The 2004 Anti-Discrimination Law bans discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, membership of organizations, education, provision of goods and services, social security and access to housing and explicitly includes direct and indirect discrimination as well as harassment, victimization and segregation. The new Criminal Code in force from April 2019 provides additional penalties for hate crimes motivated by the victim's sexual orientation. Article 14 of the Law on Family defines marriage as a legally registered community of two persons of different sexes, although in 2014 the President of the Constitutional Court said Kosovo de jure allows same-sex marriage and Article 144(3) requires Constitutional Court approval of amendments to ensure they do not infringe previously guaranteed civil rights, while a 7 July 2020 proposal for same-sex civil partnerships in the new Civil Code was rejected by the Assembly on 16 March 2022 with only 28 of 120 MPs voting in favour and on 25 April 2024 Prime Minister Albin Kurti announced intent to legalize same-sex unions. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people are allowed to serve openly in the military though they may face discrimination by peers, while a 2018 Blood Donation Week guideline bars those who have "intimate relationships with the same sex" from donating blood. LGBTQ people tend to avoid reporting discrimination or abuse to police, with 10 bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people reported to authorities in 2019 and a further 13 reported only to LGBTQ organizations. In February 2019 authorities initiated a case against a Ministry of Justice official who called for LGBTQ people to be beheaded and police took him into custody. The article states discrimination and stigmatization against the LGBTQ+ community remains very rampant amongst the general population even though it is outlawed, which refers to LGBTQ+ generally and not to transgender people specifically. The Center for Social Emancipation describes gay life in Kosovo as being "underground" and mostly secretive with one gay bar in Pristina, which refers to gay life specifically. A 2015 National Democratic Institute survey found 81% of LGBTQ+ Kosovars said they had been subject to psychological abuse and 29% reported being victim of physical violence, while a National Democratic Institute study found over 97% not willing to accept their child if they came out as lesbian or gay. Pride events celebrating the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia have been organized since 2007, with the first pride parade in Pristina in May 2016 and annual Pride Week since 2017, including the October 2019 march from Skanderbeg Square down Mother Teresa Boulevard to Zahir Pajaziti Square with the slogan "Whoever your heart beats for" held without incidence but under multiple threats especially in 2017 with anonymous threats warning people not to attend. Government support included a late 2013 Parliament bill to create a coordinating group for the LGBTQ community and a 17 May 2014 march against homophobia by politicians and diplomats welcomed by the European Union office and the government with a large LGBTQ flag covering the front of the government building that night. The article provides no documented direct quoted statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically distinct from the LGBTQ+, gay, and lesbian or gay references above.

sources.title: Basic Court of Pristina - Blert Morina ruling, December 2019
sources.summary: In December 2019 the Basic Court of Pristina granted Blert Morina legal change of name and sex marker, establishing that gender identity in Kosovo can be legally recognized without proof of surgical intervention or other medical change.

sources.title: Official websites of Center for Equality and Liberty (CEL) and Center for Social Group Development (CSGD)
sources.summary: In Kosovo CSGD provides LGBTQI+ people free confidential legal aid and psychological support in person and online via app.csgd-ks.org, tailored reproductive and sexual health services including support navigating hormonal procedures for transgender people in cooperation with the Ministry and free HIV testing, with free PrEP HIV-prevention treatment available at the QKUK Infectious Disease Clinic since June 12, 2024 following CSGD advocacy.

XKX.tangentialFactors:
Regional litigation has shaped the domestic argument over gender-marker change. In January 2019 the European Court of Human Rights ruled in X v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia that a surgical requirement for changing a gender marker violates the right to private life. Applicants in Kosovo, including Blert Morina while his own constitutional case was pending, followed that ruling closely.

The constitutional status of relationship recognition is contested even without legislation. In 2014 the President of the Constitutional Court said Kosovo de jure allows same-sex marriage, and Article 144(3) of the constitution requires Constitutional Court approval of amendments in order to ensure they do not infringe previously guaranteed civil rights. Analysis of the Civil Code's gender-neutral marriage language has argued that it would open the way for gay marriage. During Pride week the Prime Minister said he would do his utmost to get the Civil Code adopted, and a Justice Ministry working group was drafting a bill.

Two adjacent rules sit outside the trans-specific framework but bear on services. A 2018 Blood Donation Week guideline bars people who have intimate relationships with the same sex from donating blood. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people are permitted to serve openly in the military, though they may face discrimination from peers.

Advocacy reporting describes an environment of intolerance around the Civil Code debates. CSGD's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with hate speech by politicians common during those debates, and an artist received death threats over a painting.
XKX.localsOnly:
The Center for Social Emancipation (CSGD) provides LGBTQI+ people in Kosovo with free confidential legal aid and psychological support, in person and online through its app, along with tailored reproductive and sexual health services that include support navigating hormonal procedures for transgender people in cooperation with the ministry, and free HIV testing. Free PrEP HIV-prevention treatment has been available at the QKUK Infectious Disease Clinic since 12 June 2024, following CSGD's advocacy.

Discrimination and stigmatisation against the LGBTQ+ community remain widespread among the general population even though they are outlawed. The Center for Social Emancipation describes gay life in Kosovo as underground and mostly secretive, with one gay bar in the capital.

Relationship-recognition legislation is still in drafting. A Justice Ministry working group was preparing a bill, and the Prime Minister committed during Pride week to pressing for adoption of the Civil Code; Parliament had not adopted it as of February 2026.
XKX.comparisons: Pairwise: above Montenegro (0.66 — Kosovo's anti-discrimination coverage is broader, MNE's social climate calmer) and below Romania (0.67, tie region).
XKX.blindSummary:
The country's constitution was adopted on 9 April 2008 and entered into force on 15 June 2008. It guarantees equality before the law, treats human dignity as inviolable, and prohibits discrimination on grounds including gender and sexual orientation. The national anti-discrimination law was amended on 26 May 2015 and took effect in July 2015, adding gender identity to the protected grounds. It covers employment, membership of organisations, education, provision of goods and services, social security, and access to housing, and defines discrimination to include direct and indirect discrimination, harassment, victimisation and segregation. A March 2026 overview by an international advocacy organisation records that implementation of both the constitutional prohibition and the 2015 statute remains inconsistent in practice, so the protections a visitor can cite are broader than what is reliably delivered.

A criminal code in force from April 2019 provides additional penalties for hate crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity, alongside the equivalent provision covering sexual orientation.

Sexual conduct between people of the same sex has been lawful in the country since 2008. A 2004 regulation issued by the international administration then in place set the age of consent at 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation and made all sexual offences gender-neutral.

Legal gender recognition has no administrative procedure in the country and runs through the courts. The national civil registration authority rejected an applicant's request for a name and gender-marker change on his identity documents, and constitutional review of the matter was requested in July 2018. In December 2019 a court in the capital ruled in his favour, holding that his name and sex marker could be changed without evidence of surgical intervention or any other medical change. The national justice ministry and the civil registration authority have stated that the judgment will not be treated as precedent and that other transgender people will have to go through a similar court procedure. No source in the inventory identifies a standing administrative route available to applicants generally, and the only documented successful route is individual litigation.

Partnership recognition has not been extended. The family law defines marriage as a legally registered community of two persons of different sexes. The assembly rejected a civil-partnership provision in the new civil code on 16 March 2022, with only 28 of 120 members of parliament voting in favour. A news agency reported in May 2024 that the debate over same-sex unions was proceeding amid fierce opposition in the Muslim-majority country. The prime minister announced an intent to legalise same-sex unions on 25 April 2024. As of February 2026 parliament had still failed to adopt the new civil code amid opposition that included the governing party. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no legal recognition of that partnership, in the form of either marriage or civil union.

Enforcement and reporting of anti-LGBTQ violence are weak. LGBTQ people in the country tend to avoid reporting discrimination or abuse to the police. Ten bias-motivated crimes against LGBTQ people were reported to the authorities in 2019, with a further 13 reported only to LGBTQ organisations. In February 2019 the authorities initiated a case against a national justice ministry official who had called for LGBTQ people to be beheaded, and police took him into custody.

Public organising in the capital is established and visible. The first pride parade in the capital was held in May 2016, and Pride Week has been held annually since 2017; the third annual parade was accompanied by a week of exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions organised by an equality organisation, under a slogan framed as both an appeal for tolerance and an invitation to join the parade. The October 2019 march through the capital was held without incident but under multiple threats; anonymous threats warning people not to attend were especially pronounced in 2017. Government engagement has included a late-2013 parliamentary bill creating a coordinating group for the LGBTQ community and a 17 May 2014 march against homophobia by politicians and diplomats, welcomed by a regional body's office and the government, with a large LGBTQ flag covering the front of the government building that night.

Survey evidence documents widespread societal hostility, but not in terms specific to transgender people. A 2015 survey found that 81 per cent of LGBTQ respondents said they had been subjected to psychological abuse and that 29 per cent reported being victims of physical violence; the same body found that over 97 per cent of respondents would not accept a child who came out as lesbian or gay. These figures cover LGBTQ respondents generally, are not disaggregated for transgender people, date from 2015, and are given without a general-population comparison.
XKX.blindOutOfScope:
The availability of legal gender recognition as a general rule is unresolved across the sources. One overview states that transgender people in the country are not allowed to legally change their gender even if they have undergone sex reassignment surgery. That sits against the December 2019 ruling by a court in the capital, which recognised a change of name and sex marker without surgical or medical evidence for the individual applicant, and against the model of case-by-case litigation described by the national justice ministry and the civil registration authority. No source in this inventory records a later case testing whether the courts will follow the 2019 ruling, and none identifies an administrative procedure.

Data on violence and abuse are not disaggregated for transgender people. The 2015 survey figures cover LGBTQ respondents as a whole and are a decade old; the source provides no general-population rate against which to read them.

The hate-crime figures for 2019 are raw counts of reports, not incidence: 10 reports to authorities and 13 to LGBTQ organisations. Advocacy sources describe reluctance among LGBTQ people to report to police, so the recorded numbers understate what occurs and cannot be used to compare the country's risk level with any other jurisdiction.

Whether the civil code will be adopted, and whether it will retain gender-neutral marriage language or a civil-union provision, was unresolved as of February 2026.

GIB.name: Gibraltar
GIB.summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply of their own force: the Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment has been in place since the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 took effect on 1 March 2007. The Act prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of gender reassignment, defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Sexual orientation is a protected ground under the same Act.

Hate-crime coverage extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act 2011 in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with approval on 19 September, royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would urgently consider legislation to tackle what the Chief Minister, Fabian Picardo, called "disgusting lurking homophobia" on social media during Pride month, following an incident of anti-gay abuse. The proposal at that stage concerned sexual orientation; the trans-inclusive amendment came in July 2026.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy. The sourced excerpt states the offence generally without specifying whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both.

Partner recognition is established locally. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014, and same-sex marriage since 15 December 2016, after the Civil Marriage Amendment Act passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December, with the first marriage the following day. A deputy registrar may opt out, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar. Because no gender-recognition route exists, a trans visitor's legal sex for marriage purposes remains that recorded at birth; a relationship locally read as same-sex can be registered.

Adoption is open to same-sex couples. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.
GIB.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 has been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council is not established in the sourced material.

The July 2026 conversion therapy offence is stated generally; whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both is not specified in the sourced material.

No enforcement data on the 2013 or 2026 hate-crime provisions appears in the inventory, so the practical operation of the transgender-identity amendment is not sourced.

The July 2021 statement that the Ministry for Justice and Equality would urgently consider further legislation is not sourced to an enacted outcome other than the July 2026 amendments.

sources.summary: The UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories sets accountability and good-governance expectations that apply to Gibraltar as an overseas territory; it also records corruption concerns raised in Turks and Caicos.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity'. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

BMU.name: Bermuda
BMU.summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory where local legislation governs. United Kingdom law, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex services code, does not extend automatically and could be applied only by Order in Council.

Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not covered, leaving trans people without statutory protection against discrimination. The sources identify no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery.

Expression of gender identity is described as often difficult. In 2006 the Government attempted to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities.

Consensual sex between adult men is legal. The House of Assembly voted 22–16 on 14 May 1994 to decriminalise it, striking two sections of the Criminal Code; the debate divided the island, with religious leaders split and the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change. Prior liability carried up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. Lesbian activity has never been illegal, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

The age of consent is unequal: 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019, against 16 for other sexual activity. A prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct had been found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Same-sex marriage is not legally available as of 2022. The Supreme Court legalised it in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche case under the Marriage Act 1944 and the Human Rights Act. The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act on 7 February 2018, effective 1 June 2018, replacing marriage with domestic partnerships open to same-sex and opposite-sex couples and making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, but the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Recognition of a partner therefore rests on the partnership register.
BMU.outOfScopeNotes:
No transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, healthcare, enforcement, penalties or protection machinery were identified in the sources. How a trans visitor would be handled at entry, in custody or in medical settings is not sourced.

Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or its 2025 single-sex services code will be extended to Bermuda by Order in Council is unresolved.

The sources do not record whether the Human Rights Act's omission of gender identity has been tested in any Bermuda court.

sources.summary: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre', an instance of organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections. The debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

Homosexuality is legal in Bermuda; lesbian activity has never been illegal, while consensual private sexual conduct was legalised by the Stubbs Bill in 1994 after prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. As of 2022 the age of consent remains unequal at 18 years for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 versus 16 for other sexual activity, after a prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the Criminal Code provision on gross indecency between men was repealed in 2019. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation since 2013, following failed and dropped proposals in 2004-2006 and 2009. Same-sex marriage is not legally available since 2022, having been legalised by the Supreme Court in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche marriage-license case under the Marriage Act 1944 and Human Rights Act, replaced by domestic partnerships by law given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, restored by the Supreme Court on 6 June 2018 and Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, then banned again by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on 14 March 2022 with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Same-sex couples are allowed to adopt equally under the Adoption of Children Act following the February 2015 Supreme Court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and binational same-sex partners were granted equal employment and benefits by the Supreme Court in November 2015. The Bermuda Regiment, formed by random lottery-style conscription, does not discriminate on grounds of sexual orientation and officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers, though such activities have been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent one conscript described the Regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists". Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise for women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men. In November 2020 reporting, the government spent approximately £150,000 to legally appeal an unconstitutional case of a man charged and threatened with jail under the archaic "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn into Bermuda.

CYM.name: Cayman Islands
CYM.summary:
The Cayman Islands' constitutional discrimination grounds were drafted in 2009 without sexual-orientation protection. The omission drew criticism from the United Kingdom parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, which called it deplorable and warned that Cayman courts could afford less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires; the Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the list of grounds was open-ended. No enumerated constitutional ground anchors a discrimination claim, and no trans-specific ground is listed.

No domestic route to marriage exists. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the statutory prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019 and restored the ban. Recognition survives at the level of immigration administration: in December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex, an overseas marriage therefore carries immigration effects even though the territory offers no domestic route to marry.

Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, among them the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation.

No trans-specific legal provision is documented for the Cayman Islands. Nothing in the available sources addresses gender recognition, identity documents, single-sex facilities, healthcare access or hate-crime protection, and no trans-specific incident or enforcement action is recorded.
CYM.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific legal provision for the Cayman Islands appears in the available sources. The final text of the 2009 constitution, and whether the open-ended list of discrimination grounds has since been read to cover gender identity, is unresolved.

VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws across the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. The change came by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly; local legislator Orlando Smith said at the time that "there is nothing we can do."

The British Virgin Islands stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume that United Kingdom discrimination and service-access protections, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code, are available in the territory by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Whether a marriage between two people of the same sex validly contracted elsewhere is recognised under British Virgin Islands law remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid locally was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not a ruling on recognition. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be classed locally as same-sex cannot rely on recognition being settled.

No criminalisation of trans people, and no trans-specific protection machinery, appears in the sources for the territory. The visitor-relevant legal questions are the framework relationship with the United Kingdom and the unsettled recognition of marriages contracted elsewhere.

The outcome of the Forbes and Lettsome case is not sourced; whether recognition was granted or refused remains unresolved.

The GlobalGayz assessment is dated to 2012 and 2017 and is not trans-specific.

AIA.name: Anguilla
AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory and the law that governs a visitor is local law; United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only where an Order in Council extends it, so no United Kingdom-level anti-discrimination floor applies of its own force.

Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by order of the Privy Council on 5 January 2001, in a decision that also covered the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Anguillian law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's anti-discrimination clause reaches race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories and a trans visitor has no statutory non-discrimination footing in local law.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore carries legal exposure that a different-sex couple does not face.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is among the British overseas territories that have not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island states that same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic, non-legal ceremony. Non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place there.

Public LGBT life is highly constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions that the position of local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the British order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to decriminalisation imposed from outside rather than to local initiative.
AIA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory sets out Anguilla's rules on gender markers on identity documents, on entry or immigration screening, or on access to sex-segregated facilities. Those questions are unresolved here.

No trans-specific violence data and no hate-crime enforcement data for Anguilla were identified, and the inventory contains no general homicide denominator for the island, so no risk magnitude for anti-trans violence can be stated.

Sources give different years for decriminalisation: the 2023 travel account states 2000, while the Privy Council order is dated 5 January 2001 and the encyclopaedic coverage gives 2001. The 2001 date is the documented one.

Whether any Order in Council has extended United Kingdom anti-discrimination legislation to Anguilla is not established in the inventory. The sources identify the mechanism but name no such order.

The favourable accounts of how visiting same-sex couples were treated describe a different population from the residents covered by the material on secrecy and lack of protection, and the sources themselves caution that local conditions may differ from the visitor experience. No source reports how a visibly trans visitor, as distinct from a same-sex couple, was received.

MSR.name: Montserrat
MSR.summary:
Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory and stands under the United Kingdom's framework, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful since 2001, when the prohibitions were swept away retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. Lesbian conduct was never an offence. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for all persons.

The age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity and 16 for heterosexual activity. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex therefore falls under the higher threshold of 18.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. A trans visitor's partner would not be recognised as a spouse or civil partner.

Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, defining 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. Neither provision names gender identity among the enumerated grounds, which end with an open-ended 'other status'.

There are no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues on the island. Several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.
MSR.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether gender identity falls within the open-ended 'other status' ground in Article 16 of the Constitution or Article 79 of the Labour Code is unresolved; no source in the inventory addresses gender-identity-specific protections or gender marker change procedures.

No trans-specific violence data for Montserrat is sourced, and no information on police or prison treatment of trans people is available.

TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
TCA.summary:
The Turks and Caicos Islands is a British Overseas Territory standing under the United Kingdom framework, and its own ordinances and courts govern immigration status, family recognition and non-discrimination. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal there since 2001, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation.

In a Court of Appeal ruling, the Director of Immigration was ordered to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the spouse of Richard Sankar. The court read "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, and held that refusing the permit on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the constitution's equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees. The statutory definition of marriage was left untouched, so the decision creates no local right to marry. A trans visitor whose relationship local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status can rely on a marriage lawfully entered elsewhere to support residence in the territory, in the same way as the spouses of residents.

Document handling for trans people runs through United Kingdom channels. The HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the Turks and Caicos Islands, official operational guidance published in 2025, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the territory and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor presenting a United Kingdom passport with a changed gender marker can expect it to be treated as valid in the territory. No local statute or instrument giving effect to that recognition is identified in the available sources.

Visibility is low. A resident account published in 2009 described virtually no information about gay life in the territory and no visible social scene, with privacy as the everyday norm; the account attributed this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands, leaving full-citizen Belongers a demographic minority. That account is dated and impressionistic, and does not establish anything about current violence risk.
TCA.outOfScopeNotes:
No current data on the territory's social climate, and no reported trans-specific violence or hate-crime statistics for the Turks and Caicos Islands, were located in the sources; the only account of the social environment dates from 2009.

Whether local law contains any hate-crime or bias-motivated violence provision covering transgender victims is not established by the sources.

The legal instrument, if one exists, that gives local effect to the recognition of transgender citizens recorded by HM Passport Office is not documented; that recognition is visible only through the passport office's operational guidance.

No rule on access to single-sex facilities such as toilets or changing rooms for transgender people in the territory was identified in the sources.

FLK.name: Falkland Islands
FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own Legislative Assembly, which legislates locally; the United Kingdom is responsible for the territory's defence. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Islands, so legal protection and gender recognition depend on the territory's own ordinances.

Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex as well as same-sex couples, and a trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under local birth-sex status can marry or register a civil partnership on the same terms. A public consultation ahead of the bill recorded 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014 under the CPE Ordinance 2014. There is no self-identification route and no recognition of non-binary status. Holders of a UK Gender Recognition Certificate are recognised in their acquired gender under that ordinance.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The provision covers sexual orientation only; no gender-identity ground is identified in it.

Two ordinances frame the criminal-justice treatment of bias. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 provides for hate-stirring on grounds of sexual orientation, and the CPE Ordinance 2014 makes sexual orientation an aggravating factor in sentencing. On the sources available, neither ground extends to gender identity.
FLK.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not set out the requirements for legal gender change beyond the absence of self-identification and of non-binary recognition; the medical or evidentiary threshold is not described.

No gender-identity ground is identified in the Constitution Order 2008, the Crimes Ordinance 2014 or the CPE Ordinance 2014. Whether any other instrument covers gender identity is not sourced.

The content of the Prisons Ordinance 2017 is not detailed in the sources.

No data on trans-specific violence, hate-crime prosecutions or police practice in the territory appears in the sources.

SHN.name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
SHN.summary:
Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is a British Overseas Territory. United Kingdom legislation reaches it only where extended by order, so the territory's own ordinances and institutions determine what a visitor encounters. No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care or violence provision is documented in territory law.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. No penalty provision specific to transgender people is documented anywhere in the territory's instruments.

The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 has been in force since 2009 and bans discrimination on grounds including sex and sexual orientation. It defines "discriminatory" as affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status. The ban is written around sexual orientation, and no source documents it being applied to gender reassignment.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality and works towards the elimination of unlawful discrimination. Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015 it may conduct inquiries and investigations into persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or "gender reassignment". That ordinance defines "gender reassignment" as an intended, current or past process, or part of such a process, for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex, or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent with or not culturally associated with their assigned sex at birth. This is the only transgender-specific wording located in territory law, and it sits in the commission's enabling ordinance rather than in a criminal, documentation or entry instrument.

Marriage is available to same-sex couples on all three islands. The Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance 2016 commenced on 1 January 2017, the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017 took effect on 4 August 2017, and the Marriage Ordinance 2017 took effect on Saint Helena on 20 December 2017. The Tristan da Cunha ordinance defines marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extends eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples. The first same-sex marriage recorded in Saint Helena took place on 31 December 2018. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can therefore marry on any of the three islands.

Unresolved: whether the Constitution Order 2009 discrimination ban has ever been invoked on gender reassignment grounds, and whether its wording covering "sex" or "other status" has been read to include gender identity, is not sourced. No case, finding or commission decision on gender reassignment is documented in the inventory.

Unresolved: no violence or incident data for the territory appears in the inventory. No dated trans-specific incident is recorded, and no prevalence figure of any kind is available, so no assessment of physical risk can be sourced.

sources.summary: No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care, or violence provisions are documented. The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination. The Commission may conduct inquiries and investigations on persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or "gender reassignment". Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, "gender reassignment" means "an intended, current or past process (or part of such a process) for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent or not culturally associated with their assigned sex at birth". No extension of the Constitution Order 2009 sexual-orientation discrimination ban to gender reassignment, and no transgender-specific marriage, adoption, or penalty provisions, are documented. Homosexuality is legal in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining "discriminatory" as "affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status." The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes "understanding of the importance of equality" and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination, with power to conduct inquiries and investigations into suspected unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, sexual orientation means "a person's sexual orientation towards— (a) persons of the same sex; (b) persons of the opposite sex; or (c) persons of either sex". Same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 1 January 2017 under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance, 2016, on Tristan da Cunha since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance, 2017, and on Saint Helena since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017, with the first same-sex marriage in Saint Helena occurring on 31 December 2018. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010 for Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011 for Ascension Island, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, while a 2006 UK Government report recorded no adoptions in Saint Helena or Ascension Island for many years.

PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory. Defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures do not extend to Pitcairn of their own force; local ordinance governs.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a visitor faces no criminalisation exposure on that ground.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, in force since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation and not gender identity, so a trans visitor has no express constitutional protection on gender-identity grounds.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and the ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn. The ordinance was unanimously approved by the Island Council on 1 April 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair on 5 May 2015 and published on 13 May 2015.

Adoption has been legal since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.

Military service falls under United Kingdom responsibility. None of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship.

GGY.name: Guernsey
GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically; United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is lawful for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can therefore face prosecution for conduct that is lawful in the United Kingdom.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. The law permits only the issue of a new certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document. A visitor carrying both records, or documents issued at different times, should expect the earlier marker to remain on file.

The States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage on 10 December 2015 by 37 votes to 7, rejecting a civil-partnership-only scheme and a single secular status called Union Civile as insufficient. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill and commenced in 2018. Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted its own civil partnership legislation; United Kingdom civil partnerships have been recognised for succession purposes since 2 April 2012.

A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting. The States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Discrimination protections were built in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity have applied in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations. It took effect on 1 October 2023.

Les Nicolles, Guernsey's only prison, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages across 11 wings, with a capacity of 139 and about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded in the available sources, so a trans visitor has no sourced assurance about placement if detained.

No published rule or policy on how Les Nicolles houses trans prisoners by birth sex or gender identity was identified, and no separate unit or segregation practice is recorded. Placement if a trans visitor is detained is unresolved.

No trans-specific hate-crime statistics, recorded incidents, or enforcement data under the 2023 anti-discrimination Act were identified for Guernsey.

No sourced provision governs access by trans people to bathrooms, changing rooms or other single-sex facilities in Guernsey, and the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex services code does not extend to the islands.

Whether the 2023 Act's gender-identity coverage extends beyond employment, and any case law or tribunal decisions under it, is not sourced.

No data on trans-specific violence in Guernsey was identified.

IMN.name: Isle of Man
IMN.summary:
The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Its parliament, Tynwald, legislates on these questions itself, and United Kingdom statutes reach the island only by Order in Council rather than automatically.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and have the new gender recognised.

The Equality Act 2017, which received royal assent on 18 July 2017 and was largely brought into force on 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited. A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024; the Isle of Man was the first part of the British Isles to prohibit the practice.

Partner recognition is established. Civil partnerships became available to same-sex couples under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) on 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage took effect on 22 July 2016 after royal assent on 19 July 2016. A civil partnership converts into a marriage without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force, which indicates routine registration rather than discretionary approval.

Parental recognition is narrower than the marriage position. Full joint and stepchild adoption has been open to same-sex couples since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates for children born through IVF or surrogacy, and no Manx law acknowledges surrogacy. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under local law would meet that gap.

Sexual-conduct law on the island has been gender-neutral since the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3), which set a single age of consent of sixteen for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation.

A hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status was put to community consultation in July 2022. The sources reviewed do not record its enactment.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Isle of Man (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender persons to change their legal gender and to have their new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 with much of the law in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and ground of non-discrimination. A ban covering sexual orientation and gender identity conversion therapy was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the extensive sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and came into effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory and the first part of the British Isles to ban conversion therapy. In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. Private and consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with age of consent set at 21, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021 Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private, defined in Section 10 as more than two persons present or in a public-access place, and in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral. The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 passed with royal assent in July 2021 and took effect 1 July 2022 by proclamation, pardoning historical gay sex offences committed prior to 1992 explicitly based on the UK Alan Turing law of 2017. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022 on the 30th anniversary of decriminalisation the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992. Same-sex couples were granted civil partnerships by the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) effective 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage effective 22 July 2016 after royal assent 19 July 2016. By the Civil Partnership Act 2011 same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011, lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates from IVF and surrogacy and no laws acknowledge surrogacy. Under the Employment Act 2006 (c.21) effective 1 September 2006 dismissal on grounds of sexual orientation was made unlawful, and the Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation, defined to include attraction to same, opposite, either sex and lack of attraction to either sex, as a protected characteristic.

GUF.name: French Guiana
GUF.summary:
French Guiana is an overseas department of France and has no gender-identity legislation of its own. Criminal law, identity documents, anti-discrimination provisions and the marriage regime that operate here are the French national ones, applied without local variation.

Detention carries the most serious documented risk. No local protocol governs the custody of transgender detainees, so placement in French Guiana's facilities follows the national practice: assignment to a men's or women's wing is based on the detainee's legal gender and decided case by case, without a consistent protective standard.

Specialist gender-affirming care is not provided locally on the same basis as in metropolitan France. Patients travel to the mainland for surgery and specialist assessment, and the journey adds cost and delay to every medical step, including any undertaken during a stay in the department.

Transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility in the department, and abuse is less likely to be reported, including to the police. Under-reporting is a feature of the local situation rather than evidence that abuse is rare.
GUF.outOfScopeNotes:
No figures specific to French Guiana were located on transgender people: the sources reviewed contain no counts of trans-specific violence, arrests or discrimination complaints for the department, and give nothing against which to compare them with the general crime rate.

One travel guide carries sections on equality indices and gender-identity recognition but no figures, and a second guide returned no usable finding on the safety of trans visitors. Whether the national healthcare and detention findings translate into conditions specific to French Guiana's health services and detention facilities is not documented in the sources reviewed.
