sources.title: LGBTQ rights in French Guiana (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, becoming the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as mental illness, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Since 1 January 2017 under the law signed 18 November 2016 after the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November, transgender people may change legal gender marker by court order without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificate or medical diagnosis, with first-name change available at the registry office. This followed a decades-long legislative ban on legal gender change despite the 1959 change for Coccinelle and 1979 legalisation of gender-affirming surgery inside France, overturned only after the 1992 B. v France case at the European Court of Human Rights. Discrimination on the ground of "sexual identity" was prohibited from July 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" on 18 November 2016 amending Penal Code article 225-1 and Labour Code protections covering recruitment, internships, training, sanction and dismissal. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming healthcare was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to lack self-determination with extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access recommending informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine advises extreme caution and actual practice is unchanged. For youth, the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the first national guidelines in late 2024 recommending puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements, while a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under age 18 following the March 2024 Little Mermaid Observatory report has had no update since 23 July 2024 and is opposed by the Macron government. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the Penal Code of 1810 applied to nations and French colonies, ending ancien régime capital punishments including castration, dismemberment and burning with the last burning on 6 July 1750. A discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations introduced 6 August 1942 as article 334, moved to article 331 in 1945 and lowered to 18 in 1974, was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President Mitterrand, while the discriminatory 1960 Mirguet amendment to Penal Code article 330 alinea 2 doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure was repealed in 1980 with a March 2024 National Assembly unanimous compensation bill for pre-1980 Article 330 victims pending Senate vote. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of goods and services, codified in the Labour Code. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Law on Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by victim sexual orientation carries increased penalties, and created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité. Same-sex marriage following civil solidarity pacts in 1999 was legalised in 2013 with the law signed 18 May 2013 after the 17 May Constitutional Council ruling and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, and is legal in all overseas departments and territories, with French Guiana's two deputies recording one vote in favour and one abstention. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the Armed Forces, men who have sex with men blood-donation abstinence requirements of one year from 10 July 2016 and four months from 2 April 2020 were fully removed 16 March 2022 to an orientation-neutral policy, and the conversion therapy ban passed the Senate 7 December 2020, the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and was published 1 February 2022.

GLP.name: Guadeloupe
GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe is a French overseas department. Criminal law, identity-document rules, custodial conditions and the national preventive mechanism are set at the national level and carried by the parent record; this assessment covers what is specific to the island.

Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. It offers reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities.

The opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for the overseas territories. The centre's opening was presented as a concrete step toward inclusion and safety.

Community organisations Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025, described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community.

A September 2023 interview with Leïla of Secret's Out reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, and described activism on the island as advancing after neighbouring Martinique; the interview also featured Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's.
GLP.outOfScopeNotes:
Custodial conditions for trans people in Guadeloupe are governed by national prison rules, and the national preventive mechanism's 2021 opinion on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty is a national-level finding; both are carried by the parent record rather than assessed here.

No Guadeloupe-specific data on anti-trans violence, policing practice or healthcare access was identified in the sources reviewed; the island's trans-specific risk picture therefore rests on the national framework together with the community infrastructure described above.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French law applicable in Guadeloupe decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained this in the 1810 Code, while public morality laws continued to be used against LGBTQ people; in Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. The law of December 2004, passed 31 December 2004, made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. It created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, about 10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities. Transgender people have changed legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but must still appear before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change, while a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness, removing gender identity disorder by decree, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

MTQ.name: Martinique
MTQ.summary:
Martinique is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework in full: Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the island, so the identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination provisions and marriage regime a visitor would rely on are national law operating locally. A trans visitor is subject to the same substantive rules as in metropolitan France, administered through the department's own courts, administrative services and registry offices, and no island-specific procedure or exemption applies.

Martinique's correctional establishments are French prisons, so the national placement rules and the national detention watchdog's findings on transgender detainees apply to them by virtue of being French places of deprivation of liberty; no rule specific to the department governs placement, isolation or safety there. The watchdog's on-site interviews were conducted at establishments outside the department, so that finding rests on referrals and inspections elsewhere while still binding Martinique's prisons.

Same-sex conduct has been lawful in Martinique since 1815. The 2013 marriage-equality law applies in the department, discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited in goods and services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2) and in employment since 2008 (Labour Code article L1132-1), and gender-identity discrimination has been prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with the term "sexual identity" replaced by "gender identity" in 2016.

Community infrastructure operates on the island. JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, and LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.
MTQ.outOfScopeNotes:
No figures specific to Martinique on anti-trans violence, and no enforcement record specific to the island, were located in the sources consulted. National hate-crime statistics exist but cover France as a whole and are documented at national level rather than as findings about the department.

The resource page records 1815 as the date same-sex conduct was decriminalised in the department; it gives no account of enforcement or of local practice in the intervening period.

Details of legal gender recognition procedure, gender-affirming care provision and the status of youth transition care are national matters under the framework in force in the department; they are not sourced here as island-specific findings.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French law governs Martinique, and the following national provisions apply in the department. Homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments were made illegal by a National Assembly amendment approved 31 December 2004, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; the same law amended the 1881 Law on the Freedom of the Press to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Christian Vanneste, an MP in Chirac's UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people can change their legal gender without surgery or a medical diagnosis, but must still go before a court to change the gender marker, while a first name change can be done at the registry office. The bill was signed 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly, with the Constitutional Council ruling it constitutional on 17 November 2016 and dropping the original self-certification provision; before that, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims, up from about 1,380 in 2018. Penalties increase where physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published 1 February 2022. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare, including extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, with treatment covered by Sécurité Sociale under ALD 31. In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory to report on youth gender care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access. Earlier state hostility includes the 1960 Mirguet amendment treating homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism and the Vichy age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 setting 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. Gender-affirming surgery within France was legalised in 1979, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased treatment-seeking as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing actual practice, while a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report led to a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under 18 opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly with no update since 23 July 2024, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements. PYF.name: French Polynesia
PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs justice and civil status in the territory while territorial institutions in Papeete regulate much of daily life.

Gender-diverse healthcare in the territory is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France; after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed. For a trans visitor staying any length of time, the gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint.

The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.

The OutTraveler account of cultural acceptance rests on travel reporting and a visiting couple's impressions rather than on legal protection; no territorial anti-discrimination provision specific to gender identity was identified in the sources.

WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna
WLF.summary:
Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic. French civil and criminal law applies locally unless a local measure overrides it, and no provision of that framework criminalises transgender people or same-sex relations. Discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since 2012, when the statute covering employment, housing and access to services was extended to Wallis and Futuna; the term used was "sexual identity" until a 2016 amendment replaced it with "gender identity" in article 225-1 of the Penal Code. The Labour Code bars exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal and other discriminatory measures on account of gender identity.

Legal change of gender marker is available under the French reforms that took effect on 1 January 2017, following the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November and publication the next day. Applicants no longer need sex-reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, a psychiatrist's certificate or medical proof, but must still go before a court. Change of first name can be handled at a registry office, after the self-certification provision was dropped. French law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, while transsexualism remains classified under the long-term illness category ALD 31, funded by the national health insurance scheme; gender-affirming surgery has been lawful domestically since 1979.

Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for every crime punishable by imprisonment. Conversion therapy was banned by a law published on 1 February 2022, after passage by the Senate on 7 December 2020 and concurrence by the National Assembly on 25 January 2022; the offence carries two years' imprisonment and a 30,000 euro fine.

Marriage between two people of the same legal sex has been lawful since 2013, following Constitutional Council approval on 17 May 2013, signature on 18 May and the first ceremony on 29 May in Montpellier, and is stated to be legal in all French overseas departments and territories; registered partnerships (PACS) have been available since 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can expect it to be recognised.

Detention is governed by the French framework. The national preventive mechanism's opinion of 25 May 2021, extending an earlier opinion of 30 June 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals concerning about 40 transgender detainees since 2010 and on interviews with associations and experts. Trans women whose legal gender is recorded as male, largely those who have not had surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; one such case involved a transfer to a men's facility in Lille in 2014.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare is uneven. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found a lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterised the rise in demand as epidemic-like and primarily social, urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under the age of 18 passed the Senate in May 2024; it is opposed by the government and has been stalled since 23 July 2024. Guidelines issued in late 2024 by the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.

Locally, the collectivity has a population of about 11,000, and its isolation and dominant Catholic and Polynesian norms leave practical barriers to healthcare and social acceptance. Roles comparable to fakafafine coexist with stigma and concealment.
WLF.outOfScopeNotes:

Local hate-crime statistics for the collectivity are not sourced; the French figures cited in the national material are raw counts without a population denominator.

The 2024 Senate bill on medical transition under 18 remains stalled and its application to the collectivity is unresolved. Provisions of French law that are not specific to Wallis and Futuna are documented at the national level.

Detention is governed by the parent nation's framework. The national preventive mechanism's opinion of 25 May 2021, extending an earlier opinion of 30 June 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist in places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals concerning about 40 transgender detainees since 2010 and on interviews with associations and experts. Trans women whose legal gender is recorded as male, largely those who have not had surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; one such case involved a transfer to a men's facility in a city in 2014.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare is uneven. A 2022 report by a regional rights organisation found a lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The national medical academy has characterised the rise in demand as epidemic-like and primarily social, urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 upper-house-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under the age of 18 passed the upper house in May 2024; it is opposed by the government and has been stalled since 23 July 2024. Guidelines issued in late 2024 by a national paediatric endocrinology society recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.

Locally, the country has a small population, and its isolation and dominant religious and local cultural norms leave practical barriers to healthcare and social acceptance. Gender-variant roles recognised in local custom coexist with stigma and concealment.

BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy is a French overseas collectivity, and the national framework of France applies here as it does in metropolitan France: its criminal law, identity documents, anti-discrimination statute and marriage regime govern the island.

Medical capacity is the sharpest practical constraint. The island covers about 8 square miles and holds roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against it in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access. Prescriptions and ongoing gender-affirming treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally, and a visitor who depends on either should carry supplies and confirm provision before arrival.

The same aggregate index rates Saint Barthélemy 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.

Anyone detained in Saint Barthélemy falls under the French prison administration, whose placement policy recognises only biological sex; trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.

Socially the island is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are described as trained for a diverse clientele.

Politically, Saint Barthélemy's joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 overseas deputies who voted against the 2013 law opening marriage to same-sex couples.
BLM.outOfScopeNotes:
No government LGBT+ travel advice specific to Saint Barthélemy exists, and the UK FCDO records no warnings for the collectivity. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted to the aggregate index.

The aggregate rating of 7.7 out of 10, with nine positive rights and one red flag, is a composite score rather than a legal finding, and its components are not itemised in the source.

Accounts of the island's LGBTQ infrastructure conflict: one source lists gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches among the French Caribbean territories including Saint Barthélemy, while island-level guides report no LGBTQ venue or scene. The discrepancy is unresolved.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Saint Barthélemy (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: French law banned discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" in July 2012 and replaced that term with "gender identity" by the law of 18 November 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code; Chapter 2 of the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis under the law signed 18 November 2016 after Constitutional Council approval on 17 November 2016, but they must go before a court to change the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. France legalised gender affirmative surgery domestically in 1979, removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 as the first country to declassify gender dysphoria, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location for gender affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" advising extreme caution without changing practice, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first guidelines recommending puberty blockers plus calcium and vitamin D from at least Tanner stage 2. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Conversion therapy was legally banned by a bill passed by the Senate on 7 December 2020, concurred by the National Assembly on 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022, with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine. A Senate-passed bill of May 2024 to ban medical transition under age 18, following a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report criticizing youth care, is opposed by the Macron government, unlikely to pass the National Assembly and had no update since 23 July 2024. All sodomy laws were repealed in 1791 during the French Revolution with no mention of private same-sex relations in the Penal Codes of 1791 and 1810, while a 1960 ordinance inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubling the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity, adopted via the Mirguet amendment, was repealed in 1980, and the discriminatory age of consent raised to 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual in 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974 was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still awaiting Senate vote. National legislation since 1985 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services, and the law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment and increased penalties when physical assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, enforced with the first conviction in January 2006 later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples, and same-sex marriage became legal nationwide including all overseas departments and territories after National Assembly approval 12 February 2013 by 329-229, Senate approval 12 April, Constitutional Council validation 17 May 2013, presidential signature 18 May 2013 and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. The historic MSM blood-donation ban dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled 12 January 2009, replaced by one-year abstinence from 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, and fully removed 16 March 2022 so policy applies regardless of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage is legal in Saint Barthélemy but its joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 overseas deputies voting against, while Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint Martin and Saint Barthélemy are noted for gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches, and Saint Barthélemy's reputation as an international celebrity tourist destination is stated to have produced a more open and relaxed social climate for LGBTQ people than other French Caribbean territories. President Emmanuel Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as "unworthy of France" and announced future concrete measures after a rise in attacks.

ABW.name: Aruba
ABW.summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions that apply on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory ground of protection against discrimination in Aruba.

On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognise same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions, after a 2.5-year campaign sponsored by openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes and an Igualdad Aruba petition of nearly 20,000 signatures. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered.

The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

GlobalGayz describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and notes that same-sex adoption is legal. Several gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba; the last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'
ABW.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents airport or border screening practice in Aruba that treats binders, packers, breast forms or gender presentation differently from other travellers, and no source addresses gender markers on passports or identity documents as issued or read in Aruba. Whether Aruban authorities inspect or question documents whose gender marker does not match the holder's presentation is unresolved.

No source addresses access to gender-affirming healthcare, hormone prescriptions or their customs treatment for visitors, and none addresses bathroom or facility access rules on the island. These remain not sourced rather than absent.

No source records any hate-crime or violence incident in Aruba against a trans person specifically. The documented harassment (the Oduber-Lamer case, 2004 to 2007) concerns a same-sex couple; whether comparable conduct against a trans resident or visitor would be prosecuted is unresolved.

The 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement naming transgender persons is a political statement by Kingdom governments. Whether it has been implemented in Aruban statute or practice is not sourced here.

CUW.name: Curaçao
CUW.summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, with full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex faces no conduct offence on that basis.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Curaçao since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling, Curaçao recognised as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, but offered no in-island marriage, civil union or other form of recognition.

Recognition arrived by court order rather than by statute. A limited-rights proposal was put to the Estates of Curaçao in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support. In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights quickly, and the August 2015 Oliari and Others v. Italy judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, applicable to Curaçao, required legal recognition.

The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds that include heterosexual or homosexual orientation. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The protected grounds named in the source material do not include gender identity, and no Curaçao-specific authority on gender-identity coverage was identified.

Official rhetoric has not consistently governed practice. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in the local press, while her party colleague Winifred Raveneau opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

Curaçao opened an LGBT community centre, the Pink House, in 2010, and alongside Aruba and Sint Maarten has acted as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay welcoming in the region, and a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

No Curaçao-specific sourcing was found on gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry or border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, or the designation of facilities. Those areas are unassessed rather than cleared.

Gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry and border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, and facility designation are unassessed for Curaçao; no region-specific sourcing was identified.

BES.name: Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba)
BES.summary:
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The civil-status and anti-discrimination law in force on the islands is Dutch national law, applied there in the same form as in the European Netherlands, with no separate island legislation on marriage or discrimination operating alongside it.

No source in the inventory describes any provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

Travel coverage published by GayCities on 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023 places Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, citing its standing as part of the Netherlands, under whose strict anti-discrimination laws it says citizens and visitors are protected, and describing same-sex couples as warmly welcomed.

Registered unions for same-sex couples have been available in the islands since 2012. The first was recorded by the Census Office in Saba on 4 December 2012: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on Saba and both were visiting, which establishes that the island registry performs ceremonies for couples who are only passing through.

Saba Tourism's weddings page states that civil ceremonies run routinely through the island registry, that the Court Room in the Administrative Building is the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony, and that registrar Julieta Woods is flexible with couples' wishes. Caterers, florists and accommodation serving destination weddings operate on the island.
BES.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses gender-marker rules on identity documents, entry or immigration screening, access to gender-affirming care, or facilities and harassment exposure for trans visitors. The findings above rest on marriage registration and anti-discrimination provisions rather than on trans-specific legal text.

Anti-discrimination coverage is asserted in travel-facing coverage rather than documented through a statutory citation, an equality body's decisions or complaint data; no enforcement record for the islands appears in the inventory.

Sint Eustatius is not addressed separately in any source, and the documented ceremonial practice is drawn from Saba. No source reports violence, police conduct or complaints data for any of the three islands.

FRO.name: Faroe Islands
FRO.summary:
The Faroe Islands is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Danish national criminal law and document rules apply here; equality and family law are set locally by the Løgting.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent for male same-sex relations was set at 18 and remained there until 1988, when the Faroes adopted Denmark's gender-neutral age of 15, eleven years after Denmark made that change.

Since 1 January 2007 an anti-discrimination provision has made anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. On the sourced account this made the Faroe Islands the last Northern European country to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Before that provision took effect, homophobic violence went unhandled by the authorities. In 2006 the openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host Rasmus Rasmussen was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out, and he and his family then received threatening telephone calls; police refused to take the case because no Faroese law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, became mentally ill and died by suicide in 2012.

In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in Tórshavn. The group was not attacked anywhere else.

Hostility from elected officials is documented across a decade. The first gay pride march in 2005 provoked substantial controversy. In September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister and her partner, citing his religion. In July 2015 he demanded that Pride be banned, held two days before the national holiday, and the singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him; his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. In June 2015 Løgting Speaker Jógvan á Lakjuni published a letter to the editor, 'Hvar eru vit á veg?', attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. Av Rana has repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre.

Petitioning has been the main channel of advocacy. In November 2006, in a population of about 47,000, activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordic countries; neither existed at that date, and homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. Petitioning in the same period followed the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen, with eight women in Tórshavn gathering a further 2,000 signatures by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A separate petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.
FRO.outOfScopeNotes:
The sourced wording of the anti-discrimination provision lists race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion and sexual orientation as protected grounds. Whether gender identity or gender expression is separately protected is not resolved by these sources.

No sourced information covers legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, entry or visa screening, border or airport screening practices, bathroom and facilities rules, or access to healthcare for trans visitors. The Danish criminal-law and document provisions said to extend to the Faroe Islands are not itemised in the inventory.

Whether the registered-partnership law demanded in the November 2006 petition was subsequently enacted, and the current status of relationship and marriage recognition, are unresolved here; the sources record only the petition and the separate 1,262-signature petition against same-sex marriage.

The inventory supplies no enforcement record for the anti-discrimination provision after 1 January 2007 and no documented incident comparable to the 2005 or 2006 assaults in the years since.

GRL.name: Greenland
GRL.summary:
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Its parliament and courts handle domestic affairs, while Danish legislation on marriage and on official identity documents has been adopted and applies in Greenland. A visitor's legal position on those questions follows the Danish framework as received here.

Same-sex relations carry no criminal penalty. Since 2010 Article 100 of the Criminal Code has prohibited speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other protected categories, and the Code provides penalty enhancement for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation. No prosecution under either provision is recorded in the available sources.

Same-sex marriage took effect on 1 April 2016, adopting Danish legislation that passed unanimously on two occasions after the first bill lapsed in Danish elections. It replaced the registered partnership (nalunaarsukkamik inooqatigiinneq) that had run from 1 July 1996, whose application was repealed the day the marriage law commenced. The bishop of the established church supported the change. Marriage is available to a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status.

Legal change of sex designation on official documents rests on self-determination. The law, passed in 2016 and brought into force by decree, requires no sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilization or medical diagnosis. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want their documentation changed, then observe a six-month reflection period to confirm the request.

Greenlandic passports are issued with an X sex descriptor in addition to male and female.

The Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination was passed by the parliament in May 2024 and took effect on 1 July 2024. It prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics, among other characteristics. It creates an Equal Treatment Board to handle discrimination complaints and an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination.

Public expression is visible. The first pride parade was held in Nuuk on 15 May 2010 and drew about 1,000 people, and a modest march has continued since. Accounts from 2015 describe gay life as low-key, integrated and non-violent, with no reported anti-LGBT violence.
GRL.outOfScopeNotes:
No prosecution under Article 100 or under the hate-crime penalty enhancement appears in the available sources, so enforcement practice is not documented.

The 2024 anti-discrimination law took effect on 1 July 2024. No complaint outcomes or decisions by the Equal Treatment Board are recorded.

The sources do not record how the X passport descriptor is issued in practice, or whether any applicant in Greenland has obtained one.

Access to transition-related healthcare in Greenland, and the rules governing gendered facilities such as changing rooms and toilets, are not addressed in the available sources.

PRI.name: Puerto Rico
PRI.summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory and stands under the United States federal framework for entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody; the findings below are the territory's own law, its own enforcement and its own institutions.

Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors, was enacted in July 2025. It bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and penalises violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. Article 4, the operative prohibition, is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

Article 3 defines the banned chemical and surgical practice more broadly than the operative clause. It expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and it sets the protected class at anyone under 21. Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law's provisions.

The gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers leaves an unresolved question. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment on the island sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped: questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. The law's protected class is anyone under 21 and does not on its face reach patients 21 or older.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment; the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico urged Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, which it said criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated that the bill allows parents to authorise treatment where a child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth and prohibits them the same right where it does not. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona said the measure discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned did not remedy the rights violations, and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. Opposition was registered by the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. The first hate crime charges in the territory's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage is partial. The 2013 law that passed, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge was filed in March 2014 in the Ada Conde Vidal case, with intervention from Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former National Guard member and two couples already married in Canada in 2007 and in New York in 2012.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; after the United States Supreme Court's 2003 ruling invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.
PRI.outOfScopeNotes:
No court has resolved whether the definitional clause of Ley Núm. 63 de 2025 can reach a patient, or whether the statute is void for vagueness. The question is unresolved and no test case had been decided at the time of writing.

No territory-level corrections policy, dedicated unit or ruling on the housing of transgender inmates in Puerto Rico was located.

Reports differ on the surname of the health secretary who proposed amendments to the bill, rendering the attribution unresolved.

sources.title: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025 (LexJuris de Puerto Rico) — primary legal text
sources.summary: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, 'Ley para la protección de la salud y el bienestar de los menores de edad en Puerto Rico' (primary legal text, LexJuris). Article 4 — the operative prohibition — is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments altering the sex biology of a minor 'bajo el pretexto de una transición de género o como parte de un tratamiento de disforia de género'. The Article 3 definition of banned 'chemical and surgical mutilation' is drafted broader than the prohibition: it expressly includes 'el uso de bloqueadores de pubertad y hormonas sexuales (incluyendo bloqueadores androgénicos, estrógenos, progesterona o testosterona) utilizados con el propósito de tratar la disforia de género' — the USE itself of puberty blockers and sex hormones for gender-dysphoria treatment — and defines 'niño o menor de edad' as any person under 21. Article 6 then penalises 'toda persona que viole las disposiciones de esta Ley' with a fixed 15-year term, plus permanent licence loss for professionals and a $50,000 per-violation fine for juridical persons. Legal analysis of this drafting notes a structural tension: the definition speaks of patient 'use' while the operative clause restricts only providers, and the penalty catch-all says 'any person'. Under standard criminal doctrines (definitions create no offence by themselves; a protected class cannot be prosecuted as the perpetrator of its own victimisation; the principle of legality bars analogy; and travel with lawfully prescribed personal medication), a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own prescribed hormones — or of their parents for enabling it — would almost certainly fail, and the statute is a textbook void-for-vagueness candidate. But the textual ambiguity is precisely what legal advocates flag as its chilling effect: it leaves interpretive room for hostile officials to question, detain or investigate trans youth and their families on the ground, with the answer coming only after the fact. For a travelling under-21 trans person the practical reading is: carrying and using prescribed HRT in Puerto Rico sits inside the law's literal definition of banned practice, enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. The ACLU of Puerto Rico had urged a veto before signature, stating the bill 'criminalizes doctors and parents' and creates 'two distinct categories of children' divided by sex-assigned-at-birth identity, and the island's College of Physicians and Surgeons, Psychology Association, College of Social Work Professionals, Bar Association and LGBTQ+ Federation all registered opposition.

Washington Blade (26 Apr 2019): Gov. Rossello announced SB1253 ('clarify religious freedom principles') and SB1254 (conversion-therapy ban with pastoral exemption); LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors, criticizing the religious-freedom carve-out as license to refuse service on orientation/gender-identity grounds.

Washington Blade (25 Jun 2014): four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit in PR (filed March; Ada Conde Vidal case), with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening - one couple married in Canada 2007, another in New York 2012; former National Guard member among plaintiffs. Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the PR House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors; Sen. Zoe Laboy (co-sponsor) dissented publicly. Conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): Gov. Rossello asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253/SB1254 amid sustained opposition; his April announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy in the conversion-therapy ban. Record of LGBT advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

Erin in the Morning (2025): PR enacted a trans youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; law is deliberately vague so doctors and affirming parents facilitating HRT or top surgery risk prosecution; mandates Education/Health department campaigns on 'risks' of trans-affirming care; Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments allowing puberty blockers and continuation of existing HRT, but the enacted text is the most extreme care restriction in US jurisdictions per the report. For a trans visitor the ban closes off all gender-affirming care on the island for anyone under 21, and the deliberately vague facilitation language reaches the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager.

sources.title: Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government") - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling was located.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, but after the U.S. Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened doctors who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and permanent loss of their licenses; the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court. An anti-discrimination bill (House Bill 1725) passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the U.S. federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488 (signed 29 May 2013) extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

sources.title: ACLU of Puerto Rico Urges Governor to Veto Senate Bill 350 (ACLU-PR press release)
sources.summary: The ACLU of Puerto Rico called on Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, 'which criminalizes doctors and parents and aims to prohibit gender-affirming medical treatments for individuals under the age of 21'. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated the bill 'creates two distinct categories of children: one that allows parents to access and authorize treatments if the child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth, and another that prohibits parents the same right if their child's identity is different'. The release records that the bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned 'do not remedy the violation of fundamental constitutional, civil, and human rights', and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. It states the bill's 'text is clearly and exclusively aimed at minors whose identity does not correspond to the sex assigned to them at birth' and that it disregards the specialist consultation process that precedes parents authorising puberty blockers or hormonal treatments, 'and instead, criminalizes them'. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona: the measure 'directly discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth, whose very lives may be at risk'. The release lists local opposition from the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

sources.title: Senate Bill 350 — ACLU of Puerto Rico legislation page
sources.summary: The ACLU of Puerto Rico opposed Senate Bill 350 'because of its direct impact on access to gender-affirming care for trans people, particularly trans youth and trans children, as well as on the rights of families and minors. The measure bans gender-affirming medical treatments for people under 21 years of age.'

sources.title: Puerto Rico bans hormone therapy and gender surgery for transgender youth (AP News)

GUM.name: Guam
GUM.summary:
Guam's own law governs legal gender recognition, and it requires surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a transgender person must give the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery, after which the office amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed.

A 2018 attempt to remove the surgery requirement failed. Senator Fernando Esteves introduced a bill in May 2018 to permit legal gender change on judicial permission with a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional, with no surgery required. The Legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 pending medical and law enforcement process issues, and the bill failed on 17 December 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote. Surgery remains the condition for both documents.

Marriage recognition for a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship rests on the 2015 ruling. Chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 after an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

Private consensual adult non-commercial sexual conduct has been lawful since the 1978 reform of the Criminal Code; the penal code in force before that, ordained in 1933, had criminalised sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus with between one and ten years' imprisonment.

Guam hosts a large permanent United States military presence, so federal policy on transgender service members bears directly on personnel stationed on the island.
GUM.outOfScopeNotes:
No transgender-specific violence, hate-crime enforcement, or policing data for Guam was identified in the source inventory. The societal-attitude material available is framed as general LGBTQ findings rather than transgender-specific ones, so it does not establish conditions for trans visitors.

Hate-crime coverage based on gender identity and sexual orientation derives from federal law rather than Guam statute, and federal military service policy is likewise national in scope.

VIR.name: U.S. Virgin Islands
VIR.summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands is a United States territory; entry, travel documents and airport screening follow United States federal rules. What is specific to the territory is its own anti-discrimination and family law.

The territory's human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation and gender identity. That statute is the operative protection a trans visitor can invoke while in the territory.

In March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation holding that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending the protection explicitly into the education setting.

Marriage is settled in the territory. In 2015 the Superior Court of the U.S. Virgin Islands struck down the refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional, and later federal recognition settled the question nationwide. A married trans visitor can rely on their marriage in the territory, including where the couple would previously have been refused a licence as a same-sex couple.

The historic sodomy statute, applicable to the territory since 1957, has been replaced and is no longer in force.
VIR.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no territorial-level record of enforcement actions, complaints or outcomes under the anti-discrimination law, and no trans-specific violence data for the territory.

The July 2017 reporting on setbacks and prospects for the territory's LGBTQ community is not itemised in the inventory, so the specific measures at issue are unresolved.
