ASM.name: American Samoa
ASM.summary:
American Samoa's criminal law does not punish consensual sodomy. The 1979 revision of the criminal law, which took effect in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and persons unable to consent. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, criminalised male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian sex. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed in American Samoa. In July 2015 Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing whether the United States Supreme Court's marriage-equality ruling applied to the territory, and the Governor stated at the time that it did not, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application for a marriage licence then, and none has applied to date.

A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements, and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. The article sets out the litigation route: the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Reporting from the territory in July 2024 described the local ban as still treated as operative on the island and its durability under the Fourteenth Amendment as an open question, with a survey by a constitutional and comparative law professor testing the issue.

Birth certificates in American Samoa are altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, under a High Court ruling that the Office of Vital Statistics applies to applications from transgender individuals. The office changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Protection machinery has been used locally. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, following a June 2023 federal civil action that cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

American Samoan society is highly religious, and conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality tend to dominate. Reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. Against that, fa'afafine, boys raised as girls to take an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, are described in the sources as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the territory is described as tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities.
ASM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2015 marriage-equality ruling is operative in American Samoa is unresolved. Official statements from 2015 and on-island reporting from July 2024 treat the local ban as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question, while the 2026 law review article concludes the ruling applies and that a certificate would have to be issued; no court in the territory has decided the point, and no same-sex couple has applied for a licence.

No sourced material documents hate-crime provisions covering gender identity in the territory, their charging practice, or their enforcement. The February 2023 sexual-abuse charge is a single documented incident and no denominator-based figure for violence against transgender people in American Samoa appears in the sources.

Access to gender-affirming care, prison or detention placement rules by gender, and airport screening treatment specific to gender-nonconforming travellers in the territory are not sourced here. How the territory's birth-certificate gender-marker rule interacts with federal passport policy for residents is likewise not addressed by the sources.

The 2009 travel column's characterisations of local acceptance are descriptive and dated, and carry no legal force.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.summary: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

The Office will change the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order. The Office may change the gender marker on a birth certificate with medical documentation of the sex change. In 1979 the Fono revised criminal law so that consensual sodomy was no longer illegal unless it involved public acts, prostitution, minors or people unable to give consent due to mental illness, with the law taking effect in 1980. The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage but refers to the age of "the male" and "the female" and prescribes a form in which parties identify as "son" and as "daughter," and a 2003 bill to ban same-sex marriage was voted against by the House Judiciary Committee and then the full Senate. Hodges and the Governor stating the ruling does not apply due to preamble, constitution, Christian values and unorganized and unincorporated political status. Under the Respect for Marriage Act passed by the 117th United States Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022, all territories including American Samoa are required to recognize, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. The article states American Samoa remains the only part of the United States along with select Native American tribal jurisdictions to enforce a ban on same-sex couples marrying, while same-sex couples married legally in other jurisdictions are recognized and must be treated equally under US federal law since 13 December 2022. The article states "American Samoa, like the neighboring country of Samoa, tends to be tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities." It states open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. The main LGBTQ organization is the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (S.O.F.I.A.S.) which annually organizes events and festivals and campaigns for the betterment of the fa'afafine community. The first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry choral competitions, beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are quite popular, and families generally turn up en masse to support candidates.

ASM.blindSummary:
The state/province's criminal law does not punish consensual sodomy. The 1979 revision of the criminal law, which took effect in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and persons unable to consent. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, criminalised male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian sex. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed in the state/province. In July 2015 the national justice department was reviewing whether the national supreme court's marriage-equality ruling applied locally, and the state/province governor stated at the time that it did not, citing the state/province's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application for a marriage licence then, and none has applied to date.

A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in the state/province concludes that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements, and that the state/province would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. The article sets out the litigation route: the state/province high court first, with the state/province registrar as defendant, then the national interior department. Reporting from the state/province in July 2024 described the local ban as still treated as operative and its durability under the Fourteenth Amendment as an open question, with a survey by a constitutional and comparative law professor testing the issue.

Birth certificates in the state/province are altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, under a high court ruling that the state/province vital statistics office applies to applications from transgender individuals. The office changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Protection machinery has been used locally. In September 2023 the national justice department secured a settlement with the state/province government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, following a June 2023 national civil action that cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the state/province government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local society is highly religious, and conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality tend to dominate. Reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. Against that, members of a locally recognised gender category, boys raised as girls to take an important domestic role in communal life, are described in the sources as a recognised and integral part of traditional local culture, and the state/province is described as tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities.

MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
MNP.summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth. Travel documents, immigration and airport screening are governed by United States national rules rather than by commonwealth law, and the national layer of this assessment sits with the United States record.

Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised. Marriage between same-sex couples has been recognised in the commonwealth since 2015, and the first such marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can expect that relationship to be recognised. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015.

Legal gender change is permitted in the Northern Mariana Islands provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process, so identity documents can be brought into line with presentation, subject to that medical requirement.

Commonwealth law provides for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes. Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal commonwealth-level protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence.

There is no comprehensive commonwealth nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity. Commonwealth-level protections extend to government employees only, and recourse beyond federal complaint channels is limited.

As of 27 September 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scored the territory's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a negative gender-identity score.
MNP.outOfScopeNotes:
The specific medical process required for legal gender change is not detailed in the sources reviewed, so which procedures satisfy the requirement is unresolved.

No record of how often the enhanced-sentencing provision in Public Law 22-32 has been applied, or of any prosecution brought under it, appears in the sources reviewed.

The Movement Advancement Project figures are an advocacy index of policy coverage rather than a legal measure or an enforcement record, and the date of the territory's first Gay Pride event is not established in the sources reviewed.

COK.name: Cook Islands
COK.summary:
The Cook Islands is self-governing in free association with New Zealand, which supplies nationality and passport rules; criminal and marriage law on the islands is made and applied locally.

Sex between men was decriminalised by the Crimes Amendment Bill, which Parliament passed on 14 April 2023 and which took effect on 1 June 2023. The provisions removed were sections 154 and 155 of the Crimes Act 1969, covering sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, with consent expressly excluded as a defence. Sources disagree on the maximum penalties: coverage from 2017 records up to seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while reporting on the repeal cites up to ten years for indecent acts between males. No source records a prosecution under these sections in living memory, and the note attached to the amending bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands.

The same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. It did not change the marriage law.

Marriage is defined by the Marriage Amendment Act 2000 as between a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing in the Cook Islands, and a marriage entered into abroad on that basis is not recognised locally.
COK.outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material in the inventory addresses gender-marker or passport policy for trans travellers, gender-recognition procedures, healthcare access, facility use, hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection, or police practice in the Cook Islands. Nothing in the available sources documents a trans-specific prosecution, enforcement action or violent incident.

The maximum penalties recorded for the repealed sections 154 and 155 are inconsistent across sources: seven years and five years in the 2017 reporting, up to ten years in reporting on the repeal. The discrepancy is unresolved, and whether the offences were ever applied before living memory is not established either.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

NIU.name: Niue
NIU.summary:
Niue sets its own criminal law on sexual conduct. Consensual male homosexual activity is no longer an offence: the Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May 2024, in force from June 2024 (enacted 5 June 2024), removing buggery, attempted buggery and indecent assault on males from the Criminal Law Code. The age of consent was equalised in May 2011.

Before that repeal, sections 43 and 44 of the Criminal Law Code criminalised male homosexual conduct: consensual sodomy carried up to ten years' imprisonment and indecency between males up to five years, with attempted buggery and indecent assault on males falling under the same provisions. The offences were inherited from New Zealand through the 1901 annexation, retained when Niue took self-government in 1974, and left in place by New Zealand's 1986 decriminalisation, which amended New Zealand law only.

Marriage and partner recognition are closed to couples the law reads as same-sex. Same-sex unions are not recognised in Niue even though they are recognised in New Zealand, and section 6 of the Family Relationships Act 2022 expressly prohibits same-sex marriage. Couples and households headed by such couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classified locally as same-sex has no route to recognition or to the protections attached to marriage.

A 2015 UN Free & Equal information sheet on the Pacific records the fakafifine of Niue among the region's pre-colonial gender identities, which it describes as important parts of the region's cultural heritage.
NIU.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records enforcement practice under the repealed sections, the number of prosecutions brought under them, or police and court treatment of trans and gender-nonconforming people in Niue.

No source records Niue's rules on gender markers or identity documents, or access to transition-related healthcare.

No source records hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, or its enforcement.

The 2015 UN Free & Equal information sheet predates the 2024 repeal and does not describe current conditions.

The age of majority figures rest on a third-party compilation of the Niue Act 1966 rather than an official text in this inventory.

HKG.name: Hong Kong
HKG.summary:
Hong Kong is a special administrative region of the People's Republic of China with its own legal system under the Basic Law. Trans rights there have been settled by court judgments rather than by statute, and no comprehensive gender recognition framework exists. As of 2026 there are no laws prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no hate crime legislation.

Identity documents can be changed on the identity card and the passport but not on the birth certificate. Historically a marker change required full sex reassignment surgery including removal of reproductive organs. A revised policy in force since April 2024 requires applicants to have undergone specified gender-affirming surgeries, mastectomy for trans men and penectomy with orchiectomy for trans women, to supply medical proof, to have lived in their identified gender for at least two years, and to be on continuous hormone therapy. The same surgical and hormonal criteria apply to trans youth seeking an identity card change. Cross-dressing in itself is not illegal.

In February 2023 the Court of Final Appeal ruled that full sex reassignment surgery must not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on the official identity card. The High Court had ruled against the trans men Henry Tse, Q and R in February 2019; Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the only objectively ascertainable criterion and rejected self-identification as producing uncertainty and arbitrariness. The men had already changed their legal gender in Britain, and counsel argued the surgery requirement was out of proportion.

On 23 July 2025 the High Court ruled in K v Secretary for Environment and Ecology that a government regulation barring trans people from public toilets matching their lived gender identity was unconstitutional under the Basic Law's right to equality. Trans people report verbal, physical and sexual abuse in public toilets.

At the border, trans woman Eliana Rubashkyn was discriminated against and sexually abused by Hong Kong airport customs officers in 2013 and subjected to an invasive body search lasting more than nine hours. She was left stateless and required assistance from UN bodies and nongovernmental organisations.

Marriage and civil unions between partners the authorities class as same-sex are not recognised. In September 2023 the Court of Final Appeal directed the government to establish an alternative recognition framework within two years while ruling that no constitutionally guaranteed right to marry exists. In July 2025 the government introduced the Registration of Same-sex Partnerships Bill, which would have granted limited medical decision rights covering hospital visits, shared medical information, organ donation and dealing with remains; the legislature rejected it on 19 September 2025 by 71 votes to 14, leaving such partners without recognised medical decision-making rights.

Other partner rights exist. A Court of Final Appeal ruling of 4 July 2018 in the QT case required immigration authorities to grant spousal visas to partners married or in civil unions abroad, effective from 19 September 2018, when the Director of Immigration announced favourable consideration of such applications. Joint tax filing took effect on the same date, limited domestic violence protection dates from 2009, and equal public housing rights were established by a Court of Final Appeal ruling of 26 November 2024.

A 2025 report concluded that LGBTQ people in Hong Kong face exclusion across several domains, including health and personal security.
HKG.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2025 public-toilet ruling establishes a legal basis for facility access, but the sources do not describe how it is being implemented, whether it reaches government premises only or private venues as well, or what complaints mechanism exists.

Whether the September 2023 Court of Final Appeal direction to create an alternative recognition framework within two years has produced any draft instrument after the September 2025 rejection of the registered-partnerships bill is unresolved in the sources. No alternative framework has been enacted in the material available.

Hong Kong has no hate crime legislation, so no official disaggregated figures on anti-trans violence are available; the sources provide no incident counts for the jurisdiction.

The sources do not state whether the April 2024 identity card criteria have any application to visitors whose identity documents were issued elsewhere, or how a visitor's existing gender marker is handled at the border.

MAC.name: Macau
MAC.summary:
Macau is a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China. It stands under the national framework of the Basic Law and administers its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation.

Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1996, and the Penal Code treats homosexual and heterosexual sex offences identically. The general age of consent is 14 for both. Penal Code Article 166 prescribes 3 to 10 years' imprisonment for anal intercourse with a person under 14, and up to 4 years where a 14-to-16-year-old's inexperience is taken advantage of.

There is no legal pathway to gender recognition. The Identification Services Bureau maintains no policy for changing the sex marker on Macau identity cards, and the gender-marker-change study carried out in 2015 never produced legislation. Between 2004 and 28 February 2026 the bureau received eight written requests to change gender on identity documents; all were rejected.

In April 2026 the Legal Affairs Bureau (Direcção dos Serviços de Assuntos de Justiça) said there are "no plans" to revise the framework, pending "prudent study" of core societal values, civil law and family relations. The UN Human Rights Committee noted in 2017 that Macau still does not allow transgender people to change gender markers on birth records and identity documents.

The absence of a marker-change route produces border-crossing confusion. A trans man holding a Hong Kong identity card marked male remains registered female in Macau, so his documents disagree at the frontier.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. A March 2013 bill by Legislative Assembly member José Pereira Coutinho to give same-sex civil unions the same rights as heterosexual couples was rejected 17 votes to 1 with 4 abstentions and expressly excluded the right to adopt. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples remain ineligible for some legal rights available to opposite-sex couples.

Domestic-violence legislation excludes relationships the law classes as same-sex, because same-sex partners are not treated as "family members". A 2011 public consultation had included "same-sex cohabitants in an intimate relationship" in scope; the government's 2012 concluding report removed the reference citing "a lack of social consensus", and in 2016 it insisted on the exclusion. Rainbow of Macau complained to the UN Committee against Torture in October 2015, which urged Macau to protect all domestic-violence victims "without discrimination"; the group said the enacted law signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

Sexual orientation is absent from the non-exhaustive list of prohibited discrimination grounds in Basic Law Article 25. Sectoral protections exist in employment (Law No. 7/2008, Article 6/2, fines up to MOP$50,000 per affected worker), personal data (Law No. 8/2005) and the ombudsman (Law No. 4/2012); each is framed around sexual orientation.
MAC.outOfScopeNotes:
No source addresses whether gender expression is criminalised; the Penal Code's identical treatment of homosexual and heterosexual offences is the only sourced statement on the criminal law's scope.

The content and findings of the 2015 gender-marker-change study are not in the sourced material; only that it produced no legislation.

Whether the eight rejected identity-document requests included applications from non-residents is not stated.

Enforcement data on the domestic-violence law's application to same-sex or transgender victims is not sourced.

No sourced figures on prosecution or sentencing for violence against transgender people in Macau.

Whether the sectoral anti-discrimination laws (employment, personal data, ombudsman) extend to gender identity is not stated; the sourced descriptions frame them around sexual orientation.

The lesbian-themed film I'm here, directed by Tracy Choi, won the Macau Indies 2012 Jury's Award at the Macau International Film and Video Festival, depicting problems homosexuals face living in a small town like Macau.

The Macau LGBT Rights Concern Group was created in late 2012 and Rainbow of Macau registered in April 2013; gay culture in Macau remains mostly invisible.

MAC.localsOnly:

In February 2015 a transgender student, Avery (pseudonym), told Macau media about abuse and bullying experienced while studying at a local school.

ESH.name: Western Sahara
ESH.summary:
Western Sahara has no single legal order running through it. Morocco controls most of the ground, and Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate there. The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims sovereignty over the whole territory and governs through exile institutions and refugee camps in Algeria. Which framework a visitor stands under depends on which part of the territory they are in.

Moroccan jurisdiction is exercised in practice, not merely asserted. On 9 December 2005 Human Rights Watch reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The report documents Moroccan security services, courts and detention operating on Sahrawi political cases. The dossier records no comparable proceeding against Sahrawi activists after that date, so the 2005 case stands as historical evidence of how Moroccan authority is applied rather than as a description of current enforcement.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. In the areas Morocco controls, Moroccan law applies. Under the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, several catalogues of LGBT law (Council for Global Equality, Equaldex, ILGA) record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both males and females and punishable by up to three years in prison, and a July 2017 PinkNews roundup listed the territory as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and stated that it had been illegal there for decades. For a trans visitor, the operative question is how a relationship would be classified locally: a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls inside the prohibition as the sources describe it.

Detention on these charges has been documented in the camps. A 2009 USCRI report found that Sahrawi government officials running refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges even while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape.

No protection machinery is documented for either framework. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) states that there is no type of protection for LGBTQ individuals in case of discrimination or violence. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it', and CEAR concludes that this ambiguity leaves LGBTQ people without legal protection against discrimination or violence.

The sources describe most residents as Muslim and same-sex relationships as viewed as a foreign phenomenon, which bears on how a visible trans or gender-nonconforming visitor is likely to be received alongside the legal exposure.
ESH.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no trans-specific sourcing for this territory. Nothing is sourced on identity documents or gender markers, entry and visa screening, airport or custody screening, bathroom and facilities rules, healthcare or transition-care access, hate-crime protection, or recognition of a partner or marriage. These areas are unresolved rather than absent from the territory's law.

No trans-specific violence or killing figure with a denominator is available for Western Sahara, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made and none is asserted.

The sources do not map which parts of the territory stand under which framework, and they do not establish whether Moroccan statute extends to the territory by formal legal instrument or is applied through control on the ground. The 2005 trial and the 2009 camp-detention finding are historical; the dossier holds no current enforcement data for either.

GMB.name: Gambia
GMB.summary: Same-sex conduct is criminalised in Gambia, an offence retained from historic-era rule and from the 1933 Criminal Code implemented in 1934 as carnal knowledge against the order of nature. Section 158 punished homosexual acts by up to 14 years imprisonment for men and women, the provision being extended to women as gross indecency by the Criminal Code (Amendment) Act 2005. The Criminal Code (Amendment) Act signed in October 2014 created aggravated homosexuality with a mandatory life sentence, applicable to serial offenders, to gay or lesbian people living with HIV, to acts with persons under 18, with disabled or drugged persons, or where the accused was a parent, guardian or authority figure. The Criminal Code adopted in March 2025 removed the life clause and instead sets a five-year minimum for unnatural offences, defined in statute as any homosexual act, with no stated maximum, and three years for gross indecency. Section 147(1) of the Criminal Code (Cap 10:01, 2009) makes gross indecency between males a felony punishable by a mandatory five years imprisonment, and Section 147(3) defines the offence to include any homosexual act whether committed in public or in private.
GMB.outOfScopeNotes:
The US State Department's 2020 report describes the aggravated homosexuality provision as arising from a 2013 amendment, while other sources date the amendment act to October 2014. The discrepancy in dating is unresolved.

Whether the 14-year maximum under Section 158 survives the Criminal Code adopted in March 2025 is not stated in the sources.

The November 2014 arrest figures are internally inconsistent in the source material: at least eight persons are reported to have been apprehended, with the components given as four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women. The true total is unresolved.

The source material contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. The 93 per cent neighbour-attitude figure and the general statements about homosexuality concern attitudes toward homosexual neighbours and must not be read as trans-specific findings.

No trans-specific violence figures with a population denominator were identified in the source material, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary:
Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in the Gambia, and the country prohibits LGBTQ people from adopting children. No law or regulation protects residents against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and citizens cannot change their legal gender. Since 2013, section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress "as women," punishable by up to 5 years in jail or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi, effectively restricting gender expression.

The 2014 Criminal Code (Amendment) Act defines "aggravated homosexuality" to include sexual acts with persons of the same gender under 18 years of age, carrying a mandatory life sentence, and imposes a mandatory life sentence specifically on gay or lesbian people living with HIV, a direct barrier to testing and treatment. In November 2014 state forces launched an investigation under that law producing at least eight arrests, including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women. Detainees were held at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly tortured to compel confessions.

Enforcement under President Jammeh was broad. On 15 May 2008 he gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the Gambia Immigration Department to conduct mass patrols to "weed bad elements in society," warning that "any hotel, lodge or motel that lodges this kind of individuals will be closed down." In June 2008 two Spanish men in their 50s, alleged to be gay, were arrested and detained at Kotu police station after taxi drivers reported them, and were released reportedly after the Spanish government intervened. On 10 April 2012 a court remanded 18 men, 16 Senegalese, one Gambian and one Nigerian, arrested at a bar in the Tourism Development Area for "indecent practice" after police said they were wearing women's clothes; all charges were dropped on 1 August 2012. Arrests of gay people are believed to have been common during Jammeh's presidency, though data is lacking. On 23 December 2008 Frank Boers, a 79-year-old Dutch national, was arrested at Banjul International Airport when officials found him in possession of pornography including nude photos of himself and Gambian men; he was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 dalasis in lieu of a two-year sentence.

No LGBTQ+ organizations exist in the country after 2016 because it is considered too dangerous. In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honor LGBTQ+ people's privacy, which has negatively impacted HIV care for LGBTQ+ Gambians. No incidents of conversion therapy or of surgeries on intersex children or non-consenting adults were reported. A 2021-2023 survey found 93% of Gambians would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. Children are raised within strict male and female gender norms, with non-conformity to the heterosexual norm treated as deviant and taboo, and the country's media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ+ people. The Barrow government promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, though it has stated there are no plans for liberalisation of homosexuality laws.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Gambia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2013, section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress "as women", effectively discriminating against transgender women. Cross-dressing is punishable by up to 5 years in jail or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi. The Gambia makes no provision for any official change of gender and does not allow citizens to change their legal gender. There is no law or regulation protecting residents against discrimination based on gender identity. Human Rights Watch reports regular organised actions by law enforcement against persons suspected of gender non-conformity. On 9 April 2012, 18 men were arrested at a bar in the Tourism Development Area on charges of "indecent practice among themselves at a public place" after police testified the men were "wearing women's clothes", carrying handbags, and "walking like ladies", with the prosecutor dropping all charges on 1 August 2012. Consensual same-sex sexual activity is illegal for both men and women, with criminalisation commencing under British colonial rule and retained from the 1933 Criminal Code implemented in 1934 as "carnal knowledge against the order of nature". Section 158 punishes homosexual acts by up to 14 years imprisonment for both men and women, extended to women in 2005 as "gross indecency" by the Criminal Code (Amendment) Act, 2005. The Criminal Code (Amendment) Act 2014 signed in October 2014 created "aggravated homosexuality" carrying a mandatory life sentence, applying to "serial offenders" and gay or lesbian people living with HIV, and to acts with persons under 18, disabled or drugged persons, or where the accused is a parent, guardian or authority figure. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, LGBTQ people are prohibited from adopting children, and there is no protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation. Enforcement is described as rarely applied but with arrests occurring, including June 2008 detention of two Spanish men at Kotu police station after taxi drivers contacted police, released after Spanish government intervention, and December 2008 conviction of 79-year-old Dutch national Frank Boers for indecency with men resulting in a 100,000 dalasi fine in lieu of a two-year prison sentence. In November-December 2014 following the aggravated law, at least eight persons including four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women were apprehended for aggravated homosexual conduct, confined at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly subjected to torture and ill-treatment to compel confessions, with three more men interrogated in December 2014. In March 2026, Muhammad Jawo and Muhammad Krubally were each sentenced to five years imprisonment by the Brusubi Magistrates' Court for violating Section 147(1) for indecent conduct between men in an unfinished building. The current government has promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts despite stating no plans for liberalisation of homosexuality laws. Gambian society is described as conservative with strict religious and traditional beliefs where children are raised within male and female gender norms and not conforming to the expected heterosexual norm is seen as deviant and taboo. The media is described as promoting misinformation, harmful stereotypes, and violence towards LGBTQ+ people, with a 2021-2023 survey finding 93% would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbor and strong societal discrimination with some individuals shunned. There are no LGBTQ+ organizations as it is considered too dangerous, many LGBTQ+ Gambians fear arrest or killing and flee to other countries, religious leaders are widely opposed with some calling for LGBTQ+ people to be killed, and safety concerns likely prevent LGBT+ testimony to the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission. In care and livelihood, 2023 reports describe healthcare workers refusing to honor LGBTQ+ people's privacy negatively impacting HIV care alongside reported employment discrimination, with no reported conversion therapy or surgeries on intersex children or nonconsenting adults. Official hostility contributed to abuses, including former President Yahya Jammeh vowing to "cut off the head" of any homosexual, issuing a 24-hour expulsion order and threatening closure of hotels lodging them and dismissal of gay soldiers, while President Adama Barrow stated "homosexuality is not an issue in Gambia" with officials downplaying any liberalisation. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically, only general LGBTQ and homosexual-neighbor statements, which must not be conflated with transgender-specific law above.

sources.title: Gambia Criminal Code Section 147(1) - Brusubi Magistrates' Court ruling, March 2026
sources.summary: Gambia Criminal Code Section 147(1) (Cap 10:01, 2009) makes gross indecency between males, defined in Section 147(3) to include any homosexual act whether in public or private, a felony punishable by a mandatory five years' imprisonment, and in March 2026 the Brusubi Magistrates' Court applied that provision to convict two men for same-sex conduct on 18 May 2025 in Old Yundum and imposed five-year prison terms with no reduction under Section 34 of the Criminal Offences Act, expressly holding that claimed rights to gender identification and LGBT rights do not legalize homosexuality in Gambia and that such acts in public or private remain punishable to protect societal norms and morality.

GMB.tangentialFactors:
The 2014 aggravated homosexuality provision imposed a mandatory life sentence specifically on gay or lesbian people living with HIV, which operated as a direct barrier to testing and treatment. The March 2025 Criminal Code removed that clause without decriminalising the underlying conduct: the change lowered the penalty ceiling for the aggravated category while leaving a five-year minimum in place for unnatural offences.

The offence of carnal knowledge against the order of nature is retained from historic-era rule, and the 1933 Code implemented in 1934 remains the base text on which the 2005, 2014 and 2025 amendments were layered. The current statutory position is the product of successive amendments to that base text rather than of a single consolidated enactment.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Gambia, version 3.0 of February 2023, assesses risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims and records country information on law and treatment. It is an asylum decision-making instrument rather than a visitor-facing assessment, and its conclusions on internal relocation and certification are not set out in the source material.
